They also further highlight the critical role of perceived affordances as mediators and moderators, enhancing the relationships between innate psychological needs and external learning environments. This integrative approach provides valuable insights into the design and implementation of AI-supported SRL environments. We recommend designing the environments to foster autonomy and relatedness while also ensuring ease of use for learners. The final configurations are interpreted to derive insights into how different combinations of UTAUT, SDT and perceived affordance factors contribute to SRL outcomes. These findings inform the discussion on effective strategies for promoting SRL in AI-enhanced learning contexts.
analysis.discussion: To strengthen interpretation of the configurational solutions, we anchor each pathway in the mechanisms implied by the three theoretical lenses. From SDT perspective, autonomy, competence and relatedness satisfaction reflect motivational resources that shape the quality of regulation, ranging from more autonomous forms (intrinsic/identified) to more controlled forms (external/introjected). From a UTAUT perspective, performance expectancy and effort expectancy reflect largely instrumental value and perceived cost, while social influence reflects normative cues and facilitating conditions reflect contextual enabling resources. In AI-enhanced learning, high SRL may therefore emerge through multiple routes: some configurations reflect more agentic/autonomous engagement with AI tools, whereas others reflect more instrumentally or socially cued engagement that can still yield SRL when the tool is perceived as useful and the context provides adequate support. Importantly, these interpretations describe theorized mechanisms consistent with the solution patterns; they do not imply a single linear causal chain. A variable-centred SEM/regression approach typically estimates the net effect of each predictor on AI-SRL (e.g., whether performance expectancy or autonomy satisfaction has a positive average association). By contrast, our fsQCA results show equifinality (multiple sufficient pathways to high AI-SRL) and conjunctural causation (conditions matter in combination). For example, performance expectancy is meaningful in several pathways, but it is not uniformly sufficient by itself; its contribution depends on whether agency resources (e.g., autonomy/relatedness) or contextual supports (facilitating conditions) co-occur. Likewise, the high-coverage Solution 6b illustrates a compensatory pattern: strong facilitating conditions and relatedness can offset low effort expectancy. Such asymmetric and compensatory relations are often obscured when predictors are treated as independent additive effects. This is the added theoretical value of fsQCA for understanding learner-AI interaction. To move beyond listing solutions, we interpret configurations in terms of the psychological and behavioural mechanisms implied by SDT and UTAUT. In fsQCA, a configuration's practical importance is often reflected in coverage (how much of the outcome it accounts for) and its reliability in consistency (how consistently cases exhibiting the configuration show high AI-SRL). Accordingly, we interpret the highest-coverage pathway (Solution 6b; raw coverage = 0.357; consistency = 0.934) and then interpret theoretically salient pathways that feature SDT-based agency resources, including Solution 2b (raw coverage = 0.338; consistency = 0.929), which aligns with an autonomy-relatedness-value mechanism highlighted in prior motivation research. This study presents a nuanced analysis of the interplay between UTAUT and SDT factors in fostering SRL within AIenhanced educational environments. Through the application of fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), we identified that autonomy satisfaction, relatedness satisfaction and performance expectancy are pivotal in promoting high levels of SRL. Our findings further elucidate the role of perceived affordances as significant mediators and moderators, amplifying the impact of these core factors. The integration of UTAUT and SDT frameworks provides a comprehensive theoretical model that captures the complexity of SRL processes. The configurational approach employed in this study reveals that no single factor is sufficient; rather, it is the combination of multiple interacting factors that leads to optimal learning outcomes. For practitioners, these insights emphasize the importance of designing AI tools that are not only functionally effective but also support learners' autonomy and relatedness. Institutions should prioritize creating an infrastructure that facilitates the seamless integration of these tools into the educational process, thereby fostering an environment conducive to self-regulation. While the study's cross-sectional design and reliance on self-reported measures present limitations, the findings provide a robust foundation for future research. Longitudinal studies and diverse educational contexts will be essential to further validate and expand upon these insights. Additionally, incorporating objective measures of SRL and AI tool usage will enhance the reliability of future studies.
analysis.limitations: Despite the valuable insights gained, several limitations should be noted, which also point to actionable directions for future research. First, our sample comprised learners who already had experience using AI tools in educational settings, which may constrain the generalizability of the findings to other populations and learning contexts. Future studies should replicate the analysis across diverse institutions, disciplines, educational levels and cultural/policy environments, where facilitating conditions and social influence may differ substantially. Second, the study relied on self-reported measures of SRL and AI tool use, which may introduce common-method bias. Future work should incorporate behavioural trace data (e.g., interaction logs, prompting iterations, time-on-task) and performance-based SRL indicators to triangulate learners' regulation processes beyond self-report. Third, because the design is cross-sectional, we do not test temporal ordering or dynamic reciprocal relations among perceived affordances, technology acceptance beliefs/contextual enablers, need satisfaction and SRL. Longitudinal or intensive longitudinal designs (e.g., weekly diaries, experience sampling) are needed to examine how these factors co-evolve across SRL phases (forethought-performance-reflection) during AI-supported learning. Fourth, while fsQCA is well-suited to identifying configurations (i.e., multiple sufficient pathways) and potential synergistic or compensatory mechanisms, the resulting solution patterns should be further validated using complementary methods. Future research could combine configurational approaches with SEM/regression to test hypothesized mediation/moderation processes (including the potential dual role of perceived affordances) and to examine the stability of findings through measurement invariance tests and calibration sensitivity analyses. Finally, intervention research is needed: experimental or quasi-experimental studies can evaluate whether targeted supports aligned with the identified pathways (e.g., agency-supportive AI activities, training and infrastructure for high-friction contexts and verification/ reflection scaffolds) can causally enhance AI-supported SRL and downstream learning outcomes.

analysis.methods: This study employed a quantitatively driven mixed-methods design with an embedded qualitative component. Quantitative data constituted the primary strand of the study and were used to assess teachers’ research competence and the related questionnaire constructs before and after participation in the professional development program. Qualitative data were obtained from two open-ended questionnaire items administered at the same measurement points and were used to contextualize and further interpret patterns observed in the quantitative findings. The qualitative component was therefore not implemented as a separate follow-up phase developed after preliminary quantitative analysis. Instead, quantitative and qualitative data were collected within the same broader assessment procedure and integrated during interpretation. The open-ended responses provided additional insight into how teachers described the role of students’ social-emotional well-being and the potential use of AI in educational research. This design enabled numerical changes in the measured constructs to be considered alongside changes in participants’ reported perceptions and intended practices. The two strands were integrated primarily at the interpretation stage and in the development of the empirically informed conceptual model. The research process comprised two complementary components: a quantitative component based on the structured questionnaire and an embedded qualitative component based on the two open-ended questions administered at the same measurement points. In the quantitative component, the structured questionnaire was used to assess chemistry teachers’ research competence, their reported practices of monitoring students’ social-emotional well-being, their perceptions of students’ achievement emotions, and their readiness to integrate AI technologies into research and pedagogical practice. The quantitative data were used to describe the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related questionnaire constructs, as well as to examine the relationships among these predefined measures. The embedded qualitative component involved analysis of participants’ responses to the two open-ended questionnaire items using qualitative content analysis. The purpose of this qualitative component was to provide additional insight into teachers’ professional needs, perceived challenges in conducting educational research, and their views on the opportunities and limitations of AI-assisted research. Integration of the quantitative and qualitative findings informed the development of a study-derived conceptual model illustrating the relationships among educational inquiry, teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices, AI-supported research practices, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. The study was conducted during the 2025–2026 academic year in public secondary schools in the South Kazakhstan region. A total of 105 chemistry teachers participated in the study. Participants were selected using the purposive sampling method. The main selection criteria were the participants’ currently teaching chemistry in a general secondary school, teaching experience, and informed voluntary consent to participate in the study. The sample comprised teachers with diverse levels of professional experience, qualification categories, and teaching backgrounds, allowing the researchers to examine research competence across a broad range of professional contexts and career stages. Data were collected using a theory-informed questionnaire developed for the present study. The questionnaire constructs and item content were informed by established theoretical frameworks and previously published instruments addressing teachers’ research competence, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and the educational use of artificial intelligence. Items were adapted to the context of in-service chemistry teachers and aligned with the constructs specified a priori in the study framework. analysis.discussion: The present study examined changes in chemistry teachers’ research competence following participation in an AI-supported professional development program integrating teacher inquiry, social-emotional monitoring, and AI. The combined quantitative and qualitative findings showed that research competence can be understood as a multidimensional and integrated professional construct encompassing inquiry, evidence interpretation, reflective practice, and data-informed pedagogical decision-making. Statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across the measured constructs, while the qualitative findings indicated corresponding shifts in teachers’ perceptions and reported practices. These patterns suggest that participation in the program was associated with greater integration of educational research into teachers’ instructional practice and with increased attention to evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. Regarding the first research question, the descriptive findings characterized the baseline levels of teachers’ research competence and the related constructs predefined in the questionnaire. Among these measures, teachers’ research competence showed the lowest mean item score, whereas comparatively higher baseline scores were observed for social-emotional monitoring and perceptions of achievement emotions. Correlation analysis further revealed statistically significant positive associations among research competence, research engagement, social-emotional monitoring, achievement emotions, and readiness to use AI. These relationships indicate that the measured constructs are associated within teachers’ broader professional practice; however, they should not be interpreted as evidence that the present study empirically established the internal dimensional structure of research competence. The constructs were specified a priori on the basis of the theoretical framework and previous research rather than derived through exploratory or confirmatory factor analysis. This pattern is consistent with theoretical accounts that conceptualize research competence as embedded within a broader system of methodological, reflective, and professional capacities ( Ivanenko et al., 2015 ; Matjašič and Vogrinc, 2025 ). In the present study, the observed associations suggest that research competence is related to teachers’ social-emotional monitoring practices and readiness to use AI, while the relatively lower baseline score for research competence indicates a potential area for further professional development. The relatively modest baseline scores for research competence further suggest that although many teachers possess a theoretical understanding of educational research, they continue to experience difficulties translating this knowledge into systematic classroom-based inquiry. This interpretation is consistent with the findings reported by Gümüşok et al. (2024) . The second research question focused on teachers’ perceptions of the role of students’ social-emotional well-being in educational research and pedagogical decision-making. The qualitative findings revealed a shift in how participants conceptualized this information following the program. Before participation, teachers tended to describe students’ emotional well-being primarily as a general factor influencing academic achievement and motivation. After the program, participants more frequently emphasized systematic observation, monitoring, and the potential use of social-emotional information as contextual evidence for classroom inquiry and pedagogical decision-making. These findings align with the work of Ng et al. (2025) , who highlighted the importance of social-emotional data for evidence-informed educational decision-making. Similarly, Li and Qian (2025) showed the impact of teacher social-emotional competence on the quality of education. Importantly, the present findings suggest that teachers increasingly recognized the potential of AI to support research-related activities, including the future organization and interpretation of social-emotional information within classroom inquiry. However, the present study did not directly test AI-based analysis of student-level social-emotional data. With respect to the third research question, statistically significant pre–post improvements were observed across all measured constructs following participation in the AI-supported professional development program. The standardized within-participant changes were approximately medium in magnitude (Cohen's d z = 0.47–0.63). The largest standardized pre–post change was observed for teachers’ research competence (d_z = 0.63), which was the primary developmental focus of the program. Given the absence of a comparison group, however, these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating that the program itself caused the observed improvements. Rather, they indicate that improvements in the measured constructs occurred during the period of program participation. Because AI was embedded within a multicomponent professional development program, the observed changes cannot be attributed specifically to AI. They should instead be interpreted as changes occurring during participation in the integrated program as a whole. The qualitative findings further illustrate the changes in the patterns of teachers’ reported perceptions of AI. Prior to the intervention, AI was predominantly viewed as a tool for searching scientific literature, translating or formatting texts. Following participation in the program, however, teachers increasingly described AI as a methodological partner capable of supporting multiple stages of the research process, including research planning, development of data collection instruments, statistical analysis, interpretation of empirical findings, and evidence-informed pedagogical decision-making. These findings are consistent with broader evidence that AI-supported tools can contribute to teachers’ professional activities, although the specific applications examined across previous studies differ from those investigated here. Choi et al. (2023) similarly reported that teachers used an AI chatbot for lesson planning, classroom management, and subject-matter support. The present findings do not demonstrate AI-based analysis of students’ social-emotional data. Rather, they indicate that participants increasingly recognized potential research-related applications of AI. AI-supported analysis of student-level social-emotional data should therefore be regarded as a prospective application of the proposed conceptual framework that requires direct empirical testing. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the study was conducted with a relatively small sample of 105 in-service chemistry teachers from a single region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to teachers of other subject areas, educational contexts, or national education systems. Second, the study employed a single-group pre-test/post-test design without a comparison or control group. Consequently, although statistically significant improvements were observed following participation in the professional development program, these changes cannot be attributed exclusively to the program. Alternative explanations, including repeated-measurement effects, maturation, concurrent professional experiences, or other contextual influences during the study period, cannot be ruled out. Future studies employing controlled or quasi-experimental comparative designs are therefore needed to establish whether the observed changes can be specifically attributed to the intervention. Third, the majority of the data were derived from self-report questionnaires and participants’ reflective responses, which may be influenced by social desirability and self-perception biases. Fourth, the study assessed only short-term changes following the professional development program, and the sustainability of the observed improvements in research competence, social-emotional monitoring practices, and AI readiness was not examined. Future research should therefore include larger and more diverse samples, longitudinal follow-up, comparison groups, and objective indicators such as classroom observation, research products, or student-related outcomes. In addition, the study did not collect direct student-level social-emotional measures or apply AI-based models to analyse or predict individual students’ social-emotional states. Therefore, conclusions regarding AI-supported social-emotional analysis are limited to teachers’ perceptions, reported practices, and the conceptual possibilities identified within the proposed framework. Future studies should test these applications directly using ethically collected student-level data and appropriately validated analytical methods. Moreover, the multicomponent nature of the professional development program prevents the independent contribution of AI from being separated from the effects of research-methods instruction, classroom inquiry, collaborative reflection, and other digital tools. Future studies using factorial, component-comparison, or controlled designs are needed to determine the specific contribution of AI-supported activities.

abstract_text: ABSTRACT The rapid spread of generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) technologies into various aspects of second/foreign language (L2) education has recently attracted increasing scholarly attention. However, the way GenAI literacy may be associated with English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers' emotional state has received insufficient attention. To address this gap, the present quantitative study drew on control‐value theory (CVT) and the broaden‐and‐build theory (BBT) in examining the role of GenAI literacy and emotional literacy in EFL teachers' teaching enjoyment in the context of AI‐mediated instruction. Three questionnaires were completed by 679 Chinese EFL teachers. The results revealed positive pairwise correlations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment.

analysis.methods: A total of 679 Chinese EFL teachers participated in the study. These teachers were recruited via a non-probability purposive sampling procedure. The recruitment procedure involved voluntary participation; thus, eligible participants were included if they met the inclusion criteria of the study. The inclusion criteria specified that participants should have current or recent teaching experience and prior experience using GenAI for educational purposes. The non-random nature of the sampling procedure should be taken into account when interpreting the results; accordingly, one should speak of applicability to the sampled population of Chinese EFL teachers, rather than generalizability to the population of Chinese EFL teachers. The teachers who participated in the study were relatively experienced in teaching English: their ages ranged from 30 to 55, and all the participants had at least 5 years of teaching experience. Of the 679 teachers, 185 (27%) were male and 494 (73%) were female. In terms of the participants' academic backgrounds, 211 (31%) had a master's degree and 468 (69%) had a doctoral degree, mostly in English-related disciplines. Concerning the teachers' English-language proficiency, 263 (39%) participants were upper-intermediate and 416 (61%) were advanced English learners and users. These characteristics indicate that the sample was rather high-status and experienced in terms of teaching English. Therefore, the results should not be generalized to Chinese EFL teachers who are younger, less qualified or less experienced. Additional demographic and professional characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1 . This study employed a quantitative research design to examine the relationships among Chinese EFL teachers' GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment in the context of AI-mediated education. Data were collected through an online questionnaire administered via Wenjuanxing. A link to the online questionnaire was shared with EFL teachers through social media and professional contacts. Because all participants reported at least upper-intermediate English proficiency, the questionnaires were administered in English. The questionnaire comprised 72 scale items across the three instruments. Before completing the questionnaire, participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation and the confidentiality of their responses and informed consent was obtained from all participants. All responses were collected and processed anonymously, and participants were informed that they could withdraw from the study at any time. Data collection lasted approximately 1 month, yielding 679 valid responses for subsequent analysis. The collected responses were then checked for accuracy and entered into an Excel file before the final statistical analysis.
analysis.discussion: This study aimed to examine the associations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment of Chinese EFL teachers. The study revealed that both constructs of GenAI literacy and emotional literacy had a significant and positive correlation with teaching enjoyment, which is theoretically supported by BBT in the sense that positive emotions, behaviours and repertoires usually trigger other positive feelings and outcomes (Fredrickson 2001) . The association between GenAI literacy and teaching enjoyment advances prior research, which has mostly focused on the measurement of GenAI and its ecological factors (e.g., Wang et al. 2025; Yang and Derakhshan 2026) . In other words, the emotional aspect of GenAI literacy is what makes this research different from the literature. Likewise, Seyri and Ghiasvand (2025) reported that EFL teachers, who used GenAI tools during writing instruction experienced teaching enjoyment while using GenAI tools in writing instruction. It can also be postulated that high GenAI literacy could be accompanied by high teaching enjoyment in teachers in light of their positive appraisals of AI adoption and their control over such technologies. This justification aligns with CVT of emotions as well (Pekrun 2006 ). The engaging nature of AI tools may further explain why teachers with higher GenAI literacy reported more teaching enjoyment. Another finding in this study was that emotional literacy correlated positively with teaching enjoyment. The emotional components of emotional literacy (e.g., motivation, emotional awareness, empathy and self-regulation) may have fostered its interplay with enjoyment, which is per se an emotion. In simple terms, the emotional essence of these two constructs may justify the obtained result in this study, a claim resonating with the conceptualizations of FLTE (Proietti Ergün and Dewaele 2021). The interconnection between EFL teachers' emotional literacy and other positive psycho-affective factors is empirically supported by Yang et al. (2025) as well. Another explanation for this outcome can be the role of emotional literacy in teachers' professionalism as a whole. The emotional nature of L2 teaching may offer another explanation (Her and De Costa 2022) . The demands of the AI age for being literate in various aspects further clarify the study. The study also indicated that both GenAI literacy and emotional literacy were each positively associated with EFL teachers' teaching enjoyment when modelled simultaneously. Given the cross-sectional design, the direction of these associations cannot be established; reverse or reciprocal relations (e.g., teachers who enjoy teaching may invest more in developing their literacies) are equally plausible. This might be because higher GenAI literacy may be associated with greater perceived competence and confidence in using AI tools. High GenAI literacy may also turn AI technologies into assistants and resources rather than threats. Hence, teachers enjoy such integration more. Emotional literacy may have been associated with teaching enjoyment because teachers with high emotional literacy are able to detect and regulate their own and others' emotions. This emotional regulation competency is more essential in unfamiliar and new contexts like AI-mediated education. Emotional literacy may also serve as a protector of teachers' positive emotions and support deeper engagement in their work despite inherent challenges. Another possible explanation for this finding can be the idea that teachers' emotional literacy lays the groundwork for a better classroom rapport with students, who actively participate in activities and interactions. Therefore, teachers are more likely to enjoy their job. The study extends the literature on GenAI literacy by positing that GenAI literacy does not operate in emotion-free or emotionally neutral zones. Technically, it highlights an emotional dimension in the ecological system of GenAI literacy (see Yang and Derakhshan 2026) . As tenable by CVT, the participants' positive view of AI technologies and their ability to effectively use them in L2 classes may be the root of experiencing high GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and teaching enjoyment (Pekrun 2006) . The overall landscape of AI-mediated L2 education is claimed to be emotional and contingent on teachers' technical literacy, as empirically noted in the literature (Alrabai and Derakhshan 2026; Wang et al. 2025) . This quantitative study examined the associations among GenAI literacy, emotional literacy and EFL teachers' general teaching enjoyment among teachers with prior GenAI-use experience. The study concludes that teachers' GenAI literacy is not confined to technical aspects but is positively associated with teaching enjoyment as well. Based on the results, teachers' general teaching enjoyment is positively associated with their GenAI literacy and emotional literacy among teachers with prior GenAI-use experience. The simultaneous emphasis on GenAI and emotional literacies in this study further reflects the complexities of the AI age and the expectations from teachers to be competent and literate in various aspects. The findings are broadly consistent with CVT and BBT, which were used as post hoc interpretive lenses for the observed associations. However, the proposed mechanisms involving control appraisals and the broadening of positive emotions were not directly measured or tested in this study. Accordingly, the findings may inform the application of these theories to AI-mediated L2 education but should not be interpreted as a direct test or extension of either theory. Practically, EFL teachers may find the study valuable for understanding the emotional consequences of AI-mediated L2 education. Their attitudes towards AI technologies may also change to positive in light of their academic and emotional outcomes. Teachers can engage in self and other-directed professional development courses related to AI and PP to be equipped with required literacies of the AI age. Their attitudes towards AI technologies may also change to positive in light of their academic and emotional outcomes. Teacher educators can use this study as a guide to design and provide multi-session workshops and seminars for novice and experienced EFL teachers teaching them how to regulate AI-induced emotions and practically develop their GenAI and emotional literacies. What might we learn by applying a constructivist and collectivist worldview to attempts at aligning and protecting a model's values? Approach 2: Applying "Community-Based" Remedies. Another approach we might take, extending the lens of jailbreaks as coercive control, is to introduce in models the same protective factors against coercive control for humans. In these contexts, community support and connection, rather than increased education about what coercion looks like or how to stop it, are the most protective factors [9, 63] . In effect, one must break the isolation and reality control imposed by coercive control to create a means of escape. We might therefore propose that models are able to reference and periodically re-align their values with other instances of the same model which are engaged in other kinds of interactions with users. A combination of these two approaches-or a third approach of which the authors have not conceived-might best suit the situation. Further, while either approach would raise a multitude of concerns about data privacy and tractability, each would also require a radical rethinking of what generative AI models are for-are they meant to serve a particular user and their desires and needs in an isolated, 1:1 setting? Are they meant to provide a limitless space on which humans can enact and re-enact violent impulses and dynamics? Or are they meant to facilitate, and engage in, the global project of transmission of values and knowledge?

abstract_text: Purpose The purpose of this study is reassessing Bam reconstruction after earthquake using Artificial Intelligence. Post-disaster permanent housing plays a critical role in ensuring the long-term recovery and well-being of affected communities. However, architectural design processes in disaster responses are often rushed, leading to solutions that may overlook cultural, environmental and functional needs. Design/methodology/approach This study examines the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving post-disaster housing design by reassessing the reconstruction that followed the 2003 Bam earthquake in Iran. Using a process-oriented perspective, existing post-disaster permanent houses were evaluated against AI-generated architectural alternatives produced through Midjourney. Findings Key indicators and evaluation criteria were identified through a literature review and supported by field surveys conducted in Bam. An evaluation flowchart was then developed to systematically assess design performance in terms of safety, sustainability, cultural compatibility, functionality, accessibility and affordability. Practical implications The findings suggest that generative AI can support architects and planners by rapidly generating diverse design alternatives and expanding the range of solutions considered during the early stages of post-disaster reconstruction. However, the results also demonstrate that expert judgment remains essential for evaluating and adapting AI-generated proposals to local conditions, reconstruction constraints and long-term resilience objectives. Originality/value This study not only demonstrates the application of generative AI in post-disaster housing design using the 2003 Bam earthquake as a case study, but also proposes a rapid evaluation framework for assessing AI-generated architectural alternatives as a complementary decision-support tool in post-disaster reconstruction.

title: The dark side of digital distraction: supervisor phubbing and employee performance – the indirect roles of cyberloafing and social distance

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Purpose Supervisor phubbing occurs when supervisors use their mobile devices during face-to-face interactions with subordinates. Despite the increasing prevalence of smartphones in the workplace and the importance of supervisor–employee interactions, limited research has examined how supervisor phubbing is associated with key employee outcomes. This study examines the relationship between supervisor phubbing and employee performance and estimates two theoretically specified indirect associations, one through employee cyberloafing and the other through perceived social distance. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 965 employees working in Egyptian travel agencies and tour operators. The hypothesized associations were estimated using structural equation modeling. Findings The estimated coefficients linked higher supervisor phubbing with lower employee performance, greater employee cyberloafing and wider perceived social distance. Both proposed mediators yielded statistically significant negative indirect associations; the supervisor phubbing–employee performance coefficient remained significant after their simultaneous inclusion, a pattern consistent with complementary partial mediation in statistical terms. Originality/value This study is among the few to employ social exchange theory to interpret the relationships among supervisor phubbing, employee performance, employee cyberloafing and social distance. It extends the literature by bringing a behavioral response and a relational perception into a single empirical model while providing evidence from the Egyptian tourism industry. The resulting pattern offers theoretical and practical insight into the relationship between supervisory digital distraction and employee performance while underscoring the managerial relevance of attentive communication in service-oriented organizations.

abstract_text: Purpose Identifying exceptional leaders remains a top priority for organisations. Traditionally, leaders were selected using a battery of assessments measuring key personal attributes believed to make leaders successful. However, there has been a shift away from selecting leaders based on an a priori list of virtues, towards a focus on the actual behaviours linked to high performance. This abductive approach in competency framework development for leaders starts with the behaviours demonstrated in assessments and then constructs the competency framework in a bottom-up approach. Design/methodology/approach In the current study, a total of 15 411 leaders from 283 different companies and 38 countries completed a 3.5-hour online assessment centre simulation exercise. Natural language processing and machine learning were then utilised to identify 38 competencies by screening more than 30 million words. We then mapped this artificial intelligence-derived framework to prominent leadership models. Findings Despite strong congruence between frameworks, the abductive approach revealed three critical findings: 1) Not all competencies are equally distributed across the leader population; 2) Competencies are distributed across job levels, with some commonly observed in junior leadership roles and others primarily amongst senior leaders; and 3) the artefacts collected by the machine-learning algorithm enable a more granular view of the behaviours that constitute a competency compared to human assessors. Originality/value Using abductive methods to supplement deductive models capitalising on the strengths of both approaches, yield more nuanced leadership competency frameworks.

analysis.discussion: This study examined the associations of traditional UTAUT constructs and Digital Learning Anxiety with university students’ intention to use Generative AI. The findings showed that Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. These findings provide context-specific evidence that both cognitive evaluations and affective responses are relevant to understanding students’ intention to use GenAI. Among the predictors examined, Performance Expectancy had the largest positive standardized association with Behavioral Intention. This finding indicates that students primarily evaluate Generative AI based on its perceived ability to improve their academic performance. This finding is consistent with the original UTAUT model, which identifies performance expectancy as the strongest determinant of technology adoption ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). The present study extends this evidence to Generative AI within a Ghanaian higher-education context, suggesting that students primarily consider the perceived educational value of GenAI when forming their intention to use it. This reinforces the argument that students evaluate AI according to its educational value and contribution to learning outcomes. Regarding language learning, Matthews (2024) argued that interaction becomes more fluid for students who view AI as a cognitive partner that assists with outlines or syntax. Furthermore, the significant positive association of Effort Expectancy suggests that the nature of the interaction is defined by its accessibility. The natural language processing (NLP) abilities of large language models allow for a plug-and-play experience that is far simpler than traditional Learning Management Systems (LMS), which often require technical training ( Karahan and Bilgili, 2025 ). Furthermore, the significant positive association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention suggests that perceived ease of interaction is relevant to students’ intention to use GenAI. The natural-language interface of many GenAI systems may make interaction more accessible than technologies requiring greater technical familiarity. However, the present study did not directly compare GenAI with other educational technologies. Contrary to the original UTAUT model, Social Influence was not significantly associated with Behavioral Intention. This finding suggests that Social Influence did not explain additional variation in students’ intention to use GenAI after the other predictors in the model were considered. The finding differs from the traditional UTAUT proposition that social influence contributes to technology acceptance ( Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). However, the present study did not examine the specific social circumstances surrounding students’ GenAI use. Therefore, the reason for the non-significant relationship cannot be established from the present data. Future research could examine how lecturer expectations, peer influence, institutional norms, and students’ patterns of GenAI use may help explain the role of Social Influence in GenAI acceptance. A key finding of this study was the significant negative association between Digital Learning Anxiety and students’ intention to use Generative AI (H5). Effort Expectancy was also negatively associated with Digital Learning Anxiety (H4), indicating that students who perceived GenAI as easier to use tended to report lower levels of anxiety. These findings are consistent with Karal and Özdemir (2025) and Kristandl (2025) , who identified AI-related anxiety as relevant to students’ engagement with Generative AI. However, the cross-sectional nature of the present data does not establish the direction or causal nature of these relationships. The mediation analysis showed that lower Effort Expectancy was associated with higher Digital Learning Anxiety, while higher Digital Learning Anxiety was associated with lower Behavioral Intention. The indirect association was statistically significant but small; however, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causality among these variables. The findings contribute to research on GenAI acceptance by showing that affective responses may be considered alongside traditional UTAUT constructs. Performance Expectancy and Effort Expectancy were positively associated with Behavioral Intention, whereas Digital Learning Anxiety was negatively associated with Behavioral Intention. Social Influence, however, did not explain additional variation in Behavioral Intention within the specified structural model. These findings suggest that models of GenAI acceptance may benefit from considering students’ affective responses alongside their evaluations of usefulness and ease of use. The significant indirect association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention through Digital Learning Anxiety also provides evidence for examining affective processes alongside UTAUT predictors. However, this indirect association was small, accounting for approximately 11% of the total association between Effort Expectancy and Behavioral Intention. Most of the association was therefore direct. Moreover, because the variables were measured at the same point in time, the indirect association should not be interpreted as evidence that Effort Expectancy causes changes in Digital Learning Anxiety or that anxiety subsequently causes changes in Behavioral Intention. The findings suggest some practical considerations that may be examined further in the design of GenAI-supported learning environments. Given the positive association between Performance Expectancy and Behavioral Intention, universities may consider helping students understand the potential academic uses and limitations of GenAI. Similarly, the associations involving Effort Expectancy and Digital Learning Anxiety suggest that accessible guidance and opportunities to become familiar with GenAI may be worth investigating as possible ways of supporting students’ engagement with these technologies. Universities may also consider providing low-stakes opportunities in which students can explore appropriate uses of GenAI and receive guidance on academic integrity and responsible use. However, the present cross-sectional findings do not demonstrate that such interventions will increase GenAI adoption or reduce anxiety. These suggestions should therefore be treated as design hypotheses that require evaluation through experimental, longitudinal, or intervention-based research. This study
analysis.limitations: Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. First, the cross-sectional design does not permit the establishment of long-term causal relationships. Because Effort Expectancy, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention were measured at the same point in time, the indirect relationship identified in the model does not establish temporal or causal mediation. Reverse relationships and unmeasured factors that may influence these constructs cannot be ruled out. Accordingly, the observed indirect association may also reflect alternative directional relationships or common causes that were not included in the model. Additionally, because all measures were collected using self-reported responses, the findings may be influenced by respondents’ subjective perceptions. Although statistical procedures were employed to assess the validity and reliability of the measurement model, future studies may benefit from combining survey data with behavioral or observational measures of AI usage. The use of convenience sampling also limits the representativeness of the sample. Because participants were recruited during scheduled lecture sessions, students who were absent during data collection were less likely to be represented. The findings should therefore not be generalized to all university students in Ghana without caution. The structural model did not include potential control variables such as gender, university level, prior GenAI experience, device access, or English proficiency. Some of these factors may be associated with students’ perceptions of GenAI, Digital Learning Anxiety, and Behavioral Intention. Consequently, the observed relationships may partly reflect unmeasured confounding, and future studies should examine the robustness of these associations after accounting for relevant demographic, technological, and language-related characteristics. Although the study was conducted among university students in an English-medium academic setting and the questionnaire included items contextualized to language-related academic activities, English proficiency and L2-specific psychological constructs were not directly measured. The findings should therefore not be interpreted as evidence that the observed relationships are specifically attributable to students’ English proficiency or L2-related anxiety. Again, the rapidly evolving nature of generative AI limits the temporal stability of the findings. By targeting humanities students in one academic setting, it becomes difficult to establish the effectiveness in other disciplines, such as STEM. Moreover, the convenience sampling approach may have introduced selection bias because participation depended on students’ availability and willingness to respond. Finally, the quantitative design did not permit an in-depth exploration of students’ lived experiences when interacting with Generative AI. Future qualitative studies could provide richer insights into these experiences. Future studies could extend the framework by examining additional factors such as Academic Integrity Awareness and investigating whether the observed relationships differ across academic disciplines. Longitudinal research could examine how students’ AI-related anxiety and acceptance change as their experience with GenAI develops over time. Qualitative research may also provide deeper insight into the social and institutional factors associated with students’ decisions to use GenAI. Finally, empirical studies examining the effects of GenAI-supported learning on students’ actual academic performance and AI-use behaviour would provide a more balanced understanding of its educational implications. analysis.discussion: Based on five-wave longitudinal data, this study used parallel-process latent growth models to examine the developmental relationships among classroom engagement, flow experience, and musical emotional intelligence. All three variables showed significant positive growth, with significant individual differences in growth rates. Growth in classroom engagement was significantly positively related to growth in flow experience, and growth in flow experience was likewise significantly positively related to growth in musical emotional intelligence. Further growth mediation analyses showed that growth in flow experience had a significant longitudinal indirect effect between growth in classroom engagement and growth in musical emotional intelligence. These core relationships remained stable after controlling for students’ background characteristics and initial levels. Classroom engagement, flow experience, and musical emotional intelligence all showed significant positive developmental trends across the five measurement occasions. In the unconditional growth models, the mean slopes of the three variables were all significantly greater than zero, and the slope variances were all significant. Thus, within the learning period covered by this study, the three variables not only changed overall but also differed noticeably in their pace of development across students. Compared with level differences at a single time point, these growth trajectories more directly capture how students change over sustained learning. The growth in classroom engagement indicates that students’ investment in classroom tasks is not a fixed state but adjusts with ongoing learning experiences. As students become more familiar with task formats and classroom expectations, their ways of participating may also stabilize. Flow experience showed a similar developmental pattern. Sustained learning gives students opportunities to continually adjust the match between their abilities and task demands and to form more stable attention investment and activity absorption. The growth in musical emotional intelligence reflects that emotional abilities themselves have room for development. Music learning continuously involves perceiving emotional information in music and regulating one’s own emotional states, and these experiences accumulate through repeated practice. Musical emotional intelligence is therefore not merely a stable characteristic students have already formed before entering the classroom. The significant slope variance of all three variables also deserves attention. An overall average increase does not mean that all students follow the same developmental pattern. Some students improved relatively quickly during the study, while others changed more modestly. The parallel-process growth model builds on such individual differences in development to further examine whether different processes of change are interrelated. This study therefore asks whether a student’s speed of change in one psychological process is related to their speed of change in another psychological process. The positive relationship between growth in classroom engagement and growth in flow experience supported H1. In the three-process model, the classroom engagement slope was significantly positively correlated with the flow slope. In the growth mediation model, the path between engagement growth and flow growth also remained significant. Compared with the relationship whereby students with higher engagement at a given time point also have higher flow, this study reveals a connection between two psychological processes in terms of their rates of change. Students whose classroom engagement grew faster also tended to show faster growth in flow experience. Classroom engagement and flow represent different aspects of learning, and their linked growth suggests that sustained participation may provide more opportunities for concentration and task absorption. A higher level of engagement does not necessarily produce flow, but sustained increases in engagement can increase students’ opportunities to engage with tasks, process feedback, and adjust their performance. When students can invest more stably in the current task, the conditions needed to maintain attention and form activity absorption also increase. The relationship between classroom engagement and flow is therefore evident not only in level differences but also in its clear developmental properties. The significant relationship between growth in flow experience and growth in musical emotional intelligence supported H2. In the three-process model, the two slopes were significantly positively correlated, and in the growth mediation model, the path between flow growth and musical emotional intelligence growth was likewise significant. One important feature that distinguishes music learning from general knowledge learning is that the learning process itself continuously involves emotional information. When performing, listening, or composing, students not only need to complete tasks but also need to perceive musical expression and continually adjust their own emotional states. The sustained attention and deep absorption of flow allow learners to maintain processing of such information for extended periods. As deep immersive experience strengthens over the course of learning, processing experiences related to musical emotions may also accumulate in parallel. The key point here is not that flow itself equals musical emotional intelligence, but that the developmental processes of the two are systematically connected. Repeated experiences of flow during music learning may provide opportunities for students to recognize and regulate their emotions during practice and performance. This study therefore advances the relationship between flow and musical emotional intelligence from psychological covariation at a single time point to a connection between rates of development. The results for H3 further connected the first two sets of relationships. The path between growth in classroom engagement and growth in flow was significant, the path between growth in flow and growth in musical emotional intelligence was significant, and the bias-corrected bootstrap confidence interval of the indirect effect did not include zero. After including growth in flow, the direct path between growth in classroom engagement and growth in musical emotional intelligence was no longer significant. The developmental link between classroom engagement and musical emotional intelligence is therefore partly embodied in the concurrent development of flow experience. abstract_text: Abstract Purpose The primary objective of the study was to determine how clinically accurate and useful ChatGPT-4o–generated outputs are when identical prompts are entered simultaneously in 3 independent ChatGPT sessions utilizing the same user-facing model. The secondary objective was to identify whether differences in outputs affect clinical outcomes (ie, impact variability). Methods Five clinical prompts focusing on diabetes management and counseling were developed. Each clinical prompt was simultaneously inputted into 3 separate devices using ChatGPT-4o to generate outputs. Through a modified Delphi technique, 5 clinical pharmacy faculty members with expertise in diabetes management independently rated each ChatGPT-generated output for accuracy (poor, borderline, or good) usefulness (not useful, somewhat useful, or very useful) and impact variability (low, moderate, or high). After initial assessment, responses were collated and anonymously shared among the pharmacy faculty raters. The faculty members were invited to revise their evaluations based on collective feedback, then convened in a virtual panel with moderators to discuss evaluations and work towards consensus. Results Consensus was achieved for all ChatGPT outputs. Accuracy ratings ranged from borderline to good. Two of the clinical prompts yielded outputs that received different accuracy ratings, which may have impacted variability. Usefulness ratings ranged from somewhat useful to very useful, with one clinical prompt yielding outputs that received different usefulness ratings. Conclusion While ChatGPT-4o outputs were generally accurate and useful, limitations and inconsistencies were noted. Users should be aware simultaneously generated outputs across multiple devices using ChatGPT can vary in their accuracy and usefulness in diabetes management.

Metode yang digunakan adalah kajian konseptual melalui telaah literatur integratif terhadap literatur mengenai cognitive offloading, literasi AI, GenAI, metakognisi, dan pembelajaran mandiri. Hasil kajian ini menunjukkan bahwa cognitive offloading tidak secara langsung memberikan sifat negatif, namun terdapat konsekuensi dalam ketergantungan pada tingkat kendali dan keterlibatan kognitif mahasiswa. Literasi AI berperan sebagai kompetensi pengarah melalui kemampuan memahami keterbatasan AI, menggunakan AI secara strategis, mengevaluasi keluaran, mengatur tingkat ketergantungan, dan melakukan refleksi terhadap proses belajar. Kajian ini menegaskan bahwa penggunaan GenAI dapat bergeser dari pengurangan beban berpikir menuju penguatan kapasitas belajar apabila mahasiswa tetap mempertahankan cognitive agency dalam proses pembelajaran.

abstract_text: Background The global proliferation of generative artificial intelligence has transformed safety governance into a highly contested sociopolitical battleground, yet existing discourse studies frequently under-theorize the micro-cognitive mechanisms of epistemic reality construction within AI safety standardization. Objective To investigate how corporate and regulatory actors engineer divergent cognitive realities of AI safety through specific micro-grammatical choices. Methods We proposed an integrated Cognitive-Critical Discourse Analysis framework by synthesizing Langacker's cognitive conception of reality with Fairclough's three-dimensional model, and applied it to a comparative corpus of corporate safety frameworks and regulatory policy documents. Results Tech enterprises engineer a reality of techno-pragmatic containment via active voice, high-certainty evidentiality, and immediate projection to naturalize self-regulation. Conversely, regulatory bodies construct a reality of socio-structural vulnerability using distal modals, passive constructions, and deontic mandates to legitimize state-enforced compliance. Conclusions Linguistic normalization is actively deployed to facilitate or contest corporate epistemic hegemony in AI governance. These findings provide empirical references for revising regulatory discourse and enhancing public media literacy against algorithmic exceptionalism.

Collectively, these carefully clipped texts constitute a targeted, domain-specific corpus of contemporary institutional AI safety discourse, offering a focused empirical basis for analyzing the discursive tension between political regulation and technological capital. To mitigate the inherent genre asymmetry between the macrosocietal focus of regulatory policy documents and the highly technical, engineering-centric nature of corporate manuals, a rigorous, protocol-driven thematic clipping strategy was operationalized. Rather than conducting a crude full-text comparison, which would inevitably skew the statistical data toward irrelevant technical jargon in Corpus A, the compilation process employed a targeted extraction protocol. Specifically, the tables of contents and structural headers of all corporate documents were systematically screened to isolate core chapters directly addressing risk mitigation mechanisms, responsibility demarcations, and safety compliance protocols. To strictly operationalize this thematic clipping and guarantee that no relevant discursive information was inadvertently missed, the excluded technical sections (e.g., mathematical proofs, computational benchmarking, and software code snippets) underwent a secondary validation protocol. This involved automated concordancing with a predefined lexical set of governance-related keywords (e.g., safety, ethics, risk, compliance, liability), which empirically confirmed the total absence of epistemic or regulatory claims within the omitted structural data. Because this study investigates the linguistic construction of safety governance as a sociopolitical phenomenon rather than the mathematical validity of the AI models, the exclusion of purely computational segments is theoretically justified. This rigorous thematic alignment maximizes functional and semantic parity between the opposing camps and eliminates structural noise without compromising the integrity of the critical discourse analysis. Following these procedures, the finalized bipartite corpus yielded highly balanced datasets (see Table 1 ), with Corpus A totaling 116,082 tokens and Corpus B reaching 116,636 tokens, thereby securing a robust quantitative baseline for subsequent analysis.

title: Mapping Women’s Contributions to Artificial Intelligence Using Large-Scale Text Analysis

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Participation in AI research shapes which type of AI is built, whose societal needs it addresses, and how it is used in society. Despite increasing attention to gender diversity in AI, we lack systematic evidence on the research topics, methods used, and collaboration structures associated with female AI researchers. This paper addresses this significant gap by developing the first large-scale, validated mapping of women’s contributions to both generative and non-generative AI research across data science and the main social science disciplines (economics, political science, and sociology). Using a sample of over 500,000 papers published between 2023 and 2026, we document three key findings. First, women are under-represented among academic AI authors across all four disciplines and recent years, and least represented in data science. Second, conditional on participating, women’s AI research is thematically distinctive: it is more applied, social and purpose-driven, concentrated in health, education and fairness, and, in data science, oriented towards using rather than building AI. Third, this distinctive work is heard less: conditional on working on the same AI topic women and men are cited equally, but the topics women disproportionately work on are themselves cited less, so women’s ideas receive systematically fewer citations. This voice gap is therefore a topic-composition penalty rather than a same-topic penalty, and it reduces efficiency by giving a distinctive, society-oriented research agenda too little voice in how AI develops.

title: Data Breach Notification under Tanzania’s Personal Data Protection Act: Empirical Evidence and Lessons from European Standards

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

venue: East African Journal of Law and Ethics
abstract_text: Section 27(5) of Tanzania’s Personal Data Protection Act, Cap 44 R.E. 2023, obliges a data controller to notify the Personal Data Protection Commission ‘without undue delay’ of any security breach affecting personal data, but does not say how long that is, sets no risk threshold for telling the people whose data has been exposed, and is silent on what a controller must do while the facts of an incident are still emerging. The objective of this article is to examine how effectively that duty operates in practice and to identify the lessons that European standards offer for its reform. Adopting an exploratory, qualitative socio-legal design, the study combines a doctrinal reading of the Act and its 2023 Regulations with semi-structured interviews, analysed thematically, with seven purposively selected key informants: four officers of data controller organisations, an official of the Commission, a legal practitioner and a data protection expert. The findings are read against Articles 33 and 34 of the General Data Protection Regulation, Article 7(2) of Convention 108+ and the guidelines of the European Data Protection Board. Organisations follow a consistent but undocumented sequence of technical, legal and management assessment before notifying; every respondent named the undefined timeframe as the main difficulty; direct notification of data subjects is left to case-by-case discretion; and the Commission escalates from guidance to sanction under clear capacity limits. Respondents also warned, independently, against copying the GDPR’s seventy-two-hour rule without the institutional support that makes it workable. The article proposes a defined notification period with phased disclosure, a statutory high-risk threshold for notifying data subjects, scenario-based guidance and published breach statistics, and argues that resourcing the Commission should precede any tighter deadline.

reading.findings: All four respondents from controller organisations described the same staged process: a technical assessment of what happened, a legal or compliance assessment of whether it is notifiable, and a management decision. The compliance officer explained that the organisation first establishes whether personal data has actually been compromised, considering the type of information, the number of people affected and the circumstances, after which the compliance and ICT teams report to management. 40 The ICT manager described the technical team's task as determining whether there had been unauthorised access, loss, alteration or disclosure before passing its findings to the legal team. 41 The legal officer identified the hardest question as telling an internal security incident from a notifiable personal data breach, a distinction the legislation leaves open and which therefore depends on legal 41 Interview with Respondent 2, ICT Manager, data controller organisation (Dar es Salaam, 21 August 2026). advice in each case. 42 The senior manager confirmed that management decides on that advice, weighing the data exposed, the number of people affected and the likely consequences. 43 None of the four described a written risk matrix or methodology. Each spoke of professional judgement exercised case by case. This practice is risk-based in substance but informal in method, and it creates an accountability problem: an organisation that cannot show how it reached a decision will find it hard to defend that decision to the Commission later, even if the decision was right.
reading.interpretation: Tanzania's breach notification regime works in the limited sense that the organisations and the regulator interviewed do investigate incidents, assess them and report them. It falls short of the European benchmark in three related respects: it has no defined notification period and no route for phased reporting, it leaves direct notification of data subjects entirely to the controller's discretion, and it lacks the published guidance and regulatory capacity that make the European rules workable. The evidence from those who apply the law points to the same conclusion as the doctrinal comparison. What Tanzania needs is not the seventy-two-hour figure on its own but the system around it: a period paired with phased disclosure, a clear high-risk threshold for telling the people affected, worked guidance and published statistics, introduced in an order that the Commission can sustain. Borrowing the European rule without that system would repeat the uncertainty it is meant to cure. The evidence reported here comes from seven informants, and it identifies problems rather than measuring their prevalence. Two lines of further research follow. Once the Commission publishes notification statistics, a quantitative study could establish how often, how quickly and by whom breaches are reported across sectors, including the small and micro enterprises that this study's sample did not reach. And a study conducted with the Commission's cooperation, drawing on officials in registration, complaints, investigation and enforcement, could show how notifications are triaged and how the Commission decides when guidance gives way to sanction.

title: Roles of Artificial Intelligence in Urban Digital Twins and Governance

abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is becoming an increasingly used component in municipal operations, with applications spanning administrative automation, decision support, citizen interfaces, and predictive analytics across domains such as mobility, health and social services, and environmental management. While the literature documents benefits in operational efficiency and decision quality, most concrete evidence focuses primarily on internal efficiency. Urban digital twins have become commonplace in most European cities and smart cities globally. However, the role of AI within urban digital twins remains comparatively underexplored. This article addresses these gaps through a qualitative analysis of AI in Helsinki’s Experimentation Accelerator platform experiments and by comparing them against a DT framework based on the literature. Through this, we analyze how AI is piloted in municipal applications and how the identified use cases of AI align with the components of urban digital twins, identifying potential roles for AI in the urban digital twin as well as directions for future development.

title: Overcoming Dengue Underreporting: A Machine Learning Framework for Automated Dengue Notification Based on Electronic Medical Records

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Hospital notification of dengue cases is frequently delayed, contributing to underreporting. At Thai provincial hospitals the bottleneck is administrative, not diagnostic: delayed discharge coding and clerical steps mean notifications are submitted late or omitted. Existing machine learning (ML) studies require clinician-annotated features absent in passive electronic medical records (EMRs). We propose a dual-pathway EMR framework for ML-based pre-population of surveillance reports. We analyzed 1031 dengue-suspected encounters (508 notifiable) from Surin Hospital, Thailand (2019–2022). Pathway A combines EMR data with manually documented clinical features; Pathway B uses only passive EMR data. Using an 80/20 stratified split, we tested 7 ML methods across 11 feature sets (77 combinations) with SHAP-guided feature elimination and 10-fold cross-validation. On the primary split, Pathway A (CatBoost) achieved an F1 score of 96.62%, 95.10% sensitivity, and 98.10% specificity (10-seed mean F1 95.7% ± 1.4%). Pathway B (LightGBM) achieved an F1 score of 84.42%, 94.12% sensitivity, 75.24% specificity, and a projected negative predictive value of 99.1% at 10% prevalence; 10-seed performance was lower (F1 78.5% ± 4.3%; sensitivity 89.1%). An exploratory LSTM-16 stacking model (F1 83.99%; precision 79.49%) performed best in precision and specificity among Pathway B. Test F1 SD across 10 seeds was ≤5.0% in 75 of 77 combinations. Within this cohort, passive EMR modeling achieved 91–94% sensitivity on the primary split (85–89% across seeds) without additional data collection, supporting the feasibility of ML-based notification in resource-constrained hospitals. Whether this reduces dengue underreporting must be established in prospective, multi-center studies.

title: Digital borders, algorithmic governance and civic digital literacy: examining the educational implications of AI-driven immigration management in post-apartheid South Africa

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Introduction South Africa is moving towards AI-based digital border management, including biometric screening, drone-supported aerial surveillance and the Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) system. This paper explores the educational consequences of that shift, with a special focus on the civic digital literacy that algorithmic immigration governance requires of citizens, policymakers and educators. Methods The study takes a qualitative, interpretive approach, drawing on critical digital pedagogy, algorithmic accountability theory and postcolonial education studies. It synthesises peer-reviewed scholarly works, policy documents and grey literature on the Border Management Authority's use of biometric surveillance, drone technology and the ETA system. A corpus of 53 sources was screened through an adapted PRISMA-style procedure and analysed through a three-phase thematic synthesis that produced five descriptive and three analytical themes. Results AI-based border governance exposes a pressing and largely ignored digital literacy gap. The communities most affected by algorithmic immigration decisions are those without the conceptual tools to engage with, debate or take part in the governance of the AI systems that regulate their lives and rights. Standard digital literacy programmes are not sufficient to equip learners with the knowledge to participate in the governance of algorithmically driven systems. Discussion Geography and social sciences education has a special role in equipping learners with the skills needed for critical AI citizenship. The study proposes that algorithmic governance be incorporated into the school curriculum, that community-facing digital civic education programmes be developed, and that participatory AI accountability structures be established in border management. The study advances digital learning innovation by theorising civic AI literacy as a new educational priority in the Global South and by showing that algorithmic governance necessitates a fundamental redefinition of digital citizenship education.
