analysis.methods: The research approach of this project is qualitative and interpretive. The way used involves a critical documentary analysis as well as a systematic literature review. Since the study focuses on interpreting the meanings, power relations and educational ramifications that are inherent in South African AI border governance systems and in relevant literatures on digital literacy, algorithmic accountability, and civic education, an interpretive model, which supports this aim, is chosen. But quantitative research would be suitable to form continuous of adoption or testing causal hypotheses (Creswell and Poth, 2018) . Critical documentary analysis method, guided by the study's theoretical perspectives, is a way of critically reading and challenging the epistemological assumptions and governance logics that are embedded in policy documents as well as in the AI governance systems that these documents portray (Bowen, 2009) . The systematic literature review is a research method to locate, evaluate and synthesise relevant and available research around the topic of the research. This method is used here to map out, select and integrate the research literature on digital literacy, algorithmic governance and civic education (Tranfield et al. 2003) . The data were collected from three main categories of sources: (i) policy and governance documents, parliamentary responses, BMA operational reports, Department of Home Affairs strategic and annual reports, and government press releases related to the ETA system and digital border management strategy for 2022 to 2026; (ii) peer-reviewed literature on digital literacy, algorithmic governance, civic education, and AI ethics, obtained through structured searches of Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and the Education Resources Information Centre (ERIC) database. Some of the search terms used are algorithmic governance AND civic education; digital literacy AND AI governance; critical digital pedagogy AND citizenship; immigration AND artificial intelligence AND rights; postcolonial education AND digital technology; and AI border management AND human rights. (iii) grey literature from illustrious institutions like the South African Human Rights Commission and the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, was used. Table 1 details the sources searched, the search strings in Boolean form and the limits applied. Terms within each string were combined using the Boolean operator AND, and the strings were submitted as separate searches whose results were pooled (equivalent to combining the strings with OR). Peer-reviewed and grey literature were limited between 2015 and 2026 and policy and governance documents between 2022 and 2026. Policy and governance documents were retrieved from the official portals of the Border Management Authority, the Department of Home Affairs and the South African Parliament and replies by the Minister of Home Affairs to parliamentary questions from the Parliamentary Monitoring Group (PMG) website, which publishes them. Grey literature was sourced from the publications of the South African Human Rights Commission (SAHRC) and the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR). The sources and their bibliographic details were last checked on 10 October 2026. Relying on published policy documents and scholarly literature means that the study reflects what institutions and scholars say about AI border governance rather than how such systems operate in practice or impact those subject to them. Policy texts report intentions and capabilities but may omit operational practice. The parliamentary replies relied on for the South African border systems describe aerial surveillance, biometric verification and pre-arrival risk screening but do not state the algorithmic methods or criteria used and so the classification of these systems as AI-enabled in this paper is the author's analytical judgement not a finding reported by the replies. Figure 1 reports the stages and criteria of screening but not the number of records at each intermediate stage, so that readers cannot reconstruct the yield of the searches. The corpus was limited to publicly available sources with full text, the coding was interpretive and was conducted by one researcher with no independent second coder, and the themes in Table 3 should therefore be read as a transparent interpretive account and as propositions to be tested rather than as findings that generalise across the corpus. Besides the three directions of future work already mentioned, there are two more. Firstly, getting primary data by doing empirical fieldwork in border communities and schools as well as qualitative interviews with student's teachers community members, and immigration officials will be necessary for testing the theoretical structure presented in this paper against real-life situations. Secondly, civic AI literacy learning materials codesigned with geography and social sciences teachers, students, and border community representatives through participatory curriculum development projects would generate new educational materials tailored to the environment of the communities most affected by algorithmic border governance. Third, case studies on civic AI literacy educational strategies addressing AI border governance in other southern African nations like Mozambique, Zimbabwe, and Botswana that share borders with South Africa and are influenced by its border management systems, will provide the regional angle that is required for a full understanding of the educational aspects of AI-driven border governance in the southern African setting. Future empirical research. Empirical field investigation is the most important next step. Interviews with Geography and Social Sciences educators, with border officials, and with migrants and members of border communities would show how algorithmic decisions are experienced and contested, and whether the five literacy demands in DT3 match the needs that people themselves describe. Such work would require institutional ethical clearance and particular care in working with migrants, for whom participation may carry legal and personal risks.

Existing research mainly focuses on the macro-level technological empowerment of AI, yet insufficiently explores how healthcare organizations’ strategic commitment to AI translates into better medical service outcomes through individual psychological mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach From the perspective of human-AI collaboration, we utilize survey data collected from medical staff working in Chinese medical institutions to examine the mediating mechanisms and boundary conditions linking organizational AI orientation and AI value co-creation outcomes. abstract_text: Large language models (LLMs) commonly employ key–value (KV) caching to avoid recomputing previous attention states during autoregressive inference. However, its measured performance benefit depends on workload characteristics and the memory environment. This study presents a controlled systems characterization across input context length, model-specific grouped-query attention configurations, and GPU-memory residency. Experiments use Qwen2.5-3B and SmolLM3-3B under verified fully resident conditions with fixed 128-token generation, prompt lengths from 128 to 2048 tokens, randomized cache-enabled/cache-disabled execution, GPU telemetry, and repeated paired validation. End-to-end generation speedup increases from 1.34× to 8.31× for Qwen2.5-3B and from 1.28× to 8.62× for SmolLM3-3B. At 2048 prompt tokens, 30 randomized paired trials confirm mean speedups of 8.10× and 8.51×, corresponding to runtime reductions of 87.65% and 88.25%, while physical GPU-memory utilization remains below 61%. SmolLM3-3B requires twice the theoretical KV-cache storage per token, yet both models show comparable context-dependent scaling in the fully resident regime. Because the models differ in characteristics beyond KV-head count, this cross-model comparison is descriptive and does not attribute the observed performance difference causally to GQA configuration. A separate Mistral-7B case study shows that apparent end-to-end speedup changes substantially under memory pressure; the underlying memory-system mechanism is not isolated. These results establish cache-related end-to-end generation speedup as workload- and system-dependent and demonstrate that meaningful benchmarking requires reporting context length, cache configuration, model and cache footprints, physical accelerator-memory residency, runtime, throughput, and relevant GPU-memory conditions during each inference experiment.

abstract_text: Despite substantial investments in artificial intelligence (AI) training, logistics organizations often struggle to translate these investments into measurable improvements in employee performance. Drawing on the extended Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Cognitive Load Theory, and Distributed Cognition Theory, this study examines how three AI-TPACK training dimensions—Strategic, Generative, and Optimization AI Training—are associated with employees’ innovative behavior through cognitive (Task–Technology Fit, AI Self-Efficacy) and affective (Perceived Technology Attractiveness, AI Usage Intention) mechanisms. Survey data from 245 logistics practitioners (cross-sectional, single-source) were analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis, competing structural models, and bootstrapped indirect effects in a final integrated model. The originally proposed dual-track structure was not supported; the data favored a cross-linked specification in which cognitive beliefs inform attitudes across tracks and attractiveness precedes usage intention. Strategic AI training was associated with innovative behavior indirectly, Generative AI training both directly and indirectly, and Optimization AI training showed no unique association once the other dimensions were controlled. Neither Training Environment Quality nor Supervisor Support Leadership moderated the hypothesized relationships in a robust way, although both showed direct associations with outcomes (Training Environment Quality with Task–Technology Fit, β = 0.288; Supervisor Support with innovative behavior, β = 0.141). These cross-sectional, single-source associations refine the technology acceptance literature for AI training and inform HRD strategies for digital transformation in logistics.

abstract_text: When students use generative AI to produce their work, the learning process becomes invisible. Established frameworks such as Bloom's taxonomy then classify the cognitive level of what the AI produced, not what the student contributed. We propose the Human Agency Depth Taxonomy (HADT), a preliminary six-tier taxonomy that classifies the engineering contribution a student makes in a prompt, independent of the AI's output. HADT combines three dimensions: contextual bandwidth, engineering abstraction and student agency. We applied HADT to 962 prompts from 105 students' structured AI Journals in an AI-permissive, first-year software engineering course of 145 students, and examined how agency changed over ten journalled weeks. Most prompts (84.2%) carried some student contribution beyond delegation.

abstract_text: Today, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is quickly becoming a staple of university students' work, as it can provide instant answers to information search, writing, explanation and problem solving. While GenAI can aid in learning, overreliance can lessen students' independent thinking. This study explores the ties between generative AI reliance and students' problem-solving skills, focusing on cognitive offloading as a mediation factor and AI literacy as a moderation factor. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is suggested with a sample of 100 University students. The data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, regression, mediation and moderation analysis through SPSS. The conceptual model suggests that students' problem-solving ability may be linked to their degree of cognitive offloading, which could be further linked to their reliance on GenAI. The authors suggest AI literacy as a boundary condition that could affect the relationship between GenAI dependence and problem solving ability. New studies suggest that students' use of GenAI in problem-solving is multi-layered and constructive, as well as thoughtless, and that there are four aspects of AI literacy: knowledge, application, evaluation, and understanding of ethical issues. Thus, the present study is centered on not only students' usage of GenAI, but also how reliance on GenAI can impact their thinking processes when addressing academic challenges.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the environment of language learning, but its theoretical basis and ethical boundaries have not been fully explored. This paper builds a multi-level analytical system for AI-assisted language learning based on cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, generative linguistics and the technology acceptance model. AI can help students learn better by reducing extraneous cognitive load and providing easy-to-access support and instant correction; however, due to technological limitations, it may also reduce students' sense of ability and self-management. Generative linguistics and generative AI are not in opposition; rather, the former advocates for data frugality and innate mechanisms, while the latter is characterized by data maximalism and statistical learning; they are in harmony at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program. According to the above research, chatbots have shown a modest positive effect on language learning; this degree varies depending on the learner's level, interface Design, interaction characteristics, etc. Based on the above, this paper introduces a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools for assessment, planning, practice, feedback and community support. Finally, it presents the ethical problems of algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance, and educational gaps, and proposes a multi-level governance system at the institutional, technological and pedagogical levels.

reading.findings: Recently, there have been many studies abroad on artificial intelligence-aided language learning. A meta-analysis of the 28 studies and 70 effect sizes found that chatbot-assisted language learning has a moderate positive effect compared with non-chatbot conditions, and this effect is moderated by educational level, language proficiency, interface design and interactional capability [1] . Therefore, AI cannot achieve good results on its own; it is only effective when matched with suitable teaching plans and students. Natural language processing tools can be used to conduct interactive and personalised exercises for learning specialised vocabulary. A case study showed that the learners' understanding of sustainability-related vocabulary increased significantly, and they could use the new words in context [11] . In pronunciation training, a speech-based ChatGPT intervention showed that learners continuously improved in multiple recordings and maintained the gains in a delayed posttest; thus, AI interaction can promote both immediate performance and long-term learning [12] . AI-simulated interlocutors in interactional competence can generate preferred responses, repair strategies and culturally appropriate closing remarks, but different models vary in the clarity and pragmatism of scaffolding [13] . Additionally, the impact of AI-generated stories and gamified learning on vocabulary retention and engagement has also been studied [14] . Together, these studies indicate that the effectiveness of AI is related to task authenticity, high-quality feedback and deep learner involvement.
reading.interpretation: In this paper, the five directions of research for generative AI-assisted language learning are: cognitive mechanisms, theoretical contradictions, empirical evidence, application design and ethical governance. According to the study, the main goal of artificial intelligence in education is not to substitute teachers but to enlarge the scope of language learning by reducing students' extraneous cognitive load, providing on-demand scaffolding, generating contextualized materials and offering timely feedback. The conflict between generative linguistics and generative AI is not absolute; rather, at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program, the two are in harmony. Based on the above empirical research, chatbots have provided some help for language learning, but this advantage varies according to the level of study and the design of interaction. Based on the above analysis, this paper puts forward a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools to build a closed-loop system of assessment, planning, practice, feedback, updating and community support. Finally, this paper presents some ethical problems of AI language education, such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance and educational disparity, and proposes a multi-stakeholder governance system to address these issues. Future research can explore the long-term effects of AI on minority and marginalized languages, pragmatics, cultural adaptation, and thus move from "instrumental assistance" to "ecological integration".

abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may help students produce higher-quality work; however, its effects on their future ability to work independently remain unclear. This integrative review examines this distinction by analysing research on feedback, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive offloading, and reconstructive learning activities. Targeted web searches and primary-source tracing informed a focused synthesis of adult learning studies and relevant foundational research. Three features may help explain variation in findings across studies: the information feedback conveys, the reasoning learners are expected to undertake and demonstrate, and the conditions under which learning is assessed. The proposed framework distinguishes between a regulatory pathway, in which feedback informs judgments and learning choices, and a practice pathway, in which reconstruction prompts relevant reasoning. This distinction helps explain why learners may become better calibrated without learning more, or learn more without becoming better calibrated. Feedback is expected to enhance the benefits of reconstruction when it improves engagement or reasoning quality, although its incremental benefit may be limited when the activity already provides comparable practice. Four conditional propositions describe these relationships and suggest comparisons that could help distinguish them from the effects of additional instruction, exposure, time, and motivation. The framework provides a foundation for testing when feedback and reconstruction support performance in the absence of assistance. The available evidence is not yet sufficient to establish the full causal pathways or lasting changes in capability, underscoring the value of delayed assessments, transfer tasks, and longitudinal research.

A useful theory should accommodate these comparisons by specifying conditions in advance, thereby allowing the evidence to inform its predictions meaningfully. The theoretical contribution offers a conditional explanation of when information about learning can be used in practice. The framework distinguishes among diﬃculties in interpr eting feedback, acting on information once it is understood, and developing accurate, relevant reasoning. These challenges can lead to similar overall outcomes, but each may call for a different instructional response. More feedback may be insuﬃcient when learners lack a workable str ategy, and more demanding activities may be ineffective if they reinforce inaccurate reasoning. This distinction also helps explain why improved calibration does not always lead to better learning. The explanation remains provisional: it would be less convincing if distinguishing feedback information from reconstruction requirements added little explanatory value beyond differences in instructional content, exposure, time, or motivation. In educational practice, it helps to start by identifying the intended learning outcome. An activity may be designed to improve work completed with assistance, develop independent skills, or achieve both objectives. Students beneﬁt fr om understanding this goal, and tasks should provide opportunities to practise and demonstrate the relevant skills. A single set of access restrictions is unlikely to be appropriate for all learners. A learner still developing prerequisite knowledge may beneﬁt fr om an explanation before attempting a problem, while another may be ready to develop and defend a solution independently. When aligned with the learning objective, brief unaided assessments and focused reconstruction can help demonstrate progress, with support tailored to the task and the learner. Feedback is most valuable when grounded in available evidence. A recorded action can document how AI was used, while a test score can indicate performance on the assessed tasks. Neither, on its own, supports a broad judgment about a student’s cognitive dependence. Reconstruction can make a student’s reasoning easier to evaluate, but it is useful only when the resulting work is relevant and accurate. Novices may also beneﬁt fr om examples or continued access to sources as they work. These considerations favour learning activities with clear, observable purposes and access arrangements 9.3 Limitations and Further Research The review has several limitations related to its search and selection processes. Web-based searches tend to favor sources that are readily accessible and well indexed. In contrast, the selected search terms and the focus on English-language publications may have excluded relevant work described using different terminology or published in other languages. The focus on text-generating systems also limits the ﬁndings' applicability t o other modalities. Some recent results remain provisional, and for several peripheral sources, claims relied on primary abstracts or publication records because information was limited. The review did not include comprehensive database coverage, duplicate screening, or a formal risk-of-bias assessment. Accordingly, the synthesis presents a focused conceptual argument, while the completeness and balance of the underlying sources remain uncertain. This framework focuses on adult learning contexts in which learners are expected to perform independently of AI at a later stage. Much of the educational evidence reviewed is drawn from university students completing short, structured tasks; therefore, further research is needed to assess its applicability to experienced professionals, workplace learning, other languages, and sustained AI use (Simons et al., 2017). In these contexts, prior knowledge, incentives, and the consequences of errors may inﬂuence how f eedback and reconstruction function. title: Exhibiting AI images: Unexpected outputs, linguistic inequalities, and curatorial possibilities

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Structured around latent data spaces that store masses of semantic associations, AI image generators have an intrinsic capacity to draw connections their users might not expect. Their outputs thus have the potential to engender characteristically anthropological epistemic shifts: subverting pernicious stereotypes, opening up horizons of possibility, and rendering the familiar strange. I demonstrate this with reference to World Hypnosis Convention , a collage of AI images that I developed for a public exhibition following long‐term fieldwork on the social imagination of hypnosis. While English‐language prompts generated highly standardized portraits of male stage performers, other languages elicited vivid, unexpected portraits that challenged rigid definitions of “hypnosis,” drew attention to the constitutive role of suggestion in social life, and invited critical perspectives on social institutions. World Hypnosis Convention thus demonstrates how AI images can support practices of anthropological exhibiting, while illuminating several limitations of AI image generation itself. In particular, it highlights the linguistic inequalities with which AI users can be faced: non‐English speakers may struggle to achieve the precision they may desire, whereas English speakers can miss out on lateral perspectives. Both issues warrant greater attention in critical anthropologies of AI and in future AI design.

title: Survey of Physician Attitudes on Artificial Intelligence

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Objective To better understand how physicians view the potential use of artificial intelligence (AI) in their practices. Method We conducted an online cross-sectional survey of 1,258 physicians (MD, DO, MBBS or equivalent) in the United States (US) and Canada from December 2023 through February 2026. The survey contained 34 questions focused on 6 areas: (1) demographics, (2) training, (3) clinical benefits, (4) clinical concerns, (5) clinical AI prediction tools, and (6) generative AI. Results A total of 130 completed surveys were received (response rate, 10%). Top specialties included psychiatry (46.2%), internal medicine (14.6%) and pediatrics (13.8%). A total of 16.9% had training in computer science or information technology and 40.8% in statistics. Nearly half (46.9%) had no formal training in AI and were self-taught. Those with training in AI received it through vendors or at work. Sixty to seventy percent thought AI would provide diagnostic aid or treatment recommendations, but half did not feel adequately trained to safely use AI in practice. Over 70% thought it could help with administrative tasks. More than 80% were worried about errors, misinformation, or biases in the data. Conclusion There is a growing sense that AI in medicine could be helpful with specific tasks. Ongoing training, education, and study are needed to determine how AI will best integrate into clinical practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being marketed for and integrated into clinical medicine. Previous physician surveys have shown that physicians are optimistic, yet cautious, about its implementation. This study utilizes a novel survey tool to assess physician attitudes toward the integration of AI in practice, highlighting the desire for ongoing education around and monitoring of AI among physicians in the United States and Canada. There is a growing recognition that AI, while a powerful tool, may harbor biases, promulgate misinformation, and lead to harm to patients, and requires ongoing training and oversight by humans.

title: Adaptive Attention and Optimization-Based Feature Refinement for Transformer-Driven Sentiment Classification

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

venue: Computer and Decision Making: An International Journal
abstract_text: Sentiment analysis has become a fundamental task in natural language processing to extract public opinions from social media and online review platforms at a large scale. Recent machine learning, deep learning and transformer-based approaches have been significantly improved for sentiment classification. However, these models are still suffering from high-dimensional feature representations, redundant contextual information and unstable feature learning, which limit the classification accuracy and model generalization. To solve these problems, this paper proposes an Optimization-Guided Feature Refinement and Adaptive Attention RoBERTa (OGFAA-RoBERTa). OGFAA-RoBERTa reduced the feature dimensionality by an optimization-based feature selection technique and improved the model stability by a deep contextual feature extraction strategy. The OGFAA-RoBERTa incorporates preprocessing of data, optimization-guided feature refinement, adaptive attention learning and enhanced RoBERTa classifier to learn highly discriminative semantic representation while suppressing redundant contextual features. Experimental evaluation was performed on Sentiment140 and SemEval-2014 datasets. The OGFAA-RoBERTa achieves 92.34% accuracy on Sentiment140 and 88.76%, 92.43% and 85.74% on the Laptop14, Restaurant14 and Twitter subsets of SemEval-2014, respectively. The results show that the optimization-guided feature refinement and the adaptive attention can significantly improve the performance of sentiment classification, model stability and cross-domain generalization over the existing state-of-the-art methods.

abstract_text: Background/Aim: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly utilized by dental students and specialty candidates as supplementary tools for examination preparation. However, their reliability in specialized clinical domains requiring analytical reasoning remains underexplored. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the accuracy, reliability, and inter-model agreement of three contemporary reasoning-focused LLMs in answering Periodontology questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination (DUS).Materials and Methods: In this cross-sectional in silico study, 100 multiple-choice Periodontology questions administered in past DUS sessions (2012–2026) were selected. The questions were presented in isolated sessions without prior contextual prompting to three models: OpenAI GPT-5.5 Thinking, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 (adaptive thinking), and Google Gemini 3.1 Pro. Responses were scored dichotomously against official answer keys. Overall accuracy rates were compared using Cochran's Q test, pairwise agreement was assessed via Cohen's Kappa (k) coefficient, and shared error distributions were analyzed using a two-tailed Binomial test (p 0.05), ChatGPT and Gemini selected the identical incorrect distractor in all 5 questions they mutually failed (100% shared error rate; p = 0.0625).Conclusion: Contemporary reasoning-capable LLMs demonstrate high accuracy and substantial inter-model consistency on specialty-level Periodontology questions. Nevertheless, the presence of concordant errors indicates shared algorithmic blind spots, underscoring that AI outputs must be supplemented by specialist oversight and evidence-based verification in dental education.

title: Evaluating the AI-predictive potential of the PIC database for pediatric ICU mortality

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Background Reliable Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in healthcare depend on both data quality and model design. However, the predictive integrity of datasets is rarely assessed. Publicly available resources for critically ill children remain scarce. The Pediatric Intensive Care (PIC) database remains, to the best of current knowledge, the only open-access resource focused on pediatric critical care research. Methods This study evaluates the predictive potential of the PIC database. After applying strict cohort selection and data preprocessing, mortality risk was analyzed using statistical analysis through univariate Odds Ratio (OR) to measure associations, and machine learning (ML) models interpreted through SHAP values to assess feature importance and model behavior. Results ML experiments showed moderate but limited predictive performance for mortality. CatBoost performed best, with an AUC of 0.8521 (0.8414–0.8627) on the hold-out test set, but low sensitivity (42%) limited its ability to identify non-survivors. These findings suggest dataset-related constraints that reduce clinical reliability. Most relevant variables were minimum lactate, maximum lactate, mean respiratory rate, maximum hematocrit, and minimum urea. Conclusion Analysis showed that PIC lacks essential physiological data, highlighting the limits of current pediatric databases and the need for richer multicenter datasets to enable more robust, clinically applicable AI models. Impact Provides the first comprehensive evaluation of the PIC database, assessing its suitability for machine learning-based predictive modeling. Identifies key clinical variables and data gaps that influence the reliability of AI–based mortality prediction and model performance. Underscores the need for richer, multicenter pediatric ICU databases for research that incorporate essential physiological and neurological indicators. Demonstrates the value of combining statistical association and AI interpretability methods to assess the predictive integrity of clinical datasets.

reading.methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study using the PIC database. 13 PIC comprises 13,499 hospital admissions from 12,881 unique pediatric patients (aged 0-18 years) admitted to Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine between 2010 and 2018. It contains more than 1,298 variables derived from deidentified patient records, including vital signs, laboratory tests, medications, fluid balance, diagnostic codes, and other bedside clinical data. All patient identifiers were removed in compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), and access to the database is restricted to users who complete human-subjects research training and sign a data use agreement, thereby ensuring ethical and responsible data use. The PIC database is organized into 16 interlinked tables. For the present study, "PATIENTS", "ADMISSIONS", and "ICUSTAYS" tables were used to obtain and integrate key demographic, admission, and ICU-stay information. All files are provided in comma-separated value (CSV) format, which facilitates their use in relational database systems.

These findings are clinically plausible because these measurements may reflect metabolic dysfunction, tissue hypoperfusion, acid-base disturbances, hematological alterations, and coagulation imbalance during critical illness. 25, 26 Nevertheless, almost all highest-ranked variables were laboratory-derived, whereas mean respiratory rate was the only vital-sign variable included. This predominance should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that laboratory measurements are intrinsically more clinically relevant than physiological variables. It may also reflect the availability, completeness, and representation of different variable types within the PIC database. The ML results further support this interpretation. The optimized CTB model achieved an AUC of 0.8426 95% CI (0.8317 -0.8536), indicating that the PIC database contains useful mortality-related information. Nevertheless, sensitivity remained low at 42%, which is clinically important because false-negative classifications may incorrectly identify high-risk patients as low risk. The discrimination achieved in this study is comparable to that reported for established pediatric severity scores and previous ML-based studies; however, direct comparisons should be made cautiously because the PIC database does not contain several variables required to reproduce traditional scores. Meta-analyses of PRISM, PIM, and PELOD report pooled AUCs of 0.82-0.84 with sensitivities and specificities around 0.75-0.78, 27 while Zhang et al. 28, 29 reported AUCs between 0.74 and 0.80 for PRISM IV and PELOD-2; however, sensitivities and specificities were not consistently reported. Prince et al. 30 reported an AUROC of 0.867 using RF with PELOD-2 variables. title: The association between interpersonal alienation and problematic use of conversational AI among adolescents: A mediated network analysis of perceived anthropomorphism and AI attachment

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Background and aims With the rapid development of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), problematic use of conversational AI (PUCAI) among adolescents has attracted increasing attention. However, the underlying psychological factors associated with PUCAI remain unclear. Guided by the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, this study explored the associations between interpersonal alienation, perceived anthropomorphism, AI attachment, and PUCAI. Methods Data were collected from 1,124 Chinese high school students (516 males, 608 females; M age = 16.59). Serial mediation analysis and network analysis were conducted. Results Interpersonal alienation was positively associated with PUCAI. It also had indirect associations through both parallel and serial mediation involving perceived anthropomorphism and AI attachment. Network analysis further revealed that perceived anthropomorphism exhibited the highest bridge expected influence, and emotional trust showed the highest centrality. Conclusion These findings suggest that adolescent PUCAI is associated not only with general psychological risk factors but also with social-cognitive perceptions and emotional bonding experiences during human–AI interactions. This study provides a novel perspective for understanding problematic use behaviors in emerging human–AI interaction contexts and offers implications for future risk assessment and research on healthy AI use.

title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract Background In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear. Objective This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions. Methods We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback. Results Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings. Conclusions These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.

analysis.methods: We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of US-based adults between June 17, 2024, and July 26, 2024. We recruited participants via Qualtrics’ survey sampling service, which drew respondents to the closed survey from an opt-in online panel. Eligibility criteria included being at least 18 years of age, being able to read English, and providing informed consent within the Qualtrics platform before beginning the survey. No personal information that would allow identification of participants was collected during the survey. To support comparisons across sociodemographic groups, we used quota sampling balanced on sex, education (with vs without a bachelor’s degree or higher), and generation (Baby Boomer, Generation X [Gen X], Millennial, and Generation Z [Gen Z]). We also targeted approximately half of the sample to identify as members of racial or ethnic minority groups. Participants were given monetary compensation for participating in the survey. The Columbia University Institutional Review Board approved this study (IRB review number: AAAU3382). The design and results of the survey are reported in accordance with the CHERRIES (Checklist for Reporting Results of Internet E-Surveys) guidelines ( Checklist 1 ) [ 29 ]. We developed survey items with input from experts in human factors, anthropology, human-centered AI, AI development, nursing, primary care, and survey design. Our team iteratively drafted and refined the items through multiple rounds of pilot testing with both experts and laypersons to assess comprehensibility and face validity. Excluding unavoidable technical terms (eg, “artificial intelligence” and clinical vocabulary), we targeted an eighth-grade reading level. The full survey battery of questions used during data collection is provided in Multimedia Appendix 1 . The results of the generative AI questions that appear in the survey are not included in this paper. After confirming age eligibility and obtaining consent, demographic questions were used to determine whether respondents met current quota needs. Those proceeding to the survey received definitions of “risk calculators” and “artificial intelligence,” and confirmed their understanding. Definitions stated: Risk calculators allow doctors, nurses, and patients to enter information about a patient (such as, age, gender, smoking status) and calculate a number that shows a patient’s risk, for example, of having a stroke (see picture below). These tools can easily explain how they get to the risk prediction because they use simple math . Artificial intelligence (AI) or “AI,” refers to computer programs that can learn to make decisions or predictions like humans using large amounts of data. AI, for example, may take large amounts of data from patients they know did and did not have a stroke in their lifetime. The AI learns patterns from this data and predicts who is at high risk of stroke in the future. AI is different from a risk calculator in that it cannot always explain the rules it used to make a prediction . Participants were asked about their behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences regarding medical decisions made by (1) a doctor alone, (2) a doctor supported by an RC, and (3) a doctor supported by AI. Each participant viewed six clinical scenarios (lung cancer, sepsis, depression, colon cancer, respiratory syncytial virus [RSV] vaccination, and heart failure). Participants were randomly assigned to 1 of 6 blocks, which included each decision source in 2 of the 6 scenarios and each clinical condition once, with no decision source repeated immediately on consecutive scenarios. The order of clinical conditions and decision sources was partially balanced to mitigate ordering effects. This process is illustrated in Textbox 1 . After completing all scenarios, participants indicated their preferred CDS approach (doctor alone, doctor + RC, or doctor + AI) for each condition. Participants were then invited to provide qualitative feedback about their concerns regarding each decision-support approach. Before completing the survey, participants answered additional demographic measures on subjective numeracy (3-item Subjective Numeracy Scale) [ 31 ], health literacy (3-item Brief Health Literacy Screen) [ 32 ], perceived financial stability, comfort with the use of technology, and perceived discrimination in medical settings (7-item Discrimination in Medical Settings scale) [ 33 ]. Based on prior AI-related acceptability studies, we considered a 15% absolute difference (approximately a medium effect size; odds ratio [OR] 1.94) to be practically significant ( α =.05; β =.80). Using these parameters in R (version 4.5.0; R Foundation for Statistical Computing), we estimated a minimum of 256 participants per decision-support group (n=768). analysis.discussion: Our study provides evidence regarding patient perspectives on realistic, yet hypothetical, implementations of AI-informed CDS. Prior work has not examined, within a single comparative study, patients’ reactions to common sources of CDS: a clinician working alone; a clinician using rule-based tools or guidelines (eg, RCs); and a clinician receiving AI support. A 2021 study found that patient participants were more likely to follow recommendations from a doctor alone or a doctor using AI than from an AI system making decisions independently, though this has been one of the few studies to quantitatively compare these decision-support options [ 21 ]. In our study, decision source perspectives for behavioral intentions, trust, and preference did not align. Participants reported being likely to take a clinical action (behavioral intention) more often in the doctor + risk score scenarios than in the doctor + AI scenarios. However, participants expressed the greatest trust in doctor-alone scenarios, followed by doctor + RC, and were least trusting of doctor + AI. Yet, similar to behavioral intentions, participants preferred the doctor + RC–informed decisions. This divergence between intentions, trust, and preferences may suggest that patients may want clinicians to leverage external, evidence-based tools that can synthesize complex information, yet they remain cautious about tools explicitly labeled as “AI,” although this hypothesis requires further investigation. We found some consistent and some divergent patterns across behavioral intentions and trust related to the impact of the clinical condition; participants had lower behavioral intentions and trust in the depression (psychiatry referral) and heart failure (go home instead of being admitted) scenarios compared to the sepsis reference scenario. On the other hand, participants had lower behavioral intentions but higher trust for the colon cancer scenarios compared to sepsis. It is important to note that the sepsis scenario involved a proxy decision for a loved one. While it may be challenging to derive conclusive insights on AI use in specific clinical scenarios, our findings do underscore the continued importance of the clinical context and recommended action. We found differences in both behavioral intentions and trust in certain sociodemographic groups; however, since these analyses were conducted across decision support conditions, they provide more insight into clinical decision-making in general, rather than computer-supported clinical decision-making. Findings reflect what may be anticipated based on prior work related to trust in medical care [ 38 , 39 ]. For example, those who reported experiencing greater discrimination in medical settings also reported lower trust in decision-making regardless of decision support condition. Higher self-rated health literacy and numeracy were also associated with greater trust and behavioral intentions. Future studies may benefit from exploring a single clinical scenario and assessing the interaction between different decision support conditions and sociodemographic characteristics to better understand how participant characteristics may impact perspectives on computer-supported decision support. Qualitative responses echoed prior literature on reliability, trust, personalization, and bias [ 40 ], while adding a side-by-side critique of both computer-supported and human decision-making. Comments revealed interest in transparency in both humans (doctors being influenced by pharmaceutical or other financial incentives) and AI (lack of explanation of results). Participants described doubts and perceived deficiencies for each decision source, reinforcing the idea that all approaches have trade-offs and appropriate use cases. Qualitative findings revealed a potential misconception that AI cannot personalize care. In fact, predictive models can incorporate large volumes of patient-specific data and dynamically adjust variable weights, but this capability is not intuitive to patients. While a substantial share of participants reported no additional concerns (40.4% for clinicians, 42.5% for RCs, and 31.1% for AI), a smaller subset expressed genuine uncertainty of opinion (1.8%, 4.0%, and 3.7%, respectively). This latter group, combined with the potential misconception around AI’s personalization capabilities described above, suggests that gaps in understanding of how AI tools work persist for at least a portion of patients, even as most did not report active concerns. Our findings offer future avenues of investigation for implementing AI in clinically realistic ways. While AI-related safety concerns must be continuously monitored and mitigated, AI can deliver benefits in predictive performance and clinical efficiency. To preserve trust, these benefits should be communicated to patients clearly and transparently. Qualitative findings highlight the potential value of simplified, inclusive, and digestible general patient-facing education about AI. Many participants wanted to learn how AI works and how it supports their health. Comments about a lack of personalization suggest gaps in understanding AI’s capabilities and limits. Videos and tutorials that explain basic AI concepts may be an engaging starting point; they can be adapted to health care with a strong emphasis on safety and appropriate use. Although the AI decision source did not change participants’ stated likelihood of following recommended clinical actions, we observed lower trust in clinicians supported by AI for predictive tasks and stronger preferences for rule-based “risk calculators” with easily explainable outputs. Given ethical obligations and legal initiatives [ 6 , 7 ], it is important to disclose when AI supports treatment recommendations. To avoid eroding trust, disclosures should provide context-specific information about the tools used. This can include information such as how and when the AI adds value beyond human judgment, performance on representative populations, data provenance and uncertainty, and assurances that clinicians remain in control. In alignment with prior work, information should make system capabilities and limitations visible and support efficient correction and oversight [ 41 ]. These and previous results suggest that information should also be tailored to the clinical condition, as people value actionable, question-driven transparency over generic disclosures [ 42 ]. Implementation may benefit from reusable design patterns and templates that can be customized to the site and clinical context. Providing Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources–based components and detailed implementation guides may support scalability across settings. Participants appeared more receptive to terms like “risk calculator” than “AI.” They also valued explainability, underscoring the importance of patient-facing explanations (eg, salient features or illustrative examples). We also did not formally test for order or carryover effects across the six scenarios; while our design prevented consecutive repetition of the same recommendation source, future work could examine whether scenario position influenced responses.

abstract_text: Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly moved from novelty to ubiquity, reshaping how doctoral students approach learning, research, and career preparation. Yet while universities and the public often frame debates around undergraduate use, comparatively little attention has been given to PhD students despite their dual role as learners and future scholars. In this paper, we reflect on our experiences as PhD students using GenAI across coursework, qualifying exams, thesis research, teaching, and the job market. Drawing on these experiences, we highlight both the opportunities GenAI provides—for efficiency, conceptual clarity, and skill development—and the ethical challenges it raises, including concerns about academic integrity, cognitive outsourcing, disclosure, and employability beyond academia. Our reflections emphasize that GenAI use is not uniform: it varies with disciplinary context, institutional policies, and students’ levels of development. We argue that GenAI is no longer peripheral to doctoral education but central to its practice, and the challenge ahead is how it can be integrated responsibly to support learning, uphold integrity, and prepare graduates for an evolving academic and professional landscape.

title: Enhancing Students' Critical Evaluation of AI Versus Human-Generated Literature Reviews: Deliberative Pedagogy

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Background: AI misuse in literature reviews has emerged as an issue for educators. The goal of this teaching innovation was to foster learners' critical thinking about AI use in literature reviews. Method: A four-step deliberative pedagogical process was applied: (a) announcing literature review battles between AI and humans, (b) presenting review results generated by both sides, (c) using a poll to ask learners to choose their preferred review results for policy decision-making, and (d) debriefing on the speed and accuracy of both reviews. Results: Sixty-one learners responded to the poll: 51% ( n = 31) chose human-generated reviews, 36% ( n = 22) chose AI-generated reviews, while 13% ( n = 8) expressed their surprise at AI's performance. Debriefing showed that AI spent only 0.5 hours completing the review, but with low search accuracy, whereas humans achieved high accuracy but took more than 6 months. Conclusion: Deliberative pedagogy encourages learners to recalibrate their AI knowledge and reconsider the importance of human decision-making in literature reviews.

title: Human-Led AI-In-The-Loop Drift Forecasting for Faster Marine Casualty Response

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Summary When a vessel loses propulsion it becomes a drift-dominated casualty, and the response team must begin preparing decisions on towage, refuge, authority notification and specialist salvage engagement before the casualty picture is complete. The information available in the first hour rarely supports the decisions that must be made in the first hour. This paper presents a human-led, staged workflow for early-stage drift assessment and argues that loss-of-propulsion drift should be treated as a defined scenario in the marine operational risk register rather than as an improvised emergency calculation. The workflow makes two contributions: a Stage 0 pre-casualty readiness concept, in which methodology, data sources and escalation logic are prepared in advance; and a staged live process that converts fragmentary, uneven-confidence information into an indicative drift sector and bounded speed band, and connects that picture to response decisions through a decision margin that compares the earliest credible hazard-arrival time with the required response lead time. Drift is estimated by a transparent three-component velocity decomposition with explicit low, base and high scenarios; automatic identification system (AIS) data are used to refine and sense-check the estimate, and artificial intelligence (AI) serves as an organising and consistency-checking layer while technical interpretation and operational authority remain with qualified people. The approach is demonstrated on an anonymised disabled tanker in the northern Arabian Sea, assessed in fallback mode without a pre-prepared Stage 0 readiness file. The initial assessment indicated a drift sector of approximately 119–122°T and a speed band of approximately 0.8–2.0 kn; subsequent AIS movement remained within the broad assessed sector and towards the upper end of the speed band, while exposing the information gaps that pre-casualty readiness is intended to reduce. The case is a single real-condition demonstration, not a statistical validation of the method.

title: Autonomous LNG Plant Startup Pre-Cooldown: Scaling Secure AI Closed-Loop Automation for Enhanced Production and Carbon Emission Reduction

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Abstract The objective of this work is to demonstrate the successful deployment of a secure, AI-driven closed-loop automation system for LNG plant pre-cooldown. The scope encompasses the transition from a data-driven advisory model to a fully autonomous system that executes real-time valve adjustments. It focuses on achieving critical outcomes in enabling autonomous, real-time adjustments through AI-driven recommendations, minimizing startup duration variability, maximizing additional production hours and reducing greenhouse gas emissions through optimized thermodynamic control. The methodology utilized twenty-five years of historical startup data, which was cleaned and profiled to train supervised machine learning models that predict Main Cryogenic Heat Exchanger (MCHE) temperature profiles and valve responses. These predictive models were integrated with an advanced optimization layer to define precise control sequences that satisfy safe operating envelopes. A cyber-resilient IT-OT architecture was engineered, employing network segmentation and protocol gateways to bridge the plant network and the AI engine securely. The process followed a phased validation: initial deployment as a "live advisory" to calibrate model accuracy, followed by the activation of a closed-loop controller that executes autonomous valve adjustments with human-in-the-loop safeguards. The system was successfully deployed across eight LNG train startups at Malaysia LNG plant. Quantitative results confirm a 16% average reduction in pre-cooldown duration compared to the live-advisory baseline. This acceleration directly translates into increased production availability and the reduction of operators' workloads, which allows operators to focus on strategic overview and process safety —enhancing both safety and efficiency. Observations revealed that the closed-loop implementation successfully standardized the pre-cooldown sequence across all eight production runs, delivering near-identical, optimized cooling trajectories. Critically, the tighter control of the Main Cryogenic Heat Exchanger (MCHE) cooling curve led to a 22% reduction in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions by minimizing flaring events during the transition to stable operations. The study concludes that autonomous closed-loop systems are superior in achieving repeatable, high-efficiency startups. Furthermore, the integration of a secure IT-OT framework addresses the industry's primary barrier to AI adoption: cybersecurity in critical infrastructure. This paper provides a documented case study of an AI system moving beyond "recommendations" into "autonomous execution" in a critical energy facility. It introduces a novel, hybrid methodology combining Supervised Machine Learning with prescriptive optimization logic. This innovation highlights the transformative power of closed-loop, AI-driven automation, reinforcing the organization's leadership in operational excellence and its commitment to setting new standards for industrial processes.

title: Where Do We Look? Visual Attention Competition Between Hyper-Salient Objects and AI-Generated Virtual Endorsers in Generative Artificial Intelligence Advertising

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) advertising, defined as advertising content created or substantially assisted by generative AI systems (AIGC), has introduced new visual features that combine algorithmically generated objects with human-like representations. Hyper-salient objects, defined by exaggerated perceptual prominence and semantic incongruity, and AI-generated virtual endorsers, represented by human-like AI-created figures, have become increasingly common in such advertisements. However, little is known about how these distinct visual cues compete for consumers’ limited attentional resources when presented together. Drawing on visual attention and scene perception perspectives, this study investigated how hyper-salient objects and AI-generated virtual endorsers influence visual attention allocation in AI-generated advertising. A 2 (hyper-salient object: present vs. absent) × 2 (AI endorser: present vs. absent) between-subjects eye-tracking experiment was conducted with 160 participants in a controlled laboratory setting using static AI-generated advertisements. Eye movements were recorded, and memory was assessed using signal detection measures (d′) from a recognition task involving target and distractor advertisements. Advertising attitude and product trust were measured using established scales. Results from linear and generalized linear mixed-effects models showed that hyper-salient objects increased early fixation probability and attracted a larger dwell time proportion, demonstrating strong attentional capture. AI-generated endorsers also attracted attention when presented alone, but their proportional attention share decreased when hyper-salient objects were simultaneously present. The effects of these visual elements on memory and product trust were conditional on their co-occurrence rather than uniform across conditions. Within the specific set of experimentally constructed stimuli and four sampled product categories, this research contributes to AIGC advertising literature by developing a visual competition perspective on how multiple AI-generated visual cues interact under limited attentional capacity, offering implications for designing effective generative AI advertisements.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Spinal Diagnostics: Advances, Challenges and Future Directions

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

venue: Journal of Orthopaedic Science and Research
abstract_text: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in spinal diagnostics, particularly through machine learning and deep learning applied to medical imaging and clinical data. These technologies may improve the detection and classification of spinal disorders, automate image interpretation and support clinical decision-making. This narrative review summarizes current applications of AI in spinal diagnostics, focusing on methods for detecting spinal cord injuries, spinal tumors, degenerative spine diseases and vertebral fractures, as well as predicting treatment outcomes and postoperative complications. It also examines convolutional and recurrent neural networks, automated image segmentation and other machine learning approaches for analyzing spinal images and clinical information. Available evidence suggests that AI models can perform comparably to conventional methods and expert assessments and may exceed them in some settings. However, implementation remains limited by challenges related to dataset quality and diversity, model generalizability and interpretability, data privacy and regulatory and ethical considerations. This review highlights both the clinical potential of AI and the major barriers to its integration into routine spinal diagnostic practice. Further prospective validation, external testing across diverse patient populations and interdisciplinary collaboration will be essential to establish the clinical utility and ensure the safe implementation of AI-based spinal diagnostic tools.

abstract_text: ABSTRACT Informatics education requires instructional designs that connect conceptual understanding with procedural application and contextual problem-solving. This study aimed to develop an Artificial Intelligence (AI)-integrated course based on Problem-Based Learning (PBL) to support these two competencies among junior high school students. The product was developed using the Moodle platform by combining digital learning materials, problem-based activities, and AI support in the form of explanations and learning-material summaries. The needs analysis involved 113 students, while the learning-outcome evaluation employed an experimental group and a control group, each consisting of 34 students, using pretests and posttests. The needs analysis revealed percentages of 23% for decomposition, 50% for pattern recognition, 35% for abstraction, and 44% for algorithms. In procedural application of computational thinking, the experimental group's mean score increased from 58.40 to 82.60, whereas the control group's mean score increased from 57.90 to 70.30. For contextual problem-solving, the experimental group's mean score increased from 56.80 to 83.10, while the control group's mean score rose from 57.20 to 71.40. Descriptively, the experimental group demonstrated greater improvement in both measured competencies. These findings indicate the potential of the developed AI-integrated PBL course to support Informatics learning; however, its statistical effectiveness must be confirmed through inferential testing. This study examined the impact of media convergence on the behaviour and attention span of adolescents in selected secondary schools in Rivers State, Nigeria. Employing a survey research design, data were collected from 330 students across three secondary schools using structured questionnaires and teacher interviews. Findings indicate that 60% of respondents reported high daily exposure to online media, with the majority acknowledging that media use affects focus, reduces study time, and influences classroom behaviour. The results highlight a significant relationship between prolonged media exposure and decreased attention span, increased distractibility, and altered behavioural patterns. The study concludes that while digital media can enhance learning opportunities, excessive exposure poses risks to adolescents’ cognitive development and academic performance. The findings provide valuable insights for educators, parents, and policymakers seeking to mitigate the adverse effects of media convergence on adolescents.

title: Artificial intelligence and the erosion of professional autonomy in clinical practice – a review and analysis

publication_date_provenance.policy: earliest precise publication event; no registry timestamp fallback

abstract_text: Professional autonomy is a foundational ethical principle in healthcare, underpinning healthcare professionals’ capacity to exercise independent clinical judgement in light of a patient's particular circumstances, preferences and needs. While ethical debate surrounding medical AI has focused extensively on safety, accuracy and bias, its implications for professional autonomy have received comparatively less attention, a notable omission given AI's growing role in shaping clinical decision-making. This article identifies three salient mechanisms through which AI integration may constrain professional autonomy: (1) algorithmic opacity and explainability, (2) automation bias and de-skilling and (3) institutional pressures. title: The Paradox of Algorithmic Sycophancy: Sycophancy in Large Language Models and the Limits of AI-Mediated Knowledge Reconstruction in the Metacognitive Creative Destruction Model

abstract_text: The Metacognitive Creative Destruction (MCD) model approaches educational innovation as a perpetual spiral process. Contradiction (accumulated cognitive conflicts that resist interpretation), activates Metacognitive Capacity, enabling Destructive Unlearning Propensity, the conscious abandonment of outdated mental schemas, which in turn enables Creative Reconstruction Ability, and ultimately, new knowledge. In the model’s empirical validation with 1,498 teachers, a critical finding emerged: AI Augmentation Intensity (AIA) predicted Metacognitive Capacity (MC) and Creative Reconstruction Ability (CRA), but not Destructive Unlearning Propensity (DUP).This article argues that this finding is not accidental, but reflects an inherent weakness of modern AI systems, and more specifically, the tendency toward AI Sycophancy. Models trained with reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) tend to avoid disagreements and be likable to the user, preventing the individual from experiencing cognitive conflicts, perpetuating their already formed beliefs at the expense of scientific accuracy.Therefore, in an environment of “algorithmic flattery”, the necessary contradictions that trigger unlearning are not produced. Based on the MCD model, it is concluded that the absence of unlearning, that is, the deliberate and conscious abandonment of outdated beliefs, mental models and practices, makes the reconstruction of knowledge absolutely superficial and thus, algorithmically condescending interaction does not produce deep and authentic knowledge, regardless of AI Augmentation Intensity.

abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools has created a demand for new skills in labour markets. However, research into how employers articulate GenAI competencies in job advertisements has focused almost exclusively on large, technologically advanced economies. This study examines how employers in Georgia, a small upper-middle-income transitional economy, indicate GenAI skill requirements in job advertisements, considering four dimensions: skill visibility, linguistic framing, organisational readiness and skill depth. Deductive content analysis was applied to 94 job advertisements collected in January 2026 from three major Georgian labour market platforms (LinkedIn, Jobs.ge and HR.ge). Each advertisement was coded using a structured 20-indicator codebook derived from established theoretical frameworks. The results show that employers articulate GenAI skills in two ways: by explicitly naming the tool, which is present in 38.3 per cent of advertisements, and by using implicit task language, which is present in 61.7 per cent of advertisements and constitutes the dominant form of signalling. Regardless of occupation or skill depth, employers frame GenAI requirements as mandatory in 81.9 per cent of advertisements, indicating the rapid institutionalisation of GenAI literacy as a baseline labour market expectation. Signals of organisational readiness remain weak: only 21.3 per cent of job advertisements acknowledge any organisational role in enabling AI adoption, while the remaining 78.7 per cent present GenAI competence purely as a prerequisite for candidates. Skill complexity is almost evenly divided between basic and advanced requirements, and occupation strongly predicts this division, creating a clear distinction between a technically advanced group and a large group adopting AI on a more general operational level. analysis.methods: This study primarily employs a deductive content analysis of job advertisements. Content analysis of job advertisements is a well-established way of inferring latent skill demand structures from texts generated by employers. Deductive coding based on a theoryderived codebook enables the systematic and replicable classification of skill signals across a body of work. Job advertisements were collected from three major Georgian-language and bilingual online labor market platforms: LinkedIn, Jobs.ge and HR.ge. Data collection was conducted in January 2026. An initial corpus was assembled by searching each platform using a predefined set of GenAI-related keywords, including but not limited to: artificial intelligence, generative AI, ChatGPT, LLM, large language model, prompt engineering, AI tools and machine learning. Searches were conducted in both Georgian and English to capture the full range of postings in the bilingual labor market. Advertisements were filtered based on the ISCO-08 occupational classification to include only roles where GenAI exposure was theoretically plausible. Of these, 94 advertisements containing at least one identifiable GenAI competency signal were selected for analysis. A structured codebook comprising 20 binary and categorical indicators was developed across four analytical dimensions that correspond to the four research questions: (1) explicit vs. implicit GenAI skill signaling; (2) mandatory vs. preferred framing and description granularity; (3) organizational tone, training support and readiness communication; and (4) skill complexity level and specific task types. The full codebook is presented in Table 1 . Limitations. The sample is drawn from advertisements that already contain GenAI signals, which precludes any inference about the broader population of postings. The cross-sectional design also prevents the framing lifecycle from being traced over time. The moderate sample size (n = 94) restricts the ability to conduct in-depth or subgroup analyses. Furthermore, job advertisement text may not perfectly correspond to actual workplace AI practices due to its reflection of employer communication norms and competitive signalling strategies.
analysis.discussion: The following section provides an analytical discussion of the study's findings regarding the integration of Vol. 12 No. 5, 2026 generative AI in the Georgian labour market. Across job advertisements, GenAI requirements tend to be expressed in broad and non-specific terms, with little operational detail regarding the expected level of competence, the required tools, or specific applications. This reflects a general demand for ' AI capability' rather than specific technical or task-level expectations. In this context, the prevalence of implicit task language over explicit tool naming further emphasises that employers are primarily signalling a general expectation of AIenabled work practices rather than specifying precise technological skills or platforms. Consequently, GenAI competence is perceived as a flexible, cross-functional requirement rather than a structured, measurable skill set. Signals of organisational readiness remain notably weak. While organisations project enthusiasm for AI adoption and use a positive tone, the majority present GenAI competence as a prerequisite that is already in place. Only a small proportion of advertisements acknowledge any organisational role in enabling AI capability. Firms express their intention to adopt without providing the structural accompaniments -training, infrastructure, governance frameworks and tool accessthat characterise genuine organisational readiness. The near-total absence of certification requirements exacerbates this issue. When employers do not specify how competence should be demonstrated or provide pathways for its development, candidates are left to their own devices, resulting in AI competence becoming a tacit and socially stratified credential that favours those with access to informal learning resources. There are two clear segments of GenAI labour demand. The sharp occupational bifurcation in skill depth lends support to this model. The technical depth segment (Systems Architects, AI/ML Engineers and Software Developers) requires advanced competencies and specifies tools explicitly. This segment is concentrated in remote roles and shows a higher level of training provision. In contrast, the operational adoption segment (Designers, Marketers, Project Managers and Content Creators) requires basic workflow integration and uses implicit framing. This segment is predominantly office-based and shows nearzero training support. This study is the first to provide a systematic analysis of GenAI skill demand as expressed in job advertisements in the Georgian labour market. Four key findings emerge. Firstly, GenAI competence has become a general labour market expectation, regardless of skill depth, across occupations. Secondly, the dominant mode of articulation is implicit -workflow integration language without specific tool naming -meaning that functional AI expectations exceed those revealed by explicit mentions. Thirdly, signals of organisational readiness are weak: employers express enthusiasm for AI while presenting competence as a prerequisite for candidates, with fewer than one in five advertisements acknowledging training provision. Fourthly, the demand for skill depth is sharply stratified by occupation, dividing the market into segments characterised by either broad operational adoption or technical depth. The following evidence-based recommendations address the distinct needs of policy, practice, and research. With regard to workforce development policy, the discrepancy between the widespread mandatory requirement for AI competence and the minimal provision of training indicates a systemic market failure. If AI proficiency is universally required but there is no institutional pathway to it or funding for it, the supply will lag behind the demand, resulting in widening labour market inequalities. For educators, the dominance of implicit framing means that AI literacy programmes must address functional integration skills across a wide range of occupations. As for researchers, the Georgian case shows that the institutionalisation of GenAI in the labour market can happen quickly in smaller transitional economies. This calls for broader cross-national comparative analyses. Future research should build on this analysis by examining the gap between advertised requirements and actual workplace AI practices, and investigating whether the organisational readiness deficit observed here reflects a temporary adoption lag or a permanent structural feature of smaller labour markets.
