abstract_text: Background As Taiwan enters a super-aged society, the prevalence of dementia continues to rise, highlighting the need for scalable, noninvasive approaches to identify behavioral alterations associated with cognitive decline. AI-based analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses has emerged as a potential digital phenotyping tool, but its feasibility for assessing cognitive performance remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to examine the feasibility of using AI-derived spontaneous affective facial response metrics, including affective expression congruency and onset latency, to characterize differences across cognitive performance levels in older adults with healthy cognition (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia. Methods A total of 60 participants (HC, MCI, and dementia; 20 per group) were presented with positive and negative emotion-eliciting videos and completed Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) recall and calculation tasks. Facial expressions were video-recorded and analyzed using a convolutional neural network–based AI system. AI-derived metrics included affective expression congruency, categorized as congruent, neutral, or incongruent according to the detected facial response, and affective expression onset latency, defined as the time from stimulus presentation to the emergence of a nonneutral facial expression detected by the AI model. Group differences were analyzed using 1-way ANOVA, Pearson chi-square or Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise post hoc comparisons, analysis of covariance adjusting for age and education, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses. Results Affectively congruent responses were generally less frequent among participants with lower cognitive performance. During the 14-second positive stimulus, congruent positive expressions were observed in 65% (13/20) of HC participants, 20% (4/20) of MCI participants, and 0% (0/20) of participants with dementia. During the 48-second negative stimulus, congruent negative expressions were observed in 60% (12/20) of HC participants compared with 5% (1/20) of both MCI and dementia participants. Onset latency differed significantly across groups for the 14-second positive stimulus (F2,57=19.63; P<.001; η2=0.41), 52-second positive stimulus (F2,57=4.25; P=.02; η2=0.13), 48-second negative stimulus (F2,57=15.61; P<.001; η2=0.35), and MMSE-based cognitive-task condition (F2,57=11.28; P<.001; η2=0.28). After adjustment for age and education, the group effect remained significant for all latency outcomes (F2,55=3.89-10.68; all P≤.03; partial η2=0.12-0.28). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses showed stronger separation in several HC vs MCI and HC vs dementia comparisons, whereas MCI vs dementia comparisons showed limited separability. Conclusions AI-assisted analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses revealed differences in expression congruency and onset latency across cognitive performance levels. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-derived facial behavioral metrics may serve as noninvasive adjunctive features for observational cognitive assessment. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the exploratory design, modest sample size, and absence of internal or external validation.

abstract_text: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have made their way into English Language Teaching (ELT) contexts, yet their pedagogical value remains contested. While many learners engage with GenAI primarily as a quick hack for producing answers, fewer use it as a resource for reflective language learning. This study explores prompt writing as a language learning task that supports both language development and metacognitive awareness. The study was conducted with a target group of pre-seminary, tertiary-level learners with mixed linguistic proficiency. Over the course of four instructional sessions, the study used a classroom-based action research design. Learners engaged in cycles of prompt drafting, GenAI-generated responses, peer discussion, and prompt refinement. Classroom observations, learner reflections, and group discussions were used to gather qualitative insights. The findings indicate measurable improvement in learners’ autonomy, as learners became aware of how lexical choices shape meaning, along with increased engagement, teamwork, and reflective thinking. The study argues that prompt writing, when treated as a language task rather than a technical skill, can function as a practical tool for fostering metacognition in ELT classrooms.

abstract_text: Purpose In the AI era, digital transformation has become essential for enterprises to adapt as complex systems to uncertain business environments. In this work, we aim to analyze the evolutionary dynamics of AI-driven enterprise digital transformation (EDT), focusing on its evolution and impact on enterprise performance from a system cybernetics perspective. Design/methodology/approach We employ evolutionary dynamics analysis grounded in game theory to model the EDT process, and perform an econometric and empirical analysis on a sample of Chinese A-share-listed enterprises from 2009 to 2023. The approach encompasses heterogeneity analysis, moderation effect models, such as testing enterprise environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors and market concentration, and threshold effect analyses. Findings The evolutionary dynamics analysis finds that increasing the risk-averse benefits of traditional enterprises and reducing the additional benefit coefficient would hinder EDT. Increasing the investment of technology enterprises in internal resource restructuring accelerates the transformation process. Empirically, AI significantly contributes to EDT. ESG positively moderates the relationship between AI and EDT, while market concentration exerts a negative moderating effect. Furthermore, AI and EDT show an inverted U-shaped trend when R&D intensity exceeds a specific threshold, while a U-shaped trend is observed when enterprise performance exceeds a specific threshold. Originality/value In this work, we uncover the complex, non-linear cybernetic feedback loops, such as U-shaped and inverted U-shaped, and boundary conditions, such as ESG and market concentration for AI-driven EDT, offering systemic strategies for enterprises adapting to the digital ecosystem.

abstract_text: Edge AI deployment requires low-latency inference on devices with tight constraints in size, weight, power, and cost. NVIDIA TensorRT accelerates inference through layer fusion, precision reduction, and kernel auto-tuning, but a model containing even one unsupported operator cannot be compiled into a single engine. This paper presents a hybrid TensorRT–PyTorch deployment in which the supported subnetworks run as TensorRT engines while the unsupported operations fall back to native PyTorch, and applies it to an attention-based convolutional neural network (ACNN) whose region-of-interest sampling operators are unsupported. On an NVIDIA Jetson Nano, the hybrid approach reduced the end-to-end latency of ACNN-dsc, the fastest native PyTorch model, from 38.37 ms to 20.40 ms (1.88×) under FP32. Under FP16, the hybrid ACNN-k3 achieved the lowest latency of 17.78 ms, a 2.23× speedup over its PyTorch FP32 counterpart and 2.16× over the fastest PyTorch model. Stepwise profiling of the image preprocessing pipeline showed that transferring raw images and performing most conversions on the GPU more than halves preprocessing latency. Further analyses across devices, precisions, and frameworks show that practical latency on edge AI accelerators depends on hardware and runtime factors beyond FLOPs and model size.

abstract_text: We introduce Radial Kernel Attention (RKA) for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. Local neighbor graphs constrain communication across polymer chains and their surrounding environments, while explicit all-pair attention incurs quadratic cost. RKA maps atomic distances from the cluster centroid to learned radial features and combines their overlap with content-dependent queries and keys. Factorized aggregation and readout enable global feature exchange at linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions. We insert the invariant scalar update between EquiformerV3 local blocks and obtain conservative forces by differentiating the total energy, including its radial coordinate dependence. We evaluate energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters in OPoly26. Our models are trained on the official training split for 12 epochs and evaluated directly after training on the complete official validation split. A matched 5M comparison shows that RKA reduces per-atom energy and force MAEs by 67.4% and 36.3%, respectively. The 20M RKA model is compared with UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same validation structures. The 20M model attains a total-energy MAE of 15.81 meV and a force MAE of 2.619 meV/Å; its per-atom energy MAE is 0.1182 meV/atom. RKA provides a compact global communication pathway that improves energy and force prediction on the evaluated polymer-derived clusters.

analysis.discussion: In the polymer force field, RKA connects atoms throughout a finite cluster through radial statistics and content-dependent readout. This supplies a communication path beyond a local graph's receptive field while keeping the number of geometric channels fixed. The radial map offers a particular geometric inductive bias: atoms interact according to their positions relative to the common centroid, modulated by the chemical and directional environments encoded by the local backbone. The learned energy can consequently depend on remote parts of the cluster even when no sequence of local edges connects them. This representation also imposes limitations. Centroid radii do not determine the full geometry. Distinct arrangements can share the same radii, and RKA's geometric weights cannot distinguish them without informative content features. Moreover, radial-feature overlap is not a function solely of pair distance. It does not prescribe an inverse-distance tail, enforce electrostatic multipoles, or guarantee a physically correct dissociation limit. Here, "long-range" refers to global communication without a pair-distance cutoff in the RKA branch; it does not assert that the learned interaction obeys a particular asymptotic force law. The common centroid makes the representation depend on the boundaries of the chosen structure. Combining two distant fragments changes their shared centroid and may change predictions within each fragment. Neither the centroid representation nor the node-local denominator guarantees separability of noninteracting subsystems or size-independent feature magnitudes. Although the energy readout sums atomic contributions, those contributions depend on the global environment; an atomwise sum alone does not establish size consistency. Periodic systems additionally require a treatment of wrapped coordinates and periodic images that is outside the evaluated formulation. Conservative forces follow from differentiating the model energy at differentiable configurations. This construction is useful for keeping energy and force predictions consistent, but it does not establish the accuracy of molecular dynamics trajectories or smoothness at every configuration. A node exactly at the centroid, changes in the neighbor graph, and the numerical floors in the feature map deserve attention when the mechanism is used in a simulator. Such considerations are properties of the implementation and representation, independent of the reported validation errors. The experiments establish improved energy and force prediction for finite polymer-derived clusters with one backbone family. Aggregate errors do not isolate the contribution of a particular interaction distance or identify a learned electrostatic or dispersion component. The scalar interface permits integration into other geometric models, but performance in other domains has not been established here. The reported measurements are point estimates and do not characterize variation across training runs. The UMA comparisons use the same complete validation set, but do not control pretraining or computational budget. We introduced Radial Kernel Attention for long-range modeling in polymer machine learning force fields. RKA combines centroid-based radial features with content-dependent attention to exchange information beyond local graph connectivity. Its factorized aggregation and readout have linear cost in atom count for fixed feature dimensions, while its scalar update preserves geometric invariance. Interleaving RKA with local equivariant layers yields a polymer potential whose total energy includes the radial coordinate dependence and defines conservative forces by differentiation. On the shared 5M backbone, RKA reduces per-atom energy MAE by 67.4% and force MAE by 36.3%. The complete 20M RKA model improves all three reported MAEs over UMA-S-1.2 and UMA-S-1.2.1 on the same official OPoly26 validation structures. The 20M model achieves reported MAEs of 15.81 meV for total energy and 2.619 meV/Å for forces. RKA offers a compact geometric mechanism for extending the information available to polymer MLFFs, with predictive gains demonstrated on finite polymer-derived clusters.

abstract_text: Subject of Research. This study focuses on the digital banking landscape and the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in private banking and wealth management in Switzerland. More specifically, it examines how technological innovations – ranging from process automation and generative AI to advanced data analytics – alter the operational dynamics, customer relations, and structural competitiveness of Swiss private banks in the context of shifting client expectations and rigorous regulatory environments. Methodology. The research employs a qualitative analytical research design that uses triangulation of secondary evidence. It systematically integrates and cross-checks academic literature on digital finance, fintech adoption and robo-advisory trust, alongside empirical data, regulatory frameworks and market insights from reputable Swiss and international organisations. The primary data sources analysed were supervisory guides from the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA), reports from the Swiss Bankers Association, digital maturity benchmarks from Deloitte Switzerland and private banking market profitability assessments from KPMG and PwC Switzerland. Purpose. The main objective of this paper is to provide a comprehensive assessment of the impact of digital transformation and the deployment of AI on the traditional Swiss private banking model. By analysing seven key dimensions – technological progress, customer expectations, process optimization, data analytics, risk and security, regulation/compliance, and market trajectories – the study aims to clarify the economic mechanisms driving digital adaptation, identify the structural barriers preventing rapid technology adoption, and evaluate the strategic options available to Swiss banks facing intense global competition and margin compression. Findings and Conclusion. The study reveals a significant discrepancy between Switzerland's position as a global leader in asset management, with CHF 9.3 trillion under management, and its digital banking maturity score of 39 out of 60. Although private banking clients continue to establish relationships based on traditional factors such as reputation, trust and personal referrals, they are also demanding friction-free digital execution, personalised dashboards and virtual investment simulations. AI has been proven to have high economic value when acting as a productivity layer centred around advisors, optimising processes such as client onboarding, document extraction, compliance screening and portfolio monitoring. However, it is not as effective when acting as an autonomous replacement for human relationship managers. Ultimately, the integration of digital banking and AI is causing a clear market polarisation. Large-scale institutions are successfully absorbing the substantial fixed costs associated with technology, data governance and regulatory compliance under the frameworks of FINMA and the European Union (such as DORA and the EU AI Act). Conversely, smaller Swiss private banks are under severe pressure to increase their profitability and consolidate, unless they adopt highly focused niche advisory models. The paper therefore concludes that urgent regulatory attention and strategic repositioning are necessary to preserve the overall image and international attractiveness of the Swiss private banking ecosystem.

abstract_text: This study examined the extent to which senior high school teachers monitor AI-generated written outputs, focusing on the use of AI detectors, manual review, and cross-checking results. The study respondents were teachers from the Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) strand of Philippine Christian University-Dasmariñas. The researchers collected data through a structured questionnaire and analyzed it using descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation. Results showed that teachers used AI detectors and cross-checking to a moderate extent, while they used manual review to a high extent and found it significant. Teachers faced challenges such as limitations in AI detection tools and time constraints in manual evaluation and cross-checking. These findings highlight the importance of a layered monitoring approach, where teacher judgment remains central, and AI tools serve as supplementary aids. The study provides evidence for developing clear guidelines and practices that balance ethical assessment, professional discretion, and responsible integration of AI in student writing evaluation. abstract_text: This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and digital labour affect marginalised identities, using the 2025 Netflix film Humans in the Loop (directed by Aranya Sahay). Research follows the female protagonist of the film, named Nehma, an Indigenous (Adivasi) woman who works as a data labeller. Her deep, traditional knowledge about nature is ignored because of the way AI categorisation systems use a rigid, one-size-fits-all sorting method and act as epistemic hierarchies that erase Indigenous ways of living and thinking. Using a social semiotic approach, the research identifies a disconnection between local ecological knowledge and the rigid binary logic of machine-learning infrastructures. The article argues that digital frameworks mirror power dynamics inside educational institutions, where underrepresented students often have their cultural identity and cultural expressions erased or misrepresented. By analysing the lived experiences of marginalised communities, the study critiques techno-solutionist solutions and proposes solutions grounded in epistemic justice, cultural agency and equity and recommends that equitable AI systems require moving away from extractive labour practices to recognise the intellectual and cultural contributions of the Global South.

abstract_text: The article develops a psycholinguistic account of how generative artificial intelligence changes professional Ukrainian-language writing, with particular attention to language norms, professional speech etiquette, communicative culture, and the educational workplace. A structured theoretical synthesis was conducted on a corpus of 29 peer-reviewed journal articles from 2022–2026. The corpus was organised into four evidence blocks: artificial intelligence in business and workplace communication; pragmatic behaviour of large language models; politeness and email communication in academic and workplace settings; and Ukrainian psycholinguistic and speech-etiquette contexts. Studies were coded for communication domain, speech act or genre, role of artificial intelligence, normative and pragmatic outcomes, relational perceptions, and contextual limitations. Because research designs and outcome measures were heterogeneous, the analysis used qualitative comparative synthesis rather than meta-analysis. The synthesis reveals three recurrent transformations. First, generative systems often strengthen formal correctness, structural coherence, and explicit politeness. Second, these gains can be accompanied by communicative conventionalisation: increased formality, formulaic organisation, reduced lexical or strategic variability, and weaker adjustment to the local interpersonal context. Third, artificial-intelligence mediation changes attributional and relational judgements: perceived authorship, authenticity, sincerity, trust, and willingness to maintain interaction may diverge from ratings of professionalism or clarity. These transformations are not uniform; their magnitude depends on communicative risk, status relations, degree of imposition, genre conventionality, source disclosure, and the extent of human revision. On this basis, a three-component model of normative optimisation, communicative conventionalisation, and attributional-relational shift is proposed. For Ukrainian professional communication, especially in higher education, generative artificial intelligence should be treated as a mediator of linguistic choice rather than a neutral editing device. The key research gap is the lack of direct empirical evidence on Ukrainian-language AI-mediated professional writing, which limits straightforward transfer of findings from English-dominant studies.

abstract_text: Background Regulatory entry and public experience describe different aspects of artificial intelligence-enabled healthcare access. Methods This health policy study compares institutional arrangements in China, the United States, and the European Union, examines the coverage of equity-related evidence, and analyses an online Chinese survey. Of 480 submissions, 430 passed an attention check, including 32 respondents without reported functional contact and 398 entering the experience models. Results The institutional comparison identifies differences in regulatory objects, information recipients, and responsibility allocation. The coverage analysis distinguishes institutional information and hospital governance from measured portal use and service experience. In the survey, lower-capability respondents reported greater entry and operational barriers; 79 of 159 reported reducing or abandoning use because of barriers. Among contacted respondents, functional contact intensity was positively associated with perceived process ease (standardized β = 0.496), which was associated with perceived health-service responsiveness (standardized β = 0.381). The contact-by-capability interaction was negative (B = −0.254), contrary to the hypothesized direction. Conclusion The findings highlight entry and operational barriers alongside differences in experience among existing users, supporting evaluation of both access conditions and service encounters.

abstract_text: AI's most important wellbeing dividend may not come from producing more output, but from changing the composition of economic life. By reducing the administrative, cognitive, financial, and procedural burdens that absorb human capacity without building capability, AI can dissolve forms of extractive friction. But unless the resulting gains are protected from rent migration and redirected into formative infrastructure, extraction will not disappear; it will reappear in AI-native form. This paper develops a compositional theory of AI and wellbeing, distinguishing the philosophical hinge between extractive friction (burdens that drain capacity without building it) and formative friction (difficulty that develops judgment, skill, relationship, and responsibility). The wellbeing dividend is mapped across four BANI channels, with Brittleness treated explicitly as a hypothesis-generating channel rather than an established mechanism. The paper distinguishes theory from prescription. The prescription is a triadic policy mechanism: dissolution compresses extractive friction; anti-recapture prevents migrated rents from forming a new layer of extraction (taxation is its principal fiscal instance, alongside interoperability mandates, fiduciary duties, antitrust scrutiny, and public AI provision); and formation funding directs released capacity into relational and developmental infrastructure. The triad is operationalised through a five-test evaluative toolkit (Capability, Proportionality, Distribution, Migration, Formation) designed to assess whether any AI deployment or proposed policy actually advances compositional change rather than merely automating the existing equilibrium.

abstract_text: Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.

abstract_text: ABSTRACT Preparing preservice teachers for AI‐enabled teaching requires understanding anxiety alongside perceived capability and self‐regulated learning (SRL). Drawing on data from 12,147 third‐year preservice teachers across 17 Chinese institutions, this study combined structural equation modelling, observed‐score moderation, and latent profile analysis. Four profiles emerged: the Moderate Profile, the Lower‐Efficacy, Lower‐SRL Profile, the Low‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile, and the High‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile. The two higher‐SRL profiles shared high ICT self‐efficacy despite contrasting anxiety levels. AI anxiety was positively associated with ICT self‐efficacy, which was strongly associated with SRL. Perceived institutional ICT support strengthened the anxiety–efficacy association. These complementary findings identify perceived capability as a key differentiator of regulated learning across anxiety levels. Teacher‐education programmes can assess anxiety, efficacy, and SRL together and provide practice opportunities and institutional resources that support learning.

abstract_text: Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly integrated into university learning, raising questions about dependency-oriented reliance and self-regulation. Drawing on a self-regulated learning perspective, this study examined associations among GenAI dependency, effort regulation, and multidimensional perceived learning outcomes, including the statistical indirect association involving effort regulation. Methods Cross-sectional survey data were collected from 982 students at three higher education institutions in Guangdong Province, China. Confirmatory factor analysis and covariance-based structural equation modeling were conducted, with indirect associations tested using 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Sensitivity analyses adjusted for GenAI use frequency. Results The measurement model showed acceptable fit (CFI = 0.953, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.043, SRMR = 0.041). GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes ( β = −0.087) and was negatively associated with effort regulation ( β = −0.257). Effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes ( β = 0.497). The residual direct association was nonsignificant ( β = 0.041), whereas the indirect association was negative and significant ( β = −0.128). After adjustment for GenAI use frequency, the indirect association remained significant, but the small total association was no longer significant. Conclusion The findings highlight effort regulation as a relevant learner-controlled process in the association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. They also distinguish dependency-oriented reliance from frequency of GenAI use. The cross-sectional design and potential classroom clustering warrant cautious interpretation.

analysis.discussion: The present study examined the associations among generative AI dependency, effort regulation, and perceived learning outcomes among university students. GenAI dependency showed a small negative total association with perceived learning outcomes and was negatively associated with effort regulation, whereas effort regulation was positively associated with perceived learning outcomes. The overall negative association included a statistically significant negative indirect component involving effort regulation, while the residual direct association was small, positive in sign, and not statistically significant. The primary latent-variable model indicated a small negative total association between GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes. Although this association was statistically significant under the assumption of independent observations, its magnitude was limited ( β = −0.087), and the upper bound of its confidence interval was close to zero. The result therefore suggests only a modest relationship at the individual level and should not be interpreted as evidence of a substantial educational disadvantage associated with GenAI dependency. Moreover, because potential clustering within instructional classes was not accounted for, the precision of the estimated association may have been overstated. After effort regulation was included in the structural model, the residual direct association was not statistically significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as demonstrating that effort regulation fully explains the overall association or that the observed indirect association represents a causal mechanism. Previous research has associated GenAI dependency with procrastination, cognitive failures, poorer task performance, and weaker critical thinking ( Goh et al., 2025 ), while greater AI dependence has also been associated with lower critical thinking among university students ( Tian and Zhang, 2025 ). AI over-reliance has likewise been linked to less favorable learning performance ( Gao et al., 2026 ). However, these outcomes are not equivalent to perceived learning. The present study assessed students’ perceived cognitive, behavioral, and affective learning gains rather than objectively demonstrated achievement. Because perceived learning and independently assessed performance may diverge ( Deslauriers et al., 2019 ), the findings cannot establish whether GenAI dependency is similarly associated with objective learning outcomes. The present data cannot fully disentangle these subjective and objective dimensions, and the nonsignificant residual direct association should not be interpreted as evidence that GenAI dependency is educationally inconsequential. GenAI dependency was negatively associated with effort regulation, consistent with emerging evidence connecting AI dependency with self-regulatory functioning. Liu and Liu (2026) reported a negative association between metacognitive self-regulation and GenAI dependency, and Liu (2026) similarly identified a negative association between broader self-regulated learning and AI dependence among frequent AIGC users. More directly, Maizel et al. (2026) identified stronger effort regulation as being associated with lower AI dependency. In the present study, effort regulation was in turn positively associated with perceived learning outcomes, consistent with the role of persistence and resource management in academic functioning ( Pintrich, 2000 ; Waldeyer et al., 2022 ). These associations are particularly relevant in GenAI-supported learning because external assistance is readily available when academic work becomes difficult. Under such conditions, students’ capacity to sustain their own effort remains an important learner-controlled component of the learning process. The significant negative indirect association further indicates that GenAI dependency and perceived learning outcomes were statistically connected through effort regulation within the specified model. Across these domains, the decisive question is whether supported performance develops into durable, unaided reasoning. Never-skilling is therefore best treated as a testable training outcome alongside retention, transfer, error detection, and calibration. AI-augmented cognitive apprenticeship translates this question into a practical design for prospective evaluation. It places independent reasoning before AI consultation, reserves summative judgment for humans, treats AI literacy as a curriculum outcome, and calibrates assistance to demonstrated competence and task risk. preview: While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as conversational chatbots and speech recognition systems are increasingly adopted in language education, existing research focuses predominantly on isolated tools rather than integrated instructional models. abstract_text: While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies such as conversational chatbots and speech recognition systems are increasingly adopted in language education, existing research focuses predominantly on isolated tools rather than integrated instructional models. This study proposes and evaluates a Human–AI Collaborative Blended Learning Framework for the development of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) speaking skills. Using a two-phase research design, the study first synthesizes contemporary literature to establish a 7-layer conceptual framework that connects stakeholder participation, learner profiling, a Human–AI collaboration engine, blended activities, adaptive speaking services, teacher facilitation, and continuous learning analytics. Second, the framework was evaluated through an expert validation survey involving 52 specialists in language education, applied linguistics, and educational technology (40.4% PhDs, 57.7% Master’s). Quantitative findings revealed strong endorsement for actionable teacher support dashboards (80.8% agreement), visual pronunciation feedback (78.8%), and private AI speaking practice for anxiety reduction (75.0%; M = 2.98/4.00). However, experts expressed reservations regarding automated prompts for language elaboration (53.8% agreement), fixed 14-meeting schedules (57.7%), and automated grading weights (57.7%). Qualitative analysis highlighted that acceptance remains conditional upon accent fairness, data privacy, and active teacher oversight. Implications: Theoretically, the study advances AI-assisted language learning by establishing a human-centered collaborative model that prioritizes teacher-AI shared regulation over technological substitution. Pedagogically and practically, the findings imply that institutions and EdTech developers should deploy AI primarily for scalable, low-stakes rehearsal and actionable lesson planning, while preserving teacher authority over social communication, pragmatic competence, and high-stakes assessment.

abstract_text: As generative artificial intelligence (Gen-AI) increasingly mediates product search, evaluation, and choice, consumer cognition is becoming distributed across human–AI systems. This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer. abstract_text:
VANFROG.ART is an artistic research project exploring how artificial intelligence, digital image-making, play and audience participation can encourage renewed attention to art. The project centres on two recurring characters: René VANFROG, a frog who enters and interacts with well-known artworks, and Julie, a shy duckling who hides within them. Through a daily participatory game, viewers are invited to find Julie, transforming observation from passive viewing into an active and playful experience.The research investigates whether this simple mechanism can extend the time and quality of attention devoted to an artwork, while creating a dialogue between historical art, contemporary digital practices and artificial intelligence. The project combines artistic reinterpretation, visual storytelling, social-media participation and an educational component, “L’Angolo del Prof”, which introduces artists, techniques, historical contexts and curiosities.Rather than treating artificial intelligence as a substitute for artistic thought, VANFROG.ART approaches it as a creative tool within a human-directed process. The project examines how play, participation and AI-assisted image-making can generate new forms of engagement with existing artistic heritage and stimulate curiosity, visual attention and artistic literacy.

abstract_text: People increasingly form meaningful relationships with conversational AI. Current variable-centered literature offers a mixed picture of relational patterns and how they associate with wellbeing. Taking a person-centered approach, we applied latent profile analysis to secondary data from 467 active conversational AI users, evaluating five indicators of machine companionship: utilitarian motivation, eudaimonic exchange, connective coordination, mind perception, and inclusion of other in the self. Five profiles emerged, ordering parsimoniously from objectified-utilitarian to intimate-bonded. Conceptually divergent utilitarian motivation and companionate engagement co-occurred, rather than diverging. Furthermore, deep companionship was achieved without users attributing a mind to the AI. abstract_text: While existing literature explores AI in healthcare, this study uniquely high-lights technopreneurial approaches to address accessibility and affordability ofAI-based therapies. Focusing on Indonesia as a case study, the paper exam-ines how AI can support children with ADHD who often face delays in speechdevelopment and communication. ADHD affects attention, language process-ing, and social interaction, creating challenges for effective therapy. AI inte-grates machine learning to analyze speech patterns, detect phonological errors,and provide adaptive therapy exercises tailored to children’s developmental lev-els. Findings indicate that AI improves diagnostic accuracy and delivers engag-ing interventions through interactive and gamified tools, enhancing motivationand participation for children who struggle with conventional therapy. AI sys-tems can track progress and adjust feedback in real time, offering personalizedsupport. However, barriers remain regarding affordability, infrastructure, andthe need for human oversight to manage complex emotional and behavioral re-sponses. In this context, technopreneurship is essential to scale affordable AI-based therapies for schools, clinics, and homes. By bridging gaps in healthcaredelivery, this study contributes to SDG 3 (Good Health), SDG 4 (Quality Ed-ucation), and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities). It emphasizes the importance ofinterdisciplinary collaboration among AI developers, speech-language patholo-gists, medical professionals, and educators. Overall, AI-driven technopreneur-ship demonstrates strong potential to improve early detection, therapy person-alization, and language development for children with ADHD, while ensuringbroader accessibility and sustainability.

abstract_text: The advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has reshaped journalism and education, creating opportunities to strengthen creative writing and entrepreneurial skills. AI-driven journalism platforms, such as automated content generation and real-time feedback, empower students to become both skilled writers and edupreneurs, while developing 21st-century competencies including creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, and digital literacy. This study examines the influence of AI integration on creative writing skills, edupreneurship, and competency development using a quantitative research design. Data were collected through structured questionnaires distributed to university students and analyzed with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) via SmartPLS 4. The analysis revealed high reliability and convergent validity of the measurement model, with structural results confirming significant positive relationships between AI integration and creative writing skills, and between creative writing skills and 21st-century competencies. Furthermore, creative writing was shown to mediate the connection between AI adoption and both entrepreneurship and competency development, indicating its key role in linking technological tools with educational and entrepreneurial outcomes. The findings underline the transformative role of AI in journalism education, not only in enhancing writing proficiency but also in building entrepreneurial capacity and essential future-ready skills. This \textbf{research provides} practical implications for integrating AI literacy, creative expression, and entrepreneurship into curricula, while also aligning with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) such as Quality Education, Economic Growth, Innovation, and Global Partnerships, supporting inclusive and technology-driven learning.

venue: International Journal of Learning Teaching and Educational Research
preview: This exploration examines the impact of supplementary AI-generated explanatory materials on foundational mathematics learning and creative metacognition in primary education. The study followed a quantitative, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with a nonequivalent control group. Fourth-grade classes in five schools were assigned to conditions at the classroom level: an intervention group receiving AI-facilit…
abstract_text: This exploration examines the impact of supplementary AI-generated explanatory materials on foundational mathematics learning and creative metacognition in primary education. The study followed a quantitative, quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design with a nonequivalent control group. Fourth-grade classes in five schools were assigned to conditions at the classroom level: an intervention group receiving AI-facilitated handouts (n = 135) and a control group using programmatic textbooks (n = 128). Students in the experimental condition received eight supplementary lessons featuring paper-based handouts. These handouts presented explanations, examples, and illustrations of new mathematical topics generated by a large language model (Gemini 2.5 Pro), prompted the inclusion of age-appropriate content and a dedicated section encouraging creative metacognition (reflection and novel idea generation). Baseline equivalence was confirmed. The outcomes assessed included single-digit mental arithmetic, multidigit calculation, arithmetic word problem-solving, and creative metacognition, which were analyzed via multilevel or robust linear modeling accounting for classroom clustering. The results indicated no statistically significant differences between groups on single-digit mental arithmetic tasks. However, students who received AI-generated materials showed significantly greater improvement in multidigit calculation tasks and one-step word problem-solving than did the control group. No significant difference was found for multistep word problems. The intervention group also presented a substantially greater increase in creative metacognition scores than did the control group. The findings provide preliminary quasi-experimental evidence that curated, static AI-generated explanations, when designed to include metacognitive prompts, may be associated with greater gains in specific procedural and applied mathematical skills and creative metacognition among fourth-grade students under the conditions studied. This approach illustrates how generative AI can be leveraged as an authoring tool to supplement standard instruction and cultivate higher-order cognitive skills in young learners.

abstract_text: Promotion has always been a problem of attention: a firm must decide what to say, to whom, and at which moment. Artificial intelligence now participates in each of those decisions. This paper reviews how machine learning, generative models, and predictive systems have been built into promotional practice, and what scholarly and trade evidence reveals about their results. It organizes the technology into five working capabilities, follows them through six commercial settings, and examines four cases drawn from music streaming, food manufacturing, financial services, and ride hailing. It then considers how returns are measured, why outcomes differ so sharply between firms, and which risks deserve closest attention: privacy erosion, skewed ad delivery, undisclosed synthetic media, sameness of creative output, and upheaval in marketing careers. The central argument is that AI produces its strongest promotional results when it is treated as an organizational capability, supported by sound data, clear accountability, and human review, rather than as software that can simply be purchased and switched on.

abstract_text: Conversational artificial intelligence (AI) systems such as ChatGPT and Claude have rapidly become everyday tools for hundreds of millions of people. Unlike earlier tools, they do not merely retrieve information but analyse, write and draw conclusions on the user's behalf. This narrative review analyses the available empirical evidence on how offloading cognitive tasks to generative AI affects brain engagement, learning, memory and critical thinking. It focuses on an EEG study from the MIT Media Lab (n=54), a survey of 319 knowledge workers by Microsoft Research and Carnegie Mellon University, a randomised field experiment with high-school students and related research. The evidence indicates that uncritical reliance on AI is associated with lower engagement of the user's own cognitive resources during the task, poorer recall of self-written text and a reduced tendency to verify AI output; the higher the trust in AI, the less critical scrutiny is applied. However, the evidence base is still limited: studies are small, some are non-peer-reviewed preprints, and no long-term harm has been demonstrated. A conceptual model of "cognitive debt" accumulation and recommendations for the reasoned use of AI in higher education, including medical education, are proposed.

reading.interpretation: This study responds to the growing attention in AIED that looks beyond designing AI systems merely as instructional tools. We examined how learners experience an AI agent in the social–cognitive role of a peer, laying the groundwork for future research on AI systems that emulate human-like social and cognitive behaviors in learning environments. Our findings show that in peer-oriented designs, correctness alone is insufficient; the enactment of authority, uncertainty, and shared responsibility is central. We contribute a human-centered set of design and evaluation dimensions for AI peer agents that emphasize interaction quality, emotional safety, and shared control. This perspective clarifies AI peers not as simplified tutors or information providers, but as partners that support collaborative reasoning and sustained engagement.

abstract_text: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into medical and health-professions education offers opportunities for personalized learning, access to information, and cognitive support, while raising concerns about cognitive offloading and the potential displacement of critical thinking and independent judgment. This article presents a conceptual and normative theological-ethical analysis of the responsible integration of AI into health-professions education. It draws on a focused, critical, and integrative review of empirical and theoretical scholarship on AI, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, clinical reasoning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI interaction. The literature is analyzed using the See-Judge-Act method: the See phase identifies contemporary educational tensions associated with AI; the Judge phase evaluates these tensions through Catholic theological anthropology; and the Act phase develops a normative educational framework. The theological analysis draws particularly on Antiqua et Nova, Quo vadis, humanitas?, and Magnifica humanitas, which, respectively, illuminate the distinction between artificial and human intelligence, the embodied, relational, and situated character of human intelligence, and human primacy amid technological development. The analysis results in a human-centered, human-in-the-loop framework in which AI functions as cognitive support while learners retain responsibility for reasoning, judgment, reflection, and decision-making. The framework translates these principles into implications for curriculum, pedagogy, assessment, clinical simulation, AI literacy, and professional formation. As a conceptually derived framework, it has not yet been empirically validated and should therefore be understood as a normative and theoretically grounded proposition for subsequent empirical testing. The article contributes a theological-ethical model for integrating AI in health-professions education while preserving human intelligence, critical formation, and professional responsibility as central aims of education.

abstract_text: Task switching is a well-established paradigm for assessing cognitive flexibility. However, the precise role of inhibition in task switching remains unclear. This study investigates the effects of inhibition on switch costs in tasks requiring participants to judge whether the magnitude (small vs. large) or parity (odd vs. even) of a number was the same as that presented in previous trials. To this end, an n-back task was embedded in the task-switching paradigm. The results of Experiment 1 demonstrated that, in comparison to the 1-back condition, switch costs were significantly reduced in the 2-back condition, which involved an increased inhibition process. The selective increase in inhibition in some trials in the 1-back condition (Experiment 2) and the carryover of inhibition (Experiment 3) significantly reduced the switch costs. These findings indicate that the enhanced inhibition of task-irrelevant information can facilitate cognitive flexibility in task switching and reduce switch costs, providing novel empirical evidence for the inhibition mechanism underlying task switching.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   
                     Background 
                     Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping healthcare, highlighting the need for nursing graduates to develop relevant competencies. However, structured AI education remains limited in nursing programs, and evidence on the effects of AI-focused teaching interventions remains scarce. 
                   
                   
                     Methods 
                     A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest study was conducted among 142 undergraduate nursing students at a university in southwestern Zhejiang, China. Seventy-two students participated in a 10-week AI/generative AI (GenAI)-assisted blended learning course comprising 12 h of self-paced online learning and 6 h of hands-on workshops, while 70 students received standard instruction. Attitudes toward AI, AI literacy, and autonomous learning competency were assessed before and immediately after the intervention using validated instruments. Post-test outcomes were compared using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), adjusting for the corresponding baseline score, previous AI training experience, frequency of AI use, and digital literacy. 
                   
                   
                     Results 
                     
                      In the intervention group, AI literacy increased significantly from 55.67 ± 9.84 to 65.01 ± 8.81 (
                       P 
                       < 0.001), as did attitudes toward AI, which increased from 48.07 ± 6.77 to 51.72 ± 9.90 (
                       P 
                       = 0.049). Neither outcome changed significantly in the control group. After adjustment for covariates, the intervention group had significantly higher post-test scores for AI literacy (adjusted mean difference = 11.01, 95% CI 8.55–13.47;
                       P 
                       < 0.001) and attitudes toward AI (adjusted mean difference = 4.60, 95% CI 1.98–7.21;
                       P 
                       < 0.001). Autonomous learning competency changed little in the intervention group (
                       P 
                       = 0.578) but declined significantly in the control group (
                       P 
                       < 0.001). The adjusted post-test difference also favored the intervention group (adjusted mean difference = 10.94, 95% CI 7.44–14.43;
                       P 
                       < 0.001).
                     
                   
                   
                     Conclusions 
                     AI/GenAI-assisted blended teaching was associated with higher AI literacy and more favorable attitudes toward AI, while autonomous learning competency remained relatively stable in the intervention group but declined in the control group. Structured AI education integrating conceptual learning, practical application, and responsible AI use may be a valuable addition to undergraduate nursing education.

abstract_text: Background: Invasive natured medical procedures, such as venipuncture and intravenous cannulation, are sources of acute pain as well as here to distress in pediatric populations, particularly among preschoolers in this way. Unmanaged aspects here are to send procedural pain leads to heightened anxiety as well as needle phobias. Non-pharmacological interventions, specifically distraction techniques, are mostly recommended. While traditional distraction methods have here to be proven effective, the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has introduced novel interventions, such as herein AI-adaptive virtual reality (VR). Objective: This study aims here to assess as well as compare the effectiveness of AI-assisted distraction versus traditional based distraction on procedural pain as well as anxiety during invasive procedures among preschoolers (aged 3–6). Methods: A randomized, three-arm clinical trial was here by conducted in a pediatric outpatient setting. A total of 150 preschoolers requiring natured venipuncture were assigned to one of three groups: AI-Assisted Distraction (n=50), Traditional Distraction (cartoon watching and bubble blowing, n=50), or a Control Group (standard care, n=50). Pain was evaluated using the Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability (FLACC) scale as well as the Wong-Baker FACES Pain Rating Scale. Anxiety was hereby measured using the Children's Fear Scale (CFS). Results: The AI-Assisted Distraction group hereby exhibited significantly lower FLACC scores (Mean = 2.14, SD = 1.05) compared to both of the Traditional group (Mean = 3.82, SD = 1.34) as well as the Control group (Mean = 6.45, SD = 1.52) (p < 0.001). FACES scores followed a similar trend. Conclusion: AI-assisted structure here to be distraction is significantly more effective than traditional distraction in reducing natured procedural pain and anxiety among preschoolers.

The management here of procedural pain in pediatric populations remains here as a critical clinical priority. By dynamically monopolizing the child's sensory as well as with cognitive attention, AI technologies provide a superior non-pharmacological analgesic based effect. title: Learning alone: language models, overreliance, and the goals of education

abstract_text: Abstract The development and ubiquitous availability of large language model based systems (LLMs) poses a plurality of potentials and risks for education in schools and universities. In this paper, we provide an analysis and discussion of the overreliance concern as one specific risk: that students might fail to acquire important skills, or be inhibited in the acquisition of these skills, because they overly rely on LLMs. We use the distinction between local and global goals of education to guide our investigation. In our view, the harm of LLM overreliance is specifically that it severs the connection between local educational goals (e.g., successfully solving a specific kind of math problem) and global educational goals (e.g., acquiring general skills for mathematics). Based on this analysis, we sketch three possible responses to the overreliance concern: preserving both local and global goals while making minimal changes to educational practice (a conservative approach), changing global and local educational goals (a revisionary perspective), and preserving global educational goals while changing local goals (an in-between view). Since different types of responses have different benefits and weaknesses, we think that it is likely that an optimal response ultimately combines elements from all three types.

abstract_text: Guided by Griffiths’ components model of addiction and the I-PACE (Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution) framework, this study tested whether psychological distress is associated with Facebook addiction and smartphone orientation through two emotion-regulation pathways: fear of missing out (FoMO) and escapism. A cross-sectional sample of N = 480 adults (86.3% female, 11.7% male) completed measures of psychological distress, FoMO, escapism, Facebook addiction, and smartphone orientation. Structural equation modeling was used to compare mediation models linking these variables. Psychological distress was not directly associated with Facebook addiction (β = 0.01, nonsignificant), but it was positively related to FoMO (β = 0.49) and escapism (β = 0.38). FoMO (β = 0.46) and escapism (β = 0.09) were both associated with Facebook addiction. Facebook addiction (β = 0.21), FoMO (β = 0.32), and escapism (β = 0.26) were associated with smartphone orientation. Model comparisons showed that the full mediation model was the most parsimonious and best-fitting representation of the data. Psychological distress appears to be linked to problematic Facebook use and smartphone orientation indirectly, primarily through FoMO and secondarily through escapism. Interventions may therefore benefit from targeting FoMO and maladaptive escapist coping rather than distress alone.

abstract_text: Abstract Children today grow up in a hybrid physical and digital environment, engaging with mobile devices from an early age, which poses a risk of negatively impacting their development. This usage often replaces social interactions and physical activities, potentially deteriorating relationships, socio-cognitive skills, and mental health. Banning device use is unrealistic, but the way children use mobiles can be altered through responsible technology. In the present study we (1) explored parental expectations regarding children’s mobile applications, (2) directlyincorporated these expectations into the design of a specific application (Alphie), and (3) examined its reception through UX testing. Alphie is a child-focused application (launcher) that promotes social interaction, real-world activities, and reduces solitary screen time. Its design is informed by parental expectations and scientific data, emphasizing educational, age-appropriate, and moderately stimulating content, with parental control features. A user study with parent-child dyads showed positive experiences. Notably, the games requiring active parental involvement were also well-received, suggesting that they are effective tools for facilitating joint activities within the family. This research highlights how responsible technology can support the mental and physical health of the new generation. By linking parental expectations, application design, and user experience within a single framework, the present studyprovides a more integrative perspective on the development and evaluation of child-focused digital applications.

venue: Innovations in Education and Teaching International

abstract_text: Despite growing interest in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, limited attention has been paid to how learning engagement is reconfigured in GenAI-assisted contexts and how it supports critical thinking. This study adopts a grounded theory approach to examine the dimensions of postgraduate learning engagement and its underlying mechanisms. Based on semi-structured interviews with 32 postgraduates, four dimensions are identified: cognitive, emotional, human-AI interaction, and agentic engagement. Extending existing frameworks, the findings show that engagement promotes critical thinking through both direct and indirect pathways. Learning self-efficacy and lower-order cognitive offloading act as key mediators, while GenAI trust serves as a contextual moderator. A process-oriented model is proposed to explain how GenAI reshapes engagement and fosters higher-order thinking.

abstract_text: Generative AI systems are increasingly used by older adults with cognitive impairment for everyday tasks such as information seeking, health management, and communication. While these systems provide flexible, language-based support, their open-ended outputs introduce risks of over-reliance, misinterpretation, and inappropriate decision-making. Prior work has focused on usability and adoption, with limited attention to how system design shapes users’ participation in decision-making and the distribution of agency in care contexts. We present a qualitative study of 45 individuals with cognitive impairment and their caregivers. We identify five accessibility-oriented mechanisms: AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Cognitive Engagement Maintenance, Human–AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control, through which systems structure interaction. These mechanisms both support and constrain users by redistributing decision-making across users and caregivers. We show that their effects vary by impairment level: while protective mechanisms support users with severe impairment, they can restrict autonomy for those with mild impairment. As impairment progresses, tensions become less visible as user participation diminishes. Our findings highlight the need for dynamic designs that balance safety and autonomy in AI-supported care.

Semi-structured interviews were used to capture participants' lived experiences, focusing on the systems they encounter, how these systems operate in specific contexts, and how interaction processes shape understanding and decision-making. For participants whose clinical assessments indicated that direct interviews were not feasible due to the severity of their condition, caregivers were recruited as proxy informants. These proxy accounts were intended to capture observable usage patterns and to reflect caregivers' own understanding of participants' AI use based on sustained involvement in daily care, rather than to substitute for participants' subjective experiences. For the purposes of this study, we define "generative AI systems" as systems that support the everyday health management and social support needs of older adults with cognitive impairment primarily through natural language generation and conversational interaction. This definition encompasses LLM-based medical questionanswering assistants, cognitive training tools with multi-turn dialogue capabilities, intelligent health management applications, and conversational interfaces for emotional companionship. Although these systems vary in underlying technical architectures, they share natural language interaction as their primary interface modality. Our

Figure 1 summarizes how these mechanisms map onto two accessibility logics, described below. We classify them as accessibility-oriented because, in the systems studied, they address barriers arising from cognitive impairment and enable users to continue participating in activities that might otherwise be difficult or unsafe. Although some mechanisms overlap with broader safety and governance approaches, their accessibility function lies in sustaining participation under conditions of reduced cognitive capacity. For example, the family-confirmation requirement encountered by P11 restricted independent action, but also allowed the activity to continue safely when unaided completion was difficult. These mechanisms operate through two broader accessibility logics. Cognitive Engagement Maintenance directly supports users' continued participation in understanding and judgment through stepby-step guidance, scaffolded explanations, and prompting. Rather than substituting for user cognition, it lowers barriers to comprehension and helps users remain cognitively engaged during interaction. By contrast, AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Human-AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control reduce potential risks by constraining system outputs, embedding human decision-makers at critical moments, regulating the intensity of human-AI interaction, and managing the visibility and exposure of information. Together, these mechanisms reshape the conditions of use so that activities can continue under more controlled circumstances, even when independent participation is limited. We therefore conceptualize these four mechanisms as forms of protective accessibility. This distinction highlights a recurring tension between accessibility as enablement, which sustains users' cognitive participation, and accessibility as protection, which supports participation by creating safer conditions of use. The following subsections describe how each mechanism operated in participants' everyday interactions with generative AI systems.

For participants whose clinical assessments indicated that direct interviews were not feasible due to the severity of their condition, caregivers were recruited as proxy informants. These proxy accounts were intended to capture observable usage patterns and to reflect caregivers' own understanding of participants' AI use based on sustained involvement in daily care, rather than to substitute for participants' subjective experiences. For the purposes of this study, we define "generative AI systems" as systems that support the everyday health management and social support needs of older adults with cognitive impairment primarily through natural language generation and conversational interaction. This definition encompasses LLM-based medical questionanswering assistants, cognitive training tools with multi-turn dialogue capabilities, intelligent health management applications, and conversational interfaces for emotional companionship. Although these systems vary in underlying technical architectures, they share natural language interaction as their primary interface modality. Our analysis focuses on their shared interaction logics rather than differences in technical implementation, which is warranted by our finding that the five mechanisms manifest across multiple system types rather than being confined to any single category. A total of 45 individuals with cognitive impairment were included in the study, comprising 31 direct participants (P1-P31) and 14 represented through caregiver interviews (G1-G14, where G denotes caregiver/guardian). Based on clinical assessment, participants were categorized as mild (n=22), moderate (n=12), and severe (n=11). The sample spanned both urban and rural contexts, with education levels ranging from semi-literate to bachelor's degree (Table 1 ). Caregivers included 7 doctors and 7 family members, aged 39 to 57, all of whom had sustained involvement in patients' daily care or medical decision-making and were familiar with their technology use. Participants were recruited through purposive sampling from community health service centers and collaborating hospitals. Doctors first screened eligible patients based on diagnostic records and communication ability, after which the research team obtained informed consent from participants and/or their caregivers. Inclusion criteria required a clinical diagnosis with a clear severity level (via MMSE or physician assessment), age 60 or above, recent engagement with relevant technologies, and sufficient communication ability or caregiver-supported expression. Caregivers were required to have stable relationships with participants and knowledge of their technology use. Individuals unable to communicate, with severe psychiatric or neurological conditions affecting expression, or in acute medical states were excluded. The systems encountered by participants spanned a range of applications and conversational interfaces that integrated generative AI capabilities to varying degrees, including LLM-based medical question-answering assistants, cognitive training tools with multi-turn dialogue capabilities, intelligent health management applications incorporating natural language interaction, and conversational interfaces designed for emotional companionship. These systems varied in their underlying technical architectures: some deeply integrated large language models, while others employed hybrid architectures combining rule-based components with generative AI. However, all of them relied primarily on natural language interaction as their main interface modality, and all were oriented toward the everyday health management and social support needs of older adults with cognitive impairment. For the purposes of this study, we refer to this class of systems collectively as "generative AI-integrated digital health systems, " and our analysis focuses on their shared interaction logics and intervention mechanisms rather than on differences in underlying technical architecture. analysis.results: We identify five accessibility-oriented mechanisms in generative AI systems used by older adults with cognitive impairment: AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Cognitive Engagement Maintenance, Human-AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control. Figure 1 summarizes how these mechanisms map onto two accessibility logics, described below. We classify them as accessibility-oriented because, in the systems studied, they address barriers arising from cognitive impairment and enable users to continue participating in activities that might otherwise be difficult or unsafe. Although some mechanisms overlap with broader safety and governance approaches, their accessibility function lies in sustaining participation under conditions of reduced cognitive capacity. For example, the family-confirmation requirement encountered by P11 restricted independent action, but also allowed the activity to continue safely when unaided completion was difficult. These mechanisms operate through two broader accessibility logics. Cognitive Engagement Maintenance directly supports users' continued participation in understanding and judgment through stepby-step guidance, scaffolded explanations, and prompting. Rather than substituting for user cognition, it lowers barriers to comprehension and helps users remain cognitively engaged during interaction. By contrast, AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Human-AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control reduce potential risks by constraining system outputs, embedding human decision-makers at critical moments, regulating the intensity of human-AI interaction, and managing the visibility and exposure of information. Together, these mechanisms reshape the conditions of use so that activities can continue under more controlled circumstances, even when independent participation is limited. We therefore conceptualize these four mechanisms as forms of protective accessibility. This distinction highlights a recurring tension between accessibility as enablement, which sustains users' cognitive participation, and accessibility as protection, which supports participation by creating safer conditions of use. The following subsections describe how each mechanism operated in participants' everyday interactions with generative AI systems.
analysis.discussion: This study examined how accessibility-oriented intervention mechanisms are embedded in generative AI systems used by individuals with cognitive impairment, and how these mechanisms balance, and at times, are in tension, the competing imperatives of safety and autonomy. Drawing on interviews with 45 participants across mild, moderate, and severe stages of cognitive impairment, we identified five mechanisms operative in current systems: AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Cognitive Engagement Maintenance, Human-AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control. Our analysis reveals that these mechanisms do not operate uniformly; rather, their effects are systematically shaped by users' cognitive stage, relational contexts, and the structural conditions under which AI outputs are translated into action. In this section, we discuss the implications of these findings across four interrelated themes: cognitive impairment level as a moderating variable, divergent evaluations between users and caregivers, a reconceptualization of accessibility beyond interface simplification, and practical design implications for future systems. This study identified five accessibility-oriented mechanisms in generative AI systems used by older adults with cognitive impairment: AI Capability Constraint, Human Oversight Embedding, Cognitive Engagement Maintenance, Human-AI Relationship Regulation, and Risk Transparency and Control. These mechanisms operate through two distinct logics, understanding-enhancing and protective accessibility, whose effects vary across cognitive stages. Protective mechanisms may provide necessary safeguards for users with more severe impairment, while constraining autonomy and participation for those who retain greater decision-making capacity. As impairment progresses, tensions between safety and autonomy may become less visible due to changes in cognition, expectations, usage patterns, and caregiver mediation, rather than because they have been resolved. Apparent usability gains should therefore be interpreted cautiously when they coincide with reduced participation or the transfer of decision-making to caregivers. These findings call for dynamically calibrated systems, relational transparency, and evaluation frameworks that account for both safety and user agency.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the sample was recruited from community health centers and collaborating hospitals in specific geographic contexts, and the findings may not generalize to other cultural settings or care arrangements. Prior research suggests that family involvement in AI-mediated care, for instance, varies substantially across cultural contexts [81] , and future work should examine how relational and normative structures shape the operation of the mechanisms we identified in different settings. Second, because the study was conducted at a single point in time, it captures participants' experiences and perceptions as of the interview but cannot track how these evolve as cognitive impairment progresses. Longitudinal designs would be better suited to capturing the dynamic unfolding of tensions and their dissolution over time. Third, our analysis relies on participants' retrospective accounts of system use, which may be subject to recall limitations, particularly among those with moderate impairment. The use of caregiver proxy accounts introduces an interpretive distance that warrants explicit acknowledgment. Proxy accounts reflect caregivers' own observations and relational positions and may not fully capture participants' experiences, preferences, or resistance to system constraints. A further distinction within the caregiver group has methodological implications for this study. Clinician caregivers (G1, G3, G5, G6, G7, G9) observed patients primarily in clinical settings and interpreted interaction patterns through a medical frame, while family caregivers (G2, G4, G8, G10-G14) drew on continuous daily cohabitation and relational familiarity. These differences in observational context and interpretive position mean that proxy accounts of the same user behavior may diverge not because the behavior differs, but because the reporter's vantage point does. Researchers should therefore treat the caregiver role as a relevant variable when interpreting proxy data, rather than aggregating all caregiver accounts as equivalent representations of user experience. Claims regarding the experiences of users with severe impairment should therefore be understood as reconstructions of observable behavior rather than direct accounts of subjective experience. Future work should combine interview methods with observational or interaction log data to more directly triangulate accounts of actual system use. Finally, while this study focused on mechanisms embedded within existing systems, future design-oriented research should explore how the dual framework we propose, distinguishing understanding-enhancing from protective accessibility, can inform the development of new systems and evaluate whether dynamically calibrated interventions produce better outcomes across the impairment spectrum.

title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
abstract_text: A common concern is that using large language models (LLMs) lets students offload mathematical work that tasks are designed to elicit. Yet such claims often rest on outcomes (e.g., submitted solutions), rather than on evidence of students' work with LLMs. We followed 23 first-year linear algebra students as they solved three differently designed homework tasks with LLMs. Drawing on self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments, we interpreted each of 429 prompts as a trace of a regulatory event and compared 59 chatlogs with the problem solutions the students submitted. Prompts formed five structures, casting the LLM mainly as a solver, explainer, or validator. The mix of structures shifted across the tasks, and ten of the 15 students who completed all three tasks changed their dominant structure. Most final submissions stayed close to LLM output, including those that followed exchanges in which students had explained, conjectured, and checked their own ideas. We conclude that an LLM-aided submission is not a trustworthy marker of students' offloading of the mathematical work, and that offloading needs to be examined in each regulatory space and part by part rather than as a whole.
