abstract_text: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

analysis.discussion: This study examined whether question-chain strategies can be used to structure learners' interactions with GenAI and whether different forms of question chains produce different effects. Compared with free-form questioning, both progressive and divergent question-chain strategies were associated with more learning regulation behaviors, higher metacognitive awareness, and higher academic achievement. However, no significant differences were found between the two question-chain approaches. These findings should be interpreted as effects of the question-chain conditions as a whole. Compared with the control condition, the question chains differed simultaneously in the specificity and quality of the prescribed questions, their sequence, the requirement that each question build on the preceding response, the requirement to complete every step, and the wording of the reflection prompts. The present design therefore cannot attribute the observed differences to chaining per se, and the mechanisms discussed below should be read as possible explanations rather than demonstrated causal pathways. Regarding students' regulation of learning behaviors, analysis of the interaction logs showed that both experimental groups demonstrated more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. The largest difference appeared in learning monitoring. This result is consistent with the possibility that the question-chain conditions changed how students engaged with AI responses. Under the question-chain design, each new question had to build on the previous response. This requirement may have led students to read, evaluate, and connect AI-generated information before continuing the interaction. Such engagement, if it occurred, would be consistent with the constructive and interactive forms of engagement associated with stronger learning outcomes (Chi & Wylie, 2014) . The finding is consistent with previous research showing that guided questioning promotes knowledge construction and comprehension monitoring (King, 1994; Rosenshine et al., 1996) . However, some coded behaviors, such as knowledge expansion and content evaluation, were partly embedded in the prescribed questions themselves (e.g., the final review step of the progressive chain). The higher frequencies may therefore partly reflect compliance with the prescribed prompts, and the effect of question specificity cannot be separated from that of the chained structure. The reflection data offer tentative evidence of differences in how students engaged with GenAI. This evidence is weaker than that from the interaction logs because the reflection prompts differed by condition and explicitly cued some of the coded themes. Students in the experimental groups described more deliberate interaction strategies, including precise prompting, iterative refinement, and selective use of AI suggestions. Control-group reflections, meanwhile, concerned the information GenAI provided and its perceived limitations. Taken together, the interaction logs and reflection data suggest that question-chain prompting was associated with more active forms of engagement during human-AI dialogue. In terms of students' metacognitive awareness, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition and regulation of cognition. A possible explanation is that question chains supported metacognitive processes within the interaction itself. The questions may have encouraged students to evaluate responses against their goals and consider whether to accept, revise, or reject the content; however, this process was neither explicitly required nor established by the reported analyses. These activities correspond closely to the planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes that characterize metacognitive regulation (Bannert & Reimann, 2012; Schraw & Dennison, 1994) . The present findings are consistent with previous research showing that metacognitive scaffolds can promote deeper cognitive processing in GenAI-supported learning environments (Wu et al., 2025) . The findings also contribute to ongoing discussions regarding the potential metacognitive risks of GenAI. Fan et al. (2025) reported that unstructured ChatGPT use was associated with reductions in metacognitive processes, a pattern they described as metacognitive laziness. The current results suggest that these outcomes may depend partly on how learners interact with the technology. When questioning is structured and supported by specific, well-formulated prompts, students may engage more actively in monitoring and regulating their learning. From the perspective of Winne and Hadwin (1998) , question chains provide external support that may help learners initiate and sustain monitoring processes during AI-supported learning. Furthermore, this study found that students in both experimental groups achieved significantly higher grades than those in the control group. This result is consistent with extensive evidence linking self-regulated learning to academic performance (Zimmerman, 2002) . It also aligns with previous studies showing that GenAI is most effective when integrated into structured instructional activities (Deng et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) . One possible explanation is that structured questioning encouraged students to engage more deeply with intermediate products throughout the project. Students may have examined and revised scripts and production plans during the interaction, although this process was not established by the reported analyses. This iterative process may have contributed to stronger final products and, consequently, higher grades. Alternatively, the specific and carefully formulated prompts may have elicited higher-quality AI output that directly improved the scripts, independent of any change in students' regulation. Although the question-chain groups outperformed the control group across all three outcomes, no significant differences emerged between the progressive and divergent approaches. This finding may indicate that the effectiveness of question chains depends more on the presence of structure than on the specific form of the chain. However, because both chains also shared prompt specificity and required completion, this comparison cannot isolate the contribution of chaining itself. Both approaches required students to build each question on the previous response and were intended to support active engagement with AI-generated information. This interpretation is consistent with scaffolding theory, which emphasizes structured guidance while preserving learner agency (Wood et al., 1976) . The absence of significant differences also suggests that instructors may be able to select either approach depending on instructional goals and task characteristics. The study has several theoretical and practical implications. Theoretically, it extends question-chain research from teacher-student interaction to human-AI interaction. It also points to structured questioning as a potential means through which self-regulated learning may be supported in GenAI-assisted environments, although the present design cannot determine which components of the question chains were responsible. In addition, the findings contribute to current discussions about cognitive offloading and passive AI use (Fan et al., 2025; Risko & Gilbert, 2016) . abstract_text: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) in higher education has raised concerns about its impact on students' critical thinking in academic writing, yet evidence on the conditions under which the two are related remains inconsistent. This quantitative correlational study examined the relationship between generative AI use and critical thinking among 34 Indonesian Language and Literature Education (PBSI) students participating in the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) when writing scientific articles. Drawing on Social Cognitive Theory and the cognitive offloading perspective, generative AI use was measured through four indicators (frequency, purpose, dependence, and AI literacy), and critical thinking through five aspects (analysis, evaluation, inference, synthesis–explanation, and reflection), using a four-point Likert questionnaire. Data were analyzed using simple and multiple linear regression, an independent-samples t-test, and moderated hierarchical regression. Composite generative AI use was not linearly related to critical thinking (p = .131) but showed an inverted-U pattern (p = .010), and intensive and selective users did not differ significantly (p = .097). AI literacy moderated the relationship between usage intensity and critical thinking (?R² = .222, p = .004; Holm-adjusted p = .016), with a significant positive relationship only among students with above-average AI literacy. These findings indicate that strengthening AI literacy in academic writing instruction, rather than merely restricting generative AI use, should underpin responsible, literacy-based generative AI policies in higher education.

Data were collected at one host university of the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) in the even semester of the 2024/2025 academic year. Of the 134 PMM participants, 34 PBSI students were selected purposively based on the following inclusion criteria: being a PMM participant from the PBSI study program, having completed an academic writing course, having used generative AI in writing scientific articles, and being willing to participate voluntarily; respondents who did not complete the questionnaire were excluded. These 34 respondents comprised all eligible students, making the sample close to a census. analysis.methods: This study employed a quantitative approach with a cross-sectional correlational design to examine the relationship between generative AI use (X) and students' critical thinking in writing scientific articles (Y) without manipulating participants (Creswell & Creswell, 2017; Sugiyono, 2013) ; accordingly, the results are interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. Data were collected at one host university of the Merdeka Student Exchange Program (PMM) in the even semester of the 2024/2025 academic year. Of the 134 PMM participants, 34 PBSI students were selected purposively based on the following inclusion criteria: being a PMM participant from the PBSI study program, having completed an academic writing course, having used generative AI in writing scientific articles, and being willing to participate voluntarily; respondents who did not complete the questionnaire were excluded. These 34 respondents comprised all eligible students, making the sample close to a census. Because this sample size falls below the minimum benchmarks for multiple regression (Green, 1991; Cohen, 1988) , Ha1 and Ha2 were treated as the primary analyses, whereas Ha3 and Ha4 were treated as exploratory. Data were collected through an online questionnaire (Google Form) using a four-point Likert scale, accompanied by an informed consent form. Variable X was measured with 24 items covering four indicators usage frequency, usage purpose, dependence intensity, and AI literacy with six items each, developed from the frameworks of Chan (2023) and Ng et al. (2021) . Variable Y was measured with 20 items covering five aspects of critical thinking analysis, evaluation, inference, synthesisexplanation, and reflection with four items each, based on the frameworks of Darwin et al. (2024) and Facione (1990) . Negatively worded items were reverse-scored so that higher X scores indicate more measured, purposeful, and verified use, and higher Y scores indicate stronger critical thinking. Content validity was established through expert judgment, item validity was tested on the study sample using Pearson item-total correlations (r count > r table = .339; α = .05), and reliability was tested using Cronbach's α (≥ .70). The research procedure comprised instrument development and validation, obtaining permits, screening respondents, administering the questionnaire, and data processing and analysis.

analysis.discussion: Overall, the results indicate that generative AI use was not related to students' critical thinking when measured as a single composite score (Ha1) or as a difference between intensive and selective users (Ha2), but a relationship emerged when AI literacy was taken into account as a moderator (Ha4). This finding underscores that what matters is not how much students use generative AI but whether such use is accompanied by the ability to evaluate and control AI output. The high mean levels of generative AI use and critical thinking should be interpreted in light of the respondents' characteristics. All respondents had completed a scientific article writing course, and two-thirds of them combined more than one AI tool, particularly ChatGPT, Gemini, and Quillbot. This pattern is consistent with Febriani et al. (2023) , who showed that students used Quillbot and ChatGPT mainly for paraphrasing and grammar correction, and with Chan and Hu (2023) , who found that students perceived generative AI as a useful aid that also raised academic concerns. The invalidity of four of the six usage purpose items is also substantively meaningful: items asking about the use of AI to generate ideas, outline articles, edit language, and understand concepts were answered relatively uniformly, suggesting that these purposes have become common practices that no longer differentiate students. What differentiated respondents were the items concerning the replacement of ideas, such as asking AI to write entire sections of an article or using AI to avoid generating one's own ideas. The nonsignificant Ha1 result differs from the finding of Hutauruk et al. (2025) , who reported a low but positive correlation (r = .377) between generative chatbot use and critical thinking in academic writing, and it also does not replicate the negative associations reported by Zou et al. (2023) and Gerlich (2025) . Two factors may explain this difference. First, the linearity test showed that the relationship between the composite X score and critical thinking was quadratic, with the middle-tertile group obtaining the highest critical thinking scores; this nonlinear pattern may mask the actual relationship when tested with a linear model. Second, the composite score combines dimensions that operate in different directions: more measured usage frequency tended to be accompanied by higher critical thinking (albeit nonsignificantly), whereas lower dependence was accompanied by lower critical thinking, so that the two tendencies cancel each other out at the composite level. This explanation aligns with Chan's (2023) view that generative AI use is multidimensional and cannot be reduced to a single measure. The Ha2 result also differs from Santoso and Patrissia (2026) , who found differences in critical thinking across usage-intensity groups. Although the effect size was medium (d = 0.71), the difference in this study was not significant, likely because each group contained only 12 respondents, limiting statistical power. From the perspective of Social Cognitive Theory, usage intensity alone is insufficient to explain critical thinking when cognitive factors such as AI literacy and self-regulation are not taken into account. The finding that deserves the closest attention is the partial relationship of dependence intensity (X3): respondents who reported greater dependence on generative AI rated their critical thinking higher. This finding contrasts with Zhai et al. (2024) and Gerlich (2025) , who showed that overreliance risks diminishing cognitive abilities through cognitive offloading. The discrepancy is most likely related to how variable Y was measured. Because critical thinking in this study was self-reported, students who frequently rely on generative AI may judge their thinking ability based on the quality of AI-assisted manuscripts rather than on the thinking processes they actually perform a phenomenon consistent with the concept of metacognitive laziness (Fan et al., 2025) . Faqih and Ridwan (2026) likewise found that AI improved the linguistic quality of writing without strengthening analytical or reflective thinking. Thus, the X3 finding is better interpreted as an indication of a gap between perceived and actual critical thinking ability, which should be verified through manuscript-based rubric assessment. The correlations in Table 6 suggest that the X3 finding is not confined to a single aspect, although none survived FDR correction, as the negative relationship appeared consistently across all five critical thinking aspects, with the strongest correlations for evaluation, inference, and reflection. These three aspects are precisely those that depend most on self-assessment: students must judge whether their sources are credible, whether their conclusions are supported by data, and whether their ideas genuinely originate from their own thinking. Darwin et al. (2024) reported that generative AI is helpful in the early stages of writing but may limit students' independent analysis and evaluation; if this limitation goes unrecognized, AI-dependent students may overestimate their evaluative and reflective abilities. Hamsiah et al. (2026) also showed that ChatGPT use in writing is related to students' sense of authorship and autonomy, suggesting that dependence on AI may influence how students perceive their own intellectual contribution. Another important finding is the nonlinear pattern between the composite X score and critical thinking (Figures 1 and 2 ), supported by the significant quadratic model and three-group ANOVA. The middle-tertile group had the highest mean critical thinking score (M = 3.42) with the narrowest dispersion (SD = 0.26), whereas both extreme groups had lower means with much wider dispersion. This pattern is consistent with the cognitive offloading perspective (Gerlich, 2025) : delegating some cognitive tasks to AI in moderate doses can free cognitive resources for higher-order work, whereas excessive delegation replaces thinking practice. However, the selective group who reported the most measured use did not obtain the highest scores, suggesting that strictly limiting AI use is not necessarily accompanied by better critical thinking. This finding is in line with Nasr et al. (2025) , who showed that the quality of human-AI collaboration, rather than merely the amount of use, is associated with critical thinking outcomes. The Ha4 finding is the principal result of this study. Among students with high AI literacy, higher usage intensity was significantly accompanied by higher critical thinking, whereas among students with low AI literacy, the direction of the relationship reversed. This pattern corroborates the finding of Santoso and Patrissia (2026) that AI literacy acts as a moderator and aligns with Nasr et al. (2025) , who distinguished passive use from verified human-AI collaboration. Theoretically, this result supports the combined framing proposed in this study: Social Cognitive Theory explains that AI literacy is a cognitive factor that regulates usage behavior, whereas the cognitive offloading perspective explains that delegating tasks to AI can support critical thinking when accompanied by evaluation but undermine it when done without reflection. abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and automated decision systems has resulted in a fundamental shift in human-technology interaction. This scoping review aims to map the breadth of empirical evidence and original conceptual models regarding human-artificial intelligence (AI) functional displacement. The objective is to synthesize findings across disparate fields into a unified framework of task substitution, cognitive offloading, and behavioral dependency. This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Systematic searches were executed across PubMed, Scopus, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, and ScienceDirect. The studies were screened for research addressing thinking substitution (e.g., reasoning, clinical diagnosis, and creative synthesis) over simple digital assistance. A total of 36 studies met the inclusion criteria. Neurophysiological data from functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) indicate that digital saving triggers cognitive offloading, characterized by significantly lower activation in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). In academic settings, randomized controlled trial data showed that students using ChatGPT scored significantly lower on 45-day retention tests (57.5% correct) compared to traditional learners (68.5% correct, p = 0.002). Professional judgment is increasingly subject to biases; MRI interpretation exhibited substantial self-anchoring bias (score: 6.94), while the automation bias index was high for ECG tasks (0.30). Senior executives receiving AI recommendations acted more actively (M = 5.05) than human-led controls (M = 4.61; p = 0.020), and 89% of educators surveyed reported perceptions of quantifiable skill atrophy. Socially, AI usage and human interaction were moderately and negatively correlated (r = -0.443; p < 0.01), with participants delaying the revelation of intentions in parallel-play settings with digital agents. Task substitution may create a "sovereignty trap" where individuals cede intellectual judgment to automated systems, confusing operational fluency with epistemic mastery. This reliance carries the risk of bypassing the desirable difficulties essential for long-term knowledge retention and the development of professional expertise. As "quiet dependency" becomes an evolving reality of professional and academic life, institutional and design-level interventions must prioritize trust-enabling mechanisms and robust AI literacy to preserve human critical character and professional autonomy.

reading.interpretation: The use of AI tools may shift cognitive engagement toward readily available cues [35, 68] , potentially leading to overreliance on automated outputs in place of independent judgments [48, 69] . Over time, this reliance can reduce independent analytical reasoning and may contribute to cognitive or skill atrophy [35, 68] . By overrelying on large language models (LLMs), students may no longer apply their cognitive skills, thereby compromising critical thinking skills [59] . Behavioral conformity to AI-based recommendations suggests the existence of automation bias, which often leads to overconfidence in the decision-making process [66] . Thus, dependency on GenAI is observed to negatively predict academic achievement while positively predicting false self-efficacy [65] . Critical thinking remains essential to amplify the influence of AI literacy on reflective, cautious, and collaborative use [60] . Prompt-based approaches enhance question-asking skills; thus, integrating GenAI prompts into course activities can improve learning outcomes and reduce metacognitive load [62] . It is important to note that, without sufficient digital literacy, people may ascribe human agency to AI agents and shift responsibility to them (i.e., agency laundering) [3, 45] . In medical and health science education, overreliance on AI poses risks to the acquisition of foundational diagnostic skills and competencies; hence, there is a need to develop clinical problem-solving curricula that may be AImediated and supervised. There is a need for a conceptual shift where AI functions as a partner whose contributions must be meaningful and persuasive [51, 61, 70, 71] and acts as a cognitive scaffold rather than replacing human thinking [61] . reading.limitations: The current evidence depends on restricted English-language publications across four major databases and several other study-level limitations. At the study level, the current evidence relies heavily on self-reported measures, which may be susceptible to response or common-method biases and need further validation [64] . Other limitations include retrospective data; small, purposive samples from single institutions; and studies using simulated human decision-making rather than evaluating real-time responses from clinicians in live environments, limiting generalizability [44, 60] . Controlled experimental settings may not reflect the real world or capture the sustained effects of AI use over extended periods [2] . Additionally, consistent with scoping review methodology, a formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was not conducted across the heterogeneous study designs.

In coordination tasks, 70.2% of participants selected a destination different from that recommended by the RL agent [54] . Furthermore, AI tool use was shown to be moderately and negatively correlated with social interaction (r = -0.443; p < 0.01) [47] . Psychometric evaluation with the Researcher Artificial Intelligence Addiction Scale (RAIAS) in the study population helped to identify withdrawal and tolerance as key dimensions of AI dependency behaviors among study participants [56] .
analysis.discussion: The use of AI tools may shift cognitive engagement toward readily available cues [35, 68] , potentially leading to overreliance on automated outputs in place of independent judgments [48, 69] . Over time, this reliance can reduce independent analytical reasoning and may contribute to cognitive or skill atrophy [35, 68] . By overrelying on large language models (LLMs), students may no longer apply their cognitive skills, thereby compromising critical thinking skills [59] . Behavioral conformity to AI-based recommendations suggests the existence of automation bias, which often leads to overconfidence in the decision-making process [66] . Thus, dependency on GenAI is observed to negatively predict academic achievement while positively predicting false self-efficacy [65] . Critical thinking remains essential to amplify the influence of AI literacy on reflective, cautious, and collaborative use [60] . Prompt-based approaches enhance question-asking skills; thus, integrating GenAI prompts into course activities can improve learning outcomes and reduce metacognitive load [62] . It is important to note that, without sufficient digital literacy, people may ascribe human agency to AI agents and shift responsibility to them (i.e., agency laundering) [3, 45] . In medical and health science education, overreliance on AI poses risks to the acquisition of foundational diagnostic skills and competencies; hence, there is a need to develop clinical problem-solving curricula that may be AImediated and supervised. There is a need for a conceptual shift where AI functions as a partner whose contributions must be meaningful and persuasive [51, 61, 70, 71] and acts as a cognitive scaffold rather than replacing human thinking [61] . In this context, AI systems should be seen as memex-like tools that form active parts of a hybrid transactive memory, aimed at supporting human collective cognition [50] . Determining whether such an artificial consultant is reliable requires human critical thinking, including the collection and analysis of evidence [37, 72] . Because it is highly improbable that evidence will ever be sufficient to justify a general policy of blindly relying on AI, experts demand intelligent design with risk-control measures to force human review and prevent blind trust [37, 58] . Artificial intelligence is becoming an evolving reality of professional and academic life; it is imperative to strike a balance that preserves human critical character. This potential dependency can be further exacerbated by automation bias and premature task delegation. The review shows that there is a cascading chain of ethical and cognitive implications, and without AI literacy training and thoughtful integration, there is an increased risk of compromising core competencies. While AI tools offer immediate efficiency and comprehensive outputs, there will always be a need to preserve and strengthen human critical thinking. These dynamics pose potential threats to clinical and professional autonomy and contribute to psychological dependency. Future research needs to focus on trust-enabling mechanisms that can maintain clinician autonomy and preserve core competencies, independent initiative, and interpersonal collaboration.
analysis.limitations: The current evidence depends on restricted English-language publications across four major databases and several other study-level limitations. At the study level, the current evidence relies heavily on self-reported measures, which may be susceptible to response or common-method biases and need further validation [64] . Other limitations include retrospective data; small, purposive samples from single institutions; and studies using simulated human decision-making rather than evaluating real-time responses from clinicians in live environments, limiting generalizability [44, 60] . Controlled experimental settings may not reflect the real world or capture the sustained effects of AI use over extended periods [2] . Additionally, consistent with scoping review methodology, a formal critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was not conducted across the heterogeneous study designs.

abstract_text: Generative AI tools and conversational chatbots are increasingly embedded in education, work, and daily life, raising concerns about engagement that becomes difficult to self-regulate. This review synthesizes emerging research on problematic generative AI use, treating addiction-like language as part of a broader problematic-use construct rather than a clinical diagnosis. Following PRISMA 2020 reporting, a Scopus search executed identified 188 records. Included studies were characterised by research design and evidence type rather than scored with a formal risk-of-bias instrument. Measurement work is expanding quickly, but instruments remain partially fragmented, blurring the boundary between high engagement, habitual reliance, and impairment. Mechanism studies converge on attachment processes, anthropomorphism and perceived empathy, loneliness and social anxiety, immersive flow, and self-regulatory strain, suggesting that social presence and immersion amplify reliance for some users. In learning and knowledge work, performance pressure and incentive structures can normalize overreliance, with reported risks for cognitive offloading, independent thinking, academic integrity, and skill development. Outcome studies associate compulsive or dependent use with technostress, psychological distress, and lower wellbeing, while mitigation discussion highlights reinforcement-friendly interface cues, privacy and memory governance, and sustainability trade-offs. Because the corpus is almost entirely cross-sectional and self-reported, these relationships are associations rather than causal effects. The key distinction is not between users and non-users, but between bounded, purpose-driven use and escalating reliance with reduced self-regulation. An Antecedents–Decisions–Outcomes structure is used only to frame a forward-looking agenda for longitudinal and intervention research. A sensitivity analysis comparing studies published in 2026 with those published earlier showed that no conclusion was reversed: the design profile and principal gaps held, while the most recent longitudinal studies strengthened the evidence on temporal order and outcomes.

title: Too Long to Watch, Too Short to Leave: Designing for Agent Micro-Waits
abstract_text: Agentic systems increasingly carry out complex work, where a single turn routinely runs for minutes. This produces a micro-wait that is too long to watch and too short to leave. In a formative study with 12 daily agent users, we found that staying felt like wasted time, while switching away fragmented attention and forfeited the context needed to re-engage. We introduce Sidecar, a parallel assistant situated in the same interface as the agent, which reads the run and surfaces implicit decisions the agent made, along with task directions worth exploring. In a within-subjects study (N=16), Sidecar helped participants stay focused on their main task, freely workshop unfinished ideas without fear of unwanted action, and recognize under-specification in their own prompts. Together, these findings contribute to designs that help users stay context-aware and engaged during agent micro-waits.

abstract_text: Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. reading.methods: A preregistered randomized classroom experiment assigned 144 Danish high-school students to standard ChatGPT, an AI chatbot that guided self-regulated learning (SRLbot), or the same approach with emotional support (Emotional SRLbot), with 48 participants in each condition. One learning session lasted about 25 minutes. Tests and surveys were administered before and after, and 85 students completed a four-week follow-up. Interaction traces were coded to examine self-regulatory behaviors.
reading.findings: All three groups improved on immediate conceptual-knowledge and learning-transfer tests; however, condition-by-time comparisons were not statistically significant for either outcome (p = .980 and p = .953). At the four-week follow-up, knowledge and transfer change likewise did not differ significantly between groups. Both SRL-based chatbot groups showed larger improvements in enjoyment and reductions in boredom than the general-purpose ChatGPT group. Emotional SRLbot also showed higher task-level performance and reflection indicators in the interaction traces. Hopelessness fell across all groups without a differential treatment effect, and self-efficacy and chatbot trust did not show clear between-group benefits.
reading.interpretation: The authors interpret the findings as preliminary support for combining AI prompts about planning, monitoring and reflection with encouragement sensitive to students' emotional states. An intervention that makes learning feel better and increases momentary self-regulatory behavior is not yet evidence of lasting independent learning gains. Theoretical expectations about emotional regulation pathways were not themselves fully tested as causal mediators.
reading.limitations: The intervention lasted only one 25-minute session. The pretest and follow-up knowledge measures had internal consistency below .60, making the learning estimates less reliable. Only 85 of the original 144 returned for follow-up, and dropout related to prior AI experience and initial boredom. Some self-report and trace-based measures diverged, and trace coding was aggregated across each session rather than modeling the sequence of regulatory behaviors. Several outcome comparisons were tested and longer-term effects remain uncertain.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

The study followed a non-experimental design. No variables were manipulated, and no pedagogical intervention was implemented to assess changes in participants’ linguistic performance. Instead, participants engaged with GenAI within self -directed learning e xperiences in which they were able to interact with the technology according to their own learning interests and purposes. This design was consistent with the study’s interest in informal learning as a context in which learners exercise varying degrees of control over what, how, and when they learn. The study involved four Colombian adults selected through purposive criterion -based sampling. Participants were required to be over 18 years of age, have previous experience or an interest in learning English, and engage in an informal English learning exp erience involving a GenAI tool as part of the study. A specific level of English proficiency or previous experience with GenAI was not established This decision allowed the study to incorporate participants with different educational, occupational, linguistic, and technological trajectories. The participants differed in their self -perceived English proficiency as well as in their previous familiarity with GenAI. Some reported frequent use of generative AI tools prior to the study, including their use for English learning, whereas others reported occasional use or limited previous experience with GenAI for language learning. This variation was considered analytically relevant because the study sought to understand different ways in which adults approached, interpreted, and incorporated GenAI into their informal learning practices rather than to compare homogeneous learner profiles. Participants’ identities were anonymized through participant codes throughout the data organization, Data were generated through three complementary sources: a record of GenAI interactions for English learning, a participant characterization form, and individual semi -structured interviews. When available, screenshots or other records of participants’ inte ractions with GenAI were also incorporated as complementary documentary evidence. The GenAI Interaction Record for English Learning, administered through Google Forms, was designed to document concrete experiences of GenAI use. Participants reported the tool they used, the type of English learning activity they carried out, what occurre d after receiving an AI-generated response, whether and how they continued the interaction, and how they evaluated the usefulness of the experience. The purpose of this record was to capture specific episodes of interaction rather than participants’ genera l attitudes toward artificial intelligence. Exploring generative AI appropriation in Colombian adults’ informal English learning The participant characterization form collected contextual information regarding age range, occupation, educational background, self -perceived English proficiency, previous informal English learning practices, and prior experience with GenAI. These data we re used to contextualize the individual cases and interpret participants’ accounts in relation to their previous learning and technological trajectories. The original study design explicitly incorporated these dimensions to contextualize the interpretation The third source consisted of individual semi -structured interviews conducted in Spanish. The interviews comprised ten open -ended questions organized around participants’ experiences before, during, and after their interaction with GenAI. Questions first e xplored participants’ previous informal English learning practices and the resources they typically used independently. Participants were then invited to reconstruct a specific GenAI -mediated learning experience in detail, paying particular attention to what occurred throughout the interaction and to the decisions they made as it developed. Subsequent questions explored how participants decided whether to continue an interaction, how they evaluated the adequacy of AI -generated responses, what made them trust or question the information provided, and whether they decided to accept, modify, exp and, or verify those responses. The interviews also examined perceived facilitators and constraints, changes in participants’ perceptions of GenAI after the experience, possible implications for their future learning practices, and the place they assigned to GenAI within their broader repertoire of learning resources. This structure is consistent with the interview protocol used with the participants, which explicitly asked them to reconstruct their experience and explain the decisions made during interacti on with the technology. When available, screenshots and other interaction records were incorporated as complementary documentary evidence. These materials were not treated as a separate data -generation instrument but as an additional source through which participants’ retrospecti ve accounts could be examined alongside traces of their actual interactions with GenAI. Data were examined through thematic analysis following the general principles proposed by Braun and Clarke (2006). The analysis was predominantly inductive, as the initial coding process was grounded in participants’ accounts and documented experiences rat her than organized in advance according to predetermined theoretical categories. Concepts such as learner autonomy, self -regulation, and learner agency were therefore not used as an initial coding framework. Instead, they were subsequently employed as interpretive resources to examine the patterns emerging from the data. The analysis proceeded through an iterative process rather than as a strictly linear sequence. First, the interview transcripts were read repeatedly to develop familiarity with each participant’s experience and to reconstruct each case as a whole. analysis.discussion: This study sought to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through generative artificial intelligence and what decision -making and self-regulation processes emerge from these experiences. The findings indicate that incorporating GenAI into informal language learning is not a straightforward process of technological adoption. Rather, participants configured their relationship with these tools through decisions concerning the direction of interactions, the evaluation of AI-generated responses, the use of personalized feedback, and the integration of GenAI with other learning resources. Across the four cases, learners exercised different degrees and forms of control over their interactions with GenAI. Some participants deliberately structured the interaction through specific instructions and learning purposes, whereas others recognized mo ments in which the technology influenced the direction or duration of the activity. Catalina’s experience, for instance, showed that even when learners independently initiate an AI -mediated activity, they may still need to establish boundaries over interactions that the technology continuously extends. Luisa, in contrast, perceived her interaction as largely directed by the precision of her own instructions. These differences reinforce the idea that learner control in GenAI -mediated environments is neither fixed nor guaranteed by independent The findings also demonstrate that appropriation involves an evaluative dimension. Participants developed different criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying AI -generated feedback. In some cases, trust was established through correspondence with pr ior knowledge; in others, it emerged from the explanatory quality and perceived usefulness of the feedback. Consequently, meaningful engagement with GenAI requires more than knowing how to obtain a response from the technology. It also involves developing the judgment necessary to determine what should be accepted, further At the same time, participants valued GenAI for characteristics that distinguish it from more static digital resources, particularly immediate feedback, conversational responsiveness, repeated practice, accessibility, and the possibility of requesting furt her explanations. These affordances contributed to perceptions of GenAI as a personalized learning resource and, in some cases, as a form of continuously available tutor. Nevertheless, participants did not consistently interpret these affordances as reason s to replace other forms of learning. Instead, they selectively positioned GenAI alongside structured educational platforms, audiovisual resources, independent study practices, and human interaction. Edgar’s preference for more structured platforms for som e grammar activities illustrates this selective The main contribution of this study is therefore the conceptualization of GenAI appropriation as situated orchestration. Appropriation, as observed in these cases, extends beyond access, frequency of use, or Exploring generative AI appropriation in Colombian adults’ informal English learning technological familiarity. It refers to the learner’s developing capacity to coordinate the possibilities offered by GenAI with personal purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, learning routines, alternative resources, and human interaction. From t his perspective, appropriation involves not only knowing how to use GenAI but also deciding when to use it, how much control to delegate to it, what contributions to trust, when to question its responses, when to discontinue an interaction, and when another resource may better serve a particular learning purpose. This interpretation also prevents an automatic association between GenAI use and learner autonomy. The experiences examined in this study suggest that GenAI does not inherently produce autonomous or self-regulated learners. Instead, it creates new conditio ns under which autonomy, self -regulation, and agency may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated. The educational significance of GenAI therefore lies not only in what the technology can provide but in learners’ capacity to regulate their relationship From a pedagogical perspective, these findings suggest that preparing learners to engage with GenAI should extend beyond technical competence or prompt formulation. Language education may need to foster learners’ capacity to establish purposes for AI-mediated activities, critically evaluate generated information, recognize when additional verification is necessary, regulate the duration and direction of interactions, and make strategic decisions about when AI or alternative resources are more appropriate. Such capacities become particularly relevant in informal learning environments, where learners operate without the continuous guidance of a teacher or predetermined instructional sequence. The findings should nevertheless be interpreted within the scope of the study. The analysis involved four Colombian adults with different linguistic, educational, occupational, and technological trajectories. The purpose was therefore interpretive rather than statistically representative, and the findings should not be generalized to Colombian adult English learners as a population. In addition, documentary evidence of GenAI interactions was not equally available across all cases, meaning that some interpretations relied more extensively on participants’ retrospective accounts. The diversity of participants enriched the cross-case analysis but also limits direct comparison among experiences. abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, is increasingly used to explain concepts, support research, and provide individualized learning assistance. Its growing presence raises questions about independent reasoning, creativity, verification, and equitable access. This exploratory cross-sectional survey examined respondents? reported AI use, perceived educational benefits, and cognitive abilities they considered important to protect. A total of 66 respondents participated in this exploratory cross-sectional survey, which combined descriptive quantitative analysis with summaries of open-ended responses. Sixty-four respondents (97.0%) reported using ChatGPT or a similar AI assistant. Personalized learning was selected as an expected benefit by 50 (75.8%), while 48 (72.7%) identified understanding difficult concepts as an AI use or benefit. Critical thinking was the most frequently selected cognitive skill to protect (55; 83.3%), followed by creativity (52; 78.8%), problem-solving (48; 72.7%), and decision-making (47; 71.2%). Reported themes included individualized explanations, convenient information access, dependence concerns, verification, equity, and teacher guidance. Based on these findings and relevant literature, the article proposes a preliminary six-principle Future Minds Framework. The small exploratory sample and self-reported data do not support generalization or causal conclusions about cognition. Further research should evaluate the framework and examine measurable learning outcomes.

abstract_text: In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has seen a significant growth in its integration with the field of Education. This has started many concerns about the effect it has on the process of learning, academic integrity and skill development. This paper examines the effects of AI use within the context of higher education institutions, as it investigates Moroccan postgraduate students’ perceptions on their academic achievements. The targeted sample consisted of 15 postgraduate students enrolled in the English departments of two public universities. This research follows a qualitative approach, as it aims to capture the students’ experience of AI use in their academic life. The findings highlight potential risks of heavy reliance on AI, which include a diminished confidence in the students’ performance, reduced engagement in independent learning and more. However, AI also presents many opportunities for enhancing the process of learning and education when used as a complementary tool instead of replacing the whole cognitive process. This study puts an emphasis on the need for a balanced AI integration while focusing on the development of the students’ cognitive skills in the process. This study contributes to the persisting debate regarding the implementation of AI tools in education and examines how they can be used ethically without diminishing students’ efforts or undermining their original contributions.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has raised fundamental questions about its effects on critical thinking and cognitive development. Evidence from recent empirical studies suggests a dual pattern: structured forms of AI assistance can sustain users’ cognitive activity and enhance engagement and performance, whereas more substitutive forms of use are associated with reduced autonomous reasoning and poorer subsequent independent performance. This article argues that these findings can be understood by considering how cognitive work is distributed between users and AI systems and how this distribution may evolve over time. In particular, I examine a six-step sequence in which successful complementary assistance can increase trust and delegation; greater delegation can remain complementary or become increasingly substitutive; and increasingly substitutive interactions can reduce the autonomous exercise of critical thinking and potentially hinder the development or maintenance of critical-thinking capacities over time. The available evidence provides substantial support for the first five steps considered individually and substantial, though less direct, support for the sixth. The article concludes by discussing educational, design, and social implications, arguing that preserving cognitive agency requires fostering complementary rather than progressively substitutive forms of interaction.

abstract_text: With the widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning, helping learners use AI effectively to solve language-related problems while maintaining independent judgment and critical thinking has become a key issue in technologyenhanced language education. However, existing studies have largely focused on EFL learners’ acceptance of AI, intentions to use it, and usage behaviors, offering limited explanations of how AI literacy shapes learners’ interactions with AI and relates to critical thinking. To address this gap, the present study drew on self-regulated learning theory and adopted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Questionnaire data from 450 university students with generative AIassisted EFL learning experience were analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrapping. Subsequently, 20 participants selected through stratified purposive sampling took part in semi-structured interviews, which were analyzed thematically. Quantitative results showed that AI literacy was positively associated with AI-assisted problem-solving ability and indirectly associated with critical thinking through AI-assisted problem-solving ability and AI reliance. Thematic analysis further revealed how learners translated AI-related knowledge and skills into effective problem-solving practices and how different levels of cognitive control were associated with distinct patterns of AI use and cognitive outcomes. This study deepens the understanding of the internal cognitive mechanisms underlying EFL learners’ adaptation to AI and provides practical implications for the systematic development of AI literacy and critical thinking in EFL education.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is changing how university students study, research and write. It can explain difficult topics, help with research and improve students' academic language. However, depending on AI too much may lead students to let the technology do the thinking for them. This can weaken critical thinking and raise questions about academic integrity. This article discusses both the benefits and risks of GenAI and suggests that universities should teach students to use it responsibly while keeping their own ideas and reasoning at the centre of learning.

title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis
preview: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining appro…
abstract_text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the “digital distraction load,” “psychological-academic exhaustion,” and “academic engagement” dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the “high stress-exhaustion” group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

The variable selection results of LASSO not only reduced model complexity but also provided a focused feature set for subsequent network analysis and machine learning modeling.

The SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern, with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 h for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear pattern for stress level, consistent with a threshold-like pattern of association between social media use duration and academic impact. Fourth, latent profile analysis identified three heterogeneous subgroups, among which the "high stress-exhaustion" group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%, indicating that the combination of high stress and insufficient sleep constitutes the pattern most strongly associated with the most severe academic impairment. The above findings have clear practical implications for the prevention and intervention of academic impact in adolescents. First, school-based mental health education should incorporate stress management as a core component of the curriculum and establish routine stress screening mechanisms to identify adolescents under high stress and provide timely psychological support. Second, interventions targeting digital media use should not adopt a one-sizefits-all approach of simply limiting screen time. Instead, attention should be paid to the modifiability of external distraction factors such as push notifications, and for those who have already reached high levels of social media use, cognitive-behavioral training focusing on self-regulation skills and time management should be emphasized. Third, based on the three subgroups identified by latent profile analysis, a stratified intervention approach is recommended: the "low-risk type" should receive preventive education, the "high digital exposure type" should focus on habit restructuring and self-monitoring training, and the "high stress-exhaustion type" requires multidisciplinary comprehensive interventions integrating mental health care, sleep hygiene, and digital use management. Given the cross-sectional nature of the data, these practical implications should be regarded as hypothesis-generating suggestions based on observed associations rather than as causal recommendations.
analysis.limitations: The present study has several limitations. First, the data were cross-sectional in design, which precludes the establishment of causal directions between variables. For instance, excessive social media use may lead to academic difficulties, but academic difficulties may also drive individuals to escape into social media. Second, the data were derived from self-reports, which may be subject to recall bias and social desirability effects. Third, although the SHAP explanations from the XGBoost model provided both global and local feature contribution information, they have not yet been directly linked to individualized interventions. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs to track the dynamic causal relationships between digital behaviors and academic impact, and integrate ecological momentary assessment to capture real-time changes in attentional states in daily contexts. In addition, efforts could be made to translate the individual-level explanations provided by SHAP into personalized feedback interventions, thereby facilitating the effective translation of research findings into educational practice.

abstract_text: This study examines how algorithmic management in the gig economy is related to gig workers' workplace wellbeing. Specifically, we explore how algorithmic management corresponds with (positive) challenge appraisal and (negative) threat appraisal. We also examine the moderating role of psychological resilience in these relationships, as well as the implications of appraisal processes for workplace wellbeing. Data were collected from 389 food delivery workers in China. We find that algorithmic management is positively associated with both challenge appraisal and threat appraisal. Challenge appraisal is positively associated with workplace wellbeing, whereas threat appraisal is negatively associated with workplace wellbeing. Psychological resilience strengthens the challenge-appraisal pathway and the corresponding positive indirect relationship with workplace wellbeing, but it does not significantly buffer the threat-appraisal pathway. These findings show that algorithmic management is associated with both positive and negative appraisal processes and that psychological resilience may play different roles across these pathways. The study therefore offers a more nuanced explanation of the relationship between algorithmic management and gig workers' workplace wellbeing.

Thus, a well-designed questionnaire and a scientific survey process contribute to improving the reliability and validity of the study, thereby ensuring credible results and conclusions. Therefore, we carefully designed the research questionnaire. The questionnaire in this study consists of a main section and a demographic information section. The main section includes the independent variable (algorithmic management), mediating variables (challenge appraisal and threat appraisal), moderating variable (psychological resilience), and dependent variable (workplace wellbeing). The demographic information section included information such as gender, age, marital status, job type, educational level, and monthly income. All constructs were measured using a 7-point Likert scale (1 = Strongly disagree, 7 = Strongly agree), where participants rated each item accordingly. The 7-point Likert scale provides higher resolution and sensitivity than a 5-point scale, and can capture the respondents' psychological states and behavioral tendencies in more detail. Therefore, it improves the accuracy and reliability of the collected data (Joshi et al., 2015) . The detailed measurement items, item codes, and sources for all variables in this study are presented in Appendix A. The questionnaire was originally developed in English and was translated using a translation-back-translation procedure to ensure equivalence in item meanings. Specifically, we invited three professional translators to conduct the translation and backtranslation procedures, ensuring accurate semantic representation of the measurement items. In addition, before the formal survey, we conducted a pilot test by distributing 50 questionnaires and received 37 valid responses. Cronbach's α and principal component analysis were used to assess the reliability and validity of the measurement scales. The results showed that the Cronbach's α values of all five scales exceeded 0.7, and all factor loadings were above 0.5, suggesting satisfactory reliability and construct validity. Furthermore, based on feedback from our pilot test, items with unclear wording, ambiguity, or limited comprehensibility were discussed and revised. The final version was then used for the formal survey. . Data collection process Data were collected from August to November 2025 in Shanghai, Nanjing, and Suzhou. The participants were food delivery workers aged 18 years or older. To recruit participants, we first contacted the regional managers of food delivery platforms in these three cities. With the assistance of these managers, the research team gained access to delivery stations in the three cities and invited food delivery workers to participate in the study. We then shared the recruitment information and online survey link with eligible delivery workers. The managers only assisted with recruitment and did not influence the workers' decisions about whether to participate. Before the data collection, all participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the content of the survey, and the procedures for participation. The researchers explicitly stated that participation was entirely voluntary and that participants could withdraw from the study at any time. The research team also assured participants that all collected data would be used solely for academic purposes, and that their personal information and responses would be kept strictly confidential and would not be accessed by platform managers or any other third parties. To reduce the possible impact of common method bias (CMB; Podsakoff et al., 2012) , data were collected at two time points. Specifically, at Time 1, a total of 657 participants entered the survey. Participants completed a questionnaire measuring demographic characteristics, the independent variable (algorithmic management), and the moderating variable (psychological resilience). After screening, 86 questionnaires were excluded, leaving 571 valid Time 1 responses, including 206 from Shanghai, 178 from Nanjing, and 187 from Suzhou. To match responses from the same participant across the two waves, participants were asked to provide the last four digits of their mobile phone number as a temporary matching identifier. This identifier was used only to match the two questionnaires and was deleted after matching was completed. The final dataset used for statistical analysis did not contain these four digits or any other information that could directly identify the participants. Three weeks after the first survey, participants who completed the Time 1 survey were invited to complete a second questionnaire assessing the mediating variables (challenge appraisal and threat appraisal) and the dependent variable (workplace wellbeing). A total of 496 participants completed the Time 2 survey. Some participants did not complete the second survey because they had left their jobs or declined to continue participating. In addition, questionnaires completed in less than 5 minutes were excluded based on the predefined data-quality criterion. This five-minute threshold was established before formal data collection based on the actual questionnaire completion times observed in the pilot study. Finally, 389 valid questionnaires were successfully matched across the two waves, including 153 from Shanghai, 115 from Nanjing, and 121 from Suzhou. The retention rate across the two waves was 68.1%. Upon completion of each survey wave, participants received CNY 20 (approximately USD 3) as compensation. In this survey, we found that the majority of food delivery workers in China are unmarried, accounting for over 60% of the sample (62.2%). The sample is predominantly male (86.9%), with a large proportion aged between 18 and 25 years (43.2%). More than 80% of respondents work full time (82.0%). In terms of education, most participants have completed high school (40.1%), and monthly income is primarily concentrated in the range of CNY 5,001-6,000 (37.5%; see Table 1 ). The demographic characteristics of our sample are consistent with those reported in previous studies and reflect the general profile of food delivery workers in China. For example, Lei (2021) reported that Chinese food delivery workers are predominantly male (92%), are mostly in their twenties, and typically have a middle school or high school education. Similarly, Huang (2023) found that the vast majority of Chinese food delivery workers are unmarried men, with 79% engaged in full-time work. . Measurement of variables (1) Algorithmic management. Challenge appraisal was measured using the challenge appraisal sub-scale developed by LePine et al. (2016) .
