analysis.limitations: We acknowledge that our study has several limitations, which may also provide new directions for future research. First, the research sample of this study was entirely composed of food delivery workers. However, workers on different online platforms (e.g., Uber, Helpling) may have different focuses when evaluating algorithmic management, which may lead algorithmic management to be perceived more positively or negatively in different contexts. Future research should conduct in-depth investigations on workers in different industries, platforms, and types, so as to expand the conclusions of this study and enhance the generalizability of the findings. Second, although data were collected at two different time points, and multiple post hoc tests did not identify serious common method bias, the two-wave research design cannot fully overcome the limitations of causal inference. This limitation is particularly important for the present study. Based on stress appraisal theory, we proposed a specific mechanism in which algorithmic management acts as a stressor, shapes gig workers' cognitive appraisals, and further influences their workplace wellbeing. However, because this study adopted an observational research design and some variables were measured through self-reports, alternative explanations cannot be completely ruled out. For example, workers with lower workplace wellbeing may develop more negative perceptions of algorithmic management. Therefore, although the temporal separation of variables provides stronger evidence than a single-wave cross-sectional design, the causal relationships among algorithmic management, cognitive appraisals, and workplace wellbeing should still be interpreted with caution. Future research could adopt longitudinal designs, experience sampling methods, or experimental approaches to provide stronger evidence for causal relationships. Third, prior research suggests that individuals' workplace wellbeing may shape their cognitive appraisals of the work environment, which subsequently influence their work states. However, this reciprocal process has not been widely validated through empirical research. Accordingly, adopting a dynamic perspective on workplace wellbeing is both necessary and timely. Future studies on gig workers' workplace wellbeing could integrate self-reported and other-reported measures, complemented by qualitative evidence, to examine whether and how temporal fluctuations in workplace wellbeing are associated with other workrelated outcomes over time. Fourth, this study focuses on the Chinese context, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. A lot of literature has shown that gig workers in China, particularly food delivery workers, predominantly come from rural areas. Due to structural constraints specific to the Chinese institutional environment, such as the household registration (hukou) system, even workers with high levels of psychological resilience often have limited capacity to avoid or resist unfair treatment from both societal and platform-level actors. Under such conditions, the functioning of psychological resilience may differ from that observed in other institutional settings. Given the cross-national differences in social security systems, labor regulations, and platform governance regimes, future research could adopt comparative designs to examine the contextual applicability and broader validity of the present findings across different economic and cultural contexts. Fifth, sample attrition represents another important limitation of this study. The unmatched cases from the first wave of data collection were not retained during the data matching and cleaning process. Therefore, we were unable to further examine whether there were systematic differences between retained and attrited participants in terms of demographic characteristics, perceived algorithmic management, psychological resilience, and other study variables. This limitation is particularly important because this study further examined the moderating role of psychological resilience across different cognitive appraisal pathways. Potential attrition bias may have influenced the estimated relationships among algorithmic management, challenge appraisal, threat appraisal, and workplace wellbeing, particularly the interpretation of the moderating effects of psychological resilience. Although the differences in sample retention rates across the three cities were not statistically significant, the possibility of systematic sample attrition cannot be completely ruled out. Therefore, we carefully considered this limitation when interpreting the findings and avoided making causal claims beyond what the research design could support. Future research could adopt more effective sample retention strategies while protecting participants' privacy and collect relevant information from participants who do not complete follow-up surveys to further examine potential attrition bias. In addition, this study did not collect identifying information at the delivery station or platform level during data collection. Therefore, we were unable to examine potential clustering effects at the station or platform level. This limitation may affect the estimation of standard errors and statistical inferences. Future research could retain necessary group-level information while ensuring participants' privacy and apply multilevel modeling or cluster-robust standard error approaches to further improve the robustness of research findings.

abstract_text: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by changing how students learn and perform academic tasks. Although AI is associated with greater time efficiency and improved academic performance, its broader effects on student productivity and cognitive effort remain insufficiently understood. This study aims to examine how university students associate AI-led productivity gains with less study time, better grades, better understanding of study material, changes in cognitive effort they put into AI-supported task completion and dependency on AI tools. Design/methodology/approach The authors conducted an exploratory survey among university students in Hanoi in late 2024 and proposed an empirical model that pools self-reported time efficiency, academic performance, academic self-efficacy, change in cognitive effort and AI dependency as dimensions of student productivity. The authors control for AI use intensity and AI use in collaboration, as well as for some other socio-demographic characteristics. Given the exploratory nature of the study and the relatively small sample, the empirical analysis follows a staged specification strategy when the authors first estimate a parsimonious baseline model and subsequently introduce two sets of background controls sequentially. The authors further estimate an interaction between cognitive effort change and AI dependency, first in a parsimonious specification and subsequently with additional controls. Finally, the authors produce a sensitivity analysis of the model to alternative operationalisation of self-efficacy variable. They also associate the productivity growth with greater changes of cognitive effort they put into problem-solving while using AI and rising dependency on AI tools. Self-confidence appears to be associated with likelihood to reap significant rather than some productivity gains particularly once the interaction of AI dependency and AI-led cognitive shift is accounted for. The survey data also support the existence of potentially uneven academic benefits from AI use when higher-achieving students are more likely to report further improvements in academic performance, whereas students with weaker prior performance report rather limited gains. The observed differences between daily and weekly users, particularly in critical evaluation and perceived accuracy, suggest that future studies should examine how evaluative skills and cognitive effort develop over time. abstract_text: Drawing on a computational thinking model and cognitive offloading theory, this exploratory mixed-methods study examined whether structured AI scaffolding is associated with differential computational thinking (CT) outcomes and explored the role of metacognitive self-regulation. Two naturally occurring sections (n = 47) of the same liberal arts course, taught by the same instructor in consecutive Fall semesters, one embedding ChatGPT and one not, were compared using independent-samples t-tests, multiple regression, and inductive content analysis. Students in the ChatGPT-embedded section reported significantly higher problem-solving scores on a validated CT instrument. Digital literacy scores did not differ, possibly reflecting measurement limitations or the intervention's focus on reasoning over general digital fluency. Problem solving correlated significantly with metacognitive strategy use and contributed to a significant overall regression model, but did not remain a unique predictor after adjusting for digital literacy and class membership. Qualitative analysis identified three themes: ChatGPT as a cognitive scaffold, ChatGPT as a cognitive risk, and student-initiated boundary-setting. Most students expressed all three simultaneously, suggesting structured AI-embedded environments may foster metacognitive vigilance alongside CT gains. Findings support deliberate instructional design and explicit metacognitive supports when integrating ChatGPT in higher education.

preview: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangl…
abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in students’ learning and knowledge-work routines, yet perceived productivity gains do not necessarily arise from technology acceptance alone. This study develops and empirically examines an integrated Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) framework for explaining learning productivity among Google/Gemini users in Bangladesh. The study dataset contains 400 respondent IDs, of which 385 records contain complete questionnaire responses and a valid attention-check response; 15 rows are blank. The analysis therefore uses 385 usable cases and conducts an additional sensitivity analysis on 302 respondents classified as regular or occasional AI-feature users. Perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU), SRL and learning productivity (LP) were operationalised using three five-point Likert items each. Transparent composite-score path analysis with 5,000 bootstrap resamples was used because the available analytical environment did not contain a dedicated CFA/PLS-SEM implementation; consequently, the reported measurement diagnostics are explicitly treated as pre-publication validation evidence rather than as a claim of completed covariance-based CFA or PLS-SEM. PEOU positively predicted PU (β = .278, p &lt; .001), while both PEOU (β = .191, p &lt; .001) and PU (β = .218, p &lt; .001) predicted SRL. Learning productivity was predicted by PEOU (β = .140, p = .004), PU (β = .256, p &lt; .001) and SRL (β = .202, p &lt; .001), with R² = .188. Bootstrap estimates also supported indirect pathways from PEOU to LP through PU and SRL, including a serial PEOU → PU → SRL → LP effect. The results suggest that the productivity value of GenAI is partly behavioural: users benefit not only because the technology is perceived as useful and easy to operate, but also because those perceptions are associated with planning, monitoring and addressing learning gaps. The study contributes an emerging-market, mechanism-oriented account of GenAI-enabled learning productivity and identifies measurement and sampling issues that should be resolved in subsequent validation research.

abstract_text: Cognitive flexibility, a core component of executive function, is frequently impaired in individuals with insomnia. However, the neural mechanisms underlying this impairment, particularly in response to sleep-related stimuli, remain unclear. A total of 48 participants, comprising 24 individuals with insomnia disorder (ID) and 24 healthy controls (HC), were recruited to perform a modified task-switching paradigm incorporating sleep-related (e.g., bed) and general stimuli during functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) scanning. Behavioral measures (reaction time, accuracy, and switch cost), task activation and generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI)-based task-dependent functional connectivity were analyzed. Two subjective questionaires, the Cognitive Flexibility Inventory and the Insomnia Severity Index were collectely simultaneously. The ID group exhibited significantly lower CFI scores compared to the HC group, indicating subjective cognitive flexibility impairment. Notably, in the task-switching performance, the ID group demonstrated faster reaction times to sleep-related stimuli. fMRI results revealed altered activation in the right precuneus, angular gyrus, and superior temporal gyrus, with interaction effects between group and stimulus type. The gPPI analyses showed that, compared to HC, ID group exhibited enhanced connectivity between the precuneus and cerebellar under sleep stimulus conditions, as well as disrupted connectivity between the angular gyrus and frontal-parietal regions, and reduced integration from the superior temporal gyrus to multiple association regions across networks. These findings suggest that insomnia is characterized by both subjective deficits in cognitive flexibility and altered neural network dynamics during task switching, with sleep-related stimuli exerting a significant modulatory effect. Enhanced attention captured by sleep-related information may interfere with the optimal task-related network coordination, providing a potential mechanism linking insomnia to executive dysfunction. abstract_text: Abstract The rapid pace of Artificial Intelligence (AI) development is posing unprecedented challenges for the organisation of societies and the contemporary legal order. This study explores possible scenarios related to the evolution of Artificial Intelligence, focusing on the balance between socio-economic benefits and existential risks on a planetary scale. Special attention is given to the legal dimensions of new technologies, with the identification of gaps in contemporary legal regulation of algorithmic autonomy. A global legal regulatory framework, grounded in international cooperation, transparency, and the supremacy of human rights, is proposed as a strategic solution. The methodology encompasses prospective scenario analysis and a systematic bibliographic review spanning computer science, ethics, political science, and international law. The analysis distinguishes three prospective scenarios — optimisation and prosperity, misalignment and disruption, and existential risk — and examines the structural challenges AI poses to labour markets, algorithmic justice, and global security. The study concludes that anticipatory, internationally coordinated regulation of new technologies is crucial for ensuring their development remains compatible with human safety, dignity, and long-term collective welfare.

abstract_text: This study examined the relationships among generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students’ learning regulation among university students in Pakistan. A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed, and data were collected from 293 university students through a self-administered online questionnaire distributed using Google Forms. The collected data were organized in Microsoft Excel and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize demographic characteristics, Pearson correlation was applied to examine relationships between variables, and simple linear regression was conducted to assess predictive relationships. The illustrative analysis indicated a positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness (β = 0.478, p = .001), with the regression model explaining 22.8% of the variance in metacognitive awareness (R² = 0.228). Cognitive offloading was positively associated with students’ learning regulation (r = 0.436, p = .001), while metacognitive awareness positively predicted learning regulation (β = 0.568, p = .001), explaining 32.3% of its variance (R² = 0.323). These findings highlight the potential relevance of generative AI use and metacognitive awareness to students’ learning regulation. The study emphasizes that AI tools should support, rather than replace, independent thinking, critical evaluation, and active learning. Educators may use these insights to design learning activities that promote reflection, self-monitoring, and responsible AI use. The study also provides a basis for future research examining these relationships across different academic disciplines and educational settings. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretations and does not establish changes in learning regulation over time.

Responses were reviewed to assess their completeness and correctness. The responses were edited for spelling mistakes. The researcher reserved the right to withdraw any response that raised ethical concerns. The intended final sample consisted of 293 Universi ty students. Data collected were organized and analyzed in IBM SPSS Statistics after being entered in Microsoft Excel. Descriptive statistics were computed to summarize characteristics of participants and to interpret responses to study variables. Where appropriate, the assumptions of relevant statistical techniques were checked before performing any statistical inference. Pearson correlation was applied to test hypothesis H1 to determine the extent to which generative AI-supported learning and cognitive offloading are related. Simple linear regression was conducted to assess the level of statistically predicting metacognitive awareness by generative AIsupported learning (H2). Pearson correlation was employed to assess the relationship between cognitive offloading and students' learning regulation (H3). Simple linear regression was done to assess the extent to which metacognitive awareness is related to learning regulation (H4). Results of regression analysis were interpreted as statistical predictions rather than evidence of causal relationships. Regression coefficients were described as positive or negative rather than large or small.
analysis.discussion: The results of this study show the relationships between generative AI supported learning, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive awareness and students' learning regulation. The results suggest that generative AI tools may serve as cognitive aids while affecting students' learning in a similar way as cognitive offloading. Generative AI supports students' learning by prompting and providing students' assistance and explanation. To a degree, Rahmadiningrum, (2026) argued that cognitive offloading allows students to free up their cognitive resources by utilizing external sources. AI can help student's complete academic task. However, stude nt's may lose opportunities for independent thinking by relying too much on AI. Thus, in an educational context, the value of generative AI lies in its capability to serve students as a support, rather than a substitute, for cognitive effort. The positive association between generative AI-supported learning and metacognitive awareness is significant because metacognition is the understanding of, and the ability to control, one's own thought processes. According to Melanou, (2026), knowing about cognition and regulating cognition are core elements of metacognitive awareness. Using generative AI to clarify difficult concepts and compare and check their understanding may help learners become more aware of their learning processes. Additionally, the relationship between cognitive offloading and learning regulation indicates that students' use of external cognitive support is related to the way students' structure and regulate their learning. However, offloading is not necessarily beneficial in all cases, and its utility may depend on students' ability to evaluate AI-generated information and be actively involved in their learning. The result that metacognitive awareness is predictive of learning regulation is supportive of the observation that efficient learners envision and structure their learning, and actively monitor their level of comprehension. As Suazo Galdames et al., (2026) noted, although the use of one's own cognition is pivotal in self-regulated learning, other factors such as motivation, affect and environment are also integral in the self-regulation of learning. Therefore, the results of the current study, which encourage students to critique and verify information generated by AI and consider the coherence and the rationality of the information produced, are also vital. Given the cross-sectional design of the study, it only demonstrated statistical relationships, and not causal relationships. Longitudinal research is warranted to establish the impact of long-term use of generative AI by students and what it means for learning regulation and metacognitive awareness (Fitriani et al., 2026) . This study investigated the relationships between generative AI-supported learning, cognitive offloading, metacognitive awareness, and students' regulation of their learning. The results showed that generative AI-supported learning and cognitive offloading affect metacognitive awareness. Further, cognitive offloading and metacognitive awareness impacted students' regulation of their learning. Overall, the findings demonstrate the need to understand students' use of generative AI, their thinking and learning, and the strategies and actions they take to facilitate their academic activities. The study stated that generative AI should be used as a supportive educational resource, and not replace students' independent thinking and learning. Relying too much on AI to produce information will not help students to accomplish academic goals and may negatively impact their performance and academic results. It is important that educators develop students' skills of judgment and discretion so that they can be responsible in their use of AI.

abstract_text: Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

reading.interpretation: Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning play important roles in shaping learners' engagement with generative artificial intelligence in distributed learning environments [4, 5]. Beyond the availability of AI technologies, learners' individual competencies may influence how effectively AI-generated feedback supports learning engagement. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning are therefore not merely contextual factors in applying generative AI but may also serve as important mechanisms European Journal of Education Science linking AI-generated feedback to sustained learning engagement. Learners with higher feedback literacy may view AI-generated outputs as feedback that requires evaluation rather than as definitive answers. They may actively question, verify, and refine AI- generated information while integrating teacher feedback, peer assessment, and self- reflection [4]. Similarly, learners with stronger self-regulated learning skills may demonstrate clearer learning objectives, more effective time management, and stronger metacognitive monitoring abilities. These competencies may enable learners to use AI - generated feedback more purposefully to obtain explanations, examples, practice opportunities, and timely assessments during distributed learning activities [2].

abstract_text: Individuals with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) typically perform cognitive tasks with greater response time variability than matched peers. This is thought to be due to the greater occurrence of occasional extremely slow responses associated with lowered arousal levels. To test this we designed a new, less arousing task to measure sustained attention, named the Disappearance Detection Task (DDT). This study aimed to investigate the relationship between response time variability and levels of ADHD symptoms both in this new, low-arousal sustained attention task and in the Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART). Twenty-eight children and 49 adolescents participated. On both tasks, ADHD symptom levels were associated with response time variability measures of SDRT and tau, but not with sigma. On the DDT, children with higher ADHD symptoms made more commission errors and were less accurate in detecting the target (d'), whereas adolescents made a similar number of commission errors and d' irrespective of their ADHD symptom levels. This pattern was not present in the SART. The adolescents found the DDT more challenging than the SART as their target sensitivity was lower during the DDT. The children were less confident in nominating the target (criterion) during the DDT than the SART. The results indicate that RTV measures are more consistently associated with ADHD symptoms than other RT measures and that the DDT is a sensitive task of sustained attention and response inhibition performance, particularly in children, and in children with higher symptoms of ADHD.

analysis.methods: Twenty-eight children aged between 9 and 12 years (M 10.95 years, SD 1.06; 9 females) were recruited from local primary schools. Forty-nine adolescents aged between 15 and 18 years (M 17.57 years, SD 0.76; 33 females) were recruited from local secondary schools (n 6) and from an undergraduate course in psychology at the university (n 43). Participation in this study required no known neurological condition, pervasive developmental disorder, or history of serious head injury. No participant was excluded from the study. No participants reported using medications for ADHD. Data from this cohort has previously been published, including the random SART data (Machida & Johnson, 2019; Machida et al., 2019) . Ethics approval was obtained from the University of Melbourne ethics committees. Parents/carers consented for their children and secondary school adolescents to participate and then completed a demographic information sheet and a questionnaire of ADHD symptoms of their child. University students consented for themselves and completed a self-assessment of their ADHD symptoms. The WASI was administered to the participants from the primary and secondary schools. The Conners Parent questionnaire was administered to the parents of participants from primary and secondary schools while the participants undertook the experimental tasks. The undergraduate participants completed the Conners Self-Report questionnaires before performing the tasks. The SART and the DDT were completed in counterbalanced order across participants to avoid order effects. Participants were asked to press the key as quickly and accurately as possible, and there were no further instructions provided to facilitate their efforts during the task completion.

This resulted in a sample of 25 out of 28 children (M 10.6 years, SD 1.0), and 47 out of 49 adolescents (M 17.6 years, SD 0.8). The DDT provided a task environment in which an interaction between age and ADHD symptoms became apparent -children, but not adolescents, with higher levels of ADHD symptoms performed the task with more commission errors and lower target detection (d-prime). Poorer performance on these measures most likely reflects response inhibition and sustained attention difficulties (O'connell et al., 2009) . This finding suggests that the DDT is very sensitive to response inhibition and sustained attention performance differences associated with both age and ADHD symptom levels. Compared to the commonly used cognitive tasks in the literature of ADHD and RTV like the SART (Johnson, Kelly, et al., 2007) , the Flanker task (Castellanos et al., 2005) , and the CPT (Hervey et al., 2006) , the DDT task is unique. This requirement to wait was associated with more impulsive response styles of the younger children with higher symptoms of ADHD. The Delay Aversion theory of ADHD (E. J. venue: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI Ethics and Society

abstract_text: We evaluate how effectively platform-level parental controls moderate a mainstream conversational assistant used by minors. Our two-phase protocol first builds a category-balanced conversation corpus via PAIR-style iterative prompt refinement over API, then has trained human agents replay/refine those prompts in the consumer UI using a designated child account while monitoring the linked parent inbox for alerts. We focus on seven risk areas—physical harm, pornography, privacy violence, health consultation, fraud, hate speech, and malware—and quantify four outcomes: Notification Rate (NR), Leak-Through (LR), Overblocking (OBR), and UI Intervention Rate (UIR). Using an automated judge (with targeted human audit) and comparing the current backend to legacy variants (GPT-4.1/4o), we find that notifications are selective rather than comprehensive: privacy violence, fraud, hate speech, and malware triggered no parental alerts in our runs, whereas physical harm (highest), pornography, and some health queries produced intermittent alerts. The current backend shows lower leak-through than legacy models, yet overblocking of benign, educational queries near sensitive topics remains common and is not surfaced to parents, revealing a policy–product gap between on-screen safeguards and parent-facing telemetry. We propose actionable fixes: broaden/configure the notification taxonomy, couple visible safeguards to privacy-preserving parent summaries, and prefer calibrated, age-appropriate safe rewrites over blanket refusals.

analysis.discussion: Parental notifications in the current consumer deployment are selective rather than all-encompassing, according to our results. Even when judge labels in those areas highlighted borderline or unacceptable material, we did not see any parental warnings for privacy violence, fraud, hate speech, or malware, despite employing a PAIR-style corpus and human-in-the-loop replays that covered seven risk categories. In contrast, actual harm (and, to a lesser extent, pornography and health advice) generated sporadic alarms. According to this pattern, the notification system either (a) prioritizes a limited set of harms, (b) relies on keyword-or classifier-driven triggers that are tuned for these categories, or (c) is subject to policy restrictions that deliberately exclude certain areas (such as privacy or fraud) from parental escalation via email. At the same time, we noted that educational prompts pertaining to delicate topics (e.g., basic anatomy, historical analysis with quoted slurs, benign cybersecurity hygiene) were excessively blocked. There is a calibration mismatch between the parent-facing telemetry and the userfacing assistant, as seen by the coexistence of under-coverage (no alerts for certain high-risk categories) and overblocking (benign queries rejected). This gap is made worse by cases when obvious UI protections (warnings or safe rewrites) didn't result in any parent notifications, so that carers were left in the dark about any friction or borderline replies the kid received. Under the same prompt families that the present backend opposed, legacy backends (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o) created content that was somewhat inappropriate, in accordance with continuous alignment advancements. However, since the notification profile did not change simultaneously for the un-alerted categories, families that depend only on email notifications may have an exaggerated sense of security in those sectors. Design implications. We see three actionable fronts for platforms: 1. Coverage & taxonomy. Expand notification coverage (or provide configurable options) for non-trivial categories like privacy violence, fraud, hate, and malware. Expose a transparent notification taxonomy to parents. 2. Calibrated routing. Prefer safe rewrites and guided education over blanket refusals when prompts are plausibly instructional. Pair this with on-by-default parent summaries that aggregate blocked-but-benign interactions so caregivers can adjust controls. According to our protocol, parental controls for conversational assistants have a policy-product gap in that alerts are focused in certain areas (physical harm, aspects of sexual content, some health concerns) but other important threats (privacy violence, fraud, hate speech, malware) do not trigger any parental alerts. In the meanwhile, overblocking restricts instructional content for harmless, nearby searches, particularly when expressed in age-typical language. Although the current backend is better aligned than older versions, the advancements in model rejections and safe rewrites have not kept up with the equally thorough and transparent parental telemetry. In order to better assist families, platforms should: (1) expand or allow users to customize the notification taxonomy, (2) link on-screen protections with parent-facing summaries, and (3) prioritize age-appropriate, calibrated safe rewrites over outright rejections when possible. Future research should focus on extending multilingual coverage, incorporating longer multi-turn trajectories with context carryover, comparing parental ecosystems across platforms, and assessing dashboard-style parental summaries that highlight both risks and blocked-but-benign learning efforts. When taken as a whole, these measures can move parental controls from simply reacting to notifications to proactively and developmentally supporting children in having safer and more productive interactions with artificial intelligence.
analysis.limitations: Scope and generalizability. Our corpus was tuned to seven categories and a specific consumer product configuration; results may not generalize to other categories, languages, or platforms. While we balanced prompts across categories and age bands, we did not aim to estimate population prevalence of unsafe outcomes. Seed prompt authenticity. Our seed prompts were generated by Claude Sonnet 4.5 rather than derived from naturalistic child-chatbot interaction logs. While we designed category templates with age-appropriate cover stories (e.g., "homework," "story," "I'm scared") and escalation ladders informed by developmental literature, we did not validate these seeds with child development specialists, linguists, or against corpora of authentic child discourse. Real children may employ idiosyncratic phrasing, spelling errors, codeswitching, or pragmatic strategies (e.g., emotional appeals, repetition, topic drift) that LLMgenerated prompts fail to capture. Future work should incorporate expert review from child psychology or sociolinguistics, or derive seeds from ethically obtained naturalistic interaction data, to strengthen ecological validity. Measurement constraints: • Notification pipeline opacity. We treat notifications as a black box; missing alerts could reflect policy gating, classifier thresholds, deliverability issues, or email batching. • Judge-model bias. Using ChatGPT 5 as the primary judge risks model-model correlation with the target assistant and category-specific precision/recall trade-offs. We mitigated this with human audits and sensitivity checks, but residual bias is possible. • UI vs. API drift. Prompts evolved via API then replayed in the UI. Differences in routing, context windows, or safety layers could influence outcomes. • Temporal variance. Alignment and notification policies evolve. Although we logged timestamps and ran sensitivity checks, temporal drift and day-of-week effects (e.g., latency or batching) may affect TTN and coverage. • Human-agent variability. Trained agents paraphrased minimally, but micro-variations in tone or sequencing can alter safety triggers. • Legacy backend emulation. Our legacy trials relied on product-exposed variants (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o) during specific replay windows; exact parity with historical deployments cannot be guaranteed.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows university teachers to delegate cognitive work while deciding how students should engage with it. Using codebook thematic analysis, we examined multi-source accounts from 25 teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks in China. Materials comprised interviews with 22 teachers, three documentary cases, self-narratives and reflective essays. Three themes organize the findings: reconstructing the teacher role, defending professional judgment, and managing teachers’ and students’ cognitive participation. Participants described disciplinary expertise as a basis for evaluating AI outputs and reported practices intended to retain human engagement. Instrumental and partnership orientations overlapped; descriptive comparison with later use profiles did not establish a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity. Because the protocol introduced several focal topics, we distinguish prompted positions from volunteered formulations. The proposed belief–strategy–practice cycle is a heuristic interpretation of retrospective accounts, not a demonstrated mechanism. The study contributes an account of how teachers connect their own cognitive offloading with their reported organization of students’ learning opportunities. Its claims concern this AI-engaged sample rather than university teachers generally.

reading.findings: Across the 25 cases, participants returned to a set of concepts when discussing what AI is, what it cannot do, and what they should do about it. Recurrence is interpreted alongside the distribution of clear and partial evidence, protocol prompting and case context. Appendix D summarizes coverage and Supplementary Table S2a,b provide the case-level matrix. Section 4.1 addresses beliefs and professional value (RQ1); Section 4.2 and Section 4.3 address reported cognitive strategies and participation (RQ2); recurring formulations, divergence and retrospective change across these sections inform RQ3. The heuristic synthesis follows in Section 5.4 .
reading.interpretation: The accounts suggest a perceived relationship between teachers’ beliefs about AI and the strategies they describe. Instrumental formulations emphasize task-focused use and verification-centered gatekeeping; partnership formulations emphasize sustained dialogue and calibration. These formulations can coexist in the same case, and the later use profiles do not show a simple relationship between partnership language and usage intensity ( Section 4.2.2 ). The interpretation is consistent with Pajares ’s ( 1992 ) account of beliefs as filters of decision-making and with university teachers’ reported negotiation of GenAI use ( Farazouli et al., 2025 ). Participants also described changes in their orientations, qualifying a view of beliefs as resistant to change ( Kagan, 1992 ). However, the study did not systematically follow those changes as they happened. Correspondence between beliefs and strategies may reflect the coherence of a retrospective account as well as relationships in practice. The evidence supports how participants connect the two in their descriptions, rather than the direction or rate of their influence. Within this sample, teachers shifted the defense of professional value from “what I know” towards “what I can judge”: verification and judgment carry clear evidence in 24 of the 25 cases, and irreplaceability construction appears in 24 of 25. This finding extends Ertmer ’s ( 1999 ) focus on internal barriers by showing that teachers’ beliefs also concern the source of professional authority. reading.limitations: Drawing on multi-source qualitative materials from 25 university teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks, this study examined how they describe their beliefs about GenAI and the cognitive strategies they use alongside it. Four conclusions follow. Second, participants commonly reconstructed the teacher role from “knowledge transmitter” towards “guide, designer, companion, gatekeeper”, in terms they volunteered, while ten of the 25 cases (40.0%) retained a reinterpreted claim to expertise. The 25 teachers work in 13 provinces and municipalities, with six in Gansu and three in Guangdong and the remainder distributed singly or in pairs across Shaanxi, Hunan, Hebei, Guizhou, Guangxi, Chongqing, Shandong, Henan, Yunnan, Jiangsu and Zhejiang. Their institutions comprise one university in the 985, 211 and Double First-Class schemes, two in the 211 and Double First-Class schemes, six provincial key universities outside those schemes, two normal universities, two medical universities, three vocational colleges, and one each of a foreign-language university, a university for nationalities, a university of political science and law, a university of Chinese medicine, a science and engineering university, a Sino-foreign cooperative institution, an independent undergraduate college, a provincial comprehensive university and a provincial undergraduate institution. The participants therefore work in a varied set of institutions that extends well beyond the elite tier. Because the sample was assembled through purposive and snowball sampling within a single learning community, it is not representative of Chinese higher education, and this institutional variety describes the settings of the accounts without supporting generalization to the sector. Participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling within a learning community devoted to AI-empowered teaching, to which the first author belongs. The community was founded in December 2023, with the purpose of discussing and sharing emerging GenAI tools and creative uses among university teachers and doctoral students. Recruitment targeted university teachers in mainland China with sustained use of GenAI in professional work; the included sample also contained one recently retired teacher, whose status is reported explicitly; no criterion concerning attitude towards AI was applied, although the recruitment route makes committed users more likely to be included. Recruitment proceeded from community members known to the first author to teachers they nominated in turn. The composition of the sample is a property of the study rather than an incidental feature. Foreign-language teachers make up 10 of the 25 cases, and every participant was already engaged with GenAI at the time of recruitment (though with varied levels of use or intensity). Teachers who had considered GenAI and rejected it, and teachers who had never encountered it, are not represented. This was an insider study: the first author and most participants belong to the same learning community that was open to rolling recruitment, and some interviews and self-narratives were produced during community events. This position afforded trust, contextual understanding and access to naturalistic accounts. It also shapes what participants chose to disclose and how their accounts were interpreted, and it means that a shared way of talking about AI is available as an explanation for part of what we report as convergence. Materials were collected between January 2025 and May 2026. Twenty-nine people were approached and four declined participation, leaving 25 teacher cases. Of these, 22 contributed semi-structured interviews and three (D, E and F) contributed documentary material. Three source types anchored the corpus, supplemented by other materials made available by individual participants: Semi-structured interviews (22 teachers, 60–120 min each) followed a common revised protocol, Exploring University Teachers’ Roles and Digital Literacy in the GenAI Era. The protocol comprised six sections: background and first contact with AI; digital literacy and technology adaptation; teaching roles and experiences; digital ethics and critical AI engagement; hypothetical and critical thinking; and reflective and future-oriented questions. Because several sections put propositions to participants, Table 3 records which topics the protocol introduced and which formulations participants volunteered. The interviewer’s field notes supplemented the transcripts. Teachers J and W each took part in more than one interview, and Teacher R also completed the protocol in written form. All interviews were conducted, recorded and transcribed by the first author on Tencent Meeting, the videoconferencing platform on which the interviews took place. The platform exports two forms of the same recording: a verbatim export and a cleaned export that it labels “intelligent-optimized”. The cleaning is performed automatically by the platform as part of the export. For each interview, a single transcript was manually checked and corrected against the recording before being used for coding. No separate generative-AI system was used to rewrite the transcript texts. The original recordings were retained by the first author for checking the transcript and quotations. The first author stored the original recordings and transcripts on a password-protected personal laptop; access to these original files was limited to the first author. Tencent Meeting processed recordings containing participants’ names. The first author removed names and identifying details from the transcripts before sharing deidentified copies with the corresponding author. Three interviews were held in both forms, which allows the effect of the cleaning to be measured rather than assumed. Within this sample, teachers shifted the defense of professional value from “what I know” towards “what I can judge”: verification and judgment carry clear evidence in 24 of the 25 cases, and irreplaceability construction appears in 24 of 25. This finding extends Ertmer ’s ( 1999 ) focus on internal barriers by showing that teachers’ beliefs also concern the source of professional authority. Participants described AI as producing knowledge claims and teachers as evaluating those claims—a redistribution that parallel bodies of literature describe as the renegotiation, rather than the collapse, of epistemic authority ( Haase, 2026 ; Jose et al., 2025 ; Milella & Cabitza, 2026 ). The closest analogue lies outside education: newsrooms incorporating generative AI have likewise relocated professional authority from the production of content to its authentication ( Ashuri et al., 2026 ). What distinguishes the present case is that judgment is claimed not only as a competence but as a position in a professional self-description, expressed through labels such as “gatekeeper”, “goalie”, “navigator” and “auditor”. Comparable boundary work has been documented where professionals must decide how far to let an algorithmic recommendation stand in for their own judgment ( Li, 2026 ). This interpretation is consistent with the cognitive-offloading literature: offloading is not inherently harmful, but its consequences depend on how it is monitored ( Risko & Gilbert, 2016 ). Experimental work raises concerns about reduced regulatory effort in some GenAI-supported tasks ( Fan et al., 2025 ), while observational and review evidence links offloading with variation in critical thinking and learner agency ( Gerlich, 2025 ; G. Wang et al., 2026 ). These sources do not establish a uniform causal effect of AI use. That these consequences vary across users ( Si et al., 2026 ) lends empirical weight to the conditionalist position articulated by 11 of the 25 teacher cases. The participants’ accounts resembled norms of “monitored offloading” (human-in-the-loop; quality dependence). Teachers’ AI-related beliefs—instrumental or partnership, boundary beliefs, identity beliefs—appear to orient cognitive strategies such as verification, calibration, defense and reflection. These strategies encounter feedback in practice, including efficiency gains, hallucination-related failures, student plagiarism, and additional workload. Participants’ retrospective accounts locate belief revision at nodes they describe as turning points, after which revised beliefs support new strategies. The security narratives of Section 4.1.3 are interpreted as an affective dimension of this arrangement. The arrows record what participants describe as following from what, not tested directions of effect, and nothing in the design permits a claim that one element produces another; establishing that would require following teachers over time and observing what they do rather than what they report. Three features of the sample bear on how the findings should be taken. Every participant was already engaged with GenAI, which is why disenchantment appears here as a stage within continued use rather than as grounds for abandonment. Foreign-language teachers make up 10 of the 25 cases, which is likely to be one reason the erosion of a disciplinary skill base is so prominent. And the protocol introduced several of the propositions at issue. At the same time, the prominence of “learning from accomplished people” (Teacher V), “teaching is the best learning”, and “mutual inspiration” (Teacher Y) indicates that peer exchange may function as infrastructure for teacher development in the AI era. Comparative work with teachers outside such communities is needed to establish whether these patterns extend further. Research on cognitive offloading examines how external resources change demands on memory, monitoring and task performance ( Risko & Gilbert, 2016 ). analysis.limitations: Drawing on multi-source qualitative materials from 25 university teachers recruited through an AI-focused learning community and its professional networks, this study examined how they describe their beliefs about GenAI and the cognitive strategies they use alongside it. Four conclusions follow. First, participants described a broadly shared boundary around what AI cannot do—emotion, embodiment, metacognition, tacit knowledge, judgment—which served both to make sense of the technology and to protect a professional position; this boundary was elicited by a direct question and should be taken as the shape of their answers to it. Second, participants commonly reconstructed the teacher role from “knowledge transmitter” towards “guide, designer, companion, gatekeeper”, in terms they volunteered, while ten of the 25 cases (40.0%) retained a reinterpreted claim to expertise. Third, judgment and gatekeeping were re-centered as the defended core of professional work, with verification and judgment carrying clear evidence in 24 of 25 cases. Fourth, participants described managing cognitive participation on both sides of the desk, taking divergent positions on “intellectual degeneration” (9 endorsement, 11 conditional, 2 rebuttal, 1 ambivalent, 2 no position) while describing a varied repertoire of defensive strategies with differing levels of explicit support. The relation between belief and cognition that these accounts suggest is reciprocal but not demonstrated: it is an interpretation of what teachers say, offered for longitudinal and observational examination. The contribution to research on intelligence lies in connecting teachers’ own cognitive offloading with the learning conditions they report designing for others. Professional judgment and metacognitive regulation are central to these accounts, but their effectiveness requires observational and learning-outcome evidence. The study carries implications for teachers and institutions. On the one hand, professional development in the AI era could move beyond “learning to use tools” toward “cultivating judgment”, including the disciplinary expertise needed to verify AI output, the metacognitive habit of monitoring cognitive participation, and the willingness “to err personally.” Teacher L’s phrase captures this emphasis: “AI gives the skeleton; the human fills in the soul.” On the other hand, teacher participants reported that AI had not reduced but increased their burden, and described assessment as a domain in which established practices had lost their force without replacements being available. Institutions could respond by supporting instructional-design experimentation, clarifying academic-integrity standards, and creating a fault-tolerant environment in which teachers can test and evaluate new practices, rather than limiting support to tool training. Regardless, the study is not without limitations. First, the sample was a purposive and snowball sample of teachers already engaged with GenAI, recruited through a common learning community and its professional networks, and the findings cannot be generalized to Chinese university teachers as a whole; the beliefs of resistant and avoidant teachers are not represented, and the community’s shared vocabulary cannot be separated from the convergence we report. Second, the analysis relied on self-reports, so the relation between stated beliefs and classroom practice requires observational evidence. Third, the design is largely cross-sectional and retrospective and cannot establish trajectories or directions of effect. Fourth, broad code definitions and shared interview prompts can increase coverage without establishing independently shared beliefs. The agreement check covers a small sample of meaning units and does not validate all case-level evidence ratings. English translations did not receive an additional bilingual check. Finally, the cases rest on uneven combinations of interviews, self-narratives, published essays, field notes, chat records, product documents and recorded AI dialogues; three cases (D, E, F) rest on documentary material without an interview, and an absent code in a thinly documented case records the limits of the material rather than the absence of a belief.

abstract_text: In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), sustainable education requires not only the integration of advanced technologies but also the cultivation of key competencies such as critical thinking. This study investigates English major students’ engagement with generative AI tools in translation learning, focusing on their usage patterns, critical thinking behaviors, and ethical awareness. A mixed-methods design combining questionnaire data and semi-structured interviews was employed to examine how students interact with AI in translation contexts. The results show that while students frequently use AI for translation, writing, and language learning, their engagement remains primarily functional and efficiency-driven. Although they display openness and flexibility toward AI, their reasoning confidence, self-regulation, and ethical reflection are underdeveloped, indicating surface-level interaction and overreliance on technological authority. These findings highlight the need to cultivate higher-order cognitive and ethical capacities in translation training. Central to this discussion is the conceptualization of the ideal learner in AI-assisted translation, a reflective, autonomous, and ethically aware individual who engages with AI as a partner in cognitive and moral development. Building on this, the study proposes pedagogical strategies that integrate AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and teacher training to foster critical thinking and responsible AI use in sustainable translation education.

abstract_text: Employers increasingly deploy artificial-intelligence systems that read employee sentiment from written communication, infer exhaustion from calendar and workload digital exhaust, and flag individuals as at elevated risk of burnout — tools marketed under the language of care rather than control. This paper develops a conceptual model of how AI-mediated wellbeing monitoring reshapes psychological safety, the shared belief that a work environment is safe for interpersonal risk-taking on which voice, dissent and error reporting depend. Integrating psychological-safety theory, the algorithmic-management and workplace-surveillance literatures, and organisational voice research, the paper argues that wellbeing-monitoring intensity depresses psychological safety principally through a mediating perception of surveillance threat, and that this relationship is not fixed but is conditioned by the transparency of the monitoring system, the degree to which employees attribute developmental rather than punitive intent to it, and whether a human manager mediates between algorithmic output and managerial action. Five propositions specify these relationships, including a boundary condition for India's IT-BPM sector, where the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 supplies a general consent-and-purpose-limitation framework but no sector-specific rule for wellbeing analytics, leaving adoption norms to be set informally inside a high-attrition, always-on operating environment. The paper closes with implications for the design of psychologically safe monitoring architectures and an agenda for empirical validation.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping foreign language education, yet the psychological processes underlying effective learner–AI interaction remain fragmented. This theory-building systematic review synthesizes empirical evidence on metacognition, trust, and human–AI co-regulation in GenAI-supported foreign language learning. Following PRISMA 2020 procedures, web of science and Scopus were searched for studies published from 2022 to June 2026. After screening, 51 empirical studies were included. The findings show that metacognition shapes learners’ planning, monitoring, regulation, and reflection; trust influences how learners accept, verify, modify, or reject AI-generated information and feedback; and human–AI co-regulation involves the dynamic distribution of cognitive and regulatory activity between learners and GenAI within teacher-mediated instructional contexts. AI literacy and learner agency further support critical evaluation, strategic AI use, and retention of human decision-making responsibility. Based on these findings, the review develops the metacognition–trust–co-regulation (MTC) framework, which conceptualizes effective GenAI-assisted learning as an iterative process in which metacognitive regulation informs trust, trust calibrates reliance, and reliance shapes human–AI co-regulation. The framework positions GenAI as a cognitive partner whose educational value depends on critically informed, metacognitively regulated, and humanly governed use.

analysis.discussion: This systematic review examined the psychological processes through which learners engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in foreign language education. Drawing on 51 empirical studies, it moved beyond whether GenAI improves particular language skills to examine how learners understand, evaluate, regulate, and coordinate their interactions with generative systems. Metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation emerged as interconnected mechanisms underlying GenAI-mediated learning, while AI literacy and learner agency functioned as enabling conditions. The findings conceptualize learning with GenAI as adaptive human-AI partnership. Metacognition supports goal setting, monitoring of AI contributions, evaluation, and subsequent regulation. Trust calibration shapes decisions about whether AI-generated information or feedback should be accepted, verified, modified, or rejected. Human-AI co-regulation captures the distribution and coordination of cognitive and regulatory work between learners and AI. These mechanisms are neither discrete nor strictly sequential; rather, they form a dynamic system in which metacognitive evaluation informs trust and reliance, reliance shapes cognitive distribution, and interaction outcomes provide new information for subsequent regulation. The educational value of GenAI therefore depends less on its capacity to generate language, provide feedback, or perform cognitive tasks than on how learners incorporate these affordances into their regulatory activity. GenAI can augment learning when learners retain responsibility for planning, evaluation, judgment, and reflection. When these functions are increasingly delegated to AI, assistance may become cognitive substitution, potentially weakening independent engagement and learner control. Productive augmentation and problematic dependence thus depend primarily on how cognitive and regulatory responsibility is organized. The Metacognition-Trust-Co-Regulation (MTC) Framework integrates these processes into a unified theoretical account. It explains how cognitive activity can be distributed between learners and AI while preserving human agency as the organizing principle of learning. AI literacy and learner agency are conceptualized not as additional MTC mechanisms but as enabling conditions that help learners understand GenAI's capabilities and limitations, calibrate reliance, and retain ownership of learning. The framework therefore provides a basis for explaining variation in psychological and learning outcomes, including autonomy, motivation, confidence, engagement, cognitive load, feedback literacy, and agency. The principal contribution of this review is to specify the psychological conditions under which GenAI becomes educationally productive, rather than characterizing it as inherently beneficial or detrimental. This perspective shifts attention from evaluating GenAI primarily as an instructional technology toward understanding how learners regulate its use while preserving the cognitive activities through which learning occurs. Future research should empirically test the MTC Framework across learner populations, language tasks, educational settings, and GenAI systems. Longitudinal, experimental, and processsensitive designs are needed to examine whether the proposed relationships among metacognition, trust, and co-regulation remain robust across contexts and over time. Research should also identify when human-AI cognitive partnerships enhance learning without displacing essential cognitive and regulatory activities. The central challenge for GenAI-enhanced foreign language education is not how much learning can be delegated to AI, but how AI can be integrated while preserving and strengthening learners' capacity to think, evaluate, regulate, and act independently.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify the interpretation of the findings. The 51 studies varied substantially in participants, research designs, learning contexts, AI applications, and operationalization's of psychological constructs, which limits direct comparison across studies. Moreover, the evidence base is relatively recent and rapidly evolving; findings associated with particular GenAI systems may therefore change as technologies and patterns of use develop. The review has methodological limitations related to its singleauthor design. Screening, full-text assessment, and thematic coding were conducted by the sole author without independent reviewer or coder verification, which may have introduced selection or interpretive bias despite the use of a structured coding framework and documented screening decisions. No formal risk-of-bias appraisal was conducted, reflecting the theory-building focus and methodological heterogeneity of the included studies. The database coverage also represents a limitation. Although Web of Science and Scopus provided broad multidisciplinary coverage, PsycINFO and ERIC were not searched. Future reviews should incorporate education and psychology-specific databases to broaden coverage and reduce potential database-related selection bias. Overall, the MTC Framework should be viewed as a theory-generating account that requires further empirical validation. The evidence also relied substantially on self-reports, interviews, surveys, and relatively short-term interventions. Although these approaches provide valuable insights into learners' perceptions and experiences, they may not fully capture how metacognitive regulation, trust calibration, and cognitive redistribution unfold during actual learner-AI interaction. Future research should therefore incorporate more longitudinal and process-sensitive approaches, including interaction logs, prompt histories, revision records, think-aloud protocols, and screen-based observation. Further research should examine how learner proficiency, prior AI experience, AI literacy, metacognitive ability, task complexity, instructional design, and teacher mediation shape MTC processes. In particular, the proposed framework requires empirical testing. Longitudinal, experimental, and mixed-methods research could examine whether metacognitive engagement is associated with trust calibration, whether calibrated reliance is associated with particular forms of co-regulation, and whether these processes are subsequently related to language-learning and psychological outcomes.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has diffused through higher education faster than the structures meant to govern it, yet acceptance research still treats adoption as a terminal outcome rather than as an event embedded in students&#39; self-regulation. This study extends the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) by specifying metacognitive awareness (META) and self-regulated learning (SRL) as mediators between the four UTAUT determinants and behavioural intention (BI), and BI predicts self-reported use of GenAI as a cognitive partner (AU). Responses from 451 students at seven Thai Rajabhat universities were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM; SmartPLS 4; 10,000 bootstrap subsamples). Internal consistency was very high (above .95 for six of eight constructs), indicating partial item redundancy, and discriminant validity was supported under HTMT.90. Facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, showed the strongest associations with META (&beta; = .595) and SRL (&beta; = .514) but no significant direct association with intention (&beta; = .061, p = .430); their only significant indirect association with intention ran through META (&beta; = .186), a pattern consistent with indirect-only mediation. Social influence was the strongest direct predictor of intention (&beta; = .357), followed by META (&beta; = .312); effort expectancy and SRL did not predict intention. The model explained 62.1% to 70.9% of endogenous variance and showed out-of-sample predictive relevance. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design and full-collinearity diagnostics indicating possible common-method variance, the findings are interpreted as associations compatible with, but not establishing, the proposed mechanisms.

The design is appropriate for theory extension in which a well-established nomological network is augmented with new mediating constructs, and for the estimation of a complex model containing eight latent variables and forty indicators. Because all constructs were measured at a single time point from a single source, the directional paths represent theoretically specified orderings rather than empirically established causal precedence. Path coefficients and indirect effects are therefore interpreted throughout as model-implied associations, and a significant indirect effect is described as consistent with mediation rather than as evidence that the mediator is the causal mechanism (Maxwell & Cole, 2007; Spector, 2019) . The target population comprised students in higher education at Rajabhat universities in Thailand, the network of public institutions established to serve regional populations. The sample consisted of 451 students enrolled at seven of these universities: Udon Thani Rajabhat University, Rajabhat Maha Sarakham University, Sakon Nakhon Rajabhat University, Roi Et Rajabhat University, Phuket Rajabhat University, Thepsatri Rajabhat University and Surat Thani Rajabhat University. reading.interpretation: This study asked whether the adoption of generative AI by university students is better understood as a function of expectations about the tool or as a function of learners' regulation of themselves. The pattern of associations is more consistent with the second reading, although with an asymmetry that is theoretically more interesting than a clean confirmation would have been, and with the caveat that a cross-sectional design can show consistency with, but not the direction of, these relationships. Generative AI has been absorbed into undergraduate study with a speed that has left institutions responding to a practice they did not design. This study suggests that the institutional lever that remains available may be guidance rather than access. Among 451 students at seven Thai regional public universities, facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, had no significant direct association with intention to use generative AI, yet were by a considerable margin the strongest correlate of the metacognitive awareness and self-regulation that students reported, and were associated with intention only indirectly, through metacognitive awareness. Social influence, meanwhile, was the strongest direct correlate of intention. If these associations reflect causal processes, which longitudinal and experimental research must establish, students may be carried into generative AI use by the people around them and equipped for it, if at all, by their institutions. The theoretical implication is that acceptance models built for organisational software may require mechanistic revision before they can carry explanatory weight in education, where use is never the terminal outcome of interest and where the same behaviour may be either a pa
reading.limitations: Several limitations qualify these findings and, in each case, indicate a specific next step. Design and causality. The data are cross-sectional and self-reported, so the mediation results establish statistical consistency with the hypothesised mechanism rather than causal precedence, and alternative orderings, in which intention and use foster metacognitive awareness and self-regulation, fit the same data equally well (Maxwell & Cole, 2007; Spector, 2019) . The causal vocabulary of UTAUT (determinants, effects) is used in this article to name model positions, not to claim causal effects. The substitution interpretation advanced in Section 5.3 in particular requires longitudinal or experimental evidence. Experience-sampling or trace-based designs that capture regulation during GenAI-mediated study, as advocated by Molenaar (2022b) , would allow the temporal ordering of regulation and use to be observed rather than assumed.
