The target population comprised students in higher education at Rajabhat universities in Thailand, the network of public institutions established to serve regional populations. The sample consisted of 451 students enrolled at seven of these universities: Udon Thani Rajabhat University, Rajabhat Maha Sarakham University, Sakon Nakhon Rajabhat University, Roi Et Rajabhat University, Phuket Rajabhat University, Thepsatri Rajabhat University and Surat Thani Rajabhat University. Prior experience of using GenAI tools for learning was an inclusion criterion, screened by a filter item at the start of the questionnaire; respondents indicating no experience were routed out and are not included in the 451. Sampling was purposive with voluntary participation. The realised sample substantially exceeds the minimum required for the most complex regressed construct in the model: with six predictors of behavioural intention, an anticipated effect size of f 2 = .15, α = .05 and power = .95, G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009) indicates a minimum of 146 cases, and the inverse-square-root rule for PLS-SEM (Hair et al., 2022) indicates approximately 155 cases for the smallest expected path coefficient of .20. The distribution of the sample across gender, year of study, duration and frequency of GenAI use, and preferred tool is reported in Table 1 . Two thirds of respondents were in their first or second year of study, and three quarters had been using GenAI for six months or longer, so the sample is weighted towards students who encountered these tools early in their programme rather than adopting them late. Because all data derive from a single self-report instrument, procedural and statistical remedies were applied. Procedurally, respondent anonymity was guaranteed, no right answers were implied, and predictor and criterion items were separated in the questionnaire (Podsakoff et al., 2003) . Statistically, the full collinearity assessment recommended by Kock (2015) was applied, in which the variance inflation factor of every construct is computed against all remaining constructs; values above 3.3 are taken as a warning sign of possible common method bias (Kock, 2015; Podsakoff et al., 2012) . The results, which are not unambiguous, are reported and discussed in Section 4.3 together with the inner-model collinearity diagnostics. Inner-model collinearity was assessed before the path coefficients were interpreted. In the equations for metacognitive awareness and self-regulated learning, variance inflation factors for the four exogenous predictors ranged from 2.68 (PE) to 3.79 (EE). In the behavioural intention equation, which contains six predictors, they ranged from 2.73 (PE) to 4.86 (SRL), with FC at 4.30 and META at 3.75. Every value therefore falls below the critical threshold of five above which Hair et al. (2019) regard structural estimates as compromised, but several exceed the more conservative benchmark of 3.3 proposed by Kock and Lynn (2012) and none attains the ideal of three. Estimates for the more strongly collinear predictors, and for SRL in particular, should accordingly be read as less stable than those for PE and META. The full collinearity procedure of Kock (2015) returned values between 2.76 (PE) and 4.96 (SRL), with FC at 4.33, AU at 4.21, META at 4.18, SI at 4.11, BI at 3.98 and EE at 3.89. Seven of the eight constructs therefore exceed the 3.3 criterion, and the model does not clear this test of common method bias. We report this without minimising it, and offer three considerations rather than a dismissal. First, the criterion is conservative in models with substantial construct correlations, because it cannot distinguish method-induced covariance from the theoretically expected covariance of proximal constructs; here META and SRL correlate at .841 and BI and AU at .833 for reasons the theory predicts. Second, the indicator redundancy documented in Section 4.1 inflates construct correlations independently of any shared method, so the two diagnostics are not independent of one another. Third, the pattern of results is not what uniform method inflation alone would be expected to produce: six of the fifteen structural paths are non-significant, one carries a negative sign, and the effect sizes are widely dispersed, whereas a dataset dominated by common method variance typically yields uniformly positive and significant estimates. These considerations are, however, arguments rather than tests. The present design cannot distinguish substantive covariance from covariance produced by shared measurement processes, so the magnitudes of the structural coefficients, including the intention-use path, should be treated cautiously and may be inflated by common-method variance (Podsakoff et al., 2012) . A marker-variable or unmeasured latent method construct design is recommended for replication (Podsakoff et al., 2003) .
analysis.discussion: This study asked whether the adoption of generative AI by university students is better understood as a function of expectations about the tool or as a function of learners' regulation of themselves. The pattern of associations is more consistent with the second reading, although with an asymmetry that is theoretically more interesting than a clean confirmation would have been, and with the caveat that a cross-sectional design can show consistency with, but not the direction of, these relationships. Generative AI has been absorbed into undergraduate study with a speed that has left institutions responding to a practice they did not design. This study suggests that the institutional lever that remains available may be guidance rather than access. Among 451 students at seven Thai regional public universities, facilitating conditions, operationalised largely as perceived institutional guidance and support, had no significant direct association with intention to use generative AI, yet were by a considerable margin the strongest correlate of the metacognitive awareness and self-regulation that students reported, and were associated with intention only indirectly, through metacognitive awareness. Social influence, meanwhile, was the strongest direct correlate of intention. If these associations reflect causal processes, which longitudinal and experimental research must establish, students may be carried into generative AI use by the people around them and equipped for it, if at all, by their institutions. The theoretical implication is that acceptance models built for organisational software may require mechanistic revision before they can carry explanatory weight in education, where use is never the terminal outcome of interest and where the same behaviour may be either a partnership or a substitution. The practical implication is narrower and more actionable: the question worth asking of any institutional AI initiative is not whether it increases use, which will increase regardless, but whether it increases the proportion of use in which the student is still doing the thinking.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify these findings and, in each case, indicate a specific next step. Design and causality. The data are cross-sectional and self-reported, so the mediation results establish statistical consistency with the hypothesised mechanism rather than causal precedence, and alternative orderings, in which intention and use foster metacognitive awareness and self-regulation, fit the same data equally well (Maxwell & Cole, 2007; Spector, 2019) . The causal vocabulary of UTAUT (determinants, effects) is used in this article to name model positions, not to claim causal effects. The substitution interpretation advanced in Section 5.3 in particular requires longitudinal or experimental evidence. Experience-sampling or trace-based designs that capture regulation during GenAI-mediated study, as advocated by Molenaar (2022b) , would allow the temporal ordering of regulation and use to be observed rather than assumed.

title: Exploring Digital Competence Configurations and Attention Performance Through fsQCA and Machine Learning

abstract_text: Digital competence among bank employees is an increasingly critical determinant of task efficiency in technology-driven financial service environments. In this study, a hybrid analytical approach is used that combines Fuzzy-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) with ten machine learning (ML) classifiers. The combination of these two approaches is designed to predict the Focused vs. Distracted attention status of bank employees based on multimodal behavioural and digital interaction features during task execution. The dataset included 1,000 observations of bank employees, capturing head orientation, facial expression, gaze direction, micro-movements, application usage, notification interruptions, and task completion time during digital work sessions. There was a marked imbalance in the class distribution with 91.2% of bank employees categorized as Distracted and 8.8% of bank employees categorized as Focused, which was consistent with the actual prevalence of digital distraction in professional banking environments. The LightGBM model performed best with all the classifiers, with an accuracy score of 98.9%, an AUC of 0.9998, and an F1 score of 0.989. Random Forest and XGBoost followed closely with an AUC of 0.9996 and 0.9995, respectively. The top 3 explainable features identified by SHAP analysis were Head Orientation, Facial Expression and Micro-Movements. The necessity analysis using the fsQCA method confirmed that forward gaze (consistency = 0.97), straight head posture (0.94) and neutral facial expression (0.99) are almost necessary conditions for focused attention. The results provide actionable insights for intelligent workforce management systems, adaptive digital workplace platforms, and real-time employee performance monitoring systems in banking and financial service organizations.

title: Generative AI Use, Self-Regulated Learning, and Creativity Among Indonesian Design Students
preview: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in design education, yet whether its use supports or substitutes for the self-directed creative process remains unclear, particularly outside the Chinese samples that dominate prior research. abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in design education, yet whether its use supports or substitutes for the self-directed creative process remains unclear, particularly outside the Chinese samples that dominate prior research. This study examined whether self-regulated learning (SRL) mediates the relationship between generative AI use and creativity among Indonesian design students. Data were collected through an online questionnaire from 120 Indonesian visual communication design students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped confidence intervals and four pre-specified sensitivity analyses. SRL was strongly and consistently associated with creativity (β = .674, f² = .962), and this association remained stable across all robustness checks. AI usage's relationships with SRL, with creativity directly, and with creativity indirectly through SRL were significant in the full sample but lost significance under two independent sensitivity analyses;. However, the sample was adequately powered to detect these effect sizes (post-hoc power ≥ .91); treat the point estimates as preliminary and confirm them in a larger, independent sample before treating them as established. A supplementary analysis found that frequency of AI use, unlike a richer measure of how AI was used, was unrelated to SRL or creativity. SRL is a robust correlate of creativity in AI-assisted design education, while AI use's own contribution requires replication; design pedagogy may be better served by cultivating self-regulation directly than by monitoring AI usage frequency alone. Keywords: generative AI, self-regulated learning, creativity, design education, PLS-SEM.

abstract_text: This study aims to examine the effects of generative AI dependency and digital multitasking habits on the quality of self-regulated learning (SRL) among university students, both individually and jointly. The study employed a quantitative approach involving 300 active students from five study programs at the Purwakarta Campus of Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia, who were selected through purposive sampling. Data were collected using four-point Likert-scale instruments that met established validity and reliability criteria. The data were analyzed using multiple linear regression, preceded by classical assumption tests for normality, linearity, multicollinearity, and heteroscedasticity. The results indicated that generative AI dependency was positively and significantly associated with SRL (B = 0.213, p = .004), as was digital multitasking (B = 0.178, p = .009). Simultaneously, both predictors were significantly associated with students’ SRL, F = 27.843, p < .001, and the regression model explained 15.8% of the variance in SRL. These findings suggest that, within the context of this study, moderate levels of generative AI use and digital multitasking did not substantially undermine students’ self-regulatory capacity. Rather than restricting generative AI use, higher education institutions should provide structured guidance on effective AI engagement, including prompt formulation strategies and reflective evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and integrate such guidance into learning task design. Such an approach may help ensure that students’ interaction with generative AI strengthens rather than substitutes for their self-regulatory capacity.

analysis.discussion: This study found that generative AI dependency and digital multitasking habits exert a positive and significant influence on the self-regulated learning (SRL) of students at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia Purwakarta Campus, both partially and simultaneously. Statistically, this is evidenced by t-test significance values of 0.004 for X1 and 0.009 for X2, along with an F-value of 27.843 with a significance level of < 0.001 in the initial hypothesis predicting negative effects, as reported in a number of prior studies (Costanzo, 2024; Georgiou, 2025; Parry & Le Roux, 2021; Suryanto et al., 2025). Rather than undermining the analysis, this unexpected finding opens a richer conversation about how digitally native students navigate technology within learning processes. The positive influence of generative AI dependency on SRL can be understood by examining how students actually engage with these tools. Not all forms of AI use reflect a dependency that weakens self-regulatory capacity. Many students employ AI strategically as a tool for planning their study sessions, organizing course material or clarifying concepts they find difficult to grasp, This type of purposeful use supports the planning and time management and task strategies dimensions of SRL (Xu et al., 2025). In this sense, AI can function as cognitive scaffolding that facilitates, rather than replaces, students’ self-regulatory processes (Liu, 2026). (Budiani et al., 2020) found that students with higher levels of self- efficacy tend to use AI in a more autonomous and independent manner, such that dependency does not automatically undermine self-directed learning instead the two can coexist. (Lund et al., 2025) similarly found that students exercise critical awareness when using AI for academic purposes, particularly regarding plagiarism risks, with the majority viewing AI- generated paper writing as a serious form of academic misconduct. (Xia et al., 2024) further note that generative AI carries broad pedagogical potential, not simply as a technical aid but as a medium for transforming assessment and fostering self-regulated learning in higher A similar pattern emerges with digital multitasking habits. Students who are accustomed to using multiple digital platform simultaneously appear to have developed a degree of cognitive flexibility that enables them to sustain self-directed learning even in distraction-heavy environments (Nakhostin-Khayyat et al., 2024). (Deng et al., 2024) also Copyright © 2026, The Author(s) 1322 Jurnal Penelitian dan Pengembangan Pendidikan Vol. 13 No. 4 : October 2026 https://e-journal.undikma.ac.id/index.php/pedagogy/index E-ISSN: 2722-4627 Email:paedagogy@undikma.ac.id pp. 1317-1327 established that the relationship between digital multitasking and learning is not straightforward, as motivational factors and self-regulatory strategies prove more determinative of learning quality than multitasking behavior per se. Within this context, the reasonably adequate SRL levels observed among Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia Purwakarta Campus students likely function as a buffer that mitigates the negative effects of digital multitasking, which would explain why both variables appear to trend positively alongside one another. (Guntur & Purnomo, 2024) further found that self-regulated learning plays a critical role in the success and adaptability of learners across varied digital learning conditions, affirming that students with strong self-regulatory capacities are better prepared to deal with distractions and sustain their learning strategies even in distraction-rich digital That said, these findings warrant careful interpretation, as the dimensional-level descriptive analysis presented in Table 1b reveals a more complex and layered picture. Dimensions rooted in self-perception, intrinsic motivation (M = 3.21) and online self-efficacy (M = 3.08), yielded the highest mean scores across all SRL dimensions. In contrast, dimensions reflecting more concrete cognitive regulatory behavior were notably lower, including effort regulation (M = 2.61), metacognition (M = 2.76), and planning and time management (M = 2.87), while task strategies (M = 2.84) fell in between. This suggests that while students feel motivated and academically confident, their capacity to sustain effort, monitor their own thinking, and plan their learning concretely remains comparatively weaker. This pattern is consistent with concerns about metacognitive laziness, a condition in which students feel capable and motivated precisely because AI is supporting them, yet unknowingly reduce their own active metacognitive engagement in the process. The result is an illusion of competence that does not fully reflect genuine self-regulatory ability. Parry & Le Roux, (2021) similarly caution that the effect of digital technology on cognition are often inconsistent and highly dependent on how the technology is used, not merely how frequently. Zimmerman, (2002) framework helps illuminate this pattern more deeply. SRL is conceptualized as an interconnected three phase cycle comprising forethought, performance, and self-reflection. The high scores on intrinsic motivation and online self-efficacy suggest that students’ forethought phase is relatively strong, they enter learning situations with adequate goal orientation and self-belief. However, the weaknesses observed in metacognition and effort regulation point to gaps in the performance and self-reflection phases, where students are not yet optimally monitoring and evaluating their own learning in an active and ongoing way. This underscores the importance of external metacognitive support, including the guided use of technology, in bridging the gaps between SRL phases (Xu et al., 2025). This affirms that SRL is a multidimensional and complex construct that cannot be adequately explained by two technological variables alone. (Luo & Zhou, 2024), in their systematic review, found that SRL in blended learning environments is shaped by a constellation of factors simultaneously, including instructional design, pedagogical support, learning styles, and individual student characteristics. title: The Prisoner's Dilemma of AI: Cognitive Offloading Among Future Mathematics Teachers

abstract_text: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into education has introduced substantial opportunities as well as challenges related to students’ cognitive processes and professional development. For pre-service teachers, generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) creates a professional paradox. While AI systems can increase efficiency, support learning processes, and provide rapid access to information, excessive reliance on such systems may lead to cognitive offloading, automation bias, and gradual weakening of critical thinking and professional autonomy. Within educational contexts, this tension may be interpreted as a conflict between short-term individual gains and long-term consequences for human expertise and independent reasoning. This study compares pretest and posttest perceptions of generative AI among first-year pre-service mathematics teachers following a targeted educational intervention focused on principles of AI functioning and related cognitive risks. The Prisoner's Dilemma is used as a conceptual and pedagogical lens for framing the tension between the immediate benefits of AI use and its possible long-term educational consequences; it is not empirically operationalised or tested as a game-theoretic model. Within this framework, delegating cognitive activities to AI may represent a rational strategy at the individual level while simultaneously producing undesirable outcomes for broader educational development. A quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design without a control group was employed. Participants consisted of undergraduate students enrolled in a Mathematics Teacher Education programme at the University of Ostrava (pretest n = 18; posttest n = 14). Data collection was conducted using a semantic differential instrument consisting of sixteen bipolar dimensions measuring students’ perceptions of AI characteristics. The intervention included instructional activities explaining principles of large language models, cognitive offloading, automation bias, and ethical implications of excessive dependence on AI systems. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and non-parametric methods, specifically the Mann–Whitney U test. The results did not reveal statistically significant differences between pretest and posttest measurements across any of the analysed dimensions. Several mean scores differed descriptively between the measurements, particularly for transparency, predictability, and the role of AI in deeper learning, but these differences were not statistically significant. Given the small, unmatched samples and the absence of a control group, they cannot be interpreted as evidence of an intervention effect. These results highlight the importance of integrating critical AI literacy into teacher education programmes.

abstract_text: ABSTRACT. Digital technologies have become inseparable from university learning, particularly in English as a foreign language (EFL), where students regularly use smartphones, learning management systems, dictionaries, social media, artificial intelligence tools, video platforms, and messaging applications. The same digital environment, however, can interrupt sustained attention and lead to off-task switching, notification checking, social-media browsing, and simultaneous use of several applications. This article examines the influence of digital distraction on university students' English learning through an integrative review of recent international studies and research conducted in the context of Uzbekistan. The analysis focuses on attention, vocabulary acquisition, reading and listening comprehension, speaking practice, learner autonomy, self-regulation, and academic performance. The review demonstrates that digital tools can strengthen access to authentic English-language input and individualized practice, but their benefits decrease when educational use is combined with uncontrolled multitasking and frequent non-academic interruptions. Evidence from meta-analyses indicates a small but consistent negative association between problematic smartphone use and academic learning, while experimental research reports stronger negative effects on immediate recall when learners switch between study and mobile-phone activities (1, 2, 3). Uzbek studies, in turn, emphasize the pedagogical value of digital resources, AI tools, and mobile applications, while also identifying insufficient digital-pedagogical competence, weak self-regulation, and distraction as emerging challenges in higher education (4, 5, 6). The article proposes a balanced model of digital English learning based on purposeful technology use, notification management, task segmentation, guided mobile learning, and metacognitive self-control.

abstract_text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the market-organizing infrastructures that coordinate exchange, reshaping consumer information environments and the allocation of economic value. Drawing on marketing systems theory and consumer emancipation scholarship, we theorize perceived misinformation threat and perceived automation inequality as system-level diagnostics that erode perceived democratic performance and, through it, consumers’ perceived economic wellbeing. We further theorize national AI interpretive climates as contextual amplifiers that condition how threat cues translate into institutional skepticism or optimism. A multilevel analysis across 22 nations supports the institutional-confidence pathway and the amplifying role of collective AI beliefs. By repositioning AI from firm-level tool to structural infrastructure, the study clarifies how AI-driven market externalities become consequential for consumer welfare, advancing macromarketing theory on emancipation, marketing governance, consumer agency, and public policy in AI-mediated markets.

abstract_text: Smoking cessation remains a complex self-regulatory challenge, often undermined by cue-triggered cravings arising from habitual, emotional, and social contexts. Existing wearable cessation systems are largely reactive, detecting smoking events only after lapses occur and thus missing the critical window for timely intervention. Guided by cue-reactivity theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT), we argue that future digital health systems should shift from retrospective feedback toward proactive craving management that supports user autonomy and competence. To inform the design of such systems, we present a formative pilot qualitative study involving semi-structured interviews with 10 smokers and ex-smokers from a multi-ethnic Asian population, a demographic underrepresented in current wearable AI and smoking cessation research. Through an iterative co-design interview process, we examine (1) the barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation and (2) the desired design features of wearable systems targeting cravings before lapses occur. Our findings identify key craving predictors across habitual, emotional, and social dimensions, alongside user-preferred intervention strategies such as social accountability, personalized support, rewards, and just-in-time distraction techniques. Participants also emphasized the importance of trust, privacy, personalization, and non-judgmental interaction styles. These insights directly inform the design of AURA, a novel smartwatch-smartphone ecosystem for proactive craving detection and intervention using commercially available wearable devices.

reading.methods: The design of our interview protocol and proposed system is grounded in established psychological theories of smoking behavior and behavior change. First, cue-reactivity theory suggests that smoking-related environmental or internal cues can automatically evoke craving responses through learned associations formed over repeated smoking episodes. These cues may include stress, specific locations, social situations, or habitual daily routines. Once triggered, cravings can rapidly override long-term intentions to quit, increasing relapse risk. Second, Self-Determination Theory (SDT) provides a strong framework for understanding sustained cessation behavior. SDT posits that long-term behavior change is more likely when interventions support the psychological needs of autonomy, competence, and relatedness. In the smoking cessation context, autonomous motivation-quitting because it aligns with personal values and goals-has been shown to predict more durable abstinence than externally imposed pressure [38] . This theoretical perspective directly informs our system design philosophy: rather than delivering prescriptive alerts, the wearable should empower users with awareness, personalized choices, and supportive interventions that reinforce intrinsic motivation. Additionally, elements of Social Cognitive Theory, particularly self-efficacy and outcome expectancy, inform our interview questions regarding trust, perceived usefulness, and confidence in managing cravings [37] . reading.interpretation: In this section, we discuss several implications of the qualitative results and resulting themes garnered from the pilot study. Smoking cessation remains a complex behavioral challenge, where spontaneous cue-triggered cravings frequently overpower long-term intentions. Our pilot study illuminates the subtle nuances in addiction management, revealing clusters across emotional, social and contextual domains, as well as various commonly used intervention types. Crucially, participants emphasized that proactive health wearables should be deeply personalized, protective of user privacy, highly accurate, and empowering rather than dictating user agency. This qualitative pilot study represents a first step toward ubiquitous, user-centered cessation management systems. We intend on experimenting with different configurations of AURA-incorporating various themes identified in the current study-in a high-fidelity setting on a wide range of users, including even those not inclined towards technological solutions, to fully assess its capabilities. In addition, a critical limitation of our qualitative study is the lack of female users, due to difficulties in recruitment and a significantly higher prevalence of male smokers. We intend on employing snowball sampling in future studies, which is often used to reach under-represented and hard-to-reach samples.

A comprehensive overview of all the frameworks used in constructing the interview questions are in Appendix 1. In this section, we detail the methodology of our study. The ethics statement for our pilot study is presented in Appendix A. A total of 10 participants were recruited for this pilot study. All participants were male and ranged in age from 19 to 60 years (M = 32.9, SD = 12.6). The sample comprised participants from diverse ethnic backgrounds, including five Chinese, two Malay, one Caucasian, and two participants of other ethnicities. In terms of nationality, the cohort included three Singaporeans, four Indonesians, and three Chinese nationals. Educational attainment varied across participants: three held a Master's degree, four held a Bachelor's degree, and three had completed high school or junior college education. Monthly income levels were distributed as follows: one participant reported an income between SGD 6,000-10,000, two between SGD 4,000-6,000, and the remaining participants below SGD 4,000. Regarding smoking status, six participants were active smokers and four were ex-smokers. Ex-smokers are interviewed for their insight on successful smoking cessation. Smoking histories varied substantially, ranging from 4 to 53 years, with average cigarette consumption ranging from 1 to 60 cigarettes per day. Among active smokers, current motivation to quit smoking was measured on a 10-point scale, yielding a mean score of 4.0 (SD = 2.45). Studies such as [1] have shown that smoking behavior is highly affected by variables that we collected such as ethnic background, residential place, income level, and education level. This diversity in smoking history, socioeconomic background, and ethnicity is desirable to better capture barriers and facilitators to smoking cessation within a multi-ethnic Asian context. Participants were recruited through purposive convenience sampling via announcements distributed across multiple online communities using WhatsApp and Telegram. analysis.discussion: In this section, we discuss several implications of the qualitative results and resulting themes garnered from the pilot study. Smoking cessation remains a complex behavioral challenge, where spontaneous cue-triggered cravings frequently overpower long-term intentions. Our pilot study illuminates the subtle nuances in addiction management, revealing clusters across emotional, social and contextual domains, as well as various commonly used intervention types. Crucially, participants emphasized that proactive health wearables should be deeply personalized, protective of user privacy, highly accurate, and empowering rather than dictating user agency. This qualitative pilot study represents a first step toward ubiquitous, user-centered cessation management systems. We intend on experimenting with different configurations of AURA-incorporating various themes identified in the current study-in a high-fidelity setting on a wide range of users, including even those not inclined towards technological solutions, to fully assess its capabilities. In addition, a critical limitation of our qualitative study is the lack of female users, due to difficulties in recruitment and a significantly higher prevalence of male smokers. We intend on employing snowball sampling in future studies, which is often used to reach under-represented and hard-to-reach samples.

title: Artificial Intelligence as Cognitive Scaffolding for Executive Functioning in Students with Special Educational Needs
venue: Journal of Educational Technology and E-Learning Innovations
preview: Executive functioning enables learners to organize work, monitor progress, and decide when a response needs revision. For some students with special educational needs, difficulties in these areas can restrict participation even when they understand the subject matter. abstract_text: Executive functioning enables learners to organize work, monitor progress, and decide when a response needs revision. For some students with special educational needs, difficulties in these areas can restrict participation even when they understand the subject matter. This critical narrative review considers whether artificial intelligence can reduce such barriers and, more importantly, what kind of support it actually provides. Research on executive functions, self-regulated learning, artificial intelligence in education, and special education was brought together to examine intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive platforms, planning tools, learning analytics, conversational agents, and generative AI. Across this literature, a recurring distinction emerges. Some applications compensate for an executive demand, others scaffold performance while a task is being completed, and a smaller group are designed to foster strategies that learners can later use without the tool. These outcomes should not be treated as equivalent. Completing a task successfully with automated prompts does not, by itself, demonstrate lasting improvement in executive functioning. AI may nevertheless be useful when support is tied to a clearly defined learning goal, interpreted by a teacher, and adjusted or faded in response to the learner’s progress. Its use also raises practical concerns about cognitive offloading, inaccurate feedback, privacy, bias, and unequal access. The review proposes a three-function framework - compensation, scaffolding, and development - for planning and evaluating AI-supported practice.

reading.methods: This study used a critical narrative review. This design was selected because the relevant evidence spans cognitive psychology, self-regulated learning, educational technology, and special education and includes theoretical papers, reviews, meta-analyses, empirical studies, and scholarly books. Narrative synthesis is suitable for integrating conceptually diverse evidence, provided that its interpretive character and limitations are made explicit (Baumeister & Leary, 1997; Ferrari, 2015) . The review was organized around three intersecting concepts: artificial intelligence in education, executive functioning or self-regulated learning, and special or inclusive education. Literature was identified through combinations of terms such as artificial intelligence in education, intelligent tutoring system, adaptive learning, generative artificial intelligence, executive function, self-regulated learning, special educational needs, learning disabilities, ADHD, and autism. Priority was given to peer-reviewed syntheses, influential conceptual works, and empirical research that clarified mechanisms relevant to planning, monitoring, attention regulation, information organization, and strategy use.
reading.findings: The reviewed literature supports a cautious interpretation of artificial intelligence as external cognitive scaffolding. Intelligent systems can structure tasks, make progress visible, provide immediate prompts, and adapt representations. These capabilities align with executive demands encountered by many students with special educational needs. They may also help teachers deliver timely differentiation that would otherwise be difficult to sustain. The available evidence does not justify broad claims that artificial intelligence improves executive functioning. Most relevant studies examine general learning outcomes, engagement, or platform use. Even when attention or planning appears to improve during tool use, three alternative explanations remain: the system may have reduced task difficulty, externally performed part of the executive work, or temporarily increased motivation. Direct executive-function measures, withdrawal phases, transfer tasks, and longer follow-up periods are needed to distinguish these possibilities.
reading.interpretation: Artificial-intelligence-supported tools can help students manage planning, monitoring, information organization, and other demands associated with executive functioning. Their most defensible role is as teachermediated cognitive support within inclusive educational environments. Improved task completion while a system is available should not be described as executive-function development unless independent performance, retention, or transfer has been demonstrated. The proposed three-function framework clarifies whether artificial intelligence is being used to compensate for a continuing barrier, scaffold current performance, or promote independent strategy use. This distinction can improve research design, educational decision-making, and the interpretation of outcomes. Artificial intelligence may contribute meaningfully to inclusive education when it strengthens access and agency, remains subject to human judgment, and is evaluated against clearly stated educational purposes.
reading.limitations: The narrative design does not permit an estimate of pooled effectiveness and remains more susceptible to selection and interpretive bias than a systematic review. The evidence base is also developing rapidly, and terminology varies across disciplines. Most importantly, many educational artificial-intelligence studies measure achievement, engagement, usability, or task completion rather than executive functions with validated instruments. Conclusions about executive-function development must therefore remain cautious.

title: Designing generative AI–powered reflective learning dashboards for enhancing self-regulated learning in higher education
preview: A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. abstract_text:
A reflective learning dashboard powered by generative artificial intelligence (AI) was developed to enhance self-regulated learning, student engagement, academic performance and learner perceptions in higher education. Grounded in learning analytics and generative feedback pedagogy, the system integrates behavioural data with AI-generated reflective dialogue to support continuous metacognitive development. Using a quasi-experimental design, 180 undergraduate students participated in a 12-week intervention comparing traditional instructor feedback with AI-generated reflective feedback. Quantitative results revealed significant improvements in self-regulated learning behaviours, time on task, login frequency and academic performance (p < .001), indicating strong effects on both cognitive and behavioural dimensions of learning. In addition, students reported high levels of perceived usefulness, trust, personalisation and positive attitudes towards AI-generated feedback, supported by qualitative insights highlighting increased motivation and learner agency. The findings demonstrate that combining generative AI with learning analytics transforms feedback into a dynamic, dialogic process that enhances reflective thinking and adaptive learning. This study contributes a scalable, human-centred and ethically grounded model for improving both learning outcomes and learner experience in digital education environments.
 
Implications for practice or policy:

University administrators should implement transparent AI dashboards ensuring ethics, privacy and accountability.
Educators can enhance reflective learning by integrating adaptive AI feedback that supports metacognitive development.
Policymakers should promote AI literacy and self-regulated learning within higher education frameworks.
Technology developers need to design user-centred and interpretable AI systems aligned with pedagogical objectives.
Higher education leaders should foster AI-supported reflection, professional development and evidence-based innovation for sustainable transformation.

title: Balancing AI-Driven Adaptation and Learner Self-Regulation: A Conceptual Framework for Enhancing Learning Outcomes in Generative AI-Supported Education
venue: Academic Journal of Research and Scientific Publishing
preview: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a d…
abstract_text: The rapid proliferation of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the potential for personalization, feedback, and immediate support within educational environments. Despite growing evidence of its ability to enhance certain learning outcomes, increased AI-driven support does not necessarily improve all cognitive and regulatory aspects; indeed, it may raise challenges regarding over-reliance and a decline in learner autonomy. This conceptual paper aims to develop a pedagogical framework to balance AI-driven adaptation with learner self-regulation in GenAI-supported educational settings. The framework was constructed based on an integrative analytical review of recent literature in the fields of GenAI in education, adaptive learning, self-regulated learning, and human-AI hybrid regulation. The framework proposes the concept of "Balanced AI–Learner Regulation," which structures the relationship across three graduated levels: AI-led regulation, co-regulation, and learner-led regulation. It also proposes the principle of "Adaptive Fading of AI Support," based on providing support according to need and then gradually reducing it as the learner’s capacity for independent self-regulation grows. The paper’s primary contribution lies in shifting the focus from maximizing GenAI usage to designing a pedagogical balance that preserves autonomy, self-regulation, and critical thinking alongside the improvement of academic performance.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 Artificial intelligence tools have permeated undergraduate academic life in India, yet their downstream cognitive and academic consequences remain poorly understood among rural students who adopt these tools in the absence of institutional guidance. Grounded in Extended Mind Theory and Cognitive Load Theory, this study develops and tests a sequential mediation model in which AI tool usage (AITU) influences academic performance perception (APP) through cognitive offloading behaviour (COB) and self-regulated learning behaviour (SRLB). Data were collected from 425 rural undergraduate students enrolled in government and private colleges in India. A three-stage analytical sequence, Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), and Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) with 2,000 bootstrapped resamples in SPSS 26 and AMOS 24, was employed. Harman's single-factor test confirmed that common method bias was not a dominant concern (single-factor variance = 38.40%, below the 50% threshold). The four-factor measurement model demonstrated acceptable fit (chi-square/df = 2.961, CFI = .925, RMSEA = .068). Structural results confirmed that AITU positively predicted COB (beta = .723, p < .001) and SRLB (beta = .586, p < .001), while SRLB significantly predicted APP (beta = .362, p < .001). The sequential AITU, COB, SRLB, APP indirect pathway was significant (p = .002, BC 95% CI excluding zero), while the COB, APP direct path was not robustly supported in bootstrap estimation. Multi-group SEM revealed that lower-performing students (academic score < 60%) exhibited a substantially stronger AITU, COB relationship (beta = .961) than their higher-performing peers (beta = .681), indicating differential vulnerability to AI-induced cognitive offloading. Findings suggest that unsupervised AI adoption elevates cognitive offloading, which erodes self-regulated learning and ultimately constrains academic performance perception, with academically weaker students disproportionately at risk. Institutions should integrate structured AI literacy curricula and metacognitive scaffolding to convert AI adoption from a convenience habit into a productive learning strategy.

abstract_text: This study investigates how generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can scaffold self-directed learning (SDL) in secondary classrooms. Focusing on the interaction between teacher facilitation and AI affordances, it examines and refines the Content–Response–AI&peers–Fusion–reflecT (CRAFT) framework as a practitioner-informed pedagogical scaffold for operationalizing aspects of the Process dimension of the Person–Process–Context (PPC) model. The study addresses a persistent gap between SDL theory and classroom practice by examining how learner agency can be cultivated within AI-supported learning environments. Adopting a qualitative multi-case study design, the research analyzed instructional practices, lesson artifacts, and reflective accounts from six experienced educators from a secondary school in Singapore across one academic year. Data were analyzed using a theoretically informed, hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis, enabling cross-case examination and iterative refinement of CRAFT in relation to the PPC model. Findings indicate that while generative AI supports goal setting, idea generation, and iterative feedback, the metacognitive and reflective dimensions of SDL remain underdeveloped without deliberate teacher mediation. Teachers remain critical orchestrators of AI and peer interactions, supporting disciplinary sense-making and learner autonomy rather than positioning AI as a standalone instructional aid. Overall, this study integrates a practitioner-informed and empirically refined pedagogical scaffold with an established theoretical model, offering a theoretically grounded, context-sensitive pedagogical guide for designing learning experiences that support opportunities for student agency.

abstract_text: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools into academic activities has raised concerns about its impact on students' core cognitive and linguistic skills. This study investigated the relationship between AI dependence and critical thinking and writing competence among English Language students. The study adopted a correlational research design. The population comprised English Language students, from which 492 students were selected using stratified random sampling technique. Data were collected using three validated instruments: AI Dependence Scale, Critical Thinking Disposition Scale and Writing Competence Scale. Mean and standard deviation were used to answer the research questions while Pearson Product-Moment Correlation (PPMC) was used to test the hypotheses at 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant inverse association between AI dependence and critical thinking, r(490) = -.38, p <.001, and between AI dependence and writing competence, r(490) = -.42, p <.001. This suggests that higher levels of AI dependence are associated with lower levels of critical thinking and writing competence. The study concluded that excessive dependence on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly and QuillBot is inversely associated with students' ability to analyze, evaluate and produce original written texts. While AI offers academic support, over-reliance weakens independent reasoning and writing skills.

abstract_text: Research on artificial intelligence (AI) and education has developed across largely separate domains, including learning outcomes, academic integrity, institutional governance, and lifelong-learning demand. This study integrates these domains through a common framework distinguishing cognitive augmentation, where AI supports human thinking, from cognitive offloading, where it substitutes for it. It synthesizes 2025–2026 evidence from the OECD, UNESCO, MIT, RAND Corporation, UC Berkeley, HEPI, Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, official Türkiye sources, and triangulated market data. PISA 2025 findings covering approximately 760,000 students across 91 countries and economies provide cross-national evidence: students who did not use AI to draft assignments outperformed those who did, while frequent users trained to critically evaluate AI-generated information performed better than those without such training. Additional evidence shows short-term AI-supported performance gains without equivalent retained learning, discipline-specific patterns of AI-assisted academic misconduct, rapidly increasing AI-generated coursework, and widespread teacher AI use despite limited formal governance. Türkiye is examined as a policy case linking economy-wide and education-specific AI strategies. Overall, the findings indicate that AI’s educational impact depends less on the technology itself than on pedagogical design, assessment redesign, and institutional governance capacity.

title: How YouTube Frames ChatGPT Use in Education: An Epistemic Network Analysis with Supporting Multimodal Metadata
preview: We examine educational YouTube videos through multimodal metadata, such as transcripts, titles, thumbnails, and viewer comments, to investigate how ChatGPT is framed across creator groups and how those framings relate to audience response and platform reach. Little is known about how large language models are presented to learners in informal, creator-driven public discourse. Following PRISMA, we selected 52 videos f…
abstract_text: We examine educational YouTube videos through multimodal metadata, such as transcripts, titles, thumbnails, and viewer comments, to investigate how ChatGPT is framed across creator groups and how those framings relate to audience response and platform reach. Little is known about how large language models are presented to learners in informal, creator-driven public discourse. Following PRISMA, we selected 52 videos for analysis. We identified three structurally distinct discourse groups: (G1) videos that positioned ChatGPT as a conceptual scaffold for thinking, (G2) videos oriented toward retrieval practice and skill-building, and (G3) videos that framed ChatGPT as a tool for output generation. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed statistically significant group differences with large effect sizes. Multimodal metadata consistently reflected these distinctions across transcript discourse, titles, and thumbnails. Viewers of learning-oriented content described ChatGPT as a thinking partner or tutor, whereas viewers of output-oriented content raised concerns about over-reliance, surface-level learning, and cognitive offloading. G3 achieved comparable platform reach to G2, yet with substantially weaker learning-oriented framing. This may suggest that output-oriented content competes for visibility despite lower pedagogical depth. These findings reveal a structural tension in self-directed AI learning: content that prioritizes quick outputs reaches far more learners than content that promotes deep engagement. This gap raises critical questions about whose vision of AI literacy scales and what learners are actually left with.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education by reducing the time and effort required to access information, solve problems, and complete academic tasks. Although these capabilities can improve learning efficiency, their implications for deeper understanding and independent learning remain uncertain. This review examines the cognitive effort paradox in GenAI-supported education: the possibility that reducing unnecessary mental effort can facilitate learning while excessive cognitive delegation may weaken the processes through which knowledge is constructed and retained. Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, desirable difficulties, self-regulated learning, and cognitive offloading research, the review distinguishes productive cognitive assistance from cognitive substitution. It examines how GenAI influences cognitive load, learning engagement, metacognitive monitoring, knowledge retention, and independent problem-solving. The synthesis suggests that the educational value of reduced cognitive effort depends on the nature of the task, learner characteristics, instructional design, and whether students remain actively involved in learning-relevant processing. An integrative conceptual framework is proposed to explain the conditions under which GenAI-supported efficiency may strengthen or constrain learning. The review offers directions for experimental research, educational assessment, and responsible GenAI integration in higher education.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   Objective: Deficits in attention have been linked to poorer performance on executive functioning tasks, particularly those requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility. While continuous performance tests are commonly used to assess sustained attention, their relationship to error based executive outcomes under increased task demand in pediatric clinical populations remains incompletely characterized. This study examined whether performance on a relatively low demand task of sustained attention, the Conners’ Continuous Performance Test–Third Edition (CPT-3), predicts performance on a higher demand executive task, the Delis–Kaplan Executive Function System (D-KEFS) Color Word Interference Test (CW). Method/Data Selection: Data were obtained from a mixed clinical sample of 213 children and adolescents ages 8–17 years (M = 11.7, SD = 2.8; 47.8% male, 52.2% female) evaluated in an outpatient private practice neuropsychology clinic. Participants completed the CPT-3 and D-KEFS CW as part of individualized comprehensive neuropsychological batteries. Multivariate regression analyses examined whether CPT-3 subscales predicted performance on D-KEFS CW conditions. Results/Data Synthesis: The overall model significantly predicted D-KEFS Inhibition Error scores (R2 = .12, adjusted R2 = .08, F(9, 198) = 3.02, p = .002) and D-KEFS Inhibition/Switching Error scores (R2 = .17, adjusted R2 = .13, F(9, 198) = 4.56, p &lt; .001). CPT-3 reaction time–based indices accounted for the majority of explained variance across both error outcomes. Conclusions: Performance on a sustained attention task was associated with error based executive performance requiring inhibition and cognitive flexibility in this pediatric clinical sample. Faster response speed and higher variability in response speed may be linked more impulsive verbal responding, resulting in higher errors on a cognitively demanding task.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now routine in university writing, making simple adoption studies increasingly uninformative. The more consequential question is how GenAI enters the writing process, how learners regulate that support, and when assistance begins to substitute for learner effort. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined AI-mediated academic writing among 186 undergraduate EFL students across three academic levels in Benin and integrated the quantitative results with thematic frequencies from 24 English lecturers. Student data captured tool use, AI support across pre-writing, drafting, revising, and proofreading, perceived linguistic, cognitive, and affective support, self-regulated writing behaviours, perceived writing benefit, and concerns about overreliance, verification, integrity, and critical engagement. ChatGPT was the most widely used platform (86.0%), but platform multiplicity itself was unrelated to perceived writing benefit (Spearman rho = .017, p = .814). By contrast, frequency of AI use was strongly associated with perceived benefit (rho = .615, p < .001), writing confidence (rho = .695, p < .001), and self-regulated writing (rho = .869, p < .001). AI support was reported most strongly during revising and proofreading (both M = 4.16 on a five-point scale), significantly above pre-writing and drafting. A notable benefit-risk coupling also emerged: students who reported greater benefit simultaneously reported stronger concerns (rho = .522, p < .001). Lecturer themes converged with this pattern, especially on linguistic scaffolding (87.5%), revision support (91.7%), overreliance (83.3%), and authorship or academic-integrity concerns (79.2%). The findings suggest that intensity and regulation of use matter more than the number of tools adopted. They support a view of GenAI as regulated scaffolding whose educational value depends on learners' capacity to plan, monitor, evaluate, and retain ownership of academic writing. Because the study relies on self-report and coded lecturer perceptions, it does not claim objective writing gains or causal effects.

title: The Influence of Digital Wallet Notifications on Spending Behaviour
venue: International Journal of Scientific Research in Engineering and Management
preview: Digital wallets have become a primary payment channel for consumers, and the push notifications they send, such as cashback alerts, promotional offers, payment reminders and transaction confirmations, are a constant feature of the payment experience. This study examines whether and how these notifications influence spending behaviour. Using a cross-sectional survey design with a sample of 300 digital wallet users, th…
abstract_text: Digital wallets have become a primary payment channel for consumers, and the push notifications they send, such as cashback alerts, promotional offers, payment reminders and transaction confirmations, are a constant feature of the payment experience. This study examines whether and how these notifications influence spending behaviour. Using a cross-sectional survey design with a sample of 300 digital wallet users, three hypotheses were tested with Excel-based statistical procedures. A chi-square test of independence examined whether notification frequency is associated with impulse purchasing; a one-way ANOVA compared monthly wallet spending across the dominant type of notification received; and a multiple linear regression estimated the effect of daily notification volume on monthly spending after controlling for age, income and notification engagement. Impulse purchasing rose sharply with notification frequency (14.0% at low, 30.9% at medium and 51.4% at high frequency; χ²(2) = 23.49, p < .001, Cramér’s V = .28). Mean monthly spending differed significantly by notification type, F(3, 296) = 16.67, p < .001, η² = .145, with cashback/offer and promotional notifications associated with the highest spending and payment reminders with the lowest. In the regression model (R² = .533), each additional daily notification was associated with about ₹332 more monthly spending (p < .001), alongside significant effects of income and engagement. The findings suggest that notifications function as behavioural nudges whose effect depends on both their volume and their content. Implications for wallet providers, regulators and consumers are discussed, together with limitations and directions for future research.

abstract_text: Artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly embedded in project management activities, including planning, scheduling, forecasting, reporting, risk identification, resource allocation, and decision support. Existing research has largely evaluated these applications through immediate performance outcomes such as efficiency, speed, cost reduction, forecasting accuracy, and project success. However, this short-term performance perspective may obscure a longer-term organizational consequence: the gradual erosion of human cognitive capability when project professionals repeatedly delegate cognitively consequential work to AI systems. Research on human-AI collaboration increasingly points to reduced independent cognitive effort, over-reliance, and skill-retention challenges as recurring risks of advanced automation (Dong et al., 2026). This article introduces the concept of cognitive debt to explain this deferred capability cost in AI-augmented project management. Cognitive debt is defined as the accumulated reduction in an individual’s or team’s capacity for independent judgment, contextual sensemaking, critical evaluation, and adaptive problem solving resulting from sustained delegation of cognitively consequential work to artificial intelligence. Drawing on research in cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, professional expertise, AI competency, and project management, the article develops a Cognitive Debt Accumulation Framework. The framework distinguishes productive cognitive offloading, in which AI removes cognitively routine work and frees attention for higher-order judgment, from debt-generating cognitive offloading, in which AI substitutes for activities that sustain professional expertise. It further proposes that cognitive debt may remain largely invisible during routine execution and become most consequential under novel, ambiguous, disrupted, or AI-failure conditions. Task ambiguity, delegation intensity, professional experience, AI competency, interaction design, and cognitive-preservation mechanisms are identified as important boundary conditions. The article contributes to AI-augmented project management by shifting attention from whether AI improves current performance to whether organizations preserve the human capabilities required to question, govern, and recover from AI-supported decisions over time. Keywords: generative AI, artificial intelligence, project management, cognitive debt, cognitive offloading, human-AI collaboration, professional judgment, deskilling, project resilience, organizational learning

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) confronts educational psychology with sharply heterogeneous evidence: meta-analyses report positive average effects on learning alongside prediction intervals spanning harm to benefit, and experiments document gains in some configurations and learning penalties in others. This article develops an augmentation–erosion framework that accounts for part of this heterogeneity by treating the educational effect of GenAI not as a property of the tool but as a property of the partition of cognitive labor between learner and machine. Integrating research on cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, cognitive load theory, and self-regulated learning, the framework holds that offloading augments learning when it discharges operations peripheral to the current learning goal, and risks erosion, whether of acquisition or of maintenance, when it bypasses the processing constitutive of that goal, unless the learner substantively processes the output or later reconstructs it. It supplies criteria for locating operations along a graded peripheral–constitutive continuum, specifies the comparison condition against which augmentation and erosion are defined, and states seven conditioned, testable propositions, each illustrated with a common example and paired with supporting and challenging patterns. On this basis, offloading regulation is proposed as a learning-oriented dimension of AI literacy with domain-general and discipline-specific components: a competence comprising partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification, and re-internalization, enacted through metacognitive control and conditioned by learners’ goals and motivation. The article closes with an intervention research program, a measurement strategy that triangulates interaction logs with process measures, and equity implications, using STEM learning as a strategically revealing case.

abstract_text: This review explores the transformative impact of AI-driven workforce analytics on organizational performance, employee wellbeing, and governance compliance within health systems and business intelligence frameworks. As healthcare institutions and corporate enterprises grapple with evolving labor dynamics, data-driven insights are increasingly essential for proactive human resource management. AI models enable granular analysis of workforce trends, skill gaps, productivity patterns, and burnout risks, facilitating precision in workforce planning and policymaking. By integrating behavioral analytics, sentiment detection, and predictive modeling, organizations can optimize talent management strategies and reduce turnover rates while ensuring regulatory adherence. The study synthesizes current methodologies and applications across health systems and business enterprises, highlighting how AI enhances decision support, transparency, and ethical compliance in workforce governance. The review further examines case studies demonstrating measurable outcomes, outlines implementation challenges, and proposes a framework for ethical, resilient, and adaptable workforce analytics in the AI era. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of how artificial intelligence can elevate strategic workforce initiatives while promoting operational excellence and employee-centric cultures.

abstract_text: This study examines how college students’ trust in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is associated with critical thinking engagement in GenAI-supported learning through multiple psychological mechanisms. Drawing on Distributed Cognition Theory (DCT), we propose and test a structural model including five constructs: trust in AI, perceived usefulness, cognitive offloading, AI self-efficacy, and critical thinking. Drawing on survey data from a convenience sample of college students who engaged in learning activities using GenAI tools (e.g., ChatGPT), we assessed hypothesized relationships using structural equation modeling (SEM). The results show that trust in AI is positively associated with perceived usefulness and AI self-efficacy, and both constructs are positively associated with critical thinking. In contrast, cognitive offloading is negatively associated with critical thinking, indicating a potential constraining pathway through which stronger reliance on GenAI may be associated with lower engagement in higher-order thinking. Overall, the findings suggest that trust in GenAI is linked to critical thinking through both supportive and constraining pathways. This study extends DCT in GenAI-supported learning by showing that trust in AI is not uniformly beneficial. The findings highlight the importance of educational approaches that cultivate students’ efficacy beliefs and strategic use of GenAI while discouraging overreliance that reduces cognitive engagement.

abstract_text: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) has been the dominant framework for instructional design research for over three decades, built on the principle that reducing extraneous load frees working memory capacity for the germane processing that produces durable learning. This principle was developed for static instructional environments in which the learner is the sole cognitive agent. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools introduces a dynamic information-processing partner whose contributions to the cognitive system are not adequately captured by CLT’s tripartite architecture. Empirical anomalies are now accumulating in the GenAI-in-education literature — most sharply the Effort–Load Paradox, in which ChatGPT improves learning outcomes without altering perceived effort or cognitive load, and without germane load functioning as the operative mediating mechanism (Ramachandran, 2026). Drawing on a quasi-experimental study (N = 184) conducted in Indian management education and a synthesis of CLT literature in technology-enhanced learning contexts, this paper proposes two theoretical extensions: (1) dependency-induced extraneous load — the novel cognitive burden generated when AI scaffolding is abruptly withdrawn, manifesting most acutely at Bloom’s application level; and (2) the efficiency pathway, through which GenAI improves outcomes by enhancing information quality rather than reducing load quantity, rendering its benefits invisible to standard rating instruments. These constructs are integrated with Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development, the Expertise Reversal Effect, and the Misinterpreted Effort Hypothesis into a revised theoretical framework for CLT in GenAI-mediated environments. Implications for instructional design, AI tool architecture, and CLT measurement methodology are discussed.

abstract_text: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, creating opportunities for flexible and personalised learning while raising questions about AI-supported learning. This study examines whether students’ attitudes toward GAI mediate the relationships between perceived ease of use (PEU), perceived usefulness (PU), and perceived Generative AI support for self-regulated learning (GAI-SRL). A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 264 undergraduate students at a public university in Indonesia. Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). PEU and PU were positively associated with attitudes toward GAI, while attitudes were positively associated with perceived GAI support for self-regulated learning. PEU and PU also showed significant direct relationships with GAI-SRL, and their indirect relationships through attitudes were significant, indicating partial statistical mediation. These findings suggest that students’ attitudes toward GAI constitute an intermediate statistical pathway linking technology-related perceptions with perceived GAI support for self-regulated learning. The study extends technology acceptance research by positioning attitudes toward GAI within a learning-oriented framework and highlights responsible, learner-centred use of GAI while preserving students’ learning agency.

Participants were recruited using purposive sampling based on predefined eligibility criteria. Data were collected through an online questionnaire during the first semester of the 2025/2026 academic year. A total of 278 questionnaires were returned. During the predefined eligibility screening procedure, 9 responses were excluded because the personal information provided could not be verified as indicating active undergraduate student status. A further 5 responses were excluded because the respondents reported very limited use of Generative AI for academic learning and therefore did not meet the study's predefined eligibility criterion concerning prior experience with Generative AI. Thus, 14 responses were excluded and 264 valid responses were retained for the final analysis. The final sample consisted of 112 male students (42.4%) and 152 female students (57.6%), with a mean age of 20.8 years (SD = 1.34). Participation was voluntary, and before completing the questionnaire, respondents were informed about the purpose of the study and provided electronic informed consent. Respondents' names and student identification numbers (NIM) were collected solely for the purpose of verifying active undergraduate student status. These identifying data were not included in the analytical dataset and were deleted before statistical analysis. Accordingly, the statistical analyses were conducted using de-identified data, while responses were treated confidentially. Data analysis was conducted using SmartPLS 3.0 following a two-stage PLS-SEM procedure. The first stage involved assessment of the measurement model, followed by evaluation of the structural model and mediation relationships. Given the cross-sectional research design, all estimated relationships were interpreted as statistical associations rather than causal effects (Hair et al., 2019) . The measurement model was assessed in terms of internal consistency reliability, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Internal consistency reliability was evaluated using Cronbach's Alpha (CA) and Composite Reliability (CR). Convergent validity was assessed using indicator outer loadings and Average Variance Extracted (AVE). Discriminant validity was examined using the Fornell-Larcker criterion and the Heterotrait-Monotrait Ratio (HTMT). The structural model was evaluated using path coefficients, coefficient of determination (R²), collinearity assessment, effect sizes (f²), predictive relevance (Q²), and out-of-sample predictive assessment using PLSpredict. Effect size f² was used to assess the contribution of each exogenous construct to the explained variance of the endogenous construct. Predictive relevance was examined using the blindfolding procedure, with positive Q² values interpreted as evidence of predictive relevance. PLSpredict was additionally used to assess out-of-sample predictive performance using the resulting Q² predict values. Mediation effects were assessed through indirect effects estimated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. The indirect effects of PEU and PU on GAI-SRL through ATT were examined using the bootstrapped estimates and confidence intervals. Consistent with the cross-sectional design, statistically significant indirect effects were interpreted as evidence of statistical mediation within the proposed model rather than evidence of a temporal or causal mechanism. Because the predictor, mediator, and endogenous constructs were measured using self-report items within the same online questionnaire and at the same measurement occasion, the potential for common-method variance was considered. Several procedural safeguards were applied, including voluntary participation, electronic informed consent, confidentiality of responses, and de-identification of the analytical dataset. Names and student identification numbers were collected only to verify active student status and were deleted before statistical analysis. The analytical dataset therefore did not contain direct personal identifiers. The outer and inner VIF values reported in the structural model were used to assess statistical collinearity and were not treated as a formal test of common-method bias. Therefore, the VIF results should not be interpreted as demonstrating the absence of common-method variance. Given the single-source, self-report measurement approach, the possibility of common-method variance cannot be completely excluded and is considered in the interpretation of the findings.

preview: The growing use of generative AI writing assistants, such as ChatGPT, in ESL/EFL academic contexts has sparked debate about their influence on self-regulated learning (SRL). abstract_text: The growing use of generative AI writing assistants, such as ChatGPT, in ESL/EFL academic contexts has sparked debate about their influence on self-regulated learning (SRL). This systematic review examines 41 empirical studies published between 2021 and March 2026 to evaluate how university students engage with AI tools in relation to SRL. Guided by PRISMA 2020 standards, the review synthesises quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods research through narrative analysis, drawing on Zimmerman’s (2000) three phase SRL model and metacognitive regulation theory. Three central patterns emerge. First, SRL phases are unevenly addressed: the performance phase dominates (92.7% of studies), while forethought (58.5%) and self-reflection (51.2%) receive less attention, suggesting an incomplete regulatory cycle. Second, AI demonstrates a dual role in metacognitive regulation, facilitating monitoring, evaluation, and revision (68.3%), yet also contributing to cognitive offloading and reduced learner agency (14.6%), with 17.1% of studies reporting mixed outcomes. Third, pedagogical design is critical: structured approaches that integrate AI literacy, guided feedback, and teacher mediation consistently enhance SRL, whereas unguided use yields weaker results. The evidence base remains limited by its concentration in Asian contexts (73.2%), reliance on self-report data, and absence of longitudinal designs, restricting claims about sustained competence. Overall, the review concludes that generative AI can strengthen self-regulated academic writing when embedded in intentional pedagogical frameworks that activate all SRL phases; without such alignment, AI may improve immediate performance but hinder the development of lasting regulatory skills.

This study employed a systematic literature review design guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 framework to ensure transparency, methodological rigour, and reproducibility (Page et al., 2021) .
