analysis.discussion: First, this study extends research on learners’ psychological outcomes in AI applications in education. Existing studies have mainly focused on using AI to improve learning efficiency, academic outcomes, and technology use, highlighting AI’s functional value as a learning tool ( Kasneci et al., 2023 ; Preiksaitis & Rose, 2023 ; Venkatesh et al., 2003 ). In contrast, research on the impact of AI assistants on learners’ psychological health has been relatively limited. This study uses a medical education context to investigate whether higher perceived AI assistant intelligence influences medical students’ mental health, treating perceived AI assistant intelligence as an important factor in the learning environment. This not only shifts AI education research from a predominant focus on learning performance toward greater attention to mental health but also broadens the spectrum of outcome variables examined in research on AI applications in education ( Gordon et al., 2024 ; Jia et al., 2022 ; Mohmand et al., 2022 ). Second, this study demonstrates the relevance of SDT for understanding AI-mediated learning contexts. Previous SDT studies have mostly examined the effects of conventional educational factors (e.g., teacher support and peer interaction) on motivation to learn and psychological development ( Bureau et al., 2022 ). As AI assistants become more integrated into learning, intelligent systems are becoming a major environmental resource that influences learning ( Kasneci et al., 2023 ). From an SDT perspective, AI assistants perceived as highly intelligent may create a more supportive learning environment by facilitating experiences related to autonomy, competence, and relatedness, which may in turn contribute to study goal progress and psychological adaptation. In this sense, the present findings suggest that SDT provides a useful theoretical lens for understanding how AI-supported learning environments may influence students’ learning and psychological outcomes, thereby extending SDT’s relevance to emerging human–AI collaborative learning settings. Third, this study clarifies the mechanisms and boundary conditions through which perceived AI assistant intelligence affects medical students’ mental health. While research shows that AI can positively influence learning experiences and outcomes, systematic explanations of how AI affects learners’ mental health remain lacking ( Klug & Maier, 2015 ). This study develops and validates a serial mediation mechanism through which perceived AI assistant intelligence affects mental health, with study goal progress and academic anxiety playing pivotal roles ( Pekrun, 2006 ). In addition, this study includes AI literacy as a moderating variable, indicating that the positive association between perceived AI assistant intelligence and mental health is not universal but depends on individual AI literacy ( Ng et al., 2021 ). This finding contributes to understanding how AI influences the psychological aspects of learning in educational contexts and provides a theoretical basis for further research on individual differences in AI-assisted learning environments. First, this study found that higher perceived AI assistant intelligence is associated with improved mental health among medical students by facilitating progress toward study goals and reducing academic anxiety. This suggests that AI in medical education should focus on whether it provides effective learning support ( Gordon et al., 2024 ). Thus, when designing and implementing AI learning aids, medical schools should consider how students perceive the intelligence and learning-support capabilities of AI assistants rather than focusing solely on system usability and adoption, including their ability to understand questions, provide accurate feedback, adapt to different learning situations, and support individual students ( Hale et al., 2024 ). Highly intelligent AI assistants can offer continuous interaction, personalized feedback, and learning guidance, which may be more effective than simple information retrieval or standardized question-and-answer functions in helping medical students progress toward learning goals and maintain a positive psychological state ( Meng et al., 2024 ; Preiksaitis & Rose, 2023 ). Second, this study found that study goal progress and academic anxiety play a serial mediating role between perceived AI assistant intelligence and mental health. This indicates that one important way AI assistants perceived as highly intelligent may influence mental health is by supporting students’ progress toward their learning goals ( Harkin et al., 2016 ). Thus, teachers and educational administrators can make greater use of AI assistants for learning planning, milestone management, identifying learning gaps, and providing learning feedback, thereby helping students continuously progress toward their learning goals ( Wanberg et al., 2010 ). For medical students who are continuously exposed to high-pressure learning environments, such support may enhance their sense of control over learning and reduce anxiety arising from academic uncertainty ( Pekrun, 2006 ; Quek et al., 2019 ). Third, this study revealed that AI literacy further strengthens the role of perceived AI assistant intelligence in promoting study goal progress. This indicates that even when students interact with AI assistants offering similar levels of support, the extent of their benefit may differ depending on their AI literacy ( Laupichler et al., 2024 ). Thus, while medical schools improve AI-supported education, they should not only provide the technology but also emphasize developing students’ AI literacy ( Long & Magerko, 2020 ). In particular, AI literacy courses, case-based teaching, and critical evaluation training can help students understand AI’s functional capabilities and limitations, develop effective questioning skills, and critically evaluate AI-generated content ( Pupic et al., 2023 ). Improving students’ AI literacy may therefore help them better translate the learning and psychological benefits of highly intelligent AI assistants into positive learning outcomes. While this study has contributed to the literature on the use of artificial intelligence in education and medical students’ mental health, it has weaknesses that future research should address. First, although this study used a research design integrating experimental techniques and questionnaire surveys, the experimental environment was primarily based on a short-term, simulated AI-assisted learning task, which may not fully reflect medical students’ actual and sustained experiences using AI in educational settings. analysis.limitations: While this study has contributed to the literature on the use of artificial intelligence in education and medical students’ mental health, it has weaknesses that future research should address. First, although this study used a research design integrating experimental techniques and questionnaire surveys, the experimental environment was primarily based on a short-term, simulated AI-assisted learning task, which may not fully reflect medical students’ actual and sustained experiences using AI in educational settings. In addition, Study 2 assessed the outcome variables immediately after the experimental task and framed them as task-proximal, post-intervention states. Therefore, Study 2’s findings should not be interpreted as evidence that a brief interaction with a more capable AI assistant produces enduring changes in students’ study goal progress, academic anxiety, or mental health. In particular, the mental-health measure in Study 2 reflects participants’ immediate psychological state following the task rather than their longer-term or clinical mental-health status. Future studies could use real learning platforms, repeated AI-assisted learning sessions, or longitudinal designs to examine whether these short-term effects persist over time and further enhance the ecological validity of the findings ( Gordon et al., 2024 ). Second, this study mainly collected data through self-report scales, so participants’ subjective perceptions and social desirability may have influenced the variables. Future studies could incorporate more objective indicators, such as academic performance, learning behavior logs, or teacher assessments, to cross-validate findings and strengthen their robustness ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Third, this study examined only study goal progress, academic anxiety, and AI literacy. Future studies could further consider other relevant factors, such as academic self-efficacy, learning engagement, and trust in technology, and test the model across different majors and educational levels to deepen the theoretical explanation of how perceived AI assistant intelligence influences learner development. Finally, this study focused specifically on medical students. Given the high levels of stress, competition, and competency-based training in medical education, it remains unclear whether the findings generalize to other student populations. Future studies could replicate the study across different disciplines, educational levels, and cultural contexts to enhance the external validity and generalizability of the findings.

abstract_text: Purpose This study aims to examine how customers perceive and engage with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled services provided by small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), with a particular focus on value co-creation and well-being outcomes. While prior studies have mainly investigated GenAI adoption from the firm perspective, this research shifts attention to customer-level psychological and experiential mechanisms in an emerging economy context. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on service-dominant logic and Sustainable Development Goal 3, the study adopts a quantitative approach. Data were collected from 180 Vietnamese consumers, predominantly educated youths aged 18–24, who had prior experience with GenAI-powered services offered by SMEs. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to test the proposed hypotheses. Findings The results indicate that perceived knowledge about GenAI and perceived marketplace influence are positively associated with customers’ value co-creation behavior. Value co-creation is positively associated with both value-in-use and emotional well-being. In addition, value-in-use is positively associated with perceptions of social well-being, whereas emotional well-being is not significantly associated with social well-being. Originality/value This study extends GenAI research by moving beyond firm-level adoption to examine customer-centric outcomes in SME service contexts in an emerging economy. It highlights perceived knowledge and marketplace influence as critical antecedents of value co-creation and demonstrates how AI-enabled services contribute to social value primarily through functional value-in-use rather than emotional pathways.

To reduce method bias, variables are randomly placed on questionnaire pages to reduce order effects and discourage respondents from detecting causal correlations (Hulland et al., 2018). Two statistical analyses were undertaken to evaluate the severity of the common method bias. Using Harman’s single factor test, the study found that a single common factor explained 42.597% of variation, which was below the 50% threshold (Ooi and Tan, 2016; Wang et al., 2022; Wong et al., 2023). We found that the variance inflation factor (VIF) of all variables in the research model ranged from 1.000 to 3.298. The VIF score below 3.3 shows no structural model collinearity (Hew et al., 2020; Lim et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021). Assessing Cronbach’s alpha (α), item loading, composite reliability (CR) and average variance extracted (AVE) values determined the reliability and validity of the research variables. Table 2 demonstrates that all constructs have strong internal reliability, with Cronbach’s α and CR exceeding the threshold of 0.7 (except PEK4 and PEM1, however, the AVE of PEK and PEM are 0.5 (Hair et al., 2011; Tan and Ooi, 2018), the study still keeps these items). For convergent validity, we set a threshold of 0.7 item loading and AVE of 0.5. Table 2 also shows that all item loadings and constructs’ AVE are above the indicated threshold values, indicating high convergent validity. Similarly, H2 supports the notion that perceived marketplace influence is positively associated with value co-creation behavior – an insight that extends beyond Hammedi et al. (2024), who focused on the voice of the consumer, by showing how normative beliefs about market impact can also drive participatory behavior. In line with previous literature emphasizing the experiential nature of value (Grönroos and Voima, 2013), H3 confirms that value co-creation is positively associated with value-in-use. This result strengthens the understanding that collaborative interactions between customers and GenAI-enabled SMEs lead to enhanced personalized service outcomes. Furthermore, H4 highlights the emotional benefits of co-creation, aligning with affective events theory (Weiss and Cropanzano, 1996) and extending the findings of Kim (2023), who observed emotional satisfaction in service innovation contexts, but without the GenAI lens. The Downloaded from www.​emerald.​com/​jsibr/​article-pdf/​2/​3/​128/​11866458/​jsibr-04-2025-0042en.​pdf by guest on 24 September 2026 relationship between value-in-use and social well-being offers a novel contribution by linking microlevel service outcomes with macrolevel societal perceptions, a connection that remains underexplored in GenAI literature (Creely and Blannin, 2025; Emerald Publishing, 2025). Finally, the results for H6 indicate that emotional well-being is not positively associated with perceptions of social well-being, providing an interesting insight to the broader validation of SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) in AI-powered service contexts. While emotional well- being contributes to individual satisfaction and psychological fulfillment, its effect may not extend to how customers evaluate collective or societal well-being. This outcome could stem from measurement boundaries that capture primarily individual affective states rather than socially oriented outcomes, or from cultural tendencies that distinguish personal emotions from community-based judgments. It may also reflect a theoretical misalignment, as affective responses often occur at an individual level, whereas social well-being reflects evaluative, relational and ethical considerations. These findings suggest that SMEs should make their societal and community contributions more visible and explicitly connect personalized GenAI services with inclusive, transparent and socially responsible practices. This study makes several important contributions to the literature on GenAI, value co- creation and social impact within the context of SMEs. First, this study advances the social impact literature by providing empirical evidence on how customers experience and derive value from GenAI-enabled services. It establishes that social impact in AI-mediated SME contexts is not solely a technological outcome, but a human-centered process shaped by customer perceptions, engagement and co-creation behaviors (Baabdullah, 2024; Dwivedi et al., 2023). The findings show that GenAI can serve as a social enabler when customers perceive transparency, control and personalization, reinforcing the idea that responsible AI deployment in SMEs can enhance community trust and shared well-being. Second, by integrating perceived knowledge and perceived marketplace influence as antecedents of value co-creation, this study enriches SDL theory (Vargo and Lusch, 2004, 2008) with a dual-path cognitive–normative model that explains why customers engage with Downloaded from www.​emerald.​com/​jsibr/​article-pdf/​2/​3/​128/​11866458/​jsibr-04-2025-0042en.​pdf by guest on 24 September 2026 GenAI-driven services. Third, the nonsignificant relationship between Research emotional well-being and social well-being offers a nuanced theoretical contribution. It suggests that while GenAI interactions may enhance individual emotional satisfaction (e.g. personalization and convenience), they do not automatically translate into perceived social 141 connectedness or collective benefit. This finding highlights a “human disconnect” in GenAI- mediated service encounters, where emotional gratification remains individual rather than communal, signaling a need for SMEs to design AI experiences that visibly foster inclusion, empathy and societal contribution (Lin Li et al., 2025; Modgil et al., 2025). Finally, drawing on the Yi and Gong (2013) co-creation framework, this study identifies that behaviors such as providing feedback, adapting preferences and cooperating with AI interfaces contribute more strongly to social well-being perceptions than mere information sharing. These behaviors embody the “human touch” in GenAI contexts, demonstrating that meaningful social value arises not from the algorithm itself, but from customers’ willingness to humanize their interactions with AI-enabled services (Saha et al., 2020; Simón et al., 2024). From a practical standpoint, the findings offer concrete guidance for SME service owners seeking to leverage GenAI for both business growth and positive social outcomes. title: Born into the Algorithm: Global Law, Cognitive Autonomy, and Children’s Rights in the Age of Artificial Intelligence
preview: Children born today enter a world in which artificial intelligence systems collect, categorize, and predict from the moment of birth, often before any digital engagement and well before the capacity to consent. abstract_text: Children born today enter a world in which artificial intelligence systems collect, categorize, and predict from the moment of birth, often before any digital engagement and well before the capacity to consent. Existing legal frameworks address children primarily as platform users defined by an age threshold or as natural persons without operational protection during incapacity, and none adequately addresses the newborn as a rights-bearing subject of algorithmic systems from the moment of birth. This paper proposes sovereignty-in-trust as the doctrinal frame within which children’s rights attach at birth and are held in trust during the period before consent capacity, with cognitive autonomy as the substantive content of what is held. The framework is derived from a literature review of the established provisions of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, read with the Committee’s General Comments, supported by data-protection and AI-governance instruments in the European Union, and refined through the supported-decision-making framework of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. The paper highlights four key failure modes in current frameworks: regulatory overload, commercial monetization, dependence on political will, and the limitations of current doctrinal structures. It outlines five legal measures to enhance resilience: mandatory disclosure during neonatal data collection, a bankruptcy-proof restriction on transferring data from minors, automatic deletion or anonymization of identity data not explicitly retained, a safeguard against predictive profiling without prior consent, and ongoing ethical reform and liability across the AI product lifecycle. The paper advocates that the United Nations Committee on the Rights of the Child issue a new General Comment specifically addressing children’s rights in algorithmic systems, with dedicated provisions for the period before children have the capacity to give consent. The doctrinal objective is not to establish a new right but to articulate the operational form of existing rights as they apply to a subject who is currently unable to exercise them at the moment they attach.

analysis.methods: The study used a cross-sectional survey design. Convenience sampling was used to administer paper-and-pencil questionnaires to undergraduate students at universities in mainland China during the 2024–2025 academic year. After data screening for completeness and inattentive responding, 421 valid questionnaires were retained for analysis. Of these participants, 128 (30.4%) identified as male and 293 (69.6%) as female. The sample comprised 116 first-year (27.6%), 101 second-year (24.0%), 164 third-year (39.0%) and 40 fourth-year (9.5%) students, drawn from a range of disciplines. The sample size comfortably exceeds the minimum required for PLS-SEM with the present model complexity, satisfying both Cohen’s power conventions and the inverse-square-root rule ( Hair et al., 2021 ; Kock and Hadaya, 2018 ). All participation was voluntary and anonymous. Before completing the questionnaire, students were informed of the study purpose and the protections in place; they gave written informed consent and were assured that responses would be used solely for academic research and that they could withdraw at any time. The study was conducted in accordance with the ethical guidelines of the authors’ institution and approved by the relevant Institutional Review Board. To reduce potential common method bias, the questionnaire was pilot-tested on 30 undergraduates not included in the final sample, items were arranged so that the predictor and criterion measures were separated, and procedural remedies recommended by Podsakoff et al. (2003) were applied (e.g., guaranteed anonymity, balanced item polarity, and clear instructions emphasising that there were no right or wrong answers). All scales were administered in Chinese; English-language scales were translated and back-translated by two bilingual researchers, with discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer and the wording revised after a small-scale pilot. Items were rated on a five-point Likert-type scale (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) unless otherwise noted. Scale scores reported in Table 1 were calculated as the sum of the constituent items, with higher scores indicating higher levels of the construct; for the PLS-SEM measurement model, dimension and parcel scores were computed as item means (Section 3.3), which is immaterial for estimation because PLS-SEM standardises all indicators. Means, standard deviations and zero-order correlations. GenAI use was measured with the 17-item College Students’ Generative AI Use Survey developed by Li et al. (2024) . The instrument captures students’ use of GenAI across four typical scenarios identified through literature review and semi-structured interviews with undergraduates: course learning, research activities, daily life, and further-study and job seeking. Sample items include “I use generative AI to answer the questions my teachers ask in class”, “I use generative AI to assist me in selecting research questions”, “When I encounter difficulties in life (such as diet, financial management or social relationships), I turn to generative AI for help”, and “I ask generative AI to help me create or revise my résumé”. The scale has demonstrated acceptable reliability in prior Chinese university samples. The critical-thinking outcome was operationalised as self-reported critical analytical skills using the eight-item Critical Analytical Skills sub-scale of Hou et al.’s (2022) Chinese Critical Thinking Scale. The sub-scale assesses individuals’ perceived ability to systematically gather and analyse problem-relevant background information and evaluate its veracity. Sample items include “I prefer to follow a structured set of steps when solving problems”, “I often consider the views of my parents and elders when making decisions”, and “I make different decisions in different situations when faced with a problem”. The Chinese Critical Thinking Scale was developed and validated specifically for Chinese university samples and has demonstrated good psychometric properties; higher scores indicate stronger self-reported critical analytical skills. Following the item-to-construct balance approach ( Little et al., 2002 ), the eight items were aggregated into three parcels for use as indicators of the latent critical analytical skills construct. Specifically, the items were first ranked according to their standardised factor loadings, and relatively higher- and lower-loading items were systematically distributed across the three parcels to balance their relationships with the underlying construct. Parcel scores were calculated as the mean of their constituent items. The resulting three parcels, labelled CT Parcel 1, CT Parcel 2, and CT Parcel 3, were specified as reflective indicators of a single latent critical analytical skills construct. They therefore represent aggregated measurement indicators rather than theoretically distinct dimensions of critical thinking ( Little et al., 2002 ; Matsunaga, 2008 ). GenAI feedback literacy was assessed using the 39-item Generative AI Student Feedback Literacy Scale (GenAI-SFLS) developed and validated for Chinese college students by Cui et al. (2026) . The instrument is organised around four dimensions and nine specific factors: a cognitive dimension (feedback knowledge and feedback appreciation); a behavioural dimension (feedback prompting skills, feedback judgement and enaction of feedback); an affective dimension (emotional recognition, readiness to engage and commitment to change); and an ethical dimension (feedback ethics). The four-dimension architecture extends Carless and Boud’s (2018) general feedback-literacy framework to AI-mediated environments, where prompt engineering and ethical engagement become central to the construct ( Cui et al., 2026 ; Jin et al., 2025 ; Zhan and Yan, 2026 ). Reflective thinking was measured with the Reflective Thinking Scale (RTS) developed by Kember et al. (2000) , one of the most widely used instruments in this area; in the present study, the Chinese-context revised version validated by Fu and Hali (2025) for use with students in mainland Chinese universities was adopted. The RTS captures four dimensions on a continuum of reflection: habitual action, understanding, reflection and critical reflection, with habitual action representing the least reflective level and critical reflection the most advanced. A sample item is “I often re-appraise my experience so I can learn from it and improve for my next performance”. Items were rated on a five-point Likert scale (1 = definitely disagree, 5 = definitely agree). The four-factor structure has shown good reliability and construct validity in Chinese university samples ( Fu and Hali, 2025 ; Kember et al., 2000 ). The analysis proceeded in two stages. analysis.results: To evaluate the discriminant validity of the four study constructs, a series of nested confirmatory factor analyses was conducted in AMOS 26.0 with maximum likelihood estimation ( Table 3 ). The four-factor model best represented the underlying factor structure (χ 2 /df = 2.189; CFI = 0.731; TLI = 0.723; IFI = 0.732; RMSEA = 0.053), with all factor loadings statistically significant. Although the incremental fit indices (CFI, TLI and IFI) fall below conventional thresholds (a well-documented consequence of model size: incremental fit indices such as CFI and TLI decline as the number of indicators per factor increases, even when RMSEA remains acceptable, and the present item-level model comprises 80 indicators, 39 of them from the GenAI-SFLS; Kenny and McCoach, 2003 ; Shi et al., 2019 ), the four-factor model fit was clearly superior to the three-, two- and single-factor alternatives, indicating adequate factorial differentiation amongst GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking and reflective thinking. Model 2 is the hypothesised four-factor model (GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking, reflective thinking). Model 1 adds an unmeasured common method factor, on which all indicators load, to the four substantive factors. Model 3 combines critical thinking and reflective thinking into one factor; Model 4 additionally combines GenAI feedback literacy with critical thinking and reflective thinking; Model 5 loads all indicators on a single factor. Common method bias was further checked with Harman’s single-factor test ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Twenty-one factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted from the unrotated solution; the first factor accounted for only 21.46% of the variance, well below the 40% threshold. In the unmeasured method factor approach ( Tang and Wen, 2020 ), adding a common method factor to the four-factor model (Model 1 in Table 3 ) did not improve model fit (CFI 0.699 vs. 0.731; TLI 0.688 vs. 0.723), indicating that a common method factor does not account for the covariance amongst the indicators ( Wen et al., 2018 ). Both procedures suggest that common method bias is unlikely to be a serious concern in the present data. Table 1 reports means, standard deviations and zero-order correlations amongst the four study variables. GenAI use, GenAI feedback literacy, critical thinking and reflective thinking were significantly and positively inter-correlated (all p < 0.001). analysis.discussion: This study set out to test a moderated mediation model linking generative artificial intelligence use to university students’ self-reported critical thinking, with GenAI feedback literacy as the mechanism and reflective thinking as a boundary condition. Three findings stand out. First, GenAI use was positively related to critical thinking, both directly when modelled alone and through GenAI feedback literacy when both were entered together. Second, the inclusion of feedback literacy reduced the direct effect to non-significance and accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total effect, a pattern consistent with feedback literacy as a principal mechanism. Third, the model was conditional on reflective thinking: at low reflective thinking the link was direct and the indirect path was not significant, whereas at high reflective thinking the indirect path through feedback literacy strengthened and the direct path disappeared. Read together, these results are consistent with a dual-route interpretation of the inconsistent existing evidence on GenAI and critical thinking, in which the structure of the association is sensitive to learner disposition. Each finding warrants discussion. Before turning to each finding, one interpretive boundary should be made explicit. Critical thinking was measured with the critical analytical skills sub-scale of the Chinese Critical Thinking Scale, on which students rate their own habitual analytical behaviour. The outcome therefore represents self-reported critical analytical skills, not critical-thinking performance demonstrated on a task, a test or an expert-rated piece of work. Self-reports of this kind capture students’ perceptions of how they approach problems rather than the observed quality of their reasoning, and they share a method with the self-reported predictors. Accordingly, where we write that GenAI use, feedback literacy or reflective thinking “predicts” critical thinking, the claim is that these variables are associated with higher self-rated analytical skill in a cross-sectional model, not that they produce better critical-thinking performance. This boundary applies to every finding discussed below. Generative AI is rapidly becoming part of the cognitive infrastructure of higher education, and a settled empirical answer to whether its use is associated with stronger or weaker critical thinking has remained elusive. The present study reframes the question. In a cross-sectional sample of Chinese undergraduates, GenAI use was positively associated with self-reported critical analytical skills, but the association was largely indirect: it was carried by students’ capacity to interpret, judge and act on AI-generated feedback, and its structure depended on students’ reflective stance. At low reflective thinking the association was direct and modest; at high reflective thinking it ran through feedback literacy, yielding a stronger indirect association. If these associations reflect the hypothesised causal ordering, a question that longitudinal and experimental designs must settle, the cognitive dividend of GenAI is unlikely to come from access alone, and universities that pair AI integration with explicit feedback-literacy training and reflective pedagogical practises may be better placed to convert ubiquitous AI use into the analytical capacity that higher education is meant to cultivate. The moderated mediation model presented here offers a tractable framework for the next wave of empirical work on GenAI and higher-order cognition.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations bound the study’s claims. First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. All variables were measured concurrently, so the mediation and moderated-mediation estimates describe patterns of association that are consistent with the hypothesised ordering but cannot establish it; reverse or reciprocal orderings (for example, students with stronger analytical skills making heavier or more sophisticated use of GenAI, or feedback literacy shaping use rather than the reverse) are equally compatible with the data. Although PLS-SEM with bootstrapped indirect effects and theoretically motivated path direction is well suited to estimating complex models, the findings should be replicated using longitudinal panel data or randomised intervention designs that track how GenAI use, feedback literacy and reflective thinking co-evolve over time. Second, the sample is drawn from Chinese universities and is skewed female (69.6%); cross-cultural and gender-balanced replications are needed to assess generalisability across educational systems with different assessment cultures and AI-policy environments. Third, all measures are self-reported, and the outcome in particular represents self-reported critical analytical skills rather than demonstrated critical-thinking performance. Although the study’s common-method-bias diagnostics did not flag a serious problem, behavioural and performance-based measures of critical thinking and feedback engagement (e.g., analyses of think-aloud protocols, log data from AI interactions, expert ratings of student work) would strengthen inference ( Fan et al., 2025 ). Fourth, critical thinking was operationalised through the analytical-skills sub-scale of a Chinese instrument; future studies could examine the model with broader operationalisations covering inference, evaluation, explanation and self-regulation ( Facione, 2011 ) and across disciplines, since GenAI’s affordances and risks may differ between, say, the humanities and STEM. Relatedly, the dual-route interpretation in this study rests on the pattern of moderation, not on direct observation of cognitive processing; the study did not measure whether students engaged with GenAI outputs shallowly or deeply, and process-tracing methods such as interaction logs, think-aloud protocols or eye-tracking are needed to test the proposed routes directly. Fifth, the incremental fit indices of the item-level measurement model fell below conventional thresholds, as is common with long instruments such as the 39-item GenAI-SFLS ( Kenny and McCoach, 2003 ; Shi et al., 2019 ); future work could refine the GenAI-SFLS for shorter administration without losing dimensional coverage. Finally, GenAI tools are evolving rapidly, and the empirical model captures a snapshot of usage patterns at a given moment; tracking the moderated mediation structure across model generations and modalities (text, voice, multimodal agents) is an important agenda for the field.

Three findings stand out. First, GenAI use was positively related to critical thinking, both directly when modelled alone and through GenAI feedback literacy when both were entered together. Second, the inclusion of feedback literacy reduced the direct effect to non-significance and accounted for nearly three-quarters of the total effect, a pattern consistent with feedback literacy as a principal mechanism. title: From digital companionship to capability building: reframing conversational artificial intelligence and older adults' psychological wellbeing in active aging
preview: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. abstract_text: The rapid diffusion of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped the landscape of digital interaction in later life, with growing attention to its implications for older adults' mental health and wellbeing. Existing research has predominantly interpreted conversational AI through the lens of digital companionship, emphasizing its capacity to simulate social presence, reduce loneliness, and provide emotional support. While this perspective captures important affective outcomes, it offers a limited account of the developmental processes through which AI engagement may influence psychological wellbeing in aging populations. This conceptual analysis proposes a shift from a companionship-oriented paradigm to a capability-building perspective grounded in the Capability Approach. It argues that the primary value of conversational AI lies not in its ability to substitute social interaction, but in its potential to expand older adults' cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capabilities. Building on this argument, this paper develops an AI-Augmented Active Aging Framework that explains how conversational AI affordances, responsiveness, personalization, accessibility, and availability, interact with personal, social, environmental, and system-level conversion factors. Under supportive conditions, these affordances may facilitate cognitive, emotional, social, and digital capability formation, thereby supporting autonomy, competence, social integration, and active aging. Under adverse conditions, however, conversational AI may contribute to capability erosion through over-reliance, cognitive offloading, reduced human contact, or diminished autonomous judgment. The framework therefore emphasizes heterogeneous and conditional outcomes rather than assuming uniform benefits across older adults.

title: Structure-Aware Rendering: How Code Reveal Shapes Programmers' Visual Attention

abstract_text: AI coding interfaces present generated code either all at once or token-by-token. These rendering strategies reflect model generation rather than how programmers actually read code: selectively, non-linearly, and guided by the structure. We argue that code rendering is a first-class interaction primitive that shapes how programmers read and understand code. To explore this design space, we introduce structured rendering, a technique that reveals code in semantically meaningful chunks derived from its syntactic hierarchy, exposing high-level structure before low-level details. To isolate rendering effects on visual attention, we conducted an eye-tracking study with 53 participants comparing static, character-based, and structured rendering. Our findings show that rendering alters visual attention and reading behavior: dynamic rendering induces fewer but longer fixations and more sustained focus, while structured rendering further guides attention toward semantically meaningful units and supports high-level understanding. We release the anonymized dataset with an interactive demo (https://codegaze.vercel.app/) to support future research.

abstract_text: Purpose of Review: To synthesize recent literature on the relationships between generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use and adolescents' mental health, with particular attention to problematic use and psychiatric vulnerabilities. Recent Findings: Emerging evidence suggests associations between GenAI use and a range of adolescent mental health outcomes, including depression, anxiety, psychosis-related experiences, externalizing behaviors, eating disorder risk, and suicidality. Problematic patterns of use, including dependency and emotional reliance, may be particularly relevant among adolescents with preexisting psychiatric vulnerabilities. Current evidence suggests that these relationships may be bidirectional: psychological distress can motivate GenAI use for companionship, emotional support, or escape, while problematic use may reinforce maladaptive beliefs, displace real-world relationships, and amplify existing vulnerabilities. However, evidence remains predominantly cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. Summary: GenAI may interact with and amplify underlying psychiatric vulnerabilities during adolescence, highlighting the importance of understanding patterns and motivations of use. Pediatricians and other clinicians caring for adolescents could consider not only the frequency of GenAI use but also motivations for use, problematic dependency, and socioemotional reliance. Identifying high-risk usage patterns of GenAI through longitudinal research, particularly among youth with preexisting psychiatric risks, may inform the development of tailored screening, intervention, and prevention strategies.

abstract_text: The importance of critical thinking when using generative AI in personal, professional, and educational contexts is widely acknowledged by scholars, educators, and politicians. There are contradictory hypotheses regarding the influence of AI on critical thinking, and research thus far has produced mixed results. In this paper, we present a critical scoping review of 80 research papers from Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) that study critical thinking with or about AI, focusing on how “critical thinking” is defined, measured, and how the papers claim critical thinking to be influenced by AI, according to current HCI research. Our findings demonstrate that critical thinking is rarely defined in HCI research about AI, and there are fundamental construct and criterion validity challenges in this line of research. We present a research agenda for more theory-grounded empirical research in critical thinking with or about AI, based on cognitive-psychological, philosophical, or educational research traditions.

We first describe the general challenges that pervade the study of critical thinking with or about AI in HCI research. We then outline some potential approaches to meet these challenges, both by looking at exemplars from the corpus, and then by revisiting the three theoretical traditions and what these might be able to offer in terms of designs of future studies. In this paper, we presented a scoping review of 80 research papers that empirically studied critical thinking in the context of using AI, a new but increasingly popular topic in HCI, and found that the included studies were highly heterogeneous in terms of their definitions of critical thinking and their studies of it. The studies are conducted especially in the USA, with students as participants, and using LLMs as the AI technology. Most of the studies evaluate a system designed to influence critical thinking, and most are based on short-term interventions and attitudinal rather than behavioral assessment. Human-Computer Interaction is interpreted broadly as "research in our ability to solve important problems related to human use of computing" (Oulasvirta & Hornbæk, 2016) . Since HCI draws on theories and methods from multiple other fields, we expect that studies published at HCI venues are likely to represent (in terms of methods and findings) findings published in other, specialized venues (such as education or psychology). The phenomenon of interest is specifically critical thinking, and a mapping of the emerging evidence in HCI about AI as a claimed influence on critical thinking. The complex and heterogeneous nature of recent findings within this theme makes it suitable for a scoping review rather than a systematic review (Peters et al., 2015) . We focuson the term critical thinking, and not on related concepts or skills, e.g., reflection in practice (Cho et al., 2022) , critical reflection (Iivari et al., 2024) , analytical thinking (Buc ¸inca et al., 2021) or stop-and-think behavior (Gauthier et al., 2022) . While these terms would be relevant if we wanted to systematically assess how AI affects critical thinking ability, this review is focused on how HCI interprets and uses the lexical term critical thinking. Critical thinking is particularly interesting because the term is commonly used across different disciplines, while related skills and behaviors often have roots in one discipline (for instance, "critical reflection" and "reflective practice" tend to be used in design research, while "analytical thinking" and "stop-and-think behavior" stem from a cognitive psychology tradition). These terms are also far less frequently used than the notion of critical thinking, both inside and outside academia (see Table 1 as an example of academic research prevalence). analysis.discussion: The goal of this section is to lay out potential paths forward. We first describe the general challenges that pervade the study of critical thinking with or about AI in HCI research. We then outline some potential approaches to meet these challenges, both by looking at exemplars from the corpus, and then by revisiting the three theoretical traditions and what these might be able to offer in terms of designs of future studies. In this paper, we presented a scoping review of 80 research papers that empirically studied critical thinking in the context of using AI, a new but increasingly popular topic in HCI, and found that the included studies were highly heterogeneous in terms of their definitions of critical thinking and their studies of it. The studies are conducted especially in the USA, with students as participants, and using LLMs as the AI technology. Most of the studies evaluate a system designed to influence critical thinking, and most are based on short-term interventions and attitudinal rather than behavioral assessment. Several observations about the corpus indicate construct validity challenges, such as a lack of clear and/or shared definitions of critical thinking and how this is assessed, especially in the question of perceived versus demonstrated critical thinking. A majority of the studies in the corpus rely on selfassessment as a measure of critical thinking; in fact, self-assessment measurements account for half (25 of the total 50) of the submissions that claim that AI has a primarily positive influence on people's critical thinking ability. Of the studies that base their assessment on a demonstrated effect of AI on critical thinking specifically, only 10 submissions provide explicit and reproducible criteria for how their assessment is made. We also identified potential criterion/content validity challenges, and a notable absence of in vivostudies or studies which focus on professionals rather than students. This means that it is difficult to know whether the studies actually predict or explain the type and scope of critical thinking we may be interested in assessing. Finally, we suggested some ways forward for HCI research that attempts to evaluate the influence of AI on critical thinking, based on the three theoretical foundations of cognitive psychology, philosophy, and education. We suggest that future studies of critical thinking in the context of using AI could make even clearer contributions by making explicit, at least, what their definition of critical thinking is, how they evaluate the influence, and finally, why their chosen method can reasonably be believed to measure what it is intended to measure.
analysis.limitations: A main limitation of this review is the possibility of misrepresenting the actual body of research about "critical thinking and related concepts." Searching with keywords is inherently reductionist, and our search is likely to have missed some existing work. Because we limited our search to the specific term "critical thinking" (as opposed to related terms such as "decision-making," "critical evaluation," or "reflective thinking"), we may have excluded work using a different terminology. However, as described in the methodology, this scoping review is about critical thinking-other definitions would be a matter for different (systematic rather than scoping) reviews. A second limitation is our focus on the HCI domain and our venue-based definition of this domain. Our search was confined to the ACM Digital Library, the International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction, and International Journal of Human-Computer Studies as representative for HCI work. Outside these databases, there is likely HCI-work to be found. Most importantly, we have not reviewed work from psychology or education, which could topically be characterized as at least HCI-adjacent research. However, our intention with this review was to bring attention to the gaps of work conducted in the domain of HCI. We believe that because this field draws upon many psychological and educational traditions, it is important to articulate more clearly which foundations are drawn upon in individual work. A third limitation is that we did not perform any quality assessment of the articles included in the corpus. When we report "claimed influence," it should not be interpreted as evidence for proven influence. A fourth limitation is that extraction of data was performed primarily by the first author. This may have biased the judgment in cases where decisions had to be made between assigning one category or another. We deem the influence of this acceptable, considering our focus was on relatively objective categorizations and not qualitative analysis. Finally, the rapidly evolving research area makes it likely that the corpus will become outdated or misrepresentative relatively fast. We do believe our scoping review merits further systematic review of work in this area. Especially the heterogeneity of the studies in terms of use of the term "critical thinking," their divergent focus on critical thinking with/about AI, and their varying levels of detail about data used as basis for the conclusions warrant this.

abstract_text: The proliferation of notification-driven, multi-device digital environments has produced widespread everyday experiences of scattered, discontinuous focus. Researchers and commentators frequently label this experience “attention fragmentation” (AF), yet the term is used loosely in the literature and has not been formally distinguished from adjacent constructs such as distraction, multitasking, attention span, task-switching, mind-wandering, and smartphone addiction/compulsive use. No dedicated, psychometrically validated scale for AF currently exists; where researchers have needed to quantify AF, they have relied on proxy measures built for other purposes — most recently a reverse-scored trait-mindfulness scale (Bayaskar &amp; Sharma, 2026). This manuscript (a) proposes a formal operational definition of AF grounded in the interruption and attentional-control literatures, (b) systematically differentiates AF from six related constructs and the instruments used to measure them, (c) documents a genuine, current, and specific measurement gap, (d) proposes a tentative five-dimensional structure to guide item generation, and (e) outlines a three-phase empirical program: item development, exploratory factor analysis, and confirmatory factor analysis with convergent, discriminant, and incremental validity testing for developing and validating an Attention Fragmentation Scale (AFS). This manuscript reports no new empirical data; it establishes the conceptual and methodological foundation for the validation studies that follow.

abstract_text: With the rapid development of generative artificial intelligence, AI feedback in EFL writing instruction has gained increasing attention. Grounded in social cognitive theory and self-regulated learning theory, this mixed-methods study compared AI-mediated and teacher-mediated feedback delivery modes and examined their relationships with writing performance, learning motivation, and self-regulated learning among 120 s-year English majors at Henan Normal University. A 16-week quasi-experimental pretest-posttest-delayed test design was combined with semi-structured interviews. Repeated measures ANOVA and mediation analysis (PROCESS macro) were used for quantitative analysis; thematic analysis was applied qualitatively. The AI-mediated feedback condition was associated with greater improvement in writing performance (group × time interaction: p < 0.001, η2p = 0.12), with the largest effect on grammatical accuracy (η2p = 0.16), higher writing self-efficacy (4.42→5.82), and reduced writing anxiety (3.95→2.78). Learning motivation and self-regulated learning positively correlated (r = 0.64, p < 0.001) and partially mediated the feedback condition to performance relationship (indirect effects: b = 0.38 and b = 0.45, respectively). Qualitative themes revealed learners’ adaptive progression from passive acceptance to critical AI usage. These findings extend feedback theory to the digital context and offer an integrated framework for AI-assisted language learning.

abstract_text: This study explored the lived experiences of high school students using ChatGPT in mathematics learning through a student engagement framework and the interpretive lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using a descriptive phenomenological design, data were gathered from 58 students through eight focus group discussions and analyzed using Colaizzi's method. The findings revealed that participants described ChatGPT as shaping their engagement in multiple ways. Students valued its accessibility, immediate feedback, and step-by-step explanations, which they described as supporting their participation, conceptual understanding, and confidence in learning mathematics. Emotional engagement was reflected in students' experiences of psychological safety and perceived support, while cognitive engagement was reflected in participants' perceptions that ChatGPT supported their understanding and critical evaluation of AI-generated responses. However, participants also reported disengaging experiences, including overreliance on ChatGPT, reduced interaction with teachers and peers, challenges in using mathematical symbols, and concerns regarding inaccurate responses. These findings suggest that participants perceived ChatGPT as creating both opportunities and constraints for meaningful mathematics learning. Interpreted through SDT, participants' accounts reflected experiences that may be interpreted as supporting or frustrating psychological needs related to autonomy, competence, and relatedness. This study contributes to the growing literature on AI-assisted learning by integrating student engagement and SDT to provide a nuanced understanding of students' experiences. The findings underscore the importance of guided AI use, critical evaluation, teacher support, and collaborative learning to promote meaningful and sustainable engagement in mathematics.

abstract_text: Effective collaboration and communication are vital to developer productivity and well-being, yet remain constrained by human factors such as attention, intrinsic motivation, and interpersonal accountability. These constraints are particularly vital for developers identifying with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), who navigate persistent environmental barriers in modern hybrid workplace settings. While developers with ADHD frequently rely on collaborative copresence practices (such as body doubling or pair programming) to support executive function, the recent emergence of agentic AI coding assistants has begun reshaping these collaborative dynamics. To investigate how developers with ADHD engage in human and AI-based copresence practices, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 14 software engineers with ADHD. Our findings reveal that while traditional human-human copresence provides critical social support and onboarding structure, it forces developers to constantly manage professional reputation and sacrifice personal privacy. Conversely, developers leverage emerging human-AI copresence to maintain accountability and cognitive flow without the social anxiety, performance judgment, or surveillance associated with human observation. Based on these empirical insights, we map developer copresence practices onto core dimensions of Goffman's copresence theory and Forsgren et al.'s SPACE framework of developer productivity, and provide design recommendations for AI-based tools that promote inclusive collaboration for developers with ADHD.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 Drawing on cognitive offloading theory and levels-of-processing theory, this study examined how conversational artificial intelligence (AI) learning support is related to university students’ critical thinking. Survey data from 426 students were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The results revealed two contrasting pathways. Conversational AI learning support was positively associated with both scaffolded cognitive offloading and substitutive cognitive offloading. Scaffolded cognitive offloading was positively associated with post-response deep processing, whereas substitutive cognitive offloading was negatively associated with it. Post-response deep processing was further positively associated with critical thinking. The moderating effect of AI evaluation literacy was not significant. The configurational results provided supplementary evidence that high critical thinking was more likely to occur when scaffolded cognitive offloading was present and substitutive cognitive offloading was low. These findings suggest that conversational AI may be more closely associated with critical thinking when learners continue to verify, question, reflect on, and revise AI-generated responses rather than simply accept them.

reading.interpretation: This study suggests that the relationship between conversational AI learning support and critical thinking depends not only on response quality, but also on how learners process AI-generated responses after receiving them. This argument is consistent with recent research indicating that generative AI may reshape cognitive offloading and learning processes (Yin et al., 2025; Seung & Basham, 2026) . The PLS-SEM results showed opposite scaffolding and substitution pathways, and the fsQCA results provided supplementary evidence that high critical thinking was more likely when scaffolded offloading was present and substitutive offloading was low. The findings should be interpreted cautiously because CT explained variance was modest and AEL moderation was nonsignificant. Overall, the findings suggest that conversational AI may have greater educational value when learners are encouraged to verify, question, compare, reflect on, and revise AI-generated responses rather than simply accept them.
reading.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample was mainly drawn from one university, so future studies should test the model across educational stages, disciplines, and institutions. Second, the cross-sectional self-report design limits causal interpretation; experimental designs, behavioral indicators, or longitudinal tracking would support stronger causal interpretations. Third, future work could compare text-based and multimodal tools and examine how interaction turns, feedback types, and prompt strategies shape cognitive offloading and critical thinking (Hutler et al., 2025) . Finally, the measurement of AI evaluation literacy, especially AEL1, should be refined.

Experts in educational technology, learning sciences, and research methodology reviewed conceptual relevance, clarity, and contextual appropriateness; pilot-test feedback further refined wording. The development and content validity procedures for the self-developed constructs are summarized in Table 3 . The full measurement items and scoring scheme are provided in Supplementary Material 1. The construct measurement and item design are summarized in Table 4 . Procedural controls for common method bias included anonymous responses, randomized item presentation, attention checks, and instructions that there were no right or wrong answers. Harman's single-factor test and full collinearity VIF diagnostics were also conducted. The results did not indicate a serious common method bias concern. Harman's single-factor test extracted six factors with eigenvalues above 1, and the first factor explained 24.86% of the variance, below the 40% threshold. The common method bias results are reported in Table 6 . Full collinearity VIF values ranged from 1.18 to 1.57, below 3.3. The full collinearity VIF results are shown in Table 7 . Descriptive statistics showed no substantial skewness or kurtosis problems. Correlations supported the dual-path logic: AIQ correlated positively with both SCO (r = 0.410) and SUCO (r = 0.329); SCO correlated positively with PRDP (r = 0.222), whereas SUCO correlated negatively with PRDP (r = -0.380). PRDP correlated positively with CT (r = 0.245), while SUCO correlated negatively with CT (r = -0.252). The near-zero correlation between AIQ and PRDP (r = 0.001) suggests possible offsetting effects between scaffolding and substitution. Descriptive statistics and correlations are reported in Table 8 .
analysis.results: For fsQCA, continuous variables were calibrated using the 95th percentile as full membership, the 50th percentile as the crossover point, and the 5th percentile as full non-membership. The variable calibration anchors are reported in Table 15. No single condition reached the 0.90 consistency threshold for necessity, and the necessary condition test results are shown in Table 16. Truth-table analyses used a frequency threshold of 3, with consistency cutoffs of 0.808 for high CT and 0.802 for low CT. The high-CT configurations showed recurring presence of SCO and absence of SUCO. HC1 linked high CT with SCO, low SUCO, and PRDP even under relatively low AIQ; HC2 linked high CT with high AIQ, SCO, low SUCO, and high AEL. Low-CT configurations more often involved absence of SCO and presence of SUCO, sometimes combined with insufficient PRDP or low AEL. The typical configurational results are reported in Table 17 and illustrated in Fig. 6 . Because several configuration-level and solution consistency values were below 0.80, these findings are interpreted as supplementary and exploratory configurational evidence rather than definitive causal pathways. The fsQCA solution coverage and consistency were 0.266 and 0.775 for high CT and 0.281 and 0.747 for low CT, indicating that the configurational evidence should be interpreted cautiously. The fsQCA solution parameters are summarized in Table 18 . IPMA further showed that PRDP had the highest importance for CT (total effect = 0.245, performance = 49.897), SUCO had a negative total effect (-0.106), and SCO had a positive but modest total effect (0.072). The IPMA results are reported in Table 19 . Within the current model, this pattern suggests that support quality and evaluation literacy alone were not strongly related to critical thinking; learners' continued verification, comparison, questioning, reflection, and revision showed a more direct association with critical thinking. The importanceperformance map for critical thinking is shown in Fig. 7 . The results provide preliminary support for the dual-path assumption. Conversational AI learning support was associated with both scaffolded and substitutive offloading. In the scaffolding pathway, AIQ was associated with SCO, which was positively related to PRDP and, indirectly, CT. In the substitution pathway, AIQ was associated with SUCO, and SUCO was negatively related to PRDP, which in turn was associated with lower CT. These opposing mechanisms may explain why the overall association between support quality and critical thinking was weak. PRDP emerged as the proximal explanatory process, suggesting that learners' continued active monitoring is central to whether conversational AI use is associated with more favorable critical thinking outcomes. The nonsignificant moderation of AEL suggests that evaluative knowledge alone may not automatically become verification behavior. Learners may understand that generated responses contain errors or biases but still rely on them for convenience, efficiency, or perceived authority. The fsQCA results provide a complementary view: AEL may matter more as part of specific configurations than as a simple linear moderator. High CT tended to appear when learners showed scaffolded offloading and low substitutive offloading, whereas low CT was more often associated with insufficient scaffolding, increased substitution, and weak post-response processing. However, given the modest R² for CT and the exploratory consistency of fsQCA solutions, these findings should be interpreted as evidence for a specific cognitive mechanism rather than as a comprehensive prediction model.
analysis.discussion: This study suggests that the relationship between conversational AI learning support and critical thinking depends not only on response quality, but also on how learners process AI-generated responses after receiving them. This argument is consistent with recent research indicating that generative AI may reshape cognitive offloading and learning processes (Yin et al., 2025; Seung & Basham, 2026) . The PLS-SEM results showed opposite scaffolding and substitution pathways, and the fsQCA results provided supplementary evidence that high critical thinking was more likely when scaffolded offloading was present and substitutive offloading was low. The findings should be interpreted cautiously because CT explained variance was modest and AEL moderation was nonsignificant. Overall, the findings suggest that conversational AI may have greater educational value when learners are encouraged to verify, question, compare, reflect on, and revise AI-generated responses rather than simply accept them.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the sample was mainly drawn from one university, so future studies should test the model across educational stages, disciplines, and institutions. Second, the cross-sectional self-report design limits causal interpretation; experimental designs, behavioral indicators, or longitudinal tracking would support stronger causal interpretations. Third, future work could compare text-based and multimodal tools and examine how interaction turns, feedback types, and prompt strategies shape cognitive offloading and critical thinking (Hutler et al., 2025) . Finally, the measurement of AI evaluation literacy, especially AEL1, should be refined.

title: Freirean Pedagogy for Equitable Assessment, Decolonial Governance, and Cognitive Wellbeing in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review
preview: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical frameworks and institutional policies, raising fundamental questions about the purposes of education in an algorithmic age. abstract_text: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence into higher education has outpaced the development of pedagogical frameworks and institutional policies, raising fundamental questions about the purposes of education in an algorithmic age. Paulo Freire’s critical pedagogy offers a powerful lens for interrogating the epistemological, ethical, and political dimensions of AI-mediated education, yet its application remains fragmented across disciplinary boundaries. This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and employed a systematic literature search across the Scopus database, supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. The search strategy combined terms related to Freirean pedagogy and liberating education with terms related to artificial intelligence, yielding a final corpus of 15 peer-reviewed open access journal articles published between 2021 and 2026, within the 2020–2026 eligibility window. Data extraction and thematic synthesis were conducted using the PEO framework, and risk of bias was assessed using appropriate tools. The synthesis identified four thematic clusters: epistemological foundations for critiquing algorithmic neutrality; redesign of assessment and governance practices; intersectional and decolonial dimensions of algorithmic harm; and psychological consequences of cognitive offloading. Key findings reveal that uncritical AI integration reproduces the banking model of education, systematically marginalizes nondominant epistemologies, and risks eroding critical thinking through cognitive debt. A critical framework organized around recognition, voice, and power, operationalized through credibility, comprehensibility, and control, is proposed. Freirean pedagogy retains transformative relevance when translated into design principles, governance mechanisms, and evaluative criteria that challenge algorithmic reductionism and center epistemic justice, relational agency, and collective liberation. The framework offers actionable guidance for equitable assessment redesign, participatory governance, and psychologically sustaining pedagogies in AI-mediated higher education.

Joseph & Areepattamannil (2025) document a decisive shift among faculty from "policing to design," demonstrating that educators reject detection tools in favor of assessments that foreground process, provenance, and critical judgment. Young et al. (2021) complement these analyses by proposing four organizing processes for human-machine partnerships, emphasizing accountability mechanisms, role freedom, and the awakening of critical consciousness as antidotes to workplace oppression. The synthesis thus demonstrates that sustainable assessment reform is inseparable from broader institutional governance, demanding transparent collaboration, infrastructural equity, and the active participation of all stakeholders. A third convergent finding concerns the pervasive and structurally patterned nature of algorithmic harm, which manifests most acutely along axes of gender, caste, language, and geography, systematically marginalizing non-dominant epistemic traditions. Begum et al. (2025) provides compelling empirical evidence from India, demonstrating that students from tribal and Indigenous language backgrounds face an 8.85-fold increase in algorithmic misrecognition compared to Hindi speakers, while those from Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe communities experience proctoring discomfort at rates 2.3 times higher than their privileged peers. Syamsiah & Aisyah (2025) examine gender justice in Indonesian Islamic higher education, revealing how patriarchal norms are both reinforced by conservative religious interpretations and potentially disrupted through digital platforms that enable anonymous feminist discourse. Omodan & Ngubane (2026) offer a systematic theoretical response through their CCC framework, which operationalizes epistemic justice by requiring that AI systems ensure credibility, comprehensibility, and control for marginalized learners. Karatsiori et al. (2026) extend this decolonial imperative to the global scale, critiquing universalist pretensions in Global Citizenship Education and advocating for a cartographic, ethical, and reflexive framework that resists epistemic extractivism and centers relational ethics and Indigenous ontologies. A fourth significant finding addresses the psychological and cognitive consequences of uncritical AI integration, revealing that the primary risk is not academic dishonesty but the cumulative erosion of critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and professional judgment through chronic cognitive offloading. Watts (2025) develops the concept of "cognitive debt," drawing on cognitive load theory and neuroscientific evidence to demonstrate that uncritical AI use results in skill decay and diminished capacity for independent judgment. Crimmins et al. (2026) empirically substantiate these concerns, finding that faculty resistance to AI reflects a form of "pedagogical care," a principled commitment to preserving the epistemic struggle through which genuine understanding is forged, and that faculty frame academic integrity as the preservation of judgment and meaning-making rather than rule compliance. Alqarni (2025) contributes a psychometric instrument, the Artificial Intelligence-Critical Pedagogy Scale, validated with 800 teachers, which identifies four dimensions of critical pedagogical competence and provides a measurable pathway for professional development. The synthesis thus establishes that the primary ethical imperative is the deliberate design of learning experiences that sustain cognitive engagement, metacognitive reflection, and durable mental models. Omodan & Ngubane (2026) articulate this most systematically, insisting that agency depends on being treated as a credible knower (recognition), having channels to shape meaning and criteria (voice), and holding decision rights over data and learning pathways (power). Young et al. ( 2021 ) complement this through their emancipatory organizing processes, emphasizing role freedom, mutual learning, and the identification of alternative futures as prerequisites for synergistic human-machine partnerships. Karatsiori et al. (2026) extend this vision to the planetary scale, urging institutions to move beyond neoliberal metrics and embrace a values-based pedagogy grounded in care, shared responsibility, and epistemic humility. The synthesis thus arrives at its definitive conclusion: the future of liberating education in the algorithmic age depends not on technological sophistication but on the sustained, collective cultivation of critical consciousness that alone can subvert algorithmic domination and reclaim education as a practice of freedom. analysis.limitations: The present synthesis, while offering a comprehensive critical framework for understanding AI-mediated education through the lens of Freirean critical pedagogy, is subject to several important limitations that must be acknowledged to appropriately contextualize its contributions and guide its application. First, the framework developed in this synthesis remains conceptually robust yet empirically unvalidated. As Espartinez (2026) explicitly acknowledges in his systemic framework, the model constitutes a "theoretically grounded hypothesis rather than an empirically established model," pending validation through prospective implementation studies. Similarly, Watts (2025) frames his cognitive debt model as a conceptual proposition that requires quasi-experimental evaluation to establish its efficacy in diverse educational settings. This conceptual nature implies that the practical feasibility, scalability, and transformative potential of the proposed framework have not been tested through longitudinal, mixed-methods implementation research across varied institutional contexts. Second, the geographical concentration of the reviewed empirical studies introduces significant contextual limitations. The synthesis draws predominantly on research conducted in Australia, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, the United States, and the United Kingdom, with limited representation from Sub-Saharan Africa, Latin America, and other regions of the Global South where infrastructural conditions, colonial histories, linguistic diversity, and educational governance structures differ substantially (Espartinez, 2026; Joseph & Areepattamannil, 2025; Syamsiah & Aisyah, 2025) . Begum et al. (2025) demonstrates how algorithmic biases manifest distinctly in postcolonial, multilingual contexts, suggesting that findings from one national setting may not transfer directly to others without careful contextual adaptation. Third, the rapid and ongoing evolution of generative AI technologies imposes temporal limitations on the synthesis, as the specific tools, policy frameworks, and institutional practices analyzed in the reviewed literature may become outdated within short timeframes, necessitating continuous updating and periodic reassessment of the framework's relevance (Joseph & Areepattamannil, 2025; Laidlaw, 2026) . Fourth, the synthesis privileges institutional and academic perspectives, with limited direct incorporation of student voices, particularly those from the most marginalized communities who are most affected by algorithmic governance and epistemic exclusion. As Laidlaw (2026) explicitly acknowledges, future work must centre student voices and engage with non-Western epistemologies to enrich theoretical understanding and global applicability, a gap that constrains the framework's capacity to fully represent the lived experiences, resistance strategies, and agency of learners themselves. Fifth, the reliance on English-language publications, while methodologically necessary, introduces a linguistic bias that may exclude regionally specific scholarship published in other languages, thereby potentially underrepresenting Indigenous epistemologies, local pedagogical innovations, and grassroots resistance movements that are not mediated through global academic publishing circuits (Begum et al., 2025; Karatsiori et al., 2026) . These limitations do not invalidate the synthesis but rather underscore the provisional, situated, and contestable nature of its claims, demanding that readers exercise critical reflexivity in adapting its insights to their specific institutional, cultural, and political contexts.

abstract_text: AI coding assistants are rapidly transforming software development, but are known to produce insecure code. Prior work has measured whether AI-assisted developers produce secure code, but less is known about how they evaluate AI-generated code: whether they can identify vulnerabilities, what cues they use, and how trust shapes their decisions. This evaluation step is foundational to secure development with AI, whether using auto-complete, chat tools, or AI agents. As a first step, we conducted a remote observational study with 100 participants isolating this evaluation stage. Participants were tasked with producing secure and functional code for four C linked-list tasks. For each, participants were able to cycle through five AI-generated suggestions varying in security and functionality, select one, and edit their choice into a final submission. Participants also completed a post-study survey about their decision-making and perception of AI-generated code's security and 23 completed a more in-depth interview.
