analysis.methods: The most frequently highlighted theme here was the need for chatbots to reflect the workplace realities of young women, providing support that is both personalised and empathetic, and attentive to genderspecific challenges shaping daily professional experiences. This section outlines the methodological approach used to investigate the ways in which young female workers experience and perceive the use of LLM-based chatbots for workplace mental health support. It describes the ethical considerations, subject scope and guiding research questions, before detailing the research design, participant recruitment process, survey materials, and analytical procedures of the study. The section concludes with an overview of both quantitative and qualitative data analysis strategies. Collectively, this methodology evidences the commitment of the study to rigour and ethical integrity, while affording space for exploring the possibilities and challenges suggested by this emerging area of digital mental health research. Participants were recruited in August 2023 via Prolific 55 , a reputable online crowdsourcing platform recognised as a high-quality, efficient medium through which to conduct behavioural and mental health research. These considerations are vital when nuanced, demographic-specific recruitment and data integrity are central to the research process 56 . Prior to full-scale distribution, seven pilot studies of 45 participants were conducted to determine average completion times; refine question wording; and optimise technical operation. 1. Age 25-34 years (inclusive) 2. Self-identified as female 3. Employed full-time 4. Having residence in the UK Participants received monetary compensation ranging from £1.00 to £1.50 for their time. Of 200 participants who completed the survey, 31 were excluded based on the following predefined criteria: duplicate responses; irrelevant answers to open-ended questions; responses that were overly brief or non-informative, completion times below five minutes; male gender identification; and non-targeted age group. The resulting sample included 169 female workers aged 25-34, representing diverse industries. The largest sectors included human health and social care (16.6%), education (16.6%), and professional, scientific, and technical activities (10.1%). Occupation types skewed towards skilled, non-manual roles: professional (39.6%), associate professional (28.4%), and managerial (14.2%), with sales and customer service accounting for 12.4%. Participants were primarily employed in the private (50.9%) and public (41.4%) sectors, with smaller proportions in non-profit (5.3%) and freelance/self-employed roles (2.4%). Working arrangements included hybrid (49.1%), on-site (36.1%), and fully remote (14.8%). Almost half of participants (45.0%) were employed by large organisations with over 1,000 employees. This sample provides a representative cross-section of young female workers in the UK, encompassing a range of organisational contexts, job roles, and workplace arrangements, and affording a meaningful exploration of mental health experiences and technology adoption behaviours. An online survey format was selected for both practical and methodological reasons. This approach enables efficient recruitment across multiple sectors, simplifying logistics and facilitating timely data collection. Importantly, the online format enhanced participant anonymity, a factor known to be critical when addressing sensitive topics such as mental health, reducing social desirability bias 57 . Meanwhile, the use of open-ended questions within a context of anonymity and convenience encourages participants to articulate nuanced experiences naturally and expansively, complementing quantitative insight in order to better understand the participant's experience of engaging LLM-based tools for mental health purposes, and draw out design implications. Survey development was informed by prior research on workplace mental health, the use of DMHIs broadly, and the use of LLM-based chatbots specifically 5, 31, 37, 38, 58 . Survey items were designed to capture both behavioural engagement and attitudinal drivers of adoption. To complement these structured measures, open-ended questions were included following Braun and Clarke's (2006) qualitative framework, enabling participants to share lived experiences and expectations beyond the constraints of numerical scales. The first part of survey consisted of 20 structured questions, organised into five domains: 1. Demographics: age; gender; industry; job role; organisation type and size; and working arrangement. 2. Perception of workplace mental health supports: managerial support; workplace culture; and employer initiatives. 3. Use of non-DMHIs: experiences and types of non-digital mental health interventions (e.g., physical activity, in-person counselling, mindfulness, and peer support). 4. Use of DMHIs: experiences; types of digital mental health interventions and digital devices (e.g., smartphone applications, wearable devices, or web-based resources); source of discovery; current usage, usage frequency and usage intentions; and willingness to share mental health-related data with employers. 5. Use and perception of LLM-based chatbots: experience using for work and workplace mental health purposes; perception of comfort, trust, willingness to use as a workplace mental health support, privacy concerns, and complementarity with human support; and desired functionality. This was followed by five open-ended exploratory questions: (1) the lived experience of participant workplace mental health challenges; (2) prior experience with DMHIs; (3) the perceived benefits of LLMbased chatbots as a workplace mental health support; (4) the perceived barriers to LLM-based chatbot adoption; and (5) suggestions for feature development to better support the mental wellbeing of young female workers in the workplace. Participants were provided with an anonymous link to a survey hosted on Qualtrics 59 , a secure and widely used platform in social and health research. On accessing the survey, participants were asked to review the information sheet and consent form, marking a confirmation checkbox accordingly, thereby confirming that informed consent was obtained from all participants and/or their legal guardian(s), before completing six sections: ( 1) demographic questions; (2) items on perception of workplace mental health supports; (3) use of non-DMHIs; (4) use of DMHIs; (5) use and perception of LLM-based chatbots; and (6) open-ended questions. After completion, participants were thanked and directed to a confirmation page.

analysis.discussion: This study examined how young female workers in the United Kingdom engage with LLM-based chatbots for workplace mental health support, highlighting both gender-specific and transferable design implications. Participants reported repurposing general-purpose LLMs to manage stress, regulate emotions, and organise workloads, demonstrating user-driven adaptation beyond their initial productivity-oriented purpose. This dual use reflects the evolving role of AI in professional environments, where tools can simultaneously address practical tasks and mental wellbeing. Beyond task support, participants' use of LLM-based chatbots also demonstrated potential to foster positive psychology in the workplace by enhancing resilience, emotional regulation, reflective capacity, and strengths-based coping strategies-aligning with the introduction's emphasis on digital interventions that not only reduce distress but actively cultivate employee engagement and flourishing. Analysis revealed two interrelated dimensions: gender-specific considerations and broader, transferable implications for workplace populations. Although the study focused on young women, many findings are applicable across demographics, particularly regarding the balance of trust, empathetic interaction, practical utility, and hybrid AI-human approaches, consistent with broader digital mental health research. Young female workers actively seek mental health support even in organisations perceived as promoting wellbeing, highlighting the need for gender-and user-sensitive design. Specific stressors identified included imposter syndrome, workplace inequality, burnout, anxiety in hierarchical or male-dominated contexts, and biological influences such as hormonal cycles. LLM-based chatbots that acknowledge these lived experiences are more likely to be perceived as relevant, empathetic, and supportive, suggesting that systems incorporating gender-sensitive guidance may enhance engagement. Prior research indicates that DMHIs tailored to contextual and user-specific factors improve adherence and perceived utility 31, 32 , aligning with Human-Centred Design (HCD) principles that emphasise alignment with social, psychological, and environmental contexts of users 33 . Beyond functional assistance, participants valued empathetic and nuanced communication. Research suggests that women are particularly attuned to relational and emotional cues in both face-to-face and digital interactions 34 . Effective workplace chatbots must therefore extend beyond information provision to acknowledge emotional states, validate experiences, and offer reassurance. Empathy in AI-mediated support has been associated with stronger engagement and greater perceptions of legitimacy and trustworthiness35. In workplace contexts, where psychological safety and perceived judgment are salient, empathetic communication may be critical for adoption 35 . Participants further emphasised integrating chatbots into existing workplace systems, such as workload management tools, while maintaining strong privacy protections. Clear guidance, transparent communication of system limitations, and structured onboarding were seen as essential. These findings align with HCD and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which highlight perceived usefulness and ease of use as central to adoption 33, 36 . When tools are embedded into workflows and endorsed organisationally, they are more likely to be perceived as legitimate components of workplace wellbeing ecosystems. Designing gender-sensitive LLM-based chatbots calls for empirically grounded frameworks that integrate contextual, psychosocial, and biological factors. For employers, integrating chatbots tailored to young women offers a practical avenue to enhance workplace wellbeing and demonstrate commitment to equity and inclusion. Effective deployment requires technological infrastructure, staff training, transparent governance, and alignment with human support systems. At a societal level, investing in empathetic and inclusive AI may help reduce gender-related disparities in mental health and workplace participation, fostering healthier and more equitable professional environments. Responsibly designed chatbots can extend beyond individual support to function as tools of organisational and social change. Alongside gender-specific considerations, participants highlighted transferable challenges influencing adoption across diverse groups. Key barriers included concerns regarding privacy, limited empathy, and the reliability of information and advice. Prior research indicates that reliability fosters cognitive trust, empathy cultivates affective trust, and privacy ensures moral and legal trust. These 'trust factors' provide a multidimensional foundation for technology adoption in sensitive domains such as mental health 37, 38 . The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT, 2003), and its health technology extensions, consistently show that trust mediates behavioural intention and actual use. For LLM-based technology, reliance on trust is amplified by hallucinations, biases, and unpredictable outputs. Combined with privacy risks, users bear the burden of validating information 39, 40 , highlighting the importance of trust for safe, ethical use. Privacy was the most prominent barrier to uptake, centring on concerns about data storage, access, sharing, and potential misuse of confidential information. Although anonymity was recognised as facilitating disclosure, participants feared data breaches or unintended exposure to managers or colleagues, consistent with literature emphasising confidentiality as critical for DMHI adoption, particularly in workplace contexts where disclosure carries professional risk 12 . Participants expressed ambivalence: while more comfortable sharing sensitive information with LLM-based chatbots than with colleagues, they remained wary of how data might be used or governed. Nearly half reported discomfort sharing personal information, whereas comfort was higher for voluntary or work-related data, such as workload indicators (30.0%) and self-reported stress (29.5%). These findings highlight a central design tension: anonymity can reduce stigma and create a safe reflective space, yet insufficient organisational transparency may erode trust. Robust safeguards, including transparent data policies, end-to-end encryption, and user control, are therefore essential for adoption, consistent with HCD principles emphasising clarity, accountability, and user empowerment 33 . Another uptake barrier was the inability of LLM-based chatbots to replicate human empathy and relational depth. Although LLMs can simulate aspects of cognitive empathy by recognising emotions and offering supportive responses, participants emphasised that the technology cannot match the emotional understanding and interpersonal support by humans 41 . In particular, trust-based 'interhuman bonds' were highlighted as essential not only for effective mental health support, but also for the adoption of the technology 42 . This aligns with Bickmore and Picard's [2005] work on relational agents, showing that users value AI companions primarily when they demonstrate empathy, continuity, and sensitivity to emotional states 37 . Human-AI companionship can complement, but not replace, human support in mental health interventions. LLM-based chatbots function effectively as both task and emotional supports. abstract_text:
Abstract 
                   Contemporary generative artificial intelligence software poses a threat to the development of critical thinking skills that sets it apart from the litany of prior technological developments that have raised similar concerns. This article adopts a metacognitive perspective on critical thinking in order to show that AI poses a risk of a critical thinking “death spiral” where AI use degrades critical thinking skill and thereby induces further harmful use. While the evidence on the harmful effects of cognitive offloading on critical thinking is not yet definitive, this article supports the case that AI risks undermining critical thinking abilities by appealing to two lines of evidence. The first is the alignment of features of contemporary AI software with psychological biases that will incline us to trust AI more as our reasoning capacities are degraded. The second draws on social epistemology to show that in the case of expertise identification, consideration of opposing perspectives, and use of evidential “stoppers,” AI undermines social practices and conventions that are constitutive of critical thinking. In light of these considerations, a precautionary principle requires that we do not teach AI skills as part of critical thinking skill development, at least until such time as we have stronger empirical evidence on how to do so without eroding the metacognitive capacity to recognize the right contexts for using rational strategies.

abstract_text:
Abstract 
                 This study investigates mechanisms and predictors associated with patterns and frequency of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) use among pre-service teachers. Traditional technology acceptance models often pay limited attention to context-specific issues such as cognitive offloading and institutional conditions for transparent AI use. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was applied to a subsample of active GenAI users (N = 629) drawn from a broader institutional sample of pre-service teachers (N = 695). The UTAUT framework was extended by incorporating perceived rules clarity, psychological safety, self-reported cognitive offloading, and pedagogical readiness conceptualized as AI-TPACK self-efficacy. The results indicate a strongly efficiency-driven pattern of GenAI use: Performance Expectancy (PE) emerged as the only significant UTAUT predictor of usage frequency (β = 0.66, p < 0.001), whereas Effort Expectancy, Perceived Academic Authority Influence, and Facilitating Conditions showed no significant independent associations. Perceived rules clarity was strongly associated with psychological safety (β = 0.61, p < 0.001). Usage frequency was positively associated with self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). AI-TPACK self-efficacy was positively associated with performance expectancy of GenAI (β = 0.20, p < 0.001), but it was not directly associated with lower self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.01, p = 0.839). These findings suggest that pre-service teachers’ perceived pedagogical readiness to work with AI may increase performance expectations, but does not automatically translate into lower self-reported reliance on GenAI for cognitively demanding study tasks. The study highlights the need for teacher education programmes to combine clear institutional rules, transparent AI-use practices, and metacognitive AI literacy.

The results suggest that GenAI use in teacher education cannot be understood merely as a matter of technical availability or general digital competence. In the tested model, Performance Expectancy emerged as the dominant factor associated with usage frequency (β = 0.658, p < 0.001), whereas Effort Expectancy, Perceived Academic Authority Influence, and Facilitating Conditions were not independent statistically significant predictors. GenAI use in this sample is therefore associated primarily with the perceived usefulness and efficiency of the tool. analysis.methods: The study employs a quantitative cross-sectional survey design. Its aim is not only to provide a descriptive analysis of the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), but primarily to test complex relationships between latent variables using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). This approach enables robust testing of a theoretical model that integrates an adapted technology acceptance framework (UTAUT) with pedagogical and psychological constructs: AI-TPACK, cognitive offloading, and psychological safety. Data were collected through an online questionnaire survey administered via the MS Forms platform. The target population consisted exclusively of students enrolled in teacher education programmes, that is, pre-service teachers, at the Faculty of Education, Masaryk University. Data collection targeted students in these programmes across all forms of study, both full-time and combined, including lifelong learning programmes aimed at obtaining a teaching qualification. The instrument was distributed through official institutional communication channels using the university information system between 3 January 2026 and 17 February 2026. Participation was voluntary, anonymous, and without any external incentives. The average completion time was 9 minutes and 33 seconds. The questionnaire began with informed consent and emphasized that the use of GenAI was not normatively evaluated in the context of the study, thereby reducing the likelihood of social desirability bias. The questionnaire was distributed by e-mail to the entire population of students in teacher education programmes (N = approximately 4,300). Data collection yielded 695 valid responses, representing an estimated response rate of approximately 16%. The study uses a large institutional sample of students in teacher education programmes at a single faculty of education. However, given the voluntary nature of participation and the response rate of approximately 16%, the risk of non-response bias cannot be excluded. The electronic data collection tool did not allow incomplete responses to be submitted for key constructs, thereby preventing the occurrence of missing values (missing data = 0%). Given the absence of missing values in this analytical sample, it was not necessary to test missingness mechanisms (MCAR/MAR/MNAR) or to apply advanced imputation techniques, such as FIML. The original dataset contained 698 responses. Systematic data cleaning was subsequently conducted. Three cases were excluded from the analysis due to extreme and invalid values indicating careless completion, specifically unrealistic age values. The final sample for analysis therefore consisted of N = 695 pre-service teachers in full-time and combined forms of study. The respondents' mean age was M = 24.3 years (SD = 6.62), ranging from 18 to 57 years. The higher maximum age and higher standard deviation are due to the presence of students in combined forms of study and in lifelong learning programmes, which is typical of Czech faculties of education. Of the total number of 695 respondents, women constituted the majority (n = 523; 75.3%), whereas men accounted for a smaller share of the sample (n = 172; 24.7%). The marked predominance of women in the sample (75.3%) is consistent with the national trend of feminization of the teaching profession and the demographic composition of faculties of education in the Czech Republic. In terms of study phase, the largest share consisted of students in bachelor's degree programmes (52.2%), followed by students in follow-up master's programmes (30.2%) and five-year master's programmes (17.6%). The detailed demographic composition of the research sample is summarized in Table 1 . The datasets analysed during the current study are not publicly available due to the need to protect respondents' privacy, but may be made available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.
analysis.discussion: This study aimed to examine the predictors and mechanisms of generative artificial intelligence This study examined the relationships between the use of generative artificial intelligence, technology acceptance constructs, perceived clarity of institutional rules, psychological safety, AI-TPACK selfefficacy, and self-reported cognitive offloading among pre-service teachers. The results suggest that GenAI use in teacher education cannot be understood merely as a matter of technical availability or general digital competence. In the tested model, Performance Expectancy emerged as the dominant factor associated with usage frequency (β = 0.658, p < 0.001), whereas Effort Expectancy, Perceived Academic Authority Influence, and Facilitating Conditions were not independent statistically significant predictors. GenAI use in this sample is therefore associated primarily with the perceived usefulness and efficiency of the tool. A second important finding is the strong positive association between perceived clarity of institutional rules and students' psychological safety when using GenAI (β = 0.607, p < 0.001). This result supports the conclusion that institutions should not leave GenAI use under implicit, inconsistent, or individually interpreted expectations. Clear rules alone do not resolve all issues of academic integrity, but they create conditions for more transparent communication about when AI use is legitimate, when it requires disclosure, and when it already replaces the student's own work. The results further show a positive association between the frequency of GenAI use and self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.554, p < 0.001). This relationship cannot be understood as direct evidence of a decline in cognitive abilities or learning quality, but it suggests that more intensive GenAI use may, for some students, be associated with a higher tendency to delegate certain study-related cognitive operations to an external tool. This points to a key pedagogical challenge: distinguishing the productive use of GenAI as support for learning from situations in which the tool replaces processes required for understanding, argumentation, and professional judgement. The pattern of relationships between AI-TPACK self-efficacy, Performance Expectancy, and cognitive offloading is particularly important. AI-TPACK self-efficacy was positively associated with Performance Expectancy (β = 0.197, p < 0.001), but was not significantly associated with lower levels of self-reported cognitive offloading (β = 0.013, p = 0.839). This result suggests that declared pedagogical readiness to work with GenAI may be linked to higher Performance Expectancy of the tool, but in this model it did not emerge as a factor associated with lower offloading. The supplementary analysis also showed a substantial difference between students' self-efficacy for personal study-related AI use and for its didactic integration into future teaching (Cohen's d z = 1.59). In other words, among pre-service teachers, personal experience with AI does not automatically translate into confidence that they can integrate it meaningfully and didactically into teaching. Two practical implications for teacher education follow from these findings. First, the development of AI literacy should not be reduced merely to the technical operation of tools or to general training in digital competencies. The preparation of pre-service teachers should also include a metacognitive and ethical dimension: the ability to recognize when AI supports learning, when it merely accelerates routine work, and when it may replace cognitive processes that should be part of one's own learning. Second, institutional policy should combine clear institutional rules with a safe space for transparent disclosure of AI use. In connection with the discussion on academic integrity, Academic Integrity Reporting (AIR) appears to be a suitable framework, shifting attention from mere detection to disclosure of use, interpretation of intent, feedback, and remediation (Peterson, 2025; An et al., 2025) . In this conception, the role of instructors is not limited to sanction-based control, but also includes guidance, critical validation, and support for responsible AI use. Institutional support should therefore aim to create conditions that may strengthen students' psychological safety and enable transparent disclosure of AI use to become part of dialogic assessment rather than a stigmatizing admission (AlBlooshi, 2026; An et al., 2025) . The study therefore suggests that it is important not only to teach students how to use GenAI, that is, to build AI-TPACK, but also to develop a responsible approach to their own learning. Future research should further test the identified relationships using longitudinal or experimental designs and complement self-report data with more objective indicators of learning quality, process data, or analyses of student outputs. Particular attention should also be paid to the design of academic tasks that allow GenAI to be meaningfully integrated without replacing key phases of learning, as well as to the group of students who consciously reject AI for ethical, environmental, or professional reasons.
analysis.limitations: The results of this study must be interpreted with awareness of its methodological, contextual, and conceptual limitations. First, the research is based on a cross-sectional design and uses self-report instruments. Although Structural Equation Modeling makes it possible to test theoretically specified relationships between latent variables, it does not allow strict causal conclusions to be drawn. The identified relationships should therefore be understood as directional associations interpreted within the proposed model, rather than as evidence of causal mechanisms. Since all main variables were measured through a single questionnaire at the same time point, common method bias cannot be fully excluded. The study is also based on data from a single faculty of education, which, together with the specific Czech cultural and institutional context, limits the generalizability of the results to different national, institutional, or educational systems. Given the voluntary nature of participation and the response rate of approximately 16%, the risk of non-response bias must also be acknowledged, as students with different levels of interest in GenAI, different experiences with these tools, or more pronounced attitudes may have been represented unevenly in the sample. Second, the study did not measure objective learning outcomes, the quality of student work, or the actual processes of working with GenAI. The observed relationship between frequency of use and self-reported cognitive offloading therefore cannot be interpreted as evidence of an actual "cognitive cost" of GenAI, a decline in critical thinking, or deterioration in academic performance. To examine these effects more directly, a longitudinal, experimental, or mixed-methods design would be necessary, including objective learning outcomes, process data, or analysis of student outputs. A major conceptual limitation is also the fact that the instrument used does not allow for a fine-grained distinction between adaptive offloading, that is, the strategic delegation of routine load in order to free up capacity for more complex cognitive operations, and maladaptive offloading, in which GenAI replaces one's own understanding, argumentation, or independent task solving. Similarly, AI-TPACK in this study was operationalized as self-efficacy, not as an objectively measured pedagogical, technological, or ethical competence. The interpretation of the results is further limited by the marginal fit of the structural model and by the rapidly changing GenAI environment, in which tools, institutional rules, and student practices are evolving quickly.

title: Reframing the human–robot ratio: Collaborative autonomy and the attention‐demand economy

abstract_text: Abstract The human–robot ratio is a useful design heuristic for supervisory robot control. However, advances in AI, computation, and reliable autonomy enable existing systems to extend beyond hierarchical supervision to more flexible organizations of interdependent team members. The human–robot ratio can be misleading for such organizations, so there is a need for a new way to understand teams of interdependent humans, robots, and AI agents. We propose the attention‐demand economy , a graph‐theoretic abstraction in which agents generate and transform attentional demands subject to bounded capacity. This abstraction exposes nonlinear scaling behavior, cascading supervisory requirements, and coordination bottlenecks that are masked under models that rely solely on the human–robot ratio. We demonstrate how the model can be used to (1) develop new system‐level metrics and (2) discover the source and extent of cascading failures. This paper also shows how a radar chart can be used to understand the overall difficulty of managing a human–robot team. The paper briefly demonstrates how the radar chart can be used to design the attention‐demand model. The primary message of this paper is a call to shift from optimizing human–robot ratios to designing organizations with justified attention flows.

title: Cognitive Offloading in the Age of AI: Are Students Thinking Less or Learning Differently?
venue: International Journal of Technology & Emerging Research

abstract_text: The rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into education has transformed the way students learn, solve problems, and access information. AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and intelligent tutoring systems have emerged as valuable learning companions, providing instant explanations, personalized guidance, and academic support. However, the increasing dependence on these technologies has raised concerns about cognitive offloading, a phenomenon in which individuals rely on external tools to perform cognitive tasks that would otherwise require memory, reasoning, or critical thinking. This paper provides an analytical review of recent research to examine whether AI is causing students to think less or enabling them to learn differently. By analyzing existing studies, the paper explores the impact of AI-assisted learning on critical thinking, memory retention, problem-solving abilities, creativity, academic performance, and learner autonomy. The findings indicate that while AI can enhance personalized learning, improve accessibility, and reduce cognitive workload, excessive dependence may weaken deep learning, independent reasoning, and long-term knowledge retention. The study concludes that AI should be viewed as a supportive educational partner rather than a replacement for human thinking. A balanced approach that combines AI-assisted learning with active cognitive engagement is essential to ensure meaningful learning and the development of higher-order thinking skills in the age of artificial intelligence. Keywords: artificial intelligence; AI in Education; Cognitive Offloading; Critical Thinking; Student learning

title: Academic Stress, Digital Distraction, and Student Engagement: Examining Their Impact on Learning Outcomes in Higher Education
preview: The issue of academic stress and constant connectivity to digital devices is a growing concern in higher education, and students' reactions to this stress are likely to impact their engagement, learning experiences and academic results. abstract_text: The issue of academic stress and constant connectivity to digital devices is a growing concern in higher education, and students' reactions to this stress are likely to impact their engagement, learning experiences and academic results. While there has been some scholarship on academic stress, on the use of the smartphone, on digital distraction, and on engagement with learning, there has been less scholarship on how these factors are linked and intertwined as part of the contemporary university learning environment. This gap is filled by this qualitative study that uses an interpretivist approach to explore the scholarly literature on how academic stress, digital distraction, student engagement, and learning outcomes relate. This study uses documentary analysis and thematic analysis of the existing peer-reviewed literature with an emphasis on literature from the past few years in higher education, educational psychology and digital-learning scholarship. The four interconnected patterns revealed by the thematic synthesis include: academic stress as a demand that reduces cognitive and emotional resources; digital distraction as a competing demand that fragmentates attention and can lead to disengagement; students' engagement as a learning process which is mediated by behavioral, emotional, and cognitive conditions; and learning outcomes as a result of the cumulative interaction between the demands of academic stress and the self-regulatory resources of students. In recent times, there's also growing evidence that overuse of the smartphone and digital multitasking can have a negative impact on academic performance, while strategic and goal-oriented technology use can enhance engagement (Martin et al., 2025; Troll et al., 2021). The literature also indicates that academic stress can adversely affect engagement and academic functioning, yet the relationship between academic stress and the respective outcomes can vary depending on the contextual and individual resources (Wunsch et al., 2021). Findings align with a demands–resources perspective of student wellbeing and engagement, suggesting that a combined analysis of academic and digital pressures is relevant. In practice, the study highlights the importance of institutional strategies that rely on student-centered engagement with the subject, a supportive learning environment, digital self-regulation, and workload management.

The main point is that academic pressure may diminish the psychological resources that support longer-term learning and digitally mediated distractions can further break them down. The implications vary significantly based on context, coping skills, digital behaviours, pedagogical approaches, and institutional support (Hsieh, 2025; Nkomo et al., 2021; Wunsch et al., 2021) . Based on the thematic synthesis, engagement seems to play a special role in this relationship. Students who are academically stressed might be emotionally drained, on the other hand, notifications, social media, entertainment, and multitasking can vie for focused attention that is needed for sustained academic processing. The findings of this study prove that mobile-phone distraction can affect students' immediate recall ability, highlighting the need to safeguard students' attentional resources when learning ( Chen et al., 2025) . But it can also enable communication, collaboration, information and meaningful participation when integrated purposefully into learning activities, through digital technology (Nkomo et al., 2021) . What is important is not the technology itself but whether its use facilitates purposeful engagement or creates cognitive and behavioral competing demands. Theoretically, the study is an integrated interpretation of student learning in discussing the student learning process by integrating Stress and Coping Theory, Cognitive Load Theory, Self-Regulated Learning Theory and Student Engagement Theory. These viewpoints collectively imply a learning outcome is forged through the dynamic interplay of academic requirements, coping capacities, attentional abilities, regulatory mechanisms, and involvement with learning contexts. This is a holistic view, which goes beyond looking at academic stress, smartphones or engagement as stand-alone variables. It also emphasizes the need to think about the kinds of engagement that are not necessarily the same as the kinds of learning that it is assumed they will bring. The conceptualization and measurement of engagement in technology-mediated learning (TML) has also been found to be a lot different across existing studies (Nkomo et al., 2021) . The development of behavioural participation, emotional involvement, and cognitive investment in a changing academic and digital environment should therefore be explored and researched further in higher education. The applications are as significant. Universities should steer clear of policies that only ban the use of the cell phone or that blame students for distracting themselves. Rather, institutions should put in place comprehensive wellbeing and learning strategies that integrate wellbeing and stress-management, digital self-regulation, healthy technology, distraction-aware learning spaces, supportive teaching and institutional wellbeing policy. Academic advising and counseling services can be used to provide effective suggestions for adapting to workload, tests, procrastination, and competing demands. Teachers can create learning tasks that promote continued engagement without undue disruptions to technology. Institutions can also offer guidance on how to manage notifications, practice focused learning, use social media responsibly, and how to balance connect and recover. Such interventions should take into account the fact that students' self-regulatory skills are shaped by their academic context and that whilst selfcontrol may be a personal responsibility, it is also a contextually influenced skill. The results highlight that students are aware of the importance of making informed digital habits a habit for themselves. Adjusting to a better environment can be achieved by silencing unnecessary notifications, setting periods for focused study, limiting technology use during leisure time, organizing workloads, taking breaks when necessary, and seeking assistance if workloads become too high. However, individual strategies should supplement not supplant institutional responsibility. Universities play an important role in developing realistic workloads, facilitating assessments in a supportive manner, providing easy access to counselling, psychologically supporting classrooms and establishing a learning environment that acknowledges students' cognitive and emotional needs. There are a number of caveat. The study was a qualitative one of the type documentary and so relied solely on previous studies of the students and on secondary literature. The synthesis is not able to identify cause and effect links among academic stress, digital distraction, engagement, and learning outcomes. Second, because of the varying definitions, measurement tools, educational setting, and methodology applied in the existing literature, it is not easily possible to compare the results. Third, while this review was primarily based on recent scholarship, the evolving technology landscape of digital makes it possible that evidence can become outdated as new platforms, applications, and patterns of technology use emerge. Finally, the credibility of documentary interpretation is always dependent upon the use of researcher judgements, even when such efforts have been made as systematic source selection, thematic comparison, and reflexivity. Documentary synthesis should thus be complemented by qualitative interviews and focus groups which would give further insight into how students themselves construe academic pressure, digital distraction, coping, and engagement, and, hence, how they speak about them. Longitudinal research can explore these relationships over the semesters and over testing periods more of the time than cross sectional research. Cross-cultural studies are also required since the academic and technological practices, institutional support systems and conceptions of students' wellbeing differ between societies. This study might provide information on the extent to which the patterns found in this study may be widely generalizable or strongly influenced by specific educational and cultural environments. Academic stress and digital distractions should be treated together as they can merge in the way students engage with the digital world. abstract_text: The integration of AI in higher education presents both opportunities and challenges, reshaping how students learn, collaborate, and produce knowledge. While AI offers benefits such as personalized feedback and expanded access to information, it also introduces risks, including cognitive offloading and the potential erosion of critical thinking. This chapter advocates for a shift towards critical AI literacy, which extends beyond technical proficiency to encompass analytical evaluation, ethical engagement, and metacognitive reflection. Set within the context of an online asynchronous course redesigned to prepare students for academic success with AI technology, the chapter explores design experiences, implementation strategies, and their implications. Further, the authors distill a framework for learning experience design focused on cultivating AI literacy. The chapter underscores the need for reflective engagement with AI and the development of pedagogical frameworks to ensure students are prepared for responsible, thoughtful participation in an AI-mediated world.

title: Why Young Consumers Regret the Click: Attention Economy Interruptions and Micro-Regret in Social Media Marketing
venue: International Journal of Computer Information Systems and Industrial Management Applications
preview: The study investigates how social media notification design shapes young consumers’ emotional and behavioural responses across the dominant platforms of Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and Twitter. Extending affect infusion theory, interruption science and digital choice architecture, the research introduces and validates micro-regret as an immediate, interruption-induced emotional reaction that arises prior to cogniti…
abstract_text: The study investigates how social media notification design shapes young consumers’ emotional and behavioural responses across the dominant platforms of Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and Twitter. Extending affect infusion theory, interruption science and digital choice architecture, the research introduces and validates micro-regret as an immediate, interruption-induced emotional reaction that arises prior to cognitive message processing. A cross-sectional survey of 300 young Indian social media users is analysed through structural equation modelling. Results demonstrate that four notification design attributes; frequency, timing, modality and persuasive message framing significantly increase micro-regret, which in turn negatively affects brand attitude and purchase intention while elevating disengagement behaviours. Mediation analyses confirm micro-regret as a central affective pathway linking design level features to downstream consumer outcomes. The study presents novel theoretical contributions by reconceptualising regret as a pre-decisional micro-emotion, reframing notification design as an affective architecture, and positioning disengagement as an emotional self-preservation strategy. Managerial implications highlight the need for emotionally sensitive notification systems, reduced digital intrusiveness and ethical attention practices. The research advances an emotionally grounded understanding of digital consumer behaviour in a hyper-connected environment.

abstract_text: Digital ecosystems collapse the same way physical ecosystems do: through extraction that outpaces regeneration. This paper argues that attention extraction and data-commons depletion constitute unpriced externalities in AI and platform governance, analogous to the unpriced carbon externalities that preceded the emergence of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) accounting. Two extraction vectors are identified: attentional extraction, evidenced by engagement-maximizing design features now subject to regulatory scrutiny, including the European Commission's July 2026 preliminary finding that Meta's Facebook and Instagram breach the Digital Services Act through addictive design; and data-commons extraction, evidenced by model collapse, the documented degradation of AI systems trained on recursively generated synthetic data. The paper argues that both vectors reflect a deeper structural pattern: a decoupling of reward from risk, in which the party capturing the value of extraction is not the party bearing its cost. Building on this diagnosis, the paper proposes DAESG: a three-layer accountability framework, comprising disclosure, standards, and capital allocation, structured to give financial governance functions a basis for treating digital ecosystem extraction as a material, disclosable, and manageable risk. The paper distinguishes DAESG from existing “Digital ESG” (DESG) literature, which addresses how digitalization improves corporate ESG performance rather than the extraction risks of digital ecosystems themselves.

title: From Gradual Release of Responsibility to Gradual Release of Technology: A Case for the Staged Use of AI in Formal Education
abstract_text: Debate over the role of generative artificial intelligence in formal education is marked by sharply divergent claims about its effects on student learning. Much of this disagreement reflects a failure to distinguish immediate performance gains from durable learning. This article addresses a central gap in the literature by focusing on when and how students should be permitted to rely on AI. It introduces the Gradual Release of AI-Technology (GRAIT) model, extending Pearson and Gallagher’s gradual release of responsibility to the staged use of cognitively substantive AI-technologies in formal education. The model distinguishes gradual release of responsibility, which concerns who performs the cognitive work, from gradual release of technology, which concerns when and how that work may be scaffolded, augmented, or offloaded. Three phases are proposed: independent cognition, where foundational knowledge and skill are developed without AI substitution; shared (entangled) cognition, where AI is introduced through constrained, teacher-guided interaction; and offloaded cognition, where learners strategically delegate and reallocate aspects of thinking once risks to learning are minimal and opportunities emerge elsewhere. Progression depends on demonstrated knowledge, skill proficiency, and epistemic readiness. The central question is not whether students should use AI, but who should use it, when, how, and under what conditions it should be embraced or avoided.

abstract_text:
This randomized controlled experimental study examined the impact of intermittent digital distraction on cognitive executive functions within simulated social and work environments. The primary objective was to evaluate potential cognitive interference induced by audiovisual stimuli across behavioral (error rate), neurophysiological (spectral EEG parameters), and subjective (perceived workload via NASA-TLX) dimensions. The research sample comprised 87 adult participants (students, managers, and employees), randomly assigned to an experimental group (

The experimental protocol utilized a battery of psychodiagnostic tasks assessing working memory (Dual N-back), inhibitory control (Stroop task), and selective attention (d2-R), synchronized with continuous 7-channel EEG recording via the LSL protocol. Data were analyzed using Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMM), ANCOVA, and Spearman partial correlations. Behavioral analysis revealed no statistically significant main effect of digital distraction on overall error rates in the Dual N-back and Stroop tasks. A potential interaction between group and stimulus congruency in the Stroop task was observed (

Subjective perceived workload significantly correlated with error rates exclusively during working memory tasks. In conclusion, under the current experimental conditions, intermittent audiovisual distraction did not result in a statistically significant degradation of primary task accuracy, suggesting that participants maintained behavioral performance over short time intervals.

analysis.methods: The scientific research is conceived as a complex experimental design carried out in a controlled environment of a psychological laboratory with the aim of objectifying the impact of intermittent digital distraction on executive functions in a heterogeneous sample of students and employees. The main methodological pillar is the integration of a proprietary software application that synchronizes behavioral psychodiagnostic tasks (Dual N-back, Stroop test) with continuous neurophysiological recording using a 7-channel EEG system Brain Products X.on. The experimental procedure simulates common digital interference in real time through standardized audiovisual notifications with an intensity of 60 dB, which are inserted into the process at pseudo-random intervals. The accuracy of data collection is ensured by the LSL protocol, which allows for rigorous segmentation of neurophysiological markers, namely spectral analysis of fm-Theta and Alpha rhythms, as well as analysis of event-related potentials (P300 amplitude). Objectively measured parameters of executive error rate and reaction times are supplemented in the final phase with subjective scaling of mental load using the NASA-TLX questionnaire and measurement of residual capacity of selective attention using the d2-R test. The research sample ( n = 87) consisted of male ( n = 12) and female ( n = 18) psychology teachers aged 19–24 (AM = 21.4; SD = 1.2) from the University of Constantine the Philosopher in Nitra, who were selected for our research by purposive sampling. Our research also included male ( n = 16) and female ( n = 13) managers from various companies aged 28–54 (AM = 41.2; SD = 7.8) who participated in the research based on an online call. Ordinary employees from various companies ( n = 28) aged 24–58 (AM = 36.7; SD = 9.4) also participated in the research. We randomly divided the research participants into an experimental ( n = 45) and a control ( n = 42) group by drawing lots. The study took place in the psychological laboratory at the Department of Educational and School Psychology, Constantine the Philosopher University in Nitra, Slovakia. Data collection was carried out over a period of 4 months, from October 2024 to March 2025. The laboratory environment was sound-attenuated, temperature-controlled ( 21 ∘ C − 22 ∘ C ), and maintained under constant artificial lighting to minimize external sensory noise. The experimental protocol consisted of a battery of five methods ordered by cognitive demand and measurement goal, with an emphasis on objectifying working memory and inhibition processes. The duration of the measurement for one participant was 30 min. This multimodal task is considered one of the most demanding paradigms for measuring working memory ( Jaeggi et al., 2008 ). It requires simultaneous processing of auditory and visual stimuli, while activating the fronto-parietal network, especially the dlPFC and ACC ( Kerns et al., 2004 ). The method tests the limited capacity of working memory slots ( Cowan, 2001 ) through the processes of updating, inhibition and attention switching. A multidimensional rating scale ( Hart, 2006 ) serves to objectify the subjective perception of cognitive load. It tracks six dimensions: mental, physical and time demands, performance, effort and frustration. The design allows for a comparison of objective performance with the degree of conscious effort expended on suppressing distractions via the rIFG-STN pathway. A neuropsychological method ( Stroop, 1935 ) aimed at measuring cognitive interference arising from a conflict between automated reading and conscious color naming. The test serves as a detector of the effectiveness of inhibitory control, while monitoring the interference score and the prolongation of reaction time to incongruent stimuli. A performance test ( Brickenkamp et al., 2010 ) measures selective attention and visual discrimination under time pressure. The inclusion of the “pencil-paper” method at the end of the battery allows for the quantification of residual mental fatigue and stability of concentration (CP index) after previous exposure to intermittent digital distractors. A 7-channel wireless system using active sensor technology to eliminate electromagnetic noise. The device allows millisecond synchronization with the stimulation software via the LSL protocol, which is crucial for the analysis of event-related potentials and spectral analysis of waves (fm-Theta, Alpha) in the prefrontal regions of the brain. Data analyses were performed in the statistical software environment R (version 4.4.3), using several specialized packages. The dplyr, tidyr, and readr packages were used for data manipulation and transformation. The lme4 and lmerTest packages were used for mixed models, sandwich and lmtest for calculating robust standard errors and testing models, and robustbase for robust regression. The effsize package was used for calculating effect sizes. Inferential analysis of RQ1 examined the effect of audio-visual distraction on error rates (ER%) in the Dual N-back and Stroop tasks. Given the non-normal distribution of error rates (Shapiro–Wilk; Stroop: W = 0.486, p < 0.001; Dual N-back: W = 0.866, p < 0.001) and the presence of a floor effect in the Stroop task (skewness = 3.34), a generalized linear mixed model with logit transformation was applied. The model did not reveal a statistically significant interaction between group and task type ( b = −0.41, SE = 0.38, z = −1.07, p = 0.285, OR = 0.66), indicating that the effect of distraction did not differ between the working memory and inhibition domains. The main effect of task type was significant ( b = −1.71, SE = 0.28, z = −6.20, p < 0.001, OR = 0.18), with the error rate in the Dual N-back task ( M = 23.9%) being significantly higher than in the Stroop task ( M = 6.8%). The main effect of group was not statistically significant ( b = 0.22, SE = 0.29, z = 0.76, p = 0.448, OR = 1.24), which is also confirmed by the descriptive data: Dual N-back : control group ( M = 23.69, SD = 20.50) vs. experimental group ( M = 24.14, SD = 20.42). Stroop test : control group ( M = 7.50, SD = 15.97) vs. experimental group ( M = 6.22, SD = 12.14). Analysis of covariates (age: p = 0.880; gender: p = 0.305; education: p = 0.403) showed no systematic effect on error rates. The results do not provide empirical support for the assumption that intermittent digital distraction increases error rates in working memory or inhibitory control tasks. Research Question 2 (RQ2) examined whether a significant difference exists in total concentration performance (CP) on the d2-R test between the experimental group (exposed to distractions) and the control group. All assumptions for the Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA) were met, including the normality of distribution (Shapiro–Wilk: W = 0.978, p = 0.148), normality of residuals ( W = 0.981, p = 0.255), and homogeneity of variances [Levene’s test: F (1,84) = 0.003, p = 0.954]. Homogeneity of regression slopes was confirmed, and multicollinearity was negligible (VIF < 1.10 for all predictors). Descriptive statistics indicated a numerically higher average performance in the experimental group ( M = 120.57, SD = 43.61) compared to the control group ( M = 113.29, SD = 48.53), though high inter-individual variability was observed in both samples. The ANCOVA revealed no statistically significant main effect of the group ( F = 1.77) = 0.47, p = 0.496, partial n 2 =0.006. The regression coefficient for the difference between groups remained non-significant [ b = −6.91, SE = 10.11, t (77) = −0.68, p = 0.496, 95% CI (−27.04, 13.22)] after controlling for all covariates. Among the included covariates, age ( p = 0.461), gender ( p = 0.944), education ( p = 0.675), and accuracy in the Stroop task ( p = 0.129) showed no significant effect. In contrast, accuracy in the Dual N-back task was a significant predictor of concentration performance [ F (1,77) = 4.64, p = 0.034, partial n 2 = 0.57, b = 54.70, SE = 25.40, t (77) = 2.15]. This indicates that higher working memory accuracy was associated with higher concentration performance in the d2-R test. The overall model explained 13.5% of the variance in concentration performance ( R 2 = 0.135, adjusted R 2 = 0.045). In conclusion, the results do not suggest that intermittent audio-visual distraction leads to a decrease in concentration performance on the d2-R test. Instead, performance differences appear to be driven by individual differences in working memory capacity rather than the experimental manipulation itself. Research Question 3 investigated the relationship between cognitive error rates and subjective mental workload measured by the NASA-TLX subscales (Effort, Frustration, Mental Demand). Due to the non-normal distribution of error variables, Spearman’s correlation ( ρ ) was employed. To control for Type I error across nine correlations, the Holm–Bonferroni correction was applied. To investigate whether increased error rates are associated with a specific neurophysiological profile (RQ4), two separate hierarchical linear regressions were conducted for the Stroop and Dual N-back tasks. The models were based on 76 participants, with the experimental group included as a covariate in the first step and log-transformed EEG indicators (frontal theta and parietal alpha) added in the second step. The hierarchical regression analyses provide no evidence that increased error rates in either task are significantly associated with specific theta or alpha activity. In both cases, neurophysiological indicators failed to add predictive value beyond the group covariate. Furthermore, the extreme correlation between the EEG bands suggests that any potential relationship with performance would likely be tied to a shared neural component rather than specific frequency band activity. We validated our RQ5 in which we investigated to what extent subjectively felt cognitive load (NASA-TLX) correlates with objective neurophysiological parameters (Alpha and Theta bands) in the studied groups? To examine the relationship between subjectively felt cognitive load and neurophysiological parameters, we used Spearman partial correlations, while also controlling for the group variable. We conducted the analysis separately for the Stroop and Dual N-back tasks and included the relationships between the total NASA-TLX score and log-transformed measures of frontal theta and parietal alpha activity. The results of the analysis in the Stroop task showed no significant relationship between subjectively felt workload and EEG parameters, which indicates the absence of a consistent link between the internal experience of effort and neurophysiological indicators in this domain. In contrast, in the Dual N-back task, a statistically significant negative relationship was identified between subjective cognitive workload and parietal alpha activity, indicating that an increase in perceived mental effort was directly correlated with a decrease in alpha oscillations. Overall, it can be stated that the correlation between subjective effort and neurophysiological activity was selectively manifested only in tasks focused on working memory, while this relationship was not confirmed in other cognitive tasks.
analysis.discussion: The interpretation of the findings in the framework of the presented scientific research brings a comprehensive view of the dynamics between digital interference and the executive apparatus of the human brain. When analyzing the first research question (RQ1), which examined the error rate in tasks focused on working memory and inhibitory control under the influence of audio-visual distraction, the results indicate a remarkable ability of short-term adaptive resilience of the executive system. Although Ward et al. (2017) postulate that the suppression of irrelevant stimuli itself consumes a critical amount of energy and leads to cognitive drain, our participants were able to maintain performance accuracy even under experimental conditions. This phenomenon can be explained through the lens of Kurzban et al.’s (2013) cognitive effort model, according to which subjective psychological experience and mobilization of internal resources enable the suppression of distractors without immediate performance degradation. In practice, it was shown that participants perceived digital notifications as unwanted noise and consciously increased cognitive input to eliminate the error rate, which is also confirmed by the observed “floor effect” in the Stroop task. However, the higher error rate in the Dual N-back test compared to the Stroop test ( p < 0.001) indicates that the working memory updating processes are more executively demanding than pure motor or cognitive inhibition, although in neither case did distraction cause system collapse. Reflecting the findings of Aron et al. (2014) , the absence of prolongation of reaction times suggests that the hyperdirect rIFG-STN pathway was not paralyzed by the presence of digital stimuli, which indicates the stability of cognitive control across demographic covariates such as education or gender, thereby partially correcting the assumptions of Knox and Wolohan (2014) about the influence of cognitive reserve on short-term resilience. In the second research question (RQ2), which monitored the stability of concentration in the d2-R test after exposure to distractions, it was shown that cumulative cognitive fatigue did not leave a significant trace in the subsequent selective attention ability ( p = 0.496). This result is scientifically intriguing, especially in the context of Cowan’s model (2011), which assumes that the suppression of distractors occupies slots in working memory, which theoretically should lead to subsequent exhaustion. However, our data suggest the presence of cognitive plasticity and compensation ( Ding et al., 2025 ), where the increased alertness (arousal) induced by distraction persists and paradoxically stabilizes subsequent performance. The key finding of VO2 remains that the strongest predictor of concentration in the d2-R test was accuracy in the Dual N-back test ( p = 0.034), confirming that individual working memory capacity and prefrontal circuit stability are more dominant for performance than external stimuli. From a neuropsychological perspective, this implies that individuals with a more robust central executive are able to switch more effectively between demanding cognitive operations and routine administrative control, with this stability acting as a protective factor against residual fatigue from digital interference. The third research question (RQ3) focused on the relationship between error rate and subjectively felt mental effort (NASA-TLX), with the results yielding a differentiated picture depending on the type of task. A significant correlation between error rate and subjective load (effort ρ = 0.34; frustration ρ = 0.41) was confirmed exclusively in the Dual N-back test. We explain this finding through metacognitive processing ( Menon and D'Esposito, 2022 ), where participants were clearly aware of moments of failure and loss of continuity during demanding information updating, which led to an increase in perceived frustration. On the contrary, this correlation was absent in the Stroop and d2-R tests, suggesting that inhibition processes controlled by more autonomous rIFG-STN pathways ( Aron et al., 2014 ) may not be perceived by consciousness as enormously demanding unless they lead to massive interference. Thus, digital distraction appears to increase the “cost of performance” especially where there is a direct competition for slots in working memory ( Ward et al., 2017 ), while during routine administrative tasks individuals may not be aware of the latent weakening of their attention, which may be a risk factor in a real work environment. The fourth research question (RQ4) investigated the existence of a specific neurophysiological profile associated with increased error rates. The analysis encountered methodological limitations in the form of extreme multicollinearity between theta and alpha activity (r > 0.98), suggesting that in our experimental setting these bands represented a common neurophysiological substrate of cortical excitation. Nevertheless, the results yielded a crucial finding about the stability of the alpha rhythm in the experimental group ( p = 0.002). Instead of the expected fragmentation of attention, intermittent distraction led to a significant increase in the stability of alpha activity, which we interpret as a neurophysiological “shield” or state of hyper-focus ( Ashinoff and Abu-Akel, 2021 ). This sensory gating mechanism ( Klimesch, 2012 ) allowed participants to suppress digital stimuli as irrelevant noise, thereby proactively protecting the attention devoted to the primary task ( Braver, 2012 ; Anderson and Levy, 2009 ). The stabilization of parietal neuronal networks thus serves as a reactive tool for selective resource targeting in the short term. The last research question (RQ5) analyzed the correlation between subjective workload and neurophysiological parameters (fm-Theta and Alpha). While no relationship was found in the Stroop task, a significant negative correlation was identified between perceived effort and parietal alpha activity in the Dual N-back task ( ρ = −0.31). Lower levels of alpha activity at high perceived workload indicate that the central executive had to make a massive effort to maintain the goals in memory ( Klimesch, 2012 ). However, an interesting finding is the absence of an increase in fm-Theta activity in the experimental group, which contradicts the models of Langner et al. (2018) and Guo et al. (2018) . This fact suggests that participants habituated to the distraction very quickly and their ACC did not evaluate it as a priority cognitive conflict ( Goldin-Meadow et al., 2001 ). Paradoxically, at higher perceived effort, fm-Theta activity even decreased ( r = −0.31), indicating that at maximum concentration the brain suppressed the monitoring of the external environment in favor of the primary goal. title: Impact of Smartphone Multitasking on Self-Reported Attention and Memory Difficulties among Indian Undergraduate Students

abstract_text: Smartphones have become an indispensable part of undergraduate students' academic and personal lives. While they provide convenient access to educational resources and communication platforms, frequent multitasking with smartphones during academic activities may be associated with cognitive challenges. The present study examined the relationship between smartphone multitasking and self-reported attention difficulties and self-reported memory difficulties among Indian undergraduate students. A quantitative cross-sectional correlational design was employed. Data were collected from 154 undergraduate students aged 18?24 years using a structured online questionnaire consisting of demographic questions, a Smartphone Multitasking Scale, a Self-Reported Attention Difficulties Scale, and a Self-Reported Memory Difficulties Scale. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson's Product-Moment Correlation, independent-samples t-tests, and one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). The findings demonstrated a significant positive relationship between smartphone multitasking and self-reported attention difficulties (r = .772, p < .001). A significant positive relationship was also observed between smartphone multitasking and self-reported memory difficulties (r = .659, p < .001). No statistically significant differences were identified across gender or academic year. The findings suggest that greater engagement in smartphone multitasking is associated with increased self-reported attention and memory difficulties among undergraduate students. Although causal conclusions cannot be drawn, the study contributes to the growing literature on digital behaviour and cognitive functioning and highlights the importance of promoting healthy smartphone use during academic activities.

While they provide convenient access to educational resources and communication platforms, frequent multitasking with smartphones during academic activities may be associated with cognitive challenges.
reading.methods: A quantitative cross-sectional correlational research design was adopted. The study included 154 undergraduate students aged between 18 and 24 years recruited through convenience sampling from colleges and universities across India.
reading.findings: The reliability analysis demonstrated excellent internal consistency for all three scales, with Cronbach's alpha coefficients exceeding .90. Descriptive statistics indicated moderate levels of smartphone multitasking, self-reported attention difficulties, and selfreported memory difficulties among participants. Pearson's correlation analysis revealed a significant positive relationship between smartphone multitasking and selfreported attention difficulties (r = .772, p .05). Similarly, one-way ANOVA indicated no statistically significant differences across academic years.
reading.interpretation: The findings indicate that greater smartphone multitasking is associated with increased self-reported attention and memory difficulties among undergraduate students. These findings support Cognitive Load Theory (Sweller, 1988) , which proposes that excessive cognitive demands reduce the resources available for effective learning, and Executive Attention Theory (Posner & Petersen, 1990) , which highlights the role of attentional control in managing competing information. The observed relationships are consistent with previous studies reporting that media multitasking is associated with attentional disruption, reduced academic engagement, and subjective memory complaints (Ophir et al., 2009; Wilmer et al., 2017) . However, the absence of significant differences across gender and academic year suggests that smartphone multitasking is a common behaviour among undergraduate students irrespective of demographic characteristics. The present study demonstrated that smartphone multitasking is positively associated with self-reported attention difficulties and self-reported memory difficulties among Indian undergraduate students. These findings contribute to the growing literature on digital behaviour and cognition within higher education and emphasise the importance of encouraging balanced smartphone use during academic activities. Future research should employ longitudinal designs, objective cognitive assessments, and larger, more diverse samples to further investigate these relationships.

title: Is It Mine or Not Mine? Cognitive Offloading to Generative AI and Concern over the Erosion of Cognitive Ownership
preview: Cognitive offloading—delegating cognitive work to external tools—is basic to human cognition, but generative AI (GenAI) amplifies it radically: entire cognitive products can now be produced on request. abstract_text: Cognitive offloading—delegating cognitive work to external tools—is basic to human cognition, but generative AI (GenAI) amplifies it radically: entire cognitive products can now be produced on request. This sharpens a question about agency over one’s own thinking: when cognition is habitually offloaded, does its product still feel like one’s own? We surveyed 239 pre-service teachers, operationalizing the felt loss of cognitive ownership as concern over the erosion of teaching-design subjectivity (TSC)—the metacognitive appraisal that AI-assisted work is not genuinely one’s own and that independent capacity is declining. Guided by the Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution (I-PACE) model, we tested whether AI anxiety/fear of missing out (affective) and impulsivity (self-regulatory) relate to this concern through behavioral GenAI dependency—habitual offloading. In a structural equation model with bias-corrected bootstrapping, dependency strongly predicted TSC and partially mediated the effect of AI anxiety; impulsivity raised dependency but showed a suppression pattern (a positive indirect effect offset by a null total effect), and the model explained 35% of the variance in the concern. Habitual offloading—that is, GenAI dependency—rather than generic AI use, accompanies the metacognitive loss of cognitive ownership.

analysis.methods: Participants were 239 pre-service teachers (education-major university students) in Eastern China, recruited by convenience sampling from a larger, voluntary web-based survey of university students’ GenAI use. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Qingdao University. Informed consent was obtained online: the consent statement appeared on the first screen of the questionnaire and had to be accepted before any item could be accessed. From the 264 respondents in the teacher-education track, to whom the teaching-subjectivity items were administered, we excluded those who reported never having used GenAI and a small number whose responses showed no variance across the focal items, yielding the analytic sample of 239. The sample was 92.9% female and was concentrated in the second and third years of study, and reported GenAI use ranged from monthly or less to several times per day, with most respondents using it weekly or more. Full demographic and usage characteristics are reported in Table 1 . Demographic and GenAI-Use Characteristics (N = 239). Note. n = number of respondents; percentages are column percentages. All constructs were measured on seven-point Likert scales (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). Because concern over the erosion of teaching-design subjectivity (TSC) is a newly introduced construct without existing instruments, the authors developed a scale for them following established scale-development guidance ( Clark & Watson, 2019 ; Boateng et al., 2018 ). Item development proceeded from explicit construct definitions—grounded in the teacher-agency and professional-identity literature ( Vähäsantanen, 2015 )—to an initial item pool written to reflect each definition, which the research team then reviewed and refined for clarity and content coverage; the full item wording is provided in the Appendix A . Other scales including AI anxiety and fear of missing out (ANX; six items), Impulsivity (IMP; two items), and Behavioral GenAI dependency (DEP; four items) were adopted from Jiang and Wang ( 2026 ). Analyses were conducted in R using lavaan. We used structural equation modeling because it estimates the constructs as latent variables—correcting the structural paths for measurement error—and lets the mediation hypotheses be tested directly. Because the items departed only modestly from multivariate normality, the confirmatory factor analysis and the structural model were estimated with the robust maximum likelihood (MLR) estimator, and indirect effects were evaluated with bias-corrected bootstrapping using 5000 resamples ( Preacher & Hayes, 2008 ; MacKinnon et al., 2004 ). Model fit was assessed against the criteria of CFI and TLI at or above 0.95 and RMSEA and SRMR at or below 0.08 ( Hu & Bentler, 1999 ). Two within-factor residual covariances between similarly worded items were freed on the basis of modification indices and theoretical justification ( Cole et al., 2007 ). Because all measures were self-reported, the potential for common method bias was examined ( Podsakoff et al., 2003 ). Although seven-point Likert items are ordinal, items with five or more ordered categories, provided their thresholds are not extremely asymmetric, are recovered accurately when treated as continuous under a robust estimator, and with seven categories continuous estimation is often preferable ( Rhemtulla et al., 2012 ; Robitzsch, 2020 ; C.-H. Li, 2016 ); because our items depart only modestly from symmetry, we therefore used MLR for the primary analysis and, as a robustness check, re-estimated every model with the ordinal WLSMV (polychoric) estimator ( Section 5.3 ). All standardized loadings were substantial and significant, and every construct exceeded conventional thresholds for reliability and convergent validity (composite reliability: ANX = 0.89, IMP = 0.79, DEP = 0.80, concern = 0.90; average variance extracted: ANX = 0.63, IMP = 0.65, DEP = 0.58, concern = 0.64; Table 2 ). Because impulsivity was measured with two items—for which Cronbach’s alpha is not the most appropriate reliability estimate ( Eisinga et al., 2013 )—we relied on composite reliability from the CFA. Because the focal outcome is a form of concern, its discriminant validity from AI anxiety is the critical measurement question, and we addressed it directly. The two constructs were only moderately correlated (φ = 0.42), their heterotrait–monotrait ratio of correlations was well below the recommended 0.85 threshold (HTMT = 0.44; Henseler et al., 2015 ), and a model that merged the anxiety items and the concern items into a single factor fit far worse than the four-factor model (CFI dropping from 0.97 to 0.74; scaled Δχ 2 (3) = 187.64, p < .001). Concern over the erosion of teaching-design subjectivity is therefore empirically distinct from AI anxiety rather than a relabeling of it. Discriminant validity among the remaining constructs was likewise supported, with all HTMT ratios at or below 0.50; in particular, although several concern items reference reliance on AI, the concern remained discriminant from dependency (HTMT = 0.49).
