analysis.discussion: In the present study, we investigated whether and to what extent humans offload parts of an attentionally demanding task to an algorithm-and whether prior information about this algorithm affects the human tendency for offloading. In two experiments, participants performed a multiple object tracking (MOT) task, either alone (Solo condition) or together with a socalled computer partner (Joint condition). Across experiments, participants showed a clear willingness to offload parts of the task (i.e., a subset of to-be-tracked targets) to the computer partner. In particular, participants decided to track 3.4 targets on average in the Solo compared to 2.4 targets in the Joint condition, i.e., they offloaded 1 target to the computer partner. Earlier research suggests that this difference in the number of tracked targets cannot be alternatively explained by a progressive performance decrease over time due to fatigue. This result is in line with earlier research predicting that humans will (partially) offload an attentionally demanding task to an algorithm to reduce their own cognitive effort [1] . Participants' behavior in the present study is also consistent with the offloading tendencies humans show nowadays in certain daily activities (e.g., when using Google Maps or Siri). The decision to offload a subset of targets to the computer partner resulted in a boost in participants' tracking accuracy, indicating that participants made fewer mistakes thanks to a reduction in cognitive demand [1] . This result demonstrates that offloading benefited participants' individual performance. As previous research demonstrated that the human tendency for algorithmic appreciation vs. aversion may depend on the (ascribed) reliability [5] and expertise of an algorithm [7, 8, 10] , we also explored whether the expertise factor would affect participants' behavior in the present study. To this end, participants in Experiment 1 did not receive any prior information about the expertise of the algorithm whereas participants in Experiment 2 were informed beforehand that the algorithm was flawless. Results showed that this prior information did not significantly affect the number of targets participants decided to track. Regarding our main result, i.e., the observation that participants decided to track fewer targets in the Joint compared to the Individual condition, one may wonder whether this difference could be due to the fact that in the Joint condition, participants might have tried to monitor the computer's performance in addition to performing their own tracking task. If this was true, then this might have impaired participants' individual tracking capacity, resulting in a smaller number of tracked targets in the Joint condition. Note that this worry concerns Experiment 1 only, as in Experiment 2, participants were told that the computer's accuracy was perfect such that there was no obvious need for monitoring. From participants' questionnaire responses, we know that indeed, in Experiment 1, several (i.e., 19%) participants tried to find out about the computer's accuracy through monitoring the targets selected by the computer. However, participants quickly realized that the computer's accuracy was high and stopped monitoring after only a few trials. No participant reported having monitored the computer throughout. These subjective self-reports are supported by participants' objective accuracy scores: if participants had monitored the computer throughout the entire experiment, then their own performance should have been severely impaired. Instead, participants' performed with the same average accuracy of 97% in Experiment 1 and 2, while the number of tracked targets was similar. The fact that accuracy levels did not differ between experiments suggests that participants did not perform a secondary task in Experiment 1. Moreover, our results show that participants were well aware of their tracking/offloading decisions. When asked after the experiment how many targets they had tracked in the Solo and Joint condition, the reported numbers were consistent with the numbers they had actually tracked. This suggests that participants had a high metacognitive awareness of their actions and that the offloading was likely an explicit choice participants made, which fits well with the proposition that metacognitive evaluations play a central role in offloading [1] . Finally, our questionnaire results do not provide any support for the hypothesis that participants' offloading tendencies might be related to certain personality dimensions such as desirability of control [25] , trust in automation [26] , and affinity for technological systems [27] . However, future studies with larger sample sizes are needed to rule out any influence of these personality dimensions more decisively. Alternatively, future studies could test these factors experimentally, e.g., by comparing two groups of pre-selected participants (e.g., one group with a high and one with a low affinity for technological systems). We suggest that future studies could consider the degree of cognitive load also as a moderating variable. For instance, for medical decisions, people may be more inclined to rely on the advice of an algorithm rather than a human doctor if they know that the human doctor formulated her advice under high cognitive load (e.g., at a particular busy time in the hospital). This is because people might realize that the performance of the algorithm, in contrast to that of the human, cannot be affected by any inherently human cognitive capacity limitations. Note that, as mentioned at the outset, future studies would also need to investigate the effect of cognitive load in high stakes scenarios. As the experimental task used in the present study involves considerably low stakes, our results cannot be generalized to high stakes scenarios such as the afore-mentioned medical decision-making. Investigating the latter types of scenarios seems worthwhile because it is in these scenarios that errors committed by humans under high attentional load [14] can have serious consequences, and thus, humans could substantially profit from cognitive offloading. Hence, understanding the offloading tendencies of humans (e.g., doctors) in such high stakes scenarios is critical. More generally, the conclusions drawn from the present study are limited in the sense that we have only investigated the willingness of human participants to offload a task to a computer partner, yet we did not test their willingness to offload the same task to a human partner. Thus, based on the present findings, we can report that humans are willing to (partially) offload an attentionally demanding task to an algorithm, but we do not know to what extent they would offload this task to another human, nor whether, if given the choice, they would choose the computer or the human as a partner. These questions need to be addressed by future studies to gain a more comprehensive picture of the human aversion/appreciation tendencies. A final open question one must ask in light of the results of the present study is why, in Experiment 2, participants did not decide to offload the complete task to the computer partner-given that they knew that the computer would perform the task flawlessly. abstract_text: This research aims to explore the potential impact of the ChatGPT on b-learning methodologies in engineering education, specifically in mathematics. The study focuses on how the use of these artificial intelligence tools can affect the acquisition of critical thinking, problem-solving, and group work skills among students. The research also analyzes the students’ perception of the reliability, usefulness, and importance of these tools in academia. The study collected data through a survey of 110 students enrolled in a Mathematics I course in BEng Aerospace Engineering where a blended methodology, including flipped teaching, escape room gamification, problem-solving, and laboratory sessions and exams with a computer algebraic system were used. analysis.discussion: B-learning methodologies are meant to promote the active participation of students, who complete tasks designed to improve and strengthen their knowledge, competencies, and skills [30, 33, 34, 43] . Even if a correct solution is not reached, attempting to solve problems strengthens critical thinking and improves learning and deductive abilities. Repetitive and simple tasks also aim to ensure the correct assimilation of knowledge within a broad context of questions. The subject matter addressed in this article is mathematical, which requires specific skills based on the correct assimilation of content, practice, and application, as well as reinforcement through activities. In contrast to other subjects, the use of a mathematical language different from the one used conversationally implies a need for additional learning support. However, the use of ChatGPT could weaken this support if it becomes capable of solving the problems raised and explaining the calculations made. On the other hand, ChatGPT can be helpful if used properly, as it provides a detailed description of the mathematical knowledge required to solve problems. Regarding student performance, when comparing the results to those obtained in the previous academic year, a slight increase in the scores of the practical sessions can be observed, in which the environment is not entirely controlled, as students have access to the internet. This could indicate better performance, assuming students are truthful in the survey and use ChatGPT for preparing activities. However, this increase in scores is not noticeable in exams held in more controlled environments, where no significant differences can be observed, neither for better nor for worse. Regarding the use of GBL and dEERs to promote student motivation and competency development, the use of ChatGPT has the potential to significantly affect its usage and the information collected. The data collected from the games are used to improve the students' learning experience through a feedforward strategy [44] . However, if these data are altered, the evaluation of competencies and content is highly affected, which may prevent deficiencies shown during the game from being reinforced in the future. This could have very negative repercussions on the design of future activities. The student's attitude will determine, as with other technologies, whether the use of ChatGPT in active methodologies will have benefits or drawbacks [18, 20] . Since COVID-19 pandemic, students have an improved wide range of computer and digital tools at their disposal that facilitate learning [29] , but the introduction of ChatGPT with the ability to directly customize the problem posed can greatly facilitate the search process. Consequently, the focus of attention shifts from an active search to mainly analyzing whether the answer is correct or not. If students rely solely on ChatGPT to find answers instead of training their skills, the effectiveness of FT-based methodologies could be significantly diminished. In the STEM area, the response capabilities of ChatGPT pose a risk to the integrity of the learning process if they prevent the acquisition of skills. However, the doubts generated regarding the viability and correctness of the responses generated so far can promote critical thinking. Nevertheless, ChatGPT has also positive features for blended learning environments such as, easy access to vast information to supplement their learning resources, quick assistance with homework, assignments, or clarifying doubts, and a strong capability to adapt to users based on individual needs. In the authors' opinion, this new tool can facilitate obtaining answers and facilitate knowledge acquisition. However, its potential effects on educational development and the design of activities require evaluation, as ChatGPT's response capacity can alter the learning process [12] [13] [14] . A word cloud has been generated with recent literature about ChatGPT in education (see Figure 2 ). The results obtained in this study are in agreement with the findings of other studies. Table 12 examines the performance of ChatGPT, potential issues associated with ChatGPT, and the use of this tool for enhancing learning. For a more exhaustive comparison among the literature results, see [77] . Performance [78] [79] [80] [81] [82] In agreement Performance depends on the subject. Same issues found in mathematics Potential Issues [80, 82, 83] In agreement Limited accuracy and reliability. Facilitating Learning [15, 80] In agreement Helps providing answers, solving problems and preparing tests. While ChatGPT can be a valuable tool in BL methodologies, there are some concerns that should be addressed: • Reliability issues: ChatGPT can provide incorrect, inaccurate, or outdated information, which can lead to misunderstandings or misconceptions in an educational environment [80, 81] . Students' opinions show a rather lukewarm average confidence, especially when it comes to the calculations provided. Without human oversight, guidance and responsible design and operation, such generative AI applications will remain a party trick with substantial potential for creating and spreading misinformation or harmful and inaccurate content at unprecedented scale. However, if positioned and developed responsibly as companions to humans augmenting but not replacing their role in decision making, knowledge retrieval and other cognitive processes, they could evolve into highly efficient, trustworthy, assistive tools for information management. This perspective describes how such tools could transform data management workflows in healthcare and medicine, explains how the underlying technology works, provides an assessment of risks and limitations, and proposes an ethical, technical, and cultural framework for responsible design, development, and deployment. It seeks to incentivise users, developers, providers, and regulators of generative AI that utilises LLMs to collectively prepare for the transformational role this technology could play in evidence-based sectors.

abstract_text: Recently, ChatGPT, along with DALL-E-2 and Codex,has been gaining significant attention from society. As a result, many individuals have become interested in related resources and are seeking to uncover the background and secrets behind its impressive performance. In fact, ChatGPT and other Generative AI (GAI) techniques belong to the category of Artificial Intelligence Generated Content (AIGC), which involves the creation of digital content, such as images, music, and natural language, through AI models. The goal of AIGC is to make the content creation process more efficient and accessible, allowing for the production of high-quality content at a faster pace. AIGC is achieved by extracting and understanding intent information from instructions provided by human, and generating the content according to its knowledge and the intent information. In recent years, large-scale models have become increasingly important in AIGC as they provide better intent extraction and thus, improved generation results. With the growth of data and the size of the models, the distribution that the model can learn becomes more comprehensive and closer to reality, leading to more realistic and high-quality content generation. This survey provides a comprehensive review on the history of generative models, and basic components, recent advances in AIGC from unimodal interaction and multimodal interaction. From the perspective of unimodality, we introduce the generation tasks and relative models of text and image. From the perspective of multimodality, we introduce the cross-application between the modalities mentioned above. Finally, we discuss the existing open problems and future challenges in AIGC.

analysis.discussion: There have been many debates about the dangers associated with the development and application of GAI, especially ChatGPT. Potential biases, privacy and security hazards, ethical questions, and the creation of damaging or deceptive content all fall under this category. Generative AI is still being created and used in many different contexts, despite these worries, which raises serious considerations regarding the social and ethical consequences of these technologies. It is important to regulate the AI/GAI market. Advocating for the regulation of the AI market is crucial to ensure a level playing field, promote fair competition, protect intellectual property rights and privacy, and prevent potential geopolitical risks. To mitigate risks connected with a lack of information quality control, disinformation, deepfake content, and algorithmic bias, the use of diverse and high-quality pre-approved datasets and the implementation of human feedback loops is recommended. Other recommendations include establishing clear guidelines and standards for the use of ChatGPT, implementing fact-checking mechanisms, monitoring social media platforms, and educating users on how to identify and avoid disinformation. Moreover, establishing clear and strict policies and guidelines for the use of deepfake technology in various industries could improve the digital landscape. The changing job market requires workers to continuously acquire new (digital) skills through education and retraining. As the training of AI systems becomes a prominent job category, it is important to adapt and take advantage of new opportunities. To mitigate the risks related to personal data violation, social surveillance, and privacy violation, GAI developers must prioritize ethical considerations and work to develop systems that prioritize user privacy and security. To avoid social manipulation and weaken ethics and goodwill, it is important to implement responsible AI practices and ethical guidelines: transparency in data usage, bias mitigation techniques, and monitoring of generated content for harmful or misleading information. There is a need to address financial and physical capital deficits and skills gaps to tackle global disparities and avoid the emergence of 'AI divides.' Providing international financial and technical cooperation and focusing on skills development and awareness-raising are crucial actions to assist Global South countries in overcoming the cost and digital infrastructure barriers. It is imperative to establish appropriate circumstances to ensure that no one is left behind in the AI revolution and to use macroeconomic and fiscal instruments to promote AI development and usage. More research is required to fully comprehend these concerns and design adequate safeguards to limit the potential repercussions of GAI. This involves creating ethical and legal frameworks that take into account the potential benefits and drawbacks of these technologies. Researchers, politicians, and business leaders must collaborate to guarantee GAI is developed and implemented responsibly and ethically in light of the rapid pace of technological advancement in this domain. abstract_text: We performed an empirical study to investigate whether the context of interruptions makes a difference. We found that context does not make a difference but surprisingly, people completed interrupted tasks in less time with no difference in quality. Our data suggests that people compensate for interruptions by working faster, but this comes at a price: experiencing more stress, higher frustration, time pressure and effort. Individual differences exist in the management of interruptions: personality measures of openness to experience and need for personal structure predict disruption costs of interruptions. We discuss implications for how system design can support interrupted work.

abstract_text: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.

analysis.methods: The results above describe a tunnel-vision problem. Agents often reach relevant files, but their diagnoses are broad, unstable, and especially weak when the report does not name the causal code. We next summarize failure modes and their implications for future harness designs. This analysis also shows why DISTDEBUG-BENCH's fine-grained evidence breakdown is useful: it provides concrete signals for diagnosing where current agents fail and what future harnesses should improve. Failure Mode 1: Tool-call nondeterminism drives diagnosis nondeterminism. Subtle differences in command choice can move runs into different evidence scopes, so future harnesses need adaptive tools that augment context automatically when early evidence is incomplete. Tool calls are a core reason why weak-evidence diagnosis becomes unstable. The models are often good at high-level sensemaking once they are in a relevant region, but the task requires many precise execution decisions: which keywords to search, which directory to enter, which file to open, which symbol to follow, and when to abandon a branch. When the report names the relevant method, different command orders can still converge on the same local region. When the report is opaque, small differences in search terms, directory choices, or the first file opened can send attempts into different subsystems. For example, in ZooKeeper-3769, node logs are available. The core enabler for a successful diagnosis would be to identify the BufferUnderflowException inside node1.log. We observe that both successful and failed runs read node1.log early on, but successful runs searched for Exception in the log, while failed runs looked at specific line numbers or searched for election-related logs. Those reads revealed other transient errors but missed the BufferUnderflowException. Similar behavior appears in ZooKeeper-2845. The root cause is in ZooKeeperServer.java under the broader /server path, but the issue report strongly emphasizes quorum behavior. Existing agents often narrow early to the /server/quorum subdirectory. Once there, keyword search no longer surfaces the correct class, and the run is steered toward a wrong but coherent diagnosis. To reduce nondeterminism, harnesses should provide tooling layers that infer the model's intent and automatically augment the context with relevant information. For example, when an agent searches for a keyword, static analysis can return related class definitions, symbol uses, and upstream/downstream contexts. This makes tool execution more precise when two commands are semantically aligned but differ subtly. Future harnesses should not leave context construction entirely to ad hoc shell commands: they need adaptive retrieval and context-augmentation tools that can surface adjacent files, call paths, related symbols, and competing hypotheses when the current search scope is under-supported. Failure Mode 2: Agents rarely revise initial hypotheses or discover causal code beyond the initial evidence. When the first plausible code region is not the causal one, agents often keep deepening that local explanation instead of reopening the search. In our trace proxy, only 21.0% of parseable runs showed late recovery, and only 11.25% of successful runs did so. We define late recovery as a run whose final diagnosis files do not appear among the first two inspected source files. Across 124 parseable Mini-SWE-Agent and OpenCode runs with at least two inspected source files, late recovery occurs in only 26 cases (21.0%): 7/21 for Mini-SWE-Agent and 19/103 for OpenCode. Among successful runs, only 9/80 (11.25%) are late recoveries. Bugs like ZooKeeper-2845 and Ray-8889 illustrate this lock-in. Even when an agent finds code that appears to match the reported symptom (such as the downstream data consumer that raises the exception), it often stops at that obvious location instead of asking what earlier lifecycle state made the symptom possible. Trace inspections show that agents can ask relevant follow-up questions, but whether they explore those questions is highly nondeterministic and shaped by early exploration. This early lock-in reinforces Failure Mode 1: because agents struggle to adapt their scope and reasoning, small tool-execution inaccuracies can become diagnosis failures. Distributed-systems debugging requires each hypothesis path to accumulate its own evidence. Under the current single, ever-growing context, alternatives become harder to compare. This calls for context-management strategies beyond context compaction or sub-agent delegation, such as switching context when pursuing different hypotheses or actively pruning invalidated hypotheses. Failure Mode 3: Diagnosis is hard because agents lack reliable self-correction signals before finalizing. Distributed-system failures often suffer from reproducibility challenges. Agents often cannot run tests and get quick feedback on whether the diagnosis is correct; instead, they must rely on rigorous reasoning over source code and observed artifacts. Diagnosis often lacks a cheap pass/fail check for whether a proposed source region is the true root cause. Agents often cannot tell, before finalizing, whether the selected code region accounts for the full causal chain or whether another hypothesis still needs to be explored. Even when a runnable environment is available, agents can give up on testing because they prioritize reproducing the entire incident rather than decomposing it into smaller, unit-test-style checks. Similarly, when agents converge early, they sometimes stop for engineering-practice reasons and lack explicit correctness specifications for deciding whether upstream or downstream code should be blamed. Our core insight is that bug diagnosis does not inherently lack correctness signals. Rather, signals such as raised exceptions, crash sites, logs, and documentation require consistent evaluation and cross-checking before they become useful. Future harnesses should actively inject correctness signals into the agent's context, or use an evaluator sub-agent to verify whether the proposed diagnosis fully explains the buggy behavior from start to end, and whether the decision to blame one component is backed by concrete evidence.

Trace analysis highlights inconsistent tool use and limited revision of initial hypotheses. The evidence breakdown, run-to-run flakiness, and failure-mode analyses together suggest that distributed system debugging requires more than broader search or model scaling. These findings motivate future research and agent harness designs that support adaptive context construction, hypothesis-aware context management, and correctness checks, so that exploration, revision, and validation are explicit parts of agentic diagnosis workflows. Selection bias. DISTDEBUG-BENCH intentionally focuses on closed, high-impact failures in production distributed systems whose fixes support precise source-level labeling. This selection makes the task realistic and scoreable, but it excludes failures whose fixes are dominated by broad refactorings, configuration changes, test-only changes, or ambiguous cleanup. The benchmark should therefore be interpreted as covering code-level diagnosis for labelable distributed-system bugs rather than all incident-response work. We mitigate this risk with a principled, staged selection process. For each project, we first collect historical public issues and apply automatic filters for concrete fixed bugs: closed or resolved status, an associated fixing change, high-priority or user-facing failures when priority is available, sufficiently informative reports, and non-test/non-documentation components. We then filter by the fixing change itself, excluding broad refactorings and patches dominated by unrelated cleanup, and using a practical 100 changed-source-line cutoff unless the causal span is clearly separable from auxiliary edits. The ZooKeeper attrition example in Table 2 illustrates the scale of this filtering process. Finally, annotators manually audit the survivors to confirm that the issue-side context is diagnosable without post-report discussion, that the report does not reveal the root cause or patch strategy, and that the fixing change maps to precise pre-fix root-cause blocks. Each accepted issue is then independently annotated by three annotators and reconciled into the final label set. This process does not eliminate selection bias, but it makes the benchmark population the result of consistent filters and explicit audits rather than convenience sampling.

abstract_text: This qualitative study explores university students’ perceptions, ethical justifications, and trust dynamics regarding the use of generative AI tools like ChatGPT and DeepSeek in online examinations. Through phenomenological analysis of semi-structured interviews and focus groups with 20 students across diverse disciplines, the research reveals four key themes: (1) the reframing of AI as a “collaborator” rather than a cheating tool, (2) a paradox of high reliance despite awareness of AI’s limitations, (3) moral disengagement strategies to justify use, and (4) preferences for online exams due to convenience despite ethical dilemmas. Findings contrast with institutional definitions of academic misconduct, demonstrating how students rationalize AI use through critiques of traditional assessment methods. The study contributes to academic integrity literature by adapting neutralization theory to AI contexts and highlights the need for assessment reforms that address both technological realities and pedagogical values. Practical implications suggest moving beyond detection-focused approaches toward AI-integrated assessments and targeted digital literacy training. Limitations include sample specificity to one institution, suggesting need for cross-cultural replication.

analysis.methods: The study adopts a phenomenological research design (Groenewald, 2004) to explore the lived experiences of university students regarding their use of generative AI tools in online exams. This approach is particularly suited to uncovering the subjective meanings and ethical dilemmas students associate with AI-assisted assessments, as it prioritizes depth over breadth by focusing on rich, first-person narratives. By examining how students perceive, justify, and navigate the use of tools like ChatGPT and DeepSeek in exam contexts, the study aims to reveal the complex interplay between technology, trust, and academic integrity. Phenomenology's emphasis on capturing individual experiences aligns with the research objectives, allowing for a nuanced understanding of how students reconcile AI use with their personal and academic values. Data collection employs two complementary methods: semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions. Individual interviews, lasting approximately 25-40 minutes, explored personal experiences with prompts such as, "Describe a situation where you used AI during an exam. How did you feel about it?" and "What factors influenced your decision to trust or distrust AI-generated answers?" These open-ended questions encourage reflective storytelling while allowing for emergent themes. Data collection and preliminary analysis occurred concurrently. Interviews were conducted in iterative waves, and transcribed data was coded after each wave to monitor the emergence of new themes. Data saturation was determined to be reached after the 15th interview, as two subsequent interviews yielded no new thematic insights or conceptual categories. The final five interviews served to confirm and refine the existing thematic structure, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the phenomenon under study. Focus groups of 4-6 participants each then facilitated dynamic debates on broader ethical questions, such as "Is AI-assisted exam-taking fundamentally different from traditional cheating?" The group setting may reveal social norms and peer influences that individual interviews might not capture. Both methods were conducted virtually to accommodate participant preferences and recorded for accurate transcription with their consent.

This utilitarian view aligns with broader critiques of assessment design in higher education, which often prioritizes rote memorization over adaptive learning (Rudolph et al., 2023) . Nonetheless, this reframing raises ethical questions about where to draw the line between collaboration and academic dishonesty, particularly when institutional policies remain ambiguous. This reframing is not merely semantic; it redefines the moral status of AI from an external aid to an internal cognitive partner, lowering the psychological threshold for its use in high-stakes contexts.
analysis.discussion: Our findings regarding student rationalization of AI use extend beyond the local institutional context and contribute to critical global debates about the very purpose of assessment in contemporary education. The prevalent use of neutralization techniques, particularly the condemnation of condemners, reflects a growing international disconnect between traditional examination methods and the skills required in a digitally transformed workforce. This suggests that student AI use is not merely an issue of academic dishonesty, but potentially a symptom of broader systemic issues in higher education, where assessments are perceived as artificial hurdles rather than meaningful learning experiences. This aligns with global concerns about educational relevance in the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Schwab, 2017) and calls for a fundamental reevaluation of assessment design worldwide. The findings of this study further reveal a significant dissonance between institutional definitions of cheating and how students perceive the use of generative AI in exams. While traditional academic integrity policies often categorize unauthorized AI assistance as misconduct (Mulaudzi & Hamilton, 2025) , many participants reframed it as a legitimate form of "smart learning," akin to using calculators or grammar checkers. This redefinition aligns with broader shifts in educational technology, where tools once deemed disruptive, such as search engines or spell-check, have become normalized (Rudolph et al., 2023) . However, the current study extends this literature by highlighting how students' justifications are not merely pragmatic but also rooted in critiques of assessment design. For instance, participants frequently argued that exams testing rote memorization rather than critical thinking justified their AI use, echoing concerns raised by Dawson (2020) about the misalignment between assessments and real-world skills. This suggests that attempts to curb AI cheating through detection alone may fail unless paired with pedagogical reforms addressing the perceived irrelevance of traditional exams. The trust paradox observed in this study, where students relied on AI despite recognizing its flaws, also challenges prevailing assumptions about technology adoption in education. Prior research has documented overreliance on AI in low-stakes contexts (Nguyen et al., 2023) , but this study reveals how exam pressures amplify this dependency, even among skeptical users. Participants' selective trust, such as cross-checking AI outputs in fact-heavy disciplines but accepting them uncritically in subjective tasks, mirrors findings from human-automation interaction research (Pennycook et al., 2020) . This nuanced behavior underscores the need for discipline-specific AI literacy training, as blanket policies may overlook contextual variations in how students engage with these tools. Furthermore, the moral disengagement strategies employed by participants, particularly appeals to "everyone does it" and systemic unfairness, resonate with neutralization theory (Sykes & Matza, 2017) , but with a novel twist: AI's opacity allows students to downplay personal accountability more easily than in conventional cheating scenarios. This study advances current knowledge by demonstrating that student engagement with generative AI in exams is not merely a new form of an old problem, but a phenomenon that requires new theoretical and practical frameworks. Unlike prior technologies that were primarily used for content duplication, generative AI's role as a co-creator of original-seeming text leads students to employ distinct neutralization strategies, particularly denial of injury, a technique less prevalent in discussions of traditional plagiarism. Consequently, our findings suggest that institutional policies designed to prevent copy-paste plagiarism are inadequate for addressing the ethical challenges posed by AI collaboration. By providing a nuanced, qualitative account of the justifications and dilemmas students face, this research offers a critical evidence base for developing more effective and empathetic educational responses that address the root causes of AI misuse, rather than just its symptoms. This qualitative study has illuminated the complex and often contradictory ways university students perceive, justify, and utilize generative AI tools in online exam settings. By centering student voices, the research reveals that traditional binary frameworks of "cheating versus honesty" fail to capture the nuanced realities of AI-assisted assessment. Students frequently reframed AI use as legitimate collaboration, driven by pragmatic adaptation to perceived flaws in traditional testing methods. The findings underscore a critical disconnect between institutional policies and student perspectives, suggesting that current academic integrity approaches may be misaligned with both technological realities and evolving educational needs. The study's theoretical contributions include advancing neutralization theory in digital contexts and highlighting how AI's unique characteristics, particularly its ability to generate original-seeming content, challenge conventional notions of academic misconduct. Practically, the results call for a paradigm shift in assessment design, moving from prohibition to integration, where AI literacy and ethical use become core learning outcomes. Educators and policymakers must address the root causes of student disengagement that drive AI misuse, including outdated assessment formats and unrealistic performance expectations. As AI becomes increasingly embedded in educational and professional landscapes, this research emphasizes the urgent need for flexible, forward-looking policies that balance integrity with innovation. Future studies should explore longitudinal effects of AI integration and cross-cultural variations in acceptance patterns. Ultimately, the study advocates for a collaborative approach to AI in education -one that harnesses its potential while fostering critical engagement and maintaining academic rigor in the digital age.
analysis.limitations: While this study offers valuable qualitative insights, several limitations must be acknowledged. Firstly, the sample size of 20 participants, though sufficient for reaching thematic saturation in qualitative research, was drawn from a single university. This limits the generalizability of the findings, as student perspectives and institutional cultures may vary significantly across different geographical and educational contexts. Secondly, despite employing purposive sampling to ensure disciplinary diversity, the potential for self-selection bias remains, as participants volunteered for a study concerning AI use in exams, potentially attracting those with stronger opinions or experiences. Thirdly, the reliance on self-reported data introduces the possibility of social desirability bias, where participants may have underreported or rationalized ethically questionable behaviors. Finally, the study was conducted at a specific point in time, yet the landscape of generative AI tools and institutional policies is evolving rapidly. These factors collectively suggest that while the identified themes provide a robust conceptual framework for understanding student rationalizations, their prevalence and specific manifestations should be investigated further in broader, multi-institutional, and longitudinal studies to enhance their transferability.

analysis.discussion: In conclusion, the convergent validity assessment conducted for all three proposed scales provides signiicant validation for assessing perceived fairness within the TAR framework. The high coeicient values and composite reliability scores indicate strong internal consistency and convergent validity across all constructs, airming their suitability for use by both practitioners and SMEs. While the overall scale exhibited moderate reliability, the indings suggest adequate performance in capturing the complexities of fairness perceptions among various stakeholder groups. Furthermore, the factor loading analysis highlights the efectiveness of the selected items in representing the latent constructs, with minor discrepancies pointing to potential areas for future reinement. Overall, these results reinforce the efectiveness of the TAR framework in addressing concerns related to fairness and suggest a path for continued research and improvement in measurement tools within this important area. This study aims to explore the concept of fairness in ML systems, with a focus on the development process from a sociotechnical perspective. Addressing the research gap identiied in the related works section 2 and the research proposal section 1.3, two key research questions are examined: the factors that inluence perceptions of fairness and the variations in these perceptions. This study evaluates the perceived fairness of the ML development cycle as experienced by ML practitioners and SMEs, focusing on human-centered evaluation. The research introduces the TAR framework for assessing perceived fairness, emphasizing both procedural and distributive fairness as highlighted in existing literature. The three scales developed integrate the beliefs of diverse stakeholders and are validated both theoretically and empirically. Additionally, these scales facilitate the investigation of diferences in perceptions of fairness among various stakeholders. This section outlines the implications of the proposed scales for research, practice, and broader societal impact within the context of machine learning evaluation. The empirically validated scales introduce new opportunities for ine-grained comparative analyses of fairness perceptions across models, metrics, and deployment contexts. For practitioners, the proposed scales provide a structured framework for assessing, diagnosing, and improving perceived fairness in algorithmic systems. In a social context, the scales help reine normative benchmarks of fairness and support more transparent, equitable interactions between SMEs and ML-driven systems. By enabling more precise, cross-group measurement, these tools advance fairness research and contribute to a more rigorous and inclusive discourse in the evaluation of ML systems. This study presents the irst empirical investigation into fairness perceptions among machine learning (ML) practitioners and SMEs within the development process, adopting a socio-technical lens grounded in transparency, accountability, and representativeness. It ofers a human-centered, empirically validated contribution to the discourse on fairness in ML by introducing the TAR framework and associated survey instruments for assessing perceived fairness across the ML lifecycle. The framework's multidimensional design enables organizations to identify gaps between design intentions and lived experiences, monitor fairness perceptions, and inform design and policy decisions. By bridging technical evaluations with social context, this work advances the development of AI systems that are trustworthy and socially acceptable. Findings reveal statistically signiicant diferences in fairness perceptions between practitioner and SME respondents. Because respondents evaluated diferent ML projects operating within diverse organizational and application contexts, these diferences should be interpreted as relecting a combination of stakeholder perspectives and project-speciic characteristics rather than stakeholder role alone. These results support the utility of process-based fairness measurement and demonstrate the value of the TAR framework as a validated instrument for assessing perceived fairness across ML development contexts. The validated instruments, supported by reliability and factor analysis, operationalize fairness as a multidimensional construct and provide a scalable method for real-world ML contexts. This research reframes fairness as a negotiated, context-dependent concept, encouraging participatory ML-design and interdisciplinary collaboration to close practitioner-user gaps and foster inclusive, accountable ML systems. Future work may extend the TAR framework to domainspeciic applications and explore integration into participatory ML-design processes. It also opens avenues for multidisciplinary collaboration between ML researchers, HCI scholars, social scientists, and policymakers to co-produce both methodologically robust and ethically grounded frameworks. analysis.limitations: The study results should be interpreted within the context of the sample and research design. Data were collected from a combination of Proliic participants and the authors' professional networks, resulting in a inal sample (N = 197) that, while suicient for scale validation, remains modest and exhibits some imbalance between practitioners (n = 123) and SMEs (n = 74). Although Proliic provides access to a globally diverse participant pool, it does not constitute a fully representative sample of any speciic population. Consequently, the indings should be interpreted with appropriate caution when generalizing across domains or populations. Additionally, the exclusion of student participants and restriction to adult respondents may limit the applicability of indings to educational or early-career contexts. A potential limitation of this study is that participants evaluated perceived fairness based on their most recent ML project, resulting in variability across project types and contexts. However, this variability is intentional and methodologically appropriate, given that the objective of this research is construct development rather than causal inference. Established scale development guidelines emphasize the importance of capturing constructs across heterogeneous real-world settings to ensure generalizability and external validity [31, 79] . In this study, perceived fairness is explicitly conceptualized as a context-dependent, sociotechnical construct that is expected to vary across domains, stakeholder roles, and system characteristics. To support this approach, the study collected practitioners' metadata on ML project characteristics (e.g., model type, data modality, and application domain), summarized in Table 5 , and sampled across diverse industry contexts. This design enables the TAR framework to capture generalizable perceptual patterns rather than being tied to any single project or domain. At the same time, it is important to acknowledge that some observed diferences may relect both stakeholder perspectives and project-speciic characteristics. Accordingly, indings should be interpreted as patterns of perceived fairness across heterogeneous settings rather than controlled comparisons.

It examined how teachers perceive and engage with AI tools across disciplines, highlighting both the transformative potential and the ethical complexities of digital pedagogy. Drawing from a wide corpus of research (Holmes, Bialik, and Fadel, 2019; Williamson and Eynon, 2020; Luckin et al., 2016) and empirical insights, the analysis reveals a profession cautiously optimistic about AI, yet acutely aware of the practical, ethical, and pedagogical implications surrounding its adoption. One of the most consistent themes across literature and practice is the shifting role of teachers in AI-enhanced environments. AI is increasingly viewed not as a replacement for educators, but as a scaffolding mechanism that supports planning, differentiation, formative feedback, and administrative efficiency (Holmes, Bialik, and Fadel, 2019; Belloula, 2025) . Reflective journals offer a structured yet flexible method for documenting self-reflection insights throughout the action research cycle. Their ability to capture evolving, contextrich perspectives make them a valuable source of qualitative data. Leitch and Day (2000) emphasise that reflection enhances professional development by enabling researchers to critically assess their methodologies and refine their approach. This aligns with Ayton's (2025) assertion that action research depends on iterative cycles of refinement, where introspection fosters deeper understanding of how actions influence outcomes. However, reflective journals are inherently subjective. As Ortlipp (2008) notes, individual experiences, emotions, and perspectives shape reflections, potentially introducing bias, qualitative research values practitioner voice, there is ongoing debate about whether reflective journals overemphasise individual perspectives at the expense of empirical rigour. Bashan and Holsblat (2017) further highlight that the quality of reflections can vary depending on writing skills, cognitive ability, and emotional state, which may lead to inconsistent data and hinder systematic analysis. To address these limitations, reflective journals should be complemented by other methods to enhance credibility and triangulate findings (Leitch and Day, 2000) . While surveys are widely recognised for their efficiency in collecting data from large groups within constrained periods (Creswell and Guetterman, 2019) , their reliance on closed-ended questions presents notable limitations especially when investigating complex phenomena such as teacher perceptions of AI. Closed questions, by design, restrict respondents to predefined answer choices, which can inhibit the expression of nuanced views, emotional responses, or context-specific experiences (Bryman, 2016) . This constraint may lead to superficial data that lacks the richness required for deep interpretive analysis. Closed-ended formats are particularly problematic when exploring emerging or contested topics like AI in education, where respondents may hold ambivalent or evolving views. As Reja et al. (2003) notes, while closed questions facilitate statistical analysis and trend identification, they often fail to capture the "why" behind responses. For example, a teacher may select "agree" to a statement about AI improving efficiency, but without an open-ended follow-up, the rationale whether rooted in workload reduction, pedagogical enhancement, or institutional pressure remains obscured. Moreover, closed questions can introduce response bias, especially if the options do not reflect the full spectrum of participant perspectives. Merren (2025) highlights that poorly designed closed questions may inadvertently guide respondents toward socially desirable answers or exclude critical viewpoints. This is particularly relevant in AI-related surveys, where ethical concerns, job security, and pedagogical autonomy may influence responses in subtle ways. analysis.discussion: This study explored the multifaceted integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education through a critical synthesis of literature, cross-AoLE action research, and analysis of survey data on teachers' perceptions. It examined how teachers perceive and engage with AI tools across disciplines, highlighting both the transformative potential and the ethical complexities of digital pedagogy. Drawing from a wide corpus of research (Holmes, Bialik, and Fadel, 2019; Williamson and Eynon, 2020; Luckin et al., 2016) and empirical insights, the analysis reveals a profession cautiously optimistic about AI, yet acutely aware of the practical, ethical, and pedagogical implications surrounding its adoption. One of the most consistent themes across literature and practice is the shifting role of teachers in AI-enhanced environments. AI is increasingly viewed not as a replacement for educators, but as a scaffolding mechanism that supports planning, differentiation, formative feedback, and administrative efficiency (Holmes, Bialik, and Fadel, 2019; Belloula, 2025) . Yet this repositioning raises tensions. While some teachers embrace their evolving identity as "learning designers" or "AI moderators," others express unease over diminished professional autonomy, creative erosion, and the risk of pedagogical flattening when AI-generated content is misinterpreted as authoritative or curriculum-endorsed. Action research reflections from the Expressive Arts and Humanities AoLEs illustrate this tension vividly. Teachers initially apprehensive about creativity loss or shortcut misuse later articulated renewed confidence when AI was framed as a provocation for critique, adaptation, and learner agency. This finding supports Aiken and Eladhari's (2024) argument that generative tools must be purposefully embedded within dialogic, exploratory practices to preserve aesthetic and ethical integrity. The perceived benefits of AI integration are clear: workload reduction, personalisation, improved engagement, automated feedback, and resource generation. All six core advantages were widely recognised across surveyed teachers, with "reducing workload" emerging as the top priority (48%), followed by "enhanced student engagement" (35%). These priorities reflect a pragmatic orientation, particularly evident in Numeracy and Science and Technology AoLEs, where AI-supported question generation, skeleton coding, and resource tailoring enabled efficient planning and differentiated challenge (Shi and Choi, 2024; Celik et al., 2022) . Yet the findings also caution against assuming these benefits manifest automatically. Teachers repeatedly stressed the importance of curricular alignment, regional context (especially within Welsh education), and ethical moderation. In MFL, for example, the use of ElevenLabs and Canva Magic Media for listening tasks highlighted the value of accent exposure and adaptive levels but also raised concerns about linguistic accuracy and cultural relevance. This duality echoes Luckin et al. (2022) calls for AI to be both inclusive and context-sensitive, avoiding "generic personalisation" that neglects linguistic and semantic diversity. Ethical considerations emerged as a core theme throughout the literature and data analysis. Concerns around bias, job displacement, and algorithmic reliability were widely cited, with 48% of teachers expressing explicit ethical reservations and 26% unsure. Interestingly, teachers who had received formal training were more likely to articulate ethical concerns (58%), suggesting that awareness leads to more critical scrutiny rather than avoidance. This supports Celik et al.'s (2022) claim that ethical discomfort often indicates deeper professional engagement and reflective capacity. Across AoLEs, ethical dilemmas took distinct forms. Humanities teachers raised alarms over plagiarism and academic integrity; Expressive Arts educators questioned authorship and originality; Science and Technology respondents focused on data sourcing and template transparency; and Numeracy teachers stressed the need to verify AI-generated materials to prevent misrepresentation. These concerns reinforce Belloula (2025) recommendation for attribution mechanisms and professional framing. Beyond anticipated risks, teachers identified unintended consequences such as student over-reliance, surface-level editing, and false confidence. These challenges signal the importance of embedding critical digital literacy into both student learning and staff CPD. AI must be framed not as an answer engine but as a thinking partner one that invites interrogation, transformation, and synthesis. AI's capacity to scaffold inclusive, personalised learning was repeatedly emphasised across disciplines. Teachers in Humanities, MFL, and Science and Technology praised AI's ability to scaffold complexity, provide flexible entry points, and extend challenge for learners with diverse needs. These practices echo principles outlined by Chen, Chen, and Lin (2020), who argue that AI can serve as an equity mechanism when used to honour diverse learning identities. However, successful inclusivity requires more than adaptive technology. Teachers noted the need for offline alternatives to reduce inequality. In line with Holmes, Bialik, and Fadel (2023) , these reflections call for hybrid pedagogical models where AI enriches but never monopolises the learning experience. One of the most promising findings is the documented shift in teacher perceptions. Many educators moved from scepticism to advocacy as they witnessed AI's practical utility. Confidence increased as AI was repositioned not as a threat but as a collaborative support system, with teachers noting gains in planning efficiency, learner interaction, and pedagogical creativity. This evolution supports Shi and Choi's (2024) conceptualisation of AI as a "pedagogical co-creator.". However, confidence was uneven, teachers with "Fair" or "Poor" understanding were more likely to express reluctance, and 69% most hesitant respondents lacked formal training. This emphasises the critical role of structured CPD not only in building fluency but in fostering ethical discernment and disciplinary relevance (Mustafa et al., 2024) . The integration of AI into education demands systemic reflection and coordinated policy action. Literature and data agree that teacher agency must remain central, with AI framed as a support, not a replacement. Ethical guidance, training infrastructure, and design justice must be embedded into every AI-informed initiative (Williamson and Eynon, 2020; Celik et al., 2022) . As this dissertation demonstrates, ethical and pedagogically meaningful AI integration requires ongoing reflection, collaboration, and contextual sensitivity. The findings not only illuminate current practice but also provide a foundation for future professional learning and strategic development. To support this next phase, a detailed dissemination plan has been included in Appendix 7, outlining how the insights from this study will be shared with staff, leadership, and learners to promote responsible, subject-specific engagement with AI. In this way, the research extends beyond analysis to contribute directly to the evolving culture of ethical, reflective, and context-aware AI practice within the school community.
analysis.limitations: This study employed a mixed-methods approach, combining survey data with action research to explore teachers' perceptions of AI integration in educational practice. While the findings offer valuable insights, several methodological limitations must be acknowledged to contextualise the scope and reliability of the conclusions drawn. Sample size and regional concentration of the survey component included responses from forty-seven educators, all based in the South Wales region. Although this cohort provided rich qualitative and quantitative data, the relatively small sample size limits the statistical generalisability of the findings. Moreover, the regional concentration may reflect localised attitudes shaped by specific policy environments, professional development opportunities, and institutional cultures. Broader studies encompassing diverse geographic and socioeconomic contexts would be necessary to validate and extend these findings. Furthermore, as the action research was conducted within a single school setting, which introduces potential bias linked to the school's unique ethos, leadership style, and digital maturity. The culture of this institution particularly its openness to innovation and staff collaboration may have positively influenced the implementation and reception of AI tools. As such, the results may not be transferable to schools with different pedagogical priorities, resource constraints, or leadership dynamics. School culture plays a pivotal role in shaping educators' attitudes toward technological change. Factors such as leadership support, collegial trust, and existing digital infrastructure can significantly impact how AI is perceived and adopted. The cultural context of the participating school may have fostered a more optimistic or experimental stance toward AI, which could differ markedly from schools operating under more rigid or risk-averse conditions. The study relied heavily on self-reported survey responses, which are inherently subject to bias. Participants may have provided socially desirable answers or interpreted questions through varying lenses of experience and familiarity with AI. While efforts were made to ensure clarity and neutrality in survey design, the subjective nature of perception-based data remains a limitation. As this only captured a snapshot of teacher perceptions during a specific period. Given the rapid evolution of AI technologies and their applications in education, attitudes and practices may shift significantly over time.

analysis.discussion: This study examined whether algorithmic feed dependency was associated with public issue engagement across Douyin and Xiaohongshu, yielding three main findings. First, algorithmic feed dependency was positively associated with educational issue engagement on both platforms. This suggests that a preliminary perceived-reliance composite is linked to engagement, with stable educational results after excluding its continuous-scrolling item. The finding extends media system dependency theory to algorithmically governed platform environments. Whereas the original framework focused on audience reliance on media institutions, platformized media environments increasingly organize information access through algorithmic curation. In this context, the locus of dependency shifts from institutional media outlets to recommendation systems that filter, rank, and repeatedly surface issue-relevant content ( Bucher, 2018 ; Napoli, 2014 ). We therefore treat algorithmic feed dependency as a system-level form of media reliance, that is, reliance on the algorithmic and architectural arrangements through which public issues become visible. The findings also extend prior work on algorithm dependency and algorithmic content selection. Existing research has shown that algorithm dependency shapes platformized news consumption ( Schaetz, 2023 ) and that algorithmic content selection structures users’ information exposure pathways ( Zarouali et al., 2022 ). The present study adds that such reliance is associated not only with news exposure, but also with engagement in educational, social, and civic issues circulating in non-news platform environments. In doing so, it links algorithmic dependency to issue engagement rather than only to information access. The measurement contribution remains preliminary. The administered dependency measure combines access pathway, continuous scrolling, and recommendation fit, while the fourth engagement item combines confidence and discussion willingness. The exclusion checks support the stability of educational associations, but do not resolve these content-validity limitations or establish discriminant validity against validated habit and preference scales. We therefore distinguish a useful empirical proxy from a fully validated dependency construct. Second, observed educational responses differed modestly across platforms. Only sharing/forwarding remained significant within the four-item family after Holm correction; liking/commenting did not. This is partial support for H2a, rather than evidence that all reactive behaviors are higher on Douyin. Non-significant expressive and reinforcement-item contrasts also do not establish equivalence. The educational interaction was non-significant, and the 90% interval extended beyond the upper equivalence bound. Neither a slope difference nor equivalence was established. Consequently, the data cannot rank engagement-form differences as more important than slope differences simply by comparing their p -values. The title and conclusions therefore describe the observed association with engagement form and breadth without asserting that architecture determines how, but not whether, engagement occurs. The sharing result is compatible with an affordance-based account in which immediate sharing is convenient within immersive feeds. However, the study did not measure behavioral costs, experimentally vary interfaces, or observe actual actions. Selection into platforms, differing issue exposure, and self-report interpretation are plausible alternative explanations. Architectural mechanisms remain interpretive hypotheses. Third, cross-issue patterns were supported by two kinds of evidence with distinct meanings. Adjusted within-platform coefficients were significant across all three domains on Xiaohongshu and only education on Douyin. Direct interaction tests supported steeper Xiaohongshu slopes for marriage/childbearing and social pressure, but did not establish either a difference or equivalence for education. The Douyin social-pressure coefficient was sensitive to correction and item exclusion. A topic-based navigation and discussion account offers one possible explanation for the Xiaohongshu pattern ( Zhai, 2025 ). Yet issue persistence, exposure breadth, and community structure were not measured in this questionnaire. Broader issue ecology should therefore be treated as a proposed mechanism to test with content samples and behavioral logs, not an observed characteristic established by the regression results. Douyin showed a more selective pattern. Its short-video feed is organized around fast-paced content delivery and immediate interaction, which may make engagement more dependent on issue salience and personal relevance. Educational issues are directly tied to the lived experience of university students and recent graduates, whereas marriage and childbearing issues may be less immediately relevant for many respondents in this sample. This is an untested interpretation of why feed dependency on Douyin was linked more consistently to educational issue engagement than to engagement with other issue domains. Taken together, the study distinguishes three empirical questions: paired engagement means, cross-platform association slopes, and variation across issue domains. The corrected item evidence is limited to sharing/forwarding; the educational interaction is inconclusive about equivalence; and interaction evidence supports differences for marriage/childbearing and social pressure. analysis.methods: A cross-sectional survey design was adopted. This design was selected because the study’s aim was to describe and quantify the strength of association between ChatGPT adoption, self- regulated learning, academic integrity, and learning engagement as they naturally co-occur among final-year undergraduates, rather than to establish that adoption causes changes in the other constructs. Consistent with this aim, all inferential claims in this paper are correlational: the serial- mediation and multigroup results reported below describe the pattern of statistical association observed within the sample at a single point in the students’ academic year, and should not be read as evidence that ChatGPT adoption causally produces the levels of self-regulation, integrity, or Data from the academic planning units of the various public universities revealed that the population of the study comprised 1,507 final-year undergraduates at the University of Calabar, University of Cross River, and University of Education and Entrepreneurship. All these universities are public institutions in Cross River State, Nigeria. The sampling procedure combined proportionate stratification with purposive selection within strata. The population of 1,507 final-year undergraduates was first stratified by university, in proportion to each institution’s share of the total population, so that no single institution was over- or under-represented in the achieved sample. Because random selection of individual students was not administratively feasible, given the absence of a unified, up-to-date student registry accessible to the researchers across all three institutions and the constrained data- collection window imposed by students’ examination and project schedules, students within each university stratum were then recruited purposively, through research assistants stationed at high- traffic points (lecture halls, libraries, faculty common areas) until each stratum’s proportionate quota was filled. This design is consequently better described as stratified-purposive rather than stratified-random sampling, and it is reported as such here rather than as simple random sampling. The population was restricted to final-year students specifically because this group has accumulated the most sustained exposure to ChatGPT and comparable generative AI tools across their degree program, has had the longest opportunity to develop stable self-regulated learning habits relative to earlier-year students, and is typically closest to independent, high-stakes academic work (research projects, long essays, seminar papers) in which the tension between AI- assisted efficiency and academic integrity is most directly and consequentially encountered. Earlier-year students, by contrast, would have had comparatively limited and more heterogeneous exposure to both ChatGPT and independent scholarly work, making final-year students the theoretically most appropriate, rather than merely the most convenient, population for testing this study’s hypotheses. Valid replies were provided by male (n=211) and female (n=241) students, indicating that, despite the purposive element within strata, the achieved sample remained reasonably balanced across the gender groups examined in the multigroup analysis. The achieved sample of 452 exceeds not only the minimum requirement for PLS-SEM estimation of the most complex regression in the model (Hair et al., 2022) but also the sample size of approximately 306 that standard sample-size determination tables recommend for a population of this size at the conventional 95% confidence level (Krejcie & Morgan, 1970), providing two independent bases for judging the sample adequate. Table 1 shows the profile. The data was obtained using Google Forms for ease of access and participation, which is an online survey called “ChatGPT Adoption, Academic Integrity, and Learning Engagement." The questionnaire contained four sections: Section A contained demographic data, age, and gender and a cover letter stating the aim of the study, confidentiality, and rules of participation. Section B assessed students ChatGPT adoption using statements like "I regularly use ChatGPT to support my academic tasks" and "I consider ChatGPT useful for understanding course material," respectively. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = agree), together with additional items: I intend to continue using ChatGPT in my studies, I am comfortable integrating ChatGPT into my learning routine, and I use ChatGPT to generate ideas and clarify concepts. Section C examined the self-regulated learning of respondents, using statements like “I set clear goals and plan how to accomplish my academic work," “I monitor my understanding while studying," "I adjust my learning strategies when needed," and so on. Section D examined the respondents' academic integrity using statements such as “I properly acknowledge sources, including AI-generated content" and “I avoid submitting work that is not genuinely my own. " I use ChatGPT to assist learning rather than to cheat. While section E focused on learning engagement, it included statements such as “I actively participate in my courses and learning activities," “I feel absorbed and interested in my academic work," and “I persist with difficult academic tasks. " Based on the literature and previous studies, 19 questions were first generated, with 4 and 5 items, respectively, used to measure the dimensions of the constructs of ChatGPT adoption, academic integrity, and learning engagement. analysis.discussion: The findings support an integrated account of how generative-AI adoption shapes learning engagement. ChatGPT adoption promoted self-regulated learning, which strengthened academic integrity, which in turn enhanced engagement—consistent with the view that adoption translates into outcomes through self-regulatory and ethical processes (Venkatesh et al., 2003; Zimmerman et al., 2011). The significant serial chain indicates that the benefit of adoption for engagement is transmitted, in part, through self-regulation and integrity rather than operating only directly These results extend existing scholarship in three ways. First, they connect ChatGPT adoption to engagement through integrity, responding to debates about whether generative AI helps or harms learning (Kasneci et al., 2023). Second, they provide evidence from an under- researched Nigerian public-university context (Michel-Villarreal et al., 2023). Third, the multigroup analysis shows a significant gender difference specifically in the adoption–integrity link, while the remaining structural paths were invariant across gender, underscoring the value of testing demographic moderation rather than assuming it (Sarstedt et al., 2011; Henseler et al., 2016). A companion analysis of the same dataset examines age-group differences separately. This exploration further highlights the importance of understanding how various demographic factors influence interactions with generative AI in educational settings. By exploring these nuances, researchers can better tailor their approaches to enhance learning outcomes across diverse student Since academic integrity was the strongest single predictor of engagement in this, exceeding both direct paths from adoption and self-regulation, institutions should treat integrity- building as the highest-leverage intervention point in the chain rather than one of several parallel priorities. Concretely, because the measurement items retained here specifically address acknowledging AI-generated content, avoiding AI-generated content, avoiding the submission of non-original work, and using ChatGPT to assist rather than replace independent thought, course- level assessment redesign should require students to submit a brief AI-use disclosure alongside major assignments, stating which sections, if any, involved ChatGPT assistance and how. This approach operationalizes the integrity construct actually measured in this study, rather than relying on a generic honour code that students might disconnect from their specific AI use. Because self-regulated learning mediated a substantial share of the adoption–engagement relationship (indirect effect via SRL alone = 0.081, nearly double the direct AINT-only path), Cross River State universities should embed brief, structured self-regulation prompts (goal-setting and self-monitoring checklists) directly into AI-supported coursework activities, rather than offering self-regulation training as a separate, generic study-skills workshop divorced from actual ChatGPT use. Because the adoption–integrity path was significantly stronger among female students (β = 0.308 versus 0.050 for male students, Table 7), targeted orientation sessions on translating ChatGPT use into honest academic practice may plausibly yield larger integrity gains if piloted first with female student cohorts, while male students’ comparatively weak adoption– integrity link warrants separate investigation into what non-integrity-mediated pathway is instead driving their engagement, a question this study’s design cannot resolve but that institutional data (e.g., disciplinary referral records by gender) could help clarify. Because the remaining structural paths were invariant across gender, the integrity-focused interventions proposed above can be implemented as a single, unified program rather than requiring separate versions for male and female students, with the disclosure mechanism and self-regulation prompts applied uniformly while the female-first piloting recommendation targets specifically the one path found to differ. This approach not only streamlines the implementation process but also enhances the potential for collective buy-in from all students. By fostering an inclusive environment, the program aims to promote shared accountability and support among peers, ultimately driving greater engagement This study found that the adoption of ChatGPT through the serial mechanism of self-regulated learning and academic integrity directly and indirectly supports learning engagement among Nigerian undergraduates. This relationship was invariant across gender on all but a single path (adoption–integrity), which was significantly stronger among female students. Based on the technology-acceptance and self-regulation perspectives and applying multigroup PLS-SEM by gender, this study strengthens our knowledge of responsible generative AI integration and offers practical implications for undergraduate education. A companion paper reports the corresponding age-group analysis on the same dataset. These findings highlight the importance of fostering an environment that promotes ethical practices in academic settings, particularly as technology continues to evolve.
