reading.interpretation: This study applied an interpretable machine learning framework to predict SWB among Chinese women using CGSS 2023 data. Among the five algorithms compared, XGBoost was selected for SHAP-based interpretation based on the lowest cross-validated RMSE. The SHAP results indicated that fairness, mental health, loneliness, physical health, and subjective SES indicators were the leading contributors to model-predicted SWB. First, fairness emerged as the most important predictor of model-predicted SWB among Chinese women. This result is consistent with previous studies linking fairness to SWB ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Sun, 2025 ; Wu and Wang, 2024 ). In the Chinese context, fairness may serve as an important psychological link between institutional arrangements, social comparison processes, and individual life evaluations ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Ugur, 2021 ). A stronger sense of fairness may correspond to more positive evaluations of social order, opportunity structures, and personal life circumstances, whereas perceived unfairness may intensify relative deprivation, psychological stress, and social alienation, thereby corresponding to lower SWB ( Kamilçelebi and Burger, 2025 ). The SHAP results support this interpretation from a predictive perspective. Fairness had the largest mean absolute SHAP value, and both the SHAP summary and dependence plots showed that lower fairness values contributed negatively to predicted SWB, whereas higher fairness values contributed positively. The dependence plot further suggested possible heterogeneity by future subjective SES, indicating an exploratory interaction-like pattern in the fitted prediction function. analysis.methods: This study used data drawn from the CGSS. The analysis was based on the most recently released 2023 face-to-face household interview data, which included a total of 5,583 respondents, of whom 3,080 were women. Missing-value analysis revealed an overall missing-data rate of 0.7%. Some variables showed structured patterns of missingness, as shown in Supplementary Figures S1, S2 ( Little and Rubin, 2020 ). To prevent outcome leakage, missing predictor values were handled using leakage-aware imputation embedded within the tidymodels workflow. All predictors were converted to numeric codes before model fitting; nominal variables were recoded as binary indicators, so numeric coding did not impose artificial ordering across multiple unordered categories. Median imputation was applied to ordered numeric and continuous predictors. The binary nominal variables had no missing values and therefore did not require imputation. SWB was not included in the imputation process. During cross-validation (CV), all preprocessing parameters were estimated only from the analysis fold and then applied to the corresponding assessment fold. After excluding cases with missing values in the outcome variable, the final analytic sample included 3,079 respondents. In the sample of Chinese women, the average age was 54 years (range = 18–93); 90.9% of respondents were Han Chinese, 58.9% had agricultural hukou, and 72.9% were married or cohabiting. Educational attainment was primarily concentrated at the elementary, junior high, senior high, or vocational school levels, with a mean personal income of 33,014 yuan and a standard deviation of 66,336 yuan. Descriptive statistics for the sample characteristics are presented in Table 1 . All descriptive statistics were calculated without survey weights. The outcome variable in this study was SWB. Although previous studies have often used multidimensional measures to assess SWB, single indicators can also provide an intuitive reflection of overall SWB and have been widely used in large-scale social surveys ( Gan et al., 2026 ; Sun, 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ). Therefore, this study used a single self-report item to measure SWB. Respondents were asked: “Overall, how happy do you feel about your life?” Responses were coded on a five-point scale: 1 = very unhappy, 2 = relatively unhappy, 3 = neither happy nor unhappy, 4 = relatively happy, and 5 = very happy. Higher scores indicated higher levels of SWB. For detailed variable measurements, coding, and references, see Supplementary Table S1 . Although SWB was measured using a five-point scale item, it was treated as an approximately continuous outcome in the primary regression-based prediction framework. This was a pragmatic modeling choice. Five-point scale happiness, life-satisfaction, or life-evaluation items are commonly analyzed as approximately continuous outcomes in large-scale survey research, particularly when the primary objective is prediction rather than estimation of category-specific odds ratios. The observed SWB distribution was concentrated in the upper categories: 56.7% of respondents reported being relatively happy and 21.1% reported being very happy. To assess whether the regression framework generated predictions outside the possible response scale, we also examined the prediction range of the final selected model. The predicted values remained within the interpretable range of the observed SWB scale, with no substantial out-of-range prediction problem. The observed distribution of SWB and the prediction range of the final selected model are reported in Supplementary Tables S2, S3 , respectively. Building on existing theoretical frameworks and empirical research, this study included 28 candidate predictors covering fairness, health, SES, and covariates. Fairness captured respondents’ overall assessment of the fairness of social distribution, opportunities, and rewards ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Sun, 2025 ; Wu and Wang, 2024 ). Health was measured using a self-assessment method that encompassed both physical and mental dimensions, which allows for a comparison of the relative predictive contributions of these two dimensions of health to SWB ( Ji et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Sun, 2024 ). SES included both objective and subjective indicators. Objective SES was measured based on educational attainment and personal income ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Liao and Li, 2025 ). Subjective SES encompassed respondents’ self-assessments of their current and future SES, SES relative to peers, and SES mobility compared with 3 years earlier ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Shi and Jiang, 2024 ; Sun, 2025 ; Wang et al., 2019 ; Xia, 2024 ). Based on existing research, loneliness ( Chen, 2025 ), leisure activities (8 forms) ( Ji et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2023 ), language proficiency (Mandarin proficiency and English proficiency) ( Gan et al., 2026 ), work stress ( Guo et al., 2025 ), social trust ( Wu and Wang, 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ), and demographic characteristics such as age, ethnicity, marital status, hukou registration, religious affiliation, and political status were all treated as covariates. All pre-specified predictors were entered into each machine learning algorithm. The analytical workflow included data preparation, descriptive analysis, predictor-redundancy diagnostics, data splitting, leakage-aware preprocessing, model training and hyperparameter tuning, model evaluation, and model interpretation. All statistical analyses and machine learning procedures were conducted in R version 4.5.2, primarily using the tidymodels framework. The main software packages and package versions are reported in Supplementary Table S4 . To prevent information leakage and ensure a valid assessment of out-of-sample performance, the test set was held out during preprocessing decisions, hyperparameter tuning, and model selection, and was used only once for final model evaluation. All preprocessing steps were embedded within the tidymodels workflow. After the final workflow was locked, preprocessing parameters were estimated from the full training set, the final model was refitted on the full training set, and performance was evaluated once on the independent test set. After descriptive analyses, pairwise Spearman correlations were calculated to examine bivariate relationships among variables. Multicollinearity was further assessed using variance inflation factors (VIFs) based on a linear model fitted to the machine learning analysis sample after median imputation of missing predictor values. analysis.discussion: This study applied an interpretable machine learning framework to predict SWB among Chinese women using CGSS 2023 data. Among the five algorithms compared, XGBoost was selected for SHAP-based interpretation based on the lowest cross-validated RMSE. The SHAP results indicated that fairness, mental health, loneliness, physical health, and subjective SES indicators were the leading contributors to model-predicted SWB. First, fairness emerged as the most important predictor of model-predicted SWB among Chinese women. This result is consistent with previous studies linking fairness to SWB ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Sun, 2025 ; Wu and Wang, 2024 ). In the Chinese context, fairness may serve as an important psychological link between institutional arrangements, social comparison processes, and individual life evaluations ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Ugur, 2021 ). A stronger sense of fairness may correspond to more positive evaluations of social order, opportunity structures, and personal life circumstances, whereas perceived unfairness may intensify relative deprivation, psychological stress, and social alienation, thereby corresponding to lower SWB ( Kamilçelebi and Burger, 2025 ). The SHAP results support this interpretation from a predictive perspective. Fairness had the largest mean absolute SHAP value, and both the SHAP summary and dependence plots showed that lower fairness values contributed negatively to predicted SWB, whereas higher fairness values contributed positively. The dependence plot further suggested possible heterogeneity by future subjective SES, indicating an exploratory interaction-like pattern in the fitted prediction function. Substantively, this pattern is consistent with the idea that fairness perceptions may be particularly relevant when individuals evaluate their future opportunities and socioeconomic prospects. For women facing uncertainty about future SES, fairness may signal a more predictable and legitimate social order, which could be associated with lower uncertainty-related stress and more favorable SWB evaluations ( Dufhues et al., 2026 ). However, because this study used cross-sectional observational data and a predictive modeling framework, these findings should be interpreted as evidence that fairness was highly informative for predicting SWB, rather than as evidence of a causal effect. Second, health-related factors played a central role in predicting SWB. This finding is consistent with previous studies showing that health status is closely associated with SWB ( Ngamaba et al., 2017 ; Diener et al., 2018 ; Wu and Wang, 2024 ; Ni et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ). In this study, mental health showed greater predictive importance than physical health. Loneliness also ranked among the top predictors, further emphasizing the importance of psychological and socio-emotional conditions in the model’s prediction of Chinese women’s SWB. The stronger contribution of mental health may reflect the subjective and affective nature of SWB. Because SWB captures life evaluations and emotional experiences, it may be particularly sensitive to women’s emotional states, perceived stress, psychological resilience, and self-regulation capacities ( Zhang and Sun, 2024 ). Physical health nevertheless remained important, as it may be associated with mobility, independence, quality of life, and the ability to maintain family interactions and social relationships ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Huang and Shi, 2025 ). Third, SES constituted an important dimension for predicting SWB. Consistent with previous studies ( Li et al., 2023 ; Liao and Li, 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Sun, 2025 ; Shi and Jiang, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Xia, 2024 ), both objective and subjective SES indicators contributed to the model’s prediction of SWB. However, subjective SES indicators showed greater predictive importance than objective SES measures, supporting previous findings that perceived social position may be more closely related to SWB than objective socioeconomic resources alone ( Tan et al., 2020 ). Among the subjective SES predictors, current subjective SES showed the greatest predictive importance, followed by future subjective SES, relative subjective SES, and subjective SES mobility. The importance of relative subjective SES highlights the role of social comparison in shaping SWB, suggesting that women’s wellbeing may depend not only on absolute resources but also on perceived position relative to others ( Wang et al., 2019 ). The contributions of future subjective SES and subjective SES mobility further suggest that expectations about future prospects, opportunities for improvement, hope, and upward mobility are relevant to women’s SWB evaluations ( Li et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Dufhues et al., 2026 ). Objective SES indicators showed weaker predictive contributions. Consistent with previous research ( Fors Connolly and Lindh, 2025 ), educational attainment was more important than log personal income. Education may reflect long-term accumulation of cognitive abilities, cultural capital, social resources, and opportunity structures, whereas income may be more susceptible to short-term fluctuations, social comparison, consumption expectations, and macroeconomic conditions. Fourth, several psychosocial, behavioral, and demographic variables also contributed to the model’s prediction of SWB, although their predictive importance varied substantially. Loneliness was among the most important predictors, ranking third in the global SHAP importance analysis. This suggests that loneliness is not merely a lack of relational resources, but may also reflect social marginalization, weakened emotional connections, and reduced participation in social life ( Webster et al., 2021 ). Social trust, shopping, and listening to music showed moderate predictive contributions. Higher social trust may reflect more positive assessments of the reliability and safety of the social environment ( Xu et al., 2023 ). Leisure-related activities may enrich daily life, support emotional regulation, and promote life or relationship satisfaction. Listening to music may be relevant to emotional states ( Zhu et al., 2025 ), while shopping may be associated with life and relationship satisfaction ( Ni and Ishii, 2019 ). More broadly, leisure participation may be related to SWB both directly and indirectly through health-related pathways ( Ni et al., 2025 ). Other behavioral and resource-related variables, including physical exercise, internet use, language proficiency, and reading activities, showed weaker predictive contributions. Artificial Intelligence has become a transformative tool in English Language Teaching by offering personalized learning experiences, adaptive instruction, and instant feedback. The study shows that AI positively influences the development of listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills while boosting learner motivation and engagement. However, effective implementation requires proper teacher training, responsible use of AI technologies, strong institutional support, and ethical guidelines that address privacy, transparency, and academic integrity. Instead of replacing educators, AI should act as a pedagogical assistant that improves teaching effectiveness and supports a learner-centered approach. Future research should explore the long-term impact of AI on language proficiency, critical thinking, and learner autonomy in different educational contexts. Using larger and more diverse samples will provide better insights. A balanced collaboration between human expertise and artificial intelligence has the potential to create inclusive, innovative, and effective English language learning environments.

reading.overview: Abstract Platform delivery work is widely described as precarious, yet limited scholarly attention has been paid to how algorithmic systems translate workers’ lived conditions into inputs that shape the algorithms’ availability heuristics. This paper proposes a conceptual framework using interpretive synthesis including theories to platform capitalism to address that gap.
reading.methods: This article adopts a theory-building conceptual synthesis to develop a conceptual framework for understanding how worker context may become consequential within algorithmic labour platforms. Rather than testing causal relationships or estimating empirical effects, the study integrates existing theoretical arguments, conceptual contributions, and documented accounts of platform work to identify relationships that warrant further investigation. Its central objective is to connect three analytical dimensions that are often addressed separately, including the organisation of algorithmic control, the potential translation of worker-related signals into algorithmic standing, and the consequences of standing for the allocation of work and the distribution of risk. The synthesis proceeds through conceptual integration rather than empirical aggregation. reading.interpretation: This article proposes that platform AI architectures can be understood as a process that converts workers' structural disadvantage into algorithmic standing, and standing into unequal opportunity and dependence. By separating the functions of algorithmic control from the properties that strengthen it, and by specifying the institutional conditions that moderate it, the framework gives the claim that AI contributes to inequality a testable form and governance a set of points at which to intervene. Bogotá, with its informal labour market, migrant workforce and recent platform regulation, is a setting in which the framework can be examined empirically. Whether the process operates as proposed is an empirical question that the propositions are designed to answer.
reading.limitations: The framework is built from published sources and has not been tested. Worker-side evidence on how allocation and rating systems operate consists of a few small qualitative accounts and one company statement about a points system, and is thin, so the claim that learning-based allocation compounds disadvantage is theoretical. Some sources are reports and journalism and are used for context. The evidence on pay in Bogotá is limited to a single assessment, and the legal provisions summarised here need to be confirmed against primary texts and current implementation. analysis.methods: This article adopts a theory-building conceptual synthesis to develop a conceptual framework for understanding how worker context may become consequential within algorithmic labour platforms. Rather than testing causal relationships or estimating empirical effects, the study integrates existing theoretical arguments, conceptual contributions, and documented accounts of platform work to identify relationships that warrant further investigation. Its central objective is to connect three analytical dimensions that are often addressed separately, including the organisation of algorithmic control, the potential translation of worker-related signals into algorithmic standing, and the consequences of standing for the allocation of work and the distribution of risk. The synthesis proceeds through conceptual integration rather than empirical aggregation. Scholarship on platform capitalism and labour process theory establishes the organisational incentives and power relations within which algorithmic management operates. Research on algorithmic control identifies the functions through which platforms allocate tasks, monitor performance, evaluate workers, and regulate access to work. Studies of platform labour precarity, including research on delivery work in Colombia, provide contextual evidence of workers' reported experiences of scoring, tiering, opaque allocation, and restricted access to assignments. These bodies of literature are brought into dialogue to examine how worker circumstances may become legible to platform systems, how such information might affect algorithmic standing, and how standing may mediate access to work and associated risks. The conceptual framework distinguishes between the functions of algorithmic control and the computational properties of the systems through which control may be exercised. Task allocation, evaluation, ranking, and access restriction are treated as control functions, rule-based decision-making, machine-learning-based prediction, and adaptive updating are treated as analytically distinct computational possibilities. This distinction prevents the existence of a control function from being taken as evidence of a particular AI architecture. In particular, adaptive learning is treated as a theoretically relevant possibility rather than an established feature of the platforms examined. The resulting framework specifies relationships among worker context, algorithmic standing, allocation outcomes, and institutional conditions. These relationships are articulated as propositions intended to guide subsequent empirical research. The study thus makes a conceptual contribution by developing a mechanism that can be investigated through future worker interviews, platform documentation, audit studies, or other appropriate empirical designs. It does not claim to establish the actual technical operation of the platforms, demonstrate causal effects, or verify the use of individualised adaptive learning in worker-facing systems. The conceptual synthesis proceeds in five steps. First, constructs used across the sources were listed and defined. Particular attention was given to worker context, algorithmic standing, allocation outcomes, institutional conditions, and the computational properties potentially associated with algorithmic decision-making. Second, each construct was compared with Kellogg et al.'s (2020) six functions to test whether it was conceptually distinct; constructs that proved to be functions of control were separated from constructs that describe how, or how strongly, those functions operate (properties). Accordingly, allocation, evaluation, ranking, and access restriction are treated as control functions, whereas rulebased decision-making, machine-learning-based prediction, and adaptive updating are treated as distinct computational possibilities. Third, relationships among constructs were traced, and for each, the explanatory mechanism and supporting literature were identified. The analysis considered the theoretical rationale for each proposed relationship, the supporting literature, and the limits of the available evidence. Reported associations between worker standing and access to work were distinguished from demonstrated causal relationships, while documented platform practices were differentiated from inferences concerning their underlying computational mechanisms. Fourth, institutional and individual conditions under which relationships should strengthen or weaken were identified from the Global South and Bogotá studies. Fifth, propositions were formulated only where a mechanism and supporting literature could be stated; relationships that rested on assertion alone were treated as open questions. The resulting propositions specify relationships for future investigation while preserving the distinction between conceptual plausibility and empirical verification.

The SPIRIT-AI items relating to the AI intervention itself are addressed in Section 2.4.3 and, in full, in Supplementary Material S1. analysis.discussion: The present study is designed to develop a voice-based conversational AI coaching agent and to investigate its effects on competitive state anxiety, general mental health, and healthrelated quality of life in elite athletes. The phase I literature review identified no previously published RCT of an agent that analyzes athletes' speech in real time to deliver individually tailored PST. The trial is therefore believed to be among the first of its kind, although the claim rests on that review rather than on a registered systematic search. Whereas earlier app-based interventions in sport have largely delivered pre-recorded audio or text one-directionally (12, 13) , the present agent uses speech both as an input channel and as a continuous marker of arousal (14, 15) , allowing content to be adapted to the athlete's momentary state. The closest published precedent is the pilot trial of Lumen, a voice-based coach delivering problem-solving treatment to adults with mild-to-moderate depression or anxiety against a waitlist control (15) . Three differences bear on interpretation: the population is selected on competitive role rather than on symptom severity, so the expected baseline symptom burden and room for improvement are smaller; the comparator is attention-matched rather than waitlist, so the estimate is incremental and will be smaller even if the underlying effect is identical; and speech functions not only as the interface for a fixed protocol but as a continuously recorded signal that selects and paces content within the session, a feature whose specific contribution this design does not isolate. Further strengths are the structured phase I process, which combines literature review, multidisciplinary stakeholder evaluation and usability testing before efficacy testing; the fully decentralized design, which addresses the time and location constraints central to conventional face-to-face PST; and the comparator, which holds scheduled contact time, session frequency, delivery format and assessment burden approximately constant, so that the estimate is not inflated by nonspecific trial participation. That match does not extend to interactivity, content variety or delivery platform, so the estimate is the incremental effect of the complete agent rather than of voice adaptation alone, and credibility and expectancy are measured in both arms and modeled rather than assumed to be equal. Several limitations should be acknowledged. Participants and the app-based interventionist cannot be blinded, and every outcome is self-reported by a participant who knows the assigned condition, so the trial is analyst-blinded rather than assessor-blinded: the data manager and the statistician are masked to allocation, but the person who supplies each measurement is not. Masking the personnel who code and analyze the questionnaires does not remove the response bias that arises at the point of completion, and no objective blinded endpoint is available to bound it, since the one measure that is not self-reported, the AI voice-based anxiety index, is unvalidated and exists in the intervention arm only. The measured expectancy adjustment described in Section 2.3.4 estimates the size of that bias rather than eliminating it, so expectancy effects cannot be excluded. The comparator, moreover, does not isolate real-time vocal adaptation. The agent is interactive and delivers a varied curriculum of psychological skills, whereas the control condition is a single wordless recording played repeatedly on a general-purpose platform, so interactivity, content variety, content class, delivery platform and treatment expectancy differ alongside vocal adaptation. The comparator delivers no psychological skills training, so the contrast is wider than a content-matched comparison would be and any difference is correspondingly less specific to voice adaptation. The platform difference has one concrete and uncontrollable consequence: the intervention is delivered through a dedicated application that carries no advertising, whereas the comparator is hosted on a general-purpose video platform on which advertising may be served before or during playback, depending on the subscription status of the individual viewer. Exposure to advertising therefore differs between the arms and within the control arm, and it cannot be equalized without hosting the recording locally, which the licensing position of the recording does not permit. The session log records whether playback was interrupted, so the frequency of interruption is reported rather than assumed negligible. Any between-group difference is therefore attributable to the intervention package as a whole, and attributing it specifically to voice adaptation would require a dismantling trial comparing the full agent with an otherwise identical conversational agent whose real-time adaptation is disabled, or with a fixed-curriculum interactive app. Credibility and expectancy are measured in both arms and entered into a prespecified sensitivity analysis, which bounds this confounding without removing it. The comparator is deliberately conservative, and the trial is powered for an incremental effect of d = 0.60 on the primary baseline-to-T1 contrast, so a non-significant result would be compatible with a real but smaller benefit. That figure also assumes a baseline-to-T1 correlation of 0.5; a correlation appreciably below that value would leave the trial underpowered, and the observed correlation is reported with the primary results. The single-center design, modest sample, and short follow-up limit precision and long-term generalizability; all psychological outcomes are self-reported; and the AI voice-based anxiety index is exploratory, has no established measurement properties, and exists in the intervention arm only. That index nevertheless governs which module is delivered next, which is a genuine asymmetry: an unvalidated signal shapes delivery while supporting no inference. The consequences are bounded by design, since the index can reorder but cannot alter or withhold content from a fixed library of established techniques, plays no part in risk detection, and must pass the phase I gates on analyzable-utterance rate and split-half reliability before the adaptation layer is used at all (Table 2 ). What remains untested is whether the index tracks competitive anxiety in Korean-speaking athletes; establishing that would require a dedicated validation study against an accepted measure in an independent sample, which is a prerequisite for treating the index as anything other than an internal control signal. The CSAI-2R rescoring is likewise a robustness check on item composition, not an alternative endpoint, since the measurement properties of the CSAI-2R are unestablished in Korean athletes; the alpha and omega values for the 17-item subset are a first psychometric description, not a validation. Attrition, a recognized challenge in fully remote digital interventions, is countered by weekly reminders, short fixedweekday sessions, technical support, and app-log monitoring. Anchoring CSAI-2 administration to each athlete's index competition removes a major source of measurement noise but introduces variability in the interval to competition and in the importance of that competition; both are recorded and adjusted for, though residual heterogeneity cannot be eliminated. reading.interpretation: The first contribution of this study concerns how GenAI changes the starting conditions of learning to plan. A complete AI plan did not simply supply ideas. It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Later reconstruction restored part of the reasoning work that planning is meant to develop. T3’s case followed the opposite order. His self-authored framework initially kept this reasoning work with him, but it did not prevent him from later adopting an AI-generated activity without a visible warrant. From a psychological perspective, T1’s initial acceptance is consistent with research on automation bias, in which people rely on automated recommendations instead of evaluating the available information themselves ( Goddard et al., 2012 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ). Her reflection that she was “not very sure that it was a good design” but still accepted it suggests that the apparent coherence of the AI output supplanted her own evaluation. As automation bias was not measured as a psychological construct in this study, this is an interpretation informed by that research rather than evidence of the effect itself. However, this reliance was not fixed. Once she noticed a specific gap in the plan, she moved from accepting the output to revising it. It shifted planning from constructing an instructional trajectory to authorizing a ready-made one. T1’s first action was not an absence of participation—she prompted, copied, and formatted—but the mathematical or pedagogical criterion for accepting the plan remained unarticulated. Later reconstruction restored part of the reasoning work that planning is meant to develop. T3’s case followed the opposite order. His self-authored framework initially kept this reasoning work with him, but it did not prevent him from later adopting an AI-generated activity without a visible warrant. From a psychological perspective, T1’s initial acceptance is consistent with research on automation bias, in which people rely on automated recommendations instead of evaluating the available information themselves ( Goddard et al., 2012 ; Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010 ). Her reflection that she was “not very sure that it was a good design” but still accepted it suggests that the apparent coherence of the AI output supplanted her own evaluation. As automation bias was not measured as a psychological construct in this study, this is an interpretation informed by that research rather than evidence of the effect itself. However, this reliance was not fixed. Once she noticed a specific gap in the plan, she moved from accepting the output to revising it. This finding adds to existing research on preservice teachers and GenAI. Previous studies have mainly examined preservice teachers’ AI-related knowledge (AI-TPACK), their perceptions of the benefits of GenAI, and their integration of it into lesson planning ( Aldemir et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2024 ; Kılıçkaya and Kic-Drgas, 2025 ). These aspects remain important, but they do not show which instructional decisions preservice teachers actually make for themselves when AI is involved. Nor does visible human participation guarantee the kind of hybrid intelligence envisioned in human-AI collaboration ( Cukurova, 2025 ). The present cases show that participation in the process alone is not enough to meet this condition. These cases point to a more demanding standard: preservice teachers should be able to identify, warrant, and assume responsibility for consequential instructional decisions. The finding also contributes to practice-based teacher education. Approximations are valuable when they preserve the core work novices need to learn ( Grossman et al., 2009 ). Simulation-based environments similarly create protected opportunities to rehearse decisions and examine their consequences ( Dieker et al., 2014 ; Ke and Xu, 2020 ). We propose that AI-assisted planning is more likely to remain an approximation of practice when the task requires preservice teachers to decompose the problem, anticipate students, compare alternatives, and justify transformations. A task that simply asks for a complete lesson plan may allow the AI to do much of this work. A task that asks preservice teachers to examine an AI plan and revise it against explicit professional criteria is more likely to help them retain this work. The second contribution is a decision-level account of professional judgment in lesson planning. The findings show that judgment could not be inferred from the amount of prompting or editing because the same visible action carried different meanings across episodes. Prompting the AI could keep authority with the participant or leave the AI as the substantive source. Retaining an AI proposal could follow deliberate comparison or unexamined trust. Recognizing a missing response could demonstrate pedagogical awareness while leaving AI’s plan unchanged. As warrant and enactment are part of how authority was defined, the substantive finding is that neither the type nor the amount of visible activity tracked these criteria. This finding brings research on epistemic agency into direct contact with professional judgment and professional noticing. Epistemic agency has emphasized responsibility for knowledge advancement and the negotiation of what counts as legitimate knowledge ( Damsa et al., 2010 ; Scardamalia, 2002 ; Stroupe, 2014 ). In lesson planning, the knowledge object is prospective practice. Responsibility is therefore visible when a teacher’s mathematical, curricular, pedagogical, or feasibility judgment changes what students would encounter. This interpretation is consistent with accounts of teacher judgment and noticing in which teachers attend to consequential information, interpret it through professional knowledge, and connect it to action ( Shulman, 1987 ; van Es and Sherin, 2008 ; Jacobs et al., 2010 ). The source-action-warrant-enactment sequence offers a way to observe that responsibility without treating AI contribution as inherently displacing or teacher editing as inherently agentic. The decision-level analysis also qualifies participant typologies. Song et al. (2025) identified useful patterns and levels in teachers’ GenAI integration, but the present cases show that professional authority can vary across different objects within the same planning session. T1 both ceded and retained authority; T4 both enacted a student-oriented sequencing decision and left other pedagogical insights outside the plan. Typologies may summarize broad orientations, but they should not be assumed to describe every professional decision. In these cases, ecological agency offered a more plausible account of this variation than a stable user trait ( Priestley et al., 2015 ). In the present cases, knowledge of student thinking, practicum experience, mathematical structure, and judgment about lesson capacity enabled authority to remain with the preservice teacher. Uncertainty about content or curriculum, limited teaching experience, and the fluent completeness of AI output made independent evaluation more difficult. Authority therefore had to be re-established for each consequential decision rather than secured once for the whole task. The third contribution is methodological: claims about professional judgment require evidence of how decisions developed. In this study, the screen recordings established what participants did and in what order, while the interviews and reflections supplied, extended, or complicated their reasons. Together, these sources revealed two vulnerabilities that would have been difficult to identify from final plans alone. The two differ in empirical breadth. The entire review p rocess adhered strictly to the updated Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta - Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 guidelines (Sohrabi et al., 2021) ; (Page et al., 2021) . This specific framework was deliberately selected to guarantee methodological transparency, minimize systemic selection bias, and ensure the strict replicability of the search and screening procedures. Furthermore, the comprehensive progression of litera ture identification, screening, eligibility assessment, and final inclusion is visually delineated in the PRISMA flow diagram (see Figure 1), Figure 1. PRISMA 2020 flow diagram illustrating the systematic study selection process. The eligibility of the literature was systematically determined utilizing an adapted PICOC framework. To capture recent technological disruptions, the temporal context was restricted to peer-reviewed empirical articles and conference proceedings published in English between 2022 and 2026. Contextually, the literature had to explicitly focus on Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) institutions, instructors, or policymakers. Thematically, included Copyright at authors some right reserved this work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License studies were required to investigate AI governance, ethical considerations, or human -centric adaptation models. Conversely, exclusion criteria filtered out non -academic reports, opinion pieces, and studies situated within general K -12 or non-vocational higher education. Furthermore, technical studies focusing purely on algorithmic efficiency without pedagogical or governance implications were strictly excluded from the synthesis. Quality Appraisal and Data Extraction To ensure empirical robustness, a dual -layered quality appraisal mechanism was executed on the screened records. First, an adapted 10 -item Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) checklist evaluated research clarity, methodological appropriateness, and ethical considerations. Second, the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) 2018 assessed methodological rigor across diverse study designs. Articles were retained for synthesis only if they achieved a minimum score of 7 on the CASP instrument and a 60% quality rating on the MMAT. Following this rigorous appraisal, a final corpus of 51 high -quality articles was selected. Data were systematically extracted and coded into predefined matrices aligned with the conceptualization of AI in TVET, ethical tensions, and governance frameworks.

analysis.discussion: The Paradox of Technological Acceleration and Cognitive Degradation A central theme emerging from the literature is the profound paradox between technological enablement and cognitive erosion. Batsaikhan & Correia (2024) assert that generative algorithms and intelligent tutoring systems undeniably accelerate the acquisition of foundational competencies across various vocational disciplines. These advanced computational tools provide personalized cognitive scaffolding and simulated practical environments that immediately benefit technical learners navigating complex operational procedures (Adiguzel et al., 2023). By offering instantaneous diagnostic feedback, automated systems can temporarily bridge knowledge gaps and elevate baseline performance metrics. However, this aggressive technological acceleration directly precipitates a severe dependency cycle that comp romises long term analytical retention. Students frequently substitute deep intellectual engagement with superficial task completion, relying heavily on digital prompts to navigate challenges rather than developing intrinsic physical competence. This rapid digital integration directly precipitates severe analytical vulnerabilities within practical learning spaces. Elaborating on this phenomenon, Matueny & Nyamai (2025) demonstrates that the illusion of competence generated by immediate algorithmic feedback frequently masks a shallow understanding of underlying technical principles. This dynamic creates a dangerous pedagogical scenario where students can execute tasks pe rfectly within a digital interface without comprehending the fundamental physical mechanics governing those specific tasks (Thangavel et al., 2025) . Consequently, learners become highly proficient in software operation but lack the foundational mechanical intuition required for actual physical troubleshooting. When these digital scaffolds are unexpectedly removed during independent industrial assessments, vocational graduates consistently fail to apply their supposed knowledge to unstructured physical environments (Suhartanta et al., 2026) . Empirical evidence strongly dictates that unregulated algorithmic dependence facilitates severe cognitive offloading across diverse vocational cohorts. Wang (2026) highlight that students systematically transfer core analytical responsibilities to external digital systems, fundamentally undermining the constructivist principles essential for true vocational mastery. Instead of fostering autonomous problem solving an d cognitive flexibility, excessive automation forces learners into a passive state of algorithmic compliance (Avcı et al., 2025) . Furthermore, Silva (2026) explains that this functional dependency operates synergistically with profound Copyright at authors some right reserved this work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License psychological anomalies. Escalated digital anxiety and a persistent reliance on machine validation directly impair fundamental reading strategies and complex vocabulary acquisition (Liu & Li, 2026). The resulting educational output is a workforce highly proficient in executing rigid software protocols but distinctly incapable of autonomous critical evaluation. Furthermore, uncritical technology adoption propels educational institutions toward a highly mechanistic pedagogical model that threatens human centric education. Miller (2026) warns that this specific condition, often identified in academic discourse as the Turing Trap, marginalizes empathetic interaction and systematically eliminates essential human judgment from the instructional process. The immediate consequence is a sterile learning environment completely devoid of the contextual mentorship required to navigate complex industrial disruptions (Williamson et al., 2024). Addressing this existential threat, Scherz & Green (2025) argue that the primary mandate for modern vocational educators extends far beyond merely managing digital technology integration. Institutions must actively prioritize preserving human cognitive agency and preventing the complete mechanization of the learning experience to ensure sustainable professional development (Brynjolfsson, 2022). Institutional Inertia and Macro Environmental Pressures Beyond the immediate classroom environment, the synthesized literature exposes a severe structural misalignment between academic output and contemporary industrial expectations. Modern knowledge economies heavily demand high cognitive flexibility, active digital citizenship, and agile collaborative skills (Muzam, 2023). In stark contrast, vocational curricula remain deeply entrenched in static syllabi that heavily prioritize repetitive manual proficiency. Addressing this disparity, Raju et al. (2026) explains that this persistent competency gap is not merely an isolated pedagogical failure but a direct consequence of deeply rooted institutional inertia. Administrators frequently resist curriculum modernization due to entrenched bureaucratic processes, resulting in a stagnant educational ecosystem completely unable to respond to rapid technological shifts (Ichsan & Susanti, 2025). The underlying causes of this stagnation become distinctly apparent when analyzing the broader operational context. Analyses utilizing the Political Economic Social Technological Environmental and Legal framework, whose core components are visually delineated in Figure 3, reveal that institutional technology adoption is frequently driven by coercive governmental mandates rather than genuine internal motivation (de Sousa & Castañeda-Ayarza, 2022). Institutions operating under severe resource constraints frequently deploy isolated digital tools with out possessing the requisite foundational hardware or secure internet connectivity. Consequently, this superficial digitalization process actively exacerbates preexisting socioeconomic disparities and substantially widens the digital divide across vulnerab le student populations (Pettalongi et al., 2024) . PLS-SEM is a variance-based structural equation modeling method that using ordinary least squares regressions (OLS) to estimate path coefficients [46] . The methodological criteria and specific attributes of this research were used to determine the choice of PLS-SEM over covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM). However, the present study is a confirmatory nature, as hypotheses were developed based on theory, but four important considerations were given in choosing PLS-SEM over CB-SEM. The first aspect of the research objective is that it is predictive or theoretical rather than restrictive in terms of theory confirmation. The method CB-SEM is best suited for theory testing because of the global goodness of fit evaluation, while the method PLS-SEM is well suited for studies that focus on explaining variance in endogenous constructs (i.e., R 2 ) and identifying key predictor relationships [56] . With the model accounting for 40.8% in the variance of AWB and 30.6% in BPN satisfaction, showing practical significance, prediction-oriented approach of PLS-SEM is appropriate to our research goals. Second, the model has moderate complexity that includes multiple latent constructs, multiple indicators for each construct, and a mediation pathway. PLS-SEM offers several benefits over CB-SEM

The results, however, must be interpreted as reflecting associations, due to the cross-sectional design and to data being self-reported [68] . reading.limitations: While useful, there are some caveats to take into account when considering the findings. First, the empirical context, consisting of higher education context, may limit the generalizability of the findings to other institutional, disciplinary and cultural contexts. The use of technology, motivation mechanisms and attitudes towards digital tools are contextual [14] . The associations between GenAI, BPN, and AWB could thus be contingent upon the academic discipline, type of institution and cultural background. Second, the cross-sectional study design does not allow making causal inferences. analysis.methods: The study used the Partial Least Square Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS software to test the hypothesized relationships between GenAI use, basic psychological needs and academic well-being. PLS-SEM is a variance-based structural equation modeling method that using ordinary least squares regressions (OLS) to estimate path coefficients [46] . The methodological criteria and specific attributes of this research were used to determine the choice of PLS-SEM over covariance-based SEM (CB-SEM). However, the present study is a confirmatory nature, as hypotheses were developed based on theory, but four important considerations were given in choosing PLS-SEM over CB-SEM. The first aspect of the research objective is that it is predictive or theoretical rather than restrictive in terms of theory confirmation. The method CB-SEM is best suited for theory testing because of the global goodness of fit evaluation, while the method PLS-SEM is well suited for studies that focus on explaining variance in endogenous constructs (i.e., R 2 ) and identifying key predictor relationships [56] . With the model accounting for 40.8% in the variance of AWB and 30.6% in BPN satisfaction, showing practical significance, prediction-oriented approach of PLS-SEM is appropriate to our research goals. Second, the model has moderate complexity that includes multiple latent constructs, multiple indicators for each construct, and a mediation pathway. PLS-SEM offers several benefits over CB-SEM, particularly for modeling systems with high complexity, such as solution inadmissibilities and convergence problems typical of CB-SEM estimations when using complex models [57, 58] . Although our sample size (N = 528) would be sufficient for a CB-SEM approach, the robustness of PLS-SEM to model complexity offers added methodological security. Third, the study takes the direct and indirect (mediated) effect into account, and PLS-SEM has been shown to be more effective in estimating mediation effects in structural models, especially when the mediator is a latent construct, and measured with multiple indicators [59] . This is important since the study concentrates on the Mediation of BPN in the GenAI-AWB relationship. Fourth, although our data was not exhibit strongly non-normality, but PLS-SEM does not make any distributional assumptions, and is less sensitive to non-normality or deviations from multivariate normality in the sense that it yields more stable parameter estimates [60] . This conforms to the current methodological recommendation of PLS-SEM for prediction, formative measurement and models with greater complexity than data [46, 61] . Importantly, PLS-SEM is not intended to exclude the use of a rigorous model assessment. After recent methodological developments, confirmatory composite analysis (CCA) was used to assess measurement models, both Fornell-Larcker and HTMT were used to assess the discriminant validity, and the structural model was assessed using bootstrapping with 5000 resamples [46, 62] . While this is the case, it guarantees the methodological rigor for a variance-based estimator. The data, which consists of N = 528, were checked for missing and inconsistent data before estimation of the model. Descriptive statistics such as frequencies, means and standard deviations were computed to describe the sample and check the distribution of data [63] . Following the SEM literature such as the works of Fornell and Larcker [50] and [57] , the analysis was conducted in two steps, measurement model and structural model evaluation. The measurement model was evaluated in terms of reliability and validity. To assess the internal consistency reliability, Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability (CR) were conducted, and a value of 0.70 was considered acceptable [46] . The convergent validity was analysed by using the indicator loadings and the average variance extracted (AVE) was used with threshold value 0.70 and 0.50 respectively. The discriminant validity was assessed using both Fornell-Larcker and heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratios, the latter being less than 0.90 indicating construct distinctiveness [62] . Once the measurement model was analysed, the structural model was analysed to test the hypothesized relationships. The path coefficients, coefficient of determination (R 2 ), effect size (f 2 ), and predictive relevance (Q 2 ) were analyzed. As recommended for performing PLS-SEM analysis [46] , the significance of the hypothesized relationships was established using a bootstrapping procedure with 5000 resamples. This approach yielded path t and p values to test the statistical significance of path relationships. Besides, the multicollinearity among predictor constructs was checked using variance inflation factor (VIF), and if the VIF was less than 5, then there was no problem with multicollinearity. Indirect effects were estimated by bootstrapping in the mediation analysis and Variance Accounted For (VAF) was calculated to determine mediation effect. A VAF between 20 and 80% suggests partial mediation while a VAF score of 80% or greater suggests a full mediation. Methodological contribution of the study is the ability to show that PLS-SEM can be used to explore complex relationships between technological, psychological, and wellbeing constructs in education research [46] . The mediation analysis as an element of the structural model gives a subtle insight into the processes with the help of which AI technologies can affect the outcomes of students.
analysis.discussion: The theoretical framework used in this research was SDT [12, 70] , which examines correlational relationship among the variables of GenAI, BPN, and AWB. The results shown in Fig. 2 offer empirical evidence for both direct and indirect pathways that could be linked to GenAI and AWB of students in a higher education context. The results, however, must be interpreted as reflecting associations, due to the cross-sectional design and to data being self-reported [68] . The patterns observed in the data and the interpretation of these patterns included in the following discussion are limited by the context and method of the study. As it can be seen in the structural model (Fig. 2 ), both BPN and AWB are good predictors of GenAI (BPN: β = 0.553, AWB: β = 0.398) and BPN is a good predictor of AWB (β = 0.325). The model had satisfactory explanatory power in both AWB (40.8%) and BPN satisfaction (30.6%) [46] . The results are linked to the central concept of SDT, which is the need for autonomy, competence and relatedness as intrinsic psychological needs that must be met for human well-being to be fulfilled [12, 13] . Notably, the results extend SDT by empirically locating GenAI systems as a new environmental affordance that may actively influence these psychological needs when learning in a digital setting. The positive correlation of GenAI and BPN (β = 0.553) suggests that students who believe that GenAI is useful, experience high-quality interactions with it and feel it helps with learning also report a high level of satisfaction of their basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence and relatedness). It is crucial to note that this result does not imply "frequency of GenAI use predicts BPN. Instead, it shows that greater perceived quality and pedagogical value (as indicated by the items in Sect. 3.3.2) is correlated with psychological need satisfaction [33, 34] . Theoretically, the distinction is important: it suggests that the quality of pedagogical design and scaffolding in the process of using AI tools in education is more important than providing access to them, and this is based on recent SDT research on AI-assisted learning [34, 69] . This discovery resonates with recent studies showing the positive correlation between perceived competence in AI tasks and intrinsic motivation and engagement [34] . Research indicates that allowing student control over the use of AI tools can help reduce the mechanical reliance as they feel empowered and in control of the situation [10] . Likewise, self-efficacy in using AI tools mitigates learning barriers and promotes self-directed learning [10] . The results of these analyses together suggest that the quality of the perceived GenAI, rather than just frequency, is the most important factor facilitating psychological need satisfaction. There is a special attention level for the positive correlation of GenAI with relatedness. AI mediated interaction can be related, but, because of the conversational nature of GenAI systems, the concept of relatedness is complex. Although conversational agents can assume a peer-like role to induce participation and emotional bonding [71] , the use of relationship-oriented framing raises concerns about agency transfer: passing responsibility for learning from humans to the system, which can lead to cognitive offloading and less reflection [72] . In addition, the qualitative evidence suggests that teacher support is crucial for humanizing AI-based learning as it provides emotional reassurance, helps interpret AI feedback, and facilitates the proper utilization of AI tools, all of which boost student confidence and motivation [73] . The observed trajectory of relatedness must therefore be considered as indicative of the fact that AI systems can be seen as partial intermediaries of social relationships, but pedagogical support by humans is necessary to maximize the socio-affective value of the use of AI. The direct relationship of perceived GenAI utility and student well-being (β = 0.398, p < 0.001) suggests that perceived GenAI utility is positively associated with student well-being, even when controlling for the mediation pathway through BPN. This finding is consistent with the studies that suggest GenAI can reduce cognitive load, help in academic achievement and aid in the construction of knowledge [29, 74] . But, prudence is in order. Meta-analytic studies in the last few years show that interventions with ChatGPT, on average, have a positive impact on academic outcomes and affective-motivational states, though authors have drawn cautious conclusions because of the low power of the studies and because interventions were assessed only via post-intervention measures [68] . In addition, previous studies have found that the construct of engagement, self-efficacy, and anxiety is multidimensional and has different dimensions for different learner types in LLM-assisted EFL learning [16, 17] . This diversity implies that the impacts of GenAI innovation on well-being can differ across students. The relationships observed may be moderated by individual differences in digital literacy, language proficiency, and learning orientations [16, 17] . Thus, the present results should be seen as general trends rather than universal effects, given the potential benefits of GenAI. Another major theoretical finding of the study is that the partial mediation of BPN in the relationship between GenAI and AWB (β = 0.180, p < 0.001) was validated. As shown in Fig. 2 , there are both direct and indirect pathways between GenAI and academic well-being through psychological need satisfaction. This observation confirms the empirical evidence for the SDT process model of human motivation that describes the role of contextual conditions on well-being via psychological needs [12] . The relatively smaller indirect effect on AWB (VAF = 31.1%) than the direct effect (69%) indicates that the primary pathway between GenAI and AWB likely involves functional and experiential processes with BPN being a secondary pathway. Caution should be used when interpreting this pattern due to the cross sectional design. This may be due to shared method variance [67] , the novelty effect of the use of GenAI [68] , or the influence of unmeasured third variables. Future longitudinal studies are required to find out if the direct pathway continues to be the stronger pathway over time or if the indirect pathway via BPN becomes more salient as the novelty of GenAI decreases over time. The results further add to a growing body of evidence that underlines the significance of human support in an AImediated learning environment. Recently, the study based on SDT has revealed that teachers' support is highly significant to improve competence and relatedness satisfaction, and has a significant role in increasing engagement and higherorder thinking skills in GenAI-assisted simulation-based learning (SBL) [75] . In a similar manner, there is a positive correlation between teacher-led generative AI support and student agency, which in turn positively correlates with student learning gains, and the correlation between teacher-led generative AI support and student agency is mediated by perceived fairness [69] . The studies in this collection indicate that the pedagogical value of generative AI goes beyond mere access to the tool, but rather depends on its pedagogical regulation, uptake by learners, and when taught in supportive learning conditions [69] . analysis.limitations: While useful, there are some caveats to take into account when considering the findings. First, the empirical context, consisting of higher education context, may limit the generalizability of the findings to other institutional, disciplinary and cultural contexts. The use of technology, motivation mechanisms and attitudes towards digital tools are contextual [14] . The associations between GenAI, BPN, and AWB could thus be contingent upon the academic discipline, type of institution and cultural background. Second, the cross-sectional study design does not allow making causal inferences. While the structural relationships are theoretical foundations of SDT [12, 13] , the temporal dynamics through which the relationship between AI use, psychological need satisfaction and well-being emerges were not discussed. The novelty effect of AI interventions in cross-sectional studies is not adequately captured by such studies, and positive changes in affective-motivational states may not persist in the long term [68] . Longitudinal designs should be used in future studies to investigate whether positive relationships found in this study remain over time, and if repeated use results in lower returns to GenAI or even negative outcomes like dependence on AI or a decline in critical thinking skills. Third, common method bias may be a problem with self-reported measures and may not be fully reflective of actual behavioral interaction with AI systems [67] . Furthermore, the results from the study used a rigorous scale adaptation and validation process, but the change from seven to six GenAI items and five to four BPN items in the measurement model should be noted as a methodological consideration. However, the iterative deletion of items may have caused the loss of potentially meaningful variance [46, 50] , even though these refinements were needed to ensure the construct validity of the instrument and its reliability [46] . The refined scales should be cross-validated on independent samples to test the factor structure and the stability of the measurement model in further research. The GenAI scale showed good psychometric properties, but was measured in terms of perceived utility and engagement, not in terms of frequency or patterns of actions. Future studies should integrate self-report data with objective usage data (e.g., log data, interaction traces) to better capture the quality and quantity of the use of GenAI, which may impact psychological need satisfaction and psychological well-being differently [47, 48] . Fourth, there is a limitation in the present model, because there were no teacher-side or course-level variables. Recent studies have shown that teacher support is a crucial element in the humanization of AI-assisted learning, providing emotional support and reassurance, clarifying AI feedback, and ensuring effective use of the tools [73] . Also, GenAI assistance provided by teachers has been found to be positively correlated with students' perceptions of learning gains, when they are using their agency to utilize it [69] . Future studies should involve teacher-level variables to explore how pedagogical regulation and use of GenAI are related to student well-being and learning outcomes. Fifth, the study did not take into account the learner profiles and individual differences that could moderate the observed relationships. The findings of this study indicate that engagement, self-efficacy, and anxiety are multidimensional and heterogeneous concepts, which can differ substantially in terms of learner profiles in the context of LLM-assisted EFL learning [16, 17] . Future studies should use person-centered methods, including latent profile analysis, to uncover unique subgroups of learners and explore their different experiences of GenAI mediated learning environments. Overall, the current results support the idea that there is a positive relationship between perceived GenAI utility and engagement and academic well-being, which is explained by the satisfaction of basic psychological needs. These results must be taken with a grain of salt, though, as they reflect students' perceptions of the quality and utility of GenAI and its use, rather than the frequency of use. Pathway from GenAI to AWB is significant, with students who feel GenAI is useful reporting higher levels of AWB, as well as students who experience high-quality interactions and perceive GenAI as supporting their autonomous learning reporting higher levels of AWB as well. This is similar to SDT's focus on experiential quality of learning environments [12, 13] . The results do not imply that increased frequency of using GenAI is associated with greater well-being. Instead, the researchers propose that students feeling the benefits of meaningful, highquality interaction with GenAI, including its usefulness, support, and enhancement of autonomy, are linked to positive psychological need satisfaction and well-being. This is important from both a theoretical and practical point of view. The emphasis at the school should not be on giving teachers access to tools but on the pedagogical design and scaffolding of the use of AI. Future studies could utilize a longitudinal and experimental design to gain insight into causal relationships and differentiate between quantity and quality of GenAI engagement [33, 68] .

reading.interpretation: The question of how to live well has animated human inquiry across cultures and throughout history. As people increasingly interact with and rely on AI chatbots for advice, learning, support, companionship, and everyday decision-making, the design of these systems can increasingly shape the conditions under which people pursue flourishing -both individually and collectively. We have argued that designing AI for flourishing requires moving beyond any single conception of wellbeing or simple assumption that desirable outcomes can all be simultaneously maximized. Human flourishing is multidimensional, and its constituent goods can come into tension. We foreground two questions that cut across these tensions: When is flourishing being optimized, immediately or over the longer term? And whose flourishing is being optimized, the individual or that of the community? Our flourishing-centered AI framework translates these questions into a sociotechnical agenda. Behavioral science identifies and measures the outcomes that matter; interaction design determines how those objectives are experienced and negotiated in human-AI interaction; and technical systems determine how they are represented, balanced, and optimized. analysis.methods: Addressing the temporal tension requires fundamental advances in how AI systems are trained and evaluated. Current RLHF approaches optimize for immediate user approval (Ouyang et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2023) , creating a bias toward short-term satisfaction and sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2024) . Multi-objective training approaches (e.g. adapting temporal difference learning for conversational contexts) (Hayes et al., 2022) may optimize simultaneously for immediate and longerterm outcomes, thereby striking a balance between them. However, this requires new memory architectures capable of maintaining longitudinal user models that track character development and flourishing indicators across extended timeframes (Packer et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2025) . One tractable intervention is RLAIF, which replaces human raters with an AI rater that evaluates responses against explicit principles (e.g. by directly encoding the hedonic-eudaimonic tradeoff) (Bai et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2024) . A deeper approach draws on recent work training AI to evaluate not just final answers but each step in a reasoning process (Lightman et al., 2024; Uesato et al., 2022) . Applied to flourishing, this means evaluating the developmental quality of responses in an interaction: did the model's behavior encourage reflection, introduce appropriate challenge, maintain user autonomy, etc.? Such response-level signals can serve as proximal indicators of longer-term developmental processes and connect naturally to the behavioral constructs identified earlier. To complement this, systems can also learn from the behavior of people who optimize for the long-term wellbeing of others -therapists, parents, coaches, and educators -whose per-turn decisions implicitly encode longer-horizon goals; clinical frameworks such as motivational interviewing (Miller & Rollnick, 2013) and the educational practice of scaffolding (D. Wood et al., 1976) formalize precisely this kind of present-action-for-futuregrowth reasoning. The most ambitious approach would maintain separate training objectives at per-response, per-session, and longitudinal timescales, requiring memory systems that maintain structured and evolving user representations. Interaction design provides another important technical lever. Adaptive systems could calibrate challenge, reflection, and constructive friction based on individual readiness and growth trajectories (Nepal et al., 2024; P.-H. Li et al., 2025) . Technical evaluation frameworks must also expand to include measures of delayed outcomes (e.g. sustained behavior change, skill development, enhancement of character and moral capacities) integrated into multi-objective training (Hayes et al., 2022) . In this sense, the technical challenge is not merely better personalization, but personalization toward flourishing trajectories rather than a sequence of momentary preference satisfaction. The self-community tension demands technical innovations that embed collective considerations directly into system design. Multi-agent training frameworks can optimize AI chatbots to balance individual user needs against broader social outcomes, as in work formulating recommendations as long-term social-welfare optimization across a coupled ecosystem of agents (Mladenov et al., 2020) and multi-agent studies of cooperation and defection in social dilemmas (Leibo et al., 2017) . Value alignment methodologies must incorporate collective values and social norms -not merely aggregated individual preferences -requiring advances in how training data represents community-level goods. Federated learning and privacy-preserving techniques offer pathways for AI systems to learn from collective patterns while respecting individual privacy (Abadi et al., 2016; Kairouz et al., 2021; McMahan et al., 2017) , enabling optimization that considers both personal and community flourishing. Finally, technical evaluation must expand beyond individual user metrics to include measures of social impact, prosocial behaviors, and effects on human-to-human connections. Across these approaches, the central technical implication mirrors the broader framework. AI systems should not implicitly collapse flourishing into a single reward signal. Developers should instead make explicit which dimensions of flourishing are being optimized, how competing objectives are weighted, over what time horizons outcomes are evaluated, and whose outcomes enter the objective function. Behavioral science can specify and validate these outcomes, interaction design can determine how they are instantiated in the user experience, and technical development can encode and optimize them.

The case studied is the practice of using AI by teachers of ICH subjects at MAN 2 Klaten. The key informant of the research was selected purposively, namely a ICH teacher who actively and reflexively uses AI in learning, with the consideration that the informant has direct and representative experience to answer the focus of the research. The research data was collected through two main techniques: (1) in-depth semi-structured interviews with ICH teachers, who explored the experience of AI implementation ranging from planning, material delivery, learning activities, to assessment; and (2) descriptions of the learning process in the classroom delivered directly by the informant as supporting Solo Universal Journal of Islamic Education and Multiculturalism contextual data. The learning practices she developed no longer place technology as a peripheral tool, but c onvergently integrate four main platforms: ChatGPT and Gemini for text processing and idea heuristics [35], Canva for interactive media visualization, and Kahoot as a gamification -based evaluation instrument. This cross - functional integration proves the presence of a paradigm shift from conventional history learning that tends to be textual and rote learning to an instructional ec osystem that is dynamic, visual, and centered on active student involvement [36]. Theoretically, this multi-platform utilization pattern confirms the achievement of the advanced technology adoption phase in the framework of Innovation Diffusion from Rogers. Mrs. Niha has passed the single -tool experimentation phase and has successfully consolidated various artificial intelligence instruments and digital media into a single instructional flow. The functional interconnectedness between generative AI as an adaptive historical narrative builder, Canva as a visual translator of historical facts, and Kahoot as a participatory measure of knowledge retention reflects the level of compatibility and complexity of innovation that has been carefully internalized in teacher learning design [37]. This critical description of the informant's profile emphasizes that the success of the integration of AI in religious education is not determined solely by the availability of technological tools, but rather by the literacy of teachers' digital pedagogical knowledge (TPACK). reading.interpretation: This study concludes that ICH teachers at MAN 2 Klaten utilize AI in an integrated manner in three m ain areas of learning. In the delivery of materials, AI is used from the needs analysis and planning stages to compile summaries, concept maps, historical chronology, and triggering questions, as well as develop interactive media. In learning activities, A I is positioned as a learning partner whose output is mandatory compared with textbooks and other historical sources through the design of verification tasks, thus maintaining the critical Solo Universal Journal of Islamic Education and Multiculturalism thinking process of students. In assessment, AI helps to prepare mu ltiple-choice questions, descriptions, HOTS, interactive quizzes, grids, rubrics, and feedback, with teachers acting as the main validator before the instrument is used. Overall, the teacher's strategy is characterized by an integrative approach but still centered on the authority and professional responsibility of the teacher (human -centered), with the pattern of the "layered verification" strategy as the main novelty of this research in maintaining historical validity while preventing students' cognitive dependence on AI. This study has limitations in the form of a single case study design with one key informant so that the findings cannot be generalized widely. Further research is suggested to expand the number of informants, involve direct participatory observation, and develop quantitative evaluation instruments to measure the effectiveness of the layered verification pattern on students' learning outcomes in ICH subjects in a more measurable manner.
