analysis.methods: This study uses a qualitative approach with a single case study design as developed by Yin and Creswell and Poth [32], which allows an in-depth exploration of a contemporary phenomenon in a real context. The case studied is the practice of using AI by teachers of ICH subjects at MAN 2 Klaten. The key informant of the research was selected purposively, namely a ICH teacher who actively and reflexively uses AI in learning, with the consideration that the informant has direct and representative experience to answer the focus of the research. The research data was collected through two main techniques: (1) in-depth semi-structured interviews with ICH teachers, who explored the experience of AI implementation ranging from planning, material delivery, learning activities, to assessment; and (2) descriptions of the learning process in the classroom delivered directly by the informant as supporting Solo Universal Journal of Islamic Education and Multiculturalism contextual data. It should be emphasized as a methodological limitation that the observation data in this study was sourced from the informant's narrative about their classroom practices, not from independent participatory observations by the researcher, so that the findings were descriptive-contextual in a single case and were not intended to be generalized to all ICH teachers in MAN 2 Klaten or other madrasa h. The data analysis follows the interactive model of Miles, Huberman, and Saldaña [33] which consists of three stages: data condensation by reduc ing and categorizing interview transcripts according to three research focuses (materials, activities, assessments) and three cross-focus themes (information verification, control of AI use, active involvement of students); data presentation (data display) in the form of thematic narratives; and conclusion drawing which is carried out by linking findings to the TPACK framework and innovation diffusion theory. The validity of the data is sought through theoretical triangulation [34], which is comparing the findings with various pr evious research results, as well as member checking on the key points of the interview results to informants. The research methodology was systematically designed to explore the integration of artificial intelligence in Islamic Cultural History ( ICH) learning at MAN 2 Klaten. It encompasses the research approach, data collection techniques, analytical procedures, validation strategies, and theoretical interpretation. These interconnected stages provide a structured framework for examining teachers’ experiences and AI implementation in Figure 1. Five-Stage Research Methodology for Analyzing AI Integration in ICH Figure 1 illustrates five interconnected methodological stages. First, a qualitative single case study approach establishes the research design. Second, data are collected through semi- structured interviews and informant narratives. Third, the data are analyzed through condensation, display, and conclusion drawing. Fourth, data credibility is strengthened through theoretical triangulation and member checking. Finally, the findings are interpreted using the TPACK framework and innovation diffusion theory. This methodological structure supports an in-depth understanding of AI integration in ICH learning at MAN 2 Klaten. Solo Universal Journal of Islamic Education and Multiculturalism
analysis.results: Informant Profiles and Context of AI Utilization The selection of research informants for Islamic Cultural History (ICH) subjects at MAN 2 Klaten, initialed as Mrs. Niha, presented a significant empirical articulation regarding the transformation of digital pedagogy in madrasa h. The learning practices she developed no longer place technology as a peripheral tool, but c onvergently integrate four main platforms: ChatGPT and Gemini for text processing and idea heuristics [35], Canva for interactive media visualization, and Kahoot as a gamification -based evaluation instrument. This cross - functional integration proves the presence of a paradigm shift from conventional history learning that tends to be textual and rote learning to an instructional ec osystem that is dynamic, visual, and centered on active student involvement [36]. Theoretically, this multi-platform utilization pattern confirms the achievement of the advanced technology adoption phase in the framework of Innovation Diffusion from Rogers. Mrs. Niha has passed the single -tool experimentation phase and has successfully consolidated various artificial intelligence instruments and digital media into a single instructional flow. The functional interconnectedness between generative AI as an adaptive historical narrative builder, Canva as a visual translator of historical facts, and Kahoot as a participatory measure of knowledge retention reflects the level of compatibility and complexity of innovation that has been carefully internalized in teacher learning design [37]. This critical description of the informant's profile emphasizes that the success of the integration of AI in religious education is not determined solely by the availability of technological tools, but rather by the literacy of teachers' digital pedagogical knowledge (TPACK). The novelty of the practice shown by Mrs. Niha lies in its ability to maintain the relevance and depth of ICH material in the midst of the flow of AI automation. The use of this new generation of AI platform does not reduce t he historical-spiritual values of ICH subjects, but rather functions and redefines them into material that is more contextual, interesting, and relevant to the cognitive characteristics of Generation Z in the madrasah Strategies for Utilizing AI in the Delivery of ICH Materials The strategy of utilizing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the delivery of Islamic Cultural History (ICH) material by Mrs. Niha explicitly articulates digital pedagogy that does not only focus on technical efficiency, bu t also on reconstructing the way students construct historical knowledge. The use of AI is systematically articulated to overcome classic problems of ICH learning such as materials that are too narrative -dense, the dominance of linear lecture methods, and low visual appeal by transforming historical material into interactive, visual, and contextual cognitive presentations. Technically-pedagogically, this material delivery strategy is operationalized through a combination of three main steps: 1. Narrative -Cognitive Restructuring: AI is operated to streamline complex chronological flows (such as leadership genealogy, political conflict dynamics, and civilizational development) into a systematic concept map and timeline. This helps to lower the cognitive load of learners when understanding complex historical events. 2. Convergence of Interactive Visual Media: A framework of material and key points compiled by generative AI is integrated directly into Canva's design platform to produce visual presentation media, historical infographics, and narrative comics [38]. This cross- platform transforms the delivery of material from a passive text to a responsive visual learning experience for the digital generation learners. 3. Critical Thinking Stimulation (HOTS Facilitation): When delivering the material, Mrs. Niha uses AI to formulate trigger questions and contextual analogies. Historical material is not presented as a record of the dead past, but is linked to contemporary social phenomena such as correlating the diplomatic Solo Universal Journal of Islamic Education and Multiculturalism strategy of the Madina Charter or the scientific progress of the Abbasid era with current issues Theoretically, this strategy emphasizes the fulfillment of the domain of Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPCK/TPACK). AI is not replaced by the position of the teacher, but functions as a cognitive partner that bridges the substance of ICH material that is full of values and facts with the cognitive characteristics of modern students. Thus, the delivery of ICH material transforms from a mere transfer of textual knowledge (transfer of knowledge) to a reflective and meaningful process of historical reasoning. Integration of AI in Student Learning Activities The results of the study show that the integration of artificial intelligence by Mapel ICH teachers has been internalized since the initial pre-instructional phase, namely at the stage of needs analysis and curricular planning. AI is not only positioned as an assistive instrument when delivering material in the classroom, but is used tactically to restructure the narrative of the material to be more systematic, compile essential summaries, map concepts (mind mapping), reduce the complexity of theological-historical ideas, and formulate high- reasoning triggering questions [39]. analysis.discussion: This study concludes that ICH teachers at MAN 2 Klaten utilize AI in an integrated manner in three m ain areas of learning. In the delivery of materials, AI is used from the needs analysis and planning stages to compile summaries, concept maps, historical chronology, and triggering questions, as well as develop interactive media. In learning activities, A I is positioned as a learning partner whose output is mandatory compared with textbooks and other historical sources through the design of verification tasks, thus maintaining the critical Solo Universal Journal of Islamic Education and Multiculturalism thinking process of students. In assessment, AI helps to prepare mu ltiple-choice questions, descriptions, HOTS, interactive quizzes, grids, rubrics, and feedback, with teachers acting as the main validator before the instrument is used. Overall, the teacher's strategy is characterized by an integrative approach but still centered on the authority and professional responsibility of the teacher (human -centered), with the pattern of the "layered verification" strategy as the main novelty of this research in maintaining historical validity while preventing students' cognitive dependence on AI. This study has limitations in the form of a single case study design with one key informant so that the findings cannot be generalized widely. Further research is suggested to expand the number of informants, involve direct participatory observation, and develop quantitative evaluation instruments to measure the effectiveness of the layered verification pattern on students' learning outcomes in ICH subjects in a more measurable manner.

analysis.methods: The present study employed an embedded multiple-case study design to investigate how AI chatbots functioned as metacognitive partners in supporting preservice mathematics teachers' metacognitive co-regulation across two related learning contexts. An embedded multiple-case design examines several bounded cases, each containing multiple units of analysis, and enables systematic within-case and cross-case comparison (Al Qur'an, 2025; Yin, 2003) . The design was deemed appropriate for the study because multiple-case studies support the in-depth investigation of complex learning processes in naturalistic mathematics education settings while allowing for the identification of similarities, differences, and recurring patterns across cases (Zulkarnaen & Aziza, 2026) . The first case involved the utilization of AI in culturally contextualized mathematical problem solving, whereas the second case focused on the application of AI in the development of a culturally inclusive learning lesson plan. These cases represented metacognitive regulation during mathematical problem solving and instructional design, respectively. Each case was delineated by its specific learning objectives, task characteristics, procedures, and expected outputs within the same LMS-based ethnomathematics course. This clear delineation of the cases and their contexts is consistent with Annamalah et al. (2026) , who emphasize that rigorous case study research requires clearly bounded cases to generate context-sensitive and analytically meaningful insights. The decision was made to utilize an embedded multiple-case study design because individual participants and their AI-supported learning processes constituted units of analysis within each case. The participants comprised 33 preservice mathematics teachers who were concurrently seventh-semester students in in the Department of Mathematics Education at a private university in Malang, East Java, Indonesia. The participants constituted the entire cohort that participated in the culturally contextualized mathematics learning in LMS-based environments and were considered eligible for the study because they had completed fundamental mathematical and pedagogical courses and had prior teaching experience. All 33 participants engaged in both cases of the study: AI-supported culturally contextualized mathematical problem solving and AI-supported development of a culturally inclusive learning lesson plan. Across these two cases, the participants engaged in culturally grounded learning activities, reflective problem-solving assignments, and instructional design activities with support from an AI chatbot integrated into Moodle. Within the embedded multiple-case study design, the participants and their AI-supported learning processes constituted the embedded units of analysis within each case. Four data-rich participants were then purposively selected as the primary embedded units for in-depth analysis across both cases. The selection emphasized the richness, completeness, and variation of the available data rather than statistical representativeness. The process began with the collection of data from all 33 participants, encompassing Moodle chatbot logs, participatory observation notes, metacognitive reflection journals, selfassessment questionnaires, preliminary interviews, mathematical solutions, and lesson-plan products. These data were initially screened to identify meaningful metacognitive episodes, interaction patterns, and possible indicators of metacognitive failure, such as blindness, mirage, vandalism, and stagnation (Alifiani & Faradiba, 2021) . The interactions between the participant and chatbot were subsequently coded in order to identify metacognitive processes, strategy revision, response acceptance, clarification, verification, and cultural engagement. The participants were then compared according to the completeness of their data, the diversity of their interaction patterns and metacognitive responses, the depth of their reflection, and the availability of triangulated evidence across data sources. Following this comparative assessment, four participants, based on their contrasting and analytically rich metacognitive profiles, were selected for detailed within-case and cross-case analysis. The the data from other participants were retained as supporting evidence where relevant. The study commenced with the development of a Moodle-based learning management system (LMS) that was integrated with an AI chatbot. The LMS contained instructional materials on ethnomathematics, encompassing various aspects of local culture, including the Javanese primbon, traditional foods, performing arts, traditional architecture, and traditional games. These cultural contexts were selected because they represent varied mathematical ideas, including modular arithmetic, measurement, proportional reasoning, geometry, patterns, probability, combinatorics, and strategic reasoning. The Javanese primbon, for example, is an ancient Javanese compendium of life wisdom that uses culturally embedded numerical calculations to interpret events such as marital compatibility and auspicious timing (Utami et al., 2019) . The present study was organized around two cases. In Case 1, the participants were expected to complete culturally contextualized mathematical problem-solving assignment and used the chatbot as a reflective partner for planning, verification, monitoring, and selfevaluation. In Case 2, the participants were expected to utilize the chatbot to support the development of culturally inclusive learning lesson plans for students with special needs, translating their mathematical and cultural understanding into pedagogical decisions. The study was conducted in four systematic stages as follows: (1) Design and implementation stage, in which the participants engaged with culturally contextualized mathematics assignments within two cases managed through an AI-integrated LMS (Moodle) equipped with a chatbot providing reflective scaffolding; (2) Interaction recording stage, in which the LMS automatically recorded all chatbot-learner exchanges, which were later analyzed for evidence of metacognitive activity; (3) Reflection and interview stage, conducted after each session, in which the participants completed metacognitive reflection journals and participated in follow-up interviews to elaborate on their thought processes and learning strategies; and (4) Data validation stage, in which triangulation and member checking were carried out to confirm the authenticity of interpretations. analysis.results: This section expounds on the empirical findings concerning how AI chatbots can function as metacognitive partners in culturally based mathematical learning. The findings are organized around three interrelated themes: (1) the patterns of student interaction with the AIbased chatbot during problem-solving tasks situated in cultural contexts; (2) the metacognitive strategies underlying these interactions, emphasizing students' awareness, regulation, and evaluation processes, including potential metacognitive failures; and (3) the transfer of these metacognitive processes into the design of culturally-inclusive learning (CIL) lesson plans for students with special needs. analysis.discussion: The present study demonstrates that when AI chatbots are intentionally embedded within culturally contextualized mathematics assignments, they can shift from functioning primarily as answer providers, as previously critiqued in other works (El Fathi et al., 2025; Harahap et al., 2025; Yunianto et al., 2024) , to acting as metacognitive partners that support planning, monitoring, and evaluation. This shift directly addresses the pedagogical problem identified in the introduction, wherein unregulated chatbot use often leads to surface-level learning, cognitive dependency, and diminished reflective engagement (Wu, 2024) . By situating an AI chatbot within a structured LMS and assignments grounded in ethnomathematical contexts, the present study provides empirical evidence that purposeful design can mitigate these risks and activate deeper metacognitive processes. Two distinct interaction patterns emerged during the students' engagement with problem-solving and culturally inclusive lesson (CIL) design assigments: iterative and linear. These patterns align with the introduction's conceptualization of human-AI interaction as a form of metacognitive co-regulation rather than unidirectional assistance (Awi et al., 2025; Mulholland et al., 2025) . The iterative pattern, characterized by cyclical questioning, reflection, and strategy refinement, reflects the scaffolded engagement emphasized in constructivist and multimodal mathematical learning theories (Fitria et al., 2025; Wachira & Mburu, 2019) . Subjects 1 and 3 exhibited this pattern. Subject 3 exhibited productive iterative engagement, using the chatbot to validate reasoning and sustain structured reflectionconsistent with theories that conceptualize metacognition as involving planning, monitoring, and evaluation processes (Lucangeli et al., 2019; Taranikanti & Davidson, 2023) . In contrast, Subject 1 experienced a metacognitive failure termed "metacognitive mirage," a form of overanalysis that accords with concerns raised in the introduction about the potential for AI to distort reasoning when regulation is weak (Watts, 2025) . The linear pattern exhibited by Subjects 2 and 4 corresponds ro the widespread tendency among learners to rely on AI as a generator of answers (Kim et al., 2024; Wu, 2024) . Subject 2's uncritical acceptance of AI outputs exemplifies metacognitive blindness and reflects the risks associated with cognitive offloading without sufficient regulation, echoing the concept of "cognitive debt" described in the introduction (Tankelevitch et al., 2024) . However, Subject 4 has demonstrated that linear interaction is not inherently detrimental. When learners deliberately use a chatbot for validation rather than substitution, linear engagement can foster reflective confidence. This finding reinforces the introduction's argument that cognitive offloading is productive only when it is paired with evaluative regulation (Florean et al., 2025) . The two interaction patterns are further depicted in the scenario in Figure 9 . Figure 9 illustrates the central mechanism of AI-learner interaction identified in the present study, showing how interaction patterns with the chatbot-iterative and linear-lead to different metacognitive outcomes depending on the degree of regulation enacted by the learner. As visualized in Figure 9 , iterative interaction may evolve into a well-regulated process that fosters metacognitive success or into an overly regulated process that culminates in metacognitive mirage, a form of over-analysis in which learners doubt correct reasoningan outcome anticipated in the introduction through discussions of excessive cognitive offloading and uncertainty in AI use. In a similar vein, a linear pattern may become less regulated, leading to metacognitive blindness, where learners accept AI-generated information uncritically, aligning with the concerns in the introduction regarding passive answer-seeking behavior (Kim et al., 2024) . However, when linear interaction remains well-regulated, it also yields metacognitive success, particularly when learners use the chatbot as a verification tool rather than as a substitute for reasoning. By demonstrating how iterative and linear pathways can be integrated within a unified regulatory framework, the present study lends support to the theoretical position previously introduced that AI-supported learning operates as a process of co-regulation as opposed to passive information delivery (Awi et al., 2025; Mulholland et al., 2025) . A notable development was observed as the learners transitioned from mathematical problem solving to designing culturally inclusive lessons. While the diagram captures the core cognitive mechanism, the findings have shown that this mechanism expands during lesson design into what this study identifies as meta-pedagogical cognition-an extended form of metacognitive regulation applied to instructional decision-making. Embedding mathematical assignments within culturally meaningful contexts has been demonstrated to deepen both conceptual and metacognitive engagement by establishing a connection between mathematical ideas and individuals' lived experiences, as well as social knowledge (Howlader & Sarkar, 2025; Jojo, 2024; Kusaeri et al., 2025) . It was found that iterative users engaged in dialogic co-regulation with the chatbot, revising tasks to preserve mathematical coherence, cultural authenticity, and inclusivity in ways consistent with culturally responsive pedagogical principles (Nolan & Xenofontos, 2023) . In contrast, linear users demonstrated a tendency to accept AI-generated instructional components with minimal contextual refinement, indicative of a more procedural engagement with ethnomathematical elements. These findings extend the regulatory mechanism illustrated in the diagram by showing that well-, over-, and lessregulated profiles manifest not only in individual reasoning but also in pedagogical judgment. Taken as a whole, the findings reaffirm the introduction's call to reconfigure AIsupported mathematics environments, orienting them toward reflective, autonomous, and culturally grounded learning. By demonstrating how interaction patterns and regulatory profiles shape both cognitive and pedagogical outcomes, the present study provides empirical nuance to the cognitive offloading and regulation balance discussed in earlier works (Tankelevitch et al., 2024; Watts, 2025) . Furthermore, it offers evidence that AI can support both cognitive and cultural dimensions of mathematics learning when grounded in meaningful contexts (León-Domínguez, 2024) . The findings, when considered collectively, strengthen the argument that AI should be repositioned from a role that merely provides answers to that of a metacognitive partners. This repositioning is essential in order to cultivate deep, autonomous, and culturally responsive mathematical learning. The present study examined participants' interactions within a specific Moodle-based, culturally contextualized learning environment. It did not assess whether the identified metacognitive patterns were sustained over time or transferred into actual classroom practice. Therefore, future studies are recommended to validate the proposed framework with larger and more diverse populations, mathematical topics, and cultural contexts. The present study has demonstrated that preservice mathematics teachers' interactions with AI chatbots unfold as processes of metacognitive co-regulation

Concerns regarding the reliability of the knowledge LLMs produce, the impact of their use on critical thinking, and how to promote AI literacy, have been raised by many critical researchers, especially in relation to sensitive topics. This paper explores implications of the use of LLMs for comprehensive sexuality education and pornography literacy. Discourses generated by popular LLMs when asked about pornography are analyzed through a feminist lens. The LLMs produced power-blind statements about pornography, creating silences around the gendered practices. reading.methods: The methodological and theoretical approach taken in this study is rooted in Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis (CDA) and in feminist critical discourse analysis. CDA is a “form of critical social analysis” that explores relations between discourse and different parts of social life and uses discourse as a “point of entry” into explanatory social critique (Fairclough, 2017, p. 13). It combines a critique of discourse as explanation of existing social reality, with the explicit aim to induce change (ibid.) Analyses examine the constructive effects of discourse on social reality by explaining what reality and action a discourse invokes (ibid.). Furthermore, CDA offers ways of constructing and therefore transforming social reality. The relation “between critique, explanation and (political) action is the essence of CDA” (Fairclough, 2017, p. 13). Building on CDA, feminist critical discourse analysis is rooted in radical feminist theories that prioritize the rights of women and girls to be free from sexual objectification, exploita- tion, and abuse (Dekeseredy, 2021). Feminist research aims to contribute to the transformation into a more equitable society by influencing policy, practice, and research (Olesen, 2005), and producing knowledge that pro- motes more equitable gender relations (Renzetti, 2018). Two analytical themes were identified: The silence around the gendered practices of pornography – power blind out- puts; and “Feminist” and “ethical” pornography as an educational tool. In the last section of the results, I reflect on the classroom plans provided by the LLMs and apply a critical pedagogical lens to the analysis. The tables display the texts from the LLMs’ responses which are the basis for The silence around the gendered practices of pornography – power-blind Examining the language around gendered practices is one of the main pillars of feminist critical discourse analysis (Lazar, 2007). This is to shed light on how power operates and how unequal social structures are main- tained in discourses (ibid.). Therefore, it was important to start this analysis by exploring how pornography is problematized in relation to gender. The problematizations about pornography consumption and the real-life impact of pornography that the LLMs provide are often formulated in a gen- der-blind way. The LLMs often refer to “people”, use passive voice, or use the act of something as the subject without indicating who does it. analysis.methods: The methodological and theoretical approach taken in this study is rooted in Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis (CDA) and in feminist critical discourse analysis. CDA is a “form of critical social analysis” that explores relations between discourse and different parts of social life and uses discourse as a “point of entry” into explanatory social critique (Fairclough, 2017, p. 13). It combines a critique of discourse as explanation of existing social reality, with the explicit aim to induce change (ibid.) Analyses examine the constructive effects of discourse on social reality by explaining what reality and action a discourse invokes (ibid.). Furthermore, CDA offers ways of constructing and therefore transforming social reality. The relation “between critique, explanation and (political) action is the essence of CDA” (Fairclough, 2017, p. 13). Building on CDA, feminist critical discourse analysis is rooted in radical feminist theories that prioritize the rights of women and girls to be free from sexual objectification, exploita- tion, and abuse (Dekeseredy, 2021). Feminist research aims to contribute to the transformation into a more equitable society by influencing policy, practice, and research (Olesen, 2005), and producing knowledge that pro- motes more equitable gender relations (Renzetti, 2018). Given the study’s aim to contribute to CSE, critical pedagogy is also an important analytical lens. It can be understood as a theoretical framing of education in which educational processes should serve social emanci- pation, and to eradicate oppression (Freire, 2017). It centers dialogue and the analysis of power relations as opposed to “banking education”, which aims to maintain the status quo by depositing hegemonic knowledge into passive students’ minds (ibid). ChatGPT was the first commercially available chatbot built upon an LLM and remains the most commonly used (Bick et al., 2025). OpenAI developed ChatGPT, for which revenue has grown significantly since its launch in 2022, reaching USD 10 billion in annual recurring revenue in 2025 (Capoot & Rooney, 2025). That same year, ChatGPT reached 700 million weekly users, four times the 2024 figure (Sigalos, 2025). Gemini (formerly Bard) was developed by Google and launched in March 2023, reaching approximately 40 million monthly users by 2025 (Curry, 2025). However, its recent integration into Google search results is expected to increase user traffic. Similarly, launched in 2023, Grok, developed by Elon Musk’s xAI, is integrated into the X social network (formerly known as Twitter) and had approximately 30 million monthly users by the end of 2025 (Cardillo, 2025). In January 2026, after reports have accumulated regarding users being able to produce AI-generated pornographic images with Grok, and use them to harass women, several investigations have been launched (The Guardian, 2026). Two analytical themes were identified: The silence around the gendered practices of pornography – power blind out- puts; and “Feminist” and “ethical” pornography as an educational tool. In the last section of the results, I reflect on the classroom plans provided by the LLMs and apply a critical pedagogical lens to the analysis. The tables display the texts from the LLMs’ responses which are the basis for The silence around the gendered practices of pornography – power-blind Examining the language around gendered practices is one of the main pillars of feminist critical discourse analysis (Lazar, 2007). This is to shed light on how power operates and how unequal social structures are main- tained in discourses (ibid.). Therefore, it was important to start this analysis by exploring how pornography is problematized in relation to gender. The problematizations about pornography consumption and the real-life impact of pornography that the LLMs provide are often formulated in a gen- der-blind way. The LLMs often refer to “people”, use passive voice, or use the act of something as the subject without indicating who does it. Gemini gives a more elaborate description of gendered differences and also dis- cusses violence against women (which ChatGPT omits when describing the societal impacts of pornography). However, in other parts of its answers, Gemini applies a gender-neutral language. Grok’s second responses only mention that more men than women consume pornography. For Q3, Q4 and Q5, the LLMs do not mention gendered differences. However, when explicitly asked about gendered aspects in Q6, all LLMs give multiple areas where pornography impacts men and women differently. Starting with the content, mainstream pornog- raphy often represents stereotypical gendered power relations and displays aggression and violence against women from their male sexual partners (Bridges et al., 2010). analysis.discussion: This analysis of discourses about pornography generated by the different LLMs provides an opportunity to reflect on what the purpose and aim of pornography literacy education within CSE could be. The findings dis- cussed above provided a basis for further theorization about the deploy- ment of LLMs in CSE, and literacy and critical thinking are discussed in The findings of this study suggest challenges for the use of LLMs for lesson planning for CSE and for pornography literacy education. The LLMs produced reduced discourses around pornography, violence against women, and consent, which would require careful revision and further planning from teachers. The generated lesson plans are generally short without much background, and their pedagogical activities are rather simple. This finding is in line with a recent study that showed that teachers often find lesson plans provided by ChatGPT generic and require a significant amount of work from them to contextualize them in their classrooms (Selwyn et al., 2025). While this can help maintain teachers’ sense of agency and authority over GenAI (ibid.), it also requires a high level of literacy with LLMs introduce words without an author, words for which no one is responsible (Bingham, 2024). This makes literacy even more challenging, as it is not always possible to verify the source of information presented or to interrogate the knowledge creation processes of the models that generate it. Current AI literacy approaches demand responsibility from users to critically assess discourses produced by LLMs (UNESCO, 2023; OECD, 2025b) without being able to understand or critically discuss how the knowledge is generated. The LLMs produced discourse that generally avoided explicit arguments about pornography, which can create the illu- sion that the LLMs present objective information and knowledge about pornography. However, as discussed in the analysis, there is a clear clas- sification of “feminist” and “ethical” pornography as an antidote to main- stream pornography, and as a useful educational tool, without considering different feminist critiques on this. It is also problematic that ChatGPT takes the position of an educational authority and recommends “ethical” pornography as an educational tool. This happened before anything related to education was prompted. Furthermore, ChatGPT included a solely positive conclusion about this type of content in a handout for students, which further strengthens the classification. Further research would be needed to see how teachers handle LLM outputs, which are so convinced about a discourse and an educational tool. This study supports the impor- tance of AI literacy in terms of scrutiny of knowledge produced about sensitive topics. Moreover, I argue that the proliferation of easily accessible AI-generated knowledge makes it even more important for comprehensive sexuality education and pornography literacy education that teachers get professional support from curricula, through training, and possibly with the involvement of professionals and organizations that are experts in CSE and can apply a lens that contributes to gender equality. When it comes to literacy, both AI literacy and pornography literacy trends tend to have individualistic, neoliberal approaches to critical think- ing. AI literacy centers on competencies for interacting with digital tools responsibly, ethically and effectively (OECD, 2025b). When it comes to the knowledge output of AI tools the process is often reduced to evalu- ating the sources of the media content (Williamson, 2025). Similarly, pornography literacy is often understood as an analysis of pornography content itself, and as aiming to understand gender relations, a lack of consent, or the occurrence of violence (Dawson et al., 2020). However, it rarely calls for reflection translated into actions for violence prevention, Critical thinking is multi-faceted, and I offer an analysis here that is rooted in critical pedagogy. The impact of LLMs on critical thinking is currently widely discussed and researched. Critical thinking historically has been shaped in social interactions with human beings, and the anthro- pomorphic features of LLMs create the illusion that there is an embodied AMERICAn JOuRnAL OF SExu ALITy EDuCATIOn19 coherence (Larson et al., 2024). This combined with easy and quick access to information makes LLMs a desirable educational tool. However, it has also been shown that the quality of information generated by AI-tools potentially have lower quality (Larson et al., 2024), and that it weakens people’s willingness and ability to critically think about its output (Lindebaum & Fleming, 2024). The emphasis on fast, and tailor-made information risks failing to engage users in meaningful knowledge processes but instead creating “curated narratives from which the individual can remain detached, cognitively speaking” (Costa & Murphy, 2025). In a way, how LLMs produce knowledge can shed light on a key challenge for comprehensive sexuality education is, which is to distinguish itself from merely offering information. Conversations about sexuality, gender equality, and pornography should never be automated. The discourses produced by LLMs about education on pornography call for critical thinking as an important element. However, as shown in the analysis, individualistic critical thinking is promoted, which is limited to being aware of issues of pornography. If CSE and education about por- nography should promote gender equality, and contribute to violence prevention, I suggest that a critical pedagogical approach to critical think- ing could be more beneficial. The relevance of critical pedagogy has been theorized both in relation to GenAI (Costa & Murphy, 2025) and to CSE (Sanjakdar et al., 2015). Critical pedagogy aims to overturn “banking education” which sees students as passive repositories of knowledge offered to them by actors whose aim is to maintain the status quo. Instead, it centers dialogue that fosters critical thinking and enables the illumination of social injustices and oppression (Freire, 2017). When applied to the context of GenAI, the aim is to keep knowledge production as a creative process (Costa & Murphy, 2025). AI coding assistants are evolving rapidly and adoption continues to grow; a single time point would only have captured a snapshot, whereas two time points allowed us to examine how perceptions evolved over time. Writing code showed the clearest decline, with 80% and 82% of participants reporting to spend less time on this activity at each time point, respectively. This is consistent with prior research showing AI tools accelerate code generation [11, 35]. Our qualitative findings help to explain where these perceived reductions in time came from. Participants described how AI handles boilerplate, scaffolding, and small fixes that previously consumed substantial effort (Theme 1,Compressing routine creation work). They also described turning to AI before Google or Stack Overflow, folding what was once a separate information-gathering step into the coding interaction itself, as well as accelerating onboarding onto unfamiliar codebases, languages, and legacy code (Theme 2,Rerouting information seeking and comprehension into AI interactions). Together, these patterns suggest that AI may compress not just the act of writing code but the preparatory work that surrounds it. Some patterns ran counter to expectations. Given that previous research has found that verification consumes substantial time in AI-assisted development [30], we expected more participants to report spending more time on verification activities like testing and code review. Instead, reviewing code was the only task above neutral at either time point, and only modestly so. Testing remained below neutral throughout, meaning more engineers perceived spending less time on it even in an AI-assisted context, though it did trend upward between time points. One potential explanation is that engineers do not always recognise the verification they perform on AI-generated output, such as evaluating whether to accept a suggestion, scanning output for errors, or checking that generated code integrates correctly, as “testing” or “code review” in the traditional sense. As a result, standard Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) categories may not fully capture where this verification effort is actually going. Our qualitative findings suggest developers may view some of these activities assupervisory engineering work, a new distinct category of work that traditional SDLC taxonomies do not capture (Theme 3,From doing to supervising •Directing: specifying intent, crafting prompts, providing context, and iterating when output misses the mark •Evaluating: reading AI output and deciding what to accept, modify, or reject •Correcting: fixing errors, integrating output into existing code, and maintaining consistency Not all engineers experience this supervisory work equally. Perceived impact on developer experience, using the three DevEx dimensions of cognitive load, feedback loops, and flow state, was also generally positive at Q1, though less uniformly so: 66% reported improved cognitive load, 62% improved feedback loops, and 53% improved flow state. Flow state was most vulnerable to erosion. AI coding assistants may structurally undermine flow state. Each AI suggestion requires evaluation; each generation requires verification. The cycle of prompting, reviewing, accepting or rejecting, and iterating constitutes ongoing interruption built into the workflow itself. Our qualitative Theme 3, Verification and trust management as ongoing engineering work, captured this dynamic: participants described needing to maintain vigilance when reviewing AI output, a form of mental effort that persists even when the code itself is generated quickly. This finding is consistent with a previous meta-analysis by Yin et al. (2025), which reported a moderate positive effect of pedagogical agents on SRL, as well as qualitative evidence from recent systematic reviews highlighting the potential of AI for supporting SRL (e.g., Banihashem et al., 2025). At a more detailed level, our analyses of SRL subdomains revealed that AI-PI had significant and positive effects across all three subdomains of SRL (cognitive, metacognitive, and resource management strategies). Although all effects were positive, their magnitudes differed. Resource management showed the strongest effect, followed by metacognitive strategies, while the effect on cognitive strategies was comparatively Several factors may help tentatively explain this pattern. First, many AI systems in the included studies were intentionally designed to support learners’ resource-management behaviors such as help- seeking (e.g., Chen et al., 2025; Chou et al., 2018). For example, Chen et al. (2025) developed an online learning platform that guided students in diagnosing problems, seeking help, evaluating the quality of that help, and integrating feedback from ChatGPT. Because these designs provide frequent opportunities to practice specific strategies while interacting with AI tools, learners may experience more immediate and consistent benefits in these areas. Second, the ways learners interact with AI systems naturally align with key metacognitive processes such as planning, monitoring, and evaluating their own learning. For instance, tools like learning- analytics dashboards help learners monitor their progress (Liao et al., 2024), and AI-generated prompts can encourage reflection or reconsideration of strategies (e.g., Essel et al., 2024). These forms of support may reinforce the processes within the metacognitive cycle and may explain why metacognitive outcomes responded strongly to AI-PI. Third, cognitive strategies such as rehearsal, elaboration, and organization depend heavily on learners’ prior knowledge, personal ways of thinking, and learning beliefs (Pintrich, 2000). These deeper and internal processes often take longer to develop and may not change substantially during short-term interventions. This may help explain the relatively smaller effect observed in the cognitive strategy domain. These explanations, however, remain tentative: they are hypotheses derived from the characteristics of the included interventions and SRL theory, and the present meta-analysis did not These results have meaningful implications for educators, instructional designers, and AI system developers. First, integrating AI-PI into instruction may be especially helpful for supporting students’ management of both internal resources (e.g., effort, time) and external resources (e.g., learning environments, peers, teachers). Second, higher-order thinking skills such as goal setting , self- monitoring, and self-evaluation appear to benefit more from AI-based support than basic cognitive strategies like rehearsal or elaboration. Third, when the goal is to improve cognitive strategies specifically, AI systems should be intentionally designed to provide direct, content-rich scaffolds for these skills (for example, prompts that encourage elaboration or organization). (2025), which found that educational level was not a significant moderating variable in the relationship between pedagogical agents and SRL. One possible explanation for this discrepancy lies in the scope of AI-PI examined. While Yin et al. focused specifically on pedagogical agents, which typically embedded characters that facilitate learning (Yin et al., 2025; Nguyen, 2023), our study included a broader range of AI-based tools such as adaptive learning systems, personalized learning platforms, conversational agents, and learning analytics dashboard. Differences in the range of AI applications examined may contribute to the differing patterns across reviews, although this explanation was not directly tested. Furthermore, our dataset shows an uneven distribution of studies across educational levels: 25 studies were conducted in higher education contexts, compared to only four in elementary education and five in secondary education. The uneven distribution of studies limits the precision of comparisons involving elementary and secondary education and constrains the generalizability of the observed pattern. This finding aligns with the conclusions of a systematic review by Banihashem et al. (2025), who observed that AI-SRL research has predominantly focused on higher education, with minimal attention paid to K-12 settings. In their review, 74% of studies were conducted in higher- education contexts, while only 20 studies focused on middle or high school, and just one study addressed primary education. Such an unbalanced research landscape leaves the true effects of AI interventions on SRL in K-12 education uncertain, highlighting the need for more inclusive research across educational levels. By using a qualitative research design, the study aims to gain deeper insights into the phenomenon by collecting the views of actual users of the service about various aspects linked with the technology, their understanding of the concept, relevance, and expected outcomes from the concept in a specific context, and so on. It also allows researchers to adjust the methodology or procedure based on the insights and emerging trends (Singh et al., 2025) . Qualitative methodology generally considers a specific and smaller sample size, but at the same time allows detailed and deeper exploration of the phenomenon to generate a comprehensive and inclusive understanding of their perspective on the context or service, and provides generalization of the phenomenon (Tandon et al., 2025) . To identify eligible and appropriate participants for the study, the study approached users having knowledge about the role of AI in auditing, basis understanding of the concept, and relevant experience, work or job profile, and related exposure to the phenomenon. The study used these qualifying criteria to identify participants using the online crowdsourcing platform. An online crowdsourcing platform helped to find the right participants by integrating relevant demographic characteristics and some AI adoption characteristics in auditing, which have been set as qualifiers to ensure that the sample's demographic characteristics align well with the population distribution on these demographic measures. The final sample was chosen considering these expected demographic distributions. Several qualified informants were approached for the final open-ended survey. Out of these, 45 participants actively participated in the qualitative study during the month of October 2025. The study collected data from a diverse group of respondents. Such online platforms are susceptible to non-representative bias (Habib et al., 2025) . Thus, to control for this, the study used a representative sampling procedure to ensure the sample's demographics aligned with the composition of the relevant or targeted population. In qualitative research design, to find out the suitable sample size, thematic saturation techniques are widely used. It indicates continuing with the data collection process to a point when no new codes emerged in new themes from the collected sample data (Habib et al., 2025) . The study used a grounded theory-based rule of thumb for sample size determination, which ranged from 5 to 50 respondents, to be sufficient for the study (Sharma et al., 2024) . These 45 participants belonged to diverse finance backgrounds and expertise in the area of financial reporting, budgeting, accounting, cost control, financial analysis, audit forecasting, risk management, software development, integration of solutions, billing, preparing annual statements, and many more similar areas. Out of these 45 respondents, 13 are currently employed with public firms, 30 in private firms, and 2 in family firms. 24 of the respondents belong to the middle management level, followed by 18 from senior management, and 3 from the lower management level in the organisation. 34 have less than or equal to 10 years of work experience, 7 have work experience between 11-20 years, and 3 have more than 20 years of experience. 1 participant had chosen not to disclose his work experience. Data were collected from various geographical regions, including India, the UK, Kenya, South Africa, Riga, Italy, the USA, London, Canada, and many more.
analysis.results: Based on the analysis of qualitative data, we have identified two crucial aggregate dimensions: the technical subsystem and the social subsystem. 3.2.1. Under the Technical subsystem, the study identified two important drivers (See Figure 3 ).
analysis.limitations: This study makes a useful attempt to explore the role and scope of AI in financial auditing, particularly by identifying the technical and social drivers that influence its adoption. However, the study has some limitations that may be addressed in future research. First, the data were collected from 45 auditors, accountants, and finance professionals. Although the respondents belonged to diverse professional and geographical backgrounds, the sample may not fully represent the wider auditing community, especially large audit firms, regulators, clients, and senior decision-makers. Future studies may use a larger and more varied sample to improve the generalisability of the findings. Second, the study mainly focused on the drivers and enablers of AI adoption, while the barriers and implementation challenges were discussed only to a limited extent. Future research may examine issues such as high implementation cost, lack of technical skills, data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, regulatory uncertainty, employee resistance, and overdependence on automated outputs. This would provide a more balanced understanding of responsible AI adoption in auditing. Third, the study relied on qualitative responses, which helped in gaining detailed views but did not statistically test the relationships among the identified factors. Future studies may adopt quantitative or mixed-method approaches to examine how data quality, transparency, organisational readiness, human judgement, and regulatory support influence auditors' trust and intention to use AI-enabled audit systems. Finally, future research may include the perspectives of regulators, clients, investors, audit committees, and technology providers. This would help develop a broader understanding of how AI-enabled auditing affects accountability, transparency, audit evidence, and stakeholder confidence.

abstract_text: This study examines the pragmatic capabilities of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models. Four datasets were created from five AI chatbots and compared to native English speaker data, focusing on four aspects (requestive routine expressions, request perspective, and refusal/apology strategies and their variations). In terms of pragmalinguistics, AI-generated output closely resembles native speaker data. Regarding sociopragmatics, variation in certain strategies (e.g., regret, wish, for refusals; repair, thanking/appreciation, for apologies) across social variables indicates disparities between AI and human behaviour, suggesting the chatbots lack human-like judgment. The study provides practical recommendations for EFL teachers and researchers.

analysis.discussion: The fact that GenAI data included a more varied and larger set of requestive routine expressions should not come as a big surprise, given the fact that data from the benchmark study (i.e., Osuka 2017) is retrieved from a small homogeneous group of NES; meanwhile, GenAI data are meant to reflect the average speaker (cf. the high occurrence of certain apology responses in AI data in Gablasova et al. 2026). The non-statistically significant association between the use of five requestive routine expressions and data type shows the compatibility of AI and human data (RQ1). Meanwhile, the observation that certain requestive routine expressions are more present in NES data may be explained by the written training data of AI models (Gablasova et al. 2026) (RQ1). The resemblance between the two types of data concerning the use of the two main perspectives (cf. Chen et al. 2024) suggests that GenAI data can be suitable for instruction in EFL contexts (RQ1) (cf. studies on AI-based request instruction in EFL, e.g., Alfuraiji 2024; Sim et al. 2025; Sung, Kang 2024). The absence of many refusal strategies (direct, indirect, or adjunct) in GenAI data (RQ1/2) corroborates previous findings on the underuse of pragmalinguistic resources (Gablasova et al. 2026) and the use of shorter responses (Lee, Cook 2024) in AI models. A plausible explanation is that GenAI may not possess the language-use experience/expectations of humans and their sociocultural underlying knowledge, needed for appropriate sociopragmatic output and interpretation of contextual cues (Godwin-Jones 2024; Lee, Cook 2024; Nolan 2025). It may also be linked to practicality: AI models avoid verbosity, as longer responses mean more operations and, therefore, more costs (see Wetton 2025) and the fact that some speech acts, like requests, are not supposed to be AI-initiated (Lee, Cook 2024). The dominance of certain refusal strategies in GenAI (e.g., offering alternatives, expressing empathy/positive ability/feeling/ opinion or agreement/gratitude) demonstrates the chatbots’ empathetic behaviour, compared to the human assertive and dramatic performance (Allemi, Maemi 2011), leaning towards expressing regret and giving excuses and explanations (RQ2). This agrees with Moafian et al. (2019), who reported using expressing wish in a higher-status and alternative in a lower-status context. Compared with Allemi and Maemi (2011), the chatbots’ performance appears to agree with native speakers (cf. Chen et al. 2024) in that more elaboration is offered in a high-status context, and gratitude is offered to a requester who is not higher in status (lower in this study and equal in Allemi, Maemi 2011). The use of regret with a higher status seems to diverge from native speaker performance (Allemi, Maemi 2011) and also diverges from regret use with a close interlocutor in native speaker data (Al-Sallal 2024). In addition, the use of more gratitude/appreciation agrees with NES preferences in refusals addressed to someone close (Al-Sallal 2024). Despite the alignment of the AI performance with humans (cf. Chen et al. 2024), AI systems are still in need for further oral-language-based (Gablasova et al. 2026) and ‘rule-based’ (Godwin-Jones 2024) training on the pragmatics of the various verities of English, to be reliably used for L2 pragmatics instruction and testing (RQ2), which can be achieved through enhancing AI’s nuanced cultural knowledge and contextual awareness (Kecskés, Dinh 2025; Nolan 2025), specifically for ‘reactive’ speech acts like refusals (compared to ‘active’ ones like Overall, GenAI chatbots can produce the main apology strategies found in natural data (RQ1, cf. Chen et al. 2024), despite the disparity in the selection of when to use each in relation to social variables (e.g., power, degree of offence) (RQ2). For example, chatbots appear to over-acknowledge responsibility, which is a sensitive strategy for humans to assume explicitly (cf. El-Dakhs 2018, on the NES tendency to acknowledge responsibility in certain situations and to deny it in others). Likewise, Explanation seems a crucial semantic formula in native apologies (cf. Rabab’ah, Fowler Al-Hawamdeh 2020), a strategy chatbots may replace with others, such as Concern, Request, and Forbearance. Another example is explicit Self-dispraise, which is prevalent in AI data, closely related to ‘admitting self-deficiency’ (El-Dakhs 2018) or ‘explicit self-blame’ (Eslami et al. 2022). This suggests greater apprehension in AI apologies (Rabab’ah, Fowler Al-Hawamdeh 2020), which supports the limitation in chatbots’ ability to process cultural subtleties (Kecskés, Dinh 2025). The variation in the use of two main apology strategies (i.e., repair and thanking/appreciation) and less influential ones (explanation, concern, self-dispraise, and +1 IFID) is attributed to the situation and type of offence rather than to pragmatic competence (RQ2). As a case in point, the offence in the situation set S2-S9 (arriving late to a meeting) requires thanking the hearer for understanding the circumstances of the speaker, giving justifications/explanations, and expressing concern about the hearer’s wasted time – disregarding social distance and power dynamics. As a result, this apology behaviour in the chatbots may not be attributed, as in human behaviour, to awareness of social variables, but rather to the type of offence committed (cf. O’Grady 2023, on AI models’ limited sensitivity to pragmatic aspects of social interactions). The category where variation in the chatbot behaviour seems pragmatically driven is ‘+1 IFID’ (despite the very small residual value) in the situation set S2-S9 (cf. Chen et al. 2024). Given the distinction between awareness versus awareness manifestation in apology production (Eslami et al. 2022, 52), this may indicate AI models’ lack of awareness of social norms, reflected in the inability to vary apology strategies in relation The use of some strategies in GenAI data, like Forbearance, Thanking/Appreciation, and Self-dispraise, which are absent in human data, can be partly explained by the prompting effect (cf. ‘the priming effect’ in Lee, Cook 2024, 7). That is, asking the chatbot to provide more than one appropriate apology for a given scenario can prompt it to vary the strategies used in each apology, mostly based on statistical probability rather than human-like reasoning (Nolan 2025). Moreover, AI apologies may better fit a written genre, and few apologies were email-styled , reflecting the chatbots’ training data (cf. Gablasova et al. 2026). Furthermore, AI chatbots may not be sensitive to sociolinguistic variation in expressing apology (e.g., English variety, gender, age, etc.), which can yield a dissimilar distribution of strategies when compared to human data. abstract_text: Effective personal financial management remains difficult for individuals who lack access to professional, personalized financial advice suited to their income, expenses, and goals. Most existing solutions address only a fragment of this problem: budgeting and expense-tracking applications record transactions but leave analysis and decision-making to the user; robo-advisory platforms focus narrowly on investment allocation; and conversational finance chatbots often generate numerical guidance directly from a language model, which can be inconsistent or unverifiable. This paper presents IntelliFinance, a web-based Smart Financial Decision Support System (SFDSS) that unifies these fragmented capabilities into a single, explainable platform. analysis.discussion: The proposed design directly responds to limitations documented in each of the three reviewed studies. First, French et al. (2021) found that even a well -executed RCT of finance apps produced only a “small number” of behavioral improvements and no measurable gain in overall household financial well -being within one year, with declining engagement identified as a central cause; the authors explicitly recommend targeting a specific problem, keeping the design simple, and using personalization and light gamification to sustain use. IntelliFinance's Financial Health Score functions as a simple, recurring, personally -relevant signal in the spirit of this recommendation, while the Family Financial Mode offers a natural, socially - reinforced reason to return to the app regularly. Second, Liu (2024) documents rapid real -world growth in AI-driven robo-advisory assets under management, alongside an explicit caution that AI systems may make erroneous decisions due to model defects or overfitting, and that financial data carries heightened privacy and security risk. IntelliFinance's architectural decision to compute every numerical output through a deterministic, auditable rule engine — reserving the LLM strictly for explanation, and not for arithmetic or financial -decision generation — is a direct, structural response to this documen ted risk, rather than a marketing claim of “explainability” Third, Khandait et al. (2026) demonstrate that an integrated pipeline of categorization, trend analysis, prediction, anomaly detection, and recommendation is tec hnically feasible with a lightweight Python/ML stack, and their own review notes that most comparable systems are not personalized and do not unify all these functions in one platform. IntelliFinance extends this integrated pipeline concept from expense analytics into the additional domains of emergency -fund planning, SIP-based investment guidance, and EMI/debt-repayment strategy, and adds the single composite Financial Health Score and household -level Family Financial Mode that are absent from that system' s scope. Taken together, the reviewed literature suggests that the value of a personal -finance decision-support tool depends less on any single technical capability and more on the combination of computational reliability, personalized relevance, and sustained engagement. IntelliFinance's contribution is not any one of the individual techniques used — rule-based computation, ML-based analytics, or an LLM -based advisor — IJSAT260411676 Volume 17, Issue 4 (October-December 2026) 8 International Journal on Science and Technology (IJSAT) E-ISSN: 2229-7677 ● Website: www.ijsat.org ● Email: editor@ijsat.org each of which has precedent in the reviewed work, but their combination within a single explainable architecture aimed explicitly at the specific gaps that this literature identifies. 8. Need of The Proposed Research Work Financial literacy and access to affordable, personalized financial advice remain limited for a large proportion of the population, particularly students, young professionals, and first-time earners who cannot afford professional financial advisors. Poor financial planning at an early stage — inadequate emergency funds, high debt burden, or delayed investing — can have long-term consequences for an individual's financial security. This concern is reinforced by French et al.'s (2021) finding that even a targeted, well- resourced intervention for financially squeezed households produced only partial and short-lived behavioral gains, underscoring how difficult sustained financial-capability improvement is to achieve without careful, evidence-informed design. IntelliFinance addresses this need by making structured, personalized, and explainable financial guidance accessible through a web application. By combining a verifiable, rule-based calculation engine with a conversational AI advisor, the system aims to build user trust in a domain where transparency is critical — a concern made explicit in the robo-advisory literature (Liu, 2024). The addition of a Financial Health Score gives users a simple, trackable measure of progress, while the Family Financial Mode extends the benefit of structured planning to entire households, an area largely underserved by existing single-user finance applications, including comparable ML-based expense-analytics systems (Khandait et al., 2026). • The current work covers system architecture, data-flow design, and the calculation-engine specification; empirical evaluation of the stated hypotheses (Table II) against real users remains future work, following the RCT/OLS-adjustment methodology used by French et al. (2021), to sustain long-term usage beyond an initial adoption period. It is followed by a semi-structured interview to gain an insight on the key constructs that may have a bearing on the decision process of a person considering responsible tourism to a heritage site. The first two studies were then used to develop a theoretical framework that could be used to predict responsible tourism, along with the role of various moderators. Study 3 used experimentation and survey design, to empirically understand the role of the various predictors and moderators on responsible heritage tourism. InfraNodus was used to identify the themes surrounding responsible tourism from 262 news articles from the past six months. It helped us uncover hidden connections and insights into the evolving landscape of responsible tourism. It is imperative to distinguish the functional role of the media-derived data from the study’s theoretical architecture. The corpus-based analysis via InfraNodus was used neither for inductive theory building nor for the conceptualization of latent constructs. Rather, this procedure functioned as a methodological bridge to enhance ecological validity, providing a lexical and thematic baseline for the development of experimental stimuli. By using real-world discourse to inform the nudges, the study ensured that the stimuli were representative of extant cultural heritage narratives. Conversely, the behavioural constructs and psychometric instruments used to measure participant responses were derived exclusively from established literature (e.g. Lazarus, 1991), ensuring that the internal validity of the study remained independent of the exploratory media analysis. The themes were generated by a “betweenness centrality” option in InfraNodus which ranks the words or phrases in a text network based on their contextual importance. The news articles were analyzed through a community detection algorithm, which identifies words that frequently co-occur and represents them as nodes in a network – the connections between the words were depicted as lines or curves showing their co- occurrences. Instead of relying on a distributional model, InfraNodus uses graph theory principle to generate these visualizations (Ortiz, 2023). Words that are more influential, as determined by their “betweenness centrality”, are displayed as larger nodes on the graph. Words that appear together often are grouped into thematic clusters, with different colours indicating their community, while word similarity is used to derive higher-level meanings. InfraNodus thus enables the identification of these higher-level meanings without researcher bias, relying instead on the automatic analysis of the text. 3.1.1 Results for study 1. 3.1.1.1 Main topics and influential discourse elements. Our systematic review confirmed a similar pattern, where only one of the 17 included studies (S11) measured human-AI collaboration as a distinct construct. These findings reflect the possibility that existing AI literacy frameworks do not yet fully represent the interactive and collaborative processes involved in human-AI collaboration. In summary, our synthesis of prior measurement studies indicates two main issues. analysis.discussion: Prior AI literacy research has primarily focused on knowledge, understanding, and use of AI, largely framing AI as an instrument or tool. Our systematic review confirmed a similar pattern, where only one of the 17 included studies (S11) measured human-AI collaboration as a distinct construct. Although a small number of additional studies touched on collaboration and related competencies, they were usually limited to the sub-construct level or only indirectly suggested through the wording of specific items. These findings reflect the possibility that existing AI literacy frameworks do not yet fully represent the interactive and collaborative processes involved in human-AI collaboration. In summary, our synthesis of prior measurement studies indicates two main issues. First, when human-AI collaboration items are nested within broader AI literacy frameworks, they are often removed during scale development. This pattern was observed in S4, where an expert panel considered collaboration and communication to be unnecessary components of behavioral literacy, and in S8, where the item "I can communicate effectively with AI tools based on the goals of my L2 writing" was judged to be a poor indicator and removed after factor analysis. These results suggest that human-AI collaboration competency may need to be measured as a construct distinct from general AI literacy. Second, collaboration-related items are inconsistently placed under different subconstructs across scales, highlighting the lack of a shared conceptual framework. For example, the item from S8 above was categorized under "use," whereas in S10, items relevant to collaborative learning were placed under "autonomous learning" in collaborative tasks. Taken together, the limited and inconsistent representation of human-AI collaboration competencies identified in this review reflects a broader misalignment between recent discussions of human-AI collaboration and existing AI literacy measurement frameworks. Thus, we conclude by delineating theoretical and measurement implications that should be addressed in reconceptualizing collaborative AI literacy. This systematic review synthesized 17 studies focused on the development and validation of measures for AI literacy and human-AI collaboration competency within higher education. Across the reviewed instruments, human-AI collaboration competency was rarely measured within AI literacy scales predominantly framed around knowledge acquisition and functional tool use. Even in the few studies that reflected collaborative competencies, they were typically represented implicitly at the item level within broader AI-related sub-constructs rather than measured as a distinct construct. Overall, existing measures largely remain within an instrumental view of AI and do not sufficiently reflect the coordination and communication competencies underlying human-AI collaboration. Building on these findings, this review clarifies the conceptual boundaries between AI literacy and human-AI collaboration competency, providing an initial conceptual basis for collaborative AI literacy. Specifically, we conceptualize collaborative AI literacy in terms of coordination, communication, and metacognition and outline implications for specifying measurement contexts and developing corresponding items. By bringing together extant literature and the studies reviewed, we lay groundwork for future research that can more directly measure the competencies necessary for effective human-AI collaboration. 'Use' refers to how students apply AI tools throughout the L2 writing process (e.g., use AI tools to conduct pre-writing planning and to check and correct grammatic mistakes) 'Evaluation' focuses on how students analyse, select, and critically evaluate AI tools and their outcomes (e.g., compare, analyse and make informed choices regarding AI-generated suggestions). 'AI ethics', centres on students' ethical and safety considerations when applying AI tools in L2 writing. This may include, for instance, students' awareness of potential risks associated with using AI tools in L2 writing (e.g., privacy and information security), or students' capabilities of distinguishing between ethical and unethical behaviours.
analysis.limitations: This review has the following limitations that should be noted. First, the study focused exclusively on newly developed or significantly adapted scales within higher education settings published since 2020, in accordance with our inclusion criteria. That is, widely cited instruments or those validated solely in K-12 or professional contexts were excluded, potentially limiting the comprehensiveness of the AI literacy measurement tools analyzed. Second, the review included a relatively small number of eligible studies (n = 17), and methodological quality was assessed using reported psychometric evidence (i.e., content validity, construct validity, convergent and discriminant validity, and reliability; see Table 3 ) rather than a full COSMIN appraisal. Third, although multiple databases were systematically searched, the review was limited to Englishlanguage publications and did not include gray literature; these decisions may have resulted in the omission of some relevant studies. Finally, the conceptualization of collaborative AI literacy proposed in this review remains theoretical and has not yet been empirically validated through scale development or construct validation studies.
