analysis.methods: Drawing on this theory, we built an integrated "autonomy-reflection" instructional model for graphic design on a smart education platform. Design competence development is the core objective; autonomous and reflective learning serve as dual pillars; the platform provides the supporting environment. Together they form a unified teaching system, and we regard that as necessary for coherent instructional design. The system can articulate the multidimensional intended outcomes of design learning. Traditional graphic design courses tend to emphasize technical operations and the completeness of final works. This model instead divides learning goals into four dimensions: technical competence, cognitive competence, metacognitive competence, and social-emotional competence. We conducted a comparative teaching experiment across two intact classes: the 2022 and 2023 cohorts of the Educational Technology major. Notably, intact classes were retained to preserve ecological validity. The experimental group (n = 37) received a "self-directed-reflection" integrated teaching model in a smart education environment; the control group (n = 36) received a traditional project-based teaching model. Age, gender, and pretest scores did not differ significantly between the two groups (p > .05), which supports their comparability. Students' Self-Directed Learning Scale; and reflective practice ability, gauged through the researcher-developed Design Reflection Quality Evaluation Scale. Students' satisfaction ratings of the teaching model and feedback on their learning experience were also gathered as auxiliary dependent variables. Control variables included instructional duration (16 weeks for both groups, 3 contact hours per week), instructors (the same teaching team), instructional content, and hardware conditions (both groups were provided with computers and design software of the same specifications). Platform use was an intervention specific to the experimental group; the Volume 4, Issue 11, Pp 55-59, 2026 control group was not restricted from using online resources but received no dedicated learning platform or structured guidance. Participants were second-year students majoring in Educational Technology at a comprehensive university, totaling 73 students in two intact classes. The experimental group had 37 students (15 male, 22 female; mean age = 19.3 years), and the control group had 36 students (14 male, 22 female; mean age = 19.1 years). All participants had completed prerequisite courses such as Introduction to Computers and Foundations of Fine Arts and possessed basic information technology operation skills and artistic literacy, but none had systematically studied graphic design courses. The pretest of participants' "technology acceptance" showed no significant differences between the two groups in computer operation proficiency (t = .87, p = .39), online learning experience (t = 1.02, p = .31), or prior exposure to design software (t = .76, p = .45), thereby ruling out the potential influence of technical factors on the experimental results. The pretest questionnaire also confirmed that neither group had received systematic training in self-directed learning or reflection methods in their prior learning experiences.
analysis.discussion: Although the integrated "autonomy-reflection" teaching model achieved generally positive results, its implementation also faced several challenges and limitations. Differences in student adaptability constituted one of the main challenges. About 20% of students (mainly some of those in the technology-oriented and social-interaction-oriented categories) showed a lack of fit with autonomous reflective learning, reporting that they felt "uncertain about the direction" or found "reflective writing difficult." This suggests that adaptability training and differentiated support should be strengthened in the early stage of the course. As one student candidly remarked in an interview, "For the first few weeks, I was not used to deciding what to learn by myself. Later, the teacher helped me develop a more specific learning plan, and only then did I gradually find my footing." The double-edged-sword effect of technological tools also merits attention. A small number of students (15%) relied excessively on the preset effects of design software and AI generation tools, resulting in a lack of originality in their work. Analysis of reflective journals revealed that these students' reflections focused mostly on technical operations and rarely addressed the process of creative formation. This requires teachers to place greater emphasis on originality and thinking processes in task design and evaluation criteria. Teacher workload was a practical issue in implementation. The new model required teachers to invest more time in individualized guidance and reflective feedback. The teaching team reported that, compared with the traditional model, teaching preparation and guidance time under the new model increased by about 40%. How to optimize support tools (such as AI-assisted feedback) and build a teaching community (such as a teaching assistant team and peer review) is key to sustainable development. The maintenance of long-term effects still requires further verification. This study tracked teaching effects for only one semester, whereas the cultivation of autonomous learning ability and reflective habits is a long-term process. The findings lead us to propose several theoretical implications and practical recommendations. Theoretically, this study confirms that self-regulated learning and reflective learning work synergistically in graphic design education. In smart education environments, self-regulated learning gives students room for personalized exploration; structured reflective practice, meanwhile, steers that exploration toward greater depth. The two reinforce each other and jointly foster design competence. We consider this an extension of DiFrancesca et al. (2016) on selfregulated learning and Jin Xinquan et al. (2020) on reflective learning: an integrated theoretical framework particularly suited to design education, a field with a strong practical orientation. For curriculum reform in graphic design, three practical strategies are proposed. First, autonomy should be transferred progressively: structured guidance is needed early on, with autonomous space expanding as competence develops. Early projects may, for instance, specify design themes and technical requirements, whereas later ones can open up theme selection and technical pathways. Second, reflective guidance should be differentiated. We suggest diverse forms of reflective support for students with different learning styles-more specific reflective questions for technically oriented students, and more group-based reflective activities for socially oriented ones. Third, process visualization should be supported. Technological tools can be used to record and display the design process, thus providing rich materials for reflection; version comparison functions, for example, help students intuitively see the trajectory of iterative improvement. Overall, smart-platform-supported "autonomy-reflection" teaching effectively strengthens graphic design students' allround competence-most notably design innovation, self-regulated learning, and reflective practice. Implementation may bring adaptation and workload challenges; systematic support and differentiated instruction can address them. The study offers a theoretical reference and practical paradigm for digital-age graphic design education, with implications for curriculum reform in other practice-oriented disciplines.

analysis.discussion: Feedback condition, not language proficiency and not self-regulated strategy use, dominates individual-level predicted writing gains, consistently across all six analytic outcomes and every model class compared. This result is unlikely to be an artifact of the modeling pipeline: feedback condition is precisely the variable the underlying quasi-experimental design was constructed to test, and the SHAP-based attribution reported in Section 3.7 recovers this signal directly from individual-level, model-internal attribution rather than from an aggregate group-mean comparison, corroborating this literature's ANOVA-and SEM-based conclusions with an independent, cross-validated, model-agnostic method. The magnitude of the effect, GenAI-F students gaining roughly two to three times as much as IMF or AF students across every analytic subcomponent, is larger than the medium-to-large pooled effect sizes typically reported for automated writing evaluation generally, though broadly consistent with the direction of effect reported in randomized and mixed-methods evaluations of automated and AI-mediated feedback, and with recent findings that structured, SRL-cycle-aware AI scaffolding measurably outperforms unscaffolded or narrowly form-focused feedback. Within this study's engineered predictor space, the feedback-by-SRL interaction terms carry more attributed signal than SRLTotal 's own main effect for three of six traits (Section 3.7), suggesting that to the extent self-regulated strategy use matters here, it matters conditionally on feedback modality rather than uniformly. The self-regulated-learning construct's weak and unreliable relationship with writing gain is this study's second major finding, and it illustrates the diagnostic value that motivated the explainable-ML approach in the first place. A weak SRL-to-outcome path coefficient or regression weight, considered on its own, does not distinguish a genuine null substantive effect from a measurement problem; in SEM this distinction is drawn through the measurement model, for example confirmatory factor analysis and reliability estimation, and the pre-modeling reliability check plays the same role in the present predictive pipeline. The reliability check performed in Section 3.1, conducted before rather than after modeling, revealed that the 35-item SRL questionnaire does not reproduce a coherent factor structure in this sample, with an alpha of 0.279 against a published range of 0.75 to 0.84 [9] , so the weak SRL-gain relationship observed here cannot be interpreted as evidence against the substantial prior literature linking self-regulated strategy use to writing proficiency. Validity-argument frameworks for automated writing assessment [35] call for making exactly this kind of construct-validity flag explicit before deployment, and a feature-attribution pipeline is well positioned to surface it, because doing so requires inspecting the predictor's own internal structure rather than only its estimated relationship with an outcome. The comparative model-class results carry a further methodological lesson, echoing broader findings on fairness and reliability in automated scoring [15] [16] [17] that specific modeling choices, not just aggregate accuracy, determine whether a system's outputs can be trusted for individual learners. Random forest achieved the lowest cross-validated MCRMSE among the five model classes compared; SVR and elastic net performed competitively but not better; and the stacked ensemble performed markedly worse than every individual base learner, with a negative cross-validated R 2 on every trait. The negative result reflects a real limitation of the data rather than a failure to report favorably: with only 84 observations split three ways, across the outer training fold, the inner meta-learner cross-validation fold, and the held-out test fold, the two-layer stacking architecture has too little data at its innermost layer to estimate a reliable meta-model, and the resulting instability propagates directly into out-of-fold predictions. Practitioners applying stacked ensembles to comparably small educational datasets should treat this as a caution rather than a default choice. A second, more consequential methodological finding concerns hyperparameter tuning itself. Nested cross-validation with per-trait randomized search, applied to random forest and XGBoost, did not outperform a substantially simpler baseline using the same model class with fixed, conventionally reasonable hyperparameters. The fixed-hyperparameter baseline achieved a lower pooled MCRMSE, 2.197 against 2.258, and a higher mean R 2 , 0.330 against 0.293, than the tuned pipeline, and this pattern held on five of the six individual traits (Section 3.4). A supplementary check confirmed the regression was attributable to the tuning process itself rather than to the trait-specific feature engineering that accompanied it, since restoring the full covariate set under the same tuning protocol produced statistically indistinguishable results, an R 2 of 0.555 against 0.558 for random forest on the Overall trait and 0.551 against 0.525 for XGBoost, compared with the reduced-feature tuned pipeline. reading.methods: CHAT informed the precise architecture of the empirical instruments. The items in the online questionnaire and the prompts within the semi-structured interview protocol were explicitly mapped to capture students' perceptions of institutional rules, the role of their academic communities, and the shifting division of labor between student and technology. abstract_text: Motivated by short, vague, and incomplete dataset descriptions in the Digital Porous Media Portal (DPMP), we developed and evaluated an LLM-based tool to aid users in writing descriptions that comply with curation and domain science best practices. The tool, named Rocco, has two components: a grader and a writer. The grader assesses the quality of user-submitted descriptions based on their compliance with a rubric of ten guidelines, while the writer uses this feedback, along with additional user input, to iteratively enhance them. The tool integrates different LLM techniques. Few-shot prompting provides examples of expert-evaluated descriptions, and the structured rubric ensures inclusion of essential descriptive content. The curation community is viewing and readily embracing AI as a strategy to streamline many curation tasks. We introduce a diagnostic and assistive writing tool to improve the scope and content of dataset descriptions for both specialists and general audiences. Data curation focuses on trustworthiness, authenticity, and attention to detail. The LLM-based curation tool developed in this work supports these practices. It is backed up by a sound evaluation methodology and preserves user agency by involving them in each step to verify completeness and accuracy. reading.interpretation: Taken together, AI should not be regarded as a straightforward upgrade to conventional bioinformatics tools, nor should model-centered discovery be framed as a wholly unprecedented concept. Its significance resides in a shift of emphasis: away from manually predefined analytical steps toward learned representations that increasingly contribute to prediction, intervention design, and workflow orchestration. The contribution of this review is therefore not a claim of priority for that paradigm, but a cross-domain, failure-aware evaluation lens that applies the same six questions to otherwise heterogeneous model classes: what biological representation is learned, what incremental task value is gained, where the model fails under distribution shift, what causal support exists, what resources are required, and what validation or governance is needed before deployment. Classical analytical pipelines remain indispensable, as quality-control procedures, transparent statistical frameworks, standardized workflows, and experimental validation supply the critical constraints that render learned models trustworthy. reading.limitations: The limitations of AI-driven bioinformatics can be grouped into two partially overlapping categories. Technical hurdles encompass data quality, distribution shift, model interpretability, causal identifiability, data leakage, reproducibility, privacy-preserving computation, and computational resource efficiency. Social challenges emerge upon real-world deployment of these models within institutional settings, including compatibility with clinical workflows, regulatory compliance, health-economic valuation, equitable access, accountability, and dual-use governance. Robust design will require closed-loop cycles that link sequence proposal, high-throughput assays, mechanistic interpretation, and safety constraints. The most important downstream effect of AI structure prediction is the emergence of molecular design as a native bioinformatics task. Instead of asking only what shape a natural protein adopts, current models ask which sequence, backbone, or interface should exist to satisfy a desired constraint. Network hallucination showed that information captured by structure predictors can be inverted to generate new folds [90] . Binder-design frameworks, ProteinMPNN, and RFdiffusion connect prediction with therapeutic target modulation, inverse folding, and constrained backbone generation [91] [92] [93] . AlphaFold3 and RoseTTAFold All-Atom broaden this logic to complexes involving proteins, nucleic acids, small molecules, ions, and modified residues [25, 94] . The conceptual flow is straightforward: from prediction to design and then to experiment. A model generates candidate structures, experiments test expression, stability, binding, and activity, and failures shape the next design cycle. Structural bioinformatics is therefore moving from retrospective interpretation toward programmable molecular design. This shift also changes what counts as a useful bioinformatics output. A static structural model is valuable, but design requires ranking candidates across several constraints: foldability, interface geometry, specificity, stability, expression, immunogenicity, manufacturability, and assay feasibility. Many of these properties are not fully captured by current structural objectives. The next phase of protein AI will need tighter integration among structure prediction, language-model fitness scoring, molecular dynamics, experimental deep mutational scanning, and high-throughput functional assays (Figure 3 ). The goal is not merely to generate plausible molecules, but to produce designs whose predicted mechanisms can be validated by wet-lab testing.

Its significance resides in a shift of emphasis: away from manually predefined analytical steps toward learned representations that increasingly contribute to prediction, intervention design, and workflow orchestration. Classical analytical pipelines remain indispensable, as quality-control procedures, transparent statistical frameworks, standardized workflows, and experimental validation supply the critical constraints that render learned models trustworthy. Accordingly, the most illuminating question is not whether AI "replaces" existing pipelines, but which components of biological reasoning can be delegated to computational models without compromising validity, interpretability, or accountability. The merit of AI-driven bioinformatics thus hinges less on raw model scale than on the surrounding scientific ecosystem. This ecosystem encompasses diverse, well-documented datasets, leakage-robust evaluation protocols, explicitly stated causal assumptions, uncertainty quantification together with abstention mechanisms, reproducible execution, privacy safeguards, sustainable computing resources, secure deployment, and iterative experimental feedback. Near-term practical impact will most likely emerge from auditable, scientist-supervised systems that streamline execution and verification of established analytical workflows. As the quality of interventional datasets improves, causal models and multimodal foundation models can broaden the hypothesis-generating space. By contrast, digital twins and fully autonomous discovery systems ought to be treated as conditional long-term objectives rather than inevitable endpoints. Progress within this field is achieved only when learned representations yield biological claims that hold up under independent biological, experimental, and clinical validation. That draft's bibliography has been discarded in its entirety and rebuilt from independently verified sources. Several features of the evidence base may explain variation in findings. Measurement differs: self-reported effort (Gerlich, 2025; Lee et al., 2025) and neural connectivity (Kosmyna et al., 2025) are not measures of critical thinking, and only a few studies measure delayed or transfer outcomes. Populations differ: knowledge workers, university students, and secondary-school students bring different prior knowledge, which theory suggests should change how much they can scrutinise AI output. Tool design differs: unguided chatbots and guardrailed tutors are not the same intervention (Bastani et al., 2025) . Context differs: samples come from the United States, Europe, Australia, China, Turkey, and Bangladesh, with different assessment cultures and AI policies, but few studies compare contexts directly. Finally, most studies capture single sessions or a single term, whereas the concern about critical thinking is cumulative.

Across five themes, the synthesis suggests that the central cognitive task for students has shifted from retrieving information to evaluating it; that unguided GenAI use is associated with reduced cognitive engagement and, in several experiments, with performance gains that do not translate into independent learning; that fluent AI output is readily mistaken for validated knowledge, while automated detection is too unreliable and biased to serve as a remedy; that critical thinking and lateral reading are teachable and that guided AI use and process-visible assessment are promising responses; and that workload, equity, and policy constraints shape which institutions can adopt them. The evidence establishes some of these claims more firmly than others. It establishes that language models hallucinate, that AI detectors are unreliable and biased, and that critical thinking and lateral reading can be taught. It suggests, with growing but still short-term support, that unguided AI use reduces cognitive effort and can dissociate performance from learning, and that tool design moderates this. It remains uncertain whether these effects accumulate into lasting declines in critical thinking, how critical thinking should be measured when AI is part of the task, and whether process-visible assessment improves outcomes in practice. Theoretically, the synthesis refines several perspectives at once. analysis.limitations: This review synthesizes 45 purposively identified sources rather than a systematically searched, exhaustive literature base, and it should not be read as a comprehensive systematic review of a fast-moving field. No structured search of Scopus or Web of Science with PRISMA-style screening was conducted, so the search cannot be fully reproduced, and relevant studies may have been missed. Coding was conducted by a single reviewer, so inter-coder agreement could not be assessed, although the source-by-theme matrix and evidence-strength judgements are reported to make the interpretation auditable. No formal riskof-bias instrument was applied. Several of the most directly relevant empirical sources (Kosmyna et al., 2025; Roy and Jony, 2026) are very recent, and at least one (Kosmyna et al., 2025) has drawn published methodological criticism regarding sample size and analytic transparency that this review has not independently adjudicated; its findings are reported here as suggestive rather than settled. The strongest experimental evidence on delayed effects comes from a secondary-school sample (Bastani et al., 2025) . The proposed connections between classical cognitive science and contemporary GenAI-specific findings are this review's own interpretive synthesis rather than a claim directly tested by any single included study. Finally, only English-language sources were included, and although the corpus includes studies from Asia and the Middle East as well as Western contexts, most sources come from Western highereducation systems, limiting confidence in how far the findings generalize elsewhere. analysis.discussion: This study estimated differentiated associations between five critical thinking dispositions, two GenAI interaction pathways, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy. The findings are consistent with several propositions derived from distributed cognition and depth-of-processing perspectives, while the cross-sectional and self-report design limits causal and mechanistic interpretation. This study examined the associations among five dimensions of critical thinking disposition, cognitive offloading, cognitive enhancement, and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in GenAI-assisted academic learning. Inquisitiveness was positively associated with both interaction pathways, whereas open-mindedness and systematicity showed small positive associations with cognitive enhancement. Analyticity and truth-seeking were not significantly associated with either cognitive offloading or cognitive enhancement. Both interaction pathways were positively associated with perceived supportdependence discrepancy, although the association was stronger for cognitive offloading. The findings contribute to research on learner-AI interaction by distinguishing cognitively substitutive and cognitively constructive forms of GenAI engagement while recognizing that they may coexist. The significant indirect associations further indicate that critical thinking dispositions may be linked to perceived supported-versusunsupported competence through different patterns of human-AI interaction. However, the study assessed perceived support-dependence discrepancy as a monitoring-related self-report rather than as a direct measure of metacognitive monitoring, cognitive ownership, or objective calibration. The present findings should therefore be interpreted as associations with a perceived support-dependent competence gap rather than as evidence of any single established psychological mechanism. Academic stress did not significantly moderate the association between cognitive offloading and perceived support-dependence discrepancy in the present observed-score analysis. This result indicates only that the hypothesized moderation was not detected in the current sample and does not establish invariance across tasks, institutions, or stress conditions. Given the cross-sectional design, single-item outcome measure, common data source, and heterogeneous task contexts, the findings should be interpreted as evidence of conditional statistical associations. Longitudinal, behavioral, and experimental studies incorporating AI-assisted performance, unaided performance, confidence judgments, and validated support-dependence measures are needed to test the direction and mechanisms of these relationships.
analysis.limitations: First, academic stress and perceived support-dependence discrepancy were measured with single items. Reliability sensitivity analyses showed that the focal latent-path conclusions were stable across several assumed reliability values, but this does not substitute for direct evidence of reliability, construct coverage, or measurement validity. The PSD item captures learners' perceived awareness of a gap between AI-supported and unaided competence; it does not directly measure the accuracy of ongoing judgments about understanding or independent reproducibility, nor does it establish illusory self-assessment, overconfidence, or objectively verified calibration bias. Future studies should develop and validate separate multi-item measures of perceived support-dependence discrepancy and metacognitive monitoring and combine them with repeated confidence judgments, AIassisted performance scores, delayed unaided performance scores, and objective calibration indices. Second, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal or causal ordering. Structural paths and indirect associations should be interpreted as conditional covariance patterns under the specified model. Longitudinal panels, cross-lagged designs, randomized interventions, and delayed transfer tests are needed to evaluate directionality. Third, convergent and discriminant validity were not uniformly strong. Three AVE values were below 0.50, and several critical-thinking dimensions showed high HTMT values and semantically overlapping items. Future measurement studies should revise overlapping items, confirm the factor structure in an independent sample, assess convergent and incremental validity against established AI-literacy and GenAI-use measures, and test measurement invariance across institutions and disciplines. Fourth, all focal variables came from the same questionnaire. Procedural controls and the common-method-factor analysis reduced but did not eliminate common-method concerns. Future studies should combine self-reports with prompt logs, source-check records, think-aloud protocols, instructor ratings, and objective transfer tasks to determine whether reported interaction patterns correspond to observable behavior. Fifth, participants answered with reference to usual academic tasks rather than a standardized task, so task type, complexity, discipline, and permitted assistance may be confounded. Future research should use standardized tasks and systematically vary or record task complexity, disciplinary context, and the permitted level of GenAI assistance to test whether the observed associations are task-contingent. Sixth, although the stratified purposive sampling strategy provided variation across regions and institution types, the sample was not probability-based. Future multicenter studies should adopt probability-based or clearly enumerated sampling frames, document institutionspecific recruitment and exclusions, and test the model across a broader range of regions and institutions. The findings should therefore be generalized beyond the participating universities with caution.

The results demonstrate that perceived cognitive load plays an important role in shaping students' GAI-related behaviors. When students experience higher cognitive demands during learning, they are more likely to adopt cognitive offloading strategies by using GAI as external cognitive support. Cognitive offloading further contributes to overreliance on GAI feedback, indicating that students' dependence on AI feedback is not only related to technological factors but also reflects their cognitive responses to learning pressure. In addition, perceived cognitive load directly influences overreliance on GAI feedback, suggesting that cognitive demands can affect students' reliance on AI-generated information through both direct and indirect pathways. Furthermore, this study reveals the role of metacognitive monitoring in shaping the relationship between cognitive demands and GAI feedback dependence. The comparison between groups with different levels of metacognitive monitoring shows that students follow different pathways when developing reliance on GAI feedback. Students with lower metacognitive monitoring show a stronger direct association between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance, whereas students with higher metacognitive monitoring show a stronger role of cognitive offloading in explaining GAI feedback dependence. These findings suggest that metacognitive monitoring influences not only students' learning regulation but also how they manage their cognitive relationship with intelligent tools. Overall, this study extends the understanding of GAIsupported learning by demonstrating that overreliance on AI feedback emerges from the interaction between cognitive demands, external cognitive support, and self-regulatory processes. The findings highlight that effective GAI use requires more than access to intelligent tools; it also depends on students' ability to regulate cognitive resources and evaluate AI-generated information appropriately. This study provides theoretical and practical insights into how university students can develop a more balanced and productive relationship with generative artificial intelligence in learning contexts.
analysis.limitations: Although this study reveals the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, metacognitive monitoring, and overreliance on GAI feedback, several aspects require further investigation. First, the cross-sectional design of this study limits the ability to establish causal relationships among the variables. Although the structural equation model supports the hypothesized associations and mediation pathways, the findings should be interpreted as relationships among variables rather than causal effects. Students' interactions with GAI may involve dynamic processes in which cognitive load, cognitive offloading strategies, metacognitive monitoring, and feedback reliance influence each other over time. Future studies could adopt longitudinal designs, experimental methods, or experience sampling approaches to further examine the developmental and causal mechanisms underlying students' interactions with GAI. Second, this study used a single-item measure to classify students' metacognitive monitoring levels. Although this approach provides a concise indicator of students' perceived metacognitive monitoring and facilitates comparisons between groups, it may not fully capture the complexity and multidimensional characteristics of metacognitive monitoring. Metacognitive monitoring involves various processes, including monitoring understanding, evaluating learning progress, and regulating cognitive strategies, which may not be sufficiently represented by a single item. Future research could employ validated multi-item scales or combine selfreported measures with behavioral indicators to obtain a more comprehensive assessment of students' metacognitive monitoring abilities. Third, the comparisons between the low-and high-metacognitive-monitoring groups in this study were based on differences in path coefficient patterns rather than formal statistical tests of betweengroup differences. Therefore, these results should be interpreted as variations in structural relationships across metacognitive monitoring levels rather than confirmed differences between groups. Future research could apply formal multi-group analysis approaches to further examine whether the strength of relationships among variables significantly differs across different levels of metacognitive monitoring. Fourth, the present study mainly relied on self-reported questionnaires to measure students' GAI use experiences, cognitive perceptions, and behavioral tendencies. Although self-reported measures are useful for capturing students' subjective experiences, they may also be influenced by recall bias, social desirability, and individual interpretation differences, which may introduce potential common method bias. Future research could integrate multiple data sources, such as GAI interaction logs, learning behavior records, task performance data, and experimental measures, to provide a more objective understanding of students' cognitive regulation processes during GAI use. Finally, the participants in this study were recruited from a single university, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Students from different universities, academic disciplines, and educational contexts may differ in their access to AI technologies, learning environments, and patterns of GAI engagement. Therefore, future studies should include samples from multiple institutions and diverse educational backgrounds to further validate the proposed model and examine its applicability across different learning contexts.

analysis.methods: Participants were recruited from several universities through university student groups and class groups using a convenience sampling approach. The questionnaire was administered online. Following commonly used procedures (Curran, 2016; Xu and Li, 2021) , 11 participants with incomplete responses were excluded, resulting in a final valid sample of 665 college students. Among them, 312 were male (46.9%) and 353 were female (53.1%). In terms of academic year, 183 were first-year students (27.5%), 159 were second-year students (23.9%), 172 were third-year students (25.9%), and 151 were fourth-year students (22.7%). The sample size was considered adequate for item analysis and exploratory factor analysis given the initial 26-item pool and the observed sample size. The resulting participant-to-item ratio was approximately 25.6:1, providing a substantial empirical basis for estimating the factor structure. For Study 1, the questionnaire was distributed online through student groups and class groups associated with several universities using a convenience sampling approach. Before participation, students were informed of the study purpose, the voluntary nature of participation, confidentiality of responses, and the scientific use of the data. The AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) was developed through sequential stages. First, the construct definition and provisional dimensional structure were established through literature review and theoretical analysis of cognitive offloading, distributed cognition, transactive memory, and AI-assisted learning. No formal open-ended or semi-structured interviews were conducted, and no separate pilot study was conducted before the main survey. Second, an initial pool of 26 items was generated and refined for clarity, conciseness, conceptual relevance, and appropriateness to college learning contexts. Third, a panel of five experts (all holding Ph.D. degrees in Psychology or Educational Technology, with average professional academic experience exceeding 5 years) independently evaluated all 26 items using a 3-point relevance scale (1 = inappropriate, 2 = appropriate after revision, 3 = appropriate). Their judgments focused on conceptual relevance, representativeness of AI cognitive offloading, wording clarity, and suitability for college learning contexts. The item wording and conceptual fit were revised in response to this evaluation, and the 26-item preliminary questionnaire was retained for empirical evaluation. Fourth, the preliminary questionnaire was evaluated empirically in the Study 1 sample through item discrimination, item-total correlations, and reliability analysis before EFA. Thus, preliminary questionnaire evaluation in the present study refers to expert content evaluation followed by empirical item analysis rather than to a separate pilot sample. A 5point Likert response format ranging from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree" was used. Finally, SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.3 were used for item analysis and EFA. Participants for Study 2 were recruited from several universities through university student groups and class groups using the same convenience sampling approach as in Study 1. The questionnaire was administered online. Referring to the commonly used method (Curran, 2016; Xu and Li, 2021) , 58 participants whose answers were incomplete were excluded, leaving 1,123 valid participants. The final sample consisted of 1,123 valid participants, including 563 males (50.1%) and 560 females (49.9%). Regarding academic standing, 288 participants were first-year students (25.6%), 290 were second-year students (25.8%), 269 were third-year students (24.0%), and 276 were fourth-year students (24.6%). For Study 2, the questionnaire was distributed online through student groups and class groups associated with several universities, using the same convenience-sampling procedure as in Study 1. The Study 2 participants were newly recruited and did not overlap with the Study 1 sample. Before completing the questionnaire, participants were informed that participation was voluntary, responses would remain confidential, and the data would be used only for scientific research. After data collection, Mplus 8.3 was used to conduct confirmatory factor analysis, whereas SPSS 26.0 was used to examine reliability and validity indices.
analysis.discussion: The present study developed and validated the AI Cognitive Offloading Scale for College Students (AI-COS) by examining how different cognitive functions are delegated to generative AI in learning contexts. The contribution should be understood as an alternative and context-specific operationalization rather than as the first measurement of AI cognitive offloading. Recent work has already provided complementary approaches. Jiang and Chen (2026) developed the AIBCO Scale for highereducation students in China, distinguishing lower-order from higher-order cognitive offloading according to the level of cognitive demand. Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous cognitive offloading according to whether users substitute their own thinking or use AI as a scaffold while retaining cognitive agency. In contrast, the AI-COS organizes offloading by the primary cognitive function delegated to AI-memory, assistive task-related processing, and thinking-and was developed specifically for Chinese college students' learning activities. These distinctions make the AI-COS conceptually complementary to existing measures: the AIBCO framework emphasizes cognitivedemand level, the dependent/autonomous framework emphasizes the manner of delegation, and the AI-COS emphasizes the function being delegated. This function-based perspective may be useful when researchers need to distinguish information storage and retrieval from AI participation in academic task execution and from delegation of judgment or decision support. From a theoretical standpoint, the findings suggest that the influence of generative AI on college students' learning is no longer confined to information provision or efficiency enhancement. Rather, AI systems can be implicated in task execution, cognitive processing, and intellectual regulation, functioning as components of an extended cognitive system. The extended mind theory argues that external tools are not merely ancillary to cognition, but may become constitutive elements of the cognitive system itself (Clark and Chalmers, 1998) . Likewise, cognitive offloading research indicates that external resources can reduce internal cognitive load, while the consequences of offloading may depend on the nature and regulation of the delegated activity (Risko and Gilbert, 2016; Turner, 2022) . Within this framework, the present study conceptualized three functionally distinct forms of AI cognitive offloading-memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. These dimensions describe different cognitive functions that may be delegated to AI; the present cross-sectional factor structure does not establish that students move from one form to another over time. One of the important findings is that AI cognitive offloading among college students can be differentiated into three interrelated dimensions: memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. Importantly, this three-dimensional structure represents one empirically supported operationalization of the construct rather than a claim that these are the only possible dimensions. The exploratory factor analysis yielded a clear factor pattern, and the confirmatory factor analysis supported a higherorder structure. The resulting dimensions are also conceptually distinguishable from recent alternatives. Jiang and Chen (2026) separated AI-based cognitive offloading into lower-order and higher-order forms, while Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent and autonomous offloading according to the degree to which users retain cognitive agency. The AI-COS instead differentiates the functions delegated to AI within college learning: memory-related storage and retrieval, task-related assistance and execution, and higher-order thinking-related judgment and decision support. The three approaches therefore address related but non-identical questions about AI-mediated cognition. TABLE Fit indices and testing for measurement invariance across groups. Within this framework, memory offloading primarily reflects students' tendency to delegate basic cognitive operations-such as memorization, retrieval, storage, and organization-to AI systems, thereby transferring part of the cognitive burden to external technological resources. This dimension is closely aligned with the classic notion of cognitive offloading, namely the use of external media to reduce internal cognitive costs. Assistive offloading, in contrast, involves AI-supported completion and organization of learning tasks, including content generation, textual organization, expression refinement, and the handling of complex academic assignments. Thinking offloading involves the delegation of judgment support, analytic integration, logical inference, and decision assistance. These dimensions therefore differ in the type of cognitive function being delegated, but the present factor analysis does not demonstrate that they form a developmental continuum, that one dimension necessarily precedes another, or that greater endorsement of one dimension causes movement toward another. Their co-occurrence under a higher-order factor indicates shared variance in AI cognitive offloading, not temporal progression. The confirmatory factor analysis further supported the proposed multidimensional structure. The second-order model provided the best fit among the three competing specifications, and the three first-order dimensions showed strong loadings on the higher-order AI cognitive offloading factor. This pattern supports a hierarchical representation in which memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading are distinguishable functions that share substantial common variance. The model therefore provides a statistical basis for reporting both dimension-specific scores and an overall AI cognitive offloading score. Importantly, the higher-order representation should not be interpreted as evidence that the three dimensions form a temporal sequence or a developmental hierarchy. The criterion-related validity findings are particularly informative because they reveal differentiated association patterns across dimensions. The total AI cognitive offloading score and all three dimensions showed significant positive associations with AI dependence, indicating that greater reported AI cognitive offloading was associated with greater AI dependence across the three function-based forms. Similarly, the total score and all three dimensions were negatively associated with metacognitive monitoring. In relation to need for cognition, the total score and assistive offloading were negatively associated with need for cognition, whereas the memory and thinking offloading dimensions were not significantly related to this criterion. These findings should not be interpreted as evidence that cognitive offloading is inherently beneficial or detrimental. Instead, they suggest that the psychological meaning of offloading may depend on which cognitive function is delegated, the extent of delegation, and the degree to which learners continue to monitor and regulate the process. From a functional perspective, cognitive offloading may enhance cognition when external resources reduce unnecessary cognitive demands, support information organization and retrieval, or free internal resources for monitoring, integration, and other higher-order activities (Risko and Gilbert, 2016; Dunn and Risko, 2016) . analysis.limitations: Although the present study provides relatively comprehensive evidence for the development and validation of the scale, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, although the sample included a relatively large number of college students, it was still drawn primarily from undergraduate students in a specific contextual setting. Future studies should therefore further examine the external validity of the scale across different regions, types of institutions, and graduate student populations. Second, the present study employed a cross-sectional design, which does not allow for the examination of dynamic changes in AI cognitive offloading during the learning process, nor does it permit causal inference regarding its antecedents or consequences. Third, although the current scale distinguishes among memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading, the rapid evolution of generative AI may continue to reshape how students use such systems. Future research should therefore revise and refine the items in light of new model capabilities, task contexts, and educational norms. Fourth, the initial item-development stage was based on literature review, theoretical analysis, and expert content evaluation rather than formal qualitative interviews. Therefore, the present study does not provide interview-derived qualitative evidence for item generation. Future scale-development studies could incorporate systematic open-ended interviews or focus groups, together with detailed coding procedures, to further examine students' lived experiences of AI cognitive offloading and whether additional dimensions or context-specific behaviors should be represented. Combining qualitative exploration with quantitative validation has been illustrated in other domains, such as the development of a multidimensional career-success scale for Chinese employees (Zhou et al., 2013) , and offers a methodological example for future scale refinement. Fifth, future research may also combine interviews, learning logs, or behavioral data to examine whether different forms of AI cognitive offloading correspond to different actual learning outcomes, thereby gradually extending this construct from a self-report measure toward a multi-method assessment framework. Future assessments could also distinguish metacognitive knowledge, monitoring, and control and incorporate taskbased measures alongside self-report, drawing on measurement approaches reviewed in educational settings (Rivers et al., 2020) . Sixth, although three dimensions were retained, their coverage of AI cognitive offloading should be examined further across tasks, populations, and contexts. Unexplained item variance may reflect specific variance and measurement error as well as other influences. Existing research suggests that AI cognitive offloading may also vary according to the cognitive-demand level of the delegated task and the manner in which users engage with AI. For example, Jiang and Chen (2026) distinguished lower-order and higher-order AI cognitive offloading and showed that AI evaluation capability may condition associations with these forms, whereas Zhu et al. (2026) distinguished dependent from autonomous offloading according to whether users retain cognitive agency. Future research should therefore examine whether cognitive-demand level, delegation style, AI evaluation capability, task characteristics, and learner characteristics account for additional variance or function as antecedents and boundary conditions of AI cognitive offloading. Longitudinal, experimental, behavioral, and cross-context validation studies may help determine whether these dimensions represent additional components of the construct or complementary dimensions that operate alongside the function-based structure identified in the present study. Existing reviews also suggest that this field remains in a phase of rapid expansion but uneven evidence development, underscoring the need for structured measurement tools such as the present scale to address the current gap at the level of cognitive processes (Schei et al., 2024; McDonald et al., 2025) . A review of early public claims about ChatGPT highlights the need to distinguish expectations about educational transformation from empirical evidence (Jensen et al., 2025) . A review of empirical studies further identified heterogeneous approaches and limited shared theoretical grounding in research on generative AI chatbots in higher education (McGrath et al., 2025) .

reading.findings: The with-from-offloading framework. The synthesis yields three relations (Table 1 ), distinguished not by tool or prompt but by where the cognitive work the task was designed to exercise takes place. We call that work the target process: retrieving a fact, constructing an argument, setting up an equation, judging which source to trust. In learning with AI, the learner keeps the target process and the system acts on it from outside, questioning, critiquing, offering counter-arguments or checking what the learner has produced. This corresponds to the co-regulation and hybrid relations of Lodge et al. (2023) . In learning from AI, the system supplies explanations, worked examples or feedback that the learner must process, so the target process is shifted rather than surrendered: the learner studies rather than produces. Cognitive load theory predicts that this helps novices when the material is accurate and well sequenced (Sweller, 2023) , and evidence on AI hints agrees (Pardos & Bhandari, 2024 ; for a tutor combining both relations, Kestin et al., 2025) . In offloading to AI, the system performs the target process and the learner receives the product. Offloading is efficient and frequently rational (Risko & Gilbert, 2016) , and becomes an educational problem only when the offloaded process is the one the learner was meant to acquire. The central claim of the framework is asymmetric. Learning with and learning from both depend on capacities the learner brings: domain knowledge to judge an explanation, evaluative judgement to recognise a weak argument, persistence to keep thinking when the answer is one prompt away. They are built by doing the target process unaided, which is what offloading skips, so offloading practised as a default erodes the preconditions of the other two relations. General-purpose interfaces make offloading the path of least resistance, which learners take because it feels like learning (Bjork & Bjork, 2020; de Bruin et al., 2023) . The boundaries blur in three ways, and the blurring is part of the theory. One interaction can drift between relations, as when a request for an explanation becomes a request for the answer. The same request can fall into different relations, because what counts as the target process depends on the learning goal: asking for a grammatical correction is offloading in a grammar lesson and harmless in a history essay. And the relation depends on expertise: an expert who offloads a routine step risks gradual, unnoticed decay of a skill already held, whereas a novice who offloads the same step may never acquire it (Macnamara et al., 2024) . The framework is therefore a tool for analysing tasks, not for classifying behaviours. Table. 1. reading.interpretation: The synthesis answers the Introduction's four research questions. On the first, a learner can learn with, learn from or offload to a generative system; the relations differ in where the target process takes place, and the first two depend on capacities the third leaves unbuilt. On the second, four competencies gain importance, all formed through effortful unaided work and resting on domain knowledge. The propositions in Table 3 answer the third; the fourth is taken up below. No proposition is accepted or rejected here; they are offered for testing through withdrawal designs with delayed unaided tests (P1, P7, P8), seeded-error and calibration tasks (P2, P5, P6), cohort comparisons (P3), correlations between assessment components (P4), and studies of offloading under varying workload and teacher capacity (P9, P10). Read against the empirical review, the framework reconciles apparently contradictory findings. Positive effects (Deng et al., 2025; Wu & Yu, 2024) come largely from studies measuring performance while the tool is present or using systems designed to keep the learner generating, negative findings mostly from withdrawal designs and general-purpose tools (Bastani et al., 2025; Darvishi et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025) . Both can be correct: they measure different relations, and sometimes assisted performance is called learning. As for the theories in Section 2.2, the framework is consistent with cognitive load theory and the desirable-difficulties account, applying their prediction that removing constitutive processing impairs learning to a tool that removes it on request. General-purpose interfaces make offloading the path of least resistance, which learners take because it feels like learning (Bjork & Bjork, 2020; de Bruin et al., 2023) . The boundaries blur in three ways, and the blurring is part of the theory. One interaction can drift between relations, as when a request for an explanation becomes a request for the answer. The same request can fall into different relations, because what counts as the target process depends on the learning goal: asking for a grammatical correction is offloading in a grammar lesson and harmless in a history essay. And the relation depends on expertise: an expert who offloads a routine step risks gradual, unnoticed decay of a skill already held, whereas a novice who offloads the same step may never acquire it (Macnamara et al., 2024) . The framework is therefore a tool for analysing tasks, not for classifying behaviours. Table. 1. When competent-looking work is available on demand, the scarce human contribution is judging whether it is right. Four competencies follow, best understood as a dependent structure (Table 2 ). Evaluative judgement, judging quality against standards, is the competency the others serve. It requires an explicit sense of what good work looks like and how AI processes go wrong (Bearman & Ajjawi, 2023; Bearman et al., 2024) , but it draws on domain knowledge sufficient to detect error, which is the foundation of the structure. Errors cannot be recognised without a schema against which they register (Sweller, 2023) , and fluent outputs are wrong often enough for this to matter (Pardos & Bhandari, 2024) . Sustained unaided reasoning, holding a line of thought through difficulty without external completion, is both the means by which knowledge is built and the faculty offloading leaves unpractised (Bastani et al., 2025; Stadler et al., 2024) . The disposition to verify, a habitual reluctance to accept fluent output unchecked, is motivational rather than cognitive. It activates the other three; without it, knowledge and judgement sit unused, as the uniform overconfidence reported by Fernandes et al. (2026) suggests. None of these is new. analysis.discussion: The synthesis answers the Introduction's four research questions. On the first, a learner can learn with, learn from or offload to a generative system; the relations differ in where the target process takes place, and the first two depend on capacities the third leaves unbuilt. On the second, four competencies gain importance, all formed through effortful unaided work and resting on domain knowledge. The propositions in Table 3 answer the third; the fourth is taken up below. No proposition is accepted or rejected here; they are offered for testing through withdrawal designs with delayed unaided tests (P1, P7, P8), seeded-error and calibration tasks (P2, P5, P6), cohort comparisons (P3), correlations between assessment components (P4), and studies of offloading under varying workload and teacher capacity (P9, P10). Read against the empirical review, the framework reconciles apparently contradictory findings. Positive effects (Deng et al., 2025; Wu & Yu, 2024) come largely from studies measuring performance while the tool is present or using systems designed to keep the learner generating, negative findings mostly from withdrawal designs and general-purpose tools (Bastani et al., 2025; Darvishi et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025) . Both can be correct: they measure different relations, and sometimes assisted performance is called learning. As for the theories in Section 2.2, the framework is consistent with cognitive load theory and the desirable-difficulties account, applying their prediction that removing constitutive processing impairs learning to a tool that removes it on request. Where the typology of Lodge et al. (2023) maps relations by dimension, the framework ranks them by dependency. It extends the account of invisible skill decay by Macnamara et al. (2024) into schooling, where the learner has no prior skill to decay and the loss is of skills never acquired. And it gives the evaluative-judgement agenda (Bearman et al., 2024) a developmental floor. Judgement of AI output cannot be taught in the abstract to learners lacking the domain knowledge against which it is judged. Here we depart from versions of AI literacy centred on tool operation: the findings that AI literacy went with greater confidence but less accurate self-assessment (Fernandes et al., 2026) and that active use was not found to improve the ability to detect AI (Ayanwale et al., 2024) suggest that familiarity can mask a deficit in judgement. One objection is that the argument defends drudgery against a technology that could free learners for higher-order work. The objection assumes higherorder work can proceed without the knowledge it operates on, which cognitive load theory denies (Sweller, 2023) ; the framework opposes not AI use but the default relation in which the learner's thinking is replaced. Another is that well-designed tutors make the problem disappear. They may reduce it (Bastani et al., 2025; Kestin et al., 2025) , but learners do not use only such tutors, and general-purpose systems are one tab away. The question generative AI puts to schooling is what relation to it schooling will cultivate. Because the productive relations depend on knowledge, judgement and persistence that only unaided work builds, a system that lets offloading become the default undermines its capacity to use the technology well. The competencies that remain human let a person stand outside the machine's output and assess it.

reading.methods: This study was conducted using a quantitative secondary data research design to determine if Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can act as a cognitive amplifier or as a replacement for human cognitive activities. The study took a mixed-methods approach using traditional statistical methods and computational modeling to examine AI usage, reliance, cognitive engagement, cognitive offloading, perceived cognitive benefits, and substitution-related behaviors. Self-reported indicators that transformed human reasoning and decision 1093 intelligence into something that could be quantified were integrated: independent problem solving, verification behavior, development of original ideas, reliance on decisions, and dependence on AI-generated outputs.

analysis.methods: This study was conducted using a quantitative secondary data research design to determine if Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) can act as a cognitive amplifier or as a replacement for human cognitive activities. analysis.discussion: The results suggest that Generative AI is not just an amplifier or a replacement but rather a dual pathway cognitive process. Cognitive amplification was the highest across all cognitive components and cognitive substitution and cognitive offloading were also very high. The co-existence indicates that the users might benefit from both efficiency, confidence, and learning advantages, alongside entrusting parts of reasoning and problemsolving to AI systems. This trend aligns with the idea that GenAI can help enhance higher-order thinking under certain circumstances and diminish independent thinking in other contexts (Alubthane, 2026; Lim et al., 2023) . The results of the present study thus provide a context-dependent view of the use of GenAI where results are contingent on the context in which users interact with, fact-check, and use AI-generated information. Cognitive offloading proved to be the most important predictor for both amplification and substitution, thus being the core mechanism in the framework. This finding is of theoretical significance because expenditure of cognitive effort is not necessarily a problem. Releasing time from routine information processing can free up time for more complex evaluation, synthesis and decision tasks. When offloading is repeated, however, and becomes a way of life, it can also lead to dependency and reduced intellectual independence. This fits with evidence from experiments that structured offloading is associated with enhanced critical performance, whereas unstructured cognition offloading may come at psychological and intellectual costs (Hong et al., 2025; Jose et al., 2025) . Thus, the effects of offloading seem to be related to whether saved cognitive resources are allocated to reflective thinking. Another example of the dangers of over delegating is the positive correlation between relying on AI and cognitive substitution. The use of AI in solving problems could lead to issues if users take AI-generated suggestions automatically as a definitive solution without properly assessing them. The interpretation is consistent with the research revealing that greater reliance on GenAI in problem-solving tasks may affect students' mindset toward engaging in independent tasks of thought (Hou et al., 2025) . It is also one sign of a more general 'automation bias' tendency, during which folks can trust the suggestions of the computer systems they use and fail to critically examine them (Alon-Barkat & Busuioc, 2023). The continued importance of acceptance and dependence as factors in substitution thus underscores the need to distinguish productive from passive dependence. Human cognitive engagement, however, was strong predictor of amplification at the same time. Participants who verified the information with AI and then adapted it to create their own thoughts were more likely to experience positive cognitive effects. This reinforces the notion that the greatest potential benefit of GenAI lies in active synergies between humans and AI, not solely as a substitute for thought (Jou & Kao, 2026; Li & Tian, 2026) . Previous studies have demonstrated that GenAI can aid in creative idea generation and refinement while the user is still engaged in evaluating and refining the human-generated content, which is often generated by the GenAI tools (Habib et al., 2024) . Therefore, there is a need for ongoing human judgment in order for amplification to happen. Another interesting correlation to make is the fact that amplification and substitution go hand in hand, presenting a binary interpretation that proves false. Users can experience speed, confidence, and cognitive assistance at the same time, and get more and more reliant on AI. Previous studies have also found positive and negative impacts on education, such as learning advantages, dependence, and a lack of critical engagement (Gammoh, 2024; Essien et al., 2024) . The potential for long-term impacts of GenAI on critical thinking further underscores the need for ensuring verification, reflection, and independent thinking in AI-integrated workflows (Helal et al., 2025; Rana et al., 2026 ). These differences were further substantiated by a computational profiling of these results which identified specific user patterns. The high-amp, active-engagement profile had a strong use of AI with high levels of cognitive engagement and relatively low substitution, while the high-substitution profile had a high level of dependence and offloading. The profiles indicate that trust and acceptance should be fine-tuned, not optimized as over-dependency on AI is not conducive to its positive use (Kelly et al., 2023; Lukyanenko et al., 2022) . The results suggest a balanced approach to the use of GenAI for decision-making, whereby this technology can augment cognitive assessment while retaining input from humans, but can become fully substitutive as cognitive workload is gradually shifted to the GenAI system. There are important implications of this distinction in education. This research shows how General AI cannot be considered just a cognitive amplifier or a cognitive substitute. Rather, it has a dual pathway to human reasoning and decision intelligence: augmenting the human system for good and reliance on the system for cognition. The results revealed that cognitive amplification had a positive effect on efficiency, confidence, collaborative learning and active engagement, while cognitive substitution was associated with increased reliance on AI and decreased independent problem solving and cognitive offloading. Importantly, the mental effort savings needed to reduce cognitive effort also turned out to be a prominent predictor of both pathways, suggesting that saving mental effort can be a positive or negative effect depending on how users invest the effort saved in verification, reflection and independent judgment. The computational profiling also uncovered unique human-AI interaction patterns: high amplification, high substitution, moderate use, and low engagement. The findings underscore the need for maintaining human cognitive significance in the application of GenAI for reasoning and decision support. The study thus offers a computational view to see the difference between productive AI augmentation and over-delegation of cognition. Overall, there is a need to stress key verification, adjusted trust, autonomous idea generation, and hands-on supervision when engaging with GenAI. To confirm these profiles, further studies should employ objective reasoning tasks, longitudinal study designs and larger populations to establish how continued use of AI impacts on cognitive autonomy and decision-making quality over time.

reading.findings: The central insight emerging from this research is that generative AI does not merely change how quickly or easily knowledge work is performed; it can also change the relation between creators and their own cognitive processes. When AI systems produce fluent, complete, and seemingly reasonable outputs, individuals reduce not only routine Moderating effect of task complexity on the relationship between metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality: simple slope analyses. cognitive operations but also the planning, monitoring, and reflection that would otherwise accompany their own intellectual work. Importantly, metacognitive disengagement does not imply the absence of thought. Rather, it describes a systematic decline in the depth of metacognitive investment: individuals may still read, select, and even revise AI outputs, but they are less likely to question underlying assumptions, compare alternatives, or reflect on their own strategies. This partial engagement is precisely what makes metacognitive disengagement difficult to observe, yet sufficient to erode the deeper cognitive processing required for knowledge innovation. These findings extend the classic argument of Salomon and Perkins (1989) that intelligent technologies can invite users to transfer thinking responsibility to the tool. Generative AI makes this tendency more consequential because it can perform not only peripheral cognitive tasks but also core operations such as inference, synthesis, and evaluation. The resulting shift from offloading memory to offloading thinking represents a qualitatively new phase of cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert, 2016) . Our results suggest that the most important cost of this shift may not be a direct decline in task performance, but a gradual retreat from the metacognitive regulation that sustains longterm creative capability. From a metacognition perspective, the present findings extend prior work that has linked metacognitive processes to complex problem solving and creative performance (Flavell, 1979; Schraw and Moshman, 1995) . We show that in human-AI collaboration, metacognitive engagement depends not only on individual ability but also on the technological conditions under which knowledge work is performed. When AI assumes the cognitive operations that metacognitive monitoring would ordinarily track, the raw material for monitoring disappears; when AI is perceived as reliable, the perceived necessity of monitoring declines (de Visser et al., 2016) . This dual erosion mechanism provides a more specific account of how AI use can reduce cognitive engagement, going beyond existing discussions of metacognitive laziness in learning contexts (Fan et al., 2025) . It is also noteworthy that cognitive offloading only partially mediated the effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement and the effect of cognitive offloading on innovation quality. This partial mediation indicates that other mechanisms are likely involved. For
reading.interpretation: Experiment 1 provided initial evidence for the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in human-AI collaborative knowledge innovation. Participants in the high-assistance condition showed significantly higher levels of planning reduction, monitoring weakening, and reflection absence than those in the lowassistance condition, supporting H1. A particularly interesting finding was that greater familiarity with AI was associated with lower, rather than higher, metacognitive disengagement. This pattern runs counter to the intuitive expectation that familiarity breeds dependency. One possible explanation is that individuals who are more familiar with AI are also more aware of its limitations and therefore more likely to maintain critical engagement and metacognitive vigilance when using it. This interpretation points to AI literacy as a potentially important buffer against metacognitive disengagement, which informed the inclusion of individual AI literacy as a moderator in later experiments. Experiment 2 replicated the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in a different task context and provided evidence for the mediating role of cognitive offloading. Higher AI assistance increased cognitive offloading, which in turn strengthened metacognitive disengagement. Under high AI assistance, individuals outsourced core cognitive tasks such as information retrieval, framework construction, and solution generation, reducing their direct participation in the cognitive process. This offloading deprived metacognitive monitoring of its raw material and weakened the perceived necessity of self-checking, thereby producing a chain from cognitive offloading through reduced metacognitive engagement to metacognitive disengagement. This research focuses on task-level metacognitive disengagement, and the nine-item scale captures the immediate, task-specific reduction in planning, monitoring, and reflection within a single AI-assisted task rather than a habitual, cumulative decline. The experiments therefore demonstrate immediate reductions in metacognitive engagement but cannot determine whether such reductions persist or accumulate over time. Future research should employ longitudinal or repeatedexposure designs to examine this developmental trajectory. Second, the experiments relied on online samples and short, simulated tasks. This design supports causal inference but limits ecological validity, as real innovation work is longer in duration, more socially embedded, and subject to different accountability structures. In the high-assistance condition, the AI assistant provided relatively complete solution-oriented responses to task-related requests, including generating target user profiles, offering reference directions for product features, and commenting on participants' proposals. In the low-assistance condition, the AI assistant provided only brief responses to factual information queries and did not proactively offer creative suggestions or solution content. The task requirements were identical across conditions; only the degree of AI assistance differed. A pilot study was conducted before the formal experiment to calibrate task clarity, the distinctiveness of the AI response strategies, and the reasonableness of the task completion time. Pilot data were not included in the formal analysis. After reading the task materials, participants completed an attention check by briefly describing the kind of help the AI assistant would provide. Responses clearly inconsistent with the task instructions were excluded. Participants could ask the AI assistant questions during the task. After completing the task, they filled out the metacognitive disengagement scale and the manipulation check measure. The sample size was determined using the same standards as in Experiment 1: α = 0.05, d = 0.5, and power 1 -β = 0.80, requiring at least 51 participants per group. Because mediation analyses typically require larger samples than simple group comparisons, the sample size was increased. Participants were recruited through Credamo, with invalid responses screened out in real time through attention checks. The final sample comprised 162 valid participants: 73 men (45.1%) and 89 women (54.9%), with a mean age of 29.17 years (SD = 7.34). Participants were randomly assigned to a high-assistance condition (n = 82) or a low-assistance condition (n = 80). The experiment used the same single-factor two-level betweensubjects design as Experiment 1. In the community service innovation proposal task, participants were asked to design an innovative service solution addressing the daily needs of elderly and child populations in urban communities.
