analysis.results: The central insight emerging from this research is that generative AI does not merely change how quickly or easily knowledge work is performed; it can also change the relation between creators and their own cognitive processes. When AI systems produce fluent, complete, and seemingly reasonable outputs, individuals reduce not only routine Moderating effect of task complexity on the relationship between metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality: simple slope analyses. cognitive operations but also the planning, monitoring, and reflection that would otherwise accompany their own intellectual work. Importantly, metacognitive disengagement does not imply the absence of thought. Rather, it describes a systematic decline in the depth of metacognitive investment: individuals may still read, select, and even revise AI outputs, but they are less likely to question underlying assumptions, compare alternatives, or reflect on their own strategies. This partial engagement is precisely what makes metacognitive disengagement difficult to observe, yet sufficient to erode the deeper cognitive processing required for knowledge innovation. These findings extend the classic argument of Salomon and Perkins (1989) that intelligent technologies can invite users to transfer thinking responsibility to the tool. Generative AI makes this tendency more consequential because it can perform not only peripheral cognitive tasks but also core operations such as inference, synthesis, and evaluation. The resulting shift from offloading memory to offloading thinking represents a qualitatively new phase of cognitive offloading (Risko and Gilbert, 2016) . Our results suggest that the most important cost of this shift may not be a direct decline in task performance, but a gradual retreat from the metacognitive regulation that sustains longterm creative capability. From a metacognition perspective, the present findings extend prior work that has linked metacognitive processes to complex problem solving and creative performance (Flavell, 1979; Schraw and Moshman, 1995) . We show that in human-AI collaboration, metacognitive engagement depends not only on individual ability but also on the technological conditions under which knowledge work is performed. When AI assumes the cognitive operations that metacognitive monitoring would ordinarily track, the raw material for monitoring disappears; when AI is perceived as reliable, the perceived necessity of monitoring declines (de Visser et al., 2016) . This dual erosion mechanism provides a more specific account of how AI use can reduce cognitive engagement, going beyond existing discussions of metacognitive laziness in learning contexts (Fan et al., 2025) . It is also noteworthy that cognitive offloading only partially mediated the effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement and the effect of cognitive offloading on innovation quality. This partial mediation indicates that other mechanisms are likely involved. For example, when creators delegate primary cognitive responsibility to AI, their self-efficacy may shift from a sense of having solved the problem themselves to a sense of merely supervising the AI that solved it, and their sense of accountability for the output may weaken. These possibilities are consistent with the automation-augmentation paradox identified in management research (Raisch and Krakowski, 2021) , in which the same AI system can either substitute for human cognition or augment it depending on how it is integrated into work processes.
analysis.discussion: Experiment 1 provided initial evidence for the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in human-AI collaborative knowledge innovation. Participants in the high-assistance condition showed significantly higher levels of planning reduction, monitoring weakening, and reflection absence than those in the lowassistance condition, supporting H1. A particularly interesting finding was that greater familiarity with AI was associated with lower, rather than higher, metacognitive disengagement. This pattern runs counter to the intuitive expectation that familiarity breeds dependency. One possible explanation is that individuals who are more familiar with AI are also more aware of its limitations and therefore more likely to maintain critical engagement and metacognitive vigilance when using it. This interpretation points to AI literacy as a potentially important buffer against metacognitive disengagement, which informed the inclusion of individual AI literacy as a moderator in later experiments. Experiment 2 replicated the main effect of AI assistance on metacognitive disengagement in a different task context and provided evidence for the mediating role of cognitive offloading. Higher AI assistance increased cognitive offloading, which in turn strengthened metacognitive disengagement. Under high AI assistance, individuals outsourced core cognitive tasks such as information retrieval, framework construction, and solution generation, reducing their direct participation in the cognitive process. This offloading deprived metacognitive monitoring of its raw material and weakened the perceived necessity of self-checking, thereby producing a chain from cognitive offloading through reduced metacognitive engagement to metacognitive disengagement. The finding that cognitive offloading only partially mediated the relationship suggests that other mechanisms may also be at work, such as changes in self-efficacy or perceived task responsibility. These possibilities remain open for future investigation. 5 Experiment 3: the causal effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality Experiment 2 provided evidence that cognitive offloading mediates the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. However, because cognitive offloading was measured rather than manipulated, the causal direction remained uncertain. Experiment 3 addressed this limitation by manipulating the degree of cognitive delegation to AI-the core behavioral expression of cognitive offloading in human-AI collaboration-and examining its causal effect on knowledge innovation quality, with metacognitive disengagement as a mediator. Experiment 3 provided causal evidence for the effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. First, manipulating cognitive offloading produced the expected difference in metacognitive disengagement: participants in the high-delagation condition showed significantly stronger metacognitive disengagement than those in the low-delagation condition. Because cognitive offloading was experimentally manipulated rather than merely measured, these results strengthen the inference that workflow features involving greater delegation to AI lead to stronger metacognitive disengagement. Second, cognitive offloading significantly impaired knowledge innovation quality across all three dimensions. Interestingly, the between-group difference was somewhat smaller for developability than for novelty and usefulness. One interpretation is that AI-generated solutions often appear structurally complete and operationally plausible in the short term, but lack the depth and sustainability that come from genuine iterative reflection. This pattern is consistent with the illusion of competence described by Fan et al. (2025) , in which the fluent output of AI masks underlying deficiencies in quality (Tsakalerou et al., 2026) . Third, metacognitive disengagement partially mediated the effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality. This finding indicates that cognitive offloading damages innovation quality primarily, though not exclusively, by weakening metacognitive planning, monitoring, and reflection. The residual direct effect also suggests that other mechanisms may operate alongside metacognitive disengagement. At the same time, the two workflow conditions inevitably differed in other features such as the detail of AI responses, the amount of independent effort requested, and the allocation of responsibility for core content. The findings should therefore be interpreted as reflecting the combined influence of a high-delegation workflow, within which cognitive offloading is the central feature. Future research could hold these features constant while varying only the degree of cognitive delegation to isolate the unique contribution of cognitive offloading. Consistent with Amabile's (1983) componential theory of creativity, the results imply that when metacognitive skills are no longer exercised in human-AI collaborative tasks, the formal completeness of AI-generated output may conceal a loss of deeper creative quality. Experiment 4 extended the findings of Experiments 1 through 3 by identifying two boundary conditions of the indirect effect from cognitive offloading through metacognitive disengagement to knowledge innovation quality. First, task complexity strengthened the negative indirect effect. Under high task complexity, the indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement was significantly stronger than under low task complexity. This pattern is consistent with the proposition that complex innovation tasks require more extensive metacognitive processing (Campbell, 1988) . When tasks are complex, AI outputs typically serve only as a starting point, and individuals must critically evaluate, integrate, and deeply process AI-generated content. Under such conditions, metacognitive disengagement leads to particularly severe losses in innovation quality. Second, AI literacy buffered the negative indirect effect. Individuals with higher AI literacy maintained relatively higher knowledge innovation quality even under high cognitive offloading, whereas those with lower AI literacy showed stronger negative effects. This finding suggests that the value of AI literacy lies not simply in better technical operation of AI but in the ability to maintain critical distance from AI outputs and to preserve metacognitive vigilance during human-AI collaboration (Long and Magerko, 2020) . Third, the supplementary analyses clarified that neither task complexity nor AI literacy moderated the first-stage path from cognitive offloading to metacognitive disengagement. Instead, both moderators operated at the stage at which metacognitive disengagement translated into innovation quality. This distinction indicates that metacognitive disengagement may arise fairly generally under AI-assisted conditions, but its consequences depend on task characteristics and individual capabilities. For individuals with high AI literacy or for simple tasks, even if metacognitive disengagement occurs, its actual damage to innovation quality is relatively limited; for complex tasks or low-AIliteracy individuals, the same level of metacognitive disengagement leads to more substantial quality loss. analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, a critical limitation concerns the temporal scope of the present measure. This research focuses on task-level metacognitive disengagement, and the nine-item scale captures the immediate, task-specific reduction in planning, monitoring, and reflection within a single AI-assisted task rather than a habitual, cumulative decline. The experiments therefore demonstrate immediate reductions in metacognitive engagement but cannot determine whether such reductions persist or accumulate over time. Future research should employ longitudinal or repeatedexposure designs to examine this developmental trajectory. Second, the experiments relied on online samples and short, simulated tasks. This design supports causal inference but limits ecological validity, as real innovation work is longer in duration, more socially embedded, and subject to different accountability structures. The findings may therefore not generalize to high-stakes, long-cycle projects, and effect sizes may differ. Future research could use field experiments or experience sampling methods to examine metacognitive disengagement in actual knowledge work settings (Dell' Acqua et al., 2026) . Third, the cognitive offloading manipulation in Experiments 3 and 4 was compound in nature. The high-and low-delegation conditions differed not only in the degree of cognitive delegation but also in AI response detail, independent effort requested, and responsibility allocation. The findings therefore reflect the combined influence of a highdelegation workflow, with cognitive offloading as its central feature. Future research could hold these features constant while varying only the degree of delegation to isolate the unique effect of cognitive offloading. Fourth, knowledge innovation quality was assessed through expert ratings. Although interrater reliability was acceptable, expert judgment remains partly subjective. Future studies could incorporate more objective indicators, such as the originality of proposals, downstream implementation outcomes, or peer evaluations. Fifth, cognitive offloading served only as a partial mediator. The present model focuses on cognitive offloading and metacognitive disengagement because they represent the most proximal mechanisms linking AI assistance to innovation quality. However, the residual direct effect indicates that other mechanisms are also involved. Future research could examine additional mediators such as trust in AI (Jiang et al., 2025) , perceived responsibility (Yousefi et al., 2026) , and creative psychological ownership (Ma et al., 2026) , and test multiple-mediator models for a more complete account. Sixth, although we conducted Harman's single-factor tests in Experiments 2, 3, and 4, this approach is a relatively weak test of common method variance. Because all measures were self-reported, the mediation effects observed in Experiment 2 may be partly inflated by common method variance. Future research could employ CFAbased common latent factor models, multi-source ratings, or objective behavioral measures, such as platform analytics data, to further validate the proposed relationships. Finally, the present study did not directly test interventions to reduce metacognitive disengagement. The buffering effect of AI literacy was measured as an individual difference rather than experimentally manipulated. Future research should design and evaluate interventions such as metacognitive prompting, structured human-AI workflow separation, or targeted AI literacy training. Given recent work on hybrid human-AI regulation (Molenaar, 2022) and the augmentation potential of AI (Jia et al., 2024) , such interventions may help organizations capture the efficiency benefits of AI while preserving the cognitive engagement that sustains innovation quality.

reading.interpretation: AI tools offer meaningful opportunities to support students' critical thinking and independent learning through explanations, practice, feedback, and exploration of alternative perspectives. They may help learners plan study, identify gaps in understanding, and access support beyond the classroom. However, these benefits are not automatic. Overdependence, unverified information, reduced intellectual effort, and diminished ownership of learning may undermine the very competencies education seeks to develop.The key distinction is between using AI to support thinking and using it to avoid thinking. When students attempt tasks independently, critically evaluate AI-generated material, verify evidence, and reflect on decisions, AI can serve as a useful learning scaffold. When they simply copy answers or delegate judgment, the same technology may limit opportunities to develop reasoning and autonomy. Teachers and educational institutions should therefore combine clear policies with AI literacy, inquirybased learning, reflective tasks, and assessment practices that reveal students' understanding. Students must remain accountable for the work they submit and the conclusions they reach. The long-term objective should not be maximum dependence on AI or its complete exclusion, but responsible use that strengthens human judgment. AI is most educationally valuable when it helps students become more questioning, self-regulated, reflective, and independent learners.
reading.limitations: This article is a narrative review of selected research and educational guidance rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis. It does not claim to include every relevant publication, assess every study with a formal quality tool, or establish causal effects of AI use on critical thinking. The field is changing rapidly, and studies differ in participant age, discipline, AI tool, duration, outcome measures, and instructional design. Some findings concern self-reported perceptions or short-term performance rather than long-term retention and independent transfer. The conclusions should therefore be understood as a synthesis of emerging evidence and a basis for practice, not as proof that a particular AI approach will work in every context. Future research should use transparent search methods, validated measures, comparison groups where appropriate, and longer follow-up periods.

reading.findings: Cognitive Offloading and Over -Reliance on AI -Generated Outputs The reviewed literature indicates that generative AI can alter how users distribute cognitive tasks between themselves and computational systems. This finding is particularly evident in educational and research contexts, although the available evidence doe s not support a uniform or inevitable Sani et al. GHAITSA: Islamic Education Journal (2026) Vol. 6 No. 3 decline in human reasoning. Zhai, Wibowo, and Li (2024), through a systematic review of 14 studies retrieved from ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science, examined over -reliance on AI dialogue systems in research and education. Their synthesis identified concerns related to decision -making, c ritical thinking, and analytical reasoning when users accept AI -generated recommendations without sufficient evaluation. At the same time, the review also identified productive applications of AI in research and education, including support for information access, writing, data interpretation, and problem -solving. The authors therefore locate the principal concern in patterns of over -reliance rather than in AI use itself. This distinction is also reflected in Skulmowski's ( 2024) analysis of generative AI as a form of cognitive externalization. The study distinguishes between the use of AI as an assistant that reduces cognitive burden and the attribution of human -like competence or authority to the system. Generative AI may there fore function as an external cognitive resource, but the epistemic consequences depend on how users interpret and evaluate its contribution. analysis.methods: This study employed a critical integrative literature review with a qualitative interpretive design. This approach was selected because the study aims to integrate contemporary empirical research with philosophical and Islamic theological literature to examine the epistemological and theological implications of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI). An integrative review is appropriate for bringing together empirical and theoretical literature from different scholarly perspectives (Whittemore & Knafl, 2005). The study employed two complementary analytical perspectives: epistemology and Islamic theology . The epistemological perspective examined four analytical dimensions: epistemic agency, cognitive offloading, epistemic justification, and attribution of authority . These dimensions were used to assess how AI may influence the distribution of cognitive tasks, human responsibility for evaluating information, and the credibility attributed to AI -generated outputs. The Islamic -theological perspective examined religious authority, scholarly transmission and accountability, lived religious knowledge, and the relationship between rational reflection and spiritual consciousness . The concepts of sanad and Ulul Albab were examined specifically within the Islamic context and were not generalized to other religious traditions. The analysis also distinguished between AI's technological affordances, authority attributed to AI by users, institutional adoption, and the actu al decision -making role of AI. This distinction was maintained to avoid treating the technical capabilities of AI as equivalent to autonomous epistemic or religious authority. The data consisted of two categories of scholarly sources. The first category comprised contemporary peer-reviewed literature published primarily between 2021 and 2026 . These studies constituted the main analytical corpus and addressed three areas relevant to the research questions: generative AI and epistemic agency; AI, digital religion, and religious authority; and the use of AI in Islamic theological and jurisprudential contexts . The second category consisted of selected foundational theoretical and theological sources used to establish the conceptual framework for interpreting the contemporary literature. These sources included works concerning epistemology, philosophy of technology, digital religion, science and religion, and Islamic theological concepts. Foundational sources were treated as theoretical support rather than as contemporary empirical evidence. Relevant literature was identified through Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect , supplemented by backward and forward citation tracking. This finding is particularly evident in educational and research contexts, although the available evidence doe s not support a uniform or inevitable Sani et al. Zhai, Wibowo, and Li (2024), through a systematic review of 14 studies retrieved from ProQuest, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, and Web of Science, examined over -reliance on AI dialogue systems in research and education. Their synthesis identified concerns related to decision -making, c ritical thinking, and analytical reasoning when users accept AI -generated recommendations without sufficient evaluation. At the same time, the review also identified productive applications of AI in research and education, including support for information access, writing, data interpretation, and problem -solving. The authors therefore locate the principal concern in patterns of over -reliance rather than in AI use itself. This distinction is also reflected in Skulmowski's ( 2024) analysis of generative AI as a form of cognitive externalization. The study distinguishes between the use of AI as an assistant that reduces cognitive burden and the attribution of human -like competence or authority to the system. Generative AI may there fore function as an external cognitive resource, but the epistemic consequences depend on how users interpret and evaluate its contribution. The literature consequently provides stronger support for the concept of epistemic dependence or over -reliance than for a generalized claim that AI inevitably produces an “illusion of expertise.” The evidence also indicates that the relationship between AI use and cognitive performance is context-dependent. The systematic review by Zhai et al. ( 2024) focuses primarily on educational and research settings and does not establish long -term effects across all populations. Its findings therefore cannot be generalized to all AI users or treated as evidence of a population -wide decline in intellectual capac ity. Instead, the literature suggests that the transfer of cognitive tasks to AI becomes epistemically significant when users reduce independent verification, evaluation of sources, or engagement with alternative arguments. Within this context, the distinction between information access and epistemic justification becomes important. The reviewed literature therefore identifies human evaluat ion as a continuing component of responsible knowledge practices. This finding is particularly relevant to the present study because the research question concerns human epistemic agency rather than the technical capabilities of AI alone. LLMs generate linguistic outputs through learned patterns in large -scale traini ng data and computational prediction. This technical characteristic does not, by itself, establish that an LLM possesses human -like consciousness, lived experience, or intentional understanding. Similarly, Öhman ( 2024) argues that LLMs can appear to users as a unified extra -human voice because diverse traces of human -produced data are synthesized into a single conversational interface. Recent systematic reviews do not support a uniformly negative account of ChatGPT or generative AI in education. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 69 experimental studies found that ChatGPT interventions were associated with improvements in academic performance, affective-motivational outcomes, and higher-order thinking tendencies, while also reducing mental effort in some contexts. The authors nevertheless emphasize methodological limitations and the need for objective and longer-term measures. Similarly, a systematic review of 72 studies on student engagement found both engagement and disengagement associated with ChatGPT-supported learning, indicating that outcomes depend on how the technology is integrated into learning activities. These findings qualify the more critical interpretation presented in this study. Generative AI should therefore not be conceptualized as inherently detrimental to human reasoning. Its epistemic consequences appear to depend on the degree of human involvement, the structure of the task, the quality of verification, and the pedagogical or institutional context in which it is used. The empirical evidence underlying these interpretations is provided by Deng et al. (2025), who synthesized 69 experimental studies examining ChatGPT-supported learning, and Lo et al. (2024), who reviewed 72 studies addressing behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Their findings demonstrate that positive educational outcomes may coexist with problematic patterns of dependency, disengagement, and insufficient independent evaluation. Heung and Chiu (2025) further identified a positive overall relationship between ChatGPT-supported learning and student engagement while recognizing overreliance as a potential risk. Similarly, Chan and Hu (2023) reported that university students perceived generative AI as useful for learning support and information accessibility but expressed concerns regarding accuracy, ethical use, and dependency. Future research is needed to operationalise the model, develop more testable hypotheses, and examine whether the proposed processes of human-AI synergy can be observed in different learning contexts. Another related limitation concerns measurement. At present, few established measures or coding schemes exist for key constructs in the SYNC model, particularly metacognitive offloading and metacognitive onloading. While learners may delegate planning, monitoring, evaluation, or reflection to AI, it remains unclear how these processes can be reliably captured and distinguished from productive self-regulation or unproductive over-reliance. Future studies should therefore develop behavioural, selfreport, trace-based, dialogue-based and performance-based indicators to assess when AI use supports, replaces, or strengthens learners' metacognitive regulation. The proposed SYNC model, metacognitive concepts and relevant hypotheses also require further examination across domains, learning contexts, task types and learner differences (e.g., prior knowledge, age, selfregulation, and AI literacy). Our discussion has focused mainly on contexts in which learners interact directly with AI, while paying less attention to classroom implementation, collaborative learning and teacher-mediated use. Also, human-AI synergy may differ across domains such as writing, mathematics, science, language learning, and programming, as well as across tasks such as problem solving, feedback interpretation, reflection, and creative production. These differences may influence what learners offload to AI and what they internalise through continued interaction. In addition, our discussion centres on human learning and performance in human-AI interaction, rather than on AI's performance itself, including how AI capabilities may evolve, whether AI can meaningfully demonstrate forms of metacognition, and how humans and AI might coevolve toward human-AI synergy. Finally, the evidence base remains emerging, limiting strong claims about generalisability across educational, professional, and cultural contexts, especially given the rapid development of AI technologies. In summary, this perspective defines concepts of metacognitive offloading and onloading, introduces the SYNC model to explain how GenAI can decouple task performance from durable learning, and identifies four pitfalls and approaches that may shift learners from autopilot performance to synergetic mastery. We propose that researchers, educators, and developers should co-design AI agents and learning environments with contingent, fading scaffolds and process-sensitive evaluations so that AI boosts productivity without eroding learning.

Inclusion in the corpus does not imply equivalence of genre or authority. The same textual coding framework was applied across the four publications, but evidence from UNESCO (2025) was attributed to the relevant chapter authors and interpreted as commissioned commentary. The publications were purposively selected for their engagement with AI governance and legitimate AI-supported participation in education. The analysis was informed by Fairclough's three-dimensional model. On the textual level, focus was placed on the use of the recurring policy terms: responsibility, transparency, trust, authenticity, originality, human agency, augmentation, and responsible use to analyze the ways in which each was defined, enacted, linked to institutional actors, and situated in larger narratives of authorship and what constitutes legitimate participation. A full mapping across documents of the analytical role of these eight terms is made available as Supplementary Material, illustrating the semantic instability that underpins the floating signifier analysis. At the level of discursive practice, the study analyzed the policy discourse's construction of authority, responsibility, and governance in nascent AI governance regimes. At the social practice level, these forms of discourse were analysed in connection with the shifting expectations of ownership and control on the part of the institution in AI-mediated HE. The interpretation of the findings was guided by Bourdieu's theory of practice with a focus on the concepts of field, habitus, capital and illusio. Laclau's (1996) theory of floating signifiers was also used as an additional analytical tool in the textual analysis. A signifier was considered to be floating if it occurred frequently across the corpus, had no stable operational definition in itself, and changed meaning across policy contexts or positions of actors. The analysis proceeded iteratively between the theoretical framework and the corpus, with analytical categories developing through engagement with the texts rather than being established fully in advance. The analytical process involved four stages: close reading to identify recurring concepts related to academic integrity, AI governance, authorship, and responsibility distribution; contextual examination of how these concepts were framed across institutional actors; coding of selected extracts according to Fairclough's three dimensions; and cross-corpus comparison to identify ambiguity and actor positioning across the corpus, noting how responsibility is distributed among institutional actors. The contextual analysis also recorded the genre and authorial status of each source, distinguishing institutional guidance and policy outlooks from commissioned contributions. Particular attention was given to modal constructions such as should , must , may , and encourage , as well as passive constructions associated with diffuse or indirect responsibility attribution. Figure 2 presents the integrated theoretical and analytical framework. Bourdieu's theory of practice functions as the interpretive lens on the left, Fairclough's three-dimensional CDA provides the analytical structure on the right, and the lower tier presents the interpretive synthesis centred on the changing cheating habitus and the study's core finding that academic integrity under AI-mediated conditions is structurally mediated and discursively negotiated. Integrated theoretical and analytical framework. The corpus provides evidence of how policy discourse constructs academic integrity. It does not provide empirical evidence of students’ behaviour, cognitive experience, or dispositional change. The changing cheating habitus, its proposed relationship with academic capital, and the concept of detection as a capital filter are theoretical propositions derived from the discourse analysis. Testing how they operate within particular institutions will require empirical evidence from students and educators, together with data on institutional outcomes. As an Assistant Professor of Educational Leadership at a higher education institution in the United Arab Emirates, the researcher is both a scholarly analyst of AI governance discourse and an educator working within an institution responding to the same conditions of AI integration examined in the study. The context of the UAE is especially relevant since the national AI strategy places artificial intelligence at the center of education transformation. Interpretive judgments were repeatedly verified by reference to the corpus to confirm that the analytic assertions were based on texts rather than on taken-for-granted assumptions derived from professional experience. OECD (2023) illustrates this shift. In discussing the emergence of generative AI in education, the document notes that its arrival “was considered as disruptive by many and framed in terms of ‘cheating’.” It then questions this framing by suggesting that engagement with AI may instead develop the digital competences students need for contemporary working life (p. 26). By placing cheating in quotation marks, the OECD signals that the category is open to contestation. The wording does not dismiss academic integrity concerns. It suggests that what constitutes misconduct depends on institutional interpretation and cannot be treated as settled. From a CDA perspective, this reflects the discursive operation associated with floating signifiers: cheating is invoked and destabilised within the same policy text, remaining a normative reference point whose meaning is determined by context. The term ‘responsible use’ shows how this instability extends across jurisdictions. [ OECD (2026 ), p. 37] notes that the most common immediate national response to generative AI has been the introduction of system-level guidance. Such guidance “typically focus[es] on ethical and responsible use, academic integrity, data protection, and the roles and responsibilities of teachers and students.” Drawing on a 2025 European Schoolnet survey of European Union education systems, the same page reports that guidance within this narrower group emphasises “enabling informed professional judgement rather than imposing blanket bans” [ OECD, (2026 ), p. 37, citing European Schoolnet, 2025]. analysis.discussion: This study examined how international AI policy discourse constructs academic integrity in higher education and what these constructions suggest about a changing cheating habitus. Analysis of four UNESCO and OECD publications shows that academic integrity is constructed through ethical language whose operational conditions remain underdefined. Generative AI changes the relationship between submitted work and the intellectual activity it is expected to represent. Terms such as responsibility, transparency, trust, authenticity, and responsible use provide normative coherence without establishing consistent rules for practice. The resulting interpretive burden falls on institutions and educational actors working between pressures for AI integration and inherited assumptions about authorship. In theoretical terms, the study proposes that these discursive conditions may affect the dispositions through which students approach academic participation. The changing cheating habitus describes a possible recalibration of the frames through which legitimate participation is recognised under conditions of governance uncertainty. The analysis also proposes that this process may vary according to the academic capital recognised within particular institutional fields. It generates a related hypothesis that enforcement mechanisms may operate as capital filters if the visibility of AI assistance varies with students’ capacity to evaluate and revise AI-generated material. These propositions extend the discourse analysis but are not empirical findings about student behaviour or enforcement outcomes. What the paper's title names, cheating or being cheated, is not treated here as an either/or question. The analysis proposes that these conditions may occur concurrently. Students who are sanctioned for AI-assisted participation may simultaneously be cheating in the conventional sense and being cheated by governance frameworks that normalise the same technologies through which their participation is adjudicated. This concurrent conditionality acquires an additional dimension when integrity frameworks reflect particular epistemic traditions and provide limited recognition of other knowledge practices and understandings of authorship. Read alongside decolonial scholarship, the findings raise a further question: who bears the burden of governance ambiguity, and whose ways of knowing may be classified as violations when particular academic conventions are treated as universal ( Eaton, 2024 ; Langeveldt and Pietersen, 2024 )? The analysis is confined to four publications issued or commissioned by two intergovernmental organisations, and its design is conceptual. These publications differ in genre and institutional authority and cannot be treated as expressions of a unified policy position. The changing cheating habitus is theorised from policy discourse, not from an empirical study of student dispositions. The analysis identifies conditions that may enable dispositional change but cannot establish what particular students experience. Longitudinal and institutionally situated research is needed to examine how any such change develops across disciplinary fields, institutional contexts, and different distributions of capital. The contextual studies considered in the Discussion identify mechanisms through which institutional resources and local cultures may shape policy enactment, but they do not establish that these mechanisms operate in the same way in the UAE or the Gulf. The proposed relationship among field position, capital recognition, and the changing cheating habitus therefore requires examination within particular institutions. Future research should investigate how students and educators interpret AI rules under different institutional conditions and how these interpretations affect judgments of legitimate academic participation. The student in the opening vignette, whose polished essay was submitted in an unusually short amount of time and was subsequently identified as potentially reliant on AI, remains at the centre of the problem addressed here. The analysis cannot determine whether this hypothetical student committed misconduct. Such judgments depend on whether institutional and assessment-level rules clearly define the permitted extent of AI assistance. When these rules remain unclear in practice, detection may indicate reliance on AI but cannot determine how that reliance should be classified. Academic integrity is therefore being redefined under conditions that higher education institutions have yet to address fully. The original contributions presented in the study are included in the article/Supplementary Material, further inquiries can be directed to the corresponding author. abstract_text: Generative AI tools are now routinely used by Chinese Language and Literature majors for tasks once considered the province of individual literary craft: drafting verse, shaping narrative prose, revising fiction. Two competing accounts describe what this means for students' confidence in their own creative writing. A cognitive-offloading account holds that repeated reliance on AI displaces the mastery experiences through which writing self-efficacy is built, so reliance erodes confidence over time. A compensatory-use account holds the reverse: students whose confidence is already low turn to AI to avoid the discomfort of unassisted composition, so low confidence drives reliance. The resulting intervals are unequal. Wave 1 to Wave 2 and Wave 3 to Wave 4 each span approximately nine weeks of term time, while Wave 2 to Wave 3 spans the summer vacation and runs to approximately 21 weeks. Anchoring the waves to comparable points within each semester holds the instructional context constant across occasions, and every interval is long enough for meaningful within-person change in both constructs to occur. Because the equality constraint imposed on the structural paths (Section 3.4) assumes the lagged process operates comparably across all three transitions, we test that assumption directly by freeing the Wave 2 to Wave 3 transition and comparing model fit (Section 4.2). Data were collected through an anonymous online survey administered via each participating institution's course management platform; a unique, self-generated anonymous identifier allowed responses to be linked across waves without collecting identifying information. The reverse pathway, from increased reliance to subsequent declines in self-efficacy, was about a third the size and fell just short of the conventional threshold (β = −.085, p = .072). A direct comparison of the two pathways favored compensation by both a likelihood-ratio test (Δχ²(1) = 8.83, p = .003) and a 5,000-resample bootstrap whose 95% confidence interval for the difference excluded zero. The trait-level correlation between the two constructs’ stable components was negative and moderate in size ( r = −.342) but could not be distinguished from zero. The resulting intervals are unequal. Wave 1 to Wave 2 and Wave 3 to Wave 4 each span approximately nine weeks of term time, while Wave 2 to Wave 3 spans the summer vacation and runs to approximately 21 weeks. Anchoring the waves to comparable points within each semester holds the instructional context constant across occasions, and every interval is long enough for meaningful within-person change in both constructs to occur. Because the equality constraint imposed on the structural paths (Section 3.4) assumes the lagged process operates comparably across all three transitions, we test that assumption directly by freeing the Wave 2 to Wave 3 transition and comparing model fit (Section 4.2). Data were collected through an anonymous online survey administered via each participating institution's course management platform; a unique, self-generated anonymous identifier allowed responses to be linked across waves without collecting identifying information. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Hangzhou Educational Science Research Institute prior to data collection (Approval No. HZESRI-923; approved 20 November 2024) and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. analysis.discussion: This study asked a question that cross-sectional and standard longitudinal designs cannot answer on their own: when Chinese Language and Literature undergraduates’ generative AI writing reliance and literary creative writing self-efficacy move together over an academic year, which one is more reliably driving the other? Using a four-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel model estimated by full-information maximum likelihood on all 387 baseline respondents, we found a within-person pathway from declining self-efficacy to subsequent increases in AI reliance that was statistically significant and estimated with essentially complete power (β = −.276, p < .001). The reverse pathway, from increased reliance to subsequent declines in self-efficacy, was about a third the size and fell just short of the conventional threshold (β = −.085, p = .072). A direct comparison of the two pathways favored compensation by both a likelihood-ratio test (Δχ²(1) = 8.83, p = .003) and a 5,000-resample bootstrap whose 95% confidence interval for the difference excluded zero. The trait-level correlation between the two constructs’ stable components was negative and moderate in size ( r = −.342) but could not be distinguished from zero. Read plainly: H3 and H4 were supported, H1 and H2 were not, and the erosion pathway sits in a region where this design had roughly even odds of detection, which makes its non-significance uninformative about whether the mechanism operates. Before drawing any theoretical lesson from the H1 and H2 nulls, it is worth asking what this design could have detected. Taking the estimated parameters as population values and simulating 2,000 datasets at N = 387, empirical power to detect the erosion path (H2, β = −.085) at p < .05 was 53.2%, and power to detect the random-intercept covariance (H1, r = −.342) was 44.2%; the compensation path was detected in 100.0% of replications. A non-significant result from a test with roughly even odds of detection is close to uninformative in either direction. It is not evidence that erosion fails to operate, and we do not present it as such. What it licenses is the narrower statement that an erosion effect of this magnitude, if real, would be detected by this design about half the time, and was not detected here. A cognitive-offloading account in which reliance gradually displaces mastery experience [ 1 – 3 ] remains an open possibility on these data. We are explicit about the asymmetry this creates in the abstract and conclusion as well: the erosion pathway is undetermined here, and no comparison in this paper should be read as showing that erosion is absent. This also bounds what H4 can support. The compensation path was both larger and the more precisely estimated of the two, and the equality test between them was itself well powered (91.4% at N = 387), so the conclusion that the two paths differ in magnitude is on firm footing within this design. The conclusion that compensation is the stronger mechanism in general is not, because the comparison sets an estimate this design could always detect against one it could detect about half the time, and because nothing in the offloading account specifies how much cumulative exposure an erosion effect requires before it becomes visible. A one-year window may simply be shorter than the mechanism needs. The defensible reading is that compensation operates on a timescale this design resolves and erosion, if it operates, does not announce itself within four waves and one academic year. The point estimate for the random-intercept correlation ( r = −.342) was moderate and in the expected direction, and the likelihood-ratio test around it (Δχ²(1) = 2.26, p = .133) could not separate it from zero. Lüdtke and Robitzsch [ 33 ] and Zheng and Valente [ 34 ] have argued that RI-CLPM's random-intercept variance and covariance components are estimated with less precision than its within-person cross-lagged paths when the number of waves is limited, because separating a stable trait from a correlated sequence of state-level deviations requires more repeated observations than comparing two consecutive within-person changes. Our own simulation matches that argument closely: at N = 387 the trait-level covariance was the single hardest parameter in the model to detect (44.2% power, against 100.0% for the compensation path), and the sensitivity curve in Table 6 puts the sample size needed for 80% power on this parameter well beyond what a four-wave design of this kind retains. The substantive question H1 poses, whether chronically more AI-reliant students are also chronically less confident, is answerable in principle; it is not answerable at this wave count and this N, and we report the estimate as directional evidence awaiting a design built for it. The practical question institutions are actually facing is concrete: should a Chinese Language and Literature program spend its limited intervention budget on restricting or monitoring AI access in creative writing coursework, or on something else? Our results speak most directly to that choice through H3, the one path estimated with reasonable power and found significant. A restriction-focused policy implicitly assumes reliance is the causal agent eroding confidence; that is the pathway (H2) this design could detect only about half the time and did not find at conventional significance. The pathway we did find, with adequate power, ran the other way: from lower confidence to higher subsequent reliance. Two concrete implications follow. First, the compensation path was detectable across the intervals this design used, approximately nine weeks within a semester and approximately 21 weeks across the summer, and freeing the longer interval did not change the estimate. A meaningful amount of time can therefore elapse between a dip in confidence and the increase in reliance it predicts, and the relationship survives a break in instruction. This argues for front-loading confidence-focused intervention early in a course rather than waiting for a midterm check-in; we do not have the within-wave resolution to say how many weeks the lag actually takes for a given student, only that it operates on a timescale the model detects at intervals of nine weeks and longer, which is consistent with earlier being better than later. Second, “building confidence” is vague enough to be useless as a recommendation unless tied to Bandura's [ 2 ] and Pajares's [ 3 ] own account of where self-efficacy comes from: mastery experience specifically, not general encouragement. In practice, this means low-stakes, ungraded opportunities to complete a full unassisted draft early in the term, with feedback that names what the student did well in the parts they wrote themselves, in place of generic praise or generic reassurance that “AI is just a tool.” The instructional-modality literature gives this recommendation a more concrete anchor than our own data can. analysis.limitations: Several limitations qualify these conclusions. First, this design's power to detect the erosion pathway at the magnitude estimated here was 53.2%, so the four-wave, one-year window cannot adjudicate between “erosion does not operate” and “erosion operates too slowly, or too weakly, for this design to see it.” Distinguishing those possibilities requires either a longer panel or a substantially larger sample, not a different interpretation of the same data. Second, both constructs were measured exclusively via self-report; we followed procedural safeguards against common method bias [ 43 , 44 ] and additionally ran a single-factor comparison model as a baseline check, but self-reported reliance and self-reported confidence still share a measurement source that no procedural safeguard fully removes, and future work would benefit from behavioral or trace-data measures of actual AI use alongside self-report. Third, the sample was drawn from Chinese Language and Literature programs specifically; generalization to other creative writing contexts should be made cautiously given how culture- and genre-specific our operationalization of literary creative writing self-efficacy was. Fourth, we did not measure the type or sophistication of AI tool used, and a tool used for grammar-level assistance plausibly carries different implications than one used to generate entire passages of original prose; future work distinguishing levels of AI delegation within the broader reliance construct would sharpen these claims. Fifth, the composite measures for GAWR and LCWSE were assembled from items adapted across several source instruments in place of a single validated scale adopted wholesale. Section 3.3 sets out the criterion each item had to meet, the Wave-1 standardized loadings ( Table 4 ) were uniformly high, and both α and ω exceeded .93 at every wave, but internal consistency and single-occasion factor structure are not construct validation. Neither instrument has been validated against external criteria or in an independent sample, and both should be treated as study-specific composites until that work is done. Sixth, two of the cited sources [ 30 , 33 ] are unreviewed preprints rather than peer-reviewed publications, reflecting how recent this literature is; this is a limitation of the evidence base this study draws on, not only of the study itself, and readers should weight those specific claims accordingly until published versions are available. Seventh, the analysis was not preregistered. The four directional hypotheses were derived from the two theoretical accounts before the data were analyzed, and each specifies an expected sign, but no timestamped analysis plan exists that would let a reader verify the ordering independently. The distinction between the confirmatory and exploratory portions of this paper therefore rests on our account of it, and H4 in particular was framed as a hypothesis while carrying an acknowledged asymmetry in power between the two paths it compares.

analysis.discussion: The positive correlation between AI Literacy and Epistemic Justification (β = 0.452) means that the higher the level of AI literacy, the higher the engagement in evidence-based judgment [36] . Students with wider knowledge of AI systems, their capabilities, applications, and limitations might better assess the credibility and evidentially quality of AI-generated information [37] . This awareness can prompt learners to critically reflect on artificial intelligence output instead of blindly relying on it. AI Literacy has thus been identified as an important preliminary skill for developing epistemic judgment. This discovery indicates that knowledge about how AI works and its capabilities and constraints can impact the way students use information produced using AI technology [33] . Improving students' AI literacy skills could help them realize that claims made by AI are not automatically reliable, and that it should check what is true and verify those claims by comparing them to authoritative sources before using them in educational work [38] . The positive correlation of the relation between Epistemic Justification and Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation (beta = 0.429) suggests that in evaluating AI-generated knowledge, evidence-based reasoning plays an important role [39] . A student who has carried out systematic information analysis, considers the author's credibility, looks back at one's own information, compares alternate information, and recognizes inconsistencies might be better able to assess the accuracy and reliability of the information produced by their AI [40] . It sometimes seems rational, relevant and authoritative, yet it is not sufficiently supported by evidence [4] . Epistemic Justification is an important evaluative process in which students select information possessing reasonable support from information possessing good grounds for acceptance. The discovery has prompted a call for teachers to factor the capability of students in using AI tools into their assessment methods, while also allowing them to assess whether and what goes into or out of the information spiral created by such systems [42] . Adopting AI Literacy also shows a positive direct relationship with Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation with β = 0.308. The result implies that students' understanding of AI directly affects their ability to evaluate learning value and usefulness of AI-supported knowledge [38] . Students who know what AI can and cannot do, how it can be used effectively, but when such use may fail or be ineffective may be more vigilant when assessing the outputs of the AI to understand whether can be used in their academic work properly. The relationship shows that the understanding of technology and assessing knowledge is related, but not the same as competencies in AI-enabled learning [43] . Thus, AI literacy can aid students in understanding that artificial intelligence information should not be taken as gospel. The discovery also highlights a need for AI literacy: Make sure users learn how to be aware of, understand, evaluate, and engage responsibly with the information produced by AI [44] . The proposed mediating role of Epistemic Justification is reflected in the relationships observed within the structural model. AI Literacy has a positive correlation with Epistemic Justification, and Epistemic Justification has a positive correlation with Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation. Simultaneously, AI Literacy has positive feedback with Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation [39] . The pattern shows that learning AI literacy is directly linked with synthetic knowledge as well as its epistemic process in evaluating information. In the framework proposed, Epistemic Justification can serve as an important connection point [36] . The reported results do not include an indirect-effect coefficient, significance value, or confidence interval for the mediation pathway, however. The available results thus reflect the relationships as hypothesized in the mediation model but are not statistically valid to support the significance of the indirect effect alone [41] . The interaction term Critical Thinking Disposition x AI Literacy indicates a β of -0.026 [43] against the Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation, and an f2 of 0.001. The small negative correlation suggests the interaction's effect was not very large when working with the relationship between AI Literacy and Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation [42] . Thus, within the proposed model, Critical Thinking Disposition makes a limited contribution because it interacts with AI Literacy. As revealed by the explanatory results, AI Literacy explains 20.4% of the variance in the Epistemic Justification, and the predictors explain 40.8% of the variance in the Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation [44] . Moreover, the model retrievals are SRMR 0.037 and NFI 0.945 for the saturated and estimated models respectively [45] . The overall results make a point of the value, interconnectedness and importance of technological understanding, epistemic judgment, and critical evaluation in supporting responsible use of AI-produced knowledge in higher education [37] . AI Literacy is situating itself as a key tool for fostering responsible interactions with AI among students at university. The results suggest that the higher students' level of AI Literacy, the higher their level of Epistemic Justification and -somewhat unsurprisingly -their Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation. Learning about the capabilities, applications, and limitations of AI and the information it generates help students think more critically about information created by AI and their ability to evaluate its academic appropriateness and authority. The results also showed that AI Literacy spills over into Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation, thereby establishing that knowledge of technology is a part of students' ability to evaluate synthetic knowledge. Beyond simply using AI tools, AI Literacy is crucial for educating oneself with AI-generated information in a thoughtful, critical, and ethical way. The study would be of significance towards the higher education, teachers and academic programs. The results indicated that the capacities associated with epistemic reasoning and knowledge assessment should be included in education about AI technologies. Universities can promote students to check the credibility of the information source generated by AI, analyse the credibility of information sources, compare credible information, find potential limitations, and examine the proof of information generated by AI. There are opportunities to introduce aimed activities related to AI Literacy and Epistemic Justification in academic curricula and faculty development programs. Collectively, these practices in education can help students cultivate more responsible and informed attitudes toward using generative AI in their academic education, research, writing, and knowledge-building activities. The study of Synthetic Knowledge Evaluation is analysed using quantitative and crosssectional approach at university level particular focus areas are the University students of New Delhi. The findings presented may not apply to students in other geographic locations, institutions, disciplines, and environments because of this. The structured questionnaire provides measurable evidence in relation to the chosen constructs but does not provide much insight into students' reasoning processes in assessing AI generated information. reading.findings: Rather than treating AI literacy as a single general competence, the study tested a facet-level model that distinguishes cognitive, operational, reflective, ethical, and affective dimensions. Three findings are particularly important. First, AI knowledge occupied an upstream position in the model. It was strongly associated with AI awareness, operational ability, and ethical awareness, and was also positively associated with critical reflection. This suggests that conceptual understanding of AI may help students calibrate what AI can do, recognise its limitations, operate tools more strategically, and identify ethical boundaries. This finding is consistent with AI-literacy frameworks that place conceptual understanding at the centre of AI literacy, but it extends them by showing that AI knowledge may function as a connecting resource across cognitive, operational, and ethical facets in creative higher education. Second, perceived learning performance was associated with a recognise-reflect-produce pattern. AI awareness and operational ability were linked to critical reflection, and critical reflection and operational ability were linked to perceived learning performance. This pattern suggests that AI-supported creative learning is not improved by tool use alone. Students need to recognise how AI shapes creative possibilities, critically evaluate AI-generated outputs, and then use operational skills to revise and produce work aligned with learning goals. In this sense, AI literacy contributes to learning performance when technical action is combined with reflective judgement. Third, academic well-being was associated with perceived learning performance, ethical awareness, and emotional adaptability. This finding indicates that students' well-being in AI-supported creative learning is not merely a by-product of better performance. It is also connected to whether students can manage uncertainty and whether they understand the ethical boundaries of AI use. In studio-based learning, where ambiguity, authorship, and originality are central, ethical clarity and emotional adaptability may help students experience AIsupported learning as more controllable, legitimate, and psychologically manageable.

A non-probabilistic sampling method was used to recruit participants from universities across Asia, Europe, and Oceania. A total of 556 responses were initially collected. Among these, 554 participants provided informed consent and were included in the consenting sample. The consenting sample included 221 students from Asia, comprising 183 from China and 38 from other Asian countries; 138 from Europe; and 195 from Australia. This regional distribution broadened the empirical context of the study and allowed the proposed model to be examined across a diverse group of design students. The consenting sample consisted of 286 females (51.62%), 251 males (45.30%), and 17 participants who preferred not to disclose their gender (3.07%). Most participants were aged 18-22 years, 364 (65.70%); followed by 23-25 years, 130 (23.47%); ≥25 years, 55 (9.93%); and ≤18 years, 5 (0.90%). By study level, there were 248 first-and second-year undergraduates (44.77%), 127 thirdand fourth-year undergraduates (22.92%), 137 master's students (24.73%), and 42 doctoral students (7.58%). Data screening was conducted before the PLS-SEM analysis. Responses were excluded if they met one or more predefined quality-control criteria, including duplicate submissions, unrealistically short completion time, or apparent inattentive response patterns such as straight-lining across long item blocks. Cases with substantial missing data on core constructs were removed. Applying these predefined data-quality criteria resulted in a final analytic sample of 475 participants for subsequent analyses. Data were collected through a structured online questionnaire during a single academic term. Before formal data collection, the questionnaire was prepared in both English and Chinese. To ensure semantic equivalence, a translation and back-translation procedure was conducted. The initial English version was translated into Chinese by a bilingual researcher familiar with AI education, and another bilingual researcher independently back-translated the Chinese version into English. The research team then compared the back-translated version with the original version and resolved discrepancies through discussion, with particular attention to terms such as AI awareness, critical reflection, ethical awareness, and academic well-being. A small-scale pretest was conducted with 20 students from design and related programmes who were not included in the final sample. The pretest examined item clarity, wording, questionnaire flow, completion time, and the equivalence of the Chinese and English versions. Based on the feedback, several items were reworded to improve clarity, but no construct was removed. For the formal survey, the link was distributed through department-and course-related channels, including course groups, programme mailing lists, programme-related networks, and social media groups. Participants were also allowed to forward the survey link to eligible peers in design and related programmes. The questionnaire was administered through Wenjuanxing and Google Forms. After opening the survey, participants first read an information sheet describing the study purpose, potential risks, privacy safeguards, voluntary participation, and the right to withdraw. They then provided informed consent electronically before completing the demographic items and construct scales. All core constructs were assessed using a consistently formatted questionnaire with five-point Likert-scale items ranging from 1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree, and all items were positively worded. The studies involving human participants were reviewed and approved by the Ethics Committee of Guangdong University of Technology. As shown in Fig. 1 , the overall thought classification workflow and methodology of this paper which consists of four main stages are represented and explained. Social media texts are labeled with VADER and preprocessed, then passed to three branches: traditional ML classifiers with stratified 5-fold cross-validation, transformer-based encoder models, and a prompt-based Llama-2-13B-Chat classifier. All models are evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation, with performance reported as accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, mean ± SD, and 95% confidence intervals before comparative model selection. The thought classification workflow and methodology are explained as follows: 1. Data acquisition and thought labeling: using VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoning) sentiment analyzer and expert validation, 2. Text preprocessing, including cleaning, normalization, contraction expansion, custom stop-word removal, and lemmatization), 3. Model training using three branches-traditional machine-learning classifiers namely, Logistic Regression (LR) (Stoltzfus, 2011) The data collection procedure involved web scraping from Reddit and using online social networks (OSNs) such as Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram, which enabled this study to search for news, statuses, and discussions that matched both positive and negative thinking. We used the Python library (Python Reddit API Wrapper) PRAW to scrape the data from Reddit (PRAW) (Boe, 2014) . We used the polarity score method of the VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoning) sentiment analyzer to return the probability of a given input sentence being positive, negative, or neutral (Das et al., 2021) . The study then used VADER's compound score, which ranges from -1 negative to + 1 positive, and applied conservative thresholds to obtain high-confidence polarity labels. Specifically, we defined texts with a compound score greater than 0.2 as positive and less than -0.2 as negative, treating all intermediate values in the interval [-0.2, 0.2] as neutral. This wider neutral band allowed us to discard borderline or ambiguous cases and retain only clearly positive or negative thoughts, thereby reducing potential label noise in the automatically annotated dataset. Furthermore, texts were collected from August 2022 to January 2024 using specific positive keywords such as #Success, #Life, #Happiness, #Dream, etc., and negative keywords such as #Difficulties, #Feeling, #Failure, #Worry, and many more, to build the dataset. To find these keywords, as a reference, we used the dataset of Raslescu et al. (2022) consisting of 150 positive and 150 negative adjectives describing personality characteristics, and another database of English EMOtional TErms (EMOTE) (Grühn, 2016) , which provides positive and negative subjective ratings for 1287 nouns and 985 adjectives. After the construction of our dataset, we found that some data had a negative-topositive correspondence. For example, the negative thought "I am feeling bad" has a possible positive convertible thought, "I am so good". Therefore, we can use this dataset for negative-to-positive thought conversion.

Research has shown that automatic sentiment labeling enables efficient construction of large-scale datasets for social media analysis, although concerns remain regarding annotation quality, particularly for ambiguous, sarcastic, or context-dependent expressions (Hutto & Gilbert, 2014; Jain et al., 2023; Oliveira et al., 2023) .
