Future work should examine retention, transfer, scalability, and alternative instructional configurations across diverse educational settings.

analysis.methods: This study employed a cluster-assigned quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test control-group design to examine whether a structured GenAI-supported instructional intervention was associated with differences in undergraduates' mathematical problem-solving in Calculus I. Assignment occurred at the tutorial-section level rather than at the individual level to reduce contamination and preserve the ecological validity of a real university course. Because the number of clusters was small, section-level clustering was addressed analytically through a multilevel sensitivity model and is acknowledged as a design limitation. Generative AI Tool: The experimental group used an institutionally approved large-language-model interface configured for instructional support. The tool was introduced as a Socratic tutor rather than a solution generator. Students were trained to use prompts such as "Give me a hint without solving the problem," "Ask me a question that helps me identify the next step," and "Check whether my reasoning is valid without giving the final answer." Demographic and Background Questionnaire: A short form collected data on age, gender, high school GPA, and prior mathematics achievement to verify group equivalence. To ensure comparability, the intervention lasted exactly 15 weeks for both groups, during which all students worked on identical weekly problem sets drawn from the course syllabus. Experimental Group (GenAI-supported Instruction): Participants used GenAI within a structured think-pair-GenAI-share routine. They first attempted each problem independently, then discussed their reasoning with a peer, then used GenAI to obtain hints or check reasoning, and finally shared solution strategies. Weekly sessions were monitored to reinforce the rule that GenAI should support thinking rather than provide complete solutions. Control Group (Traditional Instruction): Students received standard face-to-face instruction covering the same content and problem sets, utilizing textbooks, lecture notes, and board work. No access to GenAI tools was provided. To reduce differential effects, all procedures were standardized to the extent possible within the cluster design. The findings indicate that students in the structured GenAI-supported condition had higher post-test problem-solving scores when the tool was embedded in a pedagogical design that preserved student reasoning. The experimental group outperformed the control group after controlling for pre-test scores, and the multilevel sensitivity analysis produced a group effect in the same direction after accounting for section-level clustering. The important interpretation is not that GenAI alone improves achievement, but that GenAI can be educationally powerful when it is constrained to function as a scaffold for planning, monitoring, and reflection. This interpretation directly addresses the concern that GenAI may produce superficial learning. In the present intervention, students were trained to request hints, verify reasoning, and compare strategies rather than obtain direct solutions. Thus, the observed difference is consistent with the possibility that structured interaction patterns helped keep students cognitively responsible for the solution process. Practically, the findings suggest that universities should not introduce GenAI as an unrestricted assistance tool in mathematics courses. Instead, instructors should provide prompt protocols, model appropriate use, prohibit direct solution-seeking during learning activities, and integrate GenAI within peer discussion and reflection routines. Faculty development should therefore focus on designing prompts and tasks that require students to explain, justify, and evaluate reasoning. Methodologically, the study illustrates the value of moving beyond overall achievement scores. By using a Pólyaaligned analytic rubric, the analysis identified where the intervention had the strongest impact. This approach can help future studies distinguish between performance differences associated with answer access and those associated with changes in problem-solving regulation. On the substitution account, harm arises when an optimised interaction takes over a developmental function and removes the friction through which that function builds the child's own capacity. These imperfections are not noise around the developmental signal. Largely, they are the signal. Substitution has three features. It is functional, concerning which developmental work is done rather than how many minutes pass. It is asymmetric: optimised systems often outperform humans at the surface of a function (answering accurately, staying patient, holding attention) while lacking its depth. In one trial the AI partner produced better comprehension but less affective engagement and narrative-relevant talk than parents (Xiao et al., 2025) . And it is conditional: the same technology can substitute for reciprocal interaction or scaffold it, depending on whether a human stays in the loop and whether the child must generate rather than receive. Meta-analytic co-use effects (Mallawaarachchi et al., 2024) and a parent-prompting reading agent (He et al., 2025) illustrate the scaffolding route. Section 4.2 shows how this account reconciles apparently inconsistent findings (question 2). Propositions. Eight propositions follow (Table 2 ). Table. 2. Screen time cooccurs with fewer adult words and turns (Brushe et al., 2024) , and television predicted fewer turns a year later (Coyne et al., 2026) . analysis.discussion: The first research question asked which mechanisms are most exposed. The synthesis identifies one in each system: the shift from stimulus-driven to executive attention, which engagement-maximising content can bypass; co-regulation and caregiver availability, on which device calming and technoference act; and the effortful formulation of questions and calibration of trust that anticipation pre-empts (Table 1 ). On the second question, the framework reorganises a literature that has looked contradictory. Screen time predicts poorer outcomes in some samples but not others (Takahashi et al., 2023; Beukes et al., 2026) , co-use reverses the sign of associations, and AI partners outperform parents on one outcome while underperforming on another. If the active ingredient is the fate of reciprocal interaction rather than exposure, these are not anomalies. Brushe et al. (2024) documented the association the mechanism predicts in household audio, and Mallawaarachchi et al. (2024) its moderator in pooled data. The account is also consistent with within-person sleep effects being smaller than between-person ones (Bourke et al., 2026) : the household routines in which heavy screen use is embedded may matter more than screen minutes as such. Relative to the theories in Section 2.2, the framework extends Ainsworth's (1979) sensitivity construct to machines that are contingent without being sensitive, applies Bandura's (2006) account of agency to anticipation, which removes the resistance through which efficacy is learned, and carries the coengagement principle from media to agents. It also departs from two common positions. Against alarmism, it holds that conversational agents can scaffold learning when they demand the child's own language and keep caregivers involved (M. J. Kim & Lee, 2026; He et al., 2025) . Against the view that good design suffices, it holds that an excellent agent can still substitute: in Xiao et al.'s (2025) trial, comprehension rose while the affective texture of shared reading thinned. If attachment is formed in invested responsiveness, a patient, accurate, alwaysavailable agent is not a weaker parent but a different kind of partner, one offering contingency without care. Children seem partly to sense this, extending to humans a trust they withhold from inaccurate machines (Geng et al., 2025) , although their uncertainty about whether smart speakers have feelings (Andries & Robertson, 2023) suggests the categories are not yet stable. The third question is answered by P1-P8, which locate support in caregiver participation, in agents that elicit rather than supply the child's language and in parental device use that leaves reciprocal interaction intact. These propositions are neither accepted nor rejected here. They are offered for empirical testing with the designs in Table 2 , and each would be weakened if its named mechanism or moderator failed to appear. The evidence has limits. Technoference research uses varied definitions and measures and is largely crosssectional (Komanchuk et al., 2023) , and infant studies are heterogeneous and short-term (Vélez et al., 2026) . AI learning studies are small (15 families in He et al., 2025; 23 children in P. Kim et al., 2026) , brief and concentrated in the United States, East Asia and Europe, and several evaluate systems built by the authors' own teams. None follows children over years, and children under three, whose attention and attachment systems are most plastic, are almost absent. Future research should therefore use multiyear designs with objective measures of turn-taking and device use, include children under three and AI toys, evaluate agents independently of their developers and work in African samples. On the fourth question, education, parenting guidance and regulation should judge a use by whether it takes over or carries reciprocal interaction, as Section 5 sets out. In African settings the implications cut two ways. Conditions favouring substitution are often present. Where a caregiver's phone is the household's main screen, children are likely to meet content ranked by systems never designed for them, and caregivers under heavy workloads have strong reasons to use devices to occupy or calm children. The Ethiopian finding that three-quarters of under-fives exceeded guidelines, with devices in eating, playing or sleeping rooms among the associated factors (Demeke et al., 2026) , and Malawi's urban-rural gradient in meeting movement-behaviour guidelines, which include screen time (Mwase-Vuma et al., 2025) , suggest exposure will rise with urbanisation and connectivity. Yet the same infrastructure can carry reciprocal interaction. The Zambia and Tanzania WhatsApp trial used phones to prompt shared reading and increased responsive caregiving, although child outcomes did not change at immediate follow-up (Skeen et al., 2023) , and Lesotho data show that turntaking can be measured in rural homes and is sensitive to intervention during structured interaction (Marlow et al., 2026) . The WhatsApp trial illustrates the carrying route that P8 predicts will help, though it was not AI-mediated and its null child outcomes mean it does not test P3. Three cautions follow. High-income effect sizes should not be transported directly; in Cape Town, sleep and caregiver education mattered more for executive function than screen time (Beukes et al., 2026) . Supervision appears a stronger lever than content labels; in Kakamega, supervision was associated with readiness while "educational" content was not (Okenwa-Vincent et al., 2025) . And design must be local: codesign with caregivers in Kenya, Ethiopia, Namibia, Cameroon and the Democratic Republic of the Congo reshaped a parenting app around local realities, fathers' roles and cultural values (Alam et al., 2023) . No verified earlychildhood screen or AI studies were located from Nigeria, Ghana or Rwanda; given the limits of indexing, this indicates a gap in accessible evidence rather than proof that none exists. Young children's encounters with AI are better understood through the developmental systems they engage than through hours of exposure. Attention, attachment and agency are built in effortful, imperfect and reciprocal interaction. Technologies optimised for engagement, simulated responsiveness and anticipation threaten development when they take over the functions of that interaction and remove the friction through which children's own capacities grow. They can support development when they carry interaction between people and require the child to think, speak and choose. The question for families, educators and regulators is therefore not only how much, but what each use replaces and what it carries. Early-childhood education. Centres and pre-service programmes should treat conversational turn-taking as a protected resource and judge digital tools by whether they increase or reduce educator-child and child-child talk. AI agents, where used, should prompt rather than answer and be used in small groups with an adult present. African teachereducation curricula should add developmental criteria to the technical ones that dominate procurement. Parenting guidance. Guidance should move from minute limits alone to three practical questions: is someone with the child, is the child doing the talking, and is the device being used to calm. analysis.discussion: In Study 1, trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.425, p < 0.001). This finding differs from patterns observed in general educational technology research, where performance expectancy is typically regarded as the primary driver of behavioral intention. Students’ willingness to integrate GenAI into their creative processes was associated not only with expected gains in productivity but also, and in this sample more strongly, with perceived trustworthiness ( Oc et al., 2024 ; Rana et al., 2025 ). The construct as operationalized here is primarily instrumental, supplemented by a modest art-value component. This strong association should not be read as evidence for a fully developed art-value trust dimension. The role of trust was not uniform across paths in the model. For all five antecedents, the indirect association through trust was significant (bias-corrected 95% CIs excluded zero), and the direct association with behavioral intention remained significant after trust was included. This pattern is consistent with partial mediation for each antecedent. Substantively, partial mediation means that trust is not the sole pathway connecting these antecedents to behavioral intention. Each antecedent is associated with behavioral intention both through trust and through pathways that do not involve trust. For facilitating conditions, the direct association was small but significant ( β = 0.092, p = 0.040; 10,000 bootstrap 95% CI [0.003, 0.179]). Thus, facilitating conditions are associated with behavioral intention partly through trust and partly through a direct association that is independent of trust. This direct association may reflect the possibility that resources, training, and support are associated with behavioral intention not only through their association with trust but also through their association with reduced perceived barriers to use. Because this direct association is close to the significance threshold, the partial mediation pattern should be interpreted cautiously. Overall, the mediation results suggest that trust is an important but not exhaustive explanatory pathway; the antecedents retain direct associations with behavioral intention that are independent of trust. Among the five variables associated with trust, social influence had the highest standardized coefficient ( β = 0.262, p < 0.001), and its indirect association with behavioral intention via trust was also the most pronounced among all indirect paths (indirect coefficient = 0.112), accounting for 42.1% of its total estimated association. In traditional information systems research, social influence is typically understood to operate through normative pressure or imitation mechanisms. However, in artistic creation contexts, its role may be more prominent because social influence may be closely tied to the standards used to evaluate the legitimacy of creative tools and outputs. Artistic value is not objectively given but is constructed through social negotiation and institutional recognition ( Wingström et al., 2024 ). When teachers, peers, and the broader arts community treat GenAI as a legitimate medium for artistic creation, students may perceive more than just social pressure to conform; they may update their normative beliefs about what constitutes authentic, masterful, and valuable artistic practice ( Garcia, 2024 ; Wu et al., 2026 ). This socially constructed legitimacy may be closely linked to trust in the technology. The prominent role of social influence is thus consistent with the findings of other scholars’ qualitative studies, which suggest that art students’ attitudes toward AI are deeply embedded in community norms and the process of professional identity formation ( Ursavaş et al., 2025 ). From a theoretical perspective, social influence may be more closely tied to students’ judgments of trust as a cognitive authority, rather than merely serving as a peripheral normative factor in this sample. The remaining three classic dimensions of the UTAUT model were significantly positively associated with trust in GenAI, all meeting the p < 0.001 criterion. While the strength of their associations with trust was slightly lower than that of social influence, together they may represent consistent technological and environmental correlates of trust. Educational attainment was significantly positively associated with behavioral intention ( β = 0.072, p = 0.041). This pattern suggests that, in this sample, art students with higher educational attainment reported stronger behavioral intention to use GenAI. This metric captures statistical dispersion in semantic embedding, texture-style statistics, and edge-based compositional structure rather than artistic merit. abstract_text: After the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in 2022, research on AI literacy in education is a growing field. Less attention has been given to how teacher educators engage with these technologies in practice. Drawing on a digital agency perspective on professional knowledge and AI literacy, this study reports findings from an exploratory self-study. We investigate how we, as three teacher educators, engaged with GenAI in the design and delivery of Small Private Online Courses (SPOCs). reading.overview: After the adoption of Generative AI (GenAI) tools in 2022, research on AI literacy in education is a growing field. Less attention has been given to how teacher educators engage with these technologies in practice.
reading.methods: This study relies on research methods for self-study research as outlined by Samaras (2011) and LaBoskey (2004) . Samaras (2011) describes self-study as a personally situated and critically collaborative inquiry focused on professional learning, while LaBoskey (2004) identifies five key elements: self-initiated, improvement, interactive, qualitative, and validity grounded in trust and shared results. The use of critical friendship is central (Berry, 2008) , seen as a process of collective reflection aimed at gaining deeper insight and actionable outcomes. Reflection is crucial not only for ensuring credibility and maintaining ethical standards but also, perhaps most importantly, for identifying blind spots in one's educational practice. In this study, however, self-study was used to critically examine our own decisions, assumptions, and actions in our approach to and use of GenAI. A major focus was on the exploratory and systematic potential of this approach to analyze our roles, decisions, and reflections, as well as to document how our digital agency was enacted and developed through the pedagogical choices made when designing and implementing SPOCs with GenAI. One recognized approach in self-study research is to examine the development of professional teaching practice through retrospective reflection (LaBoskey, 2004; Samaras, 2011) . reading.findings: In this section, we present the findings of our study by addressing the RQs outlined earlier. While our analysis is structured around the four dimensions of AI literacy proposed by Ng et al. (2021) , each epistemic practice is examined based on whether it stabilizes or challenges our professional knowledge. The first two epistemic practices or themes seem to be stabilizing, while the latter two appear more transgressive. That said, we aim to demonstrate how we engaged with GenAI; accordingly, our choices, reflections, and adaptations are analyzed as practices through which digital agency is enacted, negotiated, or reconfigured by us as teacher educators.
reading.interpretation: To discuss our study, we will focus on three points. The first is to propose a research contribution considering the research streams that inspired us. These suggest that the ways in which we understand professional knowledge and digital competence need to be challenged (Aagaard et al., 2025; Brevik et al., 2019; Goller & Paloniemi, 2022; Lund & Aagaard, 2020; Rajala et al., 2016) . While established understandings assume that competence is something one acquires, digital agency argues that attention should be shifted toward situated and epistemic practices, not least the importance of negotiation situations. We also showed that within the AI literacy literature, little is known about how teacher educators develop their AI literacy (Tan et al., 2025) . There is particularly little research on how this unfolds among teacher educators who teach online (Bullock, 2024; Lay & Pinnegar, 2024; Rice, 2024; Rollag Yoon et al., 2024) . To be exact, regarding our contribution, we were inspired by the work of Yang and Banks (2024) . They demonstrated that their AI literacy development was part of an iterative, process-oriented approach. While their study is important in showing how teacher educators gradually develop AI literacy through experimentation, application, evaluation, and reflection, our study makes a different nuance. Across the four themes, which align with the framework of Ng et al. (2021) , we demonstrate that our development of AI literacy is closely tied to different situated pedagogical contexts in which we, to a varying degree, must apply and enact our professional judgment. The use of critical friendship is central (Berry, 2008) , seen as a process of collective reflection aimed at gaining deeper insight and actionable outcomes. Reflection is crucial not only for ensuring credibility and maintaining ethical standards but also, perhaps most importantly, for identifying blind spots in one's educational practice. In this study, however, self-study was used to critically examine our own decisions, assumptions, and actions in our approach to and use of GenAI. A major focus was on the exploratory and systematic potential of this approach to analyze our roles, decisions, and reflections, as well as to document how our digital agency was enacted and developed through the pedagogical choices made when designing and implementing SPOCs with GenAI. One recognized approach in self-study research is to examine the development of professional teaching practice through retrospective reflection (LaBoskey, 2004; Samaras, 2011) . Self-study has no fixed methods or theories; researchers select and adapt approaches as needed, so methodological and theoretical innovation is common (Pithouse-Morgan, 2022). In our case, after designing and implementing the SPOCs, we decided to gather data through two qualitative collaborative self-interviews semistructured by an interview guide to explore our experiences with using GenAI to create online courses and the challenges and opportunities we faced during the pilot. Interviewing each other like we did is not a common approach in self-studies of teacher education practice. Usually, interaction with others has the form of critical-friendship, collegial dialogue, or collaborative self-study groups, and is framed as open-ended conversations, feedback sessions, or inquiry meetings rather than as formal collaborative self-interviews with an interview guide (Pithouse-Morgan, 2022). However, we found it a useful approach to look at and reflect on ourselves, our development as well as our professional experiences and practices. We conducted two rounds of collaborative self-interviewed and each session lasted approximately 1.5 to 2 hours. Afterward, the interviews were transcribed verbatim and prepared for data analysis. The interviews took place in the spring of 2025. The interviews followed the methodological guidelines outlined by Brinkmann and Kvale (2015) and aimed to reflect on completed teaching practice to support knowledge construction. We prepared the interview guide together in advance, covering topics and specific questions we wanted to explore, which we considered necessary for professional growth. We placed particular emphasis on our narrative accounts. For example, interview prompts included: 'Describe how you have used AI to design and develop MOOCs', 'What motivated you to begin using generative AI?' 'To what extent has your professional practice changed as a result of using generative AI?' and 'Have your attitudes toward generative AI become more critical or more enthusiastic?' During the interviews we acted as critical friends and probed each other's accounts with follow-up questions such as 'Why is that?' and 'What does that tell you?' We also asked one another to 'provide concrete examples or demonstrate artefacts'. By requesting examples and artefacts, we deliberately incorporated material traces of practice into the interview setting. Although we did not undertake an independent, systematic analysis of teaching materials, student feedback, personal notes, or course evaluations, which is a common approach in self-studies, discussion of those materials during the interviews rendered them implicit components of the dataset. Thus, our approach to self-study introduces a more structured variation to existing interactional forms and implicitly incorporates other common methods such as artefact analysis, note review, and evaluation analysis (see Appendix).
analysis.results: In this section, we present the findings of our study by addressing the RQs outlined earlier. While our analysis is structured around the four dimensions of AI literacy proposed by Ng et al. (2021) , each epistemic practice is examined based on whether it stabilizes or challenges our professional knowledge. The first two epistemic practices or themes seem to be stabilizing, while the latter two appear more transgressive. That said, we aim to demonstrate how we engaged with GenAI; accordingly, our choices, reflections, and adaptations are analyzed as practices through which digital agency is enacted, negotiated, or reconfigured by us as teacher educators.
analysis.discussion: To discuss our study, we will focus on three points. The first is to propose a research contribution considering the research streams that inspired us. These suggest that the ways in which we understand professional knowledge and digital competence need to be challenged (Aagaard et al., 2025; Brevik et al., 2019; Goller & Paloniemi, 2022; Lund & Aagaard, 2020; Rajala et al., 2016) . While established understandings assume that competence is something one acquires, digital agency argues that attention should be shifted toward situated and epistemic practices, not least the importance of negotiation situations. We also showed that within the AI literacy literature, little is known about how teacher educators develop their AI literacy (Tan et al., 2025) . There is particularly little research on how this unfolds among teacher educators who teach online (Bullock, 2024; Lay & Pinnegar, 2024; Rice, 2024; Rollag Yoon et al., 2024) . To be exact, regarding our contribution, we were inspired by the work of Yang and Banks (2024) . They demonstrated that their AI literacy development was part of an iterative, process-oriented approach. While their study is important in showing how teacher educators gradually develop AI literacy through experimentation, application, evaluation, and reflection, our study makes a different nuance. Across the four themes, which align with the framework of Ng et al. (2021) , we demonstrate that our development of AI literacy is closely tied to different situated pedagogical contexts in which we, to a varying degree, must apply and enact our professional judgment. In our understanding, AI literacy does not only unfold as a linear process but is a situated and negotiated practice that takes different forms depending on the nature of the pedagogical situation in which we engage with GenAI to make and deliver our SPOCs. This means that professional judgment is not merely something that accompanies AI use from the outside, but is ongoingly activated, intensified, and made more explicit when GenAI is used in our pedagogical practices as online teacher educators. The question, however, is what our self-study shows if we raise the discussion further, which brings us to the second point. It shows that when online courses are developed and delivered using GenAI, our understanding of professional knowledge is challenged. Our experience aligns with what more normative and critical perspectives on AI often call for (Selwyn, 2024) . They claim that one must be critical at all phases of technology use. We do not disagree with this, but our study shows that what can be formulated as 'critical' means the active exercise of professional judgment across many levels. What GenAI does is shift the conditions for professional knowledge by creating different forms of what we call tension intensification, some weaker and some stronger. By this, we mean that across the four themes, which show different situated epistemic practices, frictions arise around our professional knowledge. Some may argue that this is obvious, but the challenge may be that we lack a vocabulary for how this occurs in pedagogical practice. This argument becomes clearer when viewed considering the points in the digital agency discussion. Although the literature argues for the importance of negotiating professional knowledge and situated epistemic practice, an important nuance may remain unexplored (Aagaard et al., 2022; Brevik et al., 2019) . Our study suggests that AI literacy is flexible and situationally conditioned. It is expressed differently depending on whether technology is used in situations that resemble established pedagogical practices we normally work within, or whether it intervenes more directly in principles that we perceive as part of our professional identity. This is precisely why we have proposed the concepts of practice-stabilizing and practicetransgressive. We believe that GenAI challenges us by both mirroring and shifting where judgment must be applied explicitly. For example, one may argue that earlier digital technologies we used in teaching and academic work supported the frameworks around practice. We used them for passive organization, communication, storage, dissemination, and administration. We only expected them to respond to us to a limited extent. Now they do. GenAI is built on a statistical logic based on pattern recognition and probability calculation, and it produces language that intervenes much more directly into our epistemic processes. AI responds back with language, structures, formulations, suggestions, rewritings, and assemblages that resemble the work we ourselves usually do. There, a boundary crossing occurs, altering how we relate to knowledge work as GenAI intervenes directly in knowledge production itself. To a greater extent, we apply professional judgement, as we must assess tone, what we ask, what we accept, what we reject, and what should still stand as ours. This leads us to our third point, which lies implicitly within the digital agency discussion, but which we believe has a double consequence (Aagaard et al., 2022; Brevik et al., 2019) . Our reading of the literature is that agency refers to teacher educators as active actors who can transform the contexts in which they operate. One interpretation we make is that the assumption often made about technology is that it is non-responsive, perhaps somewhat passive. GenAI, by contrast, also has a form of active agency, which may have been underestimated until now. It not only mirrors our professional knowledge, but also our professional judgment. The technology generates responses that enter an ongoing chain of evaluations, negotiations, and rewritings to which we must constantly respond. This challenges our ideas of professional practice, which may previously have been more reserved for human judgment, and makes them more open. When this mirrors us back through a different language or meaning that nonetheless overlaps with our own values and norms, friction emerges. This creates uncertainty about what becomes of our professional knowledge. To a greater extent, we must exercise professional judgment and consider whether what we hand over is our own thinking. Our notions of authenticity, ownership, individual work, credibility, and our own understandings of work, thinking, and language are reconsidered and displaced. Perhaps, when we believe we have control over our professional judgment, we receive a response that forces us to reflect much more deeply on what constitutes the core of professional knowledge work. This also points back to our understanding of AI literacy. Beyond the literature's emphasis on the need for more teacher educator training, we believe that one important area of development will be to move AI literacy toward situated professional judgment. The interesting aspect of our self-study is that it cuts directly to a contradiction in the use of GenAI, which we believe is increasingly recognized, and to the potential role professional judgment can play in practice -that GenAI is not as productivityenhancing as we often believe. In fact, recent studies (Selwyn et al., 2025) demonstrate that when teachers engage with GenAI and apply their professional judgment, their workload increases because the quality of the outputs does not align with their professional standards as teachers. This provides evidence for the feasibility of translating structured task information into differentiated scaffolding strategies. However, MKO 2.0 should be understood as an MKO-inspired, task-sensitive computational framework, rather than as an artificial replacement for a human More Knowledgeable Other. Traditional scaffolding depends on contingent support, fading, and transfer of responsibility in response to learner performance ( Van de Pol et al., 2010 ; Wood et al., 1976 ). The present framework operationalizes task characteristics, not learner states, and is therefore more appropriately characterized as metadata-conditioned or task-sensitive than learner-adaptive. A central contribution of the study is the reinterpretation of educational metadata as a resource for scaffold generation. Automatic question-generation research has primarily concentrated on producing and evaluating questions, while feedback generation has received comparatively less attention ( Kurdi et al., 2020 ). analysis.methods: This study employed a design-and-evaluation methodology to investigate whether structured task metadata can be operationalized as instructional signals for AI-generated scaffolding in narrative comprehension. The study conceptualized MKO 2.0 as an MKO-inspired computational framework rather than as a claim that an artificial intelligence system reproduces the interpersonal role of a human More Knowledgeable Other. The central design objective was to examine whether information about the reasoning demands of a comprehension question could systematically condition the form of support generated for that question. The study comprised two related components. (1) a deterministic rule-based scaffold generator was developed to operationalize three dimensions of question metadata: the primary narrative-comprehension attribute (attribute1), explicit versus implicit evidence requirements (ex_or_im), and local versus summary comprehension scope (local_or_sum). Each dimension contributed separately to scaffold construction, allowing the rule-based implementation to serve as a transparent realization of the proposed task-to-scaffold mapping. (2) the framework was extended to an LLM-based experiment in which a narrative-grounded generic LLM condition was compared with an MKO-conditioned LLM condition. Both conditions received the same narrative context and comprehension question, while the MKO-conditioned condition additionally received the structured task metadata. This paired design allowed the analysis to examine whether metadata conditioning altered scaffold realization beyond what was produced by a generic narrative-grounded LLM. The study therefore evaluates task-sensitive scaffold generation rather than learner-level adaptation. No learner profiles, interaction histories, performance states, or learning outcomes were modeled. Similarly, because the study did not involve learners or independent human raters, the evaluation does not establish pedagogical effectiveness. Instead, it examines the computational feasibility of metadata-conditioned scaffolding and observable characteristics of the generated outputs, including linguistic realization, narrative-evidence cues, task-sensitive inference language, and lexical overlap with reference answers. The study used The Quest Dataset , 1 a publicly available dataset developed for the Learning Agency Lab's Quest for Quality Questions initiative. The analytical file contained 6,989 question-answer pairs annotated with structured information about narrative-comprehension tasks. The dataset is related to the educational orientation of FairytaleQA, a narrative-comprehension resource developed from 278 children's stories and containing 10,580 expert-authored explicit and implicit questions across seven narrative-element or relation categories ( Xu et al., 2022 ). FairytaleQA was explicitly designed around fine-grained narrative-comprehension distinctions and supports both question-answering and educational question-generation research. The Quest data used in the present study contained the fields pair_id, source_title, cor_section, question, answer, local_or_sum, attribute1, attribute2, and ex_or_im. Three metadata dimensions were used directly in scaffold generation. The first, attribute1, identified the primary narrative-comprehension category: action, causal relationship, character, feeling, outcome resolution, prediction, or setting. The second, ex_or_im, distinguished questions whose answers were explicitly represented in the narrative from those requiring implicit inference. The third, local_or_sum, distinguished questions focused on a relatively localized portion of the narrative from summary questions requiring broader integration. These dimensions were treated as task descriptors rather than direct measurements of individual learner need. For example, a causal-relation label indicates that a question requires reasoning about relationships between events; it does not establish that a particular learner personally requires causal scaffolding. This distinction was maintained throughout the study to avoid conflating task-sensitive support with learner-adaptive instruction. Narrative context was obtained from the accompanying source_texts.csv file, which contained source_title, cor_section, and narrative text. Question records were linked to their corresponding narrative sections using source_title and cor_section. Because some questions referenced multiple sections, section identifiers were parsed separately and the corresponding text segments were retrieved in their listed order. Duplicate source-section keys were consolidated by concatenating the associated text fragments before construction of the retrieval lookup. This procedure resulted in successful narrative-context retrieval for all 6,989 question-answer instances (100%). The use of narrative text represented an important component of the LLM experiment. Rather than asking the language model to generate scaffolds from the question and metadata alone, both LLM conditions were supplied with the narrative evidence associated with each question. This made it possible to distinguish narrative-grounded generic hint generation from narrative-grounded, metadata-conditioned scaffold generation. Metadata labels are therefore operationalized as structured signals describing the demands of the task. The present framework operationalizes task characteristics, not learner states, and is therefore more appropriately characterized as metadata-conditioned or task-sensitive than learner-adaptive. A central contribution of the study is the reinterpretation of educational metadata as a resource for scaffold generation. Automatic question-generation research has primarily concentrated on producing and evaluating questions, while feedback generation has received comparatively less attention ( Kurdi et al., 2020 ). Across the same 140 questions and narrative contexts, MKO-conditioned scaffolds were longer than their generic counterparts in 82.14% of cases, with an average paired difference of 5.18 words ( W = 356.5, p < 0.001). Corpus-level MATTR was also somewhat higher for MKO-conditioned scaffolds (0.785) than for generic scaffolds (0.765), although the difference was modest and should not be interpreted as evidence of superior instructional quality. More substantively, narrative-evidence cues occurred in 40.0% of MKO-conditioned outputs compared with 10.0% of generic outputs ( p < 0.001). Among implicit questions, inference-oriented cues occurred in 36.1% of MKO-conditioned scaffolds but only 2.8% of generic scaffolds ( p = 0.002). These patterns are consistent with the intended function of metadata conditioning: evidence-status information was associated with observable differences in how guidance was linguistically realized. The more distinctive contribution of MKO conditioning in the present results concerns particular forms of guidance, especially explicit reference to narrative evidence and inference-oriented language for implicit questions, rather than contextual specificity in general. The answer-overlap analysis provides an additional qualification. Lexical overlap with reference answers was almost identical in the two LLM conditions (generic: M = 0.091; MKO-conditioned: M = 0.090), and MKO conditioning did not systematically reduce overlap. The finding therefore does not establish answer leakage, but it indicates that metadata conditioning alone cannot be assumed to reduce potentially answer-revealing language. The rule-based and LLM results illustrate complementary characteristics of the two approaches. The rule-based implementation offers transparency and deterministic control: each scaffold can be traced to an explicit combination of task descriptors. The LLM conditions provide greater generative variation and question-specific realization. This stage involved 240 senior high school students and 12 senior high school teachers who teach Economics. Data were collected using needs-analysis questionnaires and analyzed descriptively using means and standard deviations. The analysis examined students' perceived needs for learning activities that support critical thinking and creativity, as well as teachers' perceived needs for an appropriate instructional model. This study developed the AI-Assisted Inquiry Discovery Learning (AI-IDL) model in response to identified needs for learning experiences that support students' critical thinking and creativity. The model integrates constructivism as its theoretical foundation, Inquiry Learning and Discovery Learning as its pedagogical foundations, and artificial intelligence as a learning support. The model comprises six stages: Problem Orientation, Inquiry Questioning, Investigation and Exploration, Discovery and Idea Generation, Evidence-Based Solution, and Reflection and Communication. Expert validation yielded a mean Aiken's V coefficient of 0.924, indicating high content validity according to the criteria used in this study. Following implementation, the mean critical-thinking score increased from 62.1542 to 79.1625, with an N-Gain of 0.4690 and a standardized effect size of 2.99. The mean creativity score increased from 60.2042 to 75.3625, with an N-Gain of 0.3978 and a standardized effect size of 2.11. Both outcomes showed statistically significant pretest-posttest differences ((p < .001)). These findings indicate positive changes in students' measured critical thinking and creativity following participation in the AI-IDL learning process.

The development process was adapted from established R&D approaches, which emphasize systematic product development, validation, revision, and evaluation (Gustiani, 2019; Pugu et al., 2024; Purba, 2024) . The teacher respondents provided information about instructional needs and the challenges associated with supporting students' critical thinking and creativity. The student respondents provided information about their learning needs in relation to these competencies. The teacher subject area applies to the teacher respondents in the needs analysis and does not, by itself, define the subject in which the AI-IDL model was implemented. Data were collected using Likert-scale questionnaires designed to identify perceived learning needs related to critical thinking and creativity. The data were analyzed descriptively using frequencies, percentages, means, and standard deviations, as appropriate. Student responses were summarized across five critical-thinking-related indicators and four creativityrelated indicators, while teacher responses were summarized across 12 indicators. The results were used to inform the model's design and instructional support requirements. The AI-IDL model was designed by integrating constructivist learning principles, Inquiry Learning, Discovery Learning, and AI as a learning support. The model comprises six stages: Problem Orientation, Inquiry Questioning, Investigation and Exploration, Discovery and Idea Generation, Evidence-Based Solution, and Reflection and Communication. Each stage was designed to provide a connected sequence of student learning activities, with the teacher acting as a facilitator and scaffold provider. AI was incorporated to support the learning process through information provision, guiding questions, alternative perspectives, feedback, and prompts for further exploration. Students were expected to examine AI-generated information critically, verify relevant claims, consider alternative explanations, and formulate their own evidence-based conclusions. AI was not positioned as a substitute for students' reasoning or as the final authority for answers. This design was intended to preserve student agency and encourage the responsible use of AI throughout inquiry and discovery activities.

If the selection process is opaque, the synthesis becomes a personal anthology rather than an examination of evidence. This section describes exactly how the studies underlying this review were located, filtered, and organized, and it acknowledges the constraints that shaped those decisions. analysis.discussion: This review set out to examine what existing peer-reviewed research suggests about AI-assisted feedback in EFL writing, with particular attention to two outcomes that are often discussed separately but are in fact deeply intertwined: writing accuracy and learner autonomy. The evidence, considered as a whole, supports a nuanced picture rather than a simple verdict. On accuracy, the included literature is cautiously positive within clear boundaries. AIassisted feedback-whether from early automated systems or more recent large language models-appears to identify and help correct surface-level errors with a consistency that can complement teacher feedback, particularly in contexts where teacher workload limits the timeliness or detail of response. Students who receive such feedback typically produce cleaner drafts, at least in the short term. But the improvement is uneven. Teacher feedback may still outperform AI on certain accuracy measures, particularly for higherorder concerns like coherence and voice. AI tools struggle with context-dependent judgments, occasionally generate inaccurate explanations, and vary in reliability depending on how they are prompted. They are competent proofreaders and incomplete writing coaches. On autonomy, the picture is more ambivalent and more interesting. AI feedback can support self-regulated learning. It can reduce anxiety, increase engagement, and create opportunities for students to monitor their own output. Studies by Nguyen and Doan Thi Hue (2025), Yang, Hussin, and Hashim (2025), and Zhai (2025) have documented these positive effects. But they are not automatic. The same tool that scaffolds independent revision can also produce passive dependence when students accept every suggestion without evaluation. The difference lies not in the algorithm but in the pedagogy surrounding it. When AI feedback is embedded in tasks that require critical judgment-when students must explain, justify, and sometimes reject the advice they receive-autonomy tends to grow alongside accuracy. When the feedback flows directly into the final text without that mediating cognitive work, accuracy may rise on paper while the writer's underlying capacity stagnates. That interdependence is the central argument of this review. Accuracy without autonomy is fragile; it depends on the continued presence of the tool. Autonomy without accuracy is unfocused; it risks selfdirection without the linguistic resources to make that direction effective. The goal of EFL writing instruction should be to cultivate both together, through pedagogical designs that treat AI feedback as a resource to be engaged with critically rather than as an authority to be obeyed. The hybrid models described by Han and Li (2024) point toward what such designs might look like: AI and teacher working in complementary roles, with the algorithm handling scale and immediacy while the human maintains judgment, relationship, and the higher-order dimensions of writing that machines do not yet perceive. For practice, this means resisting the temptation to adopt AI feedback as a costsaving convenience or as a substitute for teacher attention. It means teaching students to evaluate AI suggestions explicitly, to recognize that the tool can be wrong, and to build personal protocols for revision. It means aligning assessment with process rather than product alone, so that the grade rewards the development of the writer, not just the polish of the text. And it means attending to the ethical dimensions that UNESCO (2023, 2024) has emphasized: protecting learner agency, ensuring equitable access, and maintaining human oversight in educational decisions that affect young people's relationship with language. For research, the agenda is clear. The field needs longitudinal studies that track writers across semesters, not weeks. It needs more work with lower-proficiency learners, who may be the population most affected by AI feedback but the least studied. It needs comparative analyses of different AI tools, integrated theoretical frameworks that connect accuracy and autonomy, and process-oriented methods that reveal what students actually think and do when they encounter algorithmic advice. Until that research is available, the most defensible stance is provisional: AI-assisted feedback is a powerful tool with significant potential and significant risks, and its value in any given classroom will depend less on the sophistication of the model than on the wisdom of the teacher who deploys it. The question is no longer whether AI will shape EFL writing instruction. It already has. The question is whether we can shape its use so that it serves the development of writers who are accurate in their language and autonomous in their learning-writers who can eventually put the tool aside not because they have outgrown the need for feedback, but because they have grown into the capacity to give it to themselves.
analysis.limitations: The most immediate problem is that AI feedback is not always correct. Large language models are trained to predict plausible text, not to verify truth, and that distinction matters when the text in question is a student's emerging English. Mizumoto, Eguchi, and Oyama (2024) documented this clearly: while ChatGPT aligned well with human raters on straightforward grammatical errors, its reliability dropped on nuanced cases-sentences that were technically non-standard but contextually appropriate, or errors that required understanding the student's intended meaning to judge correctly. An AI might smooth out a deliberate stylistic choice, flattening a voice that a human teacher would have recognized and preserved. It might miss an error entirely if the mistake happens to be statistically common in its training data, or it might generate an explanation for a correction that has no linguistic basis beyond the model's confidence in its own output. This last problem-often called hallucination-appears to be a structural feature of how these models operate rather than an incidental glitch. They generate text by predicting the most probable next token, which means they can construct fluent, authoritativesounding explanations for suggestions that are simply wrong. A student who receives such an explanation has no easy way to verify it unless they already possess the grammatical knowledge that the feedback was supposed to provide. For lower-proficiency EFL learners, who are precisely the population most likely to rely heavily on AI assistance, this creates a dangerous asymmetry: the tool sounds confident, the student is not, and the student's default response is to trust what sounds authoritative. The problem is compounded by inconsistency. Mizumoto and colleagues noted that ChatGPT's error coding could shift with slight rephrasing of the prompt or different sampling settings. For a teacher, that unpredictability is manageable because human judgment is itself variable and can be discussed. For an algorithm, the variation is invisible. The student cannot ask the model why it changed its mind; they can only accept the latest output as given. That opacity undermines one of the core principles of effective feedback identified by Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) : that students should receive information they can use to close the gap between current and desired performance. If the information fluctuates without explanation, it is hard to use systematically.

These patterns should not be interpreted as fixed learner categories or sequential developmental stages. Instead, they represent different ways in which learners interact with, interpret, and regulate their use of GenAI across writing contexts. The first pattern, passive AI reliance, describes learners who primarily used GenAI as an external correction tool. They submitted their texts, received AI-generated suggestions, and often accepted revisions with limited evaluation [ 7 , 34 , 36 ]. While this approach enabled efficient access to linguistic support, it also created risks of cognitive dependency. Cotton et al. proposed that passive GenAI use may foster cognitive dependence by replacing some thought processes. Learners may become less activity involoved in cognitive processing when they can readily rely on such feature-rich system [ 35 ]. This finding suggests that access to automated feedback alone does not necessarily promote meaningful revision when learners engage with it uncritically. The second pattern, adaptive AI engagement, reflects learners’ attempts to actively shape AI-assisted revision. After analysing the model essay, students were asked to write an essay on “Differences between the younger generation and their parents’ generation”, following the linguistic features. The original task instructions were provided in Chinese to ensure accurate understanding, with an English translation provided for international readers ( Fig 1 ). All 50 students completed their first drafts without AI assistance and then used GenAI to obtain feedback and revise their writing. They submitted their drafts by uploading or manually entering the text and could use commonly available GenAI tools, including Doubao, Kimi, and DeepSeek, according to their preferences. No specific platform or prompt template was prescribed, allowing variation in how students independently interacted with GenAI. This included prompt adjustment, questioning, and acceptance or rejection of AI suggestions. Although this reduced direct comparability across participants, such variation was analytically relevant to exploring different patterns of engagement. As part of the course assignment, students transcribed the AI-revised version and marked differences from their original drafts using coloured pens. This comparison activity was intended to make AI-related changes visible and encourage students to consider whether the revisions aligned with their intended meanings. The original drafts, annotated revised versions, and AI interaction records were subsequently collected. These materials were preliminarily reviewed and grouped into three broad patterns of AI engagement to guide purposive selection for follow-up interviews. This preliminary categorisation served as a sampling strategy rather than the final analytical framework. Students representing the different patterns were invited for interviews, which continued until no substantially new information emerged.

analysis.discussion: The thematic analysis identified three patterns of learner engagement with GenAI in EFL writing revision: passive AI reliance, adaptive AI engagement, and metacognitive AI engagement. These patterns should not be interpreted as fixed learner categories or sequential developmental stages. Instead, they represent different ways in which learners interact with, interpret, and regulate their use of GenAI across writing contexts. The first pattern, passive AI reliance, describes learners who primarily used GenAI as an external correction tool. They submitted their texts, received AI-generated suggestions, and often accepted revisions with limited evaluation [ 7 , 34 , 36 ]. While this approach enabled efficient access to linguistic support, it also created risks of cognitive dependency. Cotton et al. proposed that passive GenAI use may foster cognitive dependence by replacing some thought processes. Learners may become less activity involoved in cognitive processing when they can readily rely on such feature-rich system [ 35 ]. This finding suggests that access to automated feedback alone does not necessarily promote meaningful revision when learners engage with it uncritically. The second pattern, adaptive AI engagement, reflects learners’ attempts to actively shape AI-assisted revision. These learners modified prompts, requested alternative expressions, compared outputs, and selectively accepted suggestions according to their writing goals. This pattern aligns with studies showing that well-crafted prompts can facilitate writing and enable AI to support content, organisation, grammar, and vocabulary [ 8 , 12 , 43 ]. Similarly, AI-assisted tools can help EFL learners correct linguistic errors and improve textual coherence and structure [ 10 ]. However, learners’ evaluations often focused on linguistic features such as wording, tone, and expression rather than deeper concerns related to argumentation or textual organisation. Adaptive engagement therefore represents an emerging form of learner agency, although critical evaluation remains limited ( Fig 5 ). The third pattern, metacognitive AI engagement, represents learners who actively monitored and evaluated AI-generated feedback. These learners considered whether AI suggestions matched their intended meanings, communicative purposes, and personal writing styles. They were willing to reject suggestions and reflect on their writing processes. This aligns with research emphasising that students should be empowered to think critically, contribute to disciplinary knowledge, and engage authentically with writing [ 44 ]. From this perspective, writing is not merely task completion but a cognitive and creative process requiring critical judgement and disciplinary thinking, for which AI is not a substitute [ 13 ]. Importantly, metacognitive engagement did not result from AI itself but from learners’ active interpretation and regulation of AI use. This finding is consistent with Fabio et al., who found that passive use of such resources may amplify heuristic thinking and compromise critical reasoning. Critical evaluation is therefore essential when learners select information and make revision decisions [ 45 ]. Overall, these patterns reveal a central tension between learner agency and dependency in AI-assisted writing revision. This finding resonates with research suggesting that the characteristics of AI can enable learners to assume responsibility for writing and claim greater authorship, while also creating risks to personal agency as AI becomes increasingly capable of anticipating users’ decisions and preferences. Learners must therefore avoid allowing AI to become a proxy “sage on the stage” that limits their agency and emancipatory potential [ 46 ]. These findings highlight the importance of task design and pedagogical approaches when integrating GenAI into writing instruction [ 45 ]. The findings revealed several forms of reported metacognitive engagement during GenAI-assisted revision, including noticing, monitoring, strategic decision-making, and reflection. These processes are not interpreted as sequential stages of development, but as different forms of engagement reported by learners within a single revision task. This finding extends previous research that has primarily emphasised GenAI’s capacity to provide immediate feedback and facilitate textual revision [ 10 ]. Participants reported that AI feedback drew their attention to linguistic or stylistic problems they had previously overlooked. This finding supports Schmidt’s noticing perspective, which emphasises conscious awareness of linguistic gaps as important for language development [ 14 ] and is consistent with research showing that insufficient metacognitive monitoring can prevent L2 learners from recognising discrepancies in their own writing [ 2 ]. However, noticing did not necessarily lead to deeper engagement, as some learners responded reactively by accepting corrections without further evaluation. This distinction extends previous research by showing that AI-triggered noticing and metacognitive regulation should not be treated as equivalent processes. Metacognitive regulation was more evident when learners monitored AI feedback, compared alternative expressions, and selectively accepted, rejected, or modified suggestions. This finding is consistent with research linking effective revision to self-monitoring and strategic regulation [ 47 ]. It also supports studies showing that learners may negotiate between reliance and autonomy when interacting with GenAI [ 48 ]. The present findings suggest that the pedagogical significance of AI-triggered noticing depends partly on whether learners subsequently evaluate feedback and make intentional revision decisions. Learners also reported reflecting on AI suggestions in relation to meaning, tone, rhetorical appropriateness, and authorial intention. This finding echoes research emphasising critical judgement in advanced writing and meaningful engagement with automated feedback [ 44 , 49 ]. Importantly, participants’ accounts indicated that evaluation sometimes involved protecting their intended meanings and personal voice. Rather than treating AI-generated feedback as authoritative, these learners questioned, modified, or rejected suggestions according to their writing intentions. This supports previous research on iterative AI-assisted revision [ 25 ], while demonstrating that such benefits depend on learners retaining control over revision decisions. The findings also complicate claims that GenAI either promotes or undermines learner autonomy. Some learners reported increased confidence and motivation, whereas others recognised the risk of reduced cognitive effort. This tension is consistent with studies suggesting that AI can support learner agency while simultaneously encouraging dependency when used uncritically [ 26 , 50 ]. analysis.methods: We begin by exploring how users share their in-situ thoughts with an AI as they work. Much of this reasoning-interpreting information, comparing options, and forming tentative judgmentsemerges in the moment, but these fleeting cognitive moves are rarely captured or shared with the AI. In particular, prompting requires users to reformulate these thoughts as explicit instructions, which introduces friction and often filters out process-level reasoning. To explore this, we introduce snippet memoing, a lightweight interaction method that allows users to capture and share fragments of information on screen along with their associated thoughts in situ, directly into the LLM's context. We recruited 10 participants (5 male, 5 female; age M = 26, age SD = 1.87) with extensive daily LLM experience (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini), with four participants using them every day and six using them 2-5 times a week. Participants were recruited through online recruitment postings on our university community platform. The task was designed to elicit exploratory, multi-source sensemaking, where users interpret information, compare options, and iteratively refine their understanding, allowing in-situ thought capture to naturally arise. Participants explored potential labs and advisors to build a shortlist, and then drafted a cold email to one selected professor. To ensure ecological validity, we pre-screened participants who were actively considering applying to MS, Ph.D., or postdoctoral programs, confirming that the task would be personally relevant and motivating. Each session began with a 10-minute system tutorial, followed by a 30-minute task session in which participants used the system to complete the task while we observed their process, and concluded with a 20-minute post-survey and semi-structured interview. The survey included NASA-TLX and 7-point Likert-scale items on overall satisfaction, perceived context utilization, and burden of sharing the context. The interview explored how this form of interaction differed from conventional prompting, what types of thoughts participants captured and why, and what design opportunities or pain points they perceived. All sessions were screen-recorded and transcribed for later analysis. Participants were compensated KRW 20,000 (≈ USD 14) for their time, and the study was approved by our institutional IRB. While snippet memoing enabled richer and more user-framed context sharing, the study also surfaced a key limitation. As snippets accumulated, participants found it difficult to keep track of what they had captured and how it was reflected in the AI's understanding. This made it harder to revisit prior thoughts, see what had already been considered, and ensure that the AI remained aligned with what they actually found important (P2-P10). Importantly, participants did not simply express a need for better organization of snippets. Rather, they wanted the AI's context itself to reflect their thinking in a way that they could see and influence. At the same time, relying solely on users to manage accumulated context made it difficult to maintain alignment with the AI. Participants instead preferred system support while retaining control over how their context is represented (P6-P8). Based on these observations, we derive two key design implications for supporting the structuring and use of captured context in human-AI collaboration: DI1. Ground AI context in users' cognitive processes. Systems should incorporate users' in-situ thoughts as first-class inputs in forming AI context, so that the resulting context reflects what users consider important and how they interpret information. Rather than relying solely on system-inferred signals, this allows the AI's understanding to be directly shaped by the user's perspective. DI2. Make AI context inspectable and correctable by users. The AI's context should be externalized in a form that users can directly inspect and revise. This allows users to verify how their inputs are being interpreted, identify mismatches, and adjust the context when needed [35] . By keeping users in the loop, systems can maintain alignment with users' thinking while preserving their sense of authorship and control. We recruited 12 participants (5 female, 7 male; age 𝑀 = 26.0, 𝑆𝐷 = 3.28) through online recruitment postings on our university community platform. All participants had prior experience using LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) for exploratory or sensemaking tasks. Participants were compensated KRW 40,000 (≈ USD 28) for approximately two hours of their time. To ensure comparable levels of familiarity, motivation, and initial cognitive engagement across participants, we provided three categories of exploratory sensemaking tasks: career-related tasks (e.g., exploring PhD labs, searching for internships), academic and research-related tasks (e.g., surveying related work, organizing research directions), and everyday life tasks (e.g., trip planning, product comparison). In a pre-study survey, participants rated their familiarity with each category on a 5-point Likert scale and selected the two categories they felt most familiar with. To keep the two sessions comparable, we included only participants whose familiarity ratings for the two selected categories differed by at most one point, so that neither condition was paired with a substantially more familiar task. They then brought one real-world task from each selected category that they were genuinely motivated to pursue. Rather than assigning a fixed task, we adopted this open task design for ecological validity, so that participants worked on tasks of genuine personal relevance and brought their own criteria and prior knowledge to bear. Each session lasted approximately two hours. The session began with a 10-minute introduction, during which the study was explained, and participants provided informed consent. Participants then completed two task sessions (45 minutes each), separated by a short break. In each session, participants first completed a 10-minute system walkthrough with a warm-up task to familiarize themselves with the interface, conducted the task work under the assigned condition for 30 minutes, and responded to a 5-minute post-condition survey. The session concluded with a 15-minute semi-structured interview to explore participants' subjective experiences across both conditions.

analysis.discussion: Building on our findings, we discuss (1) how systems can capture user context while minimizing user burden, (2) how such context can be represented in forms that are understandable by both users and AI, and (3) how such an approach can extend beyond single sessions to support sustainable context use over time. Our findings reveal a tension between comprehensive context capture and selective control. Passive observation contributed to a richer context by capturing information users might otherwise miss, but also introduced noise and an additional curation burden, particularly in multitasking scenarios. At the same time, relying solely on user-driven externalization places a burden on the user. Balancing these two modalities is therefore an important design challenge. One promising approach to navigating this balance is to let the system learn from users' behavior. By leveraging snippet memoing patterns-what and where users choose to capture, and the thoughts they attach as memos-alongside patterns of context items actively referenced in chat, the system can infer which types of information tend to matter to an individual user. This inference could then drive proactive surfacing of relevant signals from observed behavior, such as highlighting passages on pages similar to previously snippeted content or flagging new information related to concepts the user frequently referenced in their memos. However, as agents take a more active role in shaping and surfacing such context, there is a risk that AI-generated organizations may inadvertently steer how users understand and pursue their tasks. Ensuring that such support remains transparent and correctable by the user will be an important consideration for future work. In human teamwork, effective collaboration depends on building and maintaining a shared mental model of the task, including each other's goals, priorities, and evolving understanding [4, 25] . Our findings suggest a similar need in human-AI collaboration: making task context shared and inspectable improved users' sense of authorship, control, and perceived AI understanding of the task. Yet this raises an important open question: what should such a shared representation actually look like? Humans benefit from spatial, visual organization that supports reflection and navigation [5, 34] . AI agents, by contrast, may need more structured textual representations that can be incorporated into model inputs, such as llms.txt [12] , which encodes complex content in LLM-readable format. This suggests the need for a translation layer between human-facing and AI-facing representations of context. Contexty takes an initial step in this direction by externalizing the AI's context on a canvas that users can inspect and revise. The canvas presents context in an intuitive, spatial form, while grounding it in the underlying hierarchical memory structure used by the AI. In this way, the canvas functions as a translation layer that makes AI context accessible to users, while also allowing users' cognitive processes to be incorporated. This approach is facilitated by the form of AI context used in our system, which organizes LLM memories into a hierarchical structure inspired by recent LLM memory work [40, 46] . However, as AI context representations evolve, they may not always align with formats that are easily interpretable or editable by users. Future work should therefore explore how such translation layers can generalize beyond specific representations, and how to maintain alignment between humanmeaningful context and model-effective representations as both continue to evolve. The synergy between in-situ snippet capturing and canvas-based organization also points to a broader design opportunity of embedding cognitive trail into everyday work environments. Recent AIpowered browsers have begun to integrate AI into users' ongoing knowledge work, supporting activities such as information gathering and assistance within the browsing experience [6, 14, 28, 30] . Our findings suggest that these systems could benefit from making users' cognitive processes explicit and inspectable. Rather than leaving them implicitly inferred by AI or transient, a canvas-like layer could make users' cognitive trail visible and continuously usable within their primary work environment. Finally, the notion of user-inspectable and correctable AI context, grounded in users' cognitive traces, carries important implications beyond single-session interactions. As this context accumulates over time, it calls for more systematic approaches to managing and reusing memory. This includes distinguishing between short-term and long-term context [10, 39] , organizing information at the task or project level, and supporting selective reuse of relevant past context across sessions. This opens up opportunities for more sustainable interaction, where past cognitive traces can be maintained, refined, and brought forward when needed. To support this, future work should explore mechanisms for filtering and prioritizing accumulated context, helping users decide what to retain, revisit, or discard over time. This includes developing representations and interaction techniques that allow users to selectively surface relevant past context without being overwhelmed, while preserving their ability to inspect and correct how it is used by the AI. We presented Contexty, a system that incorporates users' in-situ thoughts into AI context and makes it visible and editable in a shared space for human-AI collaboration. Our evaluation showed that Contexty improves users' task awareness, sense of authorship, control, and perceived AI understanding. Our work highlights the importance of moving beyond implicitly inferred, system-managed context toward user-inspectable and correctable AI context that incorporates users' cognitive processes. We hope this work motivates future systems that support more transparent and collaborative ways of constructing context, keeping humans and AI aligned in complex tasks.

All thirty eligible postgraduate residents pursuing MD Pediatrics (ten each from Junior Resident Year 1, Year 2, and Year 3) were enrolled by complete enumeration of the departmental cohort, after written informed consent. Residents with prior formal SCT experience within the preceding three months and those unwilling to provide consent were excluded. Institutional Ethics Committee approval was obtained from NKP Salve institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre prior to commencement. All case material used for AI interaction was anonymized before entry into any AI platform, and no patient identifiers were disclosed at any stage, consistent with contemporary guidance on the ethical governance of AI in health professions Four complementary instruments were used. (i) The Script Concordance Test, comprising pediatric clinical scenarios developed and validated by a panel of five senior pediatric faculty and scored by the aggregate expert-scoring method, served as the primary outcome measure of reasoning under uncertainty. (ii) A 30-point SNAPPS analytical rubric assessed the quality of case presentation across all six SNAPPS domains. (iii) A 20-item MCQ test assessed factual and applied knowledge. (iv) Five-point Likert-scale perception questionnaires captured resident confidence, satisfaction and perceived learning benefit, and a parallel faculty perception survey captured educator-rated presentation quality, depth of analysis, and satisfaction. A Faculty AI-Use Monitoring Checklist was additionally completed at every AI-assisted session to confirm that independent reasoning preceded AI consultation, that AI was used only as a learning aid, that no patient identifiers were entered, that AI output was critically appraised, and that the final reasoning was faculty-validated. Data were collected at three sequential time points. In the traditional-SNAPPS phase (T1), residents presented pediatric cases using the unmodified SNAPPS framework under faculty supervision, after which the SCT, SNAPPS rubric, and MCQ were re-administered.
