analysis.discussion: This prospective, within-subject educational interventional study demonstrates that embedding AI as a faculty-supervised cognitive scaffold within the SNAPPS framework produces significantly greater improvement in clinical reasoning, structured case presentation, and knowledge acquisition than traditional SNAPPS teaching alone, and is met with high satisfaction among both postgraduate residents and faculty. These findings extend a small but growing body of evidence on responsible AI integration in postgraduate medical education and address a specific gap identified in recent scoping reviews  the near-absence of outcome-level evidence combining AI exposure with an established clinical-reasoning framework in pediatric postgraduate training Clinical reasoning is widely regarded as the cornerstone of safe medical practice. Charlin and colleagues conceptualize reasoning as the dynamic organization and application of illness scripts under conditions of uncertainty, and proposed the Script Concordance Test specifically to capture this process rather than simple factual recall [21,22]. The significant improvement in SCT scores observed after AI-assisted SNAPPS in the present study suggests that AI- generated prompts encouraged deeper analytical engagement  requiring residents to justify differential diagnoses, weigh contradictory evidence, and reconsider management options  rather than passive acceptance of AI output. This interpretation is consistent with reports that structured, question-driven interaction with AI tools promotes higher-order reasoning more effectively than simple information retrieval [9,13]. It is also consistent with the well- established observation that clinical reasoning is highly context- and case- specific rather than a single generic skill transferable in the abstract, so that repeated, case-anchored practice  of the kind provided across sequential SNAPPS cases in this study  is more likely to yield durable gains than reasoning taught in isolation from real clinical content [28,29]. The improvement in SNAPPS rubric scores reinforces the educational value of learner-centred structured teaching. Wolpaw and colleagues, who originally described SNAPPS, reported that the framework enhances learner autonomy and stimulates active discussion between residents and preceptors [6]. The present findings extend this observation by showing that AI can enrich each SNAPPS step through structured cognitive prompting, yielding better case summaries, broader differential diagnoses, stronger analytical justification, more incisive probing questions, and more deliberate self-directed learning goals. The largest gains were observed in the probing-questions and self- directed-learning domains, both of which depend on the learner’s ability to generate novel higher-order questions rather than reproduce previously acquired information  precisely the domains in which a well-supervised AI scaffold, by modelling alternative questions and unexplored angles, might be expected to exert its greatest educational leverage. A particularly notable finding was the strong positive correlation between SCT and SNAPPS rubric scores (r=0.72, p<0.001), indicating that residents who presented cases in a more structured manner also demonstrated superior This association supports the construct validity of SNAPPS as a proxy for underlying reasoning ability and is consistent with prior work linking structured clinical discussion to reasoning competence [22,23]. It also implies that interventions which strengthen structured presentation  as AI-assisted SNAPPS did in this study  are likely to yield genuine gains in reasoning rather than superficial improvements in communication style alone. Knowledge acquisition, measured by the MCQ test, improved significantly more in the AI-assisted phase than in the traditional phase. AI is sometimes criticized for potentially reducing independent thinking by supplying ready answers; the present findings, obtained under a protocol of mandatory independent reasoning before AI consultation and mandatory faculty validation afterward, suggest the opposite outcome when such safeguards are enforced. AI appeared to function primarily as a facilitator that organized concepts, clarified pathophysiological mechanisms, and prompted evidence-based review, rather than as a substitute for learner effort. This pattern aligns with Vygotsky’s concept of scaffolded learning, in which guided support enables performance beyond a learner’s unaided capability while progressively building toward independent mastery [11], and with cognitive load theory, which holds that well-structured external support reduces extraneous cognitive load and frees working memory for schema construction and illness-script formation [24]. Both resident and faculty perception data were strongly favourable, corroborating findings from recent reviews that AI-based educational tools enhance learner engagement, motivation, and personalized learning experience [16,17]. Faculty specifically noted more organized reasoning, clearer justification of differential diagnoses, and greater participation during discussions  observations that are consistent with the broader literature describing AI’s potential to augment, rather than replace, experiential and mentorship-based teaching [23]. Importantly, faculty in this study uniformly emphasized that AI should complement, not substitute, traditional teaching; the mandatory faculty-validation step built into the protocol appears to have been central to translating AI assistance into genuine educational benefit while minimizing the risk of uncritical acceptance of hallucinated or inaccurate The present findings are also directly relevant to the aims of competency-based medical education, which prioritizes milestones in reasoning, communication, and lifelong learning over factual knowledge in isolation [1,2]. By promoting metacognitive reflection, hypothesis generation, evidence appraisal, and self- directed learning, AI-assisted SNAPPS aligns closely with CBME principles and offers a practical, scalable strategy for embedding responsible digital innovation within existing postgraduate curricula, without requiring additional faculty time beyond validation of AI-generated content [3]. Such scaffolded, deliberate- practice-oriented exposure is consistent with broader educational theory linking repeated, feedback-rich practice to the development of expertise, and echoes the wider simulation- and technology-enhanced learning literature, in which structured, low-stakes rehearsal with timely feedback  whether through simulation, virtual patients, or, as here, an AI-supported scaffold  has consistently been shown to accelerate skill acquisition [25,26,27,30]. analysis.limitations: Several limitations must be acknowledged, and addressing them helps to delineate the boundaries within which these findings should be interpreted. First, the study was conducted at a single institution with a modest sample of thirty residents, which limits statistical power for subgroup analyses (for example, by postgraduate year) and constrains generalizability to other training environments; multicentric replication is needed. Second, the within-subject, sequential design  while efficient and ethically appropriate for a promising teaching innovation  cannot fully exclude an order or practice effect, whereby residents’ performance in the AI-assisted phase may have been partly attributable to the immediately preceding traditional-SNAPPS phase rather than to AI exposure alone; future studies should consider counterbalanced or randomized sequencing across cohorts to isolate this effect. Third, the intervention period was relatively short, and long-term retention of clinical- reasoning gains beyond the study period was not assessed; longitudinal follow- up incorporating delayed SCT administration would clarify durability. Fourth, large language models evolve rapidly, and the specific prompt protocol and AI platform used here may not generalize to future model versions without re- validation. Finally, faculty enthusiasm for a novel, well-supported intervention may have introduced a degree of positive-outcome bias in perception measures, which future studies could mitigate through blinded external assessment of Notwithstanding these limitations, the study has notable strengths. The use of a prospective, within-subject design allowed each resident to serve as their own control, reducing inter-individual variability that would otherwise complicate small-cohort comparisons. Multiple validated instruments  the Script Concordance Test, SNAPPS rubric, MCQ assessment, and structured perception surveys  provided convergent evidence across cognitive, behavioural and affective domains, and the significant positive correlation between SCT and SNAPPS scores strengthens confidence that the observed gains reflect genuine improvement in reasoning rather than assessment artefact. Mandatory faculty validation and a documented AI-use monitoring checklist embedded ethical safeguards directly into the educational protocol rather than treating them as an afterthought, offering a template that other departments could adopt with Taken together, these findings suggest several practical implications for departments considering similar innovations. First, the incremental faculty burden was limited chiefly to validation rather than content generation, suggesting that AI-assisted SNAPPS could be implemented without materially increasing teaching workload once a standardized prompt protocol and monitoring checklist are in place. Second, the magnitude of improvement in the probing-questions and self-directed-learning domains suggests that AI scaffolds may be particularly useful for developing precisely those higher-order skills that postgraduate curricula struggle most to teach explicitly. Third, because the intervention relies on freely or widely available conversational AI platforms rather than bespoke educational software, the model is potentially scalable to resource-limited postgraduate programmes without significant additional infrastructure investment, provided that institutions establish clear data- protection and validation safeguards beforehand. Future multicentric studies with randomized or counterbalanced sequencing, larger sample sizes, blinded outcome assessment, and longer follow-up  including delayed post-testing to evaluate durability of reasoning gains and, ultimately, correlation with clinical performance and patient outcomes  are needed to consolidate this preliminary evidence into a generalizable recommendation for postgraduate pediatric

Under editorial curation, what became visible depended, imperfectly, on judgements about importance. Under algorithmic curation, it depends on a prediction of whether a particular user will respond. The two can diverge sharply. Matters that are important but slow, complex or local generate weak engagement signals and sink; matters that provoke anger or identity-based reactions rise (Brady et al., 2023; Milli et al., 2025) . Jungherr and Schroeder (2023) warn that data-driven curation can push challenges to the status quo out of sight, because a new issue has no engagement history to learn from. South African youth on TikTok frame local events in terms of global causes that the algorithm already recognises, which gains reach but can thin out local meaning (Schoon & Bosch, 2024) . Deliberation: from shared forums to parallel monologues. Deliberation requires that claims meet objections. Personalised curation sorts audiences so that most claims reach people who already agree with them. González-Bailón et al. (2023) show that segregation increases at each step from what is available to what is seen and what is engaged with. Where curation does bring opposing sides into contact, it tends to select the most hostile material. Milli et al. (2025) found that engagement-based ranking amplified out-group hostility relative to a chronological feed, and Piccardi et al. (2025) showed that changing exposure to partisan animosity changes how people feel about the other side. The result is not the absence of cross-cutting contact but contact of the wrong kind: encounters chosen for their capacity to provoke rather than to inform. The modest effects of feed changes on attitudes found by Guess et al. (2023) are consistent with this reading. Curation may change less what people believe than how, and with whom, they argue. Opinion formation: from aggregation to algorithmic cascades. Public opinion was never a simple sum of private views, but in a mass-media public, people formed impressions of what others thought from a shared and relatively stable set of sources. Under algorithmic curation, those impressions come from feeds saturated with prestigious, in-group, moral and emotional content (Brady et al., 2023) . This distorts perceived norms: people may overestimate how extreme or angry others are. Cascades, in which visible engagement attracts further engagement, then shape which positions appear popular. Because algorithms mostly amplify existing social drivers rather than invent them (Metzler & Garcia, 2024) , the opinion that forms is neither purely algorithmic nor purely social; it is the product of a feedback loop between the two. From the framework, six propositions follow. Proposition 1: Platform-mediated publics perform the visibility function only to the extent that ranking incorporates signals of public relevance that are independent of predicted engagement. The inversion problem (Kleinberg et al., 2024) and the gap between engagement and stated preference (Milli et al., 2025; Rathje et al., 2024) imply that engagement alone will systematically under-expose matters of common concern that are slow, complex or local. The proposition would be weakened by evidence that engagement-ranked feeds surface such matters as reliably as editorially curated or preference-based feeds. Proposition 2: Algorithmic curation degrades deliberation less by isolating citizens than by structuring their encounters across lines around hostility. Segregation is high (González-Bailón et al., 2023) , but the sharper deliberative problem is that the cross-cutting content people do see is selected for out-group animosity (Milli et al., 2025; Piccardi et al., 2025) . The proposition would be weakened by evidence that the cross-cutting content in engagement-ranked feeds is no more hostile than that in chronological or randomly ordered feeds. Proposition 3: Under algorithmic curation, public opinion is shaped more by distorted perceptions of what others think than by changes in individual attitudes. Feed interventions show limited effects on attitudes (Guess et al., 2023) , while algorithmic oversaturation of moral and emotional content distorts perceived norms (Brady et al., 2023) . The proposition would be weakened by evidence that people's estimates of others' views are no less accurate among heavy users of algorithmic feeds than among others.
analysis.discussion: The framework clarifies a debate that often talks past itself. One side, represented by Habermas's diagnosis as Lafont (2023) presents it, sees filter bubbles and echo chambers isolating citizens. The other side points to experimental evidence that feed changes have small effects on attitudes and polarisation (Guess et al., 2023; Metzler & Garcia, 2024) . Distinguishing three functions shows that both can be partly right. Curation may leave individual attitudes largely stable while still reshaping what becomes visible, how encounters across lines unfold, and what people believe others think. The harm lies less in changed minds than in a changed structure of public communication. The framework also refines the post-Habermasian position. Bruns (2023) is right that the public sphere has become a network of publics, but networks have architects. In platform-mediated societies, the links between publics, the paths along which issues travel from a spherule to national attention, are set by ranking systems optimised for engagement. Jungherr and Schroeder's (2023) point about strengthened intermediaries follows: the question is no longer only whether many publics exist but who controls the connections between them and on what criteria. Implications for governance. Most current evaluation of platforms relies on user-satisfaction and engagement metrics, which measure whether individuals respond, not whether publics function. The paper therefore proposes evaluating platform governance against public-sphere criteria, set out in Table 2. For visibility, the criterion is whether matters of common concern, including local and minority issues, reach collective attention. For deliberation, it is whether encounters across lines are informative rather than merely hostile. For opinion formation, it is whether people's perceptions of others' views are accurate. For voice, it is whether reach is distributed fairly and demotion is disclosed. These criteria are compatible with the epistemicwelfare approach of Hyzen et al. (2026) and the constructive-optimisation right proposed by Naudts et al. (2025), but they translate those normative ideas into indicators that auditors and regulators can measure. African digital publics. Three features of African digital publics sharpen the framework. First, dependence on foreign platforms means that ranking decisions affecting African visibility are made without African input, and engagement signals are dominated by global audiences, which is why local activists frame issues in global terms (Schoon & Bosch, 2024) . Second, much political communication has moved into closed messaging groups (Fisher et al., 2024; Gondwe, 2025) , where curation is social rather than algorithmic but where platform design still shapes forwarding and group size. Third, states may respond to platform power with restrictive measures that marginalise critics rather than protect publicness (Owens-Ibie et al., 2026) . Nigeria's protest movements show that digital publics can still perform public-sphere functions under these conditions (Bamidele, 2026; Uwalaka, 2023) , but they do so in spite of the architecture rather than because of it. The governance task in Africa is therefore twofold: to secure public-sphere obligations from platforms, and to prevent regulation from becoming a tool of control. Counterarguments. One objection is that editorial gatekeeping was itself exclusionary and that algorithms have opened visibility to voices that editors ignored. The framework accepts this; #EndSARS and South African TikTok activism are examples. Its claim is that algorithmic visibility, although more open at the entry point, is allocated by a criterion that is indifferent to public relevance and that compounds inequalities of reach. A second objection is that public-sphere criteria are too vague to operationalise. Table 2 responds by pairing each criterion with indicators that can be measured through audits and surveys. Algorithmic curation has replaced much of the gatekeeping on which public-sphere theory was built. This paper has argued that it transforms all three public-sphere functions. Visibility follows predicted engagement rather than public relevance. Deliberation gives way to sorted audiences and hostile encounters, and opinion forms through cascades and distorted perceptions of others' views. Platform-mediated publics can still perform these functions, but only when ranking incorporates signals of public relevance, when reach is fairly distributed and demotion disclosed, and when governance is judged by public-sphere criteria rather than by engagement. Transparency and user control help individuals but cannot by themselves restore functions that belong to publics. Several recommendations follow. Regulators should require large platforms to report public-sphere indicators, including the reach of civic and local news, the hostility of cross-cutting exposure and the distribution of political reach, and should grant independent researchers the data access needed to audit them. Platforms should offer and test ranking options optimised for stated preferences and public relevance, disclose demotion to affected users, and invest in moderation and ranking expertise for African languages and contexts. African governments and regional bodies, including the African Union, should develop shared regulatory approaches that strengthen their leverage over foreign platforms while protecting freedom of expression, so that regulation serves publicness rather than control. Civil society, journalists and universities should build independent audit capacity in Africa, drawing on reranking methods that do not require platform cooperation. Researchers should study ranking in African settings directly and measure perceived-norm accuracy alongside attitudes.

abstract_text: Problem-Based Learning remains one of higher education’s most significant pedagogical contributions. Its core premise (that students learn more effectively, particularly for the application, transfer, and retention of knowledge, when actively engaging with problems than passively receiving information) is as valid as ever. analysis.methods: The study proposes a designbased research approach because Teacher Mode is an instructional innovation to be designed, implemented, evaluated, and refined in authentic classrooms. DBR links practical problems with iterative design and evidence from implementation. The protocol is prospective: the sample, measures, and outcomes below describe a plan, not completed research findings. Participants would comprise approximately 120-240 secondary or post-secondary students across mathematics, history, civics, and geography, subject to institutional access, consent, and feasibility. Within each subject, one class could use the structured framework and a comparison class could receive usual instruction or unstructured ChatGPT access. Because intact classes may differ at baseline, analyses should account for prior achievement and report group allocation and attrition transparently. The intervention spans eight weeks. Week 1 introduces the framework, responsible-use rules, and discipline-specific instructions. Weeks 2-6 embed guided AI activities in regular coursework. Weeks 7-8 use capstone tasks to assess whether students can apply reasoning practices to integrated or unfamiliar problems. Teachers document deviations and refine prompts between cycles, while keeping core design principles stable enough for comparison. Activities reflect disciplinary practice. In civics, students explain a constitutional principle before receiving feedback and then revise terminology or application. In geography, they interpret maps or graphs before proposing causal explanations. Mathematics tasks require a proposed solution and justification of steps; history tasks require claims supported by primary or secondary evidence. These examples are adaptable templates, not identical interventions across subjects. Capstone work asks students to use AI as a guide rather than an author. History students may develop a comparative argument and use feedback to examine evidence; mathematics students may solve multi-step problems and explain each transformation. An AIfree task or oral explanation can help determine whether learning transfers beyond assisted practice. Data collection aligns with the four research questions. Pre-and posttests assess learning; essays and problem solutions are scored with subject-specific rubrics; weekly journals document attempts and revisions; sampled AI feedback is rated for quality; and surveys/interviews examine trust and perceived usefulness. Instruments should be piloted, and raters trained using shared scoring guidance. Feedback quality is rated on four dimensions: specificity (identifies the issue), accuracy (is factually and conceptually sound), actionability (offers a feasible next step), and alignment (matches learning objectives and rubrics). Independent raters should score a subset of responses, with inter-rater agreement reported. AI feedback should not be presumed equivalent to teacher feedback before comparison. Quantitative analysis may use ANCOVA or an appropriate alternative to compare post-test scores while accounting for baseline performance, alongside effect sizes and confidence intervals. Assumptions and class-level clustering should be considered; where sample size or design does not support ANCOVA, the analysis plan should be adjusted transparently. Qualitative reflections and interviews can be coded thematically, with coding procedures and discrepant cases documented. Integration of both strands can explain not only whether outcomes differ but how students use feedback. Ethical procedures include informed consent, guardian consent where required, de-identification of transcripts, restricted access, data minimization, and clear retention and deletion rules. Personal or sensitive information should not be entered into AI systems. AI use supplements rather than replaces instruction and assessment; teachers retain responsibility for evaluating work and addressing errors. The protocol requires institutional review where applicable. Several design principles follow from the framework. First, cognitive responsibility should remain with the learner: AI should ask for an initial attempt and make the reasoning visible before offering support. Second, support should be graduated. A diagnostic question or small hint is preferable to a complete solution when the learning objective is to practice problem-solving. Direct explanation may still be appropriate when the teacher determines that a learner needs explicit instruction, but the choice should be intentional and aligned with the objective. Verification should be taught as a routine rather than appended as a warning. Learners should compare factual claims with authoritative sources, check calculations independently, and explain why they accept or reject a suggestion. In history, this may involve checking a quotation against a primary document; in geography, comparing an interpretation with the map legend and data; and in mathematics, substituting a result into the original equation. The evidence of learning is not simply that students receive feedback, but that they evaluate it and make defensible decisions. The framework should preserve teacher judgment and learner agency. The AI is not the final authority on subject content, grading, or student support needs. Teachers select tasks, validate materials, decide when to intervene, and interpret evidence in context. Students should be allowed to challenge a response and explain why they reject it. Such disagreement can itself become an instructional opportunity, particularly when the AI produces an incomplete or incorrect response. Assessment should separate supported practice from independent demonstration. AI-assisted tasks can reveal how learners use feedback and revise their work, whereas AI-free tasks can indicate what they can do without immediate assistance. Neither alone provides a complete picture. A balanced assessment plan uses both and explains their distinct purposes, avoiding the assumption that polished AI-supported work is equivalent to independent competence.

The framework emphasizes student attempts before assistance, verification, revision, proportionate documentation, and AI-free assessment. Because the paper presents anticipated outcomes rather than completed empirical findings, future studies must test effectiveness, implementation conditions, and longterm transfer before strong claims about impact can be made.
analysis.limitations: Teacher Mode does not remove the limitations of generative AI. Its value depends on verification, teacher oversight, equitable access, and alignment with the task. An AI system may misstate historical facts, misread data, or provide flawed explanations while sounding confident. Students should verify factual claims against textbooks, primary sources, peer-reviewed research, or authoritative datasets. Instructions to cite sources can help but do not guarantee that sources or citations are genuine (Darvishi, 2024) . Over-reliance may weaken independent problem-solving if students request hints for every step. The design therefore combines AI-supported practice with AI-free assessments, oral explanations, and tasks requiring transfer. Teachers should gradually reduce scaffolding and evaluate whether students can apply skills independently. Institutions can provide supervised access, accessible alternatives, and equivalent low-tech tasks. Participation and access barriers should be documented so that observed differences are not mistakenly attributed to the instructional design alone. Students and teachers may disagree about what constitutes legitimate assistance. Explicit green/yellow/red categories, examples modeled in class, and consistent course-level communication can reduce ambiguity. Policies should distinguish acceptable support from undisclosed substitution and provide a fair process for resolving concerns. AI may also constrain creativity or lack disciplinary nuance, especially in open-ended writing, arts, or advanced scientific inquiry. It should support foundational reasoning and revision while teachers and peers retain central roles in interpretation, creative judgment, and collaborative discussion. Inconsistent implementation can undermine comparability and trust. Teachers should share core instructions, document adaptations, and use common rubrics where appropriate. The framework also has methodological limits: proposed participants and duration may not capture long-term learning, and results may vary across institutions, age groups, languages, and access conditions. For WTC with GAI (RQ2), learners receiving prompt instruction reported higher overall WTC than those in the SD condition across measurement points, although the two groups again demonstrated similar developmental trajectories. The qualitative findings from RQ3 are explicitly integrated into Sections 5.1 and 5.2 to explain and interpret the quantitative patterns identified in RQ1 and RQ2. Section 5.3 addresses the pedagogical implications arising from the findings. 5.1 WTC with peers across prompt-instruction and self-directed conditions Importantly, both the PI and SD groups demonstrated significant increases in WTC with peers over time. Qualitative findings suggest that two complementary processes may have contributed to this development within the human–GAI–human learning cycle. First, GAI-supported https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344026100585 Published online by Cambridge University Press preparation provided linguistic scaffolding that helped learners develop ideas, rehearse language, and refine their expressions before entering peer discussions. Across both groups, learners reported greater readiness and clearer expression after preparing with GAI. This finding is consistent with Wu et al. (2025) and Zou et al. (2026), who suggest that GAI-supported preparation may increase learners’ readiness to participate in subsequent peer discussions. Such positive GAI-mediated experiences may also further foster emotional engagement, confidence, and motivation (Wang & Zou, 2026; Xin & Derakhshan, 2025), potentially creating more favorable conditions for subsequent peer communication. From a WTC perspective, these findings suggest that GAI functioned not only as a practice resource but also as a potential mediator of the cognitive and affective conditions underlying subsequent communication (Layer V). Importantly, these forms of support were also available to SD learners, who engaged in repeated cycles of GAI-supported preparation and received teacher feedback on their use of GAI. Second, peer discussion itself provided opportunities for authentic interaction, collaborative meaning-making, and negotiation of perspectives – processes that have been associated with increased WTC in previous SLA research (e.g., Tai & Chen, 2024). The combination of GAI- supported preparation and subsequent peer interaction may therefore help explain why both instructional groups demonstrated similar developmental trajectories in peer-related WTC. While previous studies have primarily examined learners’ WTC with GAI or compared WTC across GAI and human interlocutors (e.g., Zhang, 2026; Zheng et al., 2026), the present findings suggest a possible transfer process whereby communicative resources and confidence developed during GAI-supported preparation may carry over into subsequent human interaction. This possibility extends previous research, which has documented reduced anxiety and improved performance in GAI-supported learning environments (e.g., Peng & Liang, 2026; Zheng et al., 2026) but has paid less attention to whether such benefits extend to subsequent peer 5.2 WTC with GAI across prompt-instruction and self-directed conditions Within a classroom context in which both the PI and SD groups received GAI-supported preparation, both groups demonstrated similar developmental trajectories across the three measurement points. Qualitative findings help explain this pattern. Learners in both groups valued GAI’s linguistic support, immediate feedback, and psychologically safe and readily accessible communication environment, consistent with previous research on GAI-mediated communication (e.g., Tai & Chen, 2024; Zhang, 2026). Participants also reported that corrective feedback encouraged them to rehearse and refine their language repeatedly. Previous studies have similarly found that interaction with GAI chatbots can reduce communication anxiety and support learners’ confidence in L2 communication (e.g., Mei, 2026; Zhang, 2026; Zheng et al., 2026). While most applications of the WTC model have focused on human–human interaction (Peng & Liang, 2026), the present findings suggest that GAI affordances may activate multiple antecedents of WTC in human–GAI–human communication. At the situational level (Layer III), GAI may increase the perceived accessibility of the interlocutor and reduce affective barriers to communication. Repeated opportunities to rehearse language and receive feedback may further support perceived communicative competence (Layer V) and self-confidence (Layer IV), while fostering positive motivational dispositions toward communication (Layer IV). Because the study was conducted in an authentic classroom context, learners in both conditions received teacher feedback on their use of GAI rather than being left without pedagogical support when engaging with a relatively new technology. Thus, the comparison concerned two modes of supported GAI engagement – prompt-instructed and self-directed use – rather than GAI-supported and non-GAI learning. The shared GAI support may therefore have contributed to the similar trajectories https://doi.org/10.1017/S0958344026100585 Published online by Cambridge University Press The qualitative findings nevertheless revealed a distinction in how learners in the two conditions engaged with GAI. PI learners more frequently reported requesting sentence patterns, alternative viewpoints, and structured feedback, suggesting a more purposeful and strategic use of GAI resources. These practices may have enabled learners to derive greater communicative value from GAI and may help explain why the PI group reported higher overall WTC with GAI. In this sense, the more strategic prompt practices reported by PI learners suggest that prompt instruction may support the development of prompt literacy and function as a pedagogical bridge between GAI affordances and learners’ WTC by helping them access and mobilize these affordances more strategically (Zou et al., 2026). These practices may therefore represent emerging GAI-literacy practices that support communicative preparation. This interpretation should be regarded as suggestive rather than as evidence of a direct GAI-literacy effect, as GAI literacy was not directly measured. analysis.methods: This study adopts a qualitative interpretive case study design (Tisdell, Merriam, & Stuckey-Peyrot, 2025; Yin, 2009) to explore how pre-service teachers perceived engagement with GenAI tools as supporting transversal competences and AI literacy. The interpretive paradigm underpinning this study assumes that knowledge is socially and contextually constructed, and that participants' voices are central to understanding pedagogical transformation (Denzin & Lincoln, 2018) . This study was conducted at a public HE institution in Portugal within an Early and Primary Education teacher-training program. A total of 78 pre-service teachers participated in the pedagogical intervention. The students were organized into nine collaborative groups, each of which produced a collective reflective report at the conclusion of the project. The intervention was integrated into a curricular seminar focused on pedagogical innovation and digital practices. The lead researcher acted simultaneously as a course instructor and researcher. To reduce potential researcher bias, coding and interpretation procedures were independently conducted by two researchers, followed by consensus meetings to validate thematic interpretations. Data were collected through collective reflective reports written by the nine groups. In these reports, students described their experiences with GenAI tools, the collaborative dynamics established among peers, the challenges encountered, and the perceived educational impact of the activity. Reflective reports were selected as the primary data source because they provide access to participants' authentic voices and insider perspectives, enabling insights into their reasoning processes, perceptions, and emerging professional identities as future teachers (Loughran, 2002) . The written format allowed participants to articulate complex experiences on their own terms, without the potential reactivity associated with the presence of an interviewer. Quotations from the reports were integrated into the analysis in a contextually appropriate manner and accompanied by coded identifiers (e.g., Report #1, Report #2), ensuring data traceability while preserving participant anonymity. In total, nine reflective reports were collected and submitted for systematic analysis.
analysis.results: The results are organized around the five key 21st-century competences examined in this study, describing how the groups perceived these competences as being supported through the AI-based pedagogical activity. Where relevant, the findings are interpreted in relation to the four-dimensional AI literacy heuristic introduced in Section 2.3. This structure provides an account of how the collective reports associated the project's design with the perceived development of the targeted competences.
analysis.discussion: This study provides empirical and conceptual insights into how pre-service teachers perceived the role of GenAI in relation to transversal competences during initial teacher training. Interpreted through a four-dimensional AI literacy heuristic encompassing functional understanding, critical evaluation, ethical reasoning, and creative application, the nine collective reflective reports suggest that AI-based pedagogical activities were perceived as supporting creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, problem-solving, and digital literacy. These findings represent participants' reported experiences and should not be interpreted as evidence of objectively measured competence gains. Across the reports, GenAI was describeb both as a resource for pedagogical innovation and as a content for critical reflection. The groups associated the design and evaluation of educational materials with reflection on pedagogical choices, ethical implications, and the educational possibilities and limitations of AI. They also described collaborative learning processes and a shared sense of responsibility in knowledge construction. These patterns align with international calls from UNESCO, the OECD, and the European Commission for teacher training programs to integrate AI literacy, ethical reasoning, and digital competence as central dimensions of professional preparation. The study also identifies challenges that HE institutions must address, such as limited and uneven digital literacy, inconsistent institutional infrastructure, and persistent uncertainty about the ethical use of GenAI, which continue to pose barriers to full pedagogical integration. These challenges are not merely technical; they are structural and require institutional responses that go beyond individual courses or seminars. To address them, HE institutions must provide sustained, scaffolded opportunities for teacher candidates to experiment with emerging technologies in guided, critically reflective environments that are equitably accessible to all students. In conclusion, integrating GenAI into teacher training should be pursued as part of a human-centered pedagogical transformation. Rather than replacing the educator's expertise, AI should amplify teachers' creative and reflective capacities, enabling them to design meaningful, inclusive, and technologically enriched learning experiences. The fourdimensional AI literacy heuristic developed for this study offers a conceptual tool for structuring this integration in a pedagogically grounded and ethically responsible way. By cultivating these competences during initial training, universities can prepare future educators who are not only digitally skilled but also critically aware, ethically grounded, and capable of leading educational innovation in a rapidly changing world-in direct service of SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities).
analysis.limitations: The study draws on collective self-reported reflections from a single institutional context, which limits the potential transferability of findings. Future research should incorporate longitudinal and cross-institutional designs, together with additional data sources, to examine the development of AI literacy and professional competence over time. Practical implications -The findings highlight the need to embed AI literacy within teacher education curricula through structured opportunities for critical, ethical, and creative engagement with AI technologies. Teacher education programs should provide appropriate pedagogical scaffolding to support equitable participation and responsible AI use. Originality/value -This study contributes to rethinking HE pathways by examining how five transversal competences intersect with four dimensions of AI literacy in a structured GenAI-supported teacher training experience. By connecting creativity, ethics, and digital innovation, it provides an analytical lens for integrating AI into teacher education in alignment with contemporary educational challenges and Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 10 (Reduced Inequalities). This study is subject to several limitations that should inform the interpretation of its findings. First, it was conducted within a single public HE institution in Portugal, and its findings are not intended to support statistical generalization. Their potential transferability should instead be assessed according to the degree of similarity between the present setting and other teacher training contexts, including institutional conditions, curricular structure, students' prior digital experience, access to AI technologies, and the availability of pedagogical support. Second, the data consisted exclusively of nine collective self-reported reflective documents, which may be subject to social desirability bias and retrospective rationalization. The collective authorship of the reports may also have obscured individual differences, minority perspectives, or disagreements within the groups. Third, the absence of longitudinal data precludes a conclusion about whether the perceived competence development was sustained over time or transferred to authentic teaching practice. Fourth, member checking, a commonly used strategy for supporting credibility in qualitative research (Creswell & Poth, 2018; Lincoln & Guba, 1985) , was not feasible within the study's institutional timeline and is therefore acknowledged as a limitation. Future research should address these limitations through multi-institutional designs, mixed-methods data collection, and longitudinal follow-up. Comparative studies across cultural, institutional, and disciplinary contexts would be particularly valuable for examining the potential transferability of the four-dimensional AI literacy heuristic and identifying the contextual conditions that shape pre-service teachers' experiences with GenAI. Research following pre-service teachers into their initial years of professional practice could also provide insight into whether the competences they perceived as developing during the intervention are subsequently enacted and sustained in authentic teaching contexts. At a practical level, teacher education programs may operationalize AI literacy through activities that require students to critically evaluate AI-generated outputs, justify modifications made to generated materials, reflect on ethical implications, and document prompt-design processes. Such approaches position AI not as a substitute for pedagogical expertise but as a resource through which professional judgment can be exercised and strengthened.

Two caveats are built into the table. First, several expected processes (for example, reduced extraneous load and collaborative co-construction) were theoretically proposed but not directly measured; only the rightmostcolumn indicators were assessed. Second, the mapping is a design heuristic-a falsifiable specification for subsequent process-focused research-rather than a validated causal model. The study followed Developmental Research Type I [37] , encompassing (a) design and development of the AI-GBLE, (b) expert appraisal, and (c) a preliminary field validation. Type I was selected over related methodologies because the aim was the design, documentation, and initial validation of a specific product within one bounded cycle, rather than the multi-cycle theory generation characteristic of design-based research [28, 36, 47] . The epistemological stance is pragmatic: naturalistic classroom conditions were prioritised, claims are bounded accordingly, and transferability is supported through thick description rather than statistical generalisation [26] . The validation employed a one-group pretest-posttest design. reading.findings: Section 5.1 reports design and expert-appraisal outcomes; Sect. 5.2-5.4 report observed pre-post changes and acceptance ratings. Throughout, raw-score differences are the preferred primary summary; standardised effect sizes are provided for comparability with prior literature but should be read with caution given the ceiling compression documented below. Sensitivity analyses demonstrate numerical stability under re-expression of the same single-group dataset; they cannot recover the counterfactual information absent from the research design.
reading.interpretation: This article reported the design and preliminary validation of an AI-enhanced gamebased learning environment for computational thinking in Thai upper-secondary education. The work contributes, first, a theory-mapped design heuristic linking five theoretical foundations to six concrete components; second, an architectural specification-supporting conceptual replication within the documented reproducibility boundaries-of a hybrid AI system combining a GPT-4 conversational coach with a rule-based adaptive difficulty engine, including prompt-design principles, response constraints, hallucination safeguards, and data-governance arrangements; and third, transparent preliminary validation evidence-expert appraisal in which 37 of 47 criteria met the IOC threshold before revision, strong immediate satisfaction ratings, and large though causally unattributable and ceiling-inflated pre-post gains in computational thinking and achievement, with the direction of the CT gain consistent across two raters in a re-scored subsample. The environment is best characterised as a developed and preliminarily appraised prototype-with initial evidence of feasibility, acceptability, and learning-related signals-now suitable for rigorous controlled evaluation once the measurement and documentation improvements identified above are in place; it is not a proven intervention. If subsequent comparative studies bear out the preliminary signals reported here, environments of this kind could offer a practical route to adaptive, dialogic computational thinking instruction in ordinary classrooms.

The validation employed a one-group pretest-posttest design. This design cannot rule out threats to internal validity-including testing effects, maturation, history, instrumentation, regression to the mean, and expectancy effects [41] -and no control or comparison condition was available. Supplementary analyses (Sect. 5.5) contextualise several of these threats but cannot eliminate them; accordingly, no causal attribution is made anywhere in this article, and observed pre-post changes are treated as preliminary validation signals. Participants were 30 Grade 11 students (10 male, 20 female) from one public uppersecondary school in northeastern Thailand, recruited as an intact class through purposive sampling. All had completed the compulsory Computing Science strand of the Thai national curriculum in earlier grades [29] ; none reported formal programming experience beyond this requirement. Socioeconomic data were not collected under the approved protocol. Written informed consent was obtained from all students and from their parents or legal guardians before any data collection (see Declarations). All procedures received ethics approval from the Khon Kaen University Ethics Committee for Human Research, Panel 3, on 30 December 2025 (Reference No. HE683467; see Declarations). All data collection-pretest administration, the eight-session intervention, posttest administration, and the technology-acceptance survey-took place between January and March 2026, within the second semester of the 2025 Thai academic year and entirely within the approved protocol period. Expert appraisal procedure. Before classroom validation, nine specialists, three in each of three domains-subject content, instructional design, and media technologyappraised the environment using the Index of Item-Objective Congruence (IOC) [39] . Each expert rated every criterion in their own domain as congruent (+ 1), uncertain (0), or incongruent (-1) with its stated objective; criterion-level IOC was the mean rating across experts, with IOC ≥ 0.50 as the acceptance threshold and sub-threshold criteria triggering targeted revision. Outcomes are reported in Sect. 5.1. Validation procedure. Before the intervention, participants completed the CT pretest and the achievement pretest to establish baselines. Students then engaged with the AI-GBLE across eight 60-minute sessions over six weeks (Table 2 ). Within the environment, learning followed four phases spanning the six components (Fig. 3 ): Phase 1 established the problem situation through cognitive conflict; Phase 2 structured the mission around the five CT steps in the CT Enhancement Center, with iterative refinement after evaluation; and Phases 3 and 4 operated concurrently, providing on-demand resources and collaboration (C2-C3) and adaptive support at impasses (C5-C6). After the intervention, participants completed the CT posttest and achievement posttest, followed by the technology-acceptance questionnaire. Throughout Sessions 2-7 the classroom teacher acted as facilitator-managing logistics, time, and technical access-while conceptual guidance was delegated to the in-game supports, keeping instructor-delivered content assistance minimal and comparable across students. The design phase produced the six-component AI-GBLE described in Sect. 4.3, operationalising the integrated framework within the Smart Greenhouse context (representative screenshots in Fig. 3 ). Expert appraisal across the three domains indicated broad but uneven consensus on design quality. For the content domain (10 criteria), IOC values were uniformly 1.00 (M = 1.00), with all criteria meeting the 0.50 threshold [39] . For the media-technology domain (11 criteria), IOC ranged from 0.33 to 1.00 (M = 0.758); seven of eleven criteria met the threshold, and the four sub-threshold criteria-navigation consistency, video control buttons, graphic complexity, and external-link stability-were revised before validation. For the instructional-design domain (26 criteria), IOC ranged from 0.33 to 1.00 (M = 0.845); twenty of twenty-six criteria met the threshold, with revisions addressing the authenticity of the problem narrative, concept-map legibility, divergent-thinking activities, the CT-skills and procedural scaffolds, and graduated hinting. The criterion-level IOC values are the primary validity indicator; the grand-mean IOC across all 47 criteria was 0.858, provided for completeness. All identified concerns were addressed through iterative refinement prior to classroom use, consistent with systematic instructional design practice [10] . Two constraints on this appraisal cycle should be noted. Verbatim commentary from the panel was not systematically archived, so individual expert comments cannot be traced to individual design changes; the criterion-level suggestions and the revisions made are recorded in the first author's master's thesis (Khon Kaen University, 2026), from which the domain-level summary above is drawn; and the revised environment did not undergo a second formal expert round before validation. reading.findings: The literature indicates that artificial intelligence anthropomorphism plays an important role in shaping how individuals perceive, interpret, and respond to conversational AI systems. Anthropomorphism emerges when users attribute humanlike characteristics, including personality, emotional responsiveness, intentionality, and social awareness, to nonhuman technologies. In conversational AI, these perceptions are facilitated by natural language communication, personalized interactions, and responses that resemble interpersonal exchanges. Araujo (2018) demonstrated that anthropomorphic design cues influence users' evaluations of conversational agents, while Go and Sundar (2019) identified visual, identity, and conversational cues as important elements in shaping perceived humanness. These findings suggest that anthropomorphism is not exclusively determined by technological sophistication but also by how users interpret the social characteristics presented during interaction. The relationship between anthropomorphism and social presence provides an important explanation for the development of human-AI emotional experiences. Van Der Goot (2022) emphasized the conceptual distinctions and connections among anthropomorphism, source orientation, and social presence in chatbot communication. Similarly, Munnukka et al. (2022) examined the role of anthropomorphic characteristics and interaction dynamics in shaping perceived social presence, while Truong & Chen (2025) investigated how anthropomorphized chatbots generate perceptions of social presence. These studies suggest that humanlike AI characteristics may encourage users to experience conversational systems as socially responsive entities rather than impersonal technological interfaces. However, anthropomorphism should not be interpreted as a uniform psychological response. Janson (2023) highlighted the importance of communication style and personification in chatbot interactions, indicating that different design characteristics may produce different user evaluations. Furthermore, Karpinska-Krakowiak (2025) emphasized the importance of distinguishing anthropomorphism from related conceptual phenomena, such as animism. This distinction is particularly relevant because perceiving AI as humanlike does not necessarily imply believing that it possesses genuine emotions or consciousness. Therefore, anthropomorphism is better understood as a perceptual and interpretive mechanism that may influence emotional engagement without establishing actual interpersonal reciprocity.
reading.interpretation: This study concludes that artificial intelligence anthropomorphism plays a significant conceptual role in shaping how young adults perceive and experience emotional connections with conversational AI systems. The literature synthesis indicates that humanlike communication, personalized responses, and perceived emotional responsiveness may strengthen social presence and encourage emotional attachment to AI. These characteristics create opportunities for young adults to experience perceived companionship, emotional acceptance, and social support, particularly when their emotional affiliation needs are not adequately fulfilled through existing interpersonal relationships. However, the relationship between AI anthropomorphism and emotional affiliation needs is complex and potentially contradictory. While anthropomorphic AI may provide opportunities for emotional expression and perceived social connectedness, sustained engagement may also be associated with unrealistic relational expectations, emotional dependence, and difficulties maintaining boundaries between artificial companionship and reciprocal human relationships. Therefore, AI companionship should be understood as a potential supplementary source of perceived emotional support rather than an equivalent replacement for human interpersonal relationships. The theoretical contribution of this study lies in integrating anthropomorphism, perceived social presence, and emotional attachment into a conceptual understanding of emotional affiliation needs among young adults. Nevertheless, its reliance on secondary literature limits the ability to establish causal relationships or generalize findings across populations. The selected publications were drawn from academic journals associated with major scholarly publishers and discoverable through academic research platforms, including Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Emerald Insight, Taylor & Francis, and Google Scholar. The relevance of each publication was considered in relation to three principal criteria: (1) its conceptual or empirical contribution to understanding anthropomorphic AI; (2) its examination of emotional, psychological, or social dimensions of human-AI interaction; and (3) its relevance to young adults or comparable populations experiencing AI-mediated social relationships. Studies involving broader populations were included when their findings contributed to the conceptual framework, while differences in population characteristics were considered during interpretation. Data analysis was structured around a qualitative thematic synthesis of the selected literature. The analytical process comprised three interconnected stages. First, relevant theoretical concepts, research objectives, and reported findings were identified and organized according to their relationships with the research focus. Second, the literature was compared to identify recurring themes, conceptual similarities, contrasting findings, and potential explanatory mechanisms connecting AI anthropomorphism with emotional affiliation. Third, these themes were integrated into an interpretive framework addressing anthropomorphic characteristics, perceived social presence, emotional attachment, and the potential psychological implications of AI companionship. Particular attention was given to distinguishing perceived emotional support from reciprocal interpersonal relationships and identifying circumstances in which AI-mediated companionship might support or complicate emotional affiliation needs. To maintain analytical consistency, the synthesis distinguished between findings directly concerning young adults and evidence derived from other demographic groups or technological contexts. The study also considered both supportive and adverse perspectives on AI companionship to avoid interpreting anthropomorphic interaction as inherently beneficial or harmful. Since this research was based exclusively on secondary literature, no interviews, surveys, or experimental procedures were conducted. Accordingly, its findings are presented as a conceptual synthesis of existing evidence rather than as direct empirical confirmation of causal relationships between AI anthropomorphism and emotional affiliation needs.

analysis.discussion: This study examines how Filipino university students use ChatGPT in their learning practices, with particular attention to translanguaging and multilingual meaning-making. The findings reinforce and extend recent scholarship that frames ChatGPT not simply as a technical tool for language correction but as a mediational resource embedded in learners’ multilingual, academic, and affective practices. At the same time, the findings suggest an important dimension of critical GenAI literacy. Participants did not simply accept AI-generated responses as authoritative. They also questioned their accuracy and relevance, recognized limitations in ChatGPT’s treatment of local languages and cultural meanings, expressed concerns about overreliance, and sometimes preferred their own ideas to generic AI-generated responses. These practices suggest that critical GenAI literacy involves learners’ capacity to question, evaluate, negotiate, and make decisions about AI-generated language and knowledge. A notable example is participants’ frequent use of ChatGPT for grammar checking, writing refinement, and comprehensive text evaluation. This aligns with earlier research on GenAI in language education, which highlights automated feedback, reduced anxiety, and opportunities for independent practice (Chen, 2024; Kuddus, 2022; Lin et al., 2023). However, participants used ChatGPT beyond surface-level correction, viewing it as a reflective resource that could support self-monitoring, metalinguistic awareness, and academic confidence. At the same time, using ChatGPT to assess whether writing is grammatically correct, clear, or appropriately academic raises questions about linguistic authority. Although AI-generated suggestions may become one source learners use to evaluate what constitutes acceptable academic English, ChatGPT does not necessarily determine their linguistic choices, but its feedback may influence how learners negotiate linguistic norms, echoing concerns that GenAI-mediated feedback can reproduce or naturalize dominant linguistic norms (Helm et al., 2024; Participants also used ChatGPT to simplify content, summarize information, explain complex theories, and prepare for academic tasks. These practices align with emerging views of GenAI as a mediator of academic literacy that can support comprehension and more confident engagement with dense academic content (Donley, 2024; Slamet, 2024; Zhou et al., 2026). From a translanguaging perspective, such use reflects learners’ efforts to bridge disciplinary discourse and their existing linguistic resources, supporting access and meaning-making (Wei, 2018; Thongwichit & Ulla, 2024). At the same time, simplification creates a tension between accessibility and dependence. Repeated reliance on AI- generated explanations may mediate students’ engagement with complex ideas through algorithmic interpretation rather than their own reading and thinking. Participants’ concerns about overreliance, including Q2’s concern that excessive use of ChatGPT could undermine their language development, suggest an awareness of this tension. Such concerns are relevant to critical GenAI literacy because they show learners evaluating not only the usefulness of AI-generated output but also whether relying on it supports or undermines their longer-term learning (Ulla et al., 2023b). The findings further highlight how learners negotiate their multilingual repertoires when interacting with ChatGPT. Participants moved among English, Filipino, Taglish, and local languages to support comprehension, expression, and task completion. These practices reflect the flexible use of linguistic resources described in translanguaging scholarship (Creese & Blackledge, 2010; MacSwan, 2019) and align with Yu et al. (2025), who describe learners’ strategic language shifting to support comprehension and meaning-making. In the present study, students used Filipino or Taglish when English did not allow them to express an idea precisely or when they needed to clarify an unfamiliar concept. Thus, translanguaging remained an important resource within GenAI-mediated learning. However, these practices also reveal an important ambivalence. Some participants reported feeling pressure to rely more heavily on English because they perceived ChatGPT as less reliable when responding to mixed-language prompts or local languages. P3’s use of Filipino as a resource coexisted with a desire to practice English, while P4 explicitly described pressure to rely mainly on English. This tension was particularly visible in participants’ experiences with languages such as Maranao and Bisaya. One participant described inaccurate translations and difficulty with words or expressions that lacked direct equivalents, while another reported that mixed-language prompts could produce inaccurate or incomplete responses. These experiences are consistent with broader concerns about the representation of minoritized languages in digital technologies and GenAI systems (Mohamed et al., 2020; Helm et al., 2024; Ulla et al., 2024). Additionally, this study does not systematically test ChatGPT’s performance across languages and therefore cannot establish objective differences in its linguistic capabilities. The findings instead show how students perceived these limitations and how those perceptions shaped their These tensions also demonstrate that translanguaging and critical GenAI literacy are closely connected. Learners’ multilingual repertoires provide more than a means of communicating with ChatGPT. They also provide resources for evaluating what ChatGPT produces. When participants switched languages to clarify meaning, compared responses with their own knowledge, or recognized that a translation did not adequately capture a local expression, they drew on their linguistic and contextual knowledge to assess AI-generated output. Thus, multilingual meaning-making can also become a form of critical engagement with GenAI. This critical engagement is particularly evident in participants’ responses to generic or contextually inappropriate feedback. One participant noted that ChatGPT could not fully grasp the pragmatic intentions or contextual nuances behind their writing (P5). Another explained, “But most of the time, I prefer my ideas because sometimes ChatGPT gives generic answers that obviously do not have the touch of a human soul” (Q16). These accounts show that participants evaluated AI-generated language against their own communicative intentions and contextual knowledge. They did not necessarily equate linguistic fluency with communicative adequacy. Instead, they retained their own ideas when AI-generated alternatives appeared too generic. reading.methods: A natural way to enable dynamic hybrid execution is to make layer choices for each token. However, such tokenlevel gating is ill-suited for autoregressive hybrid LLM serving. During decoding, each newly generated token relies on the Attention KV caches or SSM state caches produced by previous tokens to avoid redundant computation. If different tokens from the same request choose different layers within the same block, later tokens may no longer be able to directly reuse the caches produced by earlier tokens. As a result, the runtime must recompute previous tokens under the new layer choice, introducing substantial overhead and complicating decoding. To avoid these problems, Flex adopts a coarse-grained prefill-oriented gating mechanism in the request-adaptive hybrid model. As shown in Figure 6 , this mechanism has two key properties. First, the gate is evaluated only during prefill, where each hybrid block makes one request-level choice between the Attention layer and the SSM layer based on all input tokens. Second, the selected layer choices are fixed after prefill and directly reused throughout decoding, so generated tokens do not trigger additional gating decisions. This design is reasonable for both system efficiency and hybrid adaptation. reading.findings: We evaluate Flex on the NVIDIA H100 GPU using six datasets spanning reasoning, QA, and summarization tasks. Experiments show that the proposed hybrid model achieves a better quality-efficiency trade-off than homogeneous and static hybrid baselines, obtaining the best results on 13 out of 18 quality metrics while reducing estimated TFLOPs/token by up to 67.2% relative to LLaMA. reading.interpretation: This paper presents Flex, an inference system that combines a request-adaptive hybrid model with an optimized serving runtime through algorithm-system co-design. The model uses prefill-oriented gating to select Attention or SSM branches for each request and keeps the resulting layout fixed throughout decoding. The runtime integrates selective batching and hybrid-aware context caching to support efficient mixedbranch execution and correct prefix reuse. Experiments show that the hybrid model achieves a better quality-efficiency trade-off than static hybrid baselines, while the runtime improves serving throughput and reduces inference latency.

analysis.methods: Based on the established framework, ML, with its unique performance advantages, can identify catalysts with high activity and stability, and its main advantages are reflected in three aspects. First, ML enables HT virtual screening, thereby significantly accelerating the discovery of candidate materials [135] . By learning from limited high-quality datasets (e.g., DFT calculation results or HT experimental data), ML constructs a predictive model that maps catalyst characteristics to target performance. This model can instantly evaluate the performance of massive virtual candidate materials, thus rapidly narrowing the research focus to the most promising material regions. For example, a study exploring the 15-element space for CO 2 conversion to C3 hydrocarbon catalysts, by integrating an automated experimental platform with an explainable ML model, achieved an accelerated discovery of approximately 165 times compared to traditional methods, of which about 33 times comes from the innovation of the experimental platform, and about 5 times is due to the ML guidance that integrates domain knowledge [136] . In addition, through interpretable analysis, ML can quantitatively reveal the implicit relationship between the microscopic characteristics of materials (e.g., d-electron number, bond length) and their macrocatalytic properties. This ability makes it possible to design rational catalysts at the atomic structure level and also provides guidance for the realization of specific catalytic functions. In ML workflows, feature importance analysis (e.g., analysis based on XGBoost or random forest models) and SHapley additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis can quantify the contribution of different descriptors to catalytic performance. These methods directly link macroscopic performance with microscopic electronic and geometric parameters, thus forming specific design criteria. For example, through ML analysis, the first ionization energy and the d-band center of the catalyst, two electronic structural characteristics, are identified as the most critical factors determining the reaction potential barrier [9] . These findings have led to the transformation of catalyst design from a practice that relies on experience to rational regulation based on a clear electronic structure descriptor. Besides, the products generated by electrocatalytic CO 2 RR are complex and diverse, with multiple selectivities, involving multiple competing reaction paths. After correlation analysis and pattern recognition on large-scale catalyst performance datasets, ML can infer potential common reaction mechanisms and path branches, thus improving the product selectivity of electrocatalytic CO 2 RR. This correlation analysis based on large datasets can grasp the overall catalytic trend and mechanism analysis, supplementing the shortcomings of traditional deep mechanism studies dedicated to a single system [26, 42] . More recently, reverse design has arisen as a more difficult yet potentially rewarding application, which starts from the desired catalytic performance and reversely deduces the catalyst structure that meets this performance requirement. This approach reverses the traditional forward thinking from structure design to performance testing; instead, it begins with the expected performance target to inversely identify the catalyst structure capable of achieving this goal. Intelligent algorithms like Bayesian optimization and generative adversarial networks (GANs) are powerful enablers for reverse design. These algorithms can intelligently explore the vast catalyst design space, proactively propose new SAC structures with potentially superior performance, iteratively suggest optimal candidate structures with the minimum number of attempts, and continuously optimize the model through loop feedback, ultimately guiding researchers to synthesize "on-demand customized" catalysts [32, 137, 138] . Besides, strategies such as AL are also a robust technique to tackle the challenge of scarce data to obtain the optimal model with the minimum number of samples and achieve reverse design combined an AL framework with DFT for screening highperformance catalysts for CO 2 RR. After four rounds of iterations, the model achieved an accurate prediction (R 2 ≈ 0.94) of the adsorption energies for crucial intermediates, even when only a limited amount of data is available, and successfully discovered a variety of previously unexplored high-performance catalysts. However, the practical implementation of inverse design faces several fundamental challenges. The difficulty of inverse design first stems from the inherent complexity of the catalytic system itself. Heterogeneous catalyst surfaces exhibit significant structural complexity, accompanied by coupled surface-adsorbate interactions spanning a vast chemical space that is difficult to explore effectively through conventional screening methods [141] . Taking inorganic compounds alone as an example, their chemical space encompasses approximately 10 N possible configurations (N atoms in the unit cell). Identifying novel and useful candidate materials within such a vast space is highly challenging. Although conventional forward design approaches have been widely adopted, their fundamental limitation lies in their inability to generate new materials that go beyond existing structural prototypes. Current inverse design methods also face multiple constraints: first, different generative models must be trained for different target properties, lacking universality [137]; second, ML models are often unreliable in high-dimensional spaces, prone to predictive bias, and struggle to effectively incorporate domain expert knowledge; third, the inherent "black-box" nature of generative models renders them lacking physical interpretability, limiting researchers' mechanistic understanding of the design outcomes; fourth, the conflict between the high-dimensional compositional space of materials and the limited availability of experimental data constitutes a fundamental data bottleneck [142] . Critically, in reverse design workflows, the experimental validation rate of ML-generated candidate materials remains below 5%-10%, and rare ML-designed materials have yet surpassed the current state-ofthe-art in the combined metrics of activity, selectivity, stability, and cost [143] . The primary reasons for this problem lie in the following: regarding synthetic feasibility, the core challenge facing SACs is their intrinsic thermodynamic instability. SACs are highly susceptible to Ostwald ripening under hightemperature conditions or during prolonged catalytic applications, leading to sintering and deactivation, a consequence rooted in the weak interaction between metal atoms and the support. The regeneration and recycling of deactivated catalysts will substantially increase both the time and economic costs of industrial production. Consequently, developing SACs with high thermal stability to meet industrial requirements has become an urgent priority in this field. Meanwhile, the morphology and coordination environment of metal centers during synthesis also affect the thermal stability of the resulting products, making it difficult to precisely reproduce theoretically predicted ideal coordination configurations under complex and variable experimental conditions [144] .
