analysis.discussion: The analysis suggests that academic-integrity regulation captures only part of the challenge presented by GenAI-assisted writing. Compliance with assessment requirements remains essential, but it does not by itself explain how a student's contribution was produced across an AI-mediated writing process. Authorship literacy addresses this narrower question by directing attention to where intellectual and expressive contributions are located and how they change as AI intervention moves from feedback or local language support towards restructuring or substantive generation. A communication perspective is useful here because the submitted text is not simply a container for ideas; it is the form through which a student's knowledge, argument and academic position become available to the reader. If AI materially reshapes that form, authorship cannot be determined solely by asking who originated the initial idea. Foucault's (1977) authorfunction remains relevant because it unsettles the assumption that authorship follows straightforwardly from textual production or attribution. GenAI makes this problem particularly visible within assessment: a text may remain institutionally attributed to one student while parts of its organisation or expression have been technologically mediated. These distinctions also connect authorship to assessment design. Constructive alignment requires attention to whether the contribution demonstrated in assessed work corresponds to the intended learning outcomes (Biggs, 1996) . GenAI-specific approaches such as the AI Assessment Scale similarly distinguish levels of permitted AI use in relation to assessment design (Perkins et al., 2024) . Authorship literacy complements such frameworks by focusing more specifically on what different forms of assistance mean for the student's contribution. Disciplinary expectations also differ: assumptions about individual authorship can sit uneasily beside forms of professional writing that are already more collaborative (Velez & Rister, 2025) . Where independent formulation of an argument is itself being assessed, substantial AI restructuring has different implications from an assessment in which critical use of AI is an intended part of the task. The appropriate boundary must therefore remain connected to the learning outcomes of a particular assessment, which is why Table 1 is illustrative rather than prescriptive. Within these assessment-specific boundaries, authorship literacy offers a pedagogical rather than regulatory contribution. Having the idea is relevant to authorship but does not necessarily account for the whole of it; writing is itself part of intellectual and communicative work. Nor can responsibility substitute for authorship: a student who can explain or defend an AI-assisted text has not thereby shown that they authored all of the work being assessed, and a reflective or oral defence should not become a retrospective justification for AI involvement that the assessment did not permit. AI-mediated writing also intersects with multilingual development and unequal access (Kim et al., 2025; Kohnke, 2024; Lee, 2024) , so authorship-literacy approaches should remain sensitive to students' different linguistic and material circumstances. The scope of the argument should nevertheless be recognised. This is a conceptual paper drawing on purposively selected literature and practice-informed grounding rather than a systematic review or empirical test of authorship literacy. Further research could examine how students across different linguistic and institutional contexts interpret distinctions between ideas, expression and responsibility, and whether explicit teaching of authorship changes their decisions when using GenAI. Within this scope, authorship literacy offers a conceptual and pedagogical language for connecting academic-integrity requirements with a clearer understanding of contribution in AI-mediated writing. Generative AI has brought renewed attention to questions of academic authorship because technological assistance can now contribute directly to the organisation and expression of student writing. This paper has argued that academic-integrity rules remain necessary, but that compliance alone does not fully explain what happens to authorship when AI becomes part of the writing process. The analysis has distinguished the student's underlying ideas from their textual expression and has shown why ownership of an assignment should not automatically be equated with authorship of all aspects of its final form. It has also emphasised that responsibility remains important without functioning as a substitute for authorship. Together, these distinctions provide a more precise way of considering student contribution in AImediated writing. On this basis, the paper has used authorship literacy as a focused extension of wider AI literacy. The aim is not to weaken boundaries around AI-assisted assessment or to normalise the outsourcing of writing. Rather, students need clearer ways of understanding how technological assistance affects the work they present as their own. In an increasingly AImediated writing environment, institutional guidance needs to communicate not only what students are permitted to do, but why particular forms of assistance matter for authorship.

analysis.discussion: Studies of advisory systems have evolved through three broad 'generational' stages affecting how their knowledge-related activities have been studied. These began with an initial largely descriptive one (mainly dealing with advisors in Westminster systems) (Halligan, 1995; Plowden, 1987) , which inferred the relevance and influence of policy advice by its proximity to decision-makers (Seymour-Ure, 1987; Hustedt, 2018; Mukherjee & Giest, 2020) . Second generation studies then increased the detail of the description and analysis of PAS, recognizing the diversity of systems existing outside of the Westminster model (Brans & Timmermans, 2022; Howlett, 2019; van den Berg, 2017; Jungblut et al., 2024; Emamian & Bagheripour, 2024; Belyaeva, 2019) . This work also highlighted how politicization and externalization influenced the nature of the advice provided (Hustedt, Kolltveit, & Salomonsen, 2017; Shaw & Eichbaum, 2023) , altering the characteristics and content of both its supply and demand. Recently, a third generation of PAS has further extended this analysis to how advisory systems can be managed to provide specific kinds of information and how this activity affects the quality of the advice provided (Connaughton & Devane, 2023; Migone & Howlett, 2025a) . The idea that the knowledge that is fed into the policy process is managed rather than discovered is not new (Mendelsohn, 1977; Rayner, 2012) , but has been reprised recently in third generation PAS studies (Howlett et al., 2025) . This article builds upon this third-generation initiative to consider the impact on policy advice and judgment occasioned by the arrival of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and algorithmic governance within the contemporary public policy advisory space. It examined a high profile recent case of AI-influenced policy development by DOGE to consider how the existence of AI advice and the nature of the quality of that advice impacted upon both Geoffrey Vickers' concept of an appreciative system as well as existing thinking around PAS structure, activities, quality and management. We argue that in this important case AI-generated and -mediated advice exercised a significant, independent, and harmful, influence on policy judgments and decisions. It did so by shaping the framing or appreciation of policy problems well before a human judgment is made, introducing a new set of biases of a different kind from traditional human concerns such as gender, ethnic or racial inequities into deliberations. It did this through AI-generated advice which became highly credentialized, regardless of its accuracy. Managerial strategies which promoted this AI activity undermined a traditional appreciation model whereby problems and their framing are determined by human experience, judgment, and learning, reducing the quality of decisions. Even when AI does not 'make' a final decision, it can offer a readily available and low-cost option that becomes extremely enticing given conditions like lack of resources or the demand for quick turnaround times, further undermining the development of effective appreciations on the part of decision-makers and their advisors. The case shows how the traditional coexistence of computational and judgmental forms of knowledge selection within the context of advice from the policy advisory system is highly problematic when it is augmented by AI use in the computational and appreciative space. As the DOGE experience shows, the restriction of the number of actors that conducted operations and their poor training and understanding of administrative practices and organizational routines resulted in a policy process both poorer and more opaque and prone to further problems and problematic practices. Vickers' theory of appreciative systems suggested that policy judgment should be a recursive organizational process rather than a purely computational one and that this requires time and training for both advisors and decision-makers to gain experience with both the external world and the internal world of policy-making. There is little doubt that AI will continue to progress and can improve a variety of routine policy advice activities -low-hanging fruits include assessing tens of thousands of comments on resource projects, for example, stakeholder analysis and environmental scans, but also policy calibration simulations and the like (Nguyen et al 2020) . But in less routine situations poorly managed AI deployment runs the real risk of blunting the quality of advice and rendering it unidimensional if not outright wrong. In many other areas affected by AI, from drone warfare to autonomous cars, a central principle deployed to prevent judgment failures is to retain a 'Human-in-the-Loop', where AI is allowed to replace some of the more menial aspects of human judgment but remains ultimately within and under human direction and control (Cho et al., 2026) . However, for policy advice to successfully enmesh AI within the policy-making process, this requires not simply keeping a Human-in-the-Loop as an (impotent) supervisor, but ensuring recursive appreciation by allowing actors to revisit and debate AI options and prevent general narrowing of the alternatives available to them. The recursive nature of the policy process must be maintained if we wish to cope with the risk and uncertainty that are naturally embedded in complex policy issues. To do so it will be necessary to conceive of future AI-informed PAS as Vickersian devices with institutional arrangements around them designed and operated to deliberately protect recursive appreciation. AI can be an important support for PAS in low-level and routine cases, but its usefulness is limited when decisions require a higher level and quality of judgment. Only careful management and institutional design can ensure that the values, problem definitions, and assumptions that developed and go into prudent policy decision-making are retained in the AI era (Ramesh and Howlett 2027a) .

analysis.discussion: This study developed a context-specific measure of AI acceptance for intercultural teaching and examined its cross-sectional associations with teacher resources and occupational-health indicators. The strongest contribution is the preliminary measurement work: the overall AITA score showed good internal consistency, whereas the four theory-based facets were not clearly distinguishable empirically. The structural findings provide modest association evidence rather than evidence that AI acceptance directly improves occupational health. The structural association results are compatible with a resource-related pattern rather than a direct association between AI acceptance and the occupational-health outcomes. AI acceptance was associated with both self-efficacy and autonomous motivation. Self-efficacy was associated with higher occupational wellbeing and lower emotional exhaustion, whereas autonomous motivation was associated mainly with occupational wellbeing. Within the JD-R interpretation, self-efficacy represents an efficacy-related personal resource, whereas autonomous motivation represents an internal motivational resource. This distinction helps preserve the different content of the two resource pathways rather than treating all resources as interchangeable. The pattern is also consistent with the dual-process logic of the JD-R model ( 3 , 4 ): resources are expected to relate mainly to the motivational process and its positive outcomes, such as wellbeing, whereas emotional exhaustion is expected to arise mainly from job demands through the health-impairment process. Autonomous motivation, as a motivational resource, was accordingly associated with occupational wellbeing but only marginally with exhaustion, whereas self-efficacy, which may also help teachers appraise demanding intercultural tasks as manageable, was associated with both outcomes. Because no formal coefficient-difference test was conducted, this interpretation concerns the pattern of significance rather than a demonstrated difference between the two resources. The score-based models explained R 2 = 0.141 for occupational wellbeing and R 2 = 0.052 for emotional exhaustion. The low explained variance in exhaustion is consistent with the same logic: the model contained resource variables but no measures of job demands, such as teaching workload, administrative pressure, or AI-related role demands, which JD-R identifies as the main antecedents of exhaustion. The present model therefore should not be read as an account of teachers’ exhaustion. The exploratory moderation results did not support perceived institutional support as a boundary condition. Although perceived institutional support was positively associated with intercultural teaching self-efficacy, it did not significantly change the strength of the association between AI acceptance and self-efficacy. From an occupational health perspective, this pattern is compatible with institutional support operating as a general organizational resource rather than as a moderator of the association between AI acceptance and self-efficacy. The findings are broadly consistent with both TAM and the JD-R framework, but the two frameworks serve different roles. TAM provides the theoretical content for the AITA item pool, whereas JD-R provides a framework for interpreting why a perceived AI-usability appraisal might be related to teacher resources and occupational-health indicators. The present results do not show that AI acceptance itself is an objective job resource, nor that it causes changes in self-efficacy, motivation, or occupational health. Compared with previous research on AI adoption in education, this study further highlights the importance of the teaching context. Intercultural teaching involves cultural explanation, multilingual communication, support for international students, and cross-border collaboration. These tasks differ from general classroom teaching, and recent work on AI-enabled intercultural learning and COIL further suggests that AI use may reshape intercultural learning opportunities and challenges ( 13 , 16 ). Accordingly, teachers’ acceptance of AI cannot be fully captured by a general measure of technology adoption intention; it needs to be assessed in relation to specific intercultural teaching tasks. From the perspective of teacher occupational health and public mental health, the findings reinforce the importance of resources rather than technology exposure alone. Recent research on AI, teacher wellbeing, work engagement, anxiety, and burnout has indicated that technological change may be connected to teachers’ work experiences ( 6–15 , 17 , 18 ). The present study adds that, in intercultural teaching contexts, the observed pattern is compatible with resource-related associations involving intercultural teaching self-efficacy and autonomous motivation, whereas the direct associations between AI acceptance and occupational-health outcomes were not significant. This pattern should not be interpreted as evidence of a tested mechanism. First, the findings suggest several hypotheses for universities seeking to support teachers during AI-supported intercultural or internationalized teaching. Universities may consider scenario-based guidance, ethical and data-security support, technical assistance, and opportunities for peer exchange. However, these are proposals for future implementation and intervention research: the present study did not compare training formats, evaluate institutional policies, or estimate the occupational-health effects of specific interventions. Second, future professional-development studies could examine whether training that supports intercultural teaching self-efficacy is more useful than training focused only on software functions. The present study did not compare training formats or evaluate training effects. Any occupational-health implications of such training therefore remain to be tested. Third, although perceived institutional support did not significantly moderate the association between AI acceptance and self-efficacy, it was itself positively associated with self-efficacy. Future implementation studies could therefore evaluate whether concrete and visible forms of support, such as AI teaching ethics guidelines, data-security standards, technical support, intercultural teaching resources, incentives for teaching innovation, and opportunities for peer exchange, are followed by changes in teacher resources and occupational-health indicators. analysis.methods: This study employed a cross-sectional design. An anonymous electronic questionnaire was distributed to university physical education teachers via the Wenjuanxing online survey platform between 1 June 2026 and 10 August 2026. Participants were recruited through a combination of convenience sampling and snowball sampling, both non-probability methods: the questionnaire link was first sent to teachers who could be reached conveniently, who were asked to forward it to other university physical education teachers they knew. The questionnaire link was initially sent to teachers at 18 universities in six provinces and municipalities (Sichuan, Guangdong, Chongqing, Beijing, Hainan, and Hunan; the universities are listed in Supplementary Table S1 ) and was then circulated through snowball referral. Because the link was circulated through personal and professional networks, the number of invited teachers could not be determined, so a response rate cannot be calculated; the effective rate reported below is the proportion of returned questionnaires that were valid. Because of snowball referral, the universities that the questionnaire ultimately reached cannot be determined; the questionnaire was also anonymous and did not record respondent-level institutional affiliation, so the distribution of participants across universities cannot be reported. Gender, age, and years of teaching experience were also recorded, but because of problems in the collection and compilation of these data they could not be used, and none of the analyses reported here includes them. In total, 981 questionnaires were returned. The questionnaire consisted of four sections: the Perceived AI Acceptance Scale, the Digital Well-Being Scale, the Innovative Work Behavior Scale, and the Job-related Affective Well-being Scale (JAWS). Prior to participation, all respondents provided electronic informed consent, and all data were anonymized to ensure confidentiality. Data cleaning excluded 174 questionnaires in three mutually exclusive steps applied in the following order, so that no case was counted twice. The questionnaire contained, in addition to the four scales, a screening item on professional identity, an item on whether the respondent teaches university physical education classes and an item on weekly class hours, a pair of positively and reversely worded items on the use of a teaching method, and one attention-check item. First, 30 questionnaires were excluded because the screening item showed that the respondent was not a university physical education teacher (981–30 = 951 remaining). Second, of these 951, 113 were excluded because the total completion time was outside the limits set on the Wenjuanxing platform: a minimum of 1 min (60 s) and a maximum of 30 min (1,800 s). Wenjuanxing offers several completion-time limit options (for the maximum, for example, 5, 10, 15, and 20 min), these two limits were selected from them, and questionnaires outside the limits were marked as invalid by the platform and removed (951–113 = 838 remaining). The limits were platform settings and not empirically derived criteria. Third, of the remaining 838, 31 were excluded for internally inconsistent responses, defined as failing any one of the following checks: (a) answering “no” to whether the respondent teaches university physical education classes while reporting weekly class hours greater than 0; (b) answering “agree” or “strongly agree” to both the positively worded item “I often apply this teaching method in class” and the reversely worded item “I rarely apply this teaching method in class,” or, after reverse-scoring the negatively worded item, an absolute difference of 2 or more between the scores of the two items; and (c) not selecting the instructed option on the attention-check item (“Please select ‘somewhat agree’ for this item”). A total of 807 valid questionnaires (807/981 = 82.26%) were retained for analysis. The anonymized dataset will be retained in accordance with institutional data-management practice and made available to qualified researchers upon reasonable request, subject to a formal data-sharing agreement that protects participants’ privacy. This study was conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. It did not involve invasive procedures, and all research methods complied with relevant guidelines and regulations. Ethical approval was obtained from the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Hunan Normal University (approval no. LSK2026-472) prior to the commencement of the study. The author, who is the project leader and the applicant, is affiliated with Sichuan Film and Television University; the ethical review was conducted by the Biomedical Research Ethics Committee of Hunan Normal University, which accepted the author’s entrustment to review the project (letter of acceptance of entrusted ethics review). The approved protocol specified online recruitment of university physical education teachers by convenience and snowball sampling in 18 universities in six provinces and municipalities (Sichuan, Guangdong, Chongqing, Beijing, Hainan, and Hunan) between 1 June and 10 August 2026; because of snowball sampling, the questionnaire reached universities across these provinces and municipalities. Data were collected anonymously and kept strictly confidential. All participants provided electronic informed consent and voluntarily agreed to participate; they retained the right to withdraw from the study at any time without penalty. The Perceived AI Acceptance Scale was adapted from Davis (1989) , with item wording modified to refer to AI tools used in university teaching. The Digital Well-Being Scale is a researcher-developed instrument: Gui et al. (2017) offer a theoretical framework and indicators of digital well-being but no ready-made item set, so the 12 items were compiled, translated, and reworded by the research team on the basis of that framework, and the scale should not be regarded as a previously validated instrument. analysis.discussion: This study constructed and tested a serial mediation model examining whether perceived AI acceptance is associated with university PE teachers’ occupational well-being through the sequential mediating roles of digital well-being and innovative work behavior. The data were consistent with all four hypotheses, and the pattern of results is compatible with a resource-based interpretation of how favorable technological appraisal may be linked to occupational adaptation in a digitalizing higher-education context. Given the cross-sectional, single-source design, however, the results describe statistical indirect associations and not established psychological mechanisms or temporal processes. This study found that perceived AI acceptance was significantly and positively associated with university PE teachers’ occupational well-being, supporting Hypothesis H1 and aligning with a growing body of evidence documenting positive associations between favorable technology appraisals and occupational adjustment among teachers ( Yi et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ). The association between perceived AI acceptance and occupational well-being was accompanied by indirect associations through both digital well-being and innovative work behavior, which were themselves intercorrelated. From the perspective of Conservation of Resources theory, perceived AI acceptance can be interpreted as a favorable appraisal of a potential job resource, which is consistent with lower anticipated resource loss and with higher levels of resources in digital and behavioral domains ( Hobfoll, 1989 ; Hobfoll et al., 2018 ) (these resource states were not directly measured). Higher levels of such resources are, in turn, associated with more favorable affective experiences of work, consistent with the Job Demands–Resources proposition that job and personal resources are linked to engagement and well-being ( Bakker and Demerouti, 2017 ). Notably, similar to prior chain-mediation research on teacher occupational well-being ( Nong et al., 2022 ), the serial indirect pathway identified in the present study, while statistically reliable, represented a modest proportion of the total effect (11.66%), indicating that the sequence from digital well-being to innovative work behavior accounts for only a modest part of the association between perceived AI acceptance and occupational well-being, and that other factors not measured here are likely to be involved. Given that prosocial and occupational outcomes are typically shaped by numerous factors beyond any single technological appraisal—such as institutional support, professional identity, and workload—the magnitude of the present associations is consistent with the broader literature’s understanding of teacher well-being as a multiply determined outcome, while still carrying meaningful implications for how institutions introduce and scaffold AI tools for PE faculty. This study also found a statistically significant indirect association between perceived AI acceptance and university PE teachers’ occupational well-being through digital well-being, consistent with Hypothesis H2. This result indicates that perceived AI acceptance is not only directly associated with occupational well-being but also shows an indirect association with it through digital well-being (in a statistical sense). One possible interpretation, which these data cannot test directly, is that when AI tools are appraised as useful and easy to operate, teachers may be less likely to experience the technology as an additional demand and may be more likely to adopt selective, adaptive strategies for managing digital information and communication flows ( Gui et al., 2017 ). Consistent with this reasoning, prior organizational research has shown that workplace digitization is associated with reduced digital anxiety, which in turn is linked to enhanced employee well-being ( Han Z. et al., 2025 ). Within a COR framework, a favorable technological appraisal is theoretically linked to a lower anticipated resource cost of digital engagement, which may be related to higher digital well-being as a personal resource that is, in turn, associated with broader occupational well-being ( Hobfoll, 1989 ; Diener et al., 1999 ). Thus, the emotional and cognitive experience of digital demands may be one relevant correlate linking PE teachers’ appraisal of AI and their overall occupational well-being. The results showed that innovative work behavior had a significant indirect association linking perceived AI acceptance and university PE teachers’ occupational well-being, consistent with Hypothesis H3. This finding is compatible with a role for proactive, resource-investing behavior in linking technology appraisal and occupational adaptation, although the cross-sectional data do not establish this role. When PE teachers regard AI tools as beneficial and easy to use, they appear more willing to invest cognitive and behavioral resources in generating, promoting, and realizing novel ideas in their work, consistent with recent evidence that generative AI use is associated with employees’ innovation performance through resource acquisition and integration mechanisms ( Wang et al., 2025 ). Innovative work behavior is, in turn, associated with occupational well-being, plausibly because the successful promotion and realization of novel ideas is linked to experiences of competence, recognition, and positive affect at work ( West and Farr, 1990 ; Janssen, 2000 ). This finding is consistent with prior literature indicating that innovative behavior is associated with individual well-being outcomes ( Amabile, 1988 ), and adds evidence on this association in the domain of AI-related technology appraisal among university PE teachers. Note that innovative work behavior was measured with Janssen’s general scale, which captures idea generation, promotion, and realization in one’s work role; it does not specifically capture teaching or pedagogical innovation. This study systematically examined the associations between CAS, including total score and domains, and SABA using a multi-wave longitudinal design with multiple analytical approaches. The findings provide empirical support for the proposed metacognitive model of SABA, demonstrating that CAS total score is primarily associated with SABA at the between-person level, indicating a stable trait-level comorbidity rather than a short-term dynamic process. Among the seven CAS domains, worry uniquely emerged as the most consistent predictor for SABA: it showed the strongest between-person association with SABA and the largest within-person cross-lagged association, with a directional path from worry to SABA. This within-person association remained significant even after controlling for comorbid anxiety and depression, supporting worry as a prospective within-person correlate of SABA. Methodologically, the integration of LCGM, Random Forest, and SHAP analyses provided convergent evidence across person-centered and variable-centered approaches, which extended the RI-CLPM findings by indicating that the relative influence of CAS domains differs across SABA trajectories. Machine learning analyses consistently identified worry as the most influential CAS domain in relation to SABA, ranking first in predicting both high-stable and moderate-decreasing trajectories of SABA, and further suggested a synergistic interaction between worry and substance use, corresponding to a higher likelihood of belonging to the high-stable SABA trajectory. Clinically, the dual-pathway pattern of worry observed in the RI-CLPM suggests worry can serve different functions depending on the target population and time frame. At the trait level, its strong betweenperson association with SABA supports its potential use as a screening marker for identifying high SABA-risk medical students who may benefit from early prevention for SABA. At the state level, its significant withinperson association with SABA suggests that worry fluctuations may serve as a dynamic indicator for monitoring short-term changes in SABA risk. For medical students who have already developed SABA, whether worry represents a candidate target for future intervention research, and whether reducing worry could potentially influence the maintenance of SABA requires confirmation in future experimental studies. Given that the within-person association of worry remained significant after controlling for anxiety and depression, future research could examine whether interventions targeting worry are effective regardless of individuals' current anxiety or depression levels. Future research could employ experimental designs (e.g., randomized controlled trials targeting worry) to further test whether worry prospectively predicts SABA, and whether abbreviated metacognitive therapy is effective in reducing worry and, consequently, alleviating SABA among medical students at both short-term and long-term levels.
analysis.limitations: Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the reliance on self-report measures and the specific sample of medical students in China may limit the generalizability of these findings. Future research could replicate these findings using more diverse populations and multimethod assessments (e.g., objective measures such as actual smartphone usage data) to reduce this potential bias. Second, the 35% attrition rate over the three waves needs to be considered when interpreting the findings. Although attrition analyses suggested limited bias (|d| = .168-.196), the reduced sample size may have limited statistical power to detect small effects, particularly at the within-person level. Future research with larger samples and lower attrition rates is needed. Third, although anxiety and depression were controlled as covariates in the RI-CLPM, they were not controlled for in all analyses of this research. Future research could systematically include these covariates across all analytical levels. Fourth, the entropy values for the LCGM (.69-.74) indicated moderate trajectory classification precision, suggesting that the trajectoryspecific results, particularly those involving the low-stable group (n = 84, 12.50%), warrant careful interpretation. Future research with larger samples and more waves of data is needed to replicate and refine these trajectory classifications. Fifth, the SABAS uses a single item per addiction criterion, which may limit measurement precision. The use of a 6-point Likert format for both the SABAS and MCASS, while intended to reduce neutral midpoint bias, may have influenced response distributions and warrant consideration when interpreting the findings. Although the SABAS has been validated as a brief screening tool, future research could employ multiitem measures for greater reliability. Sixth, the two-step factor-score sensitivity analysis partially accounted for measurement error in CAS. However, the CAS latent measurement model showed relatively poor fit, and the factor loadings for substance use (λ = .29-.33) and worry (λ = .46-.50) were relatively low, suggesting these domains were less well represented by the latent factor. Furthermore, the strict one-step latent RI-CLPM did not converge, and SABA remained a unidimensional construct represented by an observed total score. Estimating a fully latent RI-CLPM with seven indicators across three waves involves a large number of parameters, which may have contributed to the estimation difficulty. Therefore, measurement error was not fully addressed, and the factor-score analyses represent limited, exploratory sensitivity checks. Future research with larger samples and more stable measurement models may be needed to estimate fully latent RI-CLPMs that better account for measurement error in CAS. Seventh, the measurement invariance results warrant consideration, as the configural models for SABAS and MCASS showed relatively weak fit, and SABAS achieved partial rather than full scalar invariance. Therefore, these results provide qualified, rather than definitive, evidence of measurement equivalence across time. Eighth, the three-wave longitudinal design constrained the precision of growth trajectory estimation. Future research with more frequent assessments (e.g., ecological momentary assessment) could further clarify the short-term dynamic relationship between worry and SABA. Ninth, although RI-CLPM provides a more stringent test of temporal precedence than traditional CLPM, it does not establish causation. Future research could employ experimental designs, such as randomized controlled trials targeting worry, to further test whether worry prospectively predicts SABA, and whether abbreviated metacognitive therapy is effective.

Artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) in particular, has been proposed as a way to make diagnosis more objective…
reading.interpretation: AI has real potential in ADHD care, but the strength of the evidence differs sharply between its proposed uses. In diagnosis, machine-learning classifiers using imaging, EEG, and sensor data show that group differences can be detected in research samples, yet inconsistent accuracy, lack of external validation, and imperfect reference labels mean that none is ready to replace or reliably improve routine clinical assessment. In treatment, the best-supported digital intervention has shown benefit on an attention measure in a randomised trial, whereas computerised cognitive training and neurofeedback have limited effects on blinded outcomes. Ethical risks, in particular bias, privacy, and over-reliance, are as important as technical performance. The most defensible near-term model is a hybrid one in which AI supports, rather than substitutes for, clinical judgement: providing additional objective data, easing access to evidence-based interventions, and monitoring outcomes, all under human oversight. Getting there requires prospective trials with patient-relevant outcomes, transparent reporting, evaluation across diverse populations, and sustained collaboration between clinicians, researchers, patients, and regulators.
reading.limitations: Beyond the points above, three limitations deserve emphasis. Data are limited: large, well-characterised, demographically diverse datasets with expert diagnoses and long-term followup are scarce. Interpretability is limited: deep models in particular rarely explain their outputs in terms clinicians can check against their own judgement. And the reference standard is imperfect: a model trained to reproduce a clinical diagnosis cannot be more valid than that diagnosis, so high agreement with labels does not prove that the model has identified ADHD as a biological or functional entity.

analysis.discussion: The findings of this study demonstrate that AI adoption and implementation in developed and developing economic business vary increasingly and TAM (perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and behavioral intention) work as a driver here. This study extends the TAM idea where it showcases that perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are influenced by infrastructural and institutional elements (Table 3 ; IMO Framework), which reinforce the AI adoption and implementation. In emerging economies, lack of institutional trust, internet connectivity and poor data governance make the user intention negative towards the usage. It is evident that privacy concern lessens people's interest toward AI and its usage (Quach et al., 2022) . Hence, it can be said that this study brings a personal/micro-level perspective with macro-level barriers and enforcing adoption gaps which has not been discussed earlier. From a DCV perspective, developed economies are fully utilizing sensing, seizing and reconfiguring opportunities but emerging economies are still in the sensing zone due to the lack of infrastructural support. Reconfiguration attempts need extreme resource depth and institutional stability (Teece, 2007) . Digital transformation now excessively depends on infrastructural support and skilled manpower (Mikalef, Krogstie, Pappas, & Pavlou, 2020) . Here, the emerging economies fail to respond toward reconfiguration as they do not have the sufficient skilled workforce, regulatory enforcement and cloud access facilities. As a result, the same AI technologies bring different output for organizations based on the country's dimension. The reason behind the unequal implementation of AI between developed and emerging economies is not just due to technological constraints but also due to socio-economic roots. Developed economies usually get advantage for its enriched digital literacy, strong institutional trust, well-structured regulations and bigger financial investment capacity on technology. These factors facilitate both organizational conversion ability and consumer acceptance and adoption toward AI-enabled services. In comparison, emerging economies often struggle with internet accessibility, inadequate cloud infrastructure, shortage of AIskilled workforce and inefficient regulations and its enforcement. Economic gap and digital divides further escalate these acceptance and usage gaps, especially in rural and semi-urban areas. Moreover, data confidentiality and online scam issues decrease consumer faith toward AI-integrated e-business platforms. Cultural differences also manipulate the AI adoption segment. For example, many developing economies' consumers still depend highly on interpersonal trust and physical interaction in commercial transactions. Hence, to convert fully on these segments require both technological development as well as institutional validity, digital literacy initiatives and context-appropriate policy. Prior literature mostly showcases the barrier of skill gap and resource gap but this study contributes in projecting how this barrier (IMO) combinedly influences individual level (TAM) and organizational level (DCV) adoption and usage. This integration provides a context-based explanation regarding why emerging economies are still facing slower and more fragile AI adoption compared to the developed economies. The study contributes to highlighting the differentiation in adaptation of AI technologies in e-business from different countries' dimensions with a comparative framework along with the theoretical analysis (TAM and DCV). Comparative framework defines how infrastructural foundation, regulatory support and sufficient skills facilitate developed countries with efficiency and personalization while emerging economies are still struggling in these issues and hence, adopt just market penetration in this competitive edge. Theoretically, the framework suggests that macro (company-wide) and micro (users) level AI adoption depends on trust, digital capabilities and regulatory context. Practically, this study implies AI is not just a technological innovation and implementation; rather, it requires a proper context-based strategic implication worldwide. As a result, the key takeaways for managerial level are ensuring AI literacy, privacy norms and contextual applications while policymakers' responsibility in emerging economies implies in context-based enforceable regulation, technological reskilling and cost-effective resources. Though this research contributed through its context-based comparative framework, it is still limited by its qualitative nature and regional focus. Future research should focus on empirical testing of the IMO framework with a cross-country dataset.
analysis.limitations: At first, this research is limited by its systematic nature because this approach totally focused on secondary evidence rather than primary empirical evidence which diminish the chances of validation for the proposed framework. Secondly, although this research gives a theoretical and practical idea regarding AI adoption from emerging countries perspective, it is still limited by certain areas which create the opportunity of future research. For instance, this research examined the AI-integrated application and implementation from both developed and emerging countries' perspective where ethical issues and data privacy concerns are explicit on a general basis. Future research can examine how this privacy concern issues affect the usage of AI from developed and emerging countries' perspective. Thirdly, this research illustrates how NLP and chatbots can be a game changer for emerging e-business perspectives, but it is not stated clearly if NLP is tailored to local language, or more specifically, South Asian languages, its effectiveness and accuracy remain the same or not. So, this brings a new research scope or area. Fourthly, this research mostly focus on South Asia and Western economies' perspective regarding the AI adoption prospects and challenges in e-business and put limited focus on other emerging economies (Latin America, Africa and Southeast Asia) which open the opportunity of future research on a broader scale for these different emerging economies. Lastly, another future research area would be scalability. Based on the recommendations or prospects this paper discussed, researchers can evaluate whether these actually bring any revenue growth or changing brand loyalty in the emerging economies.

The dataset also includes answers from state-of-the-art AI algorithms (Table S1 ). Using the human and machine answers, we conducted Turing-like tests, showing that current algorithms are not far from being able to imitate humans in these tasks (Fig. 4A-C , G-I , Fig. S5A , C , E , Fig. S15A , C , E ). In contrast to human judges, even simple machine judges can distinguish human from machine answers (Fig. 4D-F , J-L , Fig. S5B , D , F Fig. S15B , D , F ). The Turing test has been extensively discussed, and contested, as a means to assess general intelligence. Our work is not intended as an evaluation of intelligence or to contribute to the discussion of Turing tests to quantify intelligence. Imitating humans can benefit humanity in many situations where we want to align machine and human outputs, such as in emulating expert decisions. However, imitating humans can also be used for evil, as in the dissemination of fake information, phishing attempts, or other scams. Regardless of whether Turing tests are good or bad metrics of intelligence, it is of high practical importance to assess whether algorithms can imitate humans or not. In some cases, we summarized results using the overall imitation detectability metric. It is important to emphasize that this summary metric does not differentiate between the two types of classification errors: (1) False Negatives -A human response misclassified as machine-generated. (2) False Positives -A machine response misclassified as human-generated. Understanding the distinction between these two error types is important for interpreting decision-making by human and machine judges. Moreover, in real-world applications, these errors may have different consequences. For example, misclassifying a machine as a human might be more problematic than misclassifying a human as a machine if the goal is to reliably detect AI-generated content. We present confusion matrices throughout to complement the imitation detectability scores and quantify the two types of errors. One approach towards mitigating the risks from evil human imitators is to build AI judges that can distinguish true human answers. The results presented here show that even simple AI judges like the ones introduced here can generally do a better job than human judges in detecting machine answers for the current tasks. There will likely continue to be an arms race between the development of better imitators and better detectors. Public attitudes oscillate between curiosity and scepticism, openness and critique, reflecting a rapidly evolving technological landscape in which artificial intelligence-often operating invisibly-has become an increasingly pervasive presence. Anticipating some of the broader conclusions of this study, it can be argued that audiences, regardless of their initial stance, have largely accommodated the ethical implications of AI in favour of a pragmatic orientation. In this context, authorship becomes a central interpretive lens through which aesthetic evaluation is filtered. A particularly revealing dimension concerns so-called "hallucinations," that is, the random or anomalous errors produced by AI systems. While these errors are frequently interpreted by audiences as evidence of machine failure, some artists deliberately incorporate them as signs of uniqueness and creative authenticity (D'Isa, 2024). Audience responses, however, often reveal an effort to "unmask" the machine, attributing to it deceptive intentions-such as imitation or dissimulation-through a process of anthropomorphising that scholars have identified as both pervasive and unavoidable in human-machine interaction (Esposito, 2022; D'Isa, 2024; Micalizzi, 2023) . Paradoxically, it is precisely interaction that enables originality, as AI-mediated creativity neither replicates human conversation nor follows a fully predetermined linguistic script (D'Isa, 2024, p. 32). These dynamics point to a fundamental ambiguity embedded in the very notion of artificial intelligence. Despite its name, AI operates without intentionality or consciousness, yet it is persistently framed through cognitive and moral categories traditionally reserved for human actors. One of the most recurrent defensive strategies identified in the data is discrediting: when prompted to reflect on creativity at a deeper level, respondents struggle to recognise the elements that define an output as creative in a strict sense. Consequently, AI is predominantly framed as a sophisticated tool capable of imitation and recombination, but not as an agent of genuine invention. In some cases, respondents express discomfort at attributing artistic value to a non-sentient entity, reinforcing the belief that creativity necessarily entails the capacity to feel, imagine, and communicate meaning beyond technical execution. The tendency to value AI's imitative competence while devaluing its creative potential also reveals a partial misunderstanding of how generative systems operate, as well as an implicit concern about the diminishing role of the artist within computational creative processes. Yet, as Barale (2020) argues, the loss of control has always been a constitutive element of creative practice. In this sense, AI-based art foregrounds-rather than negates-the encounter between human intentionality and unforeseen outcomes, transforming the medium itself into a creative partner and generating novel forms of interaction. This conversational dimension of AI-mediated creativity aligns with Esposito's (2022) view of artificial communication and supports the recognition of creative outcomes as socially validated forms of novelty (Csíkszentmihályi, 2023) . analysis.discussion: Taken together, these findings suggest that the encounter between audiences and AI-mediated creativity should not be interpreted as a simple trajectory of acceptance or rejection, but rather as an ongoing process of symbolic negotiation through which the boundaries of creativity, authorship, and agency are continuously redefined. The empirical evidence indicates that public responses to AI-generated works are structured less by technological competence than by deeply rooted cultural schemas concerning intentionality, human experience, and the social validation of artistic value. In this sense, resistance does not function merely as opposition to technological innovation, but as a cognitive and ethical strategy aimed at preserving meaningful distinctions between human and artificial production. At the same time, the data show that everyday interaction with AI gradually destabilises these rigid distinctions. While audiences remain reluctant to attribute full creative legitimacy to artificial systems, their evaluative practices reveal a growing familiarity with hybrid forms of production and a pragmatic willingness to engage with them. Rather than signalling a stable resolution, this coexistence of scepticism and acceptance points to a transitional cultural condition in which AI is neither fully integrated nor categorically excluded from the domain of creativity. The study therefore contributes to current debates by demonstrating that the key site of transformation is not the technology itself, but the interpretive frameworks through which it is understood and evaluated. AI-mediated creativity emerges as a relational phenomenon, shaped by interactions among users, cultural expectations, technical affordances, and institutional norms. From this perspective, the future of creative AI will depend less on advances in computational capability than on the evolving socio-cultural criteria through which creativity is recognised, legitimised, and valued. After the Myth of Human Creativity: Ethical Reorientations for AI Contemporary debates on artificial intelligence are marked by a persistent polarisation of interpretative positions. Floridi (2022) elucidates this divide by outlining a framework that maps the dominant stances while intentionally distancing himself from both. Drawing on a religious lexicon to highlight their conceptual fragility, he characterises these positions as forms of uncritical attitude. On one side stand proponents of technological singularity, who anticipate the transcendence of human limitations-competence, vulnerability, and finitudethrough AI, often invoking the prospect of a superintelligence whose consequences may not be benign. On the other side are what Floridi terms AItheists, who insist on the irreducible uniqueness of the human species and attribute to it exclusive qualities beyond machine replication, yet without articulating plausible scenarios for integrated coexistence. Moriggi and Pireddu (2024) suggest that reflection on the everyday appropriation of AI remains constrained by a persistent perspectival limitationan "original sin" of sorts-namely the tendency to rely on oppositional and comparative frameworks. Whether approached with enthusiasm or anxiety, AI continues to be evaluated primarily in relation to the human rather than analysed as part of a wider socio-technical ecology. This comparative reflex proves especially restrictive in the domain of creative production, where the perception of unavoidable competition between humans and machines appears conceptually difficult to escape. Creativity, much like emotion, is still widely treated as an exclusively human prerogative, reinforcing a zero-sum logic that positions AI either as a threat or as an inferior imitator. Arielli and Manovich (2024) challenge precisely this anthropocentric myth of creativity. Instead of asking whether machines can be creative on human terms, they propose revisiting the history of art and media in order to foreground the longstanding entanglement between human expression and technical mediation. From this perspective, generative AI does not constitute an unprecedented rupture; rather, it renders visible a structural condition of aesthetic production that has always been present. Creativity, in this view, emerges through interaction with tools, constraints, conventions, and infrastructures. AI therefore functions less as a competitor to human creativity than as a medium that exposes and reshapes the conventions through which creativity is culturally recognised. Within this interpretative horizon, machines-and artificial intelligence in particular-can be understood as forms of amplification and extension rather than substitution. As Manovich (2022) notes, AI systems operate as resources that facilitate recombination, exploration, and paradigm shifts in cultural production. This position resonates with de Kerckhove's notion of augmented cognition, according to which intelligence is distributed, connective, and technologically extended rather than internally contained. Framed in these terms, the relevant question is no longer whether AI diminishes human agency, but how agency is redistributed across human-machine assemblages. Moving beyond technological "ghosts" does not entail a naïve endorsement of innovation. Rather, it requires re-centring human values, sensibilities, and responsibilities within AI-mediated practices. An ethics of creative AI must therefore be grounded not in abstract opposition but in shared awareness of processes, opportunities, and consequences. Ethical concerns are not resolved through denial or idealisation, but through situated practices of use, interpretation, and governance. Given the pace of technological transformation, definitive conclusions would be premature. It is nevertheless possible to outline a set of orienting principles for guiding reflection and debate. First, the individual-together with their resources, agency, and intelligence-must remain central in defining the intentions, meanings, and directions of creative action. Second, machines should be approached not as intelligent or sentient entities but as powerful extensions of computational and mnemonic capacities, to be employed with critical awareness rather than delegated authority. Third, cultural fields and domains must be actively cultivated (Csíkszentmihályi, 2023) to prevent the flattening of imaginaries and creative production under conditions of algorithmic standardisation. Finally, ethical engagement requires sustained attention to processes rather than reductive human-machine comparisons, fostering integrated approaches capable of supporting responsible, reflexive, and culturally grounded uses of artificial intelligence.

reading.methods: This study adopted a qualitative ethnographic case study design to analyze ethnomathematical structures within local traditions and evaluate their implementation in student-led project-based learning. The research was conducted over a 16-week period in Maros Regency, South Sulawesi, focusing on the cultural communities of Lau District and Mandai District. These locations were selected due to their active preservation of Bugis-Makassar heritage and traditional game practices. Primary qualitative data were collected through purposive sampling involving six key cultural informants who possessed direct authority and knowledge regarding indigenous traditions. In addition, 15 undergraduate mathematics education students participated as trained research assistants to facilitate field documentation and learning projects. Before deployment, these assistants underwent a standardized orientation covering qualitative interview protocols, photographic documentation of cultural artifacts, and ethical data handling. Data collection instruments included semi-structured interview guides, participatory observation sheets, and focus group discussion (FGD) protocols. All participants signed written informed consent forms ensuring anonymity, voluntary participation, and institutional ethical compliance. Table 1. reading.findings: The primary pedagogical implication of this study is that abstract mathematical concepts become significantly more accessible when contextualized within culturally familiar practices. Complex topics such as proportional ratios in Peca Sura, spatial reflections in Makkellu, and Cartesian coordinate mapping in Dende-dende can be transformed from abstract formulas into concrete learning experiences. Connecting formal geometry with local heritage aligns with fundamental ethnomathematical principles, which emphasize that integrating culture into instruction enhances conceptual relevance and strengthens learners' emotional connection to mathematical logic. Furthermore, incorporating AI imageprocessing tools and digital social platforms provides an innovative instructional framework suitable for modern mathematics classrooms. AI algorithms function as visual scaffolds, enabling students to extract geometric properties and trace spatial symmetry vectors from photographic data of cultural artifacts. Concurrently, social media platforms offer collaborative spaces where students document, critique, and share their ethnomathematical project outcomes, fostering peer interaction and mathematical communication skills. These findings strongly align with Vygotsky's Social Constructivism Theory, which posits that cognitive development occurs through social interaction and mediated activity within a community of practice. In this study, AI tools and digital platforms act as technological mediators that extend students' Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) during spatial problemsolving tasks. However, educators must balance technological integration with critical thinking to prevent over-reliance on automated tools. Because AI algorithms risk generating incorrect geometric interpretations or model hallucinations, human-inthe-loop verification-involving both teachers and cultural experts-remains essential to preserve cognitive rigor and ensure authentic cultural representation. Ultimately, integrating local ethnomathematical practices with AI visualization tools and social media platforms provides a practical framework for contextual mathematics education. Rather than viewing traditional culture as static heritage, this approach positions indigenous wisdom as a dynamic resource for mathematical modeling. By connecting formal geometry with familiar cultural artifacts, teachers can present mathematics as a living, meaningful discipline deeply rooted in community life (Seo dkk., 2016) .
reading.interpretation: Based on the qualitative investigation and pedagogical modeling, this study concludes the following in alignment with the three central research questions: 1). Embedded Mathematical Concepts: The cultural practices of Maros Regency-specifically Makkellu, Mappassili, Mappacci, Dende-dende, and Peca Sura-embody authentic mathematical structures, including line reflection, bilateral symmetry, 3D cylindrical geometry, discrete sequential ordering, Cartesian grid transformations, and proportional ratios; 2). Role of AI Technology: Computer Vision and image-processing tools effectively serve as visual scaffolds to extract geometric contours and spatial coordinates from cultural artifacts. Rather than providing absolute validity, AI technology assists in bridging informal cultural observations with formal geometric representations, provided that outputs are cross-verified by human domain experts; 3). Collaborative Project Dissemination: Developing student collaborative projects supported by social media platforms enables learners to transform field data into structured educational content. This project-based model offers an engaging mechanism for communicating mathematical concepts, fostering collaborative skills, and promoting local cultural heritage preservation.
reading.limitations: This study acknowledges several methodological limitations. First, the qualitative inquiry was confined to specific Bugis-Makassar traditions in Maros Regency with a small participant sample (six key cultural informants and 15 university research assistants), which limits the direct generalizability of the findings to other cultural settings. Second, the study focused on exploring ethnomathematical concepts and designing pedagogical scenarios; it did not evaluate empirical student learning outcomes, cognitive achievement gains, or long-term classroom implementation. Third, while Computer Vision tools assisted in feature extraction, automated AI models remain susceptible to algorithmic bias and hallucination, requiring continuous human expert oversight. Future research should implement controlled classroom interventions to empirically measure the impact of AI-assisted ethnomathematical modules on student spatial reasoning and problem-solving performance.

These findings strongly align with Vygotsky's Social Constructivism Theory, which posits that cognitive development occurs through social interaction and mediated activity within a community of practice. In this study, AI tools and digital platforms act as technological mediators that extend students' Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) during spatial problemsolving tasks. However, educators must balance technological integration with critical thinking to prevent over-reliance on automated tools. Because AI algorithms risk generating incorrect geometric interpretations or model hallucinations, human-inthe-loop verification-involving both teachers and cultural experts-remains essential to preserve cognitive rigor and ensure authentic cultural representation. Ultimately, integrating local ethnomathematical practices with AI visualization tools and social media platforms provides a practical framework for contextual mathematics education. Rather than viewing traditional culture as static heritage, this approach positions indigenous wisdom as a dynamic resource for mathematical modeling. By connecting formal geometry with familiar cultural artifacts, teachers can present mathematics as a living, meaningful discipline deeply rooted in community life (Seo dkk., 2016) .
analysis.discussion: Based on the qualitative investigation and pedagogical modeling, this study concludes the following in alignment with the three central research questions: 1). Embedded Mathematical Concepts: The cultural practices of Maros Regency-specifically Makkellu, Mappassili, Mappacci, Dende-dende, and Peca Sura-embody authentic mathematical structures, including line reflection, bilateral symmetry, 3D cylindrical geometry, discrete sequential ordering, Cartesian grid transformations, and proportional ratios; 2). Role of AI Technology: Computer Vision and image-processing tools effectively serve as visual scaffolds to extract geometric contours and spatial coordinates from cultural artifacts. Rather than providing absolute validity, AI technology assists in bridging informal cultural observations with formal geometric representations, provided that outputs are cross-verified by human domain experts; 3). Collaborative Project Dissemination: Developing student collaborative projects supported by social media platforms enables learners to transform field data into structured educational content. This project-based model offers an engaging mechanism for communicating mathematical concepts, fostering collaborative skills, and promoting local cultural heritage preservation.
analysis.limitations: This study acknowledges several methodological limitations. First, the qualitative inquiry was confined to specific Bugis-Makassar traditions in Maros Regency with a small participant sample (six key cultural informants and 15 university research assistants), which limits the direct generalizability of the findings to other cultural settings. Second, the study focused on exploring ethnomathematical concepts and designing pedagogical scenarios; it did not evaluate empirical student learning outcomes, cognitive achievement gains, or long-term classroom implementation. Third, while Computer Vision tools assisted in feature extraction, automated AI models remain susceptible to algorithmic bias and hallucination, requiring continuous human expert oversight. Future research should implement controlled classroom interventions to empirically measure the impact of AI-assisted ethnomathematical modules on student spatial reasoning and problem-solving performance.

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to technologies that enable computer systems to perform tasks commonly associated with human intelligence.
